techcrunch.com/2026/11/25/sp-considers-n.headline: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
techcrunch.com/2026/11/25/sp-considers-n.author: Marina Temkin

paragraphs.text: S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/26/braz.headline: Trump tariff threat ‘unacceptable’, says Brazil, as China denounces levies as baseless

paragraphs.text: Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.
It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was particularly singled out for in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”
The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”
Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”
Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.
It added it was “preparing and submitting rebuttal comments on the preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions and allegations made by interested parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.
Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.
Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.
Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.
However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”

“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs,” Wyden added. “Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution.”
With Associated Press and Reuters

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/26/japane.headline: ‘Trapped in grief’: wife of Japanese journalist detained by Russia pleads for his release

paragraphs.text: The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi, have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.
In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”
Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”
Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.
Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/26/pow.headline: Powerful Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast with floods, damaging winds
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/26/pow.author: Tim Craig, Matthew Cappucci

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — The East Coast could experience its worst Thanksgiving storm in decades on Thursday as forecasters and local officials warn that strong winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding could severely impede travel and lead to prolonged power outages.

The large storm is expected to progress through the Mid-Atlantic region during the day, resulting in high wind and flood warnings from Virginia Beach to New York City, as well as possibly damaging conditions in Washington, Baltimore and Philadelphia.

The storm forced the postponement of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, the first time in its 100-year history that the event was moved due to weather. Officials said they made the decision because of concerns that participants and spectators would encounter dangerous conditions.
“Safety is and always will be our top priority,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said during a Wednesday news conference with Macy’s. “And this will be a heavy storm.”
Philadelphia also canceled its Thanksgiving Day parade.
On Wednesday evening, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) issued a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.

In New Jersey, all 21 counties are also under a state of emergency after Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) warned that residents faced a “serious storm that requires us all to exercise caution.” Sherrill urged residents to complete their holiday travel on Wednesday night and stay off the roads on Thursday during the worst of the storm.
In Delaware, Gov. Matt Meyer (D) said residents should keep cellphones charged and have flashlights, extra food and medications handy.
“Be ready for power outages and difficult travel,” Meyer said in a statement Wednesday evening. “Adjust your plans if you need to and follow instructions from emergency officials.”

The storm system is poised to clobber portions of the Mid-Atlantic and the Northeast with the potential for winds near hurricane force in beach communities. Farther inland, winds could reach 60 mph, including along the Interstate 95 corridor.
Officials warned that outages could stretch into the weekend if the winds bring down trees and power lines.

In some coastal communities, the National Weather Service forecast that major flooding was possible. Coastal flood warnings were in effect for the entire New Jersey coastline and most of Delmarva, the Chesapeake, the mouth of the Hudson River and southern Long Island.
A storm surge of 2 to 4 feet is likely. The National Weather Service warned that some neighborhoods could be “cut off at the peak of the flooding.”

Sherrill said flooding in southern New Jersey could “match or exceed” the height of waters that inundated beach towns during a September nor’easter. That storm severely eroded beaches and flooded some homes and businesses.
“The coastal flooding [Thursday] could be especially intense because high winds will coincide with high tide” said Sherrill, adding the worst flood risks are expected Thursday morning.
The instigating storm system organized over Florida on Wednesday evening and it was energized, and steered westward, by an approaching upper-air disturbance.

The storm swung north toward the Carolinas overnight, bringing gusty onshore winds, very heavy downpours and thunderstorms. As the system moves into the Mid-Atlantic on Thursday, strong winds are likely.
The low-pressure center will trek north up the Appalachians, much farther inland than conventional East Coast storms.

The strengthening low-pressure system will produce winds of more than 80 mph about 2,500 feet above the ground. Severe gusts are likely at those altitudes, and any downpours or possible thunderstorms would effectively push those strong winds toward the ground.
The heaviest rains and greatest wind potential will affect D.C., Baltimore, Philadelphia, Delaware and New Jersey late Thursday morning into the afternoon.
Mamdani said the rain could lead to flash flooding, and he urged residents who live in low-lying neighborhoods or basement apartments to closely monitor conditions.

Widespread 50- to 60-mph gusts are possible, and high-resolution computer models suggest a few 70 to 75 mph gusts at the immediate coastline. New York officials have barred high-profile vehicles and trucks without cargo from seven major bridges due to concerns they could be blown over.
Winds will be less dramatic in New England when the heavy rains arrive Thursday evening, though Cape Cod, Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard could see a few gusts topping 50 mph.

The same storm system will also dump snow in eastern Missouri and western Illinois. A winter storm warning is in effect for St. Louis, where 3 to 6 inches of snow is likely. A few locations west of the city could see as much as 6 to 10 inches of snow.

The storm center will be more than 600 miles to the southeast when the snow begins early Thursday. But a weak, diffuse strip of secondary low pressure — known as an “inverted trough” — will protrude to the northwest and generate the snow.
The storm system will gradually weaken Friday as it swirls remnant rain and mountain snow showers over the Ohio Valley and northern Appalachians.
Improving weather and sunshine are likely in the Northeast on Saturday.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Halfords Shares Head for Best Ever Year After Hot Summer Boost
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Rose Henderson

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Halfords Group Plc shares are firmly on track for their best year ever after Britain's long, hot summer helped the bikes and car parts seller report estimate-beating first-half results and nudge up its full-year guidance.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The stock rose as much as 13% in early London trading, extending its year-to-date gain to about 95%. Yet it's still less than half of what it was worth at its peak in 2015 and analysts see scope for further recovery.

"There is no doubt in our view that Halfords is now operating with much more confidence and momentum," Peel Hunt analysts Jonathan Pritchard and John Stevenson wrote in a note on Thursday. "The shares now trade on a more sensible valuation but we believe there is plenty of potential for upside."
Peel Hunt is one of five brokers with a buy rating on the stock, the other two having hold recommendations. Average price targets imply about 10% further upside from current levels.

Halfords is having its best year on the stock market since listing in 2004 as the business undergoes a revival under the leadership of Chief Executive Officer Henry Birch. The former head of online retailer Very Group and bingo-hall operator Rank Group Plc joined the company in April last year and has implemented a three-phase strategy for growth.

First-half results got a boost from the UK's hot summer, which fueled demand for car aircons, tents and cycling products. Halfords attributed £8 million ($10 million) of profit in the first half to the "exceptionally warm" weather, which it said will cause full-year profit to be front-end weighted. It raised the low end of its annual earnings guidance to £60 million from £55 million, while maintaining the upper end at £65 million.

Peel Hunt's Pritchard said the CEO could take "some credit" for the strong first-half results. But he noted that the retailer is in the early stages of its strategic turnaround, which has two more phases to run after the so-called Optimise program and aims to improve sales growth and make pricing more data-driven.

Halfords has been something of a standout among UK retail stocks this year as its company-specific turnaround catches the eye of investors and analysts. More broadly, Britain's consumer stocks have been under pressure, as inflation and higher interest rates erode purchasing power and make people less likely to splash out on discretionary products.
According to Shore Capital analyst David Hughes, Halfords shares have reached multiples of earnings and cash flow that now represent the average of the wider retail sector.

Still, that "does not to us reflect the opportunity if Halfords can continue to deliver on positive trading momentum as well as deliver the sustainable margin recovery we are looking for," he wrote in a note.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Trump Riles Trade Partners With Tariffs That Undercut ‘China+1’
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Philip J. Heijmans and Francesca Stevens

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's latest tariff push risks undercutting one of the signature shifts in global manufacturing since the US-China trade war began: the movement of supply chains out of China.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The levies on 14 economies in Asia and Europe would hit some of the biggest winners from the so-called "China+1" investment boom. Countries like Vietnam could end up with rates approaching or even in some cases exceeding those on Chinese goods, though there are many exemptions that keep effective charges lower than the headline rates.

Still, as well as upsetting governments — who've been lining up to condemn the latest US trade offensive — the measures announced Wednesday will likely cause unease in plenty of corporate headquarters too. They signal that shifting production away from America's superpower rival may no longer be enough to keep companies insulated.

A lot of firms "will say: 'Well, screw it, we're just going to go back to China,'" said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore. "'Why would we be dealing with this massive amount of paperwork, compliance costs and tariff changes with the threat ahead if we don't need to.'"

The Trump administration is seeking to restore tariffs that were shot down by the Supreme Court because they lacked proper legal foundations. The new ones will be imposed based on US assessments of overcapacity in manufacturing, defined as production persistently above what market conditions would support because of government policies or intervention.

Outlining its new policy, the US Trade Representative blamed China for encouraging the expansion of manufacturing capacity abroad. That's particularly relevant in Southeast Asia, where many have seen a surge in factory output and exports to the US as Chinese firms set up shop there. The US faulted the region's countries for failing to adequately address investment, and transshipment of goods, from "non-market" economies, typically code for China.

The proposed US tariffs could rise as high as 35% for Vietnam, 25% for India and 20% for Singapore, though countries could secure lower rates by cutting deals with Washington. China will be charged 20% on top of other pre-existing duties, and may face steeper levies if the trade truce breaks down.
'Challenging to Uproot'

The push to diversify from China accelerated after Washington first imposed tariffs on Chinese goods in 2018, prompting manufacturers to expand elsewhere in Asia while often retaining operations and suppliers in China. By 2025, foreign direct investment into Southeast Asia had reached a record $246 billion, surpassing East Asia for the first time since the early 1990s.

Manufacturing FDI soared almost 50% last year alone to $40 billion, according to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, as the region attracted investment in electronics, semiconductors, vehicles and other industries.

Assuming outstanding trade deals are completed, the new rates "would narrow" the advantage many Southeast Asian exports have over Chinese goods, though probably not erase it because manufacturing supply chains are "challenging to uproot," said Erica Tay, an economist at Maybank Securities Singapore.

Vietnam is among the economies most exposed. One of the biggest beneficiaries of Trump's first trade war, it has emerged as Southeast Asia's growth champion, driven by surging output of electronic products like smartphones and laptops.

Vietnam posted a $191 billion trade surplus with the US just in the first nine months of 2026, surpassing the $178 billion posted in the full year of 2025, according to US Census data. At the same time, its deficit with China, which supplies most of its imports, also ballooned.

The mooted 35% tariff "would put Vietnam at a competitive disadvantage," said Travis Mitchell, executive director of the American Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam. "Companies may have little choice but to explore shifting some of their production to other countries, potentially disrupting supply chains that have taken years to build."
Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade responded to the new rates by saying it will participate in the next steps of the US investigation and continue to work toward a reciprocal trade agreement.
Other trade partners have voiced objections, with Singapore saying it was "very disappointed" by the latest US measures and Japan calling them "regrettable."

"It sets a worrying precedent in extending an industry concept — structural excess capacity — to an economy-wide one," said Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
For businesses, said Mitchell at the American Chamber in Vietnam, it's yet another layer of confusion that makes it harder to see the road ahead.

"It is increasingly difficult for companies to make decisions on pricing, sales forecasts, production planning and future investments," he said, "without knowing what tariff rates they will be facing in the coming months."
--With assistance from Suvashree Ghosh, Patpicha Tanakasempipat and Claire Jiao.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/26/israel.headline: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes

paragraphs.text: Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).
This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.
PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.
More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.
“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies, Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.
The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.
More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.
Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.
Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.
In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.
In the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.
The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.
A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers, including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel, five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.
The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

wsj.com/business/bank-of-england-propose.headline: Bank of England Proposes Cut to U.K. Bank Capital Requirements

paragraphs.text: Capital requirements on major U.K. banks could be lowered under proposals from the Bank of England, releasing more capital to be used on dividends, buybacks or lending.
The Bank of England's Financial Policy Committee on Thursday said it has completed a review of the framework that dictates how much capital U.K. banks are required to hold.
The proposed changes would reduce Tier 1 capital requirements for major U.K. banks by around 50 basis points of risk-weighted assets in normal times.
The measures will free up more capacity to lend to U.K. households and businesses, the BOE said. The actual impact of the proposals will vary depending on the banks' business models.

As part of the reforms, the U.K. Prudential Regulation Authority will consider lower minimum requirements for domestic lending to offset the buffer provided by maintaining a 2% neutral countercyclical capital buffer rate.
This will also better reflect the risks of geographic concentration of lending, the central bank said.
The BOE said the reforms would make capital requirements more proportionate and better targeted.

The reduction would mean system-wide risk-weighted Tier 1 requirements for major U.K. banks would be in line with the committee's updated benchmark of around 13%, which was reduced from around 14% last year.
Lowering capital requirements much further would put financial stability and sustainable economic growth at risk, the BOE warned.
A further cut to capital needs could cause banks to lose market confidence more quickly in the case of losses, pushing up borrowing costs for households and businesses.

Following the completion of the review, the Financial Policy Committee and the PRA will consult on the reforms, and aim to implement them as soon as possible. Further consultations will take place in the first half of 2027.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: BOE Proposes 30 Basis Point Cut to UK Bank Capital Requirements
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Laura Noonan and Georgia Hall

paragraphs.text: Laura Noonan and Georgia Hall
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 5:33 AM EST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The Bank of England has laid out fresh measures that would cut UK lenders' capital requirements by another 30 basis points, but warned reductions beyond that point could lead to "financial instability."
Most Read from Bloomberg

In its twice-yearly financial stability update, the BOE announced the final details of its bank capital framework review, weeks after Chancellor John Healey called on officials to go further after a hike in the government's bank tax angered lenders.

Lobby group UK Finance had proposed radical reform of the domestic lending charges, arguing for changes that would release £250 billion even if half the capital freed up was returned to shareholders, with Lloyds, NatWest, HSBC and Barclays benefiting most.

Instead, the BOE is opting for more modest changes that will free up around £100 billion of lending capacity by changing add-ons known as Pillar 2A. The benefits will vary by bank, with domestically focused lenders enjoying a 60 basis point reduction in Tier 1 requirements.
The BOE will consult on the detail early next year, when it has also promised to consult on changes already announced to the leverage ratio, a cap on banks' total borrowings.

Officials said that, together, those changes will bring system wide capital requirements to a level "consistent with" the 100 basis points cut to benchmark capital announced by the BOE almost a year ago.
Banks have grown impatient for reductions to their actual requirements to the new 13% Tier 1 level, as deregulation gathered pace across the Atlantic, benefiting Wall Street rivals.

Still, the BOE moved to rein in hopes of further reprieves. Reductions in capital requirements beyond those set out by the BOE on Thursday "would put long-term economic growth at risk by undermining the banking system's ability to absorb rather than amplify shocks," according to the minutes of the FPC meeting.
"Materially lower UK capital requirements would also risk undermining international standards intended to promote financial stability and a level playing field."
Banks have argued that the easiest way to lower actual capital ratios is by reducing the neutral level of the countercyclical buffer from its current setting of 2%. Regulators rejected this.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Number of Young Brits Not in Work or Education Falls to 959,000
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Irina Anghel

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:53 AM EST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The number of young Britons shut out of work of education declined in the third quarter, offering some relief to Prime Minister Andy Burnham in his mission to fix the UK's youth jobs crisis.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Some 959,000 16-24 year-olds were not in employment, education or training (NEET), down 22,000 from the previous quarter, the Office for National Statistics said Thursday in a report. While that's down from the start of the year when it topped one million, it's still higher than a year ago and close to levels seen in 2013 in the aftermath of the global financial crisis.

Getting young people into work is a key political and fiscal challenge for Burnham. Alan Milburn's landmark 267-page report last week gave the government a roadmap for tackling the issue, setting out measures to cut the NEET rate to 5% over the next decade. The crisis is already costing Britain £125 billion ($164 billion) a year due to lost output, benefit and healthcare costs, foregone tax and long-term scarring, it found.

Milburn urged the government to cut job taxes for under-25s, subsidize firms taking on unemployed young people and avoid more steep rises to the youth national minimum wage. The report also warned that Labour's tougher employment laws are making firms less likely to create entry-level roles.

Underlying Milburn's review is an ambition to shift public spending away from benefits to employment support. He highlighted that the state currently spends £25 on benefits for young people for every pound to help them into education and employment, a ratio he said should be changed to 2:1 over the next decade.

Competition for first-jobs is at its most brutal since the economy was under lockdown during the pandemic. Payroll tax hikes, large increases in the minium wage, elevated interest rates and, more recently, AI advances have created what the Bank of England calls a "low fire, low hire" labor market that's particularly taxing for young people.

"I suspect I'm not the only person whose first job was in a shop," BOE Deputy Governor Clare Lombardelli told lawmakers on Wednesday. She said key employers of young people in sectors such as retail and hospitality have scaled back hiring dramatically and warned that a difficult start can hold back workers throughout their careers.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: All of Canada’s Big Six Banks Now See December Rate Hike
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Mario Baker Ramirez and Erik Hertzberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Canada's six largest lenders all expect the central bank to hike its key interest rate in December, even with two major economic releases still to come next week.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Economists brought forward their rate calls after Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem reinforced concerns about persistent inflation during public remarks Tuesday. He emphasized the risk that companies will pass higher energy costs on to consumers.

Toronto-Dominion Bank, the final major Canadian bank to change its forecast to call for a hike next month, said Macklem's comments on better-than-expected economic resilience suggest policymakers are "more concerned about what is to come."
"The hike looks to be a move focused on managing inflation risks," TD Senior Economist Andrew Hencic said in an email Wednesday.

Earlier this week, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Bank of Montreal said they now expect a hike in December rather than January. Bank of Nova Scotia, Royal Bank of Canada and National Bank of Canada were already forecasting a December hike.
The central bank raised its policy rate to 2.5% in October, the first increase in three years, as high energy costs stemming from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East added to inflation pressures.
Markets also appear convinced another hike will be announced in December, with traders in overnight swaps putting the odds at about 80% as of Wednesday afternoon.

That conviction comes before the national statistics agency publishes quarterly gross domestic product data and the November jobs report, two key readings that will give policymakers a final look at the strength of the economy before their decision.
Macklem warned Tuesday that higher energy costs are likely to pass through to consumer prices, even as oil prices have recently eased.

BMO strategist Benjamin Reitzes said there's still uncertainty about what happens beyond December's meeting, "but the speech doesn't talk about neutral or provide any sign that they're looking to pause after another hike."

Macklem's comments also prompted economists to reassess how the central bank may respond to future supply shocks. The bank's updated approach suggests policymakers may react more quickly and put greater emphasis on headline inflation in its communications, said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics.
The Bank of Canada's next rate decision is on Dec. 9.

wsj.com/world/uk/boe-warns-scale-and-bre.headline: BOE Warns Scale and Breadth Of AI Financing Poses Threat to Financial Stability

paragraphs.text: The artificial-intelligence investment boom is supporting global economic growth, but the scale and breadth of financing that it requires is making the global financial system more vulnerable to setbacks, the Bank of England said Thursday.

In its twice-yearly report on the health of the financial system, the BOE estimated that AI-related bond issuance by large technology firms known as hyperscalers will more than double to exceed $305 billion this year, or around 8% of total bond issuance by investment-grade corporations.

Adding bond issuance by semiconductor manufacturers and data-center operators would leave the "broader ecosystem" borrowing more than the governments of some large advanced economies, including the U.K., the BOE said.

"The growth and broadening of markets used to finance AI-related investment is deepening interconnections across the system, making it more likely for stress in one area to propagate to another," the BOE said.

The U.K.'s central bank expects the financing needs of AI-related businesses to increase further in 2027, and reach into more segments of the system to include investment-grade bonds, leveraged finance and private credit, and public and private equity.

The BOE said the scale of the financing that is driving the AI investment boom might be so large that it is "contributing to upward pressure on global real interest rates," making it more expensive for governments, households and other businesses to borrow.

An additional source of risk is the "opacity" of financing arrangements between businesses involved in the AI buildout, often carried out through special purpose vehicles supported by leases, purchase agreements, backstops and guarantees provided by the hyperscalers.
"Off-balance-sheet arrangements make assessing the serviceability of potential future liabilities more challenging," the BOE said.
The BOE estimates that the total debts and off-balance-sheet commitments of hyperscalers now exceed $4 trillion.
"The scale and nature of these financing commitments could come under strain in a stress or if expectations around future AI revenues were revised down," the BOE said.

Equity prices for AI-related businesses have swung wildly over recent weeks, led by chip maker Nvidia. Last week alone, the Nasdaq composite's members lost more than $4 trillion in market value, but prices have partly rebounded.
The BOE said recent market moves have been amplified by some hedge funds reducing their borrowing, but had not had a significant impact on broader financial markets.

"While spillovers to other markets were limited, in a more severe shock, losses on equity positions could also lead globally active investors to deleverage in other markets, including sovereign debt markets," the BOE said.
The central bank repeated its warnings about the threat posed by frontier AI models to the cybersecurity of financial firms and market infrastructure.

"The rapid development of open-weight AI models that could run more cheaply than proprietary models, with safeguards more easily disabled or removed, can make advanced AI models more readily available and useful to malicious actors," the BOE said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/26/ubs-swiss-capital-ru.headline: Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning
cnbc.com/2026/11/26/ubs-swiss-capital-ru.author: Hugh Leask

paragraphs.text: UBS's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest bank still faces a major fight over sweeping plans that would force it to hold more capital against its foreign subsidiaries.

FINMA, the Swiss markets regulator, said Wednesday that UBS's resolvability — or its ability to fail safely, without wreaking havoc on the economy — has improved since it integrated rival Credit Suisse, with progress made in implementing the emergency plan across group-wide resolution planning.

The preferred resolution strategy — involving plans to allow for recapitalization and restructuring through the use of loss-absorbing bail-in bonds — is "executable," FINMA said. The regulator formally approved UBS's recovery plan for the first time since its Credit Suisse integration.
How UBS would withstand a future crisis remains in sharp focus among Swiss authorities ever since the lender's emergency takeover of stricken rival Credit Suisse in 2023.

UBS is now the country's only global systemically important bank, and the Swiss government wants it to hold stronger capital cushions, specifically in relation to its foreign subsidiaries, which would help it withstand another banking collapse.
UBS has pushed back against the overhaul, saying the measures are disproportionate and would damage its international competitiveness, forcing it to hold an extra $16 billion in capital.
A parliamentary showdown now looms, with the National Council, Switzerland's lower house, scheduled to debate the proposal Dec. 16.

On Tuesday, the lower house's economics committee backed plans to force the bank to support its foreign subsidiaries with 90% high-quality core Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, capital. The Council of States, the country's upper house, approved the 90% plan in September.
The Swiss government had earlier proposed a 100% threshold. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%.

UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti told CNBC in an interview Oct. 28 that 90% would not allow the company to be a "competitive player" long-term. But he would not be drawn on speculation that the measures could push the bank to relocate out of Switzerland.
In a statement, the bank said the economics committee's recommendation would herald further excessive tightening of Swiss capital requirements, "which are already among the most stringent globally."
FINMA said in its Nov. 25 update that the goal is to avoid government solvency support and emergency law.

"The aim is to enable the authorities, in the event of a crisis, to choose the option that offers the best prospects of success in safeguarding financial stability and ensuring the continuation of systemically important functions," the regulator said.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/26/lana-n.headline: ‘I’m no longer a UAE official’: UN hopeful Lana Nusseibeh tries to shake off Sudan record

paragraphs.text: Lana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.
It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK, all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.
The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.
“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE, have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.
The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.
A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”
That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.
Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.

One critic said: “It is a very smart strategic play by the UAE that seeks autocratic capture, and then the asset-stripping of the UN and its standards. The UAE would end the UN’s role on climate. It would be a catastrophe.”

The next security council vote is on Monday. By then some of the backmarkers may have dropped out of the race. The diplomats of the P5 may also be clearer on the flexibility of their mandates, in which case the papal conclave may finally produce white smoke.

cnbc.com/2026/11/26/texture-maxxing-food.headline: What is ‘texture-maxxing’? The food trend putting crunch on the menu
cnbc.com/2026/11/26/texture-maxxing-food.author: Sawdah Bhaimiya

paragraphs.text: Texture-maxxing is the latest food trend taking social media by storm as consumers, driven by aesthetics and taste, look for a sensory experience.

British supermarket Waitrose's latest food and drink report highlighted "texture-maxxing" as one of the trends of the year. It describes the phenomenon as a multi-sensory indulgence that is "fuelled by texture-maxxing crunch and intense flavour hits," pushing shoppers to fill their trolleys with crunchy peanut butter, dumplings, and trifles.

"This year, the sound of food went mainstream," Waitrose's Senior Development Chef Will Torrent said in the Wednesday report. "Driven by social media's obsession with audible, multi-sensory cooking, we're creating high-contrast meals that combine shatter-crisp crunch with pillowy chew."
"The emphasis in social media content has flipped from narrative voiceovers to ASMR-inspired audio, where the evocative sounds of food are just as important as the visuals," he added.

Food trends on social media have ranged from the obvious to the absurd. Fibermaxxing and proteinmaxxing have taken off in the past few years. Meanwhile, food and beverages like Dubai chocolate, protein coffee, and ube were some of the big social media hits.
Nestlé's USA 2026 trends found that 75% of Gen Z and 80% of millennials sought out texture in snack cravings with the hashtag "crunchtok," amassing 1.5 billion views.

Waitrose noted that shoppers looking to maximize on texture bought its viral No.1 Alphonso Mango Dessert, which involves "cracking through the crisp shell" to access a "smooth mango mousse and passion fruit curd on a crunchy white chocolate base."

Waitrose's TikTok and Instagram videos of eating the dessert were watched by more than two million people, with a whopping 6,173 hours and 36 minutes of play time on TikTok. Its videos featuring crunchy toast also went viral.
The U.K. grocer's sales of jarred chili crunches, which include crispy rayu oils such as itsu Crispy Chilli Oil, saw a 13-fold jump. Meanwhile, crunchy peanut butter outsold smooth.
Dumplings also had a moment, with sales of chicken gyoza dumplings up 116% this year and searches on waitrose.com for gochujang and peanut butter udon noodles jumped 60%.
"We've seen an explosion in demand as shoppers treat dumplings not just as a quick weeknight bite, but as a total sensory experience," Waitrose's Executive Chef Stephen Parkins-Knight said.

"Driven by the rise of texture-maxxing, people want that ultimate contrast: delicate skins, juicy fillings and crispy skirts, topped with very chilli crunch. With innovation ranging from fusion fillings to rich dipping broths, dumplings have taken a delicious centre stage in 2026," he added.
Texture-maxxing also extended to desserts, as shoppers bought twice as many chocolate trifles compared to 2025, and sales of strawberry trifles increased 160%.
Tiramisu was also popular, with searches for waitrose.com's tiramisu recipe page increasing 155% year-on-year.

cnbc.com/2026/11/26/semiconductor-chips-.headline: Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why
cnbc.com/2026/11/26/semiconductor-chips-.author: Deena Zaidi

paragraphs.text: The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data.

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
AI driven demand

Yet the demand for semiconductor has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.
"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.
The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s.

Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt.

Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle.

The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.

nytimes.com/2026/11/26/business/nvidia-s.headline: Nvidia Halts Sales to Southeast Asia as U.S. Tightens China Restrictions

paragraphs.text: Nvidia has halted some sales of its most advanced A.I. chips to four countries in Southeast Asia as the Trump administration intensifies efforts to cut Chinese companies off from American computing power.

Data center operators in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia have had orders put on hold, according to two people with knowledge of the sales suspension, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private business dealings.

The freeze threatens one of the world’s fastest-growing data center markets, where billions of dollars of projects are under construction. Much of the region’s growth has been fueled by Chinese companies renting access to powerful Nvidia chips that American export controls prohibit them from purchasing directly.
Nvidia did not provide immediate comment.

The U.S. Commerce Department last week proposed new measures aimed at closing that loophole. Under the new policy, which is still under review, data center operators in several Southeast Asian countries would be required to obtain licenses to acquire Nvidia’s most advanced chips if they supply “significant volumes of computing power” to companies headquartered in a handful of countries deemed high-risk, including China, Russia and Iran.
The measures extend Washington’s efforts to restrict China’s technological development, targeting both its ability to acquire advanced American chips and its ability to use them overseas.

It is the latest turmoil facing Nvidia’s business amid widening concerns in Washington over Chinese access to its powerful chips after Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive, resigned two weeks ago following allegations of an affair with an executive at the Singaporean data center company Megaspeed.

U.S. intelligence officials believe the woman, Alice Huang, was in contact with a Chinese Ministry of State Security officer during their relationship. Beijing has denied spying. This week, the company’s board of directors reinstated Mr. Huang as chief executive following pressure from President Trump.

It is unclear how long the sales suspension will last. One person with knowledge of the halt said it was a stopgap until the Trump administration clarified how companies could obtain licenses to continue buying chips. American-owned data center operators appeared to be exempt from the freeze, which also extended to suppliers like Dell and Supermicro that package Nvidia chips onto A.I. servers, the person said.
The Financial Times first reported the sales suspension.

Southeast Asia has become a lucrative market for Nvidia, which has sold billions of dollars worth of chips to data center operators in the region. Many of those companies, known as “neoclouds,” specialize in renting out computing power to other customers. While some cater to local businesses, others count on demand from some of China’s biggest technology companies, including Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance.
For years, that arrangement has allowed Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced computing infrastructure without owning the chips themselves.

The sales freeze could have particularly wide-ranging implications in Malaysia, where investors have poured billions of dollars into one of the world’s ambitious data center build-outs. A prolonged interruption in chip supplies could stall construction and expansion plans, jeopardizing investments and putting pressure on the lenders that have financed the projects.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: De Cos Is Poised to Take ECB Presidency in Era After Lagarde
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Mark Schroers

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become European Central Bank president, directing the region's fight against inflation and possible bond turmoil.
Most Read from Bloomberg

With the Dutch government aligning itself to the consensus of European peers, leaders meeting in Brussels are poised to nominate the 55-year-old Spaniard later on Thursday. He will succeed Christine Lagarde, who will end her term early to leave the institution on Feb. 7.
While De Cos will still need to testify to the European Parliament, its opinion isn't binding, and the political agreement now in train means his appointment as president is essentially assured.

That would hand Spain the ECB's top role for the first time, coinciding with the transformation of the euro area's fourth-largest member from a onetime victim of the region's past debt crisis to become its best-performing major economy.

De Cos, a former governor of the Bank of Spain who is now chief of the Bank for International Settlements, will oversee monetary policy in a region of 21 member states and 350 million people. Among his tasks will be quelling inflation running at double the 2% target, while confronting the danger of a new sovereign debt crisis.

Market tensions over high borrowings in countries like France are a major concern. So far, ECB officials have put the onus on Paris to solve fiscal issues, but if rising yields begin to impede the effectiveness of their monetary policy, a decision on whether to step in may be needed.
De Cos was already firmly on track to win the role after securing the backing of France and Germany in recent weeks over the rival candidacy of former Dutch central bank Governor Klaas Knot.

The appointment will be the most important element to one of the biggest reshuffles of the ECB's six-strong Executive Board since the institution's inception more than 25 years ago, installing a new management team before French elections in spring.

The result means the euro will enter its fourth decade without Germany ever having had the presidency. It had little chance of winning it this time, with two of its nationals still set to hold key roles in coming years: Ursula von der Leyen at the helm of the European Commission and Claudia Buch running the ECB's bank watchdog.
Berlin opted instead to go for the chief economist position and nominated Princeton University professor Markus Brunnermeier to succeed incumbent Philip Lane when his term ends in May next year.

France, which has had the presidency twice, picked former minister and OECD chief economist Laurence Boone to join the ECB board. She will get the markets portfolio that becomes available after Germany's Isabel Schnabel exits in January — a position that may prove key in the event of a bond crisis.

As a consequence of Brunnermeier's start in June, Germany will have no seat on the board for the five months from Schnabel's departure in January, a potentially crucial period if market turbulence erupts around France's budget and elections.

"I'm not hoping for a crisis anytime soon but the interesting aspect for markets is what kind of direction the ECB toolkit will be taken in," said Michala Marcussen, chief economist at Societe Generale. "The president of course does not make decisions in isolation, but the president has an important role in guiding and pushing on the toolkit."

De Cos holds a doctorate in economics and a degree in law. The former chair of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision was widely deemed more dovish than Knot on monetary policy, but has a track record of preaching fiscal rectitude in Spain.

In a recent interview De Cos said central banks must "remain vigilant about inflation risks" stemming from high energy prices, while also signaling concern over high levels of borrowing by some nations.

He started his career at Spain's central bank in the late 1990s before working as an adviser to the ECB's Executive Board from 2004 to 2007. De Cos then led the Bank of Spain as governor for a non-renewable six-year term that started in 2018.

The exit of the BIS chief opens up another high-level position in the global central-banking community less than two years after the last change at that institution. It's unclear if Europe will be able to retain that top job against competition from global peers. De Cos's predecessor there was Mexico's Agustin Carstens.
--With assistance from William Horobin and Jorge Valero.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Lagarde Says AI Has Helped Europe Withstand Higher Energy Prices
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Jorge Valero

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 3:59 AM PST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said artificial intelligence is one factor helping the region weather the energy crisis, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

She told European leaders in Brussels on Thursday that the economy has seen more resilience than anticipated to the fallout from the Iran war, the people said, asking not to be identified because the discussion was confidential.

Lagarde said that AI and energy are among three forces shaping the outlook, with the other being the increase in global long-term interest rates, they said. While that phenomenon is partly a reflection of expectations for higher central-bank borrowing costs, the main driver has been largescale issuance of bonds from governments and companies, the people cited her saying.
The ECB president also urged leaders to ensure that legislation for the digital euro is completed before the end of 2026, according to the people.

Lagarde is set to leave her post on Feb. 7, almost nine months before her term concludes. Leaders are also discussing her succession, with Spaniard Pablo Hernandez de Cos the clear favorite for the job now that France and Germany have agreed on his candidacy.
"I believe that by the end of the day we will know for certain who will take over this key role in Frankfurt," Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic told reporters on his way into the meeting.
--With assistance from Jan Bratanic.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/trump.headline: Trump Says Revised GDP Numbers ‘Fake,’ Calls for Investigation
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/trump.author: Josh Wingrove

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 10:03 AM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump accused his own administration of a "purposeful" move to under-report US economic growth, seizing on a routine data revision to underpin an allegation of election interference with no evidence.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a social media post on Thursday, Trump pointed to GDP figures that showed the economy grew 4.3% annualized in the third quarter — revised from the 3.4% estimate in a previous release — saying it's a "major difference."
"It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE," he said without offering proof.

"I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error," the president added in the post, which was sent from his West Palm Beach golf course on the morning of the US Thanksgiving holiday.
Trump has long stoked fringe or conspiratorial explanations for election defeats, though has previously chalked up this month's midterm rout to the fact he was not personally on the ballot.
The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes GDP figures in stages, and the headline number often moves as the agency factors in additional data.
Trump has complained about unflattering economic numbers in the past. Last year, he fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a report showed weak job growth.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/as-anthropic-i.headline: As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue
techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/as-anthropic-i.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

GTA VI launched as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”
Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

“We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.
That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.
“We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder said. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”

As millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.
But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

The AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

The final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating new landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which launched earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

“The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”

Zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”
Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.
“You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”

This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

“Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder said. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”

GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.
