latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.headline: A landlord says he’s fixing Skid Row buildings. Tenants say they were pushed out
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.author: Doug Smith

paragraphs.text: In a video shot by a tenant, the landlord, in T-shirt and sandals, listens with a half-smile as he’s being showered with expletives.
“You’re a ... piece of s— landlord!” the tenant shouts when the landlord finally turns and walks away.
The object of the verbal lashing was Leo Pustilnikov, the 41-year-old budding real estate mogul who veered two years ago from high-end residential projects to the dregs of Skid Row.

Pustilnikov, a brash developer known for his aggressive use of the state’s “builder’s remedy” law to bust zoning limits in cities such as Beverly Hills, has become the steward of nearly 1,500 units of housing for the poorest Angelenos.

He has charted a course to rehabilitate 21 buildings that he obtained in such dilapidated condition no other developer wanted them. At the same time, he has tangled with legal aid and Skid Row advocacy groups that accuse him of skirting tenant protection laws and using abusive tactics to vacate buildings for repair.
“He’s very regulation averse,” said Barbara Schultz, director of housing justice at the Legal Aid Foundation of Los Angeles.

Quixotic and litigious, Pustilnikov has gained a reputation for acting first and then seeking permission. He was twice thwarted in attempts to temporarily house mental health patients, and then recovering addicts, in two Santa Monica buildings while seeking permits to convert them to luxury housing. He won a court battle with Beverly Hills and lost one with Redondo Beach over plans for high-end developments.

But he won admirers among downtown aficionados for purchasing the beloved Original Pantry Cafe. It reopened in November under an agreement with the homeless services nonprofit Hope the Mission to run it and donate net profits.
Even so, his efforts in and around Skid Row have led to bumpy relations with Los Angeles.

In the summer, he began the rehab of the Olympia Hotel on East 7th Street, taking the interior down to studs, before his application for a building permit was approved. The Los Angeles Housing Department issued a stop-work order. The project has been stalled for months.
The strained tenant relations blew up in June when the Housing Department, which was conducting weekly visits at all Pustilnikov buildings, declared the St. George Hotel uninhabitable.
As the August deadline to vacate approached, a few holdouts were unwilling to move from their home two blocks from City Hall to a building on Skid Row.
Police arrived and told some tenants they had to leave because they were trespassing. The officers left after City Councilmember Ysabel Jurado showed up and a staff member called police headquarters.
The tenants went back to their rooms. But later that night, private security guards banged on their doors, giving them a choice: accept a relocation payment or take a replacement unit on Skid Row.
“There ain’t no way I would stay on Skid Row,” said Byron Wilkerson, 86, who had lived in the St. George for more than a decade. “I just took the money and left.”
He said the $27,000 is secure, but he hasn’t found a new home and is staying with a friend.
The relocation payment came with a catch: People would lose their right to tenancy when the renovated St. George reopens.
Another tenant said she was escorted out with nothing.
“They said I didn’t live there no more,” said Yvette Valenzuela, who had switched units a few years earlier and never signed a new lease. “They said I was up for eviction.”
After a brief stay in a park, she moved in with her mother in Hesperia.

Pustilnikov, a hands-on landlord who engaged tenants by name on a tour of several buildings with The Times, takes criticism with equanimity, only occasionally lashing back at those he thinks lack gratitude for his good works.

“Even though I think we have done a good job at stabilizing one of the most troubled portfolios in recent history, we get no appreciation from the city or other government agencies,” he said in an email response to a question about two buildings that have been beset by complaints.
In an interview, Pustilnikov acknowledged setbacks along with the gains.

“When you have one building, three buildings, it’s easy to take care of whatever you need plus take care of whatever improvements you want,” he said. “When you have 21, there’s always a fire to address.”

Those 21 buildings were the most distressed in the portfolio of the Skid Row Housing Trust that failed in 2023, leaving the city on the hook for $40 million in operating costs during an 18-month receivership. Lenders and nonprofits took over the viable buildings. Pustilnikov took on the remaining 17.

His ownership group, Hope for an Affordable LA, paid $19 million, then received a $9-million rebate for renovation and repairs. Later he took over four more buildings from a nonprofit that found them too distressed to manage. He estimates he’ll spend $30 million more to complete rehabilitation of all the buildings.

The financial challenge was immense. About half the units were either too dilapidated to be rented or occupied by tenants who were allowed to stay even after their subsidies were terminated. Records were in shambles.
“We spent close to a year just figuring out who occupied each unit and getting units rent ready,” he said.

Out of 1,491 units, the Housing Authority provides subsidies for 1,240. But only 726 of those were leased, according to data provided by the agency in August. The rest were either vacant or occupied by nonpaying tenants.

Pustilnikov said he has stabilized the portfolio by moving tenants out of the worst buildings. He has emptied five buildings for rehabilitation, including the St. George, and has obtained tax credits to rehab four of them.
Two other buildings, St. Mark’s Hotel Apartments and the Crescent Hotel, are not worth saving, he said. The few remaining tenants who want to leave are being moved to other buildings.
The Sanborn Hotel on Main Street, a property whose wretched condition The Times profiled in 2023, is one of 14 that Pustilnikov considers stabilized.

During a recent visit, halls and bathrooms were clean, broken windows and doors had been repaired and entrances were secure, including an exterior door with a hole punched in it on The Times’ earlier visit.
Pustilnikov said the Sanborn had no usable units when he bought it. Now, he said, it’s 80% occupied.
He contends he has improved his tenants’ lives by moving them from dilapidated single-room occupancy units into studios with private bathrooms.
But the relocation push brought scrutiny from the Legal Aid Foundation and the Skid Row advocacy group Los Angeles Community Action Network, or LA CAN.
“We tried to work with him for the first year,” said Schultz of the Legal Aid Foundation. “Then he kept doing this so-called voluntary relocation.”
Schultz said she asked for a relocation plan so she could check that people were going into comparable units.
“He just won’t.”
There have also been hard lessons in managing supportive housing, designed for people at high levels of mental and physical disability.

Soon after taking possession of the buildings, Pustilnikov faced criticism forcutting back on the 24-hour security established during the receivership. He said the cost of security alone would have eaten up the rent he was receiving.
The St. Mark’s and Crescent, the two buildings Pustilnikov is not trying to save, have been especially problematic.
Organizers for LA CAN have documented piles of trash, broken plumbing and collapsed ceilings in the two buildings.

But St. Mark’s was clean though dreary when Ramtin Rafiee, a tenant relations liaison for Pustilnikov’s Hope for an Affordable LA, made a recent inspection. Stepping over an extension cord strung from an open door across the hall to a wall outlet, Rafiee greeted a tenant, who responded by telling him to go away.
“I hate that building,” he said. “It takes 60% of our management for 20 tenants.”
One former St. Mark’s tenant standing outside the hotel thanked Rafiee for his transfer to another building called the Cobb.
“I love the Cobb,” Michael Barnett said. “I didn’t know that kind of life existed.”

The level of management and security at Pustilnikov properties today is hard to gauge. Security guards and staff were present at every building toured by The Times on two occasions with Pustilnikov or his top aides.

But an unannounced visit by a Times reporter and photographer to one of the stabilized buildings, the New Pershing, found no security or management on site. Residents told The Times that both were present sporadically.
“The tenants I have spoken to about the new security measures find it laughable,” said Jade Arellano, an organizer for LA CAN.

Pustilnikov said he is building security into his rehabbed buildings by, among many measures, installing double-door vestibules and facial recognition cameras to identify intruders. Wooden room doors are being swapped out with steel, and elevators are getting fob activation instead of buttons that are easily damaged. Residents can now report service needs on a 24-hour hotline.

Rafiee said a gate erected to control access to an alley behind the New Pershing has kept it free of trash and drug users, dramatically reducing crime. It’s been a battle of attrition, he said, as intruders repeatedly cut the chain lock.
LA CAN sent field workers into Pustilnikov buildings to advise tenants and help them get benefits they are entitled to when displaced. Conflicts developed as organizers held tenant meetings.
“There were points where management was yelling at the tenants that they were going to be evicted,” Arellano said. Pustilnikov says they yelled at his staff.
Arellano said Pustilnikov’s management team has pressured residents with improperly issued notices to vacate and warnings that the building would be red-tagged.
Pustilnikov said the Housing Department inspected every unit he moved a tenant to and found it comparable.
“I didn’t do anything wrong,” he said.
Schultz of the Legal Aid Foundation said her review of records found 12 former tenants who did not receive relocation payments they deserved.

One of those tenants, Kevin Winn, the last resident to leave the St. George, said he refused both options offered, relocation to another building or a $17,000 relocation fee. Meeting at a Silver Lake cafe in September, Winn said he was homeless. His phone is no longer in service.
Taking the money, he said, means, “You can’t go back.”
He said the moving to the heart of Skid Row would have jeopardized his 20 years of sobriety.
“What, they want to put me in the heart of all that BS?” he said.
Another former St. George tenant, Machaela Gagnon, accepted a move to the New Pershing and is happy she did. It’s clean and has a pleasant interior courtyard, and her neighbors are nice.
But she and son William Giblin, who is also her caregiver, said they felt bullied by Pustilnikov’s managers and that they narrowly avoided a trap.

Her contact at the Housing Authority told her that the unit she was assigned to was tied to a project-based voucher. If she took it, she would lose her tenant voucher preventing her return to the St. George when it reopens. She demanded to move to a nonvoucher unit.
Giblin thinks it was a ploy to get rid of her.
“I get it, you have to give Leo some leeway,” Giblin said. “But when does leeway become negligence?”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Bitcoin Tops $60,000 as Risk Assets Rise in Holiday Trading
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Emily Nicolle

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 8:28 AM PST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Bitcoin rose above the $60,000 mark on Thursday as risky assets tracked a rebound in tech equities, pushing crypto markets higher as they head into a period of thin holiday trading.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The largest cryptocurrency rose as much as 2.2% during the Asia session before paring some of those gains, changing hands at around $60,500 in New York trading. Other tokens including Ether and XRP also rose.

Bitcoin has lost more than a fifth of its value this month, putting it on course for its biggest monthly decline since a crypto-market meltdown more than four years ago. The sector has struggled to regain investor confidence amid a string of high-profile hacks, rising macroeconomic pressure and regulatory uncertainty following the US midterm elections.
"The rebound has improved the tape," analysts at Marex wrote in a note Thursday. "It has not repaired the underlying demand picture."

A set of US exchange-traded funds tracking the price of Bitcoin recorded $453 million in outflows on Wednesday, taking the group's outflows over the past month above $5 billion. The products launched to great fanfare in January 2024, but performance has faltered under dampened demand for the underlying asset.

"With ETF selling still running at a heavy pace, Bitcoin may have found some short-term breathing room, but there is a real risk that the sellers return once the holiday dust settles, leaving the recent lows back in sight," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/thank.headline: Thanksgiving Storm Sweeps East Coast, Delays Macy’s 100th Parade
finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/thank.author: Greg Ritchie

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A powerful Thanksgiving storm is sweeping up the US East Coast toward New York, as adverse weather knocks out power to more than half a million homes and businesses across the nation while snarling holiday travel.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The strengthening storm has already led to the postponement of events including Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade, which has rescheduled for Saturday, marking the first time the annual holiday procession has been delayed. The governors of New York and New Jersey both declared a state of emergency ahead of the storm, warning of damaging winds, heavy rainfall and severe coastal flooding through Friday.

The conditions complicate journeys for those heading to family gatherings, though the days leading up to Thanksgiving tend to see greater travel than the holiday itself. AccuWeather meteorologist Alyssa Glenny said wind gusts have already reached 72 miles per hour at Stingray Point, Virginia, with coastal areas of New Jersey and Long Island bracing for gusts up to 80 mph as the storm pushes northward.

"We're looking at the afternoon going into the evening for peak rainfall in New York," Glenny said via telephone. "Once we get to midday, early afternoon, the wind is going to pick up and then the next 12 hours is the window for peak winds."

There were about 400 reported flight cancellations across the US, with Baltimore/Washington International Airport and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport among the worst impacted, according to FlightAware data. While elevated, the disruption is far below the levels recorded earlier this month after the US Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop due to an equipment outage.

Meanwhile, there are over 560,000 US power outages as of 10:50 a.m. Eastern Time, according to PowerOutage.com. That includes about 5% of customers in Virginia and Missouri, with the latter enduring heavy snowfall from a winter storm.

"With the power outages, we always are concerned with downed trees that could impact travel," AccuWeather's Glenny said. "Along the coastal areas — like those locations in Southern New Jersey, Ocean City, Maryland where they're having the coastal flooding — there are definitely some travel impacts with flooded roadways in that corridor."

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to the high winds making it too dangerous to send the balloons above the streets of Manhattan. The city adopted new wind rules after the 1997 Thanksgiving parade, when gusts hurled a gigantic Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, injuring spectators.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.
The balloons have been grounded because of weather just once in the parade's history, in 1971. In 2019, they were required to fly at lower heights because of high winds.

"Tomorrow we're going to start to see the impacts winding down and then we're kind of just dealing with cleanup," said Glenny. "By Saturday, for places like New York City, we expect a dry day. By the afternoon we could even have some breaks of sun."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: SAP Weighs Cutting at Least 10,000 Positions in AI Restructuring
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Christina Kyriasoglou

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- SAP SE is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions to transform its software business for the artificial intelligence era, according to people familiar with the matter.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The restructuring would affect at least 9% of the global workforce, the people said, asking not to be identified because discussions are ongoing. The total number of job cuts hasn't been finalized and might still change after labor negotiations, they added.

The plans come after SAP, Europe's most valuable software company, reorganized its executive board twice this year as part of a push by Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein to promote an AI-first strategy. Two of six board members will leave the Walldorf, Germany-based company in March.

"SAP continuously reviews its organization to ensure it remains aligned with its strategy and customer needs," the company said in a statement, declining to comment on whether any job cuts are planned.

As part of the changes, SAP's leadership will continue to redesign how it develops and sells products, according to the people. Klein is seeking to embed AI tools into the company's applications, after earlier attempts to introduce AI products faced problems.
All departments are being asked to identify areas for potential cuts, with product and engineering and sales departments in particular focus, according to the people.

Klein took over most of the responsibilities of product lead Muhammad Alam this year after he didn't renew his contract, which ends in March. Sales chief Thomas Saueressig, who had been given an expanded role earlier this year, said last week he will leave the company to become CEO of Ionos Group SE.

SAP historically has announced major restructurings in late January alongside its full-year results, most recently in 2024. Around 10,000 positions were eliminated in that effort, which cost around €3 billion ($3.3 billion) and took over a year. It was mainly handled through voluntary departures and retraining workers, with the total number of employees remaining relatively flat as SAP hired for new positions.
In Germany, where SAP has the largest number of employees, the labor council this year negotiated an employment guarantee through 2028. SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide.

"Our headcount has increased a little bit over the course of the year," Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley conference last week, adding he "would be really surprised" if that trend didn't reverse.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/a-month-with-t.headline: A month with the iPhone Duo has changed how I use my phone
techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/a-month-with-t.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: For years, the definition of a premium smartphone depended on its cameras, processors, and how light it felt when you stowed it in your pocket. The iPhone Duo challenges that concept by asking consumers to pay more for a fundamentally different smartphone experience, even if it means sacrificing what they’ve long thought of as high-end features.

In a little under a month of using the Duo, I’ve found that the trade-offs I was initially concerned about matter far less to me than I had expected. What’s been more interesting is how the Duo’s foldable form factor has changed my everyday habits, including how I interact with apps, which apps I use, and how I organize and personalize the phone itself.

I also easily forgot a number of my initial concerns about switching to the Duo. The apps, for the most part, are now optimized for the Duo; I’ve reacquainted myself with Touch ID; and I don’t miss the Pro Max camera on most days.

That’s not to say the Duo doesn’t have its shortcomings. I still miss that telephoto lens sometimes, and I’m still longing for Face ID — though not as much since Apple shipped a face unlock feature in the latest update. But after a month of using the Duo, I’ve found these compromises have had less of an impact on my day-to-day experience compared with the benefits that the new form factor brings.
Multitasking feels more natural

I was surprised by how much I’ve grown to appreciate the Duo’s multitasking capabilities. Initially, I didn’t think I’d regularly use it to view two apps side by side, given the still fairly limited screen space even while the phone is unfolded, especially compared with an iPad. But I’ve found myself snapping apps to both halves of the screen more often than I had imagined.

For starters, Apple has made this side-by-side mode incredibly intuitive and easy to use — you simply drag the app over to the left or right side of the screen and drop it into the target box that appears.
I have regularly taken advantage of this feature to do all sorts of things.

I really enjoy keeping X open as I read through the news, which allows me to switch back and forth between the article I’m reading and real-time reactions to it. Sometimes I’ll keep email or Slack open on the side while I’m working on something else so I don’t miss an important message or notification.
And much like the overstimulated members of Gen Z (which I am not), I sometimes like scrolling social media while engaging with some other media off to the side.

Case in point: I passively watched Netflix’s “Love is Blind” reunion while reading the gossipy tweets and Reddit posts about the main characters on the other side of the screen. This sort of TV watching behavior used to be called second-screen viewing, but now it’s morphing into something new. Everything is happening on one screen, so should we call it “Duo screen viewing,” perhaps? It makes me long for even more interactive TV experiences where commentary and content are combined.
It really is like having two phones

I’ve noticed another shift in my behavior since adopting the Duo as my main device. When I’m out and about, the Duo feels more like an (arguably heavier) iPhone mini. For those who still miss smaller iPhones, the Duo is the next best thing. Despite its weight, the phone feels small. You can cover it with one hand; you can type with a thumb; you can reach the top and bottom easily; and you can even fit it into your front and back pockets. The Pro Max now feels unbelievably strange in my hand — how was I ever comfortable wrangling this giant rectangle?

The Duo’s small screen works well when you’re on the go, especially for short interactions like responding to a quick text or pulling up directions to a destination. It’s not as great for mindless scrolling, which I appreciate, as it forces me to engage with the real world instead of killing every moment of boredom or unease by opening up apps.
But when you’re home or somewhere with time to kill, you can unfold the screen and enjoy your apps super-sized. It’s the best of both worlds.

I find that I instinctively unfold the phone when I’m preparing to watch videos, because the larger screen is best for that. It’s also unfolded if I’m shopping, as it’s more convenient for looking at products, zooming in to examine the details, or complete checkout forms.

Generally, I also unfold the Duo when I’m actively using apps. This setup has also allowed me to rethink my Home Screen layout: With the Duo closed, I prefer to see just widgets on the small screen with key information like weather, time, battery life, and so on. Meanwhile, the only app icons on the Home Screen are those in the dock.
The Duo apps are ready now

In the weeks since its launch, most of the apps that weren’t yet optimized for the Duo have been upgraded to support its foldable form factor. In mid-November, Apple said there were over 200,000 Duo-ready apps, and in my experience, that certainly feels true. A majority of my so-called “daily drivers” — with the glaring exception of key Google apps like Gmail and Drive — have dropped the black band on the side of the screen that was frustrating early testers of the phone.
Most apps now take advantage of the available space, whether that’s on the Duo’s small front screen or the wider, unfolded one.
I’ve also found it interesting to see the different interpretations developers have had for how to best optimize their app for Duo.

Some have used the form factor as a way to bring in some sort of novelty: there’s a note-taking app that opens and closes like a notebook, with pages you can write on with the Apple Pencil; a retro Walkman-like music player; a tiny typewriter; a gaming handheld; a game where you close the phone to make grilled cheese.

As much as I love the whimsy of this group of apps, I appreciate how my everyday apps feel better to use on the unfolded screen. Spotify, at last, feels less cluttered when it has more screen real estate. A number of note-taking, list-making, and calendar apps also feel somehow more usable when spread out.

The Netflix app is actually fantastic with its support for multiple viewing modes, which include playing video on the closed outer display, the “laptop” orientation with its big player controls, and the “tent” mode.
Other developers have similarly reimagined how their app would work if it had originally been designed for the Duo’s small and larger screens.

One good example of this is Sofa, a handy utility for organizing the books, movies, TV shows, podcasts, albums, and games you want to check out. When the Duo is closed, its navigation is tucked off to the right side in a vertical bar, while the main screen focuses on the items you’ve saved. But when the Duo is unfolded, the number of items displayed on the screen also expands into a two-column layout, with more of your items featured on the screen and your lists on the left side. It doesn’t feel like two different apps, but like you’ve opened up the app itself and given it more space to spread out.

In terms of your daily social media scroll, apps like TikTok and Instagram have been updated to be perfectly usable on the Duo, whether the phone is open or closed. When closed, TikTok now stretches the video to cover the screen, instead of showing the ugly black bar. Scrolling short-form videos on the Duo, while unfolded like a slightly smaller iPad mini, has become my preferred way to watch.
I’m reading more books

Here’s another surprise: I’ve spent less time with my Kindle, and am instead reading books on my Duo. Unfolded, the Duo is a decent enough replacement for an e-book reader, albeit it can be a bit more stimulating as it’s not an e-ink device. However, the matte inner screen isn’t quite as bright and distracting as your typical glossy OLED display. There’s less glare and softer reflections, but there’s also something about the display that just feels calmer than a smartphone, allowing you to more fully engage with a book’s text.

Unfolded and held vertically, reading on the Duo feels a lot like reading on the standard Kindle, at least in terms of hand-feel. And putting your phone into the “Do Not Disturb” focus mode can help you not be distracted by incoming notifications and messages while you read.

You can also unfold the device while keeping it in landscape orientation, with the screens bent slightly inward like a real book. For even more fun, you can turn on Kindle’s page-turn animation, which makes it seem as if you’re turning the page in a physical book. And I love how you can “performatively read” using an app like Book2Life or Actually Read — they display the book’s cover on the Duo’s outer screen as you read the text on the inner screen.

E-book readers will likely find they can carry one less device when they’re out and about, because the Duo can stand in for whatever Kindle or other reader you typically keep in your purse or bag. You can save the Kindle for other times, whether that’s at home, on long travel days, or when you don’t want to worry about sand getting into your $2,000 phone.
I don’t need a PopSocket

On the big-screened iPhone 17 Pro Max I used to carry, I tended to keep a PopSocket of some sort on the back because the phone was both heavy and large, which made it hard to hold for longer periods of time. The Duo is similarly heavy, but its shape makes it far easier to hold in one hand without the extra help.
Folded, you can do the usual one-handed hold where the bottom edge of the phone rests on your pinky, your other three fingers cradle the back, and your thumb is free to navigate the screen.

Unfolded, the Duo’s like using a small Kindle or iPad mini, where two hands are required. You also don’t need a PopSocket for balancing the phone on the side, because it can be propped up like a tent or opened like a tiny laptop. Or, if you prefer, Apple and others offer Duo cases with a built-in stand. (Apple’s case comes in navy and taupe, though, so if you’re not boring, you’ll probably want to shop from third-party vendors).

If you think you still might need a PopSocket at times, or you just aren’t ready to give it up, the brand now makes a slimmer version: its Low-Pro Grip. There are other competitors, like the OhSnap grips, which aren’t a bad alternative either.
It’s inspiring personalization
There’s something about the Duo that seems to have kicked off a new iPhone personalization trend, at least judging by what I’ve been seeing on social media.
Unlike a regular iPhone, where every phone case is simply a shell that offers a degree of protection based on the materials used, the Duo case lineup provides far more variety.

You can buy cases with and without built-in screen protectors, and some use adhesive to better stick to the outer screen, while others don’t. Some cases let you customize the band around the outer screen with a different color than the case that protects the rest of the phone.

Then you have cases that cover the hinge, while others leave it exposed. There are cases that offer holes where you can attach straps, wristlets, and charms. Some of those have attachment points at the bottom and others on the side.
Essentially, there are a lot of options for customizing how you want to carry the Duo and how you want to express your own style.
I’m also now starting to see whimsical cases that come with attached pens. (Thank goodness — most of the pen cases so far have been kind of plain!)

I also believe there’s something about the Duo that particularly appeals to women. Maybe because it’s small, or maybe it’s because you can attach a strap to its side and carry it like a little purse. Or maybe because, like a purse, you can deck it out with chains and charms — a choice that’s grown increasingly popular as young people have embraced whimsical, retro tech as a way to express their individuality and sense of fashion.
The Duo easily lends itself to this trend, perhaps even more than a regular iPhone. It becomes an accessory you want on display, not one buried in a bag.
Before switching to the Duo, I spent a lot of time thinking about what I’d be giving up by moving away from the Pro Max.

I’m surprised to find that, a month later, I only think about what I’d have to give up if I switched back to a traditional iPhone. It’s not just the extra space of the unfolded screen I’d miss — it’s all the little habits I’ve developed around having different screen sizes for different purposes.

The Duo makes me pause and think about how I want to use an app. That small moment of deliberation, before I even open the phone, has helped me break some of my more mindless smartphone habits, particularly around social media.
That’s not a benefit I could have anticipated if I’d judged the device by its specifications alone.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/26/travel-fatig.headline: Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/26/travel-fatig.author: Renée Onque

paragraphs.text: Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.

An estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.

High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.

The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to new experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist.

But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani says. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.

Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, says travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked."

The consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she says. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.
Use these tips to manage fatigue, from a travel expert and a sleep specialist
You might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:

• Come up with a plan before you leave to lighten the load: If you're driving, look up restaurants along your route in advance, says Tiani. Bring snacks with you to places like the airport or train station, O'Donnell suggests. Coming up with a solid itinerary for your trip can help you feel less stressed, Tiani says. She suggests scheduling a rest day in between the day you return home and when you have to get back to your everyday routine.

• Avoid trying to control how the trip will pan out: While planning is useful, rolling with the punches is necessary, too, O'Donnell says. "A lot of travel is being OK with things going wrong, and where you get exhausted is when you try to control more than you can," she says.

• Consider reasonable accommodations: Limit the number of hours you drive in a single day by adding rest stops, or pay for extra legroom on your flight if you'd benefit from it and can afford it, Tiani suggests.

• Prioritize sleep and downtime: Not everyone can comfortably sleep on planes, trains or buses. If you can, get some rest on the way to your destination, Tiani says. During your trip, your sleep routine likely won't be the same because you're in a different setting and operating on a new schedule, she notes.

• Be mindful of your diet: Stay hydrated and aim for balanced meals when you can, Tiani says. O'Donnell agrees: "For train travel and plane travel, that is one of my first sort of defenses: eating well when I get back, loading up on fresh fruits and vegetables, and refueling my body so that it can fight off anything I've been exposed to."

• Move your body: Walking around while traveling, including up and down the corridors of your train or plane when possible, can reduce your risk of blood clots, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Anyone traveling more than four hours by bus, car, train or plane may develop blood clots, according to the agency, though the risk is generally low for the average traveler. Exercise and sunlight exposure are especially useful for dealing with jet lag once you're back home, both Tiani and O'Donnell say.

• Give yourself time to decompress after your trip: After traveling, people may ask you how your travels went. Don't feel bad if you don't want to discuss the whole trip right away, O'Donnell notes. That's a form of travel fatigue itself, she says: "You will look on it differently in two weeks [or] a month's time, just let the guilt go. You don't have to feel any which way about anything. It can be an amazing trip, and also have been really hard."

nytimes.com/2026/11/26/business/dennys-j.headline: Jensen Huang Is Back, and So Is His Plaque at Denny’s

paragraphs.text: America’s diner is always open, especially for Jensen Huang.
Denny’s, the restaurant chain, has reaffirmed its ties to Mr. Huang, the co-founder of Nvidia, days after he was reinstated as the company’s chief executive.

“Every story starts somewhere. We’re proud to be part of Jensen’s,” Denny’s posted on its social media accounts on Wednesday, alluding to Mr. Huang’s path from washing dishes at a Denny’s as a teenager to becoming one of the most powerful figures in artificial intelligence and one of the world’s richest people.

Legend has it that Mr. Huang developed the idea for Nvidia in a booth at a Denny’s in San Jose, Calif., in 1993 with his co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem. In 2023, the restaurant put a plaque above that booth commemorating Nvidia’s beginnings, inviting Mr. Huang to unveil it.

Two weeks ago, Mr. Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip maker after revelations that he’d had extramarital affairs with an executive who reported to him and with a woman whom U.S. officials had identified as a Chinese spy.
The day after his resignation, Denny’s wrote in its post on Wednesday, the company learned that the commemorative plaque had come down.
“We put the plaque right back up where it belongs,” it said.

Denny’s did not say when the plaque was restored — and multiple calls to the San Jose location on Thursday morning went unanswered — but its statement came two days after Nvidia’s board of directors reinstalled Mr. Huang following pressure from President Trump.

Mr. Huang’s comeback has been met with mixed reactions. Some congressional Republicans have harshly criticized Nvidia’s decision to reinstate him and argued that the Trump administration had not provided adequate assurances that it had resolved national security concerns surrounding the company. Mr. Huang’s allies, including in the tech sector, have supported him, with Elon Musk comparing his exit to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team.”
Denny’s, too, offered its unequivocal support for Mr. Huang. “We couldn’t be prouder of the history we share,” it wrote.
The company’s statement was met with bafflement on X, where one user said it “might actually be one of the cringiest things I’ve ever seen on this website.”

If such allegiance to another company’s executive seems out of the ordinary, Mr. Huang is no ordinary executive. Having co-founded Nvidia at 30, he built it into a company worth $5.8 trillion at its peak.
But even as he cultivated a rock star persona in the tech world, leather jackets and all, Mr. Huang often evoked his humble beginnings at Denny’s.

He has said that at 15, he got his first job at a Denny’s in Oregon, where his family lived after immigrating from Taiwan. On Thursday, his LinkedIn profile listed two jobs: founder and chief executive of Nvidia (1993-present) and “dishwasher, busboy, waiter” at Denny’s (1978-1983).
“I was a dishwasher, I was a busboy, I waited tables,” Mr. Huang said, according to a Nvidia blog post in 2023 about the unveiling of the plaque. “No one can carry more coffee cups than I can.”

Denny’s has hundreds of locations across the United States, including eight in San Jose, Calif., in the heart of Silicon Valley. The chain’s slogan, “America’s diner is always open,” is meant literally — Denny’s really is open all day, every day, Thanksgiving and Christmas included — but also as a way to showcase the chain’s philosophy.
“We’re open to whomever you are, and we greet customers with open arms and have an open mind,” Peter McGuinness, the chief executive of the agency behind the slogan, told The New York Times in 2011.
For a corporate titan looking to shake off sex scandals and the whiff of espionage, that is a welcome message.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.headline: Ex-Marine admits to stealing millions of rounds of ammunition from Camp Pendleton
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.author: Iris Kwok

paragraphs.text: A former Marine corporal has pleaded guilty to stealing millions of rounds of ammunition and multiple rocket launchers in a years-long scheme to make money.

In a plea agreement dated Nov. 20, Andrew Paul Amarillas admitted to stealing “large quantities of U.S. military ammunition and weapon systems” from Camp Pendleton’s School of Infantry West between 2022 and 2025. He was, at the time, an ammunition technician specialist.

Amarillas said in the agreement that he stole between 1 million and 2 million rounds of ammunition. In addition to the rocket launchers, he also admitted to stealing several Javelin missile systems, which are portable antitank weapons designed to destroy low-flying helicopters and other objects. They are manufactured exclusively by Lockheed Martin and RTX Corp. for the U.S. military and cannot be legally possessed by or sold to the public unless demilitarized.
The ammunition and the weapons systems were not demilitarized — a fact that Amarillas was aware of — and were worth about $374,000, according to the plea agreement.

Amarillas recruited “at least three” fellow Marines to help him move stolen goods and falsify paperwork, according to the plea agreement. A Marine spokesperson confirmed to The Times that an investigation into the ammunition theft remains ongoing. The other Marines were not named.
Amarillas, who is in his 20s, faces up to 10 years in federal prison and could owe hundreds of thousands of dollars in restitution. He is scheduled to be sentenced Feb. 8.

“I abused my position of public trust as a United States Marine to facilitate the commission and concealment of this offense, and also exploited my access to Ready Service Lockers and manipulated official documentation ... to disguise significant shortages in the ammunition and weapon systems I stole,” he said in the plea agreement.

Amarillas made “dozens” of trips to transport the stolen property to his Arizona home, according to the plea agreement. He would then sell the goods to “at least five civilian associates” who were aware they were buying stolen government property, he said in the plea agreement. Some of his associates would then resell the stolen property.
In an effort to hide the evidence, Amarillas destroyed his personal cellphone, according to the plea agreement.
Amarillas’ defense attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

“The Marine Corps has strict control measures to guarantee only authorized individuals can handle munitions materials,” Marine spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said in an email. “The circumstances surrounding the allegations of ammunition theft are under investigation and further details are not available.”
Text messages sent between Amarillas and his unnamed co-conspirators were used as evidence in his prosecution.
“Just [got] some javs and some other ones,” Amarillas wrote, according to the criminal complaint. “[I] have 2 launchers that [I] think you’d like, if you want to take a look tomorrow.”
The text messages included photos, such as one of a Javelin missile system with a serial number matching one that Amarillas had signed out from the School of Infantry West.

The ammunition that Amarillas stole included M855A1 and M80A1 “enhanced performance” rifle cartridges manufactured by Olin Winchester and limited to U.S. government sales — as well as M855 rifle cartridges, which is non-performance-enhanced ammunition that can sometimes be bought directly from the manufacturer. However, M855 ammunition made for the U.S. military is packaged differently and cannot be possessed by or sold to the public.

Federal prosecutors said that, in one instance, Amarillas offered 30 cans of ammunition — about 25,000 rounds — to a co-conspirator. Over a roughly two-week period, Amarillas stole and sold 66 cans of M855 rifle ammunition, prosecutors said. Some of the ammunition was purchased from co-conspirators by undercover officers, while some was seized by federal authorities.

cnbc.com/2026/11/26/trump-gdp-revision-i.headline: Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher
cnbc.com/2026/11/26/trump-gdp-revision-i.author: Sean Conlon

paragraphs.text: Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.

Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not necessarily out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.

Notably, the advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.
Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.

Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.

Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool. They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-26/ca.headline: California pays taxes for the rest of the country. You’re welcome
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-26/ca.author: Laurence Darmiento

paragraphs.text: Once again, California led the nation in a dubious distinction: sending the federal government far more money than it receives back — to the tune of $190 billion in the last fiscal year.

The latest USAFacts study released Wednesday showed that the Golden State easily outdistanced New York at $91 billion and Texas at $69 billion as the country’s largest so-called donor state. That’s a figure arrived at by finding the difference between the taxes and other revenues sent to the Treasury and funding such as Social Security and Medicare received back.

California’s status as the leading donor state has been trumpeted by Gov. Gavin Newsom in his political fight with the Trump administration over policy disputes and right-wing figures who claim the Golden State is failing.

Last year, when President Trump threatened to cut all federal funding to the state, Newsom suggested California might want to withhold all the federal taxes its residents and businesses pay — though nothing came of it.

“Every year when folks sit down to file their federal taxes, there’s a real sense of frustration — and I feel it too — knowing just how much California sends to Washington and how little we get back,” Newsom said in an April 15 tax day statement titled “California pays Trump’s bills.”
A Newsom spokesperson did not respond to a message for comment on the latest figures.

In some ways, it’s not surprising that California finds itself as the top donor state, given its nation-leading 39.5 million population and a huge economy that has benefited from the recent boom in artificial intelligence investment and spending. California’s $4.3-trillion gross domestic product would trail only the U.S., China and Germany if it were a separate nation.

The study by the nonprofit Bellevue, Wash., data provider found that for the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, 2025, California sent $767 billion in revenue to the federal government — also more than any other state — while receiving $576 billion in federal disbursements.

At issue is that the money sent amounts to 14.5% of all state revenue collected by federal government as measured by the study, while California’s population, though large, amounts to just 11.5% of the nation’s 343 million people. At the same time, the money disbursed to California, while also more than any other state, only amounts to 10.9% of what is distributed nationally.

Chris Gilligan, a senior content analyst at USAFacts, said the outsized federal contributions can be explained by California’s wealth, which generates significant tax revenue, while it receives less in Social Security, defense and veterans’ funding than might be expected.

“California is contributing more to the federal government, in raw numbers, than any other state, and it’s also getting back more than any other state. That said, the balance isn’t one-to-one,” he said.

This is only the second year that USAFacts has conducted the study. Last year, it found that California also was the nation’s leading donor state, paying $276 billion more to the federal government than it received.

Gilligan said the difference between last year’s larger figure and this year’s smaller figure was driven at least partially by Internal Revenue Service tax relief granted in 2023 that pushed some federal tax contributions into the next fiscal year.
USAFacts, founded by former Microsoft Chief Executive and L.A. Clippers owner Steve Ballmer, is not the only organization to have studied the issue.

At least since 2015, the Nelson A. Rockefeller Institute of Government in New York has ranked California among the top five donor states as measured by its own balance of payments metric, not counting COVID-19 pandemic assistance payments in 2020 through 2022, according to a Times report last year.
Although California’s primacy as a donor state has been bandied about politically, by some other metrics in the USAFacts study it’s not the only state that might be filling a pinch.

On a per-capita basis, Massachusetts was the largest net donor state last fiscal year, another wealthy state that has benefited from the burgeoning tech industry. It sent $8,047 per person to the Treasury, followed by farm states Minnesota at $8,038 and Nebraska at $7,799.
On a per-capita net basis, California sent $4,832, ranking it seventh.

On the other side of the federal tax payment imbalance, Alaska received the largest disbursements per person at $27,670, followed by Virginia at $26,566 and Connecticut at $23,743, according to the study.

Gilligan noted that federal contracts can contribute to the differences among states. Virginia, for example, ranks as the nation’s leading recipient of defense spending, including payroll, contracts and grants, according to the state’s economic development authority.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/26/gaza-m.headline: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says

paragraphs.text: Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”
“The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16,” it added.
The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.
Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.
He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”
On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.
Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire. Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head.
“I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day,” she added.
The Israel Defense Forces have been approached for comment.
Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.
A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.
According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.
Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/x-finally-gets.headline: X finally gets parental controls after 20 years
techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/x-finally-gets.author: Ram Iyer

paragraphs.text: After 20 years of existence, X, the social network formerly known as Twitter, has finally added parental controls for teenagers, giving parents and guardians a way to manage what their kids see and interact with on the platform. But unlike most platforms’ implementation of such controls, X is putting its own spin on the system by giving teens a say in the matter.

The company said accounts belonging to 13-to-17-year-olds will be set to “protected mode” by default, meaning they won’t be able to see sensitive content, and won’t be served targeted ads. However, X is allowing teenagers to retain a measure of control over their accounts, letting them see what restrictions were made to their accounts. Parents and guardians will also not be able to read their teens’ private messages, see search or viewing history, or post as their teen.

The controls let parents see how much time their teen spends on X per week, set daily limits, require their approval for new followers, limit feed recommendations and videos to already followed accounts, filter specific words, turn off sensitive media, specify who can send their teen DMs, and see who they are messaging.

The controls arrive months after X came under fire for a lack of controls preventing the platform’s AI chatbot from being used to generate sexualized images of children and women. The social network has also long been rife with child sexual abuse material, misinformation, AI bots, and openly lets users post porn.

X has generally not been a platform aimed at teenagers, but that doesn’t mean they don’t use the platform. A 2024 study found that nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids have an X account. The platform itself requires users to be at least 13 years old, though that’s not a high bar given the kind of content on the platform.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow. With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change. Striking that balance is vital and what we set out to build.” Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, wrote in a blog post.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/is-alice-huang.headline: Is Alice Huang a spy or not?
techcrunch.com/2026/11/26/is-alice-huang.author: Lucas Ropek

paragraphs.text: The central, still-unproven claim in the Nvidia scandal is that Alice Huang, a former executive at the data-center company Megaspeed, is a Chinese spy. She had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who abruptly resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging it and was just as abruptly reinstated on Monday of this week.

What’s publicly known is murkier than the headlines suggest. U.S. intelligence has reportedly tracked Alice Huang’s contact with an officer of China’s spy agency, but officials haven’t offered public evidence that she was commissioned to target Nvidia’s chief. In the past week, while President Trump pushed to bring Jensen Huang back, the administration has played down the allegations it once circulated internally. Whether that reflects new intelligence or political pressure is the question hanging over the case.

Undisputed reporting shows the claim emerged from the White House itself. It first appeared in a highly classified memo written in March under the oversight of Secretary of State Marco Rubio and circulated to White House officials ahead of Trump’s trip to China in May. The memo formed the partial basis for the New York Times’ initial reporting on the scandal, published Oct. 29 and its existence was first reported on Nov. 8.

The memo, whose existence the White House has never disputed, did not definitively say, according to the Wall Street Journal, that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. CNN, by contrast, has reported that the memo concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset.

What’s better established is that Alice Huang was in touch with Chinese intelligence. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is Beijing’s civilian spy agency, responsible for both foreign intelligence and domestic counterintelligence. Last weekend, the Times, citing people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports, reported that Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from the spring of 2025 until this fall, a period that overlaps her relationship with Jensen Huang. (The Chinese government has called the spy claims a “smear,” and Megaspeed says Huang left the company in August 2025 and that its business is legitimate.)
Top Trump officials have nonetheless all but discredited the espionage claims, along with the suggestion that Nvidia fell prey to spying or foreign influence.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, who was Trump’s personal defense lawyer before taking over the Justice Department, told journalists on Tuesday: “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.” On the same day, Trump said a pardon was an option for Jensen Huang but that he did not think one would be needed. Senior intelligence officials reportedly told Congress that the government apparently has no actual evidence that the MSS directed Alice Huang to pursue an affair with Jensen Huang.

None of those statements necessarily exonerates Alice Huang as an intelligence agent. Instead, they support the alternate theory that the Chinese government did not tell her to begin the affair and that Jensen Huang broke no law by having it. Not being directed to have an affair isn’t the same as not being a spy, nor do the statements address the separate chip-diversion allegations around Megaspeed.

From a certain angle, the circumstantial evidence surrounding Alice Huang looks quite suspicious. She was a top executive at a company investigated for illicitly channeling Nvidia chips to China, and her husband, Kang Wei, is said to have even closer ties to the MSS, with some sources saying he worked for the agency.

The timing of the government’s reversal is at the heart of the matter. Trump has said he lobbied the board “directly and indirectly” to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, so it wouldn’t be surprising if officials who serve at his pleasure were recasting the case in terms that satisfy his agenda. That wouldn’t necessarily make their assessments wrong. But unless new intelligence has actually resolved the question, and none has been publicly identified as yet, that backdrop is critical to keep in mind. CBS has also reported that Rubio, whose office oversaw the original memo, has privately voiced concerns about aspects of Jensen Huang’s return.

Doubts persist elsewhere, too. Earlier this month, CNN reported that the intelligence community was still working to understand Alice Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang and that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove she was acting as a spy for Beijing. After a briefing by top intelligence officials earlier this month, Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, said he was unsure whether she was a spy or a “useful idiot.” And this week, the Wall Street Journal pointed out that under Chinese leader Xi Jinping, top corporate executives routinely maintain ties to the country’s intelligence service without being formally deputized as assets.

The crush of conflicting claims, most from anonymous government sources, obviously leaves large questions unanswered as to what actually transpired. Some of those questions that naturally spring to mind:

• Alice Huang is said to have been under U.S. surveillance for over a year. If the government suspected her of espionage, why wasn’t Jensen Huang warned earlier (and privately, so as not to cause the stock-market-destabilizing maelstrom that followed the more recent disclosure)? One explanation that has been given is that alerting the Nvidia chief might have tipped off Huang that her cover had been blown.
• If Alice Huang was a spy, what information did she pass to the Chinese government, and what influence did she actually have?

• Most critically, how did the allegation reach the public at all? The likeliest answer is a leak. A source told CNN that Rubio briefed Trump on the intelligence in May, yet Trump has since said he only recently learned of the concerns, and in October he presented Jensen Huang with the National Medal of Science. Officials who felt they could not get through to the president may have turned to reporters instead, which would explain how the contents of a memo whose existence has never been disputed found their way into print. What remains unclear is who leaked it, and whether they anticipated the fallout.

There are answers to all of these questions, of course, but when the public will get them is anybody’s guess. Jensen Huang is due to appear before the Senate Banking Committee next week, and by the look from the statements of some of its members, he’s likely in for a rough ride. Unfortunately, congressional hearings, particularly public ones, rarely unearth secrets that haven’t already been disclosed.
