washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/26.headline: Strobe Talbott, who helped shape Clinton-era foreign policy, dies at 80
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/26.author: Bob Drogin

paragraphs.text: In 1970, Strobe Talbott was writing his dissertation on Russian literature at the University of Oxford in England when Time magazine, for which he had interned in Moscow, hired him to translate former Soviet premier Nikita S. Khrushchev’s then-secret memoir, which had been smuggled out of the Eastern Bloc.

The crash project required working nights, and Mr. Talbott’s housemate, fellow Rhodes scholar Bill Clinton, sometimes knocked on the door with scrambled eggs and pots of tea, so the two 24-year-olds could chew over the Kremlin’s endless intrigues.

Those predawn chats did more than cement a lifelong friendship. After taking office in 1993, then-President Clinton tapped Mr. Talbott — who by then had spent 21 years at Time as a Washington correspondent, bureau chief and columnist — to shape U.S. policy toward post-Communist Russia and the former Soviet republics as they struggled to adopt democratic reforms and free market policies in the wake of the Cold War.

Over the next eight years, first as special adviser and then as second-in-command at the State Department, Mr. Talbott helped lead the administration’s efforts to quell conflicts in the Balkans, expand the NATO military alliance eastward, remove nuclear weapons from three former Soviet republics and manage Clinton’s fraught relations with Russia’s erratic leader, Boris Yeltsin.
Mr. Talbott, who led the nonpartisan Brookings Institution’s public policy research center for 15 years after he left the Clinton Administration, died Thursday. He was 80.
The death was confirmed by his son, Devin Talbott.

Known for his intellectual heft, workaholic hours and grasp of the nuances of foreign policy, Mr. Talbott rode a famously gilded academic résumé — the Hotchkiss School, Yale and Oxford — into the top tiers of government, journalism and think tanks. Tall, trim and balding, he was a highly visible presence in the nation’s capital thanks to his authoritative books on arms control, U.S.-Soviet relations, the new Russia and India’s nuclear policy.

Perhaps most importantly, he carried the ultimate Washington credential: the confidence of a two-term president who sometimes phoned him daily, often after midnight, to schmooze and discuss global strategy.

Their rapport was such that Clinton first introduced him to Yeltsin with a teasing remark. “This is my friend Strobe. His socks didn’t match until he was 40 years old,” Clinton said, according to Mr. Talbott’s recollection in a 2010 oral history with the University of Virginia’s Miller Center, which specializes in presidential scholarship. (He added that Clinton, as governor of Arkansas, often stayed at the Talbott home when visiting Washington. “My kids,” he said, “used to call him the guy who eats all the ice cream.”)

Mr. Talbott’s 1984 book, “Deadly Gambits: the Reagan Administration and the Stalemate in Nuclear Arms Control,” was arguably his most consequential. It revealed how Pentagon aides had deliberately undermined arms talks with Moscow while a “somewhat befuddled” president and his top national security aides were mostly ill-informed.

The book, which embarrassed the White House, helped set the stage for Reagan to take a less hawkish stance in his second term. He signed the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the first to eliminate an entire class of nuclear weapons, and his administration entered into talks with the Soviets that led to the 1991 Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, the largest and most comprehensive arms control agreement in history.

Sales of Mr. Talbott’s book jumped after former vice president Walter F. Mondale, the 1984 Democratic presidential nominee, read aloud from it during a campaign debate with Reagan. It didn’t help Mondale, who lost in a landslide.

As deputy secretary of state from 1994 to 2001, under two secretaries of state, Warren Christopher and then Madeleine Albright, Mr. Talbott played an outsize role as the Clinton administration struggled to find its balance as the sole superpower in the post-Cold War world.

Convinced that Russia could be transformed into a European-style democracy, Mr. Talbott pushed U.S. political and financial support for Moscow — a policy some called “Russia First” — as a strategic priority above nearly all others, and the White House agreed.

His critics, at home and in Moscow, called him naive or deluded. They contended that he held a romanticized view of Russia based on his love of its language, literature and culture, and that he failed to grasp its brutal politics and oligarchic economy.

“Fundamentally, [Mr. Talbott] is an apologist for all things Russian, even in the Soviet era,” David Pryce-Jones wrote in the conservative National Review in 2002 after reading Mr. Talbott’s first-person book “The Russia Hand: A Memoir of Presidential Diplomacy.”

Mr. Talbott insisted that America had no choice but to deal with Moscow. He decried isolationists who wanted to “turn the American eagle into an ostrich,” with its head in the sand, as he wrote in a State Department cable in 1995.

“I think it is self-evident that you have to do business” with Russia, he told The Washington Post soon after. He added, “The business that we have to do with them is to make sure they do not blow us up.”

He defended Yeltsin as the leader most likely to stop Russia from backsliding into despotism. During his 1994 Senate confirmation hearing, Mr. Talbott praised the Russian president as the “personification of reform” even though he had ordered tanks to shell the parliament several months earlier to stop hard-liners seeking to remove him from office.

Mr. Talbott found a sympathetic ear in Clinton, who felt an affinity for the embattled leader he called “Ol’ Boris.” “We can’t ever forget that Yeltsin drunk is better than most of the alternatives sober,” he told aides, Mr. Talbott wrote in “The Russia Hand.”

Yeltsin was “both a very big man and a very bad boy, a natural leader and an incurable screw-up,” Mr. Talbott wrote. “All this Clinton recognized, found easy to forgive and wanted others to join him in forgiving.”

Clinton’s 18 meetings with Yeltsin, usually choreographed by Mr. Talbott, produced notable achievements, including persuading Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan to transfer their nuclear weapons to Russia; persuading Russia to withdraw troops from the Baltic states (Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia); and halting the sale of Russian rocket parts to India, easing an arms race with Pakistan in the subcontinent.

Mr. Talbott also took part in marathon negotiations outside Moscow that produced an accord to effectively end the civil war then raging in parts of the former Yugoslavia. During the fighting there, NATO warplanes had attacked Serb forces in Bosnia and Kosovo.

But those efforts only delayed Russia’s backsliding to autocracy and runaway corruption. When Yeltsin resigned in 1999, he handed the presidency to his chosen successor, then-Prime Minister Vladimir Putin. The fledgling partnership between Washington and Moscow gradually withered, and Putin rules Russia today with an iron fist and an ultranationalist ideology.
Despite his platinum “Friend of Bill” status, Mr. Talbott’s influence had limits in the Oval Office.

He backed a United Nations convention to ban the production, use and export of antipersonnel land mines, for example, because they so often killed civilians. But Clinton would not sign the 1997 agreement, which had nearly 100 signatories, citing U.S. military needs on the Korean Peninsula.

More importantly, Mr. Talbott warned in a memo to Christopher in 1994 that granting NATO membership to the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary — all lying within what had been the Soviet Bloc — would antagonize Moscow and provoke future clashes. He later dropped his opposition, but his initial caution proved prescient.

After the three countries joined the military alliance in 1999, followed by seven other former Warsaw Pact member states in 2004, Putin increasingly condemned NATO’s expansion toward Russia’s borders. He later sent troops into Georgia and Ukraine, both former Soviet republics, partly to create a buffer zone against what he called a threat to Russian security.

Successful diplomacy takes two sides, and Mr. Talbott’s Russian counterpart, the deputy minister of foreign affairs, proved an able partner and friend. Georgiy Mamedov, Moscow’s top expert on America and a future ambassador to Canada, worked closely with him on NATO expansion, getting nuclear weapons out of Ukraine, and ending a war in Kosovo that grew out of the breakup of Yugoslavia.

The former journalist took a dim view of the highly classified reports he got from U.S. intelligence agencies, saying they rarely went beyond what he read in the newspapers. “The intelligence is ‘sexed up’ because they go to such trouble to collect it,” he told World Policy Review in 2003. “It is only useful at the margins of a particular problem. The policymaker’s view of the world is of a piece with what the intelligent public knows.”
The road to influence

Nelson Strobridge Talbott III was born in Dayton, Ohio, on April 25, 1946, and grew up in Shaker Heights, a wealthy Cleveland suburb. His father was an investment banker, and his mother raised their four children.

Like his father and grandfather, he attended the Hotchkiss School, an elite boarding school — then just for boys — in Lakeville, Connecticut. He was a sophomore during the Cuban missile crisis in 1962, the closest the world has come to nuclear war. “I remember the headmaster summoned us all into the school chapel,” Mr. Talbott told the New York Times in 1999. “We got down on our knees and prayed that the world wouldn’t blow up.”

Partly as a result of that crisis, he began to study Russian poetry at Hotchkiss, and he made Russian language and literature his major when — following his father and grandfather again — he attended Yale.

The campus was roiling with protests against the Vietnam War, and while Mr. Talbott opposed the U.S. involvement, he called for civility, not for storming the barricades. As chairman of the Yale Daily News, he urged his fellow students in an editorial to be “the coat-and-tie standard-bearers” of the anti-war movement.

New York Times columnist James Reston took note during a visit in 1967. “If the Strobe Talbotts at Yale, serious, idealistic, patriotic, progressive … did not support the war effort, the generals had better start worrying,” he wrote.

Mr. Talbott graduated summa cum laude in 1968 and spent three years as a Rhodes scholar at Magdalen College at Oxford, where he received his master’s degree. Years later, writing in Time, he admitted to a “moral discomfort bordering on guilt” that a draft deferment for a bum knee kept him “out of the Mekong delta [in Vietnam] but not off the squash courts and playing fields” at Oxford.

His growing Russian fluency helped him land a summer internship in Time’s Moscow bureau in 1969, and he impressed the editors. They hired him to translate and edit a 1,500-page transcript of hundreds of hours of tapes that Khrushchev, who led the Soviet Union for 11 years, had recorded after he was deposed in 1964. (Khrushchev died in 1971, at 77.)
Soviet officials condemned the 1970 release of “Khrushchev Remembers,” saying the tapes were fake. After a second volume appeared in 1974, they denounced Mr. Talbott as a CIA “sapling.”
More importantly, they rejected his request for accreditation to work as Time’s Moscow correspondent and barred him from Russia for five years.

While Mr. Talbott was still at Yale, his roommate, Derek Shearer, introduced him to Shearer’s younger sister, Brooke, a student at Stanford. They married in 1971 and moved to Belgrade when Time sent him to report on Soviet-dominated Eastern Europe.

But soon he was transferred to Washington, where he covered the State Department — as the Watergate scandal brought down the Nixon administration — and then the Ford White House. He spent seven years as a diplomatic correspondent and became Washington bureau chief in 1984. Ultimately he became the magazine’s editor at large and foreign affairs columnist, a position from which he called for détente with Moscow over confrontation.

After Reagan vilified the Soviet Union as an “evil empire” in 1983 and said communism was headed for the “ash heap of history,” Mr. Talbott expressed dismay, dismissing the harsh rhetoric as “bear-baiting” in Time.

But he later conceded his error. Days after the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, he confessed in a column that in none of his 30-plus visits “did I ever think I would outlive the Soviet state.”

Among his books were “Endgame: The Inside Story of SALT II” (1979); “The Russians and Reagan” (1984); “Reagan and Gorbachev,” with Michael Mandelbaum, (1987); “Master of the Game: Paul Nitze and the Nuclear Peace” (1988); “At the Highest Levels: The Inside Story of the End of the Cold War,” with Michael R. Beschloss, (1993); “The Great Experiment: The Story of Ancient Empires, Modern States, and the Quest for a Global Nation” (2008); and “Our Founders’ Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump” (2020).

After leaving government, Mr. Talbott moved to New Haven, Connecticut, to launch the Yale Center for the Study of Globalization. He quit abruptly a year later — leaving bruised feelings at Yale — to lead the far larger Brookings Institution in Washington. He retired in 2017 after overseeing a campaign that raised more than $650 million for Brookings.
Shearer died of cancer in 2009. Six years later, Mr. Talbott married Barbara Lazear Ascher, a poet, author and lawyer.

In his Miller Center oral history interview, Mr. Talbott said he turned down President Clinton’s first job offer — ambassador to Moscow — for unspecified family reasons. They remained close, however, and after Mr. Talbott spent Thanksgiving weekend bowling with the president at Camp David in 1993 — Christopher was not invited — the secretary of state picked Mr. Talbott as his top deputy to help compensate for his “own lack of access,” Mr. Talbott recalled.

Mr. Talbott added that his influence on Clinton “was very much exaggerated” in Washington. “That said,” he continued, “I did not waste time trying to correct people, for obvious reasons. The more people assumed I had the ear of the president, the more power I had. So fine.”

When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. (“Minefield” may be misleading; there were also secret pits filled with spikes.) The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed!

During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. As he reached for the door, he almost triggered the first booby trap: a fishing line wrapped around the handle that was attached to a rigged shotgun cartridge. Suddenly the contents of the house looked rather different. If one door had been trapped, any of them might be. So might any of the shoulder-high piles surrounding him.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/26.headline: Anita DeFrantz, 'outstanding advocate for Olympic values,' dies at 74
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/26.author: Casey Parks

paragraphs.text: Anita DeFrantz, a bronze medal Olympic rower who broke barriers for women and African Americans, has died after a long battle with cancer, Olympic officials announced Thursday. She was 74.

Ms. DeFrantz was captain of the first-ever U.S. Olympic women’s rowing team in Montreal in 1976. She protested President Jimmy Carter’s decision to boycott the Moscow Olympics four years later, then became the first Black woman to hold a top position on the International Olympic Committee.

She used her power to advocate for equality and against doping, among other issues. In 1989 she proposed a lifetime ban for any Olympic athlete found to have used a forbidden substance. The proposal was not adopted.

“Deeply saddened by the passing of Anita DeFrantz. A remarkable Olympian, a true pioneer and a tireless advocate for athletes and equality in sport,” five-time Olympian Abhinav A. Bindra wrote on X. “Her courage and conviction helped shape a more inclusive Olympic Movement.”
International Olympic Committee Honorary President Thomas Bach called Ms. DeFrantz “a great trailblazer and an outstanding advocate for Olympic values.”
The Olympic flag will be flown at half-staff for three days at Olympic House, officials said in a statement.
Information on survivors and the date and location of her death was not immediately available. She had been suffering from gastric cancer.

Anita DeFrantz was born Oct. 4, 1952, in Philadelphia. Two years later, her family moved to Indianapolis, a city her father described as “the northernmost Southern city.” (“That was a polite way of saying it was racist,” Ms. DeFrantz, who spent her childhood in Indiana, wrote in her memoir, “My Olympic Life.”)

None of her schools had girls sports teams. In high school, she joined the choir and a birdwatching club, and she “attempted to play” the bassoon, but she longed to compete in athletics, like her brothers.

“The closest I got to a sport was taking the football field at halftime as part of the marching band,” she wrote in her memoir. “That did not make any sense to me. Girls were being denied the right to compete solely because they were girls.”

She found rowing while studying music at Connecticut College. Congress had not yet passed Title IX, the landmark civil rights law that banned sex-based discrimination, but a growing number of colleges had begun fielding women’s teams, and Ms. DeFrantz tried out for basketball as soon as she could.

At the beginning of her sophomore year, the school’s crew coach noticed her walking across campus. Ms. DeFrantz was 5-foot-11 “with legs a little too long,” she wrote in her memoir. The coach told her she’d be perfect for rowing.
“I thought that was quite a line because I had never been perfect for anything,” she wrote.
In a boat, Ms. DeFrantz possessed the fluidity that often eluded her on the basketball court. Rowing was meditative, she wrote, an exercise that allowed her to work out her problems.

Men’s rowing has been a part of the Olympics since the very first Games. But when Ms. DeFrantz took up the sport, the Games still did not have a women’s competition. Her senior year, the Olympic board decided to add women’s rowing to the 1976 Montreal Games.

Initially, Ms. DeFrantz didn’t consider trying out. There were no paid training programs for women rowers at the time, and she didn’t have the money to cover the costs herself. The sport was “inhabited by white people,” she wrote.

Still, her coach urged her to try, so after she graduated, she enrolled in law school at the University of Pennsylvania, and she joined a new rowing club — one that had produced a long list of male gold medalists.

She rowed before dawn and in temperatures so cold her hair froze. She worked multiple jobs to pay for law school and her club dues. Most mornings, she went from a night job at the police station to the boat house.
At Olympic trials, DeFrantz outlasted her competitors and was named captain of the inaugural U.S. women’s eight — an event raced in a long, narrow boat with eight rowers and one coxswain, who steers.
“I remember calling my parents and telling them that I was an Olympian,” Ms. DeFrantz wrote. “My feelings were somewhere between ecstasy and exhaustion.”

The women’s team had never rowed together before the Olympics began, Ms. DeFrantz wrote in her memoir. They lost an oar during the first heat of the competition, but did well in their second. As they positioned themselves at the starting line for their third and final race, Ms. DeFrantz looked out.

“The water was so rough that we looked like a cement mixer coming down the course,” she wrote. “But we were rowing like there was no tomorrow — and as I would learn, when it comes to the Olympic Games, there may not be.”

Someone’s blade hit the water wrong, and they lost their rhythm long enough to fall back to third place. Ms. DeFrantz was disappointed. Still, at age 23, she had made history: She was the first Black women’s Olympic rower, and she had earned a bronze medal.

She graduated from law school and worked on behalf of children at the Juvenile Law Center of Philadelphia. She decided she would dedicate her free time to rowing and try one more time to earn the gold medal the errant blade had cost her team.
As the 1980 Moscow Games approached, Ms. DeFrantz took a leave of absence from her work as an attorney to train. She again earned a spot on the team.
Four months before the Opening Ceremonies, Carter announced that the United States would boycott the Games in protest of the Soviet Union’s invasion of Afghanistan.
The United States had never skipped an Olympics before, and Ms. DeFrantz tried unsuccessfully to change the president’s mind.
“I knew it was wrong,” she told The Washington Post last year. “I knew it wasn’t appropriate for the federal government to be intervening in private citizens’ goals.”

Ms. DeFrantz’s lawsuit was dismissed, but fighting for athletes changed the trajectory of her life. She stopped competing and joined the organizing committee for the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics as a vice president. In 1986, she became the first woman and first African American elected to the International Olympic Committee.
By the 1990s, Ms. DeFrantz was one of the committee’s most respected members and the highest-ranking Olympic official in the United States.
In 1999, some accused her of knowing about improper payments and gifts that Salt Lake Organizing Committee members paid as the Utah city made its fifth bid to host the Winter Olympics.
The scandal led to the expulsion of 10 International Olympic Committee members. Ms. DeFrantz denied any wrongdoing.
“I would never and will never mortgage the Olympic movement for a bid city,” Ms. DeFrantz told The Post in 1999. “Check my record. It’s not me.”
She later became the first female IOC vice president and was the first woman to run for the IOC presidency.

In 2021, Ms. DeFrantz learned she had gastric cancer. Her stomach was removed, but she continued to lobby for athletes and even flew to Greece in 2025 to cast her vote in an election that led to the IOC choosing its first female president, Kirsty Coventry.
Earlier this year, DeFrantz participated in the Olympic Games one last time when he helped carry the Olympic torch toward Milan, then passed it to Coventry.
In a statement Thursday, Coventry said she feels “an immense sense of loss.”
“Anita opened doors for the rest of us,” Coventry said. “But her real legacy is that she expected us to keep those doors open for those who come next.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820q9wgrpyyo.headline: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820q9wgrpyyo.author: Sarah Rainsford, Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent

paragraphs.text: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.

In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.

Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.headline: Coastal flood warnings extended in California amid high tides
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.author: Rosanna Xia

paragraphs.text: The worst of this week’s exceptionally high king tides is finally over, but weather officials spent Thanksgiving Day urging Californians to remain alert along the coast through at least Saturday — and to brace for a potentially massive storm early next week.

Coastal flood warnings and advisories for Orange County, Ventura and the Greater Los Angeles area have been extended until Friday afternoon, and beachgoers in the San Francisco Bay Area and in San Luis Obispo and Santa Barbara counties should beware of dangerous surf, sneaker waves and rip currents through Saturday.

A 7.7-foot high tide is expected to peak on Friday in Southern California at about 10:10 a.m. Even though this is lower than the astronomical 8-foot-high tides that smashed into Pacifica’s pier earlier this week and grabbed headlines across California, officials say the potential for flooding remains significant.

“We get concerned when the tide is over 7 feet,” said Joe Sirard, a meteorologist and observing program leader for the National Weather Service in Los Angeles/Oxnard. “Even though 7.7 feet is slightly lower than the 8-foot-high tides we saw this week, that is still an exceptionally high tide.”

On Thanksgiving morning, the high tide coincided with high surf and hammered several beaches in Southern California. Zuma Beach and Cabrillo Beach reported significant flooding, and videos on social media showed the Manhattan Beach pier overtopped by massive waves. The city closed the pier for several hours, reopening it shortly before 2 p.m.
In Ventura, those brave enough to be by the water were drenched by whitewash crashing over the boardwalk.
Amtrak also suspended Pacific Surfliner train service on Thanksgiving morning in parts of Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties “due to washout from high tide conditions.”

Across the San Francisco Bay Area, weather officials were cautiously optimistic that the worst of this week’s high-tide flooding was over. But they warned that hazardous beach conditions remain along the coast — including waves breaking up to 19 feet high — and urged people to “remain out of the water, stay off of waterside infrastructure, and never turn your back on the ocean!”

“Even though conditions are easing, it’s still very dangerous along the coastline with rip currents and sneaker waves,” said Joe Merchant, a lead meteorologist for the National Weather Service’s San Francisco Bay Area/Monterey office.

This week’s high tides are the first of three so-called king tides expected this winter. These higher-than-high tides occur when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon are strongest, and the next king tides — Dec. 23 to 25 and Jan. 21 to 22 — are expected to bring some of the highest tides in recorded history to California.

What remains to be seen is whether a winter storm or another Kelvin wave or big surf will coincide with the remaining two king tides. Across the state, officials acknowledged this is still just the beginning of what will probably be a very long El Niño season.

“This was a practice drill for what could come,” San Mateo County Supervisor Ray Mueller told The Times on Wednesday, amid the wreckage of Pacifica’s pier. “Imagine everything we had today, but with a storm system on top of it.”

As for the coming days, weather officials are keeping a close eye on a potentially massive storm aimed right at Southern California. Early forecasts show a chance of light showers on Sunday night, followed by a potential downpour of many inches of rain by Tuesday.

“Pay close attention to the forecast for early next week. It looks like quite a bit of potential rain, which can lead to mudslides, traffic — all of the things we get when it rains like this in Southern California,” Sirard said. “Tuesday looks very windy, very wet and very stormy at the moment. … It’s going to be busy next week for all of us, so be prepared.”
Times staff writer Rong-Gong Lin II contributed to this report.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/26/mar.headline: Maryland residents urged to conserve water after storm disrupts power
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/26/mar.author: Tim Craig, Liam Scott

paragraphs.text: Nearly 2 million people in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties in Maryland were asked to conserve water on Thanksgiving after a major storm disrupted power supplies at two water-filtration plants.
In a news release Thursday afternoon, the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission (WSSC) said it was issuing the alert “out of an abundance of caution” due to “intermittent power disruptions.”
Residents were asked to utilize “only water that is necessary” and limit showers, toilet flushing, and the use of washing machines and dishwashers.
“Following the guidance … could help preserve water for system storage and fire protection until the storm passes and power reliability is restored,” WSSC Water said.

WSSC Water’s Potomac plant, which is the larger of the two facilities and provides drinking water to about 75 percent of the region’s 1.9 million customers, had power and was producing drinking water as of around 4 p.m., according to spokesman Chuck Brown.
The problem, Brown said, is that the facility has experienced several power disruptions due to the storm.

WSSC Water’s other water-filtration plant, Patuxent, is out of service for planned maintenance, according to Brown, but crews are working to bring it back online. That facility also was experiencing power disruptions due to the storm, he said.
The agency stressed that the water remains safe to drink and cook with, and that there is no need for it to be boiled.
“This is a rapidly evolving situation, and WSSC Water will provide continuous updates to keep customers informed,” the agency said.
WSSC Water spokesman Luis Maya said the agency didn’t have an estimate on how long the conservation alert would stay in place. He said that would depend on how long the storm lasts.
“We’re hoping on the shorter end. At the end of the storm, we’ll have a better idea,” he said. “We want to make sure we’re prepared in case this is a prolonged event.”
Once power is stable again, Maya said the agency will lift the alert and notify residents that they can go back to normal water usage.

The conservation alert comes as wind gusts exceeding 60 mph rocked the Washington region Thursday. Pepco, the electric utility in suburban Maryland, reports nearly 25,000 customers had lost power as of 3 p.m.

politico.com/news/2026/11/26/cenk-uygur-.headline: Cenk Uygur goes all in on Ro Khanna for 2028
politico.com/news/2026/11/26/cenk-uygur-.author: Will Steakin

paragraphs.text: Ro Khanna hasn't launched a 2028 bid yet, but he already has a pioneer of the populist left in his corner.

Progressive firebrand Cenk Uygur is set to formally endorse the California Democrat on Thursday night during his annual appearance on nephew Hasan Piker's Twitch stream, a Thanksgiving Day debate-a-thon the pair call "Cenksgiving." Uygur told POLITICO he will pitch Khanna as the best populist progressive candidate. His Rebellion PAC will also debut its first 2028 ad promoting a Khanna candidacy Thursday night.
"For me, it's a no-brainer," Uygur said in an interview, explaining why he’s backing Khanna. "Who else would you back, and why would any progressive or any populist back anyone else?"

Along with his PAC getting behind Khanna, Uygur is also launching his own "Draft Ro" website to collect signatures and showcase other early high-profile endorsers, though he wouldn't say who just yet.

The endorsement is one of the first of the 2028 cycle, and it comes before any major candidate has formally announced. Inside Washington, Khanna’s chances are viewed as quite slim. But for Uygur, that kind of underestimation is exactly part of the draw.
"I love it," Uygur said of the skepticism. "I wouldn't have backed him if anyone in D.C. was behind him."
"We're running against Washington," he added. "So if Washington doesn't like a candidate, perfect."

Uygur is pairing his endorsement with a litmus test he’s trying to lay down for 2028 progressives: Candidates must call what Israel has done in Gaza a genocide and support ending U.S. funding for Israel. "It isn't actually about Israel," Uygur said. "It's about: Is this person going to represent us or not?"

Khanna, he said, is "among the very, very few, and maybe the only candidate, that'll pass that test." He allowed for one other: "There's also AOC. If she runs, that's another person that could pass the test."

But that's as far as the praise goes. His endorsement of Khanna comes as many other progressives are waiting to see whether Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) jumps in. Uygur isn't one of them. Asked if her entry would change his calculus, he said: "Not 1%."
"Sorry, but I don't think AOC means it," he said. "I don't think she would do any of the things that she says, and so I'm not going to back someone who is not going to deliver."
"She's obsessed with the establishment, so she's going to run a soft, weak race," he added. "She wants to make Democratic leaders and mainstream media happy. Good luck with that strategy."
Khanna has told POLITICO he plans to decide whether to run after the holidays and that whether Ocasio-Cortez gets in won't factor into his decision.

Uygur's backing could give the potential 2028 candidate some credibility on the populist left, not to mention a boost from "The Young Turks," one of the longest-running and most popular progressive shows online, which Uygur launched in 2002. He also co-founded Justice Democrats in 2017 and ran a long-shot bid of his own for the 2024 Democratic presidential nomination. His Rebellion PAC sparked controversy during the 2026 midterms with an ad tying U.S. funding for Israel to higher grocery prices, which the campaign of then-Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced itself from.
Uygur, who was also a prominent backer of Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders' presidential runs, has a blunt prediction for 2028: "I'm positive Ro Khanna is going to win."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: Gold Steadies as Fed Rate Path and AI Stocks Frame Volatile Week
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Wendy Wells

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 3:53 PM PST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Gold steadied, as traders weighed the prospect of Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes against a wider market recovery spurred by a rebound in US technology stocks.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Bullion was near $3,565 an ounce, on track for a modest weekly gain after sinking to a 15-month low earlier in a week of choppy trading. Global stocks climbed Thursday as investors in Europe and Asia took their cue from a comeback in artificial intelligence-related equities. US cash markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.

The yellow metal has remained below $4,000 an ounce since Nov. 11 as traders gauged the Fed's path for combating sticky inflation. It's on track for a third monthly loss of more than 6%, extending a fall from a record high in January that gained pace after the US-Iran war sent energy costs soaring.

The Fed's preferred measure of underlying inflation for October, released Wednesday, reinforced expectations that the central bank will tighten policy when it meets in December. Higher borrowing costs are typically negative for gold, which doesn't pay interest. The market is also weighing the likelihood of further rate hikes early next year if price pressures continue.

Spot gold was little changed at $3,567.67 an ounce at 7:45 a.m. in Singapore. Silver slipped 0.1% to $41.50 an ounce. Platinum rose, while palladium edged lower. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was on track for a fifth week of gains.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.headline: AI Risk Puts Dollar on Track for Longest Winning Run Since 2024
finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/art.author: Cole Lipsky, Melos Ambaye and Naomi Tajitsu

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The dollar is poised for its longest monthly winning streak in two years as a rupture in the artificial intelligence trade and rising interest rates spur demand for safe-haven assets.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 1.8% in November, putting it on track for a third straight month of gains. The greenback has strengthened against all of its Group-of-10 peers, including the Japanese yen and the Swiss franc.

A slump in technology stocks, coupled with robust economic growth and elevated inflation, propelled the dollar higher over the past three months. Those dynamics were on display in pre-holiday trading on Wednesday, as the greenback jumped while the Nasdaq 100 index briefly plunged into a bear market and a measure of underlying inflation hit the highest since 2023.
"It's a pretty good dollar storm," said Steven Englander, co-head of FX research and North America macro strategy at Standard Chartered.
Market repricing for a more hawkish Federal Reserve also supported the dollar this month, according to Sarah Ying, CIBC's head of FX strategy.

Traders are fully pricing a 25 basis point interest rate hike next month for the Fed, and are betting on the possibility of two additional increases by the middle of next year. Policymakers have been flagging the need for more tightening, with some calling for lifting rates at successive meetings, while others are open to the possibility of raising by more than the usual quarter percentage point in December.

Some Wall Street strategists expect the dollar rally to extend into 2027, pointing to the very AI spending binge that's making stock markets jittery as a driver of US economic growth and capital flows. The greenback has benefited from overseas investors converting local currencies to buy shares of US companies that use the tech.

"The US economy is booming and inflation is still moving away from the target," said Win Thin, chief economist at Bank of Nassau 1982. "The Fed needs to hike rates to help cool the economy, perhaps in both December and January. That's dollar positive."

The dollar's latest surge has won over short-dated options traders, but conviction further out has weakened over the past two months. The divergence suggests investors are positioning for dollar strength into early 2027 while becoming less willing to extend bullish bets much further.

The latest equities sell-off has raised concerns about the longevity of the AI boom, fueling sharp swings in global markets. In such an environment, the dollar has become "the haven of choice," according to Goldman Sachs, while MUFG believes that the prospect of higher rates is also helping the currency.

"Weakness in the US equity market is taking place at a time when there is building evidence of strengthening cyclical growth momentum in the US, which is encouraging a stronger US dollar as a safe haven play," said Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG.

"The strength of the US economy supports the view of investors that returns are likely to remain higher in the US even if they are currently being challenged by the recent sell-off in US assets," he said.
--With assistance from Anya Andrianova, Neha D'silva and Amanda Fung.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Trump Says Huang Is Excited About His ‘Second Term’ at Nvidia
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Josh Wingrove

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said Jensen Huang is looking forward to his "second term" as chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp., reiterating his praise for the man whose reinstatement he pushed hard for despite bipartisan backlash over national security concerns.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Thursday, the president said he has not spoken to Huang since Nvidia announced his return, but probably will at some point.
"When I did speak to him, he is so happy to be going back. He calls it his second term," Trump said.

The president again dismissed national security concerns over the reinstatement of Huang, who was ousted after revelations that he had extramarital affairs including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

"Based on information and belief, I think he's absolutely fine," Trump said. Pressed on what information he had, he did not give a specific answer, only saying, "The information I have, which is a lot of information."

Nvidia earlier this week restored Huang as CEO, following intervention from Trump, who also enlisted Vice President JD Vance to help make a personal appeal to the board. Trump told CNBC on Monday he spoke to Nvidia's board "directly and indirectly" and "felt very strongly" that Huang should be brought back.

Trump's efforts drew widespread criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, with lawmakers vowing to investigate ties between Huang and the Trump administration. Huang is set to testify to House lawmakers behind closed doors on Dec. 1, and then publicly before the Senate on Dec. 3.

Nvidia's stock soared more than 31% on Monday after the announcement of Huang's return, but lost more than 9.5% in the next two days. The US market was closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

"I will tell you, the market feels very good about it," Trump said. "I was a little concerned yesterday when I saw some pretty big dips, and by the end of the day, it was it was up again. So I really did, I think I did a great thing for our country and even for the world."

Trump is due to travel on Dec. 4 to Arizona to headline a groundbreaking event for a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. chip manufacturing plant expansion — a facility that produces chips for Nvidia.
The president said he hadn't considered whether Huang should join him, but added: "I would be glad to take him."
