npr.org/2026/11/26/nx-s1-6044622/this-we.headline: This week in science: anxiety in college students, potatoes on the moon and whale snot
npr.org/2026/11/26/nx-s1-6044622/this-we.author: Nathan Rott

paragraphs.text: JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:
It is time now for our science news roundup from Short Wave, NPR's science podcast. I'm joined by science reporters Nate Rott and Sanden Totten. Hey to both of you.
NATE ROTT, BYLINE: Hello.
SANDEN TOTTEN, BYLINE: Hi.
ROTT: Happy Thanksgiving.
SUMMERS: Happy Thanksgiving to you guys. So I know you have brought us three science stories that caught your attention recently. Tell us what they are.
TOTTEN: Anxiety is on the rise for Gen Z and young millennials, and scientists think they may have found something to help explain why.
ROTT: We've also got how scientists are simulating potato gardening on the moon.
TOTTEN: And a world first involving whale snot.
SUMMERS: Really considering all the things here today, it sounds like, guys.
(LAUGHTER)
SUMMERS: All right. As an anxious girlie, I think I want to start with this new research on rising anxiety among young people.
TOTTEN: Yeah. So a new study looked at a key risk factor for anxiety in college-aged people in the U.S. and Canada over the last 30 or so years.
ROTT: And one of the reasons they started looking at this is because in the last 15 years, anxiety has started rising at a noticeably faster rate than before.
SUMMERS: OK. So what happened over the past 15 years to drive that? Any ideas?
TOTTEN: Well, the researchers pointed out that 15 or so years ago marks the start of when people really began using smartphones kind of all the time.

SUMMERS: OK, I am on my phone all day, so I feel that deeply. All the social media, all the notifications, all of the alerts, they make me really anxious. But were they able to learn anything more about why?
TOTTEN: That's the big question here. Let's say phones are ticking up anxiety. It's not clear what about the phones is making people more anxious.

ROTT: So that's where this new research comes in. The team noticed that a key building block of anxiety has also risen at this time, something called intolerance of uncertainty, that might offer some clues.

JEROEN VAN BAAR: And so, for example, somebody with high intolerance of uncertainty might want to know everything about a party they're attending before they go there because they don't feel comfortable attending if they don't know what's going to happen in advance.

TOTTEN: That's Jeroen van Baar. He's the lead author on this paper, published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Psychiatry, and he's also a postdoc at Boston University School of Public Health.
SUMMERS: OK, but, like, isn't it good to know more information in advance? Wouldn't that help someone feel more comfortable?
ROTT: OK, Juana, we get it. You want to know the ending.
SUMMERS: I do.
TOTTEN: (Laughter).

ROTT: But it's a double-edged sword, too, because, like, you know, when I'm trying to buy Christmas presents and have looked at my 30th review of a type of vacuum, I might just bail and never buy it, right? Or, you know, we've all had analysis paralysis, trying to pick a restaurant, right?

TOTTEN: Yeah. And smartphones, they kind of encourage all of this because suddenly we have thousands of reviews at our fingertips for everything. So over time, we start to expect to know everything. And when you kind of want to know everything, you start to become intolerant of not knowing. And if you're me, you're also intolerant of lactose, so you're also checking every menu for vegan options, and...
ROTT: (Laughter).
SUMMERS: Oh boy.
TOTTEN: It just goes on and on. So the theory is that when we can't handle uncertainty, we actually get more anxious.
SUMMERS: Interesting. OK. So knowing all of this, is there anything we can do about it to lessen people's anxiety?

ROTT: Yeah. I mean, there is a silver lining. There's been a lot of research into how people become more chill with uncertainty, like cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure therapy. These things have shown to be really effective. So there's hope that with treatment, you know, we can address some of these root causes of anxiety.
SUMMERS: All right, crossing my fingers for that one. Let's now move on to potatoes on the moon. I have many questions. The first is why the moon?
ROTT: Well, because Matt Damon already showed us that we can do it on Mars, right Juana? "The Martian"?

ROTT: Spoiler alert. You like spoilers. OK, no, seriously though. NASA's Artemis program is aiming to get a sustained human presence on the moon by the 2030s. So that means feeding people. Enter the potato. They're nutritionally dense. They're pretty hardy plants. And they pack a lot of calories for the space they take up. So scientists want to know, could you grow potatoes in simulated lunar dirt?
SUMMERS: Interesting. And lunar dirt is not at all like the rich soil here on Earth, correct?
ROTT: That's right. Yeah. So lunar dirt real or simulated doesn't have enough nutrients. So in this experiment, the scientists added in fertilizer and compost. And they found...
AYMERIC GOYER: If you go to 30% organic matter, plants look pretty much the same than an Earth control.

TOTTEN: That's plant biologist and the lead researcher Aymeric Goyer from Oregon State University. He says, based on molecular tests, the potatoes, they seem safe to eat, and they seem to have similar nutrients to Earth potatoes. And so for future lunar missions, he pictures astronauts growing these plants in, you know, greenhouse-type structures on the moon using lunar dirt instead of having to ship it from home. But you will still need to ship some fertilizer and make some compost on the moon. They publish these results in the journal npj Microgravity.
SUMMERS: Nate, you mentioned that the lunar dirt they grew the potatoes in is simulated. Do they know how well it stacks up to the real thing?

ROTT: Yeah, so we talk to plant biologist Anna-Lisa Paul, who has sprouted seeds in actual moon dirt - how cool is that? - collected from the Apollo missions. And she was impressed by this work even though she says it is super hard to simulate just how sharp and poke-y (ph) real moon dirt is.
ANNA-LISA PAUL: There's a big difference between having a bucket full of freshly broken glass and a bucket full of sand.
ROTT: Not to mention, you know, the gravity differences, the temperature differences, the radiation differences on the moon, too. So there's a lot there.

SUMMERS: So assuming we work all of that out and we can grow potatoes in moon dirt for our future human colonies on the moon - pretty cool, I have to say - I still have one big question. Will moon fries taste as good as Earth fries?
TOTTEN: (Laughter) That is a great question. And bad news, Aymeric can only answer that one in theory.
GOYER: For some reason, we didn't taste them either. I don't know why (laughter).
TOTTEN: Lost opportunity.

ROTT: But based on chemical analysis, he assumes they'll taste the same. Not to be a buzzkill, you'd also have to, you know, ship oil up there if you want something more than boring boiled potatoes, so...
SUMMERS: I will put that on my list. Nate Rott, last one. We've got to talk about whale snot.
ROTT: Juana, I would love nothing more. So scientists have been collecting whale snot for quite a while now because, much like our snot, it is packed with, like, loads of information.
TOTTEN: You got stuff like viruses, bacteria, or cells from the whale's respiratory tract, even fragments of DNA, all of which can tell researchers a whole lot about the whale and his health.
SUMMERS: OK, I think we all remember nasal swabbing for COVID tests. It did not feel very good.
ROTT: No.
SUMMERS: Didn't like that. How do you get whale snot?
ROTT: Well, they let the snot come to them...
(SOUNDBITE OF WHALE BLOWING AIR FROM BLOWHOLE)
ROTT: ...By carefully positioning flying drones above the whales. So here's marine ecologist Éadin O'Mahony.
ÉADIN O'MAHONY: The drones have got sterile Petri dishes attached to them, literally Velcroed on. And then as that whale comes up and breathes out...
TOTTEN: Splat. Snot sample collected.
SUMMERS: That is disgusting, but also perhaps the coolest use of drones I've heard of in a while.
ROTT: Yeah, so this collection technique is not, like, new new. What's new is what Éadin and her colleagues were able to learn from this snot.

TOTTEN: Yeah, they collected dozens of snot samples from humpback whales off the coast of British Columbia. And they say in the journal Molecular Ecology Resources that they were able to use those to sequence a whole whale genome, which means, you know, they could get the full genetic code.

ROTT: And that's really important, Juana, 'cause it can tell scientists about the genetic health of the broader population, you know, which is pretty crucial information for northern humpbacks, which have been in decline. So they can now get this in a noninvasive way instead of taking a tissue sample.

SUMMERS: Did not expect to be talking about whale snot today, but here we are. That is Nate Rott and Sanden Totten with NPR science podcast Short Wave, which you can listen to for new discoveries and the science behind the headlines. Thanks to both of y'all.
ROTT: Thanks.
TOTTEN: So fun. Thank you.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/us-iran-war-trump-ho.headline: Two Italians killed in Kuwait drone attack; Trump says Iran war ends ‘whenever I want it’
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/us-iran-war-trump-ho.author: Lim Hui Jie

paragraphs.text: Two Italians have been killed after an alleged Iranian attack on Kuwait, Kuwaiti forces said Thursday.
In a post on X, Kuwait's army said the deaths followed Iranian attacks on the country, with the two Italians killed by falling missile debris. Two others were also injured.

In response, a spokesperson for Iran's military told state media that no offensive or military operations had been carried out in the area and that "these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region" by U.S. and Israeli forces.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Telegram that he had spoken with his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani, and expressed regret over their deaths, while stressing that Tehran had no role or involvement in the incident.
"The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war," Araghchi wrote on X.
He also said Iran was ready to cooperate with the governments of Kuwait and Italy in investigating the incident.

Separately, Israel said Thursday that it was prepared to carry out strikes against Iran "at any moment," even without U.S. forces joining the effort, according to Israeli military spokesman Effie Defrin on Israeli broadcaster Kan.
The comments came after U.S. envoy Jared Kushner told a podcast Wednesday that Israel "needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset."

Israel has been pushing the Trump administration to back another offensive against Tehran, with Reuters reporting on Nov. 18 that Israeli spy chief Roman Gofman pushed for joint strikes when he met U.S. officials earlier in the month.
Late Thursday, President Donald Trump said on PBS that the U.S. had "victory at hand" in the Iran conflict and reiterated that victory would come "whenever I want it to be, to be honest."
Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with U.S. military personnel, Trump said Washington was still trying to give Iran "every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives."
But he added that he was not sure whether Tehran would agree.
"Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are," Trump said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/spacex-shares-musk-d.headline: SpaceX shares jump on alternative trading platform after Musk says he will expand share donations
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/spacex-shares-musk-d.author: Jenny Lee

paragraphs.text: Shares of SpaceX jumped 7.47% in overnight trading on Blue Ocean ATS after CEO Elon Musk expanded his SpaceX share-donation plan for U.S. children.
"I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year," Musk said in a post on X.

Blue Ocean ATS is an alternative trading system for U.S. equities that operates from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, outside regular U.S. stock market hours. According to the platform's holiday schedule, overnight trading resumed at 8 p.m. ET on Thanksgiving Day. U.S. stock exchanges were closed Thursday and are scheduled to close early Friday.
SpaceX shares closed 1.30% higher on Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving.

The latest pledge follows SpaceX's announcement Wednesday that it would donate one share of its Class A stock to every active Trump Account, tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children, with Musk personally matching the gift.
In a separate post on X, Musk said SpaceX's contribution would be transferred next month, while his personal donation would follow when his lockup period expires in June next year.
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created as of October, according to the White House.

Since the program's launch in July, families and friends have contributed more than $1 billion to the accounts, bringing total deposits from all sources to more than $9 billion, CNBC reported earlier this week.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/threat.headline: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections

paragraphs.text: Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/new-ze.headline: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/new-ze.author: Eva Corlett

paragraphs.text: The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-26/.headline: Woman's body washes ashore in Newport Beach; police investigate

paragraphs.text: Police are investigating after a woman’s body washed ashore in Newport Beach on Thursday.

Details were scarce late Thursday on the case. The “identity and circumstances of the dead body are currently under investigation,” Newport Beach Police Department Lt. Court Depweg said in a statement.
Lifeguards called police to report the body on the beach near 34th Street around 12:45 p.m., police said.
The body appeared to be that of an adult female who “was washed up out of the ocean,” police said. Newport Beach police and the Orange County Coroner Division are investigating.
The department provided no further information about the case.

Although the circumstances around the death are unclear, Newport Beach is one of a number of coastal Southern California communities that have been battling king tides and high surf that have caused hazardous beach conditions. Officials have warned of huge waves, rip currents and sneaker waves even as conditions have sent water crashing over seawalls and into people’s homes.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/mad-ab.headline: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind

paragraphs.text: As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.
“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara, meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.
“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

The hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.
Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.
Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.
“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

Despite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.
“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/sap-job-cuts-ai-rest.headline: German software major SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push: Bloomberg
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/sap-job-cuts-ai-rest.author: Shikhar Gupta

paragraphs.text: SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The number could change after labor negotiations. SAP did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.

Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.
The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.
Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.
In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.

The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy. This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.
The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

wsj.com/finance/stocks/chinese-shares-li.headline: Chinese Shares Lifted as Beijing Signals More Market Support

paragraphs.text: Chinese stocks were lifted as authorities reiterated support for capital markets and vowed stabilization policies, amid increased volatility in global markets.
According to state media Xinhua News Agency, Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Friday chaired a State Council executive meeting focused on market reforms.

The meeting noted that "the capital market is crucial to the overall economic development," and China would improve its market stabilization mechanism and introduce new policies to promote stable and healthy markets, Xinhua reported.

As part of this, the role of China's state investors--the so-called "national team"--in stabilizing the markets and countering volatility would be strengthened. Also, efforts would be made to optimize the function of Central Huijin, a unit of state-owned sovereign wealth fund China Investment, as a quasi-stabilization fund.
It also said that Beijing will guide medium- and long-term funds into the markets and listed companies should be encouraged to pay more dividends and step up share repurchases.

Although the measures look to be mostly reiterating previously announced ones, the language has shifted incrementally to show a bit more urgency and tangible action, according to ING chief China economist Lynn Song.

Chinese stock markets have weakened in recent months, broadly in line with global market as investors cool on tech-related companies. The U.S.'s recent efforts to tighten AI chips exports and renewed tariffs have also weighed on investor sentiment.
The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index has fallen over 15% from its peak in May but picked up on Friday, likely supported by the signals of support from Beijing.

The Shanghai Composite Index was recently up 3.6%, the Shenzhen Composite Index was 6.8% higher and the tech-heavy ChiNext Price Index surged 10.6%, on track for its biggest one-day percentage gain in over two years.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/private-markets-reta.headline: Private markets are more accessible than ever for investors. Getting out is another matter
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/private-markets-reta.author: Hugh Leask

paragraphs.text: Retail investors are lining up to back private funds. But education on how restrictive these funds can be, particularly on when and how much money they can get back, may not be keeping pace with the influx of new capital.

PwC research has found that 77% of fund distributors surveyed said access to private markets is becoming important or very important to what they plan to offer clients, but just 15% of asset managers said they provide comprehensive education for retail investors.

Unlike the public markets retail investors are more used to, some private-market vehicles limit when investors can get their money back to set repurchase windows, and even then may return only part of what they request.
Why liquidity matters

A spike in redemption requests at several private-credit funds earlier this year exposed the tension between giving investors regular opportunities to cash out and holding assets that can be difficult to sell quickly.

Blackstone restricted withdrawals from its $79 billion flagship nontraded BCRED private credit fund to 5% of shares in June, after redemption requests hit 10% during the second quarter. Apollo also capped withdrawals in its Apollo Debt Solutions vehicle at 5% after second-quarter redemption requests surged to almost 17%. Blue Owl, Morgan Stanley and Partners Group also limited investor withdrawals from some of their funds.
Limitations on redemptions are a key trade-off in structures such as LTAFs in the U.K., ELTIFs in the EU and interval funds in the U.S., which broaden access to less-liquid assets.
It's emerged as a major pressure point as those structures come under closer scrutiny.

"Private markets can have very different characteristics from the products many wealth clients are used to, particularly around liquidity, valuations and holding periods," said Albertha Charles, global asset and wealth management leader at PwC.
"Investors and advisers need to understand how these products work, including their liquidity and valuation characteristics, so they can make informed decisions about whether they are appropriate."

PwC's 2026 Asset Management Revolution report, published Nov. 23, surveyed 250 asset managers, 100 institutional investors and 100 distributors across 36 countries and regions. More than half of respondents represented firms with over $20 billion in assets under management.

Among the study's key findings, education and liquidity are seen as the main hurdles as private markets reach a broader investor base. Distributors said better advisor and client education would help expand access, while liquidity, lock-ups and suitability requirements remain major barriers. Private equity and private credit were also the areas where distributors saw some of the biggest gaps in advisor knowledge.
Private credit appears likely to draw the strongest demand — two-thirds (66%) of distributors expect it to lead client interest in private markets, compared with 46% for private equity.
Routes to access

Regulators in several major markets are creating structures to widen access to long-term and illiquid assets. The U.K. uses long-term asset funds, or LTAFs, while the EU's European long-term investment funds, known as ELTIFs, can be marketed across member states.

In the U.S., interval funds provide periodic, rather than daily, liquidity. Singapore, Japan and Hong Kong have also taken steps to broaden retail or listed access to private assets. The frameworks differ, but all aim to make less-liquid investments workable within existing distribution, suitability and liquidity requirements.

Yen Sum, global chair of the private capital practice at Latham & Watkins, and a member of its executive committee, said access to private-market funds is generally limited to investors who certify they are qualified or sophisticated.

She told CNBC on Thursday that the key issue for investor education centers on how private assets differ in liquidity, maturities and return-of-capital terms, and how higher rates can pressure leveraged companies — rather than simply whether regulation should curb access.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw074p95ye5do.headline: Marital rape: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected - study
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw074p95ye5do.author: Geeta Pandey

paragraphs.text: Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Inflation Slows Much More Than Expected in France and Spain
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: William Horobin, Daniel Basteiro and Mark Schroers

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Inflation in France and Spain slowed much more than anticipated as energy pressures eased, offering some relief to the European Central Bank as it weighs raising interest rates further.
Most Read from Bloomberg

French prices rose 3.2% from a year ago in November, down from 3.7% in October and far below the 3.6% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of analysts. Spain's reading came in at 4.1%, easing from 4.9% and considerably weaker than the 4.7% expected.

Despite the slowdown, inflation remains well above the ECB's 2% target as the war in the Middle East continues to reverberate. Policymakers have already lifted borrowing costs twice and are expected to do so again in December.

Investors, and some officials, are indicating more action beyond that. Traders on Friday, however, pared bets on hikes by end-2027, assigning a 25% chance of three increases compared with 35% before the inflation numbers were released.

Officials at the ECB's last policy meeting in October determined that the outlook for prices had deteriorated, supporting "a continuation of the measured policy response, while noting that further tightening was likely necessary."
Speaking to Bloomberg this week, Austrian central bank Governor Martin Kocher cited "significant upside risks" to inflation as he warned that the ECB "should not fall behind the curve."

Friday's data are the first for this month from the region's major economies. The 21-nation euro zone publishes figures on Tuesday, with analysts seeing a retreat to 3.9%. The decline may be steeper, to 3.8%, based on the numbers from France and Spain, according to Daniel Hartmann, chief economist at Bantleon.

A separate ECB survey, however, pointed to a sharp increase in consumers' expectations of future inflation. As of October, they saw prices rising 3.5% over the next 12 months, up from 3.1% a month earlier, and by 3% over the next three years, up from 2.9%.
Such perceptions risk boosting wage demands. Lithuanian central-bank chief Gediminas Simkus told Bloomberg this week that he expects unions to seek compensation for lost purchasing power.
France's report attributed the retreat in inflation to energy, while the pace of price gains in the closely watched services sector eased to 2.3% from 2.6%.
What Bloomberg Economics Says:

"A sharp decline in pump prices explains the easing in France's inflation in November. From here, we expect inflation to rise only modestly over the coming months, as earlier energy price increases feed through to the index. Inflation should then gradually ease through 2027, averaging 2.3% in our baseline scenario for oil and natural gas prices."
—Jean Dalbard. Click here for full REACT

Inflation and higher rates are proving tricky for the euro area's second-biggest economy, which is to recession and is grappling with a bloated budget deficit, jittery investors and social unrest — all before spring's pivotal presidential election.
Spain's statistics agency put the sharp decline in inflation down to fuels and, to a lesser extent, clothing and footwear prices.
--With assistance from Giovanna Coi, Harumi Ichikura, Joel Rinneby and James Hirai.
(Updates with ECB survey in ninth paragraph.)

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-st.headline: Oil Stockpiling to Influence Market in 2027, Energy Aspects Says
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-st.author: Rong Wei Neo and Weilun Soon

paragraphs.text: Rong Wei Neo and Weilun Soon
Fri, November 27, 2026 at 1:31 AM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Oil stockpiling will be important factor for the next couple of years, potentially tightening the market and aiding prices even with a projected global surplus, according to Energy Aspects Ltd.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Around 600 million barrels of inventories have been drawn down worldwide since the start of the Middle East war, so there's a need to rebuild, said Amrita Sen, founder and director of the consultancy.

China will be the biggest stockpiler, and will add 160 million barrels of new storage capacity this year and next, she said in a Bloomberg TV interview. Beijing is already refilling inventories, plus the US is set to rebuild strategic stockpiles at a low level from the second quarter of 2027, Sen said.

Refiners in China, the world's No. 1 oil importer, have boosted purchases this month, taking advantage of falling prices. Global benchmark Brent has plunged over the last few months as Persian Gulf exports recovered despite continued Iranian attacks on shipping. Energy Aspects is forecasting a global surplus of 1.2 million barrels a day next year.

Traders are "getting very complacent" and want to short oil, but they're doing so at their own risk when stockpiles are low and the chance of production outages is high, Sen said, referring to recent incidents in Brazil and Norway. Refilling stockpiles would take time, she said.
"Inventory refilling is a multiyear story, with 2028 being the bigger one than 2027 especially as the conflict continues for the first half at least."

Exporting Persian Gulf oil is likely to remain costly and inefficient, with higher freight costs effectively baked into the trade, Sen said. Logistics, rather than production capacity, may become the biggest constraint, she said in a separate interview, adding that Energy Aspects was seeing Iraq deferring loadings by more than a week, while ship-to-ship transfers and uncertainty around Hormuz transits create further friction.
"From a geopolitical point of view, we think this current status quo is the new reality," Sen said in the TV interview.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: Copper Rebounds From 11-Month Low on Return of Risk Appetite
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Bloomberg News

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 10:33 PM EST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Copper extended its rebound from an 11-month low alongside technology stocks in Asia, as risk appetite returned across markets after weeks of volatility fueled by concerns over the artificial intelligence trade.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The red metal rose as much as 4.4% to trade above $12,300 a ton on the London Metal Exchange, putting the market on track for the first weekly increase since early October. The technology sector in Asia was among the biggest gainers on Friday, while US equity-index futures also climbed.

"It's concentrated short-covering triggered by the rebound in US equities," said Harry Jiang, a trader at China-Base Ningbo Group Co. "With Chinese inventories still tight, a bounce like this makes perfect sense."

The prospect of US tariffs had prompted traders to ship huge volumes of copper to the US earlier this year, tightening markets elsewhere, but a short squeeze in China has recently created a lucrative trading opportunity. Logistics companies fielded a deluge of inquiries from traders seeking to ship the metal from the US to the Asian nation, with several shipments booked.

The Yangshan premium for imported cargoes hit a record $500 a ton last week, but has since dipped to $320, according to Shanghai Metals Market. That's still well above historical levels. The spread between China's physical spot price and benchmark futures has also dropped over the past week, but still remains at a substantial premium. Inventories monitored by the exchange edged higher.

Copper in London has pulled back rapidly after hitting a record near $15,000 a ton in September, with concerns over the sustainability of spending on AI data centers weighing on sentiment. Looming US interest-rate hikes added to the pressure. The red metal was 3.7% higher at $12,314.50 a ton on the LME as of 11:32 a.m. in Shanghai. Tin, zinc and aluminum also rallied on Friday.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Liau Y-Sing

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 26, 2026 at 9:43 PM EST 1 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Treasuries fell in light trading as the market reopened after the Thanksgiving holiday, with gains in Asian equities damping demand for haven assets.

Yields climbed at least three basis points across the curve, with the rate on benchmark 10-year notes up five basis points to 4.90%. A tentative recovery in risk appetite lured investors away from the safety of US government bonds, as regional shares extended a rebound following weeks of volatility in the artificial intelligence trade.

"Positive risk sentiment is the key driver for the tick up in bond yields with the late-session rebound in US technology names on Wednesday flowing through to Asian trade," said Prashant Newnaha, a strategist at TD Securities. "Trading volumes are light ahead of an early 2 p.m. New York close."

technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149946/.headline: Cutting-edge prosthetics allow researchers to probe the human mind
technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149946/.author: Jessica Hamzelou

paragraphs.text: Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.

He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.
Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy) and writing (also not easy).
What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.

He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.

“While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?

There may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.

Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?

Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.
I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.

As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.

Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."

Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.
"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."
How far can luxury sales take Macy's?
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.

"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.
Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.
"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.
"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."
One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.
But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.
"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/rheinmetall-stock-cm.headline: Defense giant Rheinmetall embraces ‘new normal’ of caution after military contract setback; stock rises
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/rheinmetall-stock-cm.author: Elsa Ohlen

paragraphs.text: Shares of Rheinmetall rose on Friday as investors assessed the defense giant's cautious forecasting approach at its Capital Markets Day.
It follows several recent setbacks for the German arms maker, most notably the cancellation of a major contract to build F126 warships for the country's military.

Rheinmetall now expects sales of between 33 and 37 billion euros (between $36.2 billion and $40.6 billion) by 2030, down from a previous forecast of about 45 billion euros. That guidance incorporates a "more prudent approach" for its vehicle systems business as well as its weapons and ammunition unit, now adjusted for new capacities and project delays.
Shares rose 3.4% in mid-morning trading amid a European defense sector firmly in the green.
"The opportunity has not changed; the way we plan for it has," Rheinmetall said in a company presentation.
"We are becoming more cautious whilst retaining our agility in a dynamic market," it said, highlighting a "new normal level of conservatism and recalibrated ambition" in the mid-term.
