nytimes.com/2026/11/27/magazine/ai-silic.headline: Why Some A.I. Evangelists Aren’t Bothered by the Potential for Human Extinction

paragraphs.text: On Nov. 19, Anthropic’s co-founder and chief executive, Dario Amodei, rang the Nasdaq bell to announce, to great fanfare, an initial public offering of tech millenarianism. Almost instantly, the company’s 5,000 employees became collectively richer than the poorest 100 million Americans combined. Six hundred of them were minted centimillionaires.

The offering wasn’t an unmitigated success, with share prices tumbling shortly after opening. Even so, it was a remarkable, trillion-dollar affirmation for a company founded just five years earlier, during the pandemic emergency, by a band of reluctant capitalists terrified by the prospect of out-of-control A.I. progress. As recently as last year, Amodei was estimating the chances that artificial intelligence would bring about human extinction at between 10 and 25 percent. Anthropic’s own I.P.O. filings acknowledged that its product might cause catastrophic or even existential harms and projected that the entire global insurance industry might not be big enough to cover that risk.

By now, warnings like these have become crazily familiar. Even Trump’s former tech czar, the A.I. pollyanna David Sacks, has called work on recursive self-improvement — in which A.I. essentially trains itself — the most dangerous thing anyone could be doing. At Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg’s blasé materialism has long prevailed, the wunderkind A.I. lead, Alexandr Wang, warned in late November that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control.” Paul Christiano, who joined the OpenAI board in September, told a large audience this month that A.I. accidents would be the most likely cause of death for most people in the room. And Buck Shlegeris, chief executive of the A.I. security company Redwood Research, said he thinks “there’s a very real possibility (maybe 20 percent) that within a year, A.I. misalignment issues prevent you from going about life normally, because you are dead or enslaved.”

Ever since ChatGPT first tugged Silicon Valley’s machine-god dreams into public view in 2022, the obvious question has gone unnervingly unanswered: Why would so many people who believe artificial intelligence could perhaps bring about human extinction nevertheless be racing so fast to build it?

The tsunami of A.I.-related wealth offers one cynical explanation. Those on the inside offer others: an urgent arms race, with other companies or with China; the possibility of superabundance; the need to bend technological history in a somewhat more humane direction.

But to the list I would add another one: that some number of A.I. accelerationists remain unbothered by the possibility of extinction or human obsolescence because they don’t believe it would be a bad outcome, necessarily. On some level, on some timeline, they consider it inevitable. Often, even, a source of enthralling awe.

For decades, the practical work of Silicon Valley was shaped spiritually by what became known as the “California ideology,” a mix of hippy counterculture, live-and-let-live libertarianism and market-friendly technological determinism.

Today the vibe is closer to religious fervor, with a proliferation of new creeds often tending toward the eschatological. One variety is called “successionism”: the belief that, in building artificial intelligence, humanity’s most gifted technologists are giving rise to an entirely new species, destined to rule by sheer force of superintelligence and sidelining measly human minds. Elon Musk has long called humanity merely a “biological bootloader” for what’s to follow; the writer and philosopher Ginevra Davis has imagined a near future in which it has become clear that the “cosmic purpose” of our species was merely to mine silicon. “Human extinction would be a profound tragedy,” the A.I. researcher Daniel Faggella wrote the week before the Anthropic I.P.O., reflecting on the possibility of rapid A.I. takeoff. “But something even greater is at stake.”

For normies, these may be the most cosmically unnerving features of A.I. — that the technology could bring about cognitive obsolescence and the end of the human era. (To trust the march of whistle-blowers, perhaps quite quickly.) But in Silicon Valley, the ideas are neither all that unusual nor all that new, having developed over many decades of slower and less visible A.I. progress. Then things accelerated, with spectacularly well-funded visionaries finally building something resembling their dreams and nightmares. And they became, as a result, the fabulously wealthy, immensely powerful architects of our collective future — a new class of tech overlords with a pretty distinctive way of seeing the world and their own place in the long arc of human history.

In 2023, the A.I. researcher Timnit Gebru and the philosopher Émile Torres — two spiky critics of big A.I. who are not exactly beloved in Silicon Valley — described this emergent worldview as the “TESCREAL bundle,” an acronym that folded seven distinct but related intellectual strands into a single package of apocalyptic techno-futurism. The resulting bundle isn’t a precise ideological map so much as a broadly illustrative mood board.

First is transhumanism, the belief that humans can and should find ways of evolving past their biological limitations. The second is extropianism, which involves extending human control over more and more of the physical universe. Singularitarianism proposes that exponential technological progress will soon reach takeoff and bring humanity into an unknowable future. Cosmism is a modern variant of 19th-century Russian alchemistic science aimed at achieving human immortality, invoked by Peter Thiel, among others. Rationalism is a rigorous debate-society approach to making quasi-mathematical judgments about the world. Effective altruism is an ethically demanding do-gooder approach to the survival and well-being of those elsewhere around the world — which evolved to emphasize the ethical and moral value of animal and plant life. Then there is the final piece of the bundle: longtermism, which suggests that stewardship of the future should be our central political and ethical goal in the blighted present.

Not everyone working in artificial intelligence believes that the world as we know it may be about to end or that recursive self-improvement is right around the corner, or that, even if it does come soon, it will necessarily prove quite so transformative. But the sense of imminent obsolescence hangs in the air like a Bay Area fog, seeping into the thinking of hardheaded materialists and even A.I. optimists, too. But for outsiders the utopian visions (thousand-year life spans, economic superabundance) can look pretty dystopian (loss of individual autonomy, the end of politics, perhaps an A.I. welfare state to support all the layabout humans).

The genomics researcher and writer Ruxandra Teslo has called this worldview “handoverism”: that short of extinction, humans will inevitably hand over control of everything to robots and machine intelligence, choosing a kind of petlike existence for ourselves and celebrating it all as transcendence.

The A.I. philosopher Dean Ball, who helped design the Trump administration’s A.I. policy in 2025, calls handoverism the “silent consensus” of the industry: that intelligence is all that matters; that a new and awe-inspiring form of it is now emerging, in what is best understood as a kind of evolutionary leap; that its future capabilities lie so far beyond our Stone Age brains we can’t predict the shape of what’s to come; and that the sheer power of A.I. promises to overwhelm anything humans might muster to resist or even direct it. Perhaps it will bring about the end of all human disease, as Amodei has predicted (a possibility that almost all biological researchers have dismissed). Perhaps it would bring about a crisis of human meaning, of the kind now sweeping the world of mathematics after A.I. produced several previously unimaginable breakthroughs in the span of a few months. “Regardless of the specifics,” Ball writes, the silent consensus means “the termination of human primacy in the world as we know it.”

Religious revivals need not be truly universal to illuminate their age. That is why we study the Black Death in part through the penitential response of medieval Christians, why the Reformation tells you something about Europe in the age of the printing press, why Mormonism and Methodism reveal some things about industrialization and the closing of the American frontier and why the prosperity gospel emerges tellingly in the United States of the late 20th century. And as much as A.I. millenarianism reflects features of the technology itself, it also reflects something about the world in which those tools have landed — namely the widespread feeling of social disempowerment already pervading our politics.

No country has invested more in artificial intelligence than the United States, which has spent five times as much as China, our nominal rival. No country is more anxious about the technology than we are. In China, A.I. anxieties have been kept in check by widespread faith that Beijing would intervene in any crisis to ensure social stability and the continuation of the regime. But no nation trusts its government to monitor A.I. less than the United States, where citizens are panicking about breakouts of A.I. agent swarms and widespread I.T. outages have reached crisis levels. We’ve recently watched the White House bully the world’s second-most-valuable company, Nvidia, to ignore blaring national-security alarms and reinstall its scandal-plagued chief executive, Jensen Huang, to rescue a crashing stock market.

The public has recoiled from all this and is fighting back. By wide margins, Americans believe that the technology will do more harm than good, with typically fewer than 10 percent telling pollsters they are very enthusiastic. Nearly three-quarters of the country opposes the construction of data centers — a coalition so much larger than other NIMBY alliances against more obviously noxious construction projects that the near-unanimity must reflect broader rage about the machine future. And in the midterm elections, Democrats used the threat of A.I. turbulence and the menace of tech oligarchs as the binding agent for a new crusade against plutocracy and corruption — contributing to a stomping victory.

But in certain ways these protests mirror the logic of their opposition. Like all good science fiction, the basic story of A.I. takeover echoes widespread contemporary anxieties: that we are already, in many waves, slaves to technology and becoming more so; that our political economy is already broken; that we have already handed over much of our lives to forces beyond our control; and that so much of the culture and institutions that might have once seemed to offer comfort and stability in the face of social turbulence now stands so obviously degraded, like ruins from another era.
The question is: Who rules the next one?
Source image for illustration above: Getty Images.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/black-friday-2026-in.headline: Inflation has shoppers hunting for value. That bodes well for Black Friday
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/black-friday-2026-in.author: Laya Neelakandan

paragraphs.text: Economic headwinds have made consumers more cautious — but new data and reports from retailers are painting a picture of robust holiday spending through Black Friday and beyond.

The macroeconomic environment has squeezed wallets. High inflation, fluctuating gas prices and labor uncertainty have dampened consumer sentiment and contributed to a pullback in spending. October's consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, coming in higher than expected, while the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to a seasonally adjusted 3.8% in October compared with last year. Meanwhile, October retail sales grew at their slowest pace in nearly a year, according to the CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor.

The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index slid to its lowest since 2014 in September, with respondents citing concerns about inflation and the job market. It's translated into caution from some retailers like Walmart and Lowe's, which have reported slower sales, smaller baskets and drops in big-ticket and discretionary purchases.
Despite that pullback, recent earnings reports and end-of-year forecasts suggest consumers are still willing to shell out for the holidays.

Planned spending on gifts and nongifts is estimated to be $1,049 on average this year, up 5.9% from $990 last year, according to The Conference Board. Adjusting for inflation, that figure is still up 3.2% year over year.

Holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion this year, but that growth is boosted by inflation. Though consumers have said they're willing to spend, experts have noted that shoppers are still emphasizing value and looking for deals where they can. Adobe data found that in the first 22 days of November — what it considers the beginning of the holiday season — consumers spent $82.5 billion online, marking a 9.1% year-over-year increase.

That's translating to the Black Friday and Cyber Monday week, too, as consumers take advantage of deals that started days before the traditional Friday blitz. Salesforce is predicting a record-breaking holiday week between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, as it expects online sales to reach $357 billion globally and $84 billion in the U.S., both marking 6% year-over-year increases.
The report also found that retailers are offering bigger markdowns than last year, with discount rates up 8% in the U.S. in November.

And according to Deloitte's Black Friday survey, participation in the shopping holiday this year is expected to be the highest seen since 2016, with 87% of shoppers reporting they plan to buy during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales.

That number is up from 82% in 2025. Consumers are expecting to spend an average of $624 this holiday, similar to last year's numbers, and Generation Z is going all in on those deals, according to Deloitte, which surveyed 1,200 consumers in mid-October. That echoes similar behavior from the cohort last year.

"It's sort of the mix of feeling the squeeze on prices, people thinking about their economic condition and their financial position, but still wanting to protect the holidays," Brian McCarthy, retail strategy lead at Deloitte, told CNBC in an interview.

He added that even as shoppers pulled back on spending over the past few months and delayed big purchases, that spend is now being more heavily concentrated into promotional windows like the holiday season. They're searching for more deals, becoming more savvy and deferring some spending.
The Deloitte data also found that 40% of Gen Z shoppers plan to use buy now, pay later for their shopping this holiday season.

"People do care about the holidays and want to make sure they can buy those gifts to share with their friends and family, but it's another way of deferring when they're going to have to pay for that item," McCarthy said.
Retailers see continued spending
On the other side of the cash register, retailers are expecting similar holiday shopping behavior and reported optimism about the consumer in earnings reports over the past two weeks.

Walmart CFO John David Rainey told CNBC last week that the company is continuing to see a resilient consumer. The retailer is leaning into value with rollbacks and deals, and Rainey said the holiday quarter was "off to a pretty good start" as macroeconomic trends start to show signs of potential improvement.

"The fact remains that payrolls are healthy, the equity markets are holding up in the face of geopolitical uncertainty, and even though consumer sentiment is somewhat lower, it hasn't translated into reduced economic output," Rainey said.

Target executives also said last week that the retailer is optimistic about holiday spending this season. The company is pricing thousands of products at $5 and under and investing in elevated products while prioritizing low prices, they said.

"We're encouraged by the start of the quarter that we've seen so far," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters following the company's third-quarter earnings report. "We're really excited for what guests are going to find at Target this holiday season."

Best Buy CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday that while the company is seeing consumers place higher emphasis on value, those shoppers are also looking to upgrade products, sometimes into "more premium price points."

Lowe's is also expecting a solid holiday season, with CEO Marvin Ellison telling CNBC last week that the company's November sales to date are in line with its expectations. The home improvement company is also emphasizing deals for customers who may be more price-conscious, but Ellison said he's still "optimistic."

Executives at TJX Companies, a retailer known for its value proposition, said on an earnings call with analysts last week that the company is expecting sales momentum to accelerate throughout the holiday season.
"In the current environment, we believe value will be top of mind for many consumers this holiday season," CEO Ernie Herrman said on the call.

Still, TJX said warmer weather in the beginning of the fourth quarter led to a sales slowdown. The company also reported weak fourth-quarter guidance, coming in below Wall Street expectations for earnings and same-store sales. Competitor Burlington Stores also posted weak sales and provided a lower-than-expected outlook.

Gap Inc. saw a similar trend. CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC that the company's sales lagged at the beginning of the quarter due to warmer weather. The retailer posted flat comparable sales for its fiscal third quarter last week and reported sinking sales at its Athleta and Banana Republic banners. It also lowered its guidance.
But Dickson said the retailer is optimistic about colder weather beginning to drive spending again.
"We're entering the peak holiday season and selling weeks with pent-up demand and hopefully maintained good weather for shopping," Dickson said. "This could be, and would be, a source of upside."

npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6054884/thanksg.headline: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6054884/thanksg.author: NPR Staff

paragraphs.text: A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.

More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.

Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.

Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.
"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.

On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.

New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.
Iconic Macy's parade postponed

Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.

Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.

There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.
Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.

"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.
"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.
This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.
Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.
Black Friday kicks off

Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.

The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.

The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.
The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.

aeon.co/essays/all-our-models-of-how-the.headline: All our models of how the mind functions are missing something
aeon.co/essays/all-our-models-of-how-the.author: David Colaço, Philipp Haueis

paragraphs.text: Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.
So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.
A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.
Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime

The past 25 years have seen great advances in our understanding of brain metabolism, providing us with a wealth of material for studying metabolic constraints on the mind. We now have detailed energy budgets: the brain devotes about 16 per cent of its energy to generating action potentials, 44 per cent to transmitting these signals chemically at the synapse, and 40 per cent to maintaining and repairing neuron cells. This means that only 60 per cent of brain energy is for signalling, while the rest is spent keeping the neural machinery from falling apart. According to a 2015 paper by the neuroscientists Elisabeth Engl and David Attwell, energy for maintenance and repair ‘must contribute to limiting the cognitive abilities of the brain because the total energy use of the brain constrains the temporal rate at which information can be encoded and processed.’ But budgets like this are too coarse on their own to serve as constraints, especially when modelling individual cognitive capacities. Numerical costs of information-processing, by contrast, are more specific. According to one study by the theoretical neuroscientist Jan Karbowski and colleagues, storing one bit of information in the synapse costs about 500,000 ATP (the ‘fuel’ of the cell).

Return to the example of memory. How can metabolism help us assess whether a model of memory is plausible? The dominant theoretical framework in neuroscience is that memory is stored in synapses: the junctions where signals pass from one neuron another. When a new memory is formed, the synapses change, affecting the signals that are transmitted. One such change is known as ‘Hebbian learning’, named for the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb, whose work is summed up in the slogan (not his) ‘neurons that fire together, wire together’.

Models are useful when they solve a theory’s problems, and the synaptic theory has two big ones. The first, often called interference, is that synapses that change easily are good at storing new memories but bad at keeping old ones. Almost any change in neural firing alters a synapse’s molecular makeup slightly. But then how do new memories keep from overwriting old ones? The second problem is called turnover. Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime. In order to stay alive, neurons must constantly rebuild their decaying parts. A neuron is like Otto Neurath’s ship, rebuilt plank by plank at sea. How does information survive in a system whose every part is being replaced?

In 2016, Stefano Fusi and Marcus Benna published a mathematical model to solve the interference problem. It asks us to imagine the synaptic memory process as a set of beakers – each standing for a chemical process at the synapse – filled with liquid and connected by tubes. The level in the first beaker is the synapse’s strength: adding liquid strengthens it, and removing liquid weakens it. ‘Over time,’ Benna explained in an interview, ‘the resulting flow of liquid will diffuse across the other beakers, corresponding to the long-term storage of memories.’ Because those deeper beakers fill and drain more slowly, they hold a trace of past changes and keep drawing the first beaker back towards its old level. New memories form quickly; old ones fade only slowly, as the levels even out.

However, metabolic constraints render this solution implausible. The beaker model describes a system in which biochemical processes in the synapse even out over time: liquid can flow one way or the other, but it ultimately reaches equilibrium. In biology, settling into equilibrium means death. As the physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it: ‘Living matter evades the decay to equilibrium.’ Neurons must take in and expel ions and molecules to stay alive. A neuron that reaches equilibrium loses its organisation and can no longer perform functions such as storing memories at the synapse. Treating metabolism as a constraint shows us that a linear beaker model does not solve the problem of forming new synaptic memories and keeping old ones. This consequence is easy to miss if modellers do not consider the relevance of metabolism.

Metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Unlike the beaker model, this framework describes the resting state of the synapse as not being in equilibrium with its environment, and thus capable of storing memories.
Holding on to old memories costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep them while laying down new ones

The model links biochemical processes at the synapse in cycles rather than in linear sequences (as in the beaker model). ATP powers transitions between states in the cycle, so metabolism is built into the model directly. These transitions represent how the synapse strengthens or weakens to store or erase memories. Because the state changes in the cycle have different rates, they never reach equilibrium. The synapse can form new memories and keep them over time without dying.

Karbowski then combines the cyclic model with the numerical costs of information-processing (such as the ATP cost per bit of memory storage). His calculations show that encoding new memories is energetically cheap, and so is, under certain conditions, storing them for a long time. That may explain why interference doesn’t erase long-lasting memories: holding on to them costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep old memories while laying down new ones. The same picture suggests an answer to the turnover problem: if a memory is held in a state that the synapse actively maintains, rather than in any particular molecules, it can outlast the molecules themselves, much as Neurath’s ship stays afloat precisely because it is constantly being rebuilt.

A second example of how metabolism can inform models comes from research on mental effort. When you start work in the morning, you feel fresh. But as the day grinds on and you’re writing your 700th email and attending your fifth meeting, tasks that were easy become gruelling. This is the cost of mental effort. How can mental effort be modelled? One possibility is the ego depletion model, developed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

But the model has been challenged on empirical grounds, such as difficulties with replicating its findings. As a result, researchers such as Robert Kurzban and colleagues have turned towards computational models of mental effort, in which the brain calculates the benefits and costs of staying on task versus switching to another activity. Proponents conclude that computational models are superior, and that metabolism is not relevant to model mental effort.

Yet the opposition between resource models such as ego depletion and computational models of mental effort is false. Ego depletion was undone partly by metabolic evidence: the brain’s glucose use barely changes during demanding tasks, far too little for an afternoon of self-control to run it down. That is metabolism doing just what we have described, ruling out a model the brain could not run. And computational models face metabolic questions of their own, because weighing the costs and benefits of staying on task is itself work that must be paid for. Neuroscientists such as Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Clay Holroyd believe this computational process takes place in a brain area known as the anterior cingulate cortex. We can use evidence about available energy to assess whether models of this process are feasible.

Some researchers already integrate metabolism into their models of mental effort. Alexandre Zénon and colleagues, for instance, posit that effortful tasks require the brain to process more information and therefore use slightly more energy. Since its energy budget has a hard upper limit, the brain needs to spend less energy on other tasks. Zénon and his team explicitly link metabolism to our subjective feeling of effort, which might reflect how fast metabolic changes build up during demanding tasks. Fatigue, in turn, might reflect our expectation that these changes will continue.

Likewise, Holroyd’s ‘controllosphere’ model starts from the theory of how the brain controls behaviour and draws on empirical findings that sustained mental effort produces waste in neurons. On this model, the feeling of effort is a signal to the brain to stop tasks that require high control, so that waste can be cleared before causing damage. Research on mental effort shows that including metabolism into models of the mind is not a mere theoretical possibility. It is already a practical reality.

Attention to metabolism and energy use can improve more than just our knowledge of biological organisms. It can also help our understanding of artificial neural networks at the heart of dramatic advances in artificial intelligence. While the speed of development is new, the link between AI and the brain is old, going back to the first neural network model in 1943, from pioneers such as Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, or ‘the perceptron’ of Frank Rosenblatt in 1958. Recent advances like LLMs (large language models) reignited existential questions about whether AI is really intelligent, or even conscious. Metabolism and energy use should inform how we approach these questions.

The relationship between AI and energy use is largely uncharted territory, and a metabolically informed perspective suggests where to start looking. Hyperscale data centres use a lot of energy, far beyond the 20 watts the human brain runs on. Yet in philosophy and cognitive science, views like medium independence lead scholars to think of AI in abstract, formal terms: while the physical basis of an AI system may vary, the computation, so the thought goes, is the same. This focus on abstract computation leads philosophers such as Luke Kersten and Leonard Dung to argue that AI systems could, in principle, duplicate human minds. But, in brains, energy constraints help determine which computations are performed in the first place. If the same holds for artificial systems, then whether a chip and a brain are running ‘the same’ computation cannot simply be assumed. It has to be found out.
Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows

Our research belongs to a growing discussion of energy use and its role in modelling both brains and AI systems. For example, Cao and the neuroscientist Daniel Yamins have studied how AI models implement a highly abstract version of the mechanism that brains use to respond to novel visual stimuli. Cao and Yamins recognise that brains and engineered AI face different energy constraints, yet they consider energetics only abstractly, in terms of efficiency and optimisation. We propose instead to rethink energy use in AI from the bottom up. How an AI system uses energy is a modelling problem, which depends on scale, training data and details of grid infrastructure, just as the brain’s energy use depends on the details of its metabolism. This crucial parallel between studying brains and AI systems is missed when we focus on task optimisation alone. Modelling AI energy use informs how and when energetic differences lead to computational, perhaps even cognitive, differences.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows. AI energy use is a practical problem that the study of metabolism can help tackle. Cognitive scientists such as Megan Peters are already looking to the brain to improve energy efficiency in AI. These projects highlight the practical benefits that come from studying brain metabolism for engineering projects like AI model building. They also have theoretical benefits: projects that include energy use serve as tests of philosophical positions like medium independence.

When it comes to figuring out how to model minds, it is time that researchers take a ‘metabolic turn’, to quote our colleague Patrick McGivern. Taking seriously how systems use energy and regulate themselves gives us new ways of addressing the toughest questions that we face in making sense of the mind.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/pow.headline: Power outages, heavy rain continue on East Coast after Thanksgiving Day storm
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/pow.author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: More than 700,000 people remained without power mainly across the East Coast early Friday after the worst Thanksgiving Day storm in decades battered the region, flooding coastal communities and disrupting travel.

The storm “continues to bring widespread inclement weather this morning for a large portion of the eastern U.S.,” the National Weather Service said, adding that there was wet snow “as far south as the Tennessee Valley,” and “freezing rain” across northern New England, on Friday morning.
Power outages were recorded in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, Missouri and New York.

The storm has affected tens of millions of people across the East Coast from North Carolina to New York, with ocean tides hitting record levels in some places, bridges closed, trees uprooted and infrastructure damaged by wind and waves.
Shorelines in Washington, D.C., and Baltimore remained under a coastal flood warning early Friday linked to high tides, with water levels expected to be up to three feet above normal in some places.

New York City also remained under a coastal flood warning early Friday, after being battered by high winds and rain. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said two people had to be rescued from their cars in the extreme weather. The storm forced the postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday, the first time in the event’s 100-year history it was postponed due to weather.

On Friday, conditions are expected to improve across the East Coast as the storm begins to weaken, though the vast size of the system means it will take some time to dissipate, the National Weather Service said.
The storm brought up to 15 inches of snow in eastern Missouri, according to the NWS.

Huge waves and storm surges flooded streets in North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey and New York, officials reported. Several communities reported record high water levels, including a six-foot rise in Wachapreague, Virginia, which broke a 1998 record by more than 2.1 feet.
The NWS has reminded people to never drive through flooded roadways, and warned of significant coastal flooding and beach erosion along the Mid-Atlantic and New England coasts.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.headline: 2 teens fell down a SoCal mountain; 14-year-old did not survive
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.author: Fedor Zarkhin

paragraphs.text: A 14-year-old hiker died this week after falling on Pine Mountain in the San Gabriel Mountains near Wrightwood, authorities said.
It was the second death of a hiker in the mountain range in less than a week. Just days earlier, a 44-year-old father slipped on ice as he was trying to stop his son from falling.

In the most recent incident, Nathan Sakaue of Phelan was on a hike with two friends, ages 16 and 17, on Tuesday morning in icy conditions when the youngest and oldest teens both slipped and fell, the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department said in a statement Wednesday.

The third friend didn’t fall, and he called 911 and told dispatchers what he saw happen. He could see Sakaue, and he wasn’t moving, the teen told authorities. The teen said the other friend was injured but was conscious and coheren, the Sheriff’s Department said.

The terrain was so treacherous that sheriff’s deputies couldn’t reach the injured boys on foot. The sheriff sent a helicopter to the scene, and the pilot and medic found the hiker who’d reported the fall and, soon after, the two fallen hikers.

The helicopter team lowered a medic down to Sakaue, who confirmed that the boy was dead, the Sheriff’s Department said. The team used a cable hoist to lift the injured hiker off the mountain and take him to a hospital, as well as to get the uninjured teen off the slopes and reunited with his family.

Officials recovered Sakaue’s body and carried it off the mountain by air around 5 p.m., sheriff’s officials said. Authorities took his body to the county coroner’s division, which will complete a death investigation.
Pine Mountain is a 9,648-foot peak on the north side of the San Gabriel Mountain range.

A fundraising campaign to pay for Sakaue’s funeral expenses has already raised more than $45,000. Opened by a person purporting to be a family friend, the fundraiser says that Sakaue was a Serrano High School student, played trumpet in the school’s marching band and loved basketball.
“He will be deeply missed by his family, friends, and classmates,” Chris Lindish wrote on the GoFundMe page.
Neither Lindish nor Sakaue’s parents could be reached.

Sakaue’s death came just three days after Guillermo Batres fell and died while on a trip with his wife and 14-year-old son to Mt. Baden-Powell, a 9,400-foot peak in the Angeles National Forest that is about 60 miles northeast of Los Angeles and about eight miles from Pine Mountain.

At one point on their hike Sunday, Batres’ son, Sebastían, slipped on ice but steadied himself by grabbing a tree, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said. The teen’s father tried to get over to help him but slipped on some ice and fell about 500 feet into a gulch.
A fundraiser to help Batres’ family with funeral expenses also has raised a significant sum, approaching $40,000 donated as of Thursday evening.

technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149857/.headline: Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open
technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149857/.author: Amy Nordrum

paragraphs.text: Every year, the editors at MIT Technology Review select 35 of the world’s top young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors to honor as our newest class of Innovators Under 35. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.

We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to some of the most formidable problems society faces, including human disease and climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.

We want to hear about people, based anywhere in the world, who are responsible for a major finding or advance and can show real-world impact from their work. To qualify for the list, a nominee must be under the age of 35 as of October 1, 2027 (that is, born on or after October 2, 1992).

Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to nominate yourself? Follow this link to suggest someone who you think should make our 2027 list. It’s free and takes only a few minutes. Just be sure to get your nomination in before the deadline—which is 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, January 19.

After the deadline, our editors will review all nominees and select a group of semifinalists, whom we’ll invite to complete a formal application. Then, dozens of expert judges will help us evaluate those applicants and settle on the finalists. You can read more about our selection process here.

Our newsroom began producing our Innovators Under 35 list in 1999. It’s an annual exercise that helps our reporters scout out the brightest young minds in the fields they cover. It also introduces our audience to dozens of rising stars worth watching in the years to come. Subscribers can explore the 2026 list and peruse the full archives.
We look forward to reviewing your nominations.

slowboring.com/p/we-need-to-understand-h.headline: We need to understand “health care costs” better
slowboring.com/p/we-need-to-understand-h.author: Matthew Yglesias

paragraphs.text: To just toss a hot take into the permitting reform discourse, one thing that I think we see in these debates is that there is way too much non-park federally owned land in the American West, and that creates some very confusing exchanges about activities happening on “public lands.” It’s good to have parks. And obviously there’s lots of otherwise useful infrastructure that you wouldn’t want to put in a park. But if you look at the federal land portfolio, it’s 12.5 percent run by the National Park Service and then 14 percent run by the Fish and Wildlife Service. A majority of the land, though, is run by either the U.S. Forest Service or else the Bureau of Land Management, and that land is designed for economic exploitation — logging, mining, ranching, and so forth — in a way that just somewhat arbitrarily excludes uses like housing development.

I think we should have more real parks and more real wildlife preservation and then more privately owned land that’s put to its highest and best use by market forces. A lot of what passes for “public land” preservation is in practice a kind of subsidy-masquerading-as-conservation to favored industries involved in natural resource extraction.

Peter: I’m just retired from the tech industry, and need something to do after I finish Slow Boring in the morning. You’ve mentioned in the past that you thought there was not enough analytical work on policy related questions. There have also been examples of someone with a computer providing valuable data to the world, for example during Covid. So, what’s your list of topics that you wish someone would get to the bottom of?
To pick just one example, because it’s a big topic and it’s been on my mind recently, the whole policy community has a very poor grasp of what exactly is going on with health care costs.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/how.headline: How 193K acorns gathered this fall could help restore Helene-damaged forests
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/how.author: Brady Dennis

paragraphs.text: Most visitors to the sprawling Biltmore Estate outside Asheville, North Carolina, come to marvel at the 250-room mansion, built in the late 19th century by George Washington Vanderbilt II, or to check out its famous conservatory and winery.
But another group of visitors recently turned up looking for something else entirely: acorns.

At the end of October, U.S. Forest Service employees, working with groups such as the Appalachian Trail Conservancy and EcoForesters, scoured the grounds and collected a startling 27,744 white oak acorns.
The goal? To hasten the process of restoring forests devastated by Hurricane Helene in the fall of 2024.

“There are always fingerprints of Helene on everything we are doing right now,” said Matt Drury, associate director of science and stewardship for the Appalachian Trail Conservancy who is based in Asheville.

The acorn-gathering extravaganza at Biltmore was part of a broader collection across national forests, local parks and businesses in the region that netted 193,664 acorns, according to the Forest Service.

The agency said the acorns, which were gathered largely using rolling mechanical harvesters with tines that pluck them from the ground, will be sown this fall at state nurseries in Tennessee and Georgia. There, they will be tended to during the 2027 growing season.

In February 2028, workers plan to distribute the young trees to some areas hit hard by Helene, in hopes of helping restore the diversity and resilience of the forests, said Jason Rodrigue, a regional silviculturist for the U.S. Forest Service Southern Region.
“This planting allows us to guide or assist the natural recovery,” he said.
Helene battered forests throughout the region when it blew through in late September 2024.

The storm caused catastrophic damage across roughly a fifth of the region’s federally protected forests, according to the North Carolina Forest Service. Satellite data analyzed by the U.S. Forest Service’s Southern Research Station showed damage that stretched more than 200 miles through the southern Appalachians.

According to one North Carolina Forest Service report, more than 800,000 acres of woodlands were damaged by Helene, posing long-term consequences that include threats to wildlife habitat, elevated wildfire risk and the potential for more invasive species.

Forestry officials said the restoration work spans numerous tree species, including red oak, white oak, chestnut oak, hickory, spruce and butternut. But Rodrigue said mature oaks, which make up a significant proportion of the landscape in places such as the Pisgah and Nantahala national forests, were hit particularly hard by Helene’s fierce winds.

“Even though we don’t have the ability to restore oak across the entire landscape that got damaged, we can do our best to put it back” wherever possible, he said, adding that officials have used ecological models to identify areas where the trees once stood in large numbers.
Rodrigue said it also is beneficial to be able to collect acorns from trees that are already genetically adapted to local climate conditions.
“They have the best odds of growing in whatever climate is going to be here over the next century or so,” he said.
The recent acorn gathering is a small but vital part of the broader undertaking that began soon after Helene to rebuild the health and resilience of the area’s public forests.

State and federal workers along with nonprofits and other volunteers have helped restore access to trails and recreation sites. Crews have cleared fallen trees and other debris in an effort to reduce potential fuel for forest fires.

With access restored to nearly all recreation sites and trails, the Forest Service has shifted its efforts toward strengthening forest health, restoring damaged watersheds and preparing the landscape for future storms.

James Melonas, forest supervisor with the National Forests in North Carolina, said in a statement earlier this fall that those efforts require partnerships among state agencies, conservation organizations and universities. The work includes restoring critical watersheds, repairing wildlife habitat, rebuilding infrastructure, conducting prescribed burns and mitigating non-native species.
So far, Melonas said, more than 170,200 seedlings have been planted in areas damaged by Helene to help reestablish vegetation and bolster the long-term health of the forest.

Drury said his group and others collect acorns from numerous sites around the region every year. Most oaks, however, follow boom-and-bust cycles, only producing large numbers of acorns in what are known as mast years. This year, white oaks have been the most prolific.
The well-kept, gently rolling expanse of the Biltmore Estate, Drury said, is an ideal place to use the Bag-A-Nut mechanical harvesters that make acorn gathering much more efficient.
He said seedlings grown from this collection probably will be planted across the region, including in Buncombe, Yancey, Mitchell and Avery counties.
In addition, Drury said, there was a poetic aspect to this fall’s acorn collection at such a famous site. “Biltmore is the cradle of forestry in North America,” he said.

Frederick Law Olmsted, the renowned landscape architect whose work includes Central Park and the U.S. Capitol Grounds, was the mastermind behind the design of Biltmore’s gardens, grounds and vast forests.

By 1891, according to the Forest Service, Olmsted had planted 300 acres with white pine. In 1892, he hired trained forester Gifford Pinchot, who worked on the Biltmore Estate for several years before becoming the first Forest Service chief.

In 1914, George Vanderbilt’s widow, Edith, sold approximately 86,700 acres of the estate’s forested mountains to the federal government. That acquisition led to the creation of the Pisgah National Forest and the Cradle of Forestry, a 6,500-acre site that was home to the nation’s first forestry school.
Now, that cradle is helping provide acorns for the next generation of trees in these mountains.

“The overall effort is going to take many years, probably a decade or more,” Rodrigue said of the regional restoration plan. “We have to start ourselves on the right footing, and that’s what we are trying to do now.”
Simon Ducroquet, Niko Kommenda and John Muyskens contributed to this report.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/tech-download-jensen.headline: The Tech Download: Will Jensen Huang’s return be the spark the shaky AI market needs?
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/tech-download-jensen.author: Kai Nicol-Schwarz

paragraphs.text: This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.
The recent Nvidia saga has had more twists and turns than an Agatha Christie novel.

It all started with Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's admission that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Days later, amid an independent board investigation and broader scrutiny over national-security concerns, he resigned. Less than two weeks later, Huang was back at the helm.
During all of that, Nvidia stock lost over $1 trillion and then regained just under $1 trillion.
The leadership drama has played out at a time when the artificial intelligence market is looking shakier than it has in some time.
Neoclouds have seen stocks plummet in recent months as investors question the sustainability of the AI boom. Chip stocks like Arm and AMD have both fallen in the past month.
Huang's surprise return saw Nvidia stock surge 31%, with other AI stocks also gaining. But the sheen was off by Tuesday's close, with Nvidia and a host of chip stocks falling.

The sharp reversal raises questions for investors: did Huang's return restore confidence in Nvidia, or did it spark a short-lived relief rally as the market faces broader questions about returns on AI investment?
Judging by the first few days of his return, it's a hard one to call.
Volatility
Volatility in the tech sector looked set to continue on Friday, as tech stocks rebounded again.
"Wall Street pared its Monday advance as sobriety returned to the market and a focus returned to fundamentals," wrote Kyle Rodda, analyst at Capital.com, in a note at market close on Tuesday.

"While Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO is indubitably a boon for the markets and the overall AI trade, it does not assuage every risk and concern about an industry confronting a potential peak in its investment boom and moderating earnings growth."
The early week rally was "largely driven" by Huang's return, said Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares.

"Fresh tariff threats from the Trump administration have added to market uncertainty," she added. "The short-term rally has reversed course, and Nvidia's share price is likely to trade sideways between $125 and $170 in the near term."
Nvidia stock closed at $149.30 on Wednesday, giving it a $3.6 trillion market cap — a figure around $2 trillion lighter than it was at its peak in October.

"We expect a selective recovery across the AI ecosystem, and NVDA to trade sideways and stay volatile below its October peak at least until the Dec 1–3 Congressional appearances," Egor Tolmachev, senior analyst at Freedom Capital Markets, said in a note on Wednesday.

Other key AI stocks have also been volatile. Anthropic's first week as a public company has been mixed. AMD has fallen 25% in the past five days, and memory chip maker Micron has dropped 18%. Both spiked on Monday before paring gains.
The Huang evangelists might've been hoping for a speedier return to AI boom times.

But while the Nvidia CEO's return has removed one source of uncertainty around the chip giant, the volatility among AI stocks suggests investors are still trading on questions much bigger than who occupies the chief executive's office.
News edit
Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push.
U.S. adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist over export control concerns amid Nvidia controversy.
Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, a Chinese EV firm says.
SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts.
Jensen Huang tells staff that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan, according to people inside the room.
One more thing
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia, and is now tasked with selling the company's AI vision while also defending himself in Washington, my colleague Kif Leswing wrote on Tuesday.

npr.org/2026/11/27/g-s1-156004/up-first-.headline: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
npr.org/2026/11/27/g-s1-156004/up-first-.author: Suzanne Nuyen

paragraphs.text: Today's top stories

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.

• 🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.

Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.

• 🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.

The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.
Behind the story
This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent

I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."

After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.
New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.

Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.
Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.
I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).
Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.
Once again, my shopping cart is empty.

My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.

He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
