npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6055559/gerard-.headline: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6055559/gerard-.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-.headline: Iran War Updates: Trump says he's giving Iran "a chance to be smart"
cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-.author: Frank Andrews, Ahmed Shawkat

paragraphs.text: Ahmed Shawkat is a CBS News producer based in Cairo. He has worked for CBS News since 2016, prior to which he worked with several European networks including TVE, ZDF, SVT and Yle.
November 27, 2026 / 6:37 AM EST / CBS News
What to know about the Iran war today:

• President Trump said Thursday that victory in the war with Iran would be achieved "whenever I want it," and that he is giving the Islamic Republic regime "a chance to be smart," though he said he doubts they will take it.

• Mr. Trump also downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran after multiple reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target U.S. military assets in the Middle East.

• Iran denied on Thursday being behind a drone attack on a Kuwaiti military facility that killed two Italian nationals. The head of the European Commission called for more international pressure on Iran over the incident.
Iranian navy commander claims commandos took back 2 oil tankers seized by U.S. forces

Iranian Navy Commander Rear Adm. Shahram Irani made the bold claim on Friday that Iranian commandos boarded and reclaimed two oil tankers that had been seized by the U.S. while American forces on board the vessels slept, according to state media.
Irani did not offer any evidence to back up his assertion, which came in remarks carried by the Fars News Agency, which is linked with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The U.S. military's Central Command did not immediately respond to a CBS News request for comment on the Iranian navy commander's claim, but CENTCOM has rejected many previous claims by the IRGC of attacks on U.S. forces as false.
The U.S. military has not announced the seizure of any Iranian or Iran-linked commercial vessel in the region since April, when forces boarded and seized the Touska cargo ship.
Trump says victory in the war will be "whenever I want it to be," trying to give Iran "a chance to be smart"

President Trump told reporters Thursday that the U.S. would achieve victory and the war with Iran will be over, "whenever I want it to be," but that he is giving the Islamic Republic "a chance to be smart."

"We have victory at hand and it's going to be … whenever I want it to be," the president said as he took questions at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida after speaking on the phone with U.S. troops for Thanksgiving.
"We're giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I'm not sure if they are going to take advantage of that," he said of the Iranian regime.
On Sunday, Mr. Trump called Iran's negotiators "professional tap dancers" and reiterated previous remarks suggesting he would give them until the new year to agree to a peace deal.
Trump says China, Russia not providing significant support to Iran
President Trump on Thursday downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran amid reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target U.S. military bases.

Mr. Trump, during a short press conference with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, noted that the Iran conflict had been discussed during his recent trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they're very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information," Mr. Trump said.
He added: "We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too."
Regarding Russia's intelligence sharing, Mr. Trump said, "I don't think they give very much."
He said both countries want to see the conflict with Iran end.
"I think they're helping me in that regard," Mr. Trump said.
Days after the Iran war broke out, multiple sources, including a senior U.S. official, told CBS News that Russia was providing intelligence to Iran regarding U.S. positions in the Middle East.
Iran denies being behind deadly Kuwait attack that killed 2 Italians
The Iranian Embassy in Italy said the Islamic Republic wasn't behind Thursday's attack in Kuwait that killed two Italians.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Rome categorically rejects the allegation that Iran was behind today's purported drone attack on a military facility in Kuwait," the embassy said on social media.
Iran's ambassador to Italy, Ali Akbar Rezaei, expressed condolences in a separate post.
"My thoughts and prayers are with the families and loved ones of the victims during this difficult time," he said.
Trump downplays Iran's latest attacks as it vows to use all means to end U.S. blockade

finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/nv.headline: Nvidia Blackwell Chips Turn Up at China Site Tied to Alice Huang
finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/nv.author: Andy Lin, Mackenzie Hawkins and Kari Lindberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A pair of Chinese firms installed Nvidia Corp.'s powerful Blackwell semiconductors in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman at the heart of a controversy surrounding the US chipmaker.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The gear installed at the Yangtze River Delta Project included a GB300 NVL72 rack, among Nvidia's most powerful products, according to a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November. Shanghai Shuoyao offered the hardware as collateral to obtain a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, according to filings from the lender that were reviewed by Bloomberg News.

A second firm Shanghai Kezhan, controlled by a Tokyo-based parent, described a GB200 server — which also relies on Blackwell chips — at the facility. That description was provided in documents when it obtained a 90 million yuan loan in late 2025 from a finance-leasing firm wholly owned by a local Shanghai government agency.

The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license.

President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge.

Nvidia and its just-reinstated CEO have come under intense scrutiny in recent weeks for their failure to stop diversion of the company's products to China, a shadow trade that US officials believe is worth billions of dollars.

It's unclear how the GB300 rack made its way to the country, to Shanghai Shuoyao or to this specific site — described in local media as designed to house as many as 800,000 servers. By inputting the serial number for the product into a public warranty database, Bloomberg found that it was manufactured by Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology Co., which assembles Nvidia chips into servers and racks. The database also provided a model name for the serial number, which matches a GB300 NVL72 server rack manufactured by the Taiwanese company.

This sort of gear often passes through several hands — including local distribution networks — before it's installed in data centers. In many cases, products that were ultimately smuggled into China were originally sold to parties in unrestricted areas.

Bloomberg provided the rack's serial number to Gigabyte, seeking information about to whom Gigabyte had originally sold the hardware and when. It declined to answer those questions, citing company policy. The firm "conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," a spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "All transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time."

Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation."

Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country. Bloomberg does not have evidence that Megaspeed itself diverted Nvidia hardware there, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing in response to the US probe. The company has not answered repeated queries about the Yangtze River Delta Project. Nor has Nvidia, which for years insisted that there was no black market for its products and didn't respond to questions for this story.
The Trump administration this month put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, citing a significant risk of involvement in chip diversion.

Alice Huang in 2023 founded Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation, and went on to become the chipmaker's largest Southeast Asian customer. She also has ties to a number of companies that invested in the Yangtze River Delta Project, which counts Kang Wei as its president. Kang has been introduced at times as Alice Huang's romantic partner, people familiar with the matter said.

It's unclear how far along operators are in meeting their overall goal for that project, which at 800,000 servers would be on par with hyperscale facilities used by companies like OpenAI. It's also unclear what mix of servers they plan to use. The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.

Still, the smuggled hardware disclosed in the filings reviewed by Bloomberg is just a fraction of what they'd need. These documents only cover hardware offered as collateral for loans — providing a small snapshot of the operators' ambitions, while also underscoring how some Chinese financial institutions, including with government ties, were aware that restricted hardware was getting into China and willing to lend capital on those assets.

Bloomberg was unable to reach the leasing company that lent money to Shanghai Kezhan, nor Shanghai Innovation Bank, which in addition to the money it lent Shanghai Shuoyao, also provided a 200 million yuan loan to another company called Shanghai Longjie, similarly with restricted Nvidia chips as collateral.

Shanghai Longjie — which has the same parent company as Shanghai Shuoyao — disclosed in documents filed to regulators that it has servers containing Nvidia's earlier Hopper-generation chips, which are illegal to ship to China without Washington's permission, Bloomberg reported this month. That hardware was manufactured by Super Micro Computer Inc. and Dell Technologies Inc. It's unclear whether the shipments had US approval.

Those aren't the only Hopper chips at the Yangtze River Delta Project. Shanghai Kezhan, the company that described the GB200 server in filings last year, also disclosed that it has 32 servers with H200 chips there. These products had a Gigabyte prefix in their model name, but the documents didn't include serial numbers — making them harder to trace.

Shanghai Kezhan is headquartered about half a kilometer from the Yangtze River Delta Project, at the same commercial complex where Shanghai Shuoyao solicited engineers to work on Nvidia H100 and H200 chips — two restricted models. In February 2024, both of these firms added "imports and exports" to their business activities, according to data from Qizhidao, a company information provider.

The same month, Megaspeed's original parent — the Chinese gaming giant 7Road — obtained 16.7% of Shanghai Kezhan via a subsidiary the gaming company bought from Alice Huang in 2019. The other 83.3% of Kezhan is ultimately owned by NeXPower Japan, according to Qizhidao. Japan's official companies registry returned only one company named NeXPower, which was established in March 2025. Caixin, a Chinese business news outlet, said the Tokyo firm is controlled by Alice Huang.

Bloomberg has been unable to reach NeXPower for comment. Chinese-speaking staffers at the firm's registered address wouldn't confirm that was NeXPower's office, and shut the door after Bloomberg News asked about their relationship with Alice Huang and Shanghai Kezhan. On the intercom was a message saying they are working and will not respond to media questions. The registered address of the company's director appeared to be a vacated residence.

In May 2025, records compiled by Big Trade Data show, Shanghai Kezhan received a shipment worth $11 million, flown from Malaysia to Shanghai Pudong International Airport with the company as consignee.

The customs document described the shipment as "storage chassis," referring to a structure that houses components of a storage server. But the product code it was assigned to was 847150, which denotes computing servers. The shipment's unit price was $264,108, too costly for a storage chassis — but within the price range of servers powered by Nvidia's Hopper chips.
--With assistance from Mari Kiyohara, Natsuko Katsuki and Mayumi Negishi.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/heathr.headline: Heathrow and Rosebank Disputes Threaten Burnham’s Labour Unity
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/heathr.author: Lucy White

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 27, 2026 at 6:49 AM EST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Controversial decisions over a North Sea oil field and one of the world's biggest airports are threatening to shake the unity that Prime Minister Andy Burnham has brought to Britain's ruling Labour Party.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Almost 100 Labour Members of Parliament have written to the government to express concerns about the possibility that it will approve development of the Rosebank oil field — just weeks after it angered some left-wing colleagues by giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field. The letter includes four signatories from Labour's front benches, the Guardian newspaper reported.

A critical report from Parliament's Transport Select Committee on Thursday also lambasted the government for failing to "make the case" for a third runway at London's Heathrow Airport. The much-delayed project is set to deepen divides between Labour MPs who think it would help boost growth, and those who are concerned about the impact on carbon emissions and noise levels.

The contentious issues present a dilemma for Burnham, who has been credited with smoothing over rifts in the party following his appointment as premier in July. One MP said that Burnham has kept in contact with MPs and focused on more left-wing issues such as the cost of living, bringing a sense of calm to a party that had become increasingly disgruntled and fractious under his predecessor Keir Starmer — however, they warned that such tactics wouldn't necessarily be enough to maintain unity on divisive issues such as Rosebank.

In an article written for the Guardian, Labour MP Catherine Fookes — who organized the protest letter — said that "if Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil giants." She added that it would "not make an iota of difference to our constituents' energy bills" and would "accelerate the climate crisis."

Meanwhile the Transport Committee — chaired by Labour's Ruth Cadbury — said in a 96-page report on Thursday that plans for the £33 billion ($43 billion) Heathrow expansion were not compatible with climate goals and would bring only a "modest" level of economic growth.

The committee urged the government to improve its case for the runway, strengthening the air quality and noise tests, and said more detail should be provided over the cost of the expansion and plans to increase public transport to the airport.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Altria’s Interest in Imperial May Affect Its AB InBev Stake
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Eric Pfanner and Jennifer Creery

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A possible three-way deal to reshape the global tobacco industry may also spill over into another business whose products are sometimes consumed alongside cigarettes — beer.
Most Read from Bloomberg

That's because Altria Group Inc., the US tobacco company that says it's weighing a bid for Britain's Imperial Brands Plc, holds a roughly 8% stake in Anheuser-Busch InBev. The shareholding dates back to when Marlboro-maker Altria was called Philip Morris and owned Miller Brewing Co., one of the companies that evolved into the world's largest brewer after a series of deals.
To finance a deal for Imperial, likely in partnership with Japan Tobacco Inc., Altria may sell some or all of its stake in AB InBev that's worth $12.8 billion, Jefferies analysts said.

"Altria has suggested before in the past that it's something that's worthy to generate cash at any given need and that it would be open to trimming or selling altogether," Jefferies analyst Andrei Andon-Ionita said by phone.

The knock-on effect could then see AB InBev buying back a portion of this holding, analysts at Jefferies said in a note, just as it did when Altria reduced its stake from 10% about two years ago. Doing so could modestly boost AB InBev's earnings per share but also raise its debt ratios, they wrote.
The brewer had no immediate comment when contacted by Bloomberg.

AB InBev could buy back as much as $10 billion of this stake while keeping net debt at 2.9 times earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, the analysts wrote, based on the current expected leverage of 2.5 times in its fiscal year starting in January. "However we would anticipate a more modest participation in the event of a selldown," they said.

AB InBev shares traded lower on Thursday after Bloomberg reported the interest in Imperial and Altria said it was weighing a cash offer for the tobacco company. They were down as much as 1.2% in Brussels on Friday.

For Altria, selling a portion of its stake could affect its representation on AB InBev's board, which was reduced from two seats to one after the 2024 reduction in its shareholding, the analysts said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/the-sp-500-is-in-a-c.headline: The S&P 500 is in a correction. Bear markets and recessions don't always follow
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/the-sp-500-is-in-a-c.author: Deena Zaidi

paragraphs.text: The S&P 500 fell into a correction on Nov. 20 for the first time since April 2025 as stocks pulled back sharply from October's record highs.

The market correction, defined as a 10% decline from a recent high, came as investor concern mounted over a potential slowdown in AI spending, mega-cap tech valuations and the path of Federal Reserve interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Nov. 20 alone, closing at 6,910.39, its seventh consecutive daily decline. That left the index 11.6% below the Oct. 6 closing high of 7,818.93.

A correction can deepen into a bear market, defined as a drop of 20% or more from the most recent top. But history shows that even a bear market, let alone a correction, doesn't automatically mean the economy is destined for a recession.

In a CNBC analysis, eight of the 13 S&P 500 bear markets overlapped with recessions, as defined by the National Bureau of Economic Research, and five did not. The NBER says a recession is "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months."

The 1973-74 oil shock, the dot-com bust in 2000, the 2007-09 financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic downturn all overlapped with recessions. But some major bear markets also occurred without one, including in 1987 and 2022.
What Wall Street says

Deutsche Bank macro strategist Henry Allen said that every S&P 500 bear market since the 1962 "Kennedy Slide" has coincided with at least one of three factors: a recession, worsening economic data raising recession fears, or a cycle of Federal Reserve rate hikes. None of those are present today, at least so far.

"Much as last week's selloff was severe, it's worth remembering that it has several differences with many of the other big risk-off moves in recent times," the London-based strategist wrote on Tuesday.

Allen said there hasn't been any sudden reassessment of the growth outlook recently, which happened during the Covid-19 shock, when the pandemic pushed the global economy into recession and the S&P 500 plunged 33.9% in just 33 days. Nor is the current situation similar to the 2025 "Liberation Day" tariff period either, which also prompted a reassessment of the growth outlook.

Economic numbers aren't deteriorating either, with the November U.S. flash composite Purchasing Managers' Index, or PMI, at 54.6, above 50 and indicating that business activity continued to expand. Another factor that often coincides with a recession, Allen said, was a big hawkish shift from the central banks, seen in the 1966 and 2022 bear markets.

"Today however, the equity declines have not coincided with a hawkish repricing," despite widespread expectations that the central bank is set to raise rates again at its final meeting of the year, on Dec. 9, Allen said.

Today, markets are pricing fewer Fed rate hikes through September 2027 than they were on Oct. 6, when the S&P 500 set its record, Allen said. "If anything, pricing has shifted slightly dovishly with the equity declines."
Over more than six decades since 1962, bear markets have always coincided with at least one of those three circumstances, according to Allen.
"So it would be unusual to see one today without those" happening too, he said.

technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149960/.headline: The Download: Innovators Under 35 nominations are open, and a bionic window into the mind
technologyreview.com/2026/11/27/1149960/.author: Thomas Macaulay

paragraphs.text: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open

Every year, MIT Technology Review honors 35 of the world’s brightest young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors in our Innovators Under 35 list. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.

We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to society’s most formidable problems, from human disease to climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.

Nominees can be based anywhere in the world, but must be under 35 on October 1, 2027. Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to put yourself forward? Here’s how to make a nomination for our 2027 list.
—Amy Nordrum
How cutting-edge prosthetics can help probe the human mind

There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi Davidson. A horrific injury as a teenager left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, his experience informs his work as a trauma therapist. He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand.

Before the trial started, researchers scanned his brain to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs?
Here’s what a bionic hand might reveal about the mind.
—Jessica Hamzelou
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/27/t.headline: Denials soar for ‘extraordinary ability’ visa in program once used by Melania Trump
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/27/t.author: Lauren Kaori Gurley

paragraphs.text: It’s long been considered the crown jewel of visas — a ticket to a green card and legal permanent residence in the United States, designated for people of “extraordinary ability,” including winners of Olympic medals, Oscars and Pulitzer Prizes.

But since President Donald Trump retook the White House, approvals for the EB-1A visa — distributed under the EB-1 program that helped first lady Melania Trump receive permanent residence in the United States — have plummeted.

The share of petitions approved for the EB-1A visa, designated for individuals in the sciences, arts, education, business and athletics who have shown “sustained national or international acclaim,” dipped from 75 percent during the final months of President Joe Biden’s term to 32 percent in mid-2026, according to federal immigration data. The sharp decline has prompted concern from immigration advocates about the United States losing its competitive edge everywhere from Hollywood to the country’s top laboratories.

The American Immigration Council, a nonprofit advocacy organization for immigrants, said in an August report that rising denial rates for EB-1As and other restrictions on employment-related green cards have “significant implications for workforce planning and the United States’ ability to attract and retain global talent.”

“It’s a huge, huge drop,” said Kate Angustia, a former immigration officer and supervisory policy and practice counsel at the American Immigration Lawyers Association, the national immigration law bar. “It’s strange because the Trump administration has repeatedly said they want the best and the brightest.”

Major league athletes, circus performers, tech entrepreneurs, science researchers and journalists who have been denied EB-1A visas this year would have breezed through the process with their achievements in the past, several attorneys and business leaders said. And some law firms have stopped processing the visa altogether because of the high denial rate. About 5,200 individuals received approvals for the visa in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, compared with nearly 8,900 over the same period in fiscal 2024.
The Department of Homeland Security, the White House and the first lady’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

While there is no evidence that the Trump administration has directed its immigration officers to clamp down on the elite visa category, the president has overseen a widespread effort to limit legal immigration and immigrant visa issuances, which have fallen sharply this year.

Immigration attorneys who represent clients petitioning for the EB-1A said that it appears, based on their dealings with immigration officers, that many are rejecting applications because the applicants are not, in their personal view, “extraordinary.” Immigration officers have long had a great deal of latitude in deciding who has enough “acclaim” to be eligible for the visa. But in the past, they typically looked for reasons to approve the visa, not deny it, because they are already very difficult to obtain, attorneys said.

“It’s become so much more subjective,” said Rachel Baskin, a Long Island-based immigration attorney who represents clients in arts and entertainment and has had clients denied EB-1A petitions this year.

For years, the visa has sparked debate over who qualifies as “extraordinary,” including the president’s wife. The Washington Post reported during the first Trump administration that Melania Trump obtained a visa under the EB-1 program in 2001 as a working model — someone who was not considered a supermodel like Kate Moss, Gisele Bündchen or Naomi Campbell. The visa set her on the path to U.S. citizenship and put her in the position to sponsor her Slovenian parents for legal residency.

When Trump’s critics called into question her qualifications during her husband’s first administration, many legal experts argued that she probably was qualified for the visa based on legal standards that have been in place for decades given her credentials, which included a photograph of her in a bikini embracing a blow-up killer whale in the 2000 swimsuit edition of Sports Illustrated.
“Part of the problem is that over the years, people used to call it the Einstein visa,” said Angustia, “which is a misnomer because you don’t have to be Einstein.”

Immigration officers are required to use a two-part legal test to review applications for the visa. First officers must determine whether applicants meet three out of 10 criteria, or can show evidence of a one-time achievement such as an Olympic medal or Oscar. If they pass that test, the immigration officer then must issue a “final merits determination” — a subjective assessment based on the complete evidence. Many applicants have been denied on that final determination this year, attorneys said, despite meeting the other requirements.

“Before the first Trump administration, it was very letter-of-the-law. If you met the requirements and you met the standard, then you pretty much are going to have this petition approved,” Baskin said.

That has changed, according to Finn Reynolds, head of insights and strategy at Lawfully, an immigration data analytics firm that tracks millions of U.S. immigration cases, because the EB-1A program, given its designation for “extraordinary” individuals, is “the easiest place for there to be a lot more scrutiny applied.” That makes it a relatively simple way for the Trump administration to reduce immigration.

“There should be a higher focus on bringing in the best and the brightest from around the world,” said George Fishman, senior legal fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates reduced immigration. “It’s entirely conceivable that the Trump administration decided that the adjudicators have been getting too lax in approving these things.”
Some immigration experts noted that denials may be on the rise in part because of the quality of applications and a dearth of immigration officers.
Reynolds said there has been explosive growth in a lucrative legal subindustry that profits off immigrants from countries with long wait times, such as China and India.

Organizations serving these immigrants in some cases charge exorbitant amounts to help desperate individuals submit weak, self-filed petitions; some companies sell templates or use AI to write the applications, Reynolds said.

An influx of these poor-quality applications, coupled with the Trump administration’s demands for higher scrutiny on applications and the inexperience of newer officers stretched increasingly thin by a wave of buyouts and firings coordinated by the U.S. DOGE Service, could be increasing rejection rates, as well. Reynolds’s data shows that applicants are increasingly receiving requests for additional evidence to back up their claims of “extraordinary ability” — which are usually a precursor to getting denied.

“The scrutiny is probably roughly half of the equation here,” Reynolds said of the increased denials. “And then the other half is probably the fact that there are both more unqualified and underqualified petitions being submitted.”

But he said many applicants who would have been qualified in the past are getting rejected. And the approval rate probably has dipped even further, to about 27 percent in the final quarter of fiscal 2026, according to projections by Lawfully.
Even the tech sector — in which the president has called for growth — has seen reductions in approvals, attorneys say.

“They’re killing AI entrepreneurs,” said James Hollis, an immigration attorney in Memphis who processes “extraordinary ability” visas for athletes, entrepreneurs and entertainers. “They’re absolutely annihilating them.”

Hollis said he filed a petition for a tech entrepreneur in June that would have been a “slam dunk” a year and a half ago. The applicant had raised over $60 million in venture capital funding over his career, sold companies and had 20 news articles published about him, said Hollis.
The candidate was denied, with the officer determining that he met zero criteria, Hollis said.
Achievements like those of Hollis’s client are no longer enough, many attorneys said.

“You have to be very, very legitimate in AI, software engineering, software development, or somebody who’s very extraordinary in arts and performance, sports, things like that,” Reynolds said. “Those are definitely getting approved at higher rates.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/new-car-buying-deals.headline: New car prices are at a record high. Here's where to look for deals
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/new-car-buying-deals.author: Sarah Agostino

paragraphs.text: Consumers who are in the market for a new car may find the latest pricing data somewhat sobering.

The average transaction price for a new vehicle reached an all-time high of $51,109 in October, up 2.1% from a year earlier, according to a report from Kelley Blue Book, an auto valuation company. The amount excludes incentives, taxes and fees.
But for consumers who can't spend that much — or don't want to — the good news is that plenty of buyers are shelling out much less for a vehicle.
"The average is telling us as much about product mix as it is about affordability," Erin Keating, executive analyst at Cox Automotive, which owns Kelley Blue Book, said in the report.

Of the five highest-volume car types sold in October, three — compact and subcompact SUVs, and compact cars — sold at prices far below the overall average transaction price, she said. For example, the average amount paid for a compact car in October was $28,030.
Additionally, sales of vehicles priced from about $28,000 to $38,000 climbed 9.6% from a year earlier.

"Consumers are still buying plenty of vehicles well below the headline average transaction price, even as strong demand for full-size pickups and other larger, well-equipped vehicles keeps pushing the average to new highs," Keating said.
Why prices are elevated
The record price comes amid a 34% jump in the average cost of a new vehicle since October 2019, when it was $38,259, according to Kelley Blue Book data.

While pandemic-related supply shortages helped drive up prices earlier this decade, consumers' appetite for larger, more expensive vehicles like SUVs and pickup trucks has also pushed the average higher. Full-size pickups, for instance, sold for an average of $67,912 in October, according to Kelley Blue Book.
Yet buyers who would struggle to afford a $50,000-plus new car can still spend less and find deals in the current market.

For starters, automakers have been slower than usual to roll out 2027 models, at least in part because 2026 cars continue to sell well at current prices, said Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds, an automotive research company. In October, 76% of new-vehicle sales were for current-year models, compared with 59% a year earlier.
This slowdown in the annual model-year transition means more 2027 cars will hit dealer lots soon, which suggests dealers and automakers are motivated to clear 2026 inventory, Drury said.
But waiting until the last week of the year to buy — thinking dealerships are desperate to make the sale — won't necessarily get you a better deal, he said.

"You're not going to get massive savings by waiting," Drury said. "Everybody's busiest time of the year is between Christmas and New Year's, but it's not like the best deals are then — that's a perception thing."
Some 2026 models come with incentives
Some manufacturers are offering incentives on certain 2026 models, which can reduce the cost of a new car by thousands of dollars.

For example, the 2026 Nissan Pathfinder, a midsize SUV with a starting price of $41,565 — which includes destination charges — comes with a rebate of $5,000 for qualified buyers through Nov. 30, according to Cars.com, an online automotive marketplace.
Just be sure to check your local dealerships to confirm participation for any manufacturer's incentives, experts say.
Look for cars considered old inventory
Look for cars that have been sitting on dealer lots for an extended time, Drury said. In September, new cars took 58 days to sell, on average, according to Edmunds.

Generally, dealerships consider cars unsold for 60 to 90 days to be aging inventory, which may motivate them to offer a better deal, according to Autotrader.com, an online auto marketplace owned by Cox Automotive.

"You'll find the vehicles that dealers definitely want to get rid of the most," Drury said. Looking for older inventory will be "your quickest way to find a dealership that's thinking, 'Yes, I too want to get rid of this. Help me help you,'" he said.
Listings on some car-shopping websites include how long a car has been on a dealership's lot. You can also ask the dealership how long a particular car has been in its inventory.
Leasing may be a good fit for some consumers
Leasing may present an opportunity to get into a car with lower monthly payments than financing the same vehicle, depending on the terms of the lease.

However, fewer attractive leasing deals are available, a trend that started during the pandemic, Drury said. Plus, leases, which are typically for three years, usually come with mileage limits and charges for excessive wear and tear.
Nevertheless, leasing may make financial sense for a consumer who "gets that two- or three-year itch for a new car," Drury said.

This is because after the first two or three years of making payments on a car loan — a time period when the steepest depreciation generally occurs — the car's value may be less than what is still owed on the loan, depending on the specific terms. This is known as being upside down or underwater, or having negative equity. In that case, the amount must either be paid off or added to the buyer's new loan.
"We see so many cars traded in that are 3 years old, and the customer is upside down by $7,000, $8,000 or $10,000 and they roll that into another loan," Drury said.
The used-car market may have some deals
You also may be able to find a good deal on a used car that's not too old.

The average transaction price for a 3-year-old vehicle was $32,039 in the third quarter, down slightly from $32,461 in the second quarter but 3.1% higher than $31,067 a year earlier, according to Edmunds. It's also higher than the average $27,133 list price for used cars of any age in October, according to Cox.

However, these 3-year-old cars are selling for far less than they did when they were new — $16,562 below the original sticker price of $48,601, on average. That marks the largest dollar gap Edmunds has on record, surpassing the previous high of $16,252 in the last quarter of 2019.

Some 3-year-old models tend to take longer to sell than others, which may give buyers some negotiating power, according to Edmunds. For example, a 3-year-old Jeep Cherokee, with an average transaction price of $23,138 — compared with its original price of $42,263 — takes an average of 64 days to sell, according to Edmunds.
Additionally, a good credit score can help keep the cost of financing a car purchase down. The higher your score, the lower the interest rate you can get, generally speaking.
And, finally, if you're trading in a car, be sure to shop it around, Drury said.
"Get multiple offers. They can vary by thousands of dollars," Drury said. "Have those offers in hand when you're at the dealership that has the next car you want to buy."

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/27/durable-good.headline: It’s not just you: Durable goods are getting less reliable, from sputtering cars to glitching smart TVs
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/27/durable-good.author: Megan Sauer, Juhohn Lee

paragraphs.text: "They just don't make things like they used to." The phrase, formerly exclusive to grandparents, is now used by consumers of all ages.

Across the United States, durable goods like cars, appliances and electronics are becoming less reliable. In the automobile industry, owners of 3-year-old models reported an average of 204 problems per 100 vehicles as of Feb. 12, the highest level since 2022, according to a report from consumer intelligence company J.D. Power. Reliability is a growing concern for dishwashers and front-load washers too, respectively experiencing an average of 92 and 91 problems per 100 units as of Oct. 29, according to a similar J.D. Power report.

Consumers have noticed: Shoppers dealing with high inflation rates and added tariffs on imported goods are unsatisfied with all kinds of products, from cars and tech devices to furniture and kitchen gear. Just over three-quarters of Americans say they believe companies often sell lower-quality products and services at higher prices, according to an Axios and Harris Poll survey published in May 2025.

To be sure, reliability and durability aren't the only ways to define a product's quality. Aesthetics and performance matter to consumers, too. Your television today may not last as long as the one you grew up with, but it's probably larger and thinner with better picture definition — and it likely costs much less, when adjusted for inflation, says Justin Sirotin, an industrial design professor at the Rhode Island School of Design. Indeed, the average price of a television was roughly $622 in 1996 adjusted for inflation, whereas a 55-inch LCD model now costs $232 on average.

But because they're penny-pinched, consumers are becoming more focused on finding high-value products — ones that perform consistently and reliably — than on price, according to a 2025 Deloitte report.

Unfortunately for shoppers, some businesses are also economically squeezed, and may manufacture products with cheaper, less durable parts to keep their profits growing, Sirotin says. Plus, we've all gotten used to sleek products with impressive features at affordable prices, and when businesses have to deliver on those aspects to grow demand, longevity can drop down the list of priorities. Manufacturers may prioritize quality on the external parts of a product — like the picture quality on a television — and get their cost savings with cheaper internal components that you won't initially notice, says Keyana Sapp, an investigative journalist and creator of the Worse on Purpose newsletter.

In some cases, a product's durability may even be part of a "planned obsolescence," wherein businesses intentionally give goods a certain lifespan so customers need to buy replacements within a predictable timeframe. Planned obsolescence isn't necessarily rampant, and it's hard to prove that any individual company purposefully designs products to fail, Sapp says.

But historically speaking, it's not entirely a conspiracy theory. In 1924, major light bulb manufacturers formed an international coalition and agreed to lower and standardize the lifespan of incandescent light bulbs to 1,000 hours. The cartel broke up during World War II.

You can, of course, try extending the longevity of products you've already bought by paying to repair them, rather than getting a brand-new replacement. But as devices like vacuum cleaners and headphones evolve technologically, they require increasingly specialized tools and labor, says Shahram Mokhtari, lead teardown technician at online repair community and e-commerce site iFixit. Specialized screws, glued components and limited access to repair information can make some products difficult or impossible to fix, the Federal Trade Commission reported in May 2021.

Europe has right-to-repair regulations that require manufacturers of certain products to provide access to replacement parts, tools and information. Only nine U.S. states have similar legislation for consumer electronics.

If you want to know how long a product might last before you buy it, look up its reviews or do some research to understand if it's complicated to fix, Mokhtari recommends. Or, if you have the budget, you can prioritize higher-priced products that might bring both initial quality and long-term longevity. This may require intentional long-term planning for some consumers — even as online shopping has made impulse buying easier, Sirotin notes.

"It takes a lot of intentionality by the consumer to say, 'OK, well, is this chair really a chair that I want to have for 25 years? Or is this the chair I'm going to buy and sit in for six months, and then I'm just going to get another chair?'" says Sirotin.
