cnbc.com/2026/11/27/spain-election-trump.headline: Spain’s election could pull Madrid closer to Trump’s Washington
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/spain-election-trump.author: Natalie Feary

paragraphs.text: Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday for a snap election that could bring down socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has repeatedly clashed with U.S. President Donald Trump.
It could also put the far right in government for the first time in the country's modern democratic era.

The center-right Popular Party is the frontrunner, and it could win a majority with far-right Vox, according to El País's final polling averages. A government led by the PP could shift Spain's approach to Washington, Beijing and NATO.
It's the first test of whether Europe's mainstream conservatives are willing to bring the far right into government, ahead of elections in France and Poland next year.
Housing, cost of living in focus
Despite Spain's economy growing 2.7% year over year in the third quarter, more than twice the euro zone's 1.3%, the campaign has been dominated by housing and cost-of-living crises.

Inflation soared to 4.9% in the year to October, above a euro zone average of 4%. November's flash estimate published Friday showed Spanish inflation cooling to 4.1%, still well above the 2.3% reading at the start of the year. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing one of the country's two most important issues.

Home purchase prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat. In 2025, house prices rose nearly three times as fast as household incomes, the European Commission said.
Nationwide protests began after an 87-year-old woman died two weeks after being evicted from her Madrid apartment in September.

Sánchez called the snap election after lawmakers rejected two government decrees designed to broaden housing protections, including limiting rent increases and blocking certain evictions and automatic lease renewals. Congress later ratified a revised version of one decree, limiting rent increases and evictions in some circumstances.
Sánchez's 'anti-Trump' campaign

Sánchez has made a name for himself internationally after clashing with Trump over NATO spending, the war in Gaza and Spain's refusal to let U.S. forces use its bases for operations against Iran. Trump even threatened to cut off "all trade" with Spain during the dispute over the bases.
At a Nov. 21 rally in Tenerife, Sánchez asked: "What good has President Trump brought to the United States and, by extension, to the world?"

He has also told voters that the PP and Vox would roll back government cost-of-living assistance. Days before the election, Sánchez's government approved 1.21 billion euros ($1.33 billion) to extend public transport discounts through 2027 and approved a general pay increase of up to 4.5% for 2027.

But in a final pre-election survey for El Español on Nov. 23, 66% of respondents gave Sánchez a failing grade and 29.5% a passing one. His government has faced scrutiny over its handling of the Ceuta migrant crisis, two deadly train collisions this year and corruption cases involving people close to the prime minister.

PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the current favorite to replace Sánchez, has made alleged government corruption and inflation central to his campaign. At a Nov. 22 rally in Murcia, he said the government wanted voters to forget "that inflation is eating into your pay check, that you can't afford a home, that you're paying more than ever for everything."

The PP led the final El País polling average, published Nov. 24, with 31.4%, followed by Sánchez's Socialists at 29.1% and Vox at 17.9%. Several seat projections put the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat lower house. If Vox joins a government, it would be the first far-right party to do so since Spain returned to democracy after Francisco Franco, the dictator who ruled for 40 years, died in 1975.
PP looks to market solutions to housing crisis

The PP wants to repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in designated high-pressure areas. It proposes speeding up construction permits and lowering taxes on first homes for buyers under 40. Vox also wants to repeal the housing law and would prioritize Spanish citizens for subsidized housing and public services.

Sánchez's Socialists want to extend renter protections and make at least a quarter of new homes public or permanently price-restricted. It would use proceeds from a bank levy to support housing, which it says will raise a further $1.5 billion. The PP has pledged to scrap this.
The PP also favors easing climate rules, extending the life of nuclear plants and replacing a decree that sets tight new renewable-power requirements on data centers with large new grid connections.
Immigration could weigh on PP-Vox coalition

A PP-Vox coalition would have its tensions, with immigration likely to be a major pressure point as Vox has an increasingly hard line on deportation and the militarization of some borders. The parties clashed in regional governments over the distribution of unaccompanied migrant children, leading Vox to quit several coalitions in 2024.
Immigration has since gained more prominence amid the government's handling of reports that more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31.

"Immigration has played a significant role in supporting Spain's recent growth, a strong role for Vox could complicate the government's ability to sustain that," said Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.

The parties also differ on defense commitments: both support more investment, but neither has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defense. The PP pledges closer NATO cooperation, while Vox puts greater emphasis on border security.

The PP favors closer integration with the European Union, while Vox wants more independence from it. The success or failure of a PP-Vox partnership will also have wider lessons for Europe "where long-standing firewalls against far-right parties are coming under strain," added Middleton, pointing to the rise of Germany's AfD and the prospect of Marine Le Pen potentially winning next year's election in France.
U.S.-Spain relations
A shift to the right could improve relations between the U.S. and Spain. Sánchez used his tenure to strengthen ties with Beijing, the country's largest goods trading partner outside the EU.

The U.S. remained Spain's largest source of foreign direct investment. Flows more than doubled to 11.6 billion euros in the 12 months through June 2026, from 5.1 billion euros in the previous 12 months, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Carla Hobbs, head of the European Council on Foreign Relations' Madrid office, expects a PP-led government to seek closer ties with Washington and bring its China policy more in line with the EU's. Vox could complicate that. The first test for Washington would be whether a new government changes Spain's position on defense spending or the use of its bases.

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/27/poo.headline: The surprising reason some people sleep better than others
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/27/poo.author: Shannon Osaka

paragraphs.text: In the United States, wealth and socioeconomic status is a great determiner of health. The top 1 percent of male income earners, for example, live on average 15 years longer than the bottom 1 percent. (For women, the difference is around 10 years.) The reasons for this divide are legion: Access to medical care, food and housing insecurity, stress and environmental pollution.
But there’s another significant difference between the wealthy and the poor, a new study shows: quality and quantity of sleep.

A new study in the journal JAMA Network Open this month of more than 12,000 participants found sleep duration is strongly associated with economic stability; participants with greater economic stability had much less variability in their amount of sleep and also slept more total minutes per night.

The research affirms other analyses that have found a strong connection between people’s income and amount of sleep. One analysis by the Centers for Disease Control in 2015 found that 35 percent of people with incomes below the federal poverty level slept less than six hours per night, compared to 27 percent with family incomes greater than three times the federal poverty level.

Dayna Johnson, a professor of epidemiology at Emory University and one of the authors of the new study, said that poor sleep can damage many systems of the body. “Poor sleep affects our lives, our livelihoods,” she said. “It’s associated with worse cardiovascular health, obesity, hypertension, diabetes. There’s also emerging data that it’s associated with a higher risk of cancer.”

Many studies rely on self-reported measures of sleep, which can be skewed by what participants think is an appropriate amount of sleep to report. But the new analysis drew data from wearable technology, like a Fitbit, to track the amount of sleep participants got with precision.

Researchers say there many reasons low socioeconomic status can make it difficult to sleep reliably. “Sleep is an opponent process to vigilance,” said Lauren Hale, a professor of preventive medicine at Stony Brook University who was not involved in the study. “You need to turn off at night. You can’t do that if you’re worried about what’s my kid going to eat tomorrow, how am I going to get to my job.”

Higher levels of air pollution can also make patients more likely to develop sleep apnea, which in turn erodes sleep quality. Low-income families also may be more likely to live in an area with a lot of noise, or work jobs that require variable hours.

Not every study, however, has found that higher incomes lead to better sleep. Some economists have found that higher wages can actually lead to less sleep, as people trade in hours of sleep for more hours of work.

But sleep researchers say that across various studies, people of very low incomes or living in poverty are likely to sleep less, endangering their health. “Poverty leads you to be in a situation where sleep becomes difficult,” said Michael Grandner, director of the sleep and health research program at the University of Arizona.

The differences in sleep can have serious effects on mortality. Research has shown that people who sleep less than seven hours a night have a 14 percent higher risk of dying prematurely than people who sleep seven to eight hours. Interestingly, people who sleep more than nine hours a night have also been found to have higher mortality risks, likely due to a correlation with chronic illness and higher amounts of sleep.

Grandner says that lack of consistent, stable sleep creates a long-term debt from which your body has to recover. He has a few suggestions for people who feel that they chronically don’t get enough sleep. He advises that people try to at least have a regular schedule, which will help the body recover even if the amount of sleep is insufficient. If you’re struggling to fall asleep, he adds, it’s better to get up and do something else, instead of training your body that being in bed is stressful.
“You miss an oil change for a few miles, and your car won’t break down on the side of the road,” he said. “But you continue to ignore maintenance and you’re courting danger.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/25/kevin-warsh-greenspa.headline: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
cnbc.com/2026/11/25/kevin-warsh-greenspa.author: Steve Liesman

paragraphs.text: In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?

Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.

It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.
Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.
Here are some key points:

• The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.

• Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.

• The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%.
• Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%.
• Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against.

It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/israel.headline: Momentous decision looms after judges call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped

paragraphs.text: The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”
Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.
A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Beloved ‘Star Trek’ No. 1 Jonathan Frakes reveals cancer battle
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Deborah Day

paragraphs.text: Jonathan Frakes, best known as Cmdr. William Riker on “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” has revealed he battled bladder cancer.

While attending a Phoenix convention with former costar Brent Spiner, Frakes, 74, noticed his urine had turned pink, he said in the most recent episode of their podcast “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny.”

Though Frakes had hoped it was something he ate, what he had experienced was “painless gross hematuria,” said his surgeon, Dr. Ram Narayanan, the Disney Family Cancer Center section head of urologic oncology. Narayana joined the duo in the podcast episode published Nov. 21.

“So that means: ‘gross,’ which basically you can see with your eyes, [and] ‘hematuria,’ which means blood in the urine,” Narayanan explained to Frakes and Spiner. “So when it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag.
“When you come to the urologist as the specialty, what we want to do is we want to figure out, number one —”
“You don’t have to call me ‘Number One,’ ” Frakes interrupted with a laugh, referring to his “Star Trek” character’s rank.

A urologist determines where the potential bleeding is coming from, Narayanan continued, by performing a cystoscopy, in which a small camera is inserted through the urethra to examine the passageway and the bladder.

“The camera goes in through the penis, and it takes about 30 seconds. It’s very fast,” Narayanan explained. “You get numbed up and … bottom line is that you have to buy in to do that. A lot of times guys are like, ‘I don’t ... not sure if I’m ready for it right away,’ and that’s OK too, but the cystoscopy is a must.”

Frakes also had a deeper scan called a blue light cystoscopy, which uses an imaging solution and high contrast to better identify tumors and their edges, according to the Urology Care Foundation website.

“Bladder cancer is confirmed during an outpatient surgery called transurethral resection of a bladder tumor (TURBT),” the Urology Care Foundation explains. “The combination of an imaging study (such as CT scan) and the results from transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) can find out the stage of your cancer.”
Narayanan said tumors look like “ferns,” “a shrub,” or “a sea anemone” and are scraped away.
After tumors in Frakes’ bladder were identified and removed, the actor and director underwent chemotherapy.

Frakes initially hesitated to share his diagnosis publicly, but Narayanan urged him to speak out and raise awareness about a warning sign that requires prompt evaluation to avoid the cancer progressing into the bladder muscle, which may necessitate removal of the organ.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say

paragraphs.text: Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants, which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.
The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.
Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne Law School, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.
“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.
“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster”, with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators.
Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”
Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.
Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.
“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.
“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”
Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.
O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.
“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.
A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”
“We are not selling Melbourne Water. It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.
“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”
The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.
The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/eu-budget-2028-2034-.headline: EU leaders fail to break $1.7 trillion budget deadlock as political pressure mounts
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/eu-budget-2028-2034-.author: Chloe Taylor

paragraphs.text: European leaders failed to break a deadlock over the EU's next long-term budget on Thursday, leaving negotiators under pressure to meet their year-end target before a busy 2027 election cycle adds further complications.

National leaders are divided over the European Union's next long-term budget, which sets spending priorities and limits from 2028 to 2034. It requires unanimous approval from all 27 member states to pass, as well as a majority vote in favor from members of the European Parliament.

Representatives from EU member states met on Wednesday and Thursday to discuss the latest budget proposal from European Council President António Costa, which amounts to a spending plan worth 1.58 trillion euros ($1.73 trillion). It marks a downward revision of around 10% from the original proposals for the bloc's long-term budget — known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF.

The EU's budget negotiations come against a backdrop of surging government borrowing costs, spiraling inflation and sluggish growth across much of the continent, as well as concerns about rising budget deficits in various EU countries.
Failure to meet the year-end deadline for the budget to be agreed risks deepening the political deadlock at the center of the ongoing talks.
Budget talks face walk-outs

At a summit in Brussels Thursday, budget talks went on for 12 hours, according to a BBC report — with some participants said to have walked out of the meeting as conflicts emerged around spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
A spokesperson for the European Commission was not available to comment on Thursday's talks.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters on Thursday evening that the talks had brought "new movement" towards reducing the overall size of the budget, adding that leaders would reconvene in mid-December to resume talks.
But he also said: "The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."

Merz, alongside the leaders of Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria, Finland and Sweden, said in September that the original 2-trillion-euro proposal would need to be reduced by "several hundred billion euros."
"We must make choices," they said in a letter addressed to Costa and Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin, pointing out that their six countries finance almost 40% of all contributions to the budget.
They called for funding to be focused on defense spending, competitiveness and innovation and "the fight against irregular migration."

Costa labeled the revised budget plans "realistic" when he presented them last week, noting that despite the 10.2% reduction in spending the proposals still represented a 120% jump in competitiveness funding and a 232% upswing for defense compared to the current budget.

"We didn't reach an agreement," he said in a statement after Thursday's meeting. "Regarding the global volume of the budget, some member states asked for further reductions, most opposed further cuts. And some even proposed to reverse some cuts."
Some European parliamentarians also appeared unconvinced by the new proposals.
"Parliament is consistent and proposes more investments, [the] Council is inconsistent and proposes cuts," Romanian MEP Siegfried Mureşan said on Wednesday.

"When the Council finally reaches a position, that's when negotiations will start, not when they end. As prime ministers cannot dictate to national parliaments, prime ministers also cannot dictate to the European Parliament to adopt a budget that is too small, and which does not equip Europe for the future."
National elections pose EU risks

Elections are set to go ahead in key EU economies including Spain, Poland and Italy over the next 12 months, while France's spring presidential election is at the forefront of regional leaders' minds.
Current front-runner for the French presidency, far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, has previously called for the country to leave the EU and to cut its contributions to the bloc's budget.
Incumbent French President Emmanuel Macron stressed on Thursday that he had limited time left to have his say on EU spending.

"After 31 December, I will no longer be in a position, politically or democratically, to reopen discussions on the budget and bring them to a conclusion, as we will be entering a period far too close to the presidential election in France," he told reporters after the talks, according to French publication France 24.

France, the EU's second-biggest economy after Germany, is being tasked with drastically cutting spending to bring its 5.1% national deficit closer to an EU guideline of 3%, while reeling from months of mass protests, riots and strikes over education funding and a cost-of-living crisis.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.headline: Bitcoin Bounces as Optimism Returns to Markets After Holiday
finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto/article.author: Emily Nicolle

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Bitcoin bounced on Friday as traders geared up for a bumper return to US trading after the US holiday, with technology stocks set to rally when markets open.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The largest cryptocurrency rose as much as 2.3% to top $62,000 before paring gains slightly, changing hands at around $61,400 as of early morning in New York. Other cryptocurrencies also jumped amid thin trading, with overall volumes on crypto exchanges falling around 25% in the last 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data.

"A move above $64,000 would be a serious indication of a shift in market sentiment," said Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at FxPro. "However, such positivity should be taken with a pinch of salt, as it has yet to be tested for liquidity when traders return next week. A drop to $57,000 would signal a return to the short-term bearish scenario."

US stocks are expected to open higher with futures climbing ahead of the Friday session. Equities in Europe and Asia also rose, as concerns about the artificial intelligence trade bubble bursting appeared to have abated.

Cryptocurrencies have struggled to perform in recent weeks, with Bitcoin on track for its worth monthly performance in more than four years. The token is down roughly 20% in November, weakened by failing investor confidence after a series of major crypto hacks and mounting regulatory uncertainty following the US midterms.

Large Bitcoin holders have seen most of their unrealized profit margins wiped out in the recent rout, inching them closer to ending the year in the red. The average unrealized profit margin for wallets holding between 1,000 and 10,000 Bitcoin is sitting at 5.7% this quarter, CryptoQuant said in a note on Friday — the lowest level of 2026, and a stark fall from a 33.9% margin in late September.

Overall, unrealized gains belonging to addresses holding 1,000 Bitcoin or more are sitting at $23.8 billion, CryptoQuant said, down from $124.7 billion in September and a peak of $294.4 billion in August 2025.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: German Budget Passes With €210 Billion in New Borrowing Planned
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Kamil Kowalcze

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Germany's parliament approved a €556 billion ($610 billion) budget that will ramp up spending on defense and infrastructure by piling on more debt.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The finance plan for 2027 that Chancellor Friedrich Merz succeeded in passing through the Bundestag on Friday is almost 6% larger than the one for this year, and is set to require more than €210 billion in net new borrowing.

More than half of core expenditure is earmarked either for labor and social affairs or for defense, highlighting both the increasing strain caused by Germany's welfare state and the government's focus on a rapid buildup in the military.

The legislative milestone reached in Berlin follows a hard-fought deal between Merz's conservative bloc and the Social Democrats of Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil that followed months of coalition disputes over taxes, welfare spending and borrowing.
"The process of drawing up this budget certainly did not deserve a beauty prize," the chancellor told lawmakers earlier this week.
Talks continued into the final days, with the parties agreeing to lower an electricity tax for households and businesses, and to soften previously agreed welfare cuts.
The coalition is also using debt-financed special funds to modernize the military and infrastructure after decades of under-investment.

Merz warned that this round of bargaining was only the beginning, saying that Germany will no longer be able to finance everything citizens have come to expect from tax revenue. The government's financial plan still contains an unresolved shortfall of more than €20 billion for 2028.

Of the planned net new borrowing, about €123 billion is assigned to the core budget. A further €58 billion will come through the infrastructure and climate-neutrality fund, with roughly €30 billion allocated to the Bundeswehr special fund.

Much of the borrowing falls outside the normal limits of Germany's constitutional debt brake, allowing Klingbeil to increase spending on rearmament and infrastructure while seeking savings elsewhere in the regular budget.
Labor and social affairs remains the largest ministry budget at €203 billion. Defense receives about €110 billion from the core budget and almost €30 billion more from the military special fund.
Debt-servicing costs will rise by more than a third to about €41 billion.
The legislation will now go to the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house, which is due to meet on Dec. 18.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/danger.headline: Dangerous Nor’easter Storm Triggers US East Coast Power Outages
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/danger.author: Lauren Rosenthal

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 27, 2026 at 6:20 AM PST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- More than 500,000 homes and businesses along the East Coast are without power after an explosive storm uprooted trees in Queens and inundated commuter rail lines in New Jersey on Thanksgiving Day.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The nor'easter system that pummeled New York City and surrounding areas also carried heavy rains as far south as North Carolina. Though the storm is losing power Friday, beaches from Virginia to Maine are still at risk of coastal flooding during high tide, according to the US National Weather Service.

"It was not a typical nor'easter," said Brian Hurley, a meteorologist with the service's Weather Prediction Center in Maryland. "It's been a while since we saw one that had such a footprint in terms of power outages, that wasn't tied to a tropical system."

Strong wind gusts scoured the eastern seaboard, toppling trees and knocking down power lines. Electricity is out for more than 145,000 customers throughout Pennsylvania, according to PowerOutage.com, with over 120,000 outages in New Jersey and about 50,000 throughout New York State.

At the peak of the storm Thursday evening, weather gauges captured gusts of up to 66 miles (106 kilometers) per hour at LaGuardia Airport in New York City. In Manhattan's Central Park, top winds measured 54 miles per hour.
The gusts were too strong to safely fly gigantic balloons in the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. For the first time in its history, organizers postponed the parade until Saturday morning.

wsj.com/world/americas/canada-posts-curr.headline: Canada Posts 3Q Current-Account Surplus of C$4.48 Billion

paragraphs.text: OTTAWA--Canada posted a third-quarter current-account surplus, marking the first time in about four years the country has recorded two consecutive quarterly surpluses, though it was smaller than expected.

Canada's current account, the broadest indicator of its trading and investing relationship with other nations, posted a seasonally adjusted surplus of 4.48 billion Canadian dollars ($3.14 billion) in the third quarter, Statistics Canada said Friday. That fell short of expectations for a C$9.4 billion surplus, according to Bank of Nova Scotia.
The data agency revised the previous quarter's surplus to C$6.10 billion, from an earlier estimate of C$8.84 billion.

Statistics Canada said the third-quarter surplus from merchandise-goods trade was largely unchanged from the previous quarter. Exports rose 0.2% nonannualized in the July-to-September period to C$232 billion, with gains in nine of the 13 sectors tracked. Exports of energy products declined in the third quarter, but from a record high in the previous three-month period as Canada benefits from higher crude-oil prices. Imports rose 0.3% to C$221.6 billion, led by electrical equipment and industrial machinery.

The current-account report also indicated that foreign-direct investment into Canada rose nearly 13% in the third quarter to C$33.61 billion, driven by foreign-led dealmaking. More than half of the foreign-direct investment was focused on the energy and mining sector, Statistics Canada said.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckd71ypy9e8eo.headline: Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckd71ypy9e8eo.author: James FitzGerald, Freya Scott-Turner

paragraphs.text: Touring musicians from across the US who descended on New York City to perform at the Macy's Thanksgiving parade have turned to fundraising to cover their costs, after getting stuck when the event was rearranged due to a storm.
A band from Texas told the BBC's US partner, CBS News, it had raised some $350,000 (£267,000) to pay for an extended stay for its 500 members. It saluted the kindness of its supporters.
A group of student musicians from Hawaii, meanwhile, voiced their relief after friends and family rallied around to cover their additional hotel, coach and meal costs.
The parade, a famous annual event, is now scheduled to take place on Saturday.
Earlier this week, organisers said they would it push it back by two days, in part due to the concerns around flying giant inflatables in strong winds.
The balloons were temporarily deflated for a few days - and so too were the spirits of those who had journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed, although it was suspended altogether during World War Two.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, some of them from high schools, to provide music for the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions of people in person and on TV.
The leader of the Texas band described his emotions as costs for his delegation were met.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School, near Houston, in Texas, told CBS.
Demkovich said contributions had arrived from businesses and individuals in the band's home community, with the help of a social media push.

Meanwhile, the Hawaii group, the the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it would still be able to participate in the parade, as a result of the efforts of families, friends, and other supporters who raised more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It had travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional, for our students," Badua said.

But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would get the same experience he had when he first performed in the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Prof Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain that were brought by a storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes lost power, and coastal areas were flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/27/glyp.headline: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA

paragraphs.text: The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradicts a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weed killer is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup producer Bayer.

The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generates new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations.

If the EPA again finds that glyphosate is not carcinogenic, the NIH studies would complicate the legal terrain for it and Bayer. The papers also represent a major public relations hit for Bayer, which has relentlessly defended the herbicide, for which it recorded $2.8bn in sales in 2024.

Nathan Donley, environmental health science director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the studies raise further questions about chemical companies’ influence on the EPA’s pesticide division, which “parrots industry talking points” in its safety reviews.

“Americans would be smart to heed the cancer findings of the nation’s most trusted scientific institution rather than the industry-influenced claims of the EPA,” Donley said. “The EPA’s pesticide office has made a mockery of pesticide science for far too long.”
The EPA did not respond to a request for comment.

In a statement, Ruveon, a Bayer subsidiary that manages Roundup in the US, said in a statement: “The US EPA, like other leading health authorities globally, has previously and repeatedly concluded that glyphosate does not cause cancer.”

The NIH findings arrive during a year in which the White House has come under fire from across the political spectrum for its support for Bayer. That includes an executive order from Donald Trump that aimed to protect the substance’s production and provide immunity to its producers, and an amicus brief in support of Bayer in an eventual US supreme court case that partially shielded the company from lawsuits.

The NIH did not carry out new studies, but conducted a systematic review of decades of scientific literature from across the globe. It found an association with blood cancers in humans, and that the pesticide caused several types of tumors in animals.

Advocates say the NIH used proper scientific protocol, which is followed by the World Health Organization’s International Agency on Research for Cancer (IARC), and other credible research organizations.

The EPA’s pesticide division reviewed most of the same studies several years ago but came to a different conclusion because it deviated from its own methodology, Donley said. A court threw out the EPA’s findings in 2022 because it did not use proper protocol, and ordered a new risk assessment.

The EPA is expected to finish it early next year, Donley said. The EPA and NIH are often aligned on many chemicals’ risk assessments, but the pesticide division chronically underestimates cancer risks because of its flawed methodology, he added.
“This agency is completely incapable of doing a good, clear, robust cancer assessment, not just with glyphosate, but all pesticides, because they don’t follow their own methodology,” Donley said.

The administration’s support for glyphosate has driven a wedge between pro-industry figures in the White House, and the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement, which health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr spearheads.

Kelly Ryerson, a Maha advocate who has met with top agency officials to advocate for stricter pesticide policies, told the Guardian she is “extremely hopeful that glyphosate’s day of reckoning has arrived”.

“The release of the government-performed studies on glyphosate further prove what many independent scientists have claimed for decades: glyphosate can cause cancer. The EPA will be forced to change its determination of carcinogenicity in the upcoming review,” Ryerson said.

She noted the NIH papers are in addition to a recent US Department of Health and Human Services-commissioned study that similarly reviewed literature on glyphosate’s impact on hormones and found it likely reduced sperm counts and testosterone.
Donley said he is “99.9% certain the EPA is going to again find that glyphosate does not cause cancer”.

“They cannot possibly get their head around any other option, so they’re going to come out with that, then they’re going to get sued, and they’re going to get their behinds handed to them in court, again,” Donley said.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3dgpy9lem3o.headline: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3dgpy9lem3o.author: Nadine Yousif

paragraphs.text: 15 minutes ago
Nadine YousifSenior Canada reporter
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their funadamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely-watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
On Friday, the Supreme Court ruled that Quebec's use of the "notwithstanding clause" is valid, except for a section of Bill 21 that bars elected officials from wearing a face covering.
The court found that this provision of the law violates a section of the Canadian Charter protecting the democratic rights of all citizens, which is not covered by the notwithstanding clause.
Barring elected officials in Quebec's legislature from wearing a face covering would infringe on an individual's right to run for public office, the court found.

The court's majority also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the rights Charter even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/28/what.headline: ‘I felt a zap race through my body’: what happens when someone is hit by lightning?

paragraphs.text: Caitlin Thomas recalls knowing that something terrible had happened but not fully understanding what.

She and her partner had arrived at a music festival some 270km north of Melbourne in the early afternoon and began setting up their tents and a gazebo for shade when the sky suddenly turned dark and the rain became incredibly heavy. A huge gust of wind picked up and Thomas asked her partner to hold on to the gazebo so it wouldn’t fly away. “He then asked me to hold on to it also so he could crack open his beer.”

“We heard this huge crack of thunder which felt like it shook the ground underneath it,” she says. “It almost felt like we were in a dome of thunder. Within three seconds everything was in a whiteout, and I felt a zap race through my body.”
She saw her partner, Harry Gordon, lying on the ground in the foetal position, holding his left arm, not moving.

“I remember the fear of not knowing if he was okay. I recall the second my body and brain linked as I looked down at my left leg and left arm and could not feel anything … As soon as I saw Harry move, I began sprinting for my life, searching for help. I remember looking down at my body running but not being able to feel anything.”
Thomas and Gordon had been struck by lightning in a freak storm at the three-day Strawberry Fields music festival in Tocumwal, on the Victoria-New South Wales border, on 20 November.
Grant Kirkby, a lightning risk mitigation expert from Western Australia, believes they were affected by an “upward streamer leader”.

“As lightning begins to travel downwards from a thundercloud, it creates an extremely strong electrical field at ground level,” he says. “In response to this electrical field, small channels of electricity can start travelling upwards from the ground and [through] objects such as trees, buildings, metal structures and even people.

“In effect, these upward electrical currents are competing to connect with the approaching lightning. When one successfully connects, it completes the electrical pathway between the cloud and the ground, resulting in the bright lightning strike that we see.”

The gazebo’s metal frame – an excellent conductor – would have allowed the electrical current to travel through it easily, he explains. So, what Thomas and Gordon experienced would have been an electrical discharge rather than a direct strike, similar to what happened to a Chinese weather presenter on live TV who was holding an umbrella.
“A person does not necessarily have to be standing at the point where lightning strikes the ground to be injured,” Kirkby says.

Lightning (which contains a current five times hotter than the surface of the sun) can injure or kill someone indirectly by the electricity that spreads through the ground, jumps from a nearby object or travels along metal, as well as upward streamers. About 95% of people are struck indirectly, and both direct and indirect strikes can be fatal.
Thomas says her experience was “extremely painful, almost like every muscle had contracted at the same time”. It left her feeling weak and dizzy, with an instant headache.
But she and Gordon were extremely lucky. After being taken to hospital by ambulance and monitored for several hours, the 23-year-olds were given the all-clear.

Globally, deaths from lightning have been estimated at between 6,000 and 24,000 and injuries at 240,000 a year. In Australia, one to two people have been killed by lightning each year since 2023, according to Kirkby, and more than 100 have been injured. Many experience lasting effects – and not via burn injuries, as commonly thought.

“The burns are usually very minor,” says Prof Mary Ann Cooper, retired from the University of Illinois, Chicago, who has conducted medical studies of lightning victims and released a free book on reducing lightning injury.

The damage is neurological, she says. In the short term it can cause kerauno paralysis (kerauno being Greek for lightning) in the legs or arms. It may cause unconsciousness or confusion akin to concussion. Longer term injuries include learning problems, amnesia, headaches, personality changes, irritability, chronic pain, sleeping problems and dizziness. Many survivors suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.
“One of my survivors and good friends used to call it black holes that he had in his brain, and he never knew where the little black holes were going to be,” Cooper tells the Guardian.
‘When thunder roars, go indoors’
How can we protect ourselves? First, by understanding the risk.

You don’t have to be in the middle of a storm to be struck, as discovered this month by a man in his 20s who was hit by lightning under a clear blue sky while swimming on the Central Coast of NSW. He was last reported to be in a critical but stable condition.

Use the “flash-to-bang” rule to calculate how far away a pending storm is. “Light travels almost instantly,” Kirkby explains, “but sounds take about three seconds to travel one kilometre.” If you count 30 seconds or less between seeing a flash and hearing the thunder, the storm is up to 10km away and you should head for safety.

The single most important way to protect yourself is to go into a substantial building, say Cooper and Kirkby. “When thunder roars, go indoors.” The next best option is a hard-topped metal vehicle. This isn’t due to the rubber tires but because the current flows over the metal, creating a faraday cage.
After the lightning stops, you should stay sheltered for 30 minutes.

The Australian Bureau of Meteorology warns that there is no safe place outdoors during a storm. But if seeking shelter is not possible, keep your exposure low, Kirkby says. “Keep your feet together and try to find some sort of depressed area so you are not the highest object.”

But don’t seek refuge next to something that is taller than you. If you stand under a tree, for instance, you can be struck by a side flash: if the electrical current goes through the tree it could jump to you. “This happens quite regularly,” Kirkby warns.
Be mindful that lightning deposits up to 1bn volts of electricity at its impact point, which dissipate the further you get from the point of impact.

Kirkby stresses the importance of keeping your feet together – and, whatever you do, don’t lie down. It’s all about equalising the voltage. “Think about a bird sitting on a high-voltage power line with 110,000 to 130,000 volts, and he’s fine, flapping his wings and singing and having a great time,” he says.
But if his wing touches some other object, like a nearby wire, it causes a voltage differential, which causes current to flow. “And it’s the same with people.”
If your feet are apart, it causes a voltage differential that allows ground current to flow through the body, meaning cows can be struck down in whole herds.
Thomas hasn’t noticed any after-effects since the music festival. “Although it would be cool if I had superpowers,” she says.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Shell’s Arc Deal Helps Lift Foreign Investment in Canada to Two-Year High
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Erik Hertzberg

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Foreign direct investment in Canada rose to its highest quarterly level in more than two years, driven by outlays into the country's energy and mining sectors.
Most Read from Bloomberg

FDI totaled C$33.7 billion ($23.7 billion) in the third quarter, up from C$29.8 billion in the second quarter, according to data released Friday by Statistics Canada. The increase was driven by mergers and acquisitions, as well as earnings "reinvested in Canadian affiliates by their foreign parents," the agency said.

More than half of the foreign direct investment was in the energy and mining sector, with the UK and US accounting for most of the inflows. FDI from the UK was the highest in nearly two decades. Canadian direct investment abroad totaled C$31.5 billion, up from C$20.2 billion previously.
UK-headquartered Shell PLC completed its acquisition of ARC Resources Ltd., an energy company with operations in Alberta and British Columbia, during the quarter.
The data offer an early benchmark for Prime Minister Mark Carney's push to attract more capital to Canada, though most of the quarter likely predates his government's biggest investment incentives.

Carney has set a goal of "catalyzing" C$1 trillion in investment over five years. In September, he hosted some of the world's biggest money managers in Toronto for the inaugural Canada Investment Summit, where the government pitched dozens of firms on possible stakes in Canadian natural resources, manufacturing and other projects.

His government has also made the most significant changes in decades to the tax treatment of business investments. The "productivity mega deduction," announced at the summit in September, allows firms to immediately expense a broad range of capital investments.

The measure carries a C$36 billion price tag over half a decade, and is part of a shift in fiscal policy that Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne say is aimed at sparking an "investment super-cycle."

Shelly Kaushik, an economist with the Bank of Montreal, said the data is "starting to show signs of the tide turning on the attractiveness of doing business in Canada." She added that it's still early, and Carney's latest initiatives have yet to show up in the numbers.
The release shows Canada's current account surplus narrowed to C$4.5 billion, from C$6.1 billion previously.
--With assistance from Mario Baker Ramirez.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/27/the-traitors.headline: 'The Traitors' ended with a $246,300 prize—here's who won and what they told us about spending it
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/27/the-traitors.author: Mike Winters

paragraphs.text: When Shane Beatty, a contestant on NBC's "The Traitors: New Blood," deceived his fellow finalists, he walked away with the entire $246,300 prize. But the emotional toll of winning caught him by surprise.

"The second I had to reveal that I was a Traitor, everything hit me at once," Beatty, a 32-year-old ironworker from Staten Island, New York, tells CNBC Make It. "I had built genuine relationships with these people, and knowing that some of them were blindsided by my decision was difficult."

Now that he's won, Beatty has a plan for his money, starting with setting aside a sizable share for Uncle Sam. As for the rest, he's more interested in financial security than the trappings of newfound wealth.
How Beatty plans to spend his winnings
After winning, Beatty doesn't expect his day-to-day life to change much.
"I'm still going to get up, go to work, and continue doing what I've been doing as a Local 580 ironworker," he says. "I love my career, and winning this money doesn't change that."
Beatty plans to pay for a wedding he and his fiancée previously struggled to afford, help his mother pay down debt and clear his own debts before saving the rest.
"What it does give me is an opportunity to take some financial pressure off, be a little more comfortable and put myself in a better position for the future," he says.
But before spending his winnings, Beatty is accounting for what could be his single biggest expense — taxes.
"First thing I'm gonna do with the money is put at least $100,000 in a separate bank account just so I can have it ready for Uncle Sam," he told Entertainment Weekly last week.
How much Beatty could owe in taxes
Setting aside $100,000 is a reasonable move given Beatty's potential tax liability, according to tax experts.

"Taxes are often an afterthought when winning big on a gameshow," says Riley Adams, a certified public accountant and founder of Sequoia Ridge CPAs. "So, it's definitely smart on his part to get ahead with his tax planning."
Game show winnings are generally taxed as ordinary income, meaning the prize money is added to a winner's other taxable income for the year. That can push a winner into higher tax brackets.
In addition to federal income taxes, Beatty, who lives in New Jersey, will have to account for state income taxes.
While Beatty did not disclose his income to CNBC Make It, ironworkers in the New York City metropolitan area typically earn around $100,000 a year, according to 2025 Bureau of Labor Statistics data.

Assuming Beatty lives in New Jersey, earns $100,000 from his job in New York in 2026, receives his winnings this year, files as a single taxpayer with no dependents and takes the standard deduction, here's how much of his prize money he could keep, according to Adams' calculations:
• Total winnings: $246,300
• Estimated taxes on winnings: $86,105
• Estimated take-home winnings: $160,195

Under this scenario, Beatty's winnings would push him from the 22% federal income tax bracket into the 35% bracket. Factoring in state income taxes, an estimated 35% of his prize would go to taxes, according to Adams' calculations. Setting aside $100,000 would give Beatty a comfortable cushion under this scenario. His actual tax bill, however, will depend on his income, deductions and other financial circumstances.
Jim Guarino, a certified public accountant and managing director at Baker Newman Noyes in Woburn, Massachusetts, arrived at a similar estimate.
"Folks tend to get excited by the 'gross amount' of their total winnings," but Beatty is "extremely tax-aware" in recognizing how much less he'll actually get to keep after taxes, he says.
For Beatty, the money won't radically change his life, but it will give him greater financial security.

"Having a savings cushion and knowing I don't have to worry about living paycheck to paycheck or falling behind on bills means so much to me," he says. "I want to be responsible with this opportunity and make sure it gives me greater financial peace of mind."
