cnbc.com/2026/11/27/ai-shopping-agents-r.headline: AI shopping agents are having a moment, but Amazon and a growing number of sites threaten to stunt their growth
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/ai-shopping-agents-r.author: Annie Palmer

paragraphs.text: Maia Bittner urgently needed to replace her car's windshield wipers. So last month, she turned to Meta's Muse personal artificial intelligence agent.
Bittner, chief product officer at fintech startup Imprint, gave Muse the greenlight to buy some wipers on her behalf from AutoZone. Or so she thought.
About 17 hours later, she got a notification from her Muse agent, which she named Dash, saying AutoZone canceled her order due to an unspecified error.
"Honestly, the most reliable path now is you ordering on Amazon yourself," Muse said, according to a screenshot of the message.

The interaction encapsulates the current messy and complicated landscape of agentic shopping apps, the AI tools that can make purchases on behalf of users. Over the past year, tech companies like OpenAI, Meta, Google and Instinct have introduced versions of personal agents that promise to take the hassle out of browsing and buying online.
The rollout has been far from smooth.

While some major retailers like Walmart and Sephora have opened up their sites to agents, companies including Amazon, eBay, United Airlines and Kohl's limit what actions agents can take or block them outright. Others have added provisions to their terms of service spelling out that they're not liable if users' AI-driven purchases go wrong.

"It's a very mixed bag," Emily Pfeiffer, a principal analyst at Forrester, said in an interview. "It means that a consumer who's using an agent to shop and browse and learn is not going to see the full set of options because some websites are unavailable."

The hiccups threaten to stunt the growth of shopping agents by creating a clunky and frustrating experience for users who are just starting to experiment with the tools. The question of who takes the blame when a transaction goes wrong also remains unclear.

Despite those challenges, analysts remain bullish about agentic commerce's potential. U.S. revenue from agentic commerce could reach up to $1 trillion by 2030, analysts at McKinsey and ICSC forecast in April.

Retailers and tech companies are also positioning agents as a helping hand for holiday shopping. Walmart on Tuesday touted its partnership with Meta, saying consumers could "put an AI agent to work" to nab Black Friday deals.
Earlier this month, Shopify President Harley Finkelstein predicted this year would be the "first holiday season" where AI-driven shopping goes mainstream.
"I think last year we saw AI influence more in discovery," Finkelstein told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "I think now we're going to see more of that conversion."
Patchwork of permissions
For users hoping to turn their online shopping over to AI agents, the experience can be unpredictable.

Agents encounter a patchwork of permissions across various websites. Retailers like Coach and Gap allow AI bots to browse but not check out, while others such as Target sometimes "block shopping agents by accident," according to an audit conducted in August from agent security company Billions Network.
Amazon has responded the most aggressively to agents by walling off its site entirely. The company rankled Elon Musk last month after it prevented his Grok Bot from placing orders.

In September, the company also blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its platform, saying it never agreed to participate in the program. And last November, Amazon sued Perplexity, accusing the startup of concealing its Comet agent, which can purchase products on behalf of users.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said the company expects, "over time, to partner with third-party agents," but that any partnerships will require the right "value exchange" between agents and retailers.

Bots encounter issues even when retailers welcome them in. They often fumble through webpages, and get stumped by login requirements at checkout. In some cases, the agents may require human intervention to bypass a CAPTCHA test and continue browsing.

A Visa study published earlier this month instructed 22 models from 12 AI labs to carry out a range of shopping tasks like buying a TV, a laptop and a hair appliance. The agents failed about 43% of test runs, and in more than half of those failed runs, an agent purchased a product "that did not meet the customer's identified requirements," according to the study.

Bittner said she is a "big believer" in AI agents' potential. Earlier this year, she was delighted when Perplexity's shopping agent found and purchased a pair of Adidas sneakers that were sold out for months.

Other experiences have been clumsier. Last week, she asked Meta's Muse to help her find a Jellycat octopus plushie for her kids. It suggested a product marked 75% off from "Crazy Hobby Supply," a retailer she'd never heard of and that didn't appear to have any reviews.

"I sort of trust Google to only surface sites that are not scams to me in their sponsored ads," Bittner said in an interview. "In the same way, I want AI to only surface to me websites that are not scams. I don't think we're there yet."
Users have reported mishaps with other AI tools, including one case where Instinct's text-based agent booked a hotel and signed up for a loyalty program without the consumer's consent.

Many retailers are approaching agents cautiously because they're concerned about fraudulent bot activity. San Francisco-based Skyfire is trying to solve that problem by arming retailers with more data to identify which bots are visiting their site, and verify that a human has actually consented to let an agent buy a product on their behalf.
Typically, when a human visits a website, there's "all kinds of signals" to prove it's not a fraudulent user, Skyfire CEO Amir Sarhangi said in an interview.

None of those things are available to retailers when an agent accesses their site, Sarhangi said. Agents might appear even more suspicious because they mask their IP address or origin via data centers, and they often use one-time, virtual cards to check out.

"So we talked to a lot of merchants and banks and financial institutions, and the things they told us were: we want to know who the end user is, and we want to know it's a real human," Sarhangi said. "We want to know who these agents are because we're not going to just let willy-nilly anybody do these types of transactions, and we need a way to kind of verify that."
AI companies, retailers, financial institutions and other industries have announced an alphabet soup of "protocols," or rules that propose ways to make it easier for agents to transact on websites.

There's yet to be a broad consensus around who takes responsibility when an agent purchase goes sideways. American Express in April said it would protect eligible customers "from charges related to AI agent error." Stripe, whose Link digital wallet is integrated with Muse, protects some agent purchases and offers a "refund guarantee."

Others are more wary. Last month, JPMorgan Chase blocked external agents from operating on behalf of customers, citing security concerns. Best Buy is among several retailers that deem users responsible for agent purchases in their terms of service, saying it views those transactions "as if you performed them yourself."
"Best Buy is not responsible for conduct, errors, actions, or inaction by any Digital Agent," the company's terms state.
Sarhangi said he can see why retailers, especially Amazon, are shutting their doors to external agents when the user experience remains inconsistent.

"At the scale [Amazon] operates in, I would think they need it to be much more aligned with their existing processes, so that they're not going to have a bunch of unhappy users saying, 'What's going on here,'" he said.
Can't ignore them forever

For now, agents remain a niche tool for shopping, with agentic purchases making up just 0.4% of global e-commerce transactions and 0.2% of value, according to Bain & Co. research published earlier this month.

Uber disclosed last month that AI agents booked only 504 rides and Uber Eats orders during its busiest week in October. Airbnb also said it has seen little volume from agents, while DoorDash said it has recorded only "several hundred" agent orders so far.

But retailers may not be able to ignore them forever. Roughly a quarter of Muse's 10 million users are shopping online via an AI agent with an average spend of $200 per order, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in October.
Instinct CEO Noah Shinn told CNBC earlier this month that the average transaction value among its users exceeds $500 per person.
Asked about some companies' efforts to block agents, Shinn said he tries to "give them some slack."

"It's a new interface, it's a new mode of where users' attention is coming from and it might just disrupt existing large services of theirs," Shinn said at a CNBC CEO Council dinner in San Francisco. "They just need time and we've just done a lot of thinking on our side."
He added, "We can obviously move very fast and certain businesses cannot. So, how can we collaborate with them?"

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw4yrr8kz9o.headline: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw4yrr8kz9o.author: John Simpson

paragraphs.text: John Simpson: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/pre.headline: Pregnant inmate escapes from prison vehicle in New Mexico
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/27/pre.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news
Authorities are searching for a pregnant prisoner who escaped custody in Albuquerque while being taken back to prison after a medical appointment, the New Mexico Corrections Department said Thursday.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, was sentenced to six years in prison after pleading guilty to four vehicle theft charges going back to 2024, the Associated Press reported, citing court records.
She was being transported back to the Western New Mexico Correctional Facility in the city of Grants after a prenatal appointment Wednesday when she escaped, the corrections department said.
Department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said Taylor, who is in her second trimester, was not restrained during the drive, the Albuquerque Journal reported.

She was being transported by three officers who stopped to get food from a Whataburger restaurant, when she unbuckled herself and drove away, Roembach told the outlet. The vehicle was found about an hour later, but Taylor was not inside.
New Mexico authorities said Taylor has ties to the Albuquerque area and Texas, and they urged people not to approach her while a multiagency search is underway.
Reporter covering Russia
Russian Orthodox patriarch calls on Christians to tame AI, warns of ‘Apocalypse’

The head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, has said that Russia has a “crucial task” in a fight to prevent artificial intelligence from gaining the upper hand “over human will and reason.”

With advanced AI, “the fulfillment of the prophecies of the Apocalypse seems closer than ever,” Kirill said Thursday at a religious conference. He cast Russia as a keeper of “a religious perspective on global processes” and an “alternative to the civilization of consumption,” echoing rhetoric of President Vladimir Putin, who has pursued a traditionalist, conservative society cast as an alternative to the decadent West.
Kirill said taming this “incredible new power” and preventing a scenario in which humans are relegated to the margins of existence “rests specifically upon Christians.”
Russia’s biggest bank, Sber, issued a report this week that said AI can replace at least 13 percent of jobs in Russia and force another 38 percent to adapt.

Pope Leo XIV has voiced similar concerns, making AI the focus of his first encyclical. Leo called AI a powerful achievement that needs oversight and must serve the common good, while warning it could hollow out the middle class, drive unemployment and concentrate wealth among a few.
Trump’s Thanksgiving message attacks adversaries, migrants and economic data
President Donald Trump issued an acerbic Thanksgiving message Thursday that criticized the Commerce Department, members of the Somali community and opponents of his ballroom project.

Writing on Truth Social, he baselessly accused the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis of deliberately publishing “fake Economic Numbers” before the midterms. He cited updated figures published Wednesday which showed third quarter GDP growth at 4.3 percent, revised up from 3.4 percent.
The BEA updates its figures on a prescheduled basis. GDP often has big revisions after its initial release, as statisticians gather more data.
He also targeted those who sought to bring America to “the Radical Far Left,” and other political opponents.
He said Somalis in Minnesota who did not receive government assistance were “wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay … the others should be thrown out.”
Nearly 90 percent of Somalis in Minnesota are citizens, and only 1 percent are in America illegally, a demographer told The Post in 2025.
Trump also defended the time he spent on White House renovations, saying he “took time out of my very busy schedule to fix … a primary symbol of our Country.”
Many Americans have told pollsters they don’t see the renovations as a priority.
Reporter and researcher covering culture and social affairs in Asia
South Korea is cracking down on AI cheating with metal detectors and body cameras
SEOUL — South Korea has launched a nationwide crackdown on AI-assisted cheating after the top scorer on this year’s national tax accountant exam confessed to using artificial intelligence.

Han Won-seok, 34, admitted in a YouTube video that he photographed exam questions with a miniature camera, sent them to an AI tool and checked the answers on his phone. Police on Thursday were seeking an arrest warrant for him on charges including obstruction of official duties, local media reported.

In a country where students spend years preparing for one make-or-break test, the scandal has raised fears that AI is undermining trust in the system. Days after Han’s video, authorities rushed out new anti-cheating rules for the Suneung, the university entrance exam often compared to the SAT.

On exam day, Nov. 19, three emergency alerts blared on phones nationwide — to reveal any hidden devices in exam rooms — as part of last-minute changes that drew criticism from students, parents, teachers and lawmakers. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday, apologizing for the confusion it caused for half a million test-takers.
President Lee Jae Myung has ordered a review of how state exams are run and launched a task force to investigate suspected AI-assisted cheating in Suneung and national qualification tests.

The government plans to introduce metal detectors, device checks and WiFi shutdowns for middle and high school exams, as well as proctor-worn body cameras for national certification exams. Up to $373,000 is being offered for tips on major exam fraud, local media reported.
You should have a sinking fund for holiday spending. Here’s how to start one.

While some Americans are looking for ways to spend less this festive season, going into debt is still a holiday tradition for many. Pressure to spend on gifts, activities and family travel can lead to blown budgets and borrowing that many come to regret when the new year arrives.

A sinking fund offers a solution that allows you to spend without worry. Sinking funds are dedicated pools of money built by investing small amounts over time. Rather than struggling to find thousands to cover your December expenses, you can save for them all year.

While it’s likely too late to adopt this approach for the 2026 season, starting now for next year will allow you enjoy a much merrier time. Just decide how much you want to spend on the holidays, divide that amount by 12, and put the required sum into a special savings account earmarked for celebration. If you want to spend $1,500 on Thanksgiving and Christmas, set aside $125 a month until those holidays are here.
This approach allows you to truly enjoy the fun of the festivities, without the financial stress that often comes with them.
White House reporter covering President Donald Trump and his political movement
Trump to visit site for new semiconductor factory in Arizona

President Donald Trump is doubling down on boosting America’s semiconductor industry, planning to visit a chip factory in Phoenix next week after working to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in recent days.

Trump will deliver remarks and attend a groundbreaking ceremony Dec. 4 for an expansion at the multibillion-dollar Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company facility, according to a White House official.

The White House has not said whether Huang will also attend. The briefly ousted CEO is scheduled to appear before Congress next week. Trump and Vice President JD Vance helped get Huang reinstated to his position by providing assurances to Nvidia’s board members that the government does not have evidence that he poses a national security risk.
Lawmakers from both parties have pledged to investigate Huang’s romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has sought to promote the semiconductor industry, seeing it as a key driver of economic growth in the United States. The White House sees the Arizona plant as key to increasing U.S. semiconductor production.
Writer and editor for The 7, The Post’s morning briefing
What to know to start your day
Good morning. It’s Friday, Nov. 27, and if you’ve woken up with a food hangover, you probably don’t care about the news. Simply take heed of these three quick remedies and be on your way.

For those with enough mental and physical strength, catch up with today’s edition of The 7 briefing. It begins with the impacts of yesterday’s storm on the East Coast. Flights were canceled and power outages were widespread. But better weather is on the way.
The briefing also has news from Iran, the White House and SpaceX that you might have missed.

Further down, we share The Post’s gift guide to aid your Black Friday shopping. We explain why some people have worse sleep than others. And finally, do you have a fridge full of leftovers? They won’t last as long as you might think. So you should get back to eating.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy49de4xx1zo.headline: Paul Mackenzie: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy49de4xx1zo.author: Patrick Jackson

paragraphs.text: A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the Shakahola cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/canada.headline: Canada’s top court upholds Quebec law barring public sector workers from wearing religious symbols

paragraphs.text: Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.
In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning, the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.
“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.

Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.

Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.

Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The clause is the result of political comprise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.

Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters.

In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.

Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96, which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.

But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional right and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.

In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.

In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.

In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.
The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.
The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws were at risk.

Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.

The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/norse-atlantic-bankr.headline: Budget airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy in Europe after failing to secure funding
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/norse-atlantic-bankr.author: Sawdah Bhaimiya

paragraphs.text: Budget carrier Norse Atlantic filed for bankruptcy Friday, saying it failed to secure funding after soaring fuel costs strained the company's operations throughout the year.
Its parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, concluded that the Norwegian carrier no longer has a basis to continue operations.
"Despite extensive efforts, the Company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs," the firm said in a statement Friday.

It comes days after Norse said it's facing a "critical financial situation" and was considering its options from a strategic takeover to ACMI contracts, which refer to short-term capacity leasing. The company's shares closed 85% lower on Wednesday.
The board has now filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court, where a trustee will be appointed to manage the process further.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution," Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald said.

"We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald added.
The company has cancelled all flights, and ticket sales have been discontinued.
Norse was founded in March 2021 and offered cheap flights between Europe, the U.S., North America, Africa, and Asia.
Soaring fuel costs strain airlines

The U.S.-Iran war began on Feb. 28 and caused jet fuel prices to skyrocket, forcing airlines around the world to grapple with higher costs. Prices are now up nearly 72% to $155 per barrel year-on-year as of the week ending Nov. 20, according to the International Air Transport Association's Jet Fuel Price Monitor.

Norse Atlantic's Roald told CNBC in May that he wasn't "overly concerned," about access to fuel but flagged that the company had canceled over 700 flights, which impacted more than 240,000 passengers.

Ryanair's CEO Michael O'Leary warned in April that if jet fuel prices continued to stay elevated throughout the year, then other European airlines were likely to face "financial difficulties" during the winter season.

In fact, several European airlines have stopped operating this winter, including Slovakia's AirExplore, Spain's AlbaStar, Ireland's Fly4, and Spain's Plus Ultra, which has canceled all flights but hasn't permanently closed.

livescience.com/archaeology/neanderthals.headline: Why are we the last humans standing? What interbreeding with Neanderthals reveals about the differences between us.
livescience.com/archaeology/neanderthals.author: Tia Ghose

paragraphs.text: Across thousands of years, Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) interbred, leaving traces of Neanderthal DNA in people alive today. But how these encounters happened is a huge unanswered question. Answering it may shed light on what made us different from our close cousins — and why we thrived while Neanderthals died out.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Anthropic Shares Jump After Volatile First Week Since IPO
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Carmen Reinicke

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC shares climbed above their $83 initial public offering price as the artificial intelligence lab looked to end its first calendar week on the Nasdaq after its record-setting debut on a positive note.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The stock increased about 11% from the previous session to $91.90 each as of 12:05 p.m. on Friday in New York, the highest intraday level since Monday, putting it on track to end a two-day streak of closing below the IPO price. Anthropic joined a broader rally in a shortened trading day following the Thanksgiving holiday, as risk appetite returned after a slump.

Concern over the pace of AI spending had roiled tech stocks in the lead-up to the Claude Code maker's record $119.5 billion first-time share sale, and spread to Anthropic's shares after Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's return to the chipmaker as investors weighed the potential impact of the controversy on the AI ecosystem.

The trading gives the Dario Amodei-led company a market capitalization of roughly $1.7 trillion. That's below the peak of more than $2 trillion during the firm's debut on Nov. 19, when shares touched $115.10 before retreating.

The uneven debut has drawn scrutiny around the IPO's execution. Some investors have questioned the decision to allow Anthropic's underwriting banks to exercise the so-called over-allotment option after the first day, rather than preserving the ability to support the stock.

Others drew attention to the slug of as many as 315 million shares released from a lockup agreement on insiders on the first trading day, as part of the company's year-long staggered lockup releases, according to its prospectus.

A further tranche of as many as 303 million shares held by insiders are expected to become available for sale on Dec. 15, the prospectus shows. Also in December, indexes including the Nasdaq 100 could add Anthropic shares, leading to a wave of buying from tracking funds.

The rapid adoption of products such as Claude Code, Anthropic's coding agent for software developers, and the company's revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October, made for a powerful sales pitch for the company's IPO. That helped investors overlook the company's committed spending nearing $901 billion through 2045.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Banks Facing Bond Price-Fixing Trial Agree to Pay Over $400 Million
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Sridhar Natarajan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street firms including some of the industry's biggest banks are nearing an agreement to pay more than $400 million to end a high-stakes lawsuit claiming they schemed to fix prices in the muni bond market.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The deal would end a long-running federal class-action suit that reached the doorstep of the US Supreme Court and was heading to a jury trial, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The proposed payment — a fraction of the billions that plaintiffs demanded — was hashed out in recent days and may be presented to a court soon, one of the people said, asking not to be identified discussing the confidential talks.

Municipalities led by Philadelphia had accused a group of banks including JPMorgan Chase & Co., Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. of colluding to set interest rates artificially high on a certain kind of debt, positioning the firms to profit at the expense of taxpayers.
Representatives for the cities and those banks declined to comment on any settlement talks. The firms have disputed the allegations in court.

A public trial threatened to place another harsh spotlight on Wall Street's treatment of Main Street, bringing with it risks of reputational damage on top of financial demands that swelled during litigation. Documents filed to the Supreme Court showed municipalities hoped to ultimately win $12 billion.

The allegations centered on so-called variable-rate demand obligations. The long-term bonds, dubbed VRDOs, have their rates periodically reset and offer investors the opportunity to return the securities for cash if they think the yields are reset too low.

The municipalities accused the banks of conspiring to inflate those rates above competitive levels to increase the chances of placing the VRDOs with an investor rather than having to keep them in their own inventory.

The claims followed findings of manipulation in the global foreign-exchange market and in setting Libor, the London interbank offered rate. Those scandals cost dozens of traders their jobs and banks billions in fines and penalties.

In their Supreme Court appeal, the banks said municipalities hadn't met one of the class-action requirements by showing that issues common to all of the plaintiffs would predominate over individual questions. The banks hoped to overturn a federal appeals court decision that let the class action go forward.

The banks are separately defending against related claims in state court in New York and California under the US False Claims Act. Bloomberg Intelligence analysts estimated in July that settling the antitrust action would likely cost banks about $770 million along with an additional few hundred million dollars to resolve state court actions.

Though the allegations focused on an esoteric corner of a complex market, lawyers for the municipalities would have set out to make a more straightforward argument in a trial: That banks made promises to clients and didn't live up to them.
--With assistance from Todd Gillespie and Hannah Levitt.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: OpenAI Says Apple Pressured Suppliers to Shun Its Devices
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Erik Larson

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The trade-secrets fight between OpenAI and Apple Inc. is widening, with the artificial intelligence company accusing the iPhone maker of undermining its supplier relationships and using unfair employment agreements to prevent talent from jumping ship.
Most Read from Bloomberg

OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple on Friday in federal court in San Jose, California, transforming the lawsuit Apple brought earlier against OpenAI into a two-way battle over the companies' intellectual property.

The case has overshadowed OpenAI's bid to sell its own devices, a move that would put it in competition with the iPhone maker. Former Apple design guru Jony Ive is helping the AI company develop a family of products, starting with what's expected to be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker.

"Apple has responded to OpenAI's anticipated entry into the hardware market by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI and using expansive employment restraints to limit OpenAI's access to talented engineers," OpenAI said in the filing. "Apple's power over suppliers and engineers cannot lawfully be used to exclude competing purchasers and employers from the market."
Apple did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment.

Apple in July sued OpenAI and Tang Tan, the AI company's chief hardware officer, alleging the ChatGPT maker orchestrated a campaign to steal trade secrets via job candidates and hires from Apple. The companies had earlier collaborated to integrate ChatGPT directly into iPhone, iPad and Mac software, only to see that relationship cool more recently.
In the new counterclaims, OpenAI alleges Apple unfairly pressures industry suppliers to "identify their OpenAI projects and the names, locations, and assignments of workers with Apple experience."

Apple then seeks to exclude workers with OpenAI experience from doing further work for the iPhone maker, effectively discouraging suppliers from committing workers to OpenAI projects, according to the filing.

Another industry supplier that provides specialist finishing services moved its manufacturing work for OpenAI products to the night shift to avoid overlapping with work for Apple, increasing costs for OpenAI, according to the filing. The supplier did so under pressure from Apple, OpenAI says.

"Suppliers have expressed fear of losing Apple business and have moved or rescheduled meetings with OpenAI to avoid Apple seeing them," according to OpenAI's counterclaims. "Other suppliers have told OpenAI personnel that they must be cautious about devoting staff, production resources, or managerial attention to OpenAI."

OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and has asked a judge to toss out Apple's lawsuit. In October, OpenAI voluntarily agreed not to use trade secrets that Apple claims were stolen when a judge said he was likely to issue an order to that effect.
The counterclaims accuse Apple of stealing OpenAI's trade secrets, an allegation that the AI company previously made in a filing in the case.

OpenAI alleges that a former employee — who had left Apple for OpenAI but later returned to Apple — had sent "over a hundred highly confidential files" about at least one unreleased OpenAI device to personal accounts. The files included images of unreleased hardware, engineering and manufacturing data and supplier information, OpenAI said.

In response, Apple said it has policies in place to prevent the use of confidential information from former employers, that it found no evidence to substantiate OpenAI's claims and that the AI company is simply trying to distract from the "significant evidence" that its employees took Apple product information.

The new counterclaims also accuse Apple of using unfair employment agreements to prevent its engineers from leaving for OpenAI. The AI company is challenging provisions that bar former Apple employees from soliciting or recruiting Apple workers for one year.

OpenAI argues that Apple's intellectual property agreements, or IPAs, which employees must sign, use an overly broad definition of the company's private information. The agreements essentially cover all nonpublic information that employees learn from the iPhone maker, even if it isn't a trade secret, unfairly restricting former employees' professional skills and putting them at risk of being sued, OpenAI says.

"The threat of litigation, however meritless, gives the unlawful provisions in Apple's IPA teeth," OpenAI said in the filing. "Even if a former employee's rights are entirely vindicated, the process of litigation is expensive and invasive, and may even involve Apple rifling through the former employee's personal devices and accounts."

Apple's lawsuit names a former iPhone engineer, Chang Liu, who joined OpenAI in January. Apple claims he accessed confidential hardware-related files over a period of several weeks, while developing devices for OpenAI, after discovering an authentication bug that allowed him to tap into Apple's information.
The case is Apple v. Liu, 5:26-cv-07078, US District Court, Northern District of California (San Jose).

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Trump’s AI Gambit Fuels Wild Thanksgiving Week on Wall Street
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Emma Haidar

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The message from Washington this week was unmistakable: America must do whatever it takes to win the artificial-intelligence race with China, and the government is prepared to intervene to make it happen.
Most Read from Bloomberg
A jittery Wall Street has cheered the message. Yet the wild swings in financial markets show the limits of investor conviction.

President Donald Trump's intervention to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia Corp. restored to the helm not just one of the biggest AI evangelists but one of the chief financiers of its expansion. Technology stocks soared, sank and rallied again, with a 1.6% jump in the S&P 500 Friday capping a week of gains across risk assets.

The recent turbulence, which Trump acknowledged Thursday had briefly left him concerned, was an unusually intense bout of the volatility that has gripped Wall Street for months as the financial and economic stakes of the AI boom have grown.

"There was a tacit admission – or maybe not even so tacit – that Nvidia's too big to fail, Jensen is too big to fail, and if you're well enough connected with the powers that be, you'll get bailed out to some extent," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.
The euphoria over Huang's return had barely lasted a day before stocks started sliding again, while fresh tariff threats from the Trump administration added to market swings.

An average of 21 billion shares changed hands daily in the first three sessions, the busiest start to Thanksgiving week in Bloomberg data going back to 2008. The Nasdaq 100 Index had alternated between weekly gains and losses of more than 3% for four straight weeks, something not seen since July 2022.

Through Wednesday's close, a gauge of expected volatility in the Nasdaq 100 had averaged 33 in November, putting it on course for its highest monthly reading since April 2022 and the highest for any November since the global financial crisis. Relative to a diversified portfolio of global stocks, bonds and commodities, US equities have been this volatile only once before since the pandemic, going by 30-day measures of realized volatility.

At the heart of the whiplash is a question that even the full political weight of the US government cannot answer: Who will emerge as the winners and losers from one of the biggest investment booms in history? The prospect of higher borrowing costs only compounds the dilemma, raising the bar for those investments to pay off.

Uncertainty over future demand for all the computing capacity being built is making markets particularly sensitive to incremental news, said Michael Reynolds, vice president of investment strategy at Glenmede. "Every time we get a new piece of information on a headline here, investors are updating their priors."

That uncertainty is making investors more discriminating about where they put their money. At RWA Wealth Partners, which has about $22 billion under management, Chief Investment Officer JP Powers said investors are shying away from specialized cloud-computing providers and diversifying into sectors such as health care and consumer staples.

"If you just sat back for the week and looked at the weekly returns, you'd probably be happy to have missed some of these violent swings here and just stuck it out in the Dow, more value-oriented names," Powers said.

For now, the gyrations on Wall Street stand in contrast to the strength of the American economy. Data this week showed gross domestic product expanded at a 4.3% annualized pace in the third quarter. The AI spending spree, household wealth, resilient consumption and government outlays have all helped sustain the expansion.

While a prolonged slump in stocks could take a toll on consumer spending, the more immediate concern for investors is that the economy remains too hot to warrant monetary relief. Traders are all-in betting on an interest-rate increase from the Federal Reserve next month, further complicating the economics of the AI buildout.

The flip side is that the very investment boom unnerving Wall Street is helping insulate the economy against a downturn, according to Justin Bergner, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. "We also have a much stronger economic engine in AI than we have had supporting past cycles," he said.

Investors may not need to resolve the question of who ultimately profits from AI to make money in the stock market over the next few months. The recent bouts of turbulence have left hedge funds with some of their lowest net equity exposure in years, a cohort of systematic traders heavily short and demand for protection against losses elevated. In that scenario, even a modest improvement in sentiment could unleash a substantial wave of buying.
Bergner, for one, bought Nvidia shares last Friday afternoon after Huang's departure pushed the stock to recent lows, betting on a rebound.
"I am looking selectively at buying into some tech names like I did with the Nvidia position, just based on the notion that tech feels very heavily sold in the market," he said.
--With assistance from Lu Wang and Rita Nazareth.
