noahpinion.blog/p/the-coming-age-of-sodi.headline: The coming age of sodium-ion batteries
noahpinion.blog/p/the-coming-age-of-sodi.author: Alex Shoer

paragraphs.text: One source of constant frustration for me is that Americans, by and large, seem to be missing the importance of the battery revolution. Batteries represent a truly revolutionary shift in our ability to store energy and move it around at will in arbitrarily large or small pieces. The country continues to install batteries at a decent clip, and there is some dawning realization in the Trump administration that batteries are actually important (thanks to their usefulness in data centers). But many American technologists don’t seem very excited about batteries, opinion leaders aren’t paying much attention, and politicians have politicized the issue to the point where Trump and Republicans actively attack the EV industry.

I try to remind people about the importance of batteries every chance I get. So when Alex Shoer, an energy VC and founder, offered to write me a guest post about why he thinks sodium-ion batteries will create a revolution in the space, I was happy to oblige. Sodium-ion is a technology that China has really poured a lot of resources into, but America has largely slept on, so we need to catch up.

Alex Shoer is currently a managing partner at GridVest, a company that delivers end-to-end battery storage procurement, financing, and commissioning for commercial and industrial and utility-scale projects. You can learn more about Alex at his website and his X account.

A decade ago, if you’d told a room of battery engineers that lithium iron phosphate (LFP) would take over the market, most of them would have laughed. LFP held noticeably less energy per kilogram than the nickel-rich chemistries that most used, and as recently as 2020 it supplied under a fifth of the world’s EV batteries.

Then something surprising happened: LFP got cheap, stayed safe, and turned out to be good enough. By 2023 it powered about 80% of new grid storage, and by 2025 it supplied more than 55% of EV batteries worldwide, with cells now around $84 per kilowatt-hour. I watched that shift up close from Shanghai, and I think we’re about to see the same thing again. This time with a battery made from one of the most common elements on Earth: sodium.

I want to make the case for why sodium-ion batteries will win, but I also want to be clear about what “win” means, because that’s where most of the hype, and most of the skepticism, goes wrong. Sodium-ion is not cheaper or more power dense than LFP today, but economists will recognize this pattern, because it’s one of the oldest in industrial history: the product that wins isn’t always the best one. It’s the cheapest one that’s good enough, made from inputs nobody can corner.
A market growing faster than anyone could have imagined

Start with demand. Global battery demand passed 1 terawatt-hour in 2024, according to the IEA. To put that in perspective, a single average week of battery demand in 2024 exceeded the entire year’s demand from a decade earlier. Most of that went into cars. But the fastest-growing slice, and the one I spend my days on, is stationary storage: the big refrigerator and shipping-container-sized systems that store cheap solar energy during the day and release it in the evening, stabilize grids, and increasingly keep data centers and microgrids running.

Stationary storage used to be a rounding error next to EVs. That’s changing because the economics changed and the demand for more on and off-grid capacity has changed. When I started in renewables in 2011, a battery on the grid was a science project. Today, in places like California, Texas and New York, solar-plus-storage is the cheapest way to add reliable evening capacity. And now AI data centers, which need enormous amounts of firm power fast (and to smooth the spiky power draw of AI chips), are turning storage from a nice-to-have to a requirement.

Here’s the key point: stationary storage doesn’t really care much about weight. A car battery has to be light, because every kilogram costs range. A stationary/grid battery sits on a concrete pad and never moves after it’s installed. What storage buyers care about is cost per kilowatt-hour over its lifetime, safety, how many times it can cycle, and whether supply is reliable. That list describes exactly what sodium-ion is good at.
Where sodium-ion is today

Sodium-ion today is tiny. LFP manufacturing is measured in terawatt-hours of capacity; sodium is measured in tens of gigawatt-hours. CRU, a commodities research firm, forecasts sodium-ion demand of 135 GWh in 2030 and 346 GWh in 2035. At the other end, Morgan Stanley expects 830 GWh by 2030 and 2.4 TWh by 2035, which would be roughly a fifth of the battery market by 2030 and over a third by 2035. That’s a six- to sevenfold gap between forecasts, and that difference is the story. Almost nobody disputes that sodium works. The argument is about how fast it gets cheap.

The world’s largest battery makers are no longer treating sodium as a side project. CATL launched a sodium-ion platform called Naxtra in 2025 and signed large sodium supply deals for grid storage. BYD has invested in dedicated sodium-ion lines. Hithium, one of China’s biggest stationary storage-cell makers, just launched a 785 amp-hour sodium cell for grid systems. And the first grid-scale projects are running: a 50 MW / 100 MWh sodium-ion station in Hubei, built with HiNa Battery cells, came online in 2024, with expansion planned.

GetFocus, tracks how fast technologies improve rather than how big they are. By its measure, sodium-ion is improving at about 57% a year since 2010, the fastest of the 30 storage technologies it analyzed. That’s the kind of early-warning signal LFP showed against nickel chemistries a decade before it took over. Size tells you who’s winning now. Slope tells you who’s winning next.
What’s actually inside a sodium-ion battery
Most people’s understanding of sodium-ion stops at “it uses salt instead of lithium.” That’s generally correct, but the more interesting story is in what else changes.
A battery has four main parts: a cathode, an anode, an electrolyte that lets ions shuttle between them, and thin metal foils, called current collectors, that carry electricity in and out.
Three things jump out.
• The cathode options are cheap and diverse. Prussian blue is literally a chemistry related to a centuries-old paint pigment.

• Second, sodium cells use hard carbon (an organic component) instead of graphite. That turns out to be the current bottleneck: hard carbon supply chains are young and expensive (but eventually hard carbon could become a benefit as it could be derived from waste products).

• Sodium cells can use aluminum foil on both sides instead of copper. This is one of my favorite details as aluminum is cheaper and lighter, and it means sodium batteries can be shipped fully discharged, at zero volts, without damage. Lithium-ion batteries can’t do that safely (the copper will degrade). If you’ve ever dealt with the paperwork and insurance of shipping hazardous lithium cargo across the Pacific, you understand why it would make logistics so much easier and in some cases could allow for fewer dangerous goods provisions.
Are the inputs cheaper?

On paper, yes. Sodium carbonate, the raw material, costs roughly $100 to $500 per ton. Lithium carbonate in LFP has swung between about $6,000 and $86,000 per ton since 2020, and this spring it jumped about 70% in a few months. Sodium is extracted from seawater and vast mineral deposits on every continent. Lithium is concentrated in a handful of countries and refined mostly in one (and it’s a messy process).
When will sodium-ion cells be cheaper than LFP?
HiNa’s general manager estimates sodium cells at 0.5 to 0.7 yuan per watt-hour, against 0.3 to 0.5 for lithium cells. Independent trackers put the premium at roughly 13% to 25%. Why? Three reasons:
• LFP has a decade of manufacturing learning and enormous scale.
• Hard carbon is still pricey.

• Sodium cells store less energy per kilogram, about 175 Wh/kg for the best commercial cells versus up to 205 for LFP, so you need more of everything else per kilowatt-hour (including higher shipping costs per Wh).

The IEA estimates sodium-ion could cost up to 20% less than today’s batteries once it reaches scale, and some analysts put the gap at 30%. Putting the crossover around 2028 to 2029. Notably, that date keeps slipping, because LFP keeps getting cheaper: cells fell from about $115 to $84 per kWh between early 2023 and early 2026.
Sodium as a backstop technology

William Nordhaus coined the term “backstop technology” in the 1970s: a substitute available at a fixed cost, which caps how expensive a scarce resource can get. Sodium-ion is shaping up to be lithium’s backstop.

Between late 2020 and late 2022, lithium prices rose more than tenfold, battery prices rose for the first time in years, and storage projects I was working on got repriced mid-negotiation. With a mature sodium-ion industry, every storage buyer would have had a lithium-free alternative, and the spike in price would have been far less if sodium was a real alternative.
So even before sodium wins much market share, it turns lithium into an ordinary commodity with a substitute. That’s a win for everyone building the grid, whether or not they ever buy a sodium cell.
Where sodium beats LFP outright
Cost is the headline, but performance is where sodium already has real advantages.

Cold weather. Lithium batteries lose much of their capacity in deep cold and need heating systems to operate safely. Sodium-ion handles cold far better. BYD rates its sodium storage cell from −30°C to 55°C. For projects in Minnesota, Alberta, or northern China, that means less energy spent heating the battery and better winter performance.

Safety. Sodium cells are generally less prone to thermal runaway, and the zero-volt shipping capability (as mentioned earlier) makes logistics and storage simpler. Fire risk is the single biggest source of local opposition to storage projects in the US. A chemistry that eases that fear is worth a lot more than its spec sheet suggests.

Shelf life and logistics. The same zero-volt trick may matter even more for how batteries move and are stored. For stationary projects stuck a year or more in interconnection queues, that could mean equipment that sits on site without aging, spare cells that don’t degrade (or need to be cycled). So far manufacturers they can hold more cell inventory and build more in advance. For distributors and developers they can order equipment earlier. The multi-year storage data of sodium-ion batteries doesn’t exist yet. But if it holds up, it changes the economics of an industry where so much hardware spends so long waiting and being shipped as Hazardous Materials (”HazMat”).

Cycle life, with caveats. Some manufacturers are making huge claims: Hithium rates its new sodium cell for 20,000 cycles and a 30-year calendar life, and HiNa’s storage cells are rated for 8,000 cycles. These aren’t field results but if credible warranties back them up they are pretty meaningful numbers compared to LFP which is more in the 6,000 cycle range. In my work, we’ve learned to trust a spec sheet only as far as the warranty behind it. Most stationary storage projects average 1-2 cycles per day and the more they can be cycled typically the better their return on investment is and the lower the Levelized Cost of Storage (LCOS) is.

Power output / C rating: Sodium-ion batteries can often sustain higher continuous and peak discharge rates (C-rates, typically 3C to 5C) without significant damage compared to many standard lithium-ion chemistries like LFP which tend to be .5C to 1C. This is a huge benefit to microgrids and datacenters in particular that want Universal Power Supply (UPS) quick response backup or are supporting large loads.

Environmental footprint. A sodium-ion pack produces about 56.8 kg of CO₂ per kWh, roughly 25% less than LFP’s 75.5. Most of the gain comes from replacing lithium and from lower-temperature cathode processing. Not every study agrees, and hard carbon production is the main hotspot, but the direction is encouraging. Sodium-ion also avoids lithium mining, cobalt and copper.
The on-ramp: sodium-lithium hybrids

The switch to sodium probably won’t be a clean break. The more likely path runs through hybrids that put sodium and lithium cells in the same system and let software give each the job it does best. China Southern Power Grid switched on the first large-scale example in May 2025: a 200 MW / 400 MWh station in Yunnan pairing HiNa’s sodium cells with lithium-ion. Hithium is now marketing a lithium-sodium hybrid for AI data centers. The logic is a portfolio one. Lithium carries the bulk of the energy and the density, while sodium takes the fast bursts, the cold snaps and the heavy cycling, which is exactly where it’s strongest. For buyers, a hybrid is a way to put sodium to work at modest volumes, build a track record, and shift the mix as sodium gets cheaper, without betting a whole project on a young chemistry.

Hybrids aren’t risk-free, though. Two chemistries with different voltage curves and aging rates make the control software harder, and a mistake in that software becomes a safety problem as well as a performance one. Each chemistry needs its own fire testing and certification, warranties have to cover how the two interact, and lenders have even less field data on hybrids than on pure sodium. And if lithium stays cheap, the hybrid’s cost edge narrows. I think of hybrids as a bridge rather than a destination: their value is that they let the market learn while the cost curves cross.
Will sodium ever go into mainstream EVs?
This is the question I get most, and my answer is: partly, and from the bottom up.

The constraint is energy density. At about 175 Wh/kg, the best sodium cells today are roughly where LFP was several years ago, and that was good enough for standard-range cars. So the plausible path is cheap city cars, scooters and three-wheelers first, which already matter enormously in China, India and Southeast Asia, and then hybrid packs that pair sodium with lithium cells to improve cold-weather performance. Long-range SUVs and trucks will likely stay with lithium chemistries for the foreseeable future.
But notice that sodium doesn’t need EVs to win. Stationary storage alone is on track to become one of the largest battery markets in the world. Sodium can be a niche in cars and a giant on the grid.
Can the US dominate sodium-ion?
Now the uncomfortable part for Americans. Sodium-ion is often pitched as a way to escape Chinese lithium supply chains. The chemistry does escape lithium. But it doesn’t escape China.

Sodium-ion is made on largely the same equipment, with largely the same processes, as LFP. Hithium says its new sodium cell runs on its existing 1,000 amp-hour lithium-ion manufacturing platform. CATL’s sodium storage product uses the same enclosures, lines and supply chains as its lithium products. Spencer Gore, founder of the now-shuttered US startup Bedrock Materials that was attempting to manufacture sodium-ion in the US, put it bluntly: “If you lost it for lithium-ion, you’ve already lost it for sodium. It’s the same thing, same equipment, same process.” When asked what he would have done differently, “I would have gone to China the very first day that I founded the company.”

The companies that know how to build gigawatt-scale factories, and that control the hard-carbon supply chain, are mostly Chinese. Also companies like CATL can afford to lose money on sodium for years, treating it as a hedge on its LFP business.
So far in the US Natron Energy went under and Bedrock shut down. The bright spot is Peak Energy, which shipped its first grid systems in 2025 and signed a 5 GWh deal with Jupiter Power.

But, I think America’s bigger bet belongs somewhere else as it’s already way behind. Solid-state batteries are a different kind of race. Much of the underlying science was pioneered in the US, and companies like QuantumScape, Solid Power and Factorial Energy are trying to skip past China’s lithium-ion manufacturers, with cells claiming roughly 300 to 390 Wh/kg, well beyond today’s EV batteries and the batteries that will be used for electric aviation. That’s a contest where research expertise, venture capital and automaker partnerships have a huge factor.

Of course Japan and South Korea are also close to mass production and Chinese giants are working on solid-state too. But if I were setting US battery strategy, I’d deploy sodium-ion storage wherever it pencils out today, build the anode supply chain at home, encourage foreign investments in factories in the US, push for US integration of Chinese battery cells in the meantime and put the big policy bets on the next chemistry rather than trying to compete on the current ones. That argument deserves its own post but I touch on it in the Cleaning Up PodCast.
What could prove me wrong
• Lithium stays cheap (and gets cheaper) for a decade. If new supply keeps prices low, the urgency to switch fades and sodium remains a niche.
• LFP keeps outrunning sodium on cost. LFP’s learning curve has repeatedly surprised everyone. If it hits $50/kWh at scale before sodium does, the crossover may be tough to arrive.
• Cycle-life claims don’t hold up in the field. If real-world degradation looks more like the skeptical tests than the spec sheets, storage buyers will walk away.
• Hard carbon doesn’t scale. If the anode supply chain stays tight and expensive, sodium’s materials advantage stays theoretical.
The bottom line
The history of energy is not a history of the best technology winning. It’s a history of good-enough technologies made from abundant materials getting cheap at scale.

Sodium-ion probably won’t win everywhere. But it will likely win the grid, the cold environments, and on LCOS, and by simply existing at scale it will cap the price of lithium for everyone else. That might be the most interesting kind of victory: the one that makes the whole market work better, even for the people who never buy the product.

npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6054055/the-str.headline: The strategy behind those Black Friday deals
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6054055/the-str.author: Kenny Malone

paragraphs.text: A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:
If you are shopping today for Black Friday discounts, Planet Money's Kenny Malone wants you to know about the backstory for big deals.

KENNY MALONE, BYLINE: If you walk into a Target today, you will likely see a display of 50%-off games, including "Sell Me A Sasquatch," a purple-colored game secretly about economics that we have been making as a reporting project. And this Black Friday placement and sale has been in the works for almost a year.
MARTIN MARECHAL: We probably pitched it earlier this year - like, January or February.

MALONE: Martin Marechal is a VP with the company Exploding Kittens, which publishes our game. And his pitch to the big-box retailer was - Exploding Kittens makes games for different age groups that would look good together and will all start from the same price point.
MARECHAL: They like to have a story. Sometimes price is the story, especially for Black Friday.
MALONE: The story is all the same price?
MARECHAL: It's game under 20, you know?
MALONE: Used to be 20, now isn't. That's the story. Yeah.
DAISY RITZ: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
MALONE: Yeah.
RITZ: Yeah.

MALONE: That last voice there is Exploding Kittens' VP of brand, Daisy Ritz. And yeah. They have agreed to sell our game for half price. But the calculation is that this Black Friday sale gets our game out there, 'cause games are one of these products that grow exponentially from network effects.
RITZ: So there is this webbing effect that can happen with a great game where it starts to spread. We just need to ignite that to start spreading.
MALONE: But not all product categories may have the same goals on Black Friday.
DINESH GAURI: Now, for products like television or...
MALONE: Blenders? Let's talk about blenders in there.
GAURI: Yeah. So I think...

MALONE: Dinesh Gauri is a marketing professor at the University of Buffalo - has studied retail discounting. And he says maybe a manufacturer's trying to get rid of old models of a product, or maybe they're trying to build brand loyalty. Or maybe, Gauri says, selling us the physical product is just opening a door. Like, think about smart TVs. Those companies can make money off of us even after we buy the TV by collecting and monetizing our data.
GAURI: So then TV becomes a medium by which - like, they can basically advertise through there.
MALONE: There's a secondary business model here that could make up for the fact that they sold the TV at a discount.
GAURI: Yes. There is.

MALONE: Companies will often have minimum advertised price policies for retailers. And to do these Black Friday sales, they may carve out little exceptions that say, for one week only, we're cool selling our game for, you know, ten bucks instead of 20. Although, says Martin Marechal from Exploding Kittens, sometimes store-to-store price matching can mess things up.
MARECHAL: Yeah. I mean, it's every sales guy's nightmare.

MALONE: These days, Target and Walmart and Amazon have systems to immediately match competitor prices. And even if our sale on "Sell Me A Sasquatch" is supposed to expire after a week, Marechal says it doesn't mean the price-matching standoff always unwinds perfectly.
MARECHAL: Just have to - after the deals are done, the systems still look at each other and get stuck. So sometimes you get the price stuck for longer than you want.
MALONE: Oh, no.
MARECHAL: And - yeah.
MALONE: Don't say that. No.
MARECHAL: Yeah. So it's very tricky.
MALONE: Like it or not, every Black Friday discount strategy comes with its own risks and rewards.
Kenny Malone, NPR News.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
MARTÍNEZ: Find the whole series on designing and manufacturing a party game based on Nobel Prize-winning economics in the Planet Money podcast feed.

npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6052399/califor.headline: California voters pass billionaire's measure to bankroll his own medical lab
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6052399/califor.author: April Dembosky

paragraphs.text: California voters pass billionaire's measure to bankroll his own medical lab California voters passed a ballot measure backed by a billionaire to fund $8.4 billion in immunology research. Half the funding will go to the research group funded by the same billionaire.
Science
California voters passed a ballot measure backed by a billionaire to fund $8.4 billion in immunology research. Half the funding will go to the research group funded by the same billionaire.
A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

California voters rejected a proposal to fund healthcare by taxing billionaires, but they approved a ballot measure from a Southern California billionaire asking taxpayers to bankroll his new medical lab. From member station KQED, April Dembosky has more on Proposition 38.
APRIL DEMBOSKY, BYLINE: This fall, Marianne O'Malley was at one of her regular boxing classes for people with Parkinson's. Her classmates asked her if they should vote for Prop 38.
MARIANNE O'MALLEY: We're all desperate for a cure or at least treatment.

DEMBOSKY: Exercise is the top therapy proven to slow progression of the disease. Her classmates were excited by Prop 38 and its promise to find new immunotherapy treatments for Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and cancer.
O'MALLEY: The disappointing thing is to tell them, no, this measure doesn't do what you think it's going to do.

DEMBOSKY: O'Malley worked for 30 years at the state Legislative Analyst's Office in Sacramento. When she dug into the fine print of Prop 38, she says she was horrified. The measure authorizes the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund immunology research. But half the money is slated for one institute, backed by the same billionaire who put the measure on the ballot.
O'MALLEY: This measure hijacks the initiative process to steer public funds to a billionaire's philanthropic project.
DEMBOSKY: But other patients see merit in Prop 38. Laurie Adami was diagnosed with blood cancer 20 years ago. She suffered through multiple treatments, including grueling rounds of chemo.
LAURIE ADAMI: So chemotherapy is like the napalm. So they poison your whole body in the hopes of killing off your cancer, but there's a lot of collateral damage.

DEMBOSKY: In 2018, she enrolled in a clinical trial for an immunotherapy called CAR-T. Doctors extracted her immune cells and re-engineered them to attack her cancer. Put another way, these immune cells are like Pac-Mans. And scientists altered them so they'd be hungry only for Adami's cancer cells, then infused them back into her body to start eating.
ADAMI: So this idea of waking up the immune system in a much more elegant way to target the cancers.
DEMBOSKY: Adami had one CAR-T treatment and has been cancer-free ever since.
ADAMI: Why wouldn't I want more patients to be able to access the type of treatment that finally saved my life?

DEMBOSKY: But immunotherapy doesn't work for everyone. Only 15% to 20% of patients have durable results. Clinical trials in general are largely speculative. Only 14% of experimental drugs ever reach FDA approval. That's why another cancer survivor, Dan Carson, is suspicious of the claims that Prop 38 will, quote, "pay for itself" by returning 10% of licensing fees from new discoveries back to California.
DAN CARSON: I am here to tell you that won't happen. Not even close.

DEMBOSKY: Carson says the odds of finding enough successful new treatments are too low. He's also a retired legislative analyst. He says supporters of an earlier bond measure to fund stem cell research made the same claim that it would be cost-neutral, but the state only received a tiny fraction of the billions it was promised in returns.
CARSON: So here we go again with Prop 38.

DEMBOSKY: The billionaire behind the measure, Gary Michelson, is not doing interviews. But his campaign says the global immunotherapy market is worth more than $200 billion, and it's growing fast. They're confident the research will generate plenty of revenue to repay the bond with interest.
For NPR News, I'm April Dembosky in San Francisco.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy5p4gdnwvo.headline: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy5p4gdnwvo.author: Paul Kirby

paragraphs.text: Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
Pedro Sánchez's government "has betrayed us, he has robbed us and he has lied to us", Abascal told an audience earlier in Tarancón, to the south-east of Madrid.

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".

He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

wsj.com/business/energy-oil/oil-prices-r.headline: Oil Futures Settle Lower Ahead of OPEC+ Policy Meeting — 2nd Update

paragraphs.text: Oil futures settled lower Friday with traders weighing renewed threats to Middle Eastern supplies and awaiting a weekend meeting of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies to discuss output policy for 2027.

Brent crude for January delivery fell 1.2% to $95.44 a barrel, ending the week up 3.1% and snapping a three-week losing streak. West Texas Intermediate crude for January fell 0.7% to $83.08 a barrel and was down a 0.4% from a week earlier, a fourth consecutive weekly loss.

Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Thursday that an attack on the Jazan oil refinery sparked a fire and temporarily halted some operations. Authorities were assessing the damage and checking the safety of the facilities, the ministry said.

Meanwhile, an Iranian drone attack in Kuwait killed two Italian technicians, The Wall Street Journal reported. Iran denied responsibility for the attack, which comes as negotiations between Washington and Tehran remain deadlocked despite a ceasefire.

"Prices had been under pressure for roughly four weeks as the market leaned into surplus talk," Price Futures Group senior market analyst Phil Flynn said in a note. But attacks on Saudi infrastructure and continued incidents around the Strait of Hormuz have put risk premium back, he added.

Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz remain at just 31% of prewar levels, according to preliminary data from Kpler. While Iraqi crude exports remain relatively strong, delays to some November and December cargoes have raised concerns over the reliability of near-term Middle Eastern supplies, Alex Booth, head of research at the data provider, said.

OPEC and other producers in the broader group called OPEC+ are expected to discuss their collective output policy for 2027 on Sunday, with existing production agreements set to expire at the end of this year.

The group's assessment of members' sustainable production capacities will help determine individual output quotas for next year. However, disruptions to production and exports during the Iran war have complicated efforts to establish how much individual countries can pump.
It remains unclear whether Saudi Arabia--the cartel's de-facto leader--and other members will restore more supply, maintain current restrictions or consider fresh cuts to support prices.
The impact on oil prices of Sunday's OPEC+ meeting is likely to be tempered by the outlook for the regional conflict, analysts at MUFG said in a note Friday.

The meeting could end without a final decision, leaving current production quotas in place for the time being, Commerzbank analyst Barbara Lambrecht said. With the exception of Iraq, most OPEC+ members are producing well below their existing quotas, while some countries, including Russia, are unable to increase output further, she said.

"Long-running tensions within the group may surface over output quota decisions," and disputes among members could weaken the group's pricing power, Capital Economics senior climate and commodities economist Hamad Hussain said in a note. "A more fractious and less cohesive OPEC+ will lead to greater oil price volatility and skew the balance of risks towards lower oil prices over time."

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/pete-h.headline: ‘Abusive and insulting to Canadians’: campaign to oust US ambassador presented to parliament

paragraphs.text: A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.
“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico.
She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.
The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.
The US state department said it was aware of the petition.
Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.

Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.
Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.
The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.
“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.
Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.
Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.
Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.
“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV.

Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/27.headline: A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/27.author: Grey Battle

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”
Virginia sheriff’s office ends agreement with ICE after court ruling

The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia, this week ended its cooperation agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an appeals court upheld a state law limiting local law enforcement cooperation with immigration agents.

Virginia was one of several states this year to place restrictions on participation in ICE’s 287(g) program, which allows state and local officials to be deputized to conduct immigration enforcement. A federal judge temporarily blocked the provision from taking effect in July after the Justice Department sued, but a federal appeals court Monday reversed that decision.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office entered into a 287(g) agreement last year, authorizing its officers to execute ICE administrative warrants, known as detainers, on individuals already in the sheriff’s custody. In an email, sheriff’s office spokesman Tom Julia said the department will abide by the court’s decision. He said the department no longer will keep an individual scheduled for released in custody based on an ICE warrant, but it will continue to honor immigration warrants that are “concurrent” with a person’s release.

So far this year, ICE has issued 673 detainers for noncitizen inmates in the Loudoun County jail, of whom 330 were transferred to ICE custody, according to Julia. The sheriff’s office has not released anyone to ICE since the appeals court ruling, he said.
The agreement had long been a point of contention between Loudoun Sheriff Mike Chapman and the county’s Democratic-controlled board of supervisors.

Loudoun County Board Chair Phyllis J. Randall said in a statement that she was “very pleased” by the sheriff’s decision, adding: “Across our country, poorly trained ICE agents have wreaked havoc, caused death, killed American citizens and terrorized American cities.”
Latin American researcher
Mexico condemns DEA tip line asking people to report corrupt officials in Sinaloa

MEXICO CITY — The Mexican government presented a formal complaint to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico after the Drug Enforcement Administration promoted a tip line for information that would help “expose corruption” and “dismantle narcoterrorist organizations.”

DEA chief Terry Cole, in a post Wednesday on X, shared a dedicated tip line now available in Sinaloa to report alleged members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, corrupt government officials and criminal networks involved in money laundering. Another line will be opened for Jalisco state, he said.

In response, Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco presented a formal complaint to U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson in an effort to defend Mexico’s sovereignty, President Claudia Sheinbaum said. The DEA did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

“We have made it very clear to the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said during her Friday morning news conference. She described the tip line as a form of U.S. “interference” in Mexico.

While Mexico accepts its responsibility to stop drugs from crossing the border, Sheinbaum said, the U.S. also has a responsibility to reduce drug use among its own population and to detain the cartel members distributing drugs and laundering money within U.S. territory.

The spat comes after the Mexican government, aided by intelligence gleaned by U.S. drones, arrested one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives in Sinaloa. Pressured by President Donald Trump’s administration to do more against cartels, Mexico has increased its security operations in Sinaloa, where a violent turf war has taken place after the U.S. arrested drug kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada.
Reporter covering issues in national K-12 education
Illinois will not opt in to federal school voucher program
Illinois will not participate in the nation’s new voucher-style federal tax credit program when it launches in January, Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker said this week.

Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, echoed objections voiced by many Democrats, saying voucher programs subsidize tuition for families already in private schools and take money from public schools.

“At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education,” Pritzker said in a statement.

The new program puts Democratic governors who oppose vouchers in a political conundrum. It will let taxpayers donate to certain nonprofits, which will then give scholarships to private school families for tuition. The program also allows funds to go to public school students for services such as tutoring.
The federal government will reimburse eligible taxpayers for every dollar they donate, up to $1,700, via a tax credit. Governors must opt their states into the program.
Most states that plan to take part are led by Republicans.
A growing cohort of left-leaning advocates says governors who do not opt in are passing up billions of dollars that can help public schools.

Pritzker’s “decision is precisely how Democrats squander the opportunity that emerged from the recent election: focusing on fighting Trump so much that we become more driven to oppose him than to deliver for our constituents,” Jorge Elorza, chief executive of Democrats for Education Reform, said in a statement.
Additional Coverage
Reporter covering the military and national security
U.S. military jet disables commercial vessel in Gulf of Oman
A U.S. military jet fired a precision munition into the stern of a commercial ship Thursday in the Gulf of Oman and disabled it, U.S. Central Command said Friday in a statement.

The Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer had departed from Bandar Abbas, a port city in Iran, and was attempting to run the naval blockade the U.S. is enforcing on any ship departing Iran as a way to cut off Tehran’s revenue. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s approach to try forcing Iran to concede after more than nine months of military operations since the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury in February.
The strike disabled the ship but did not harm the crew, Central Command said.
The U.S. has maintained a significant naval presence in the Arabian Sea and Gulf of Oman to stop any vessels carrying Iranian oil or other exports from leaving the country.
Reporter covering Russia
‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
The release of the highly anticipated “Grand Theft Auto VI” game has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles, sweeping shelves from the United States to Japan.

The Rockstar Games crime epic, 13 years in the making, came out last week and is playable only on the Xbox Series X or S and PlayStation 5, the most recent generation of consoles from Microsoft and Sony.
The game landed in an already strained market, where console manufacturers have been hit hard by a global memory chip shortage caused by AI companies buying up components.

In the United States, Sony’s higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900.

In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones. Private-sale platforms are flooded with ads from people looking to buy used consoles at the price of new. Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price.

In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.headline: Storms headed for Southland; heaviest rain coming Tuesday, Wednesday
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.author: Ruben Vives, Carlos De Loera

paragraphs.text: As Southern California’s high tides and warm temperatures start to subside this weekend, the National Weather Service is warning of several approaching storm systems that are expected to produce widespread rain, strong, gusty winds and a chance of thunderstorms.
During a news briefing Friday, Dave Gomberg, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said the first and smallest of the two storms likely will arrive Sunday night.
“At this point, it looks like just a beneficial light rain with most areas likely receiving less than a quarter of an inch of rainfall,” he said.

The second and strongest storm system, he said, will move into the region beginning Monday night and linger through much of Wednesday, producing widespread moderate to heavy rainfall and southerly wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph.
Warm ocean waters, he said, also could help boost the second storm system’s chance of producing strong thunderstorms and intense bursts of rain.
Gomberg said much of the storm’s impact will occur Tuesday when a half-inch to 1 inch of rain per hour is expected to fall over the region.
He said the heavy rainfall could lead to overflowing creeks and riverbeds, eroding roads and rock slides and mudslides in burn areas such as Pacific Palisades and Altadena.

The coastal communities are expected to receive up to 3 inches of rain, with up to 4 inches or more along the coastal slopes and foothills. Gomberg said while the timing of lower tides is working in the coastal communities’ favor, elevated surf still could create minor to moderate risk of coastal flooding, especially around high tide.
Snow also is expected to fall in the mountains at or above 7,500 feet in elevation.

Forecasters said strong winds may create hazardous sea conditions and trigger small craft advisories along the coastal waters until Tuesday night. And the midweek storms may not be the end of the wet weather.
“Once we get past Wednesday, we do have the possibility of additional storms as we move into Friday and into next weekend,” Gomberg said.

Farther south in Orange and San Diego counties, as well as east in the Inland Empire, forecasters also were warning residents to be prepared for heavy rainfall that’s expected to hit Tuesday and into Wednesday.

National Weather Service meteorologist Dave Munyan said it was too early to tell the extent of that storm’s impact, but more would be known upon its arrival. He said about 2 to 3 inches of rain is expected to fall in the region.
The post-Thanksgiving storms will be an additional headache for coastal communities that have been experiencing record-breaking high tides, flood warnings and advisories.

In Northern California, 8-foot high tides made headlines this week when powerful waves caused portions of Pacifica’s pier to crumble into the ocean. In Laguna Beach, waves smashed a lifeguard tower into pieces. A video of it was shared on social media.

At least three so-called king tides have been forecast for this winter. These higher-than-normal tides occur when the gravitational pull of the sun and moon are strongest. The next king tides — Dec. 23 to 25 and Jan. 21 to 22 — are expected to bring some of the highest tides in recorded history to California.
Munyan said the king tides that have been affecting coastal cities across the state will continue to fall throughout the weekend.

“Tides will definitely be receding, which is again a good story that we’re kind of offsetting a big rainstorm potential like this from the king tides that we just had,” he said. “We’re going to be a good four or five days separated from some of the high tides we’ve just seen and hopefully some of those communities can get reset between now and then, and flip from coastal flood preparedness to potential rainfall and flash flood preparedness.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2898wq2qjo.headline: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2898wq2qjo.author: Brandon Drenon

paragraphs.text: Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.
If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

cnbc.com/2026/11/27/china-chip-stocks-be.headline: Chinese chip stocks notch biggest ever one-day gains as Beijing signals broader market support
cnbc.com/2026/11/27/china-chip-stocks-be.author: Evelyn Cheng, Anniek Bao

paragraphs.text: Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.

The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT, Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.

The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
State intervention offers relief
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government. Bob ChenShanghai-based venture capitalist

Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.

By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.

That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."

The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.

The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.

The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.

Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.headline: California's ocean temperatures shatter records and fuel flooding
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.author: Rong-Gong Lin II

paragraphs.text: Streets flooded across San Francisco.
A chunk of a Northern California pier was felled by 20- to 30-foot waves.
Homes were inundated with water in an Orange County neighborhood.

Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner train car windows were splashed by waves, with service suspended on Thanksgiving and Black Friday between Orange and San Diego counties because of a “washout” of its tracks.

Havoc from extreme weather has played out across California over the last few weeks and is tied to several factors, including exceptional king tides and storms fueled by El Niño. But weather experts say there is another root cause: record-high ocean temperatures.
Seawater temperatures started setting calendar-day records again this summer and have remained very high as winter approaches, leaving experts stunned as records continue to fall daily.
The seawater is so warm that surfers have been riding the waves without wet suits — in November.

“Is the ocean still ridiculously warm? ... The answer is still a heck yes,” UC Agricultural and Natural Resources climate scientist Daniel Swain said. “I would still call this record-shattering warm.”

The numbers are eye-popping up and down the California coast. Of the eight stations monitored by UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography that took measurements this week, every single one posted record-breaking temperatures.
For instance, on Friday in La Jolla, a neighborhood of San Diego, the sea surface temperature was 73.2 degrees, 12 degrees higher than normal for Nov. 27.

In Newport Beach on Friday, the ocean temperature was 71.6 degrees, compared with the average for Nov. 27 of 60.5 degrees. Zuma Beach in Malibu registered Wednesday at 70.3 degrees; the average for the calendar day is 60.2 degrees. Even farther north, the temperatures are jaw-dropping. On Sunday, the sea surface was 64.6 degrees at the Farallon Islands in San Francisco, where the average for that day is 55.2.
Scientists had expected ocean temperatures to be very warm, but the reality has been sobering.
Hot ocean temperatures are a significant reason for the unusually high sea levels, because hotter water takes up more volume — a process scientists call thermal expansion.
“The water molecules are literally taking up more volume and therefore more space,” Swain said.
Elevated seawater temperatures alone have made the ocean more than a foot higher than normal, worsening flood risks.

The water is warmer for a variety of reasons. Permanent human-caused global warming has elevated sea levels, Swain said, which will not go away and will get worse over our lifetimes. There’s also El Niño-influenced ocean warming, causing half a foot to nearly 2 feet of temporary sea-level elevation. The El Niño climate pattern, which involves a warming of ocean temperatures west of Peru, dispatches warm waters up the coast of the Americas through Kelvin waves, which have reached California’s shores, and their effects are expected to last for months.

This week brought us exceptionally high king tides — which will return again around Christmas and Martin Luther King Jr. Day — that are caused by the position of the moon and sun. “Then, if we do have a strong storm, we can on top of that get another half a foot to a foot and a half of storm surge,” Swain said. That would be a result of low barometric pressure, which allows water to expand in a low-pressure environment and, fueled by winds, pushes water toward shore.
Heat waves in ocean waters are very different from the kind of atmospheric heat waves we’re more familiar with. The ocean variety takes a long time to develop and a long time to fade.

“You can end an atmospheric heat wave, where the air is hot, essentially overnight,” Swain said. Ocean heat waves are “a lot stickier because you generally don’t have the same rapid changeover dynamics in the ocean.”
The fluid motion of the ocean is a lot slower than in the atmosphere. “You can get 100-mile-an-hour winds,” Swain said. “You generally don’t get 100-mile-an-hour ocean currents, for example.”

And the heat capacity of water is different from that of air. “Just think about how long it takes if you have a roaring flame on a pot of boiling water,” Swain said. “It takes a lot more energy to change the temperature of water than it does to [change] the temperature of air.”

So atmospheric heat waves that spike the temperature 20 to 40 degrees above average are familiar; extreme heat waves in ocean waters are not. That’s “why it is so extraordinary that we do actually now have a double-digit Fahrenheit marine heat wave along almost the entire California coast,” Swain said. “Just genuinely astonishing.”
Swain noted a phenomenon with sea-surface temperatures off California that’s a historic first for the state.

The climate scientist recently observed that “there is a region, all the way from about Ensenada, Mexico, northward to about [the] Sonoma County coast ... that is contiguously more than 10 degrees Fahrenheit above average. We have never seen that before at any point in recorded history in California.”
Fallout for the ocean’s inhabitants

Hot ocean temperatures are placing extreme stress on California’s kelp, said Jennifer Smith, marine ecologist and professor at Scripps Institution of Oceanography. Kelp is very important to marine ecosystems, forming a canopy that serves as a habitat for marine life. Marine heat waves have caused Northern California’s bull kelp habitats to decline by 90% since 2014, negatively affecting other species, including endangered white abalone, according to Nate Jaros, the Aquarium of the Pacific’s vice president of animal care for fish and invertebrates.
Kelp can be threatened by heat, either directly, causing it to essentially melt, or indirectly, by causing an abundance of a harmful bacteria, Vibrio, that targets sea stars.

“In the last El Niño event, we had a sea star wasting disease that happened as an indirect effect of the El Niño and warming. The sea stars eat the sea urchins, so when the sea stars died, the urchins rapidly exploded in abundance and subsequently ate all of the kelp,” Smith said, leaving behind urchin barrens, or a seafloor carpeted with urchins where kelp forests once stood.
In marine heat waves, wildlife that relies on kelp is pushed “past their thermal capacities,” she said.

Historically, “some of the largest continuous patches of kelp in the state of California” have thrived off La Jolla and Point Loma, Smith said, a phenomenon seen by satellites. But after the last big El Niño, in 2015-16, “we pretty much lost all of our canopy-forming species.”
There has been some limited recovery in the last year. But recent hot ocean temperatures have caused that recovery to dissipate.

“And so, if you’ve been out in the water in La Jolla, you’ve probably noted that there really is no giant kelp left. Most of it’s ended up on our beaches, drifting,” Smith said. “There are still a few patches of kelp remaining in Point Loma, which is amazing, and this is something that we’re desperately trying to study,” such as whether the surviving kelp have some ability to withstand higher temperatures.
Learning from the past
Every El Niño is different, but scientists note the alignment of several factors that when combined portend a more disastrous scenario.
Some of California’s worst El Niño disasters have happened when high tides, warm ocean waters and intense storms occur together.

During the El Niño of 1982-83, storms in December brought big waves but occurred at the lowest tides of the month, said Reinhard Flick, a researcher at Scripps Institution of Oceanography. But at the end of January, a huge storm coincided with the highest tides of the year.

This confluence caused the worst flooding in Southern California in decades, resulting in millions of dollars in damage, severely damaging piers in Santa Monica, Seal Beach and San Diego, and flooding homes in places including Malibu, Venice, Playa del Rey and Redondo Beach. Scripps Pier in La Jolla was so damaged that it had to be replaced and is now made of concrete.
“The coincidence of storms and big waves,” Flick said, “if they occur during these periods of peak high tides, that’s when the damage and the flooding and the beach erosion is the worst.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3d4y094x7o.headline: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cme3d4y094x7o.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.
"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.
Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."
But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.
For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.
Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.
The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.
In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.
"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.
"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."
The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.
He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."
* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

cbsnews.com/news/iowa-lead-detonation-ep.headline: Iowa lead detonation testing results expected soon, EPA says
cbsnews.com/news/iowa-lead-detonation-ep.author: Kierra Frazier
