paragraphs.text: The Environmental Protection Agency said Thursday it expects to begin receiving sample results as early as Friday night following the U.S. Army's detonation of a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa.

The EPA collected more than 1,600 air, water, soil and dust samples ahead of Wednesday's destruction of the lead azide stockpile, followed by more than 1,000 samples after the detonation, the agency said. Samples were sent to multiple EPA and private labs for testing.
"The agency is expecting to start receiving lab results on post-detonation sampling as early as tomorrow," the EPA said in a news release.

The EPA said it collected samples at more than 180 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, as well as at parks, nearby farms, drinking water sources and the Mississippi River watershed.
The EPA said Friday that it had completed 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes that were sampled pre-detonation, and expected to finish the remainder Friday.
As of Thursday, no airborne lead had been detected throughout the region, the EPA said.
The agency said it is also testing for other compounds that may have been released during the detonation.
"The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation," it said in Thursday's news release.

The Army on Wednesday detonated 5 tons of deteriorating explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant located in the small community of Middletown, citing the risk of an unplanned explosion. Local residents and environmental groups had sought to block the detonation over concerns that a plume of toxic lead dust could threaten public health and agriculture.

The Middletown plant housed about 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. The EPA said the lead azide had degraded over the last 20 years it had been in storage. It had undergone a recrystallization process that increased "the material's sensitivity to friction and shock" and made it more susceptible to the "risk of unintentional detonation," the EPA said.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation last week while it considered whether to impose a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups challenging the plan had failed to show they were likely to succeed.

The chaotic lead-up to the detonation reached the White House, prompting questions within the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
President Trump praised the detonation as having "exceeded expectations."

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9309nyg2vno.headline: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr9309nyg2vno.author: Kate Bowie

paragraphs.text: Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Barred from jobs
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.

This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.

Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.

But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.

Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
What is an ADHD or autism reassessment?

Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.

The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.

Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.

Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnoses but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
'I was stuck'
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.

Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.

During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.

During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment.
Fears about stigma
The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD.

"The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults.

Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society.
"That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds.
Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers.
Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair.

He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says.
Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds.
'Magic spell'
People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals.
Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed".
"It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says.
Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her.

Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change.
The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to.

"The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead.
Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis.
She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis.
"Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.
How it works

Instead of treating skip connections as a rigid, additive pipeline, DCA reframes residual learning as a dynamic routing problem. Rather than passing all prior layers forward with equal weight, DCA introduces a lightweight, layer-wise module that decides how to best combine previous embeddings on a per-token basis.
The architecture introduces two primary mechanisms:

• Dynamic layer routing: For every token processed, DCA computes a unique set of mixing weights using a static, learnable base combined with an input-dependent projection. This allows the network to adaptively shift its processing structure — ranging from purely sequential to fully parallel — based on the specific context of the token.

• Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.
By allowing the network to dynamically select and retrieve high-resolution features from earlier layers, DCA eliminates the information dilution inherent to classic residual connections.
Experiments and results

To test whether DCA can overcome information dilution in practice, we evaluated our approach across controlled synthetic setups, large-scale language modeling benchmarks, and image classification tasks.
DCA demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed, training stability, and final model quality across these experiments.

On the colossal, cleaned version of Common Crawl's web crawl corpus (C4) and 1 Billion Word Language Model Benchmark (LM1B) datasets, DCA reached the performance of standard transformers in up to five times fewer training steps. When trained for the same duration or number of steps, DCA consistently achieved lower perplexity — how well a probability model predicts a sample — than standard residual connections, effectively extracting more representational capacity from the same training budget. To achieve a perplexity of <14 on LM1B, a standard transformer with fixed width required 42 layers, whereas the DCA model achieved a lower perplexity with only 30 layers — a 29% reduction in depth and parameter count.

One of the most common trade-offs in AI is that better models are often much larger and slower to run. DCA adds a tiny number of parameters — less than 0.2% of the total model size — making it negligible in terms of compute and memory footprint, while increasing memory bandwidth, as representations from different layers are presented intact rather than blended together. Interestingly, because DCA can be initialized to behave identically to a standard residual network, it doesn’t require training from scratch: retrofitting DCA onto an already pre-trained transformer and briefly continuing training reduced perplexity by 0.19 on LM1B, compared to just 0.02 for continued standard training.
A broader shift toward dynamic residual routing

As large language models (LLMs) are used across a broader range of domains, optimizing their training processes and underlying architectures is critical for scaling and unlocking new capabilities. DCA and similar dynamic residual techniques are already seeing significant adoption and success. The rapid emergence of these methodologies highlights dynamic routing as a highly active and promising area of research.
Attention residuals

Developed by Moonshot AI, attention residuals share DCA's core principles of replacing fixed addition with selective retrieval. Instead of blindly summing every prior layer's output, they use a learnable softmax attention mechanism paired with a layer-specific pseudo-query. This allows each layer to selectively weight and retrieve representations from earlier depths. By preventing the unbounded growth of hidden states and the dilution of early-layer information, this method improves gradient stability and boosts performance on reasoning-heavy tasks like coding and mathematics. To maintain computational efficiency at scale, a "Block AttnRes" variant partitions layers into blocks, recovering the benefits of full attention with significantly less memory overhead. The recent Inkling 2 model developed by Thinking Machines also adopted this design in addition to DCA’s cross attention (Q/K/V split) mechanism.
Hyper-connections

Hyper-connections expand the residual stream into multiple parallel channels, offering a form of memory scaling that goes beyond simply increasing model width or depth. They use a fixed-size stack where layer outputs are aggregated and mixed using learnable mixing matrices. However, this unconstrained mixing breaks the traditional identity mapping property of residual connections, which can cause amplification or attenuation of signals, and lead to training instability at scale.
Manifold-constrained hyper-connections

To address instability in standard hyper-connections, manifold-constrained hyper-connections apply specific constraints to the mixing matrices. By forcing these matrices to live on a defined manifold — specifically, constraining them to be doubly stochastic using the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm — manifold-constrained hyper-connections restore stable signal propagation. This approach prevents exploding or vanishing gradients while preserving the rich information flow and expressivity of the widened residual streams, allowing models to scale robustly.
Conclusion

DCA demonstrates that transitioning from static residual connections to dynamic, attention-based routing is a powerful strategy for building more efficient models. By leveraging an expanded residual stream and depth-wise cross-attention, DCA empowers deep networks to selectively retrieve and integrate token embeddings across different layers. We expect that next-generation models will dynamically route and weigh past layer representations based on the specific tokens or inputs being processed. This will allow for the effective use of all the model layers as specialized experts working in tandem, with maximum information sharing and no redundancy, leading to more expressivity and deeper interactions. We look forward to seeing how these multi-depth interactions will shape the next generation of transformer architectures.
Acknowledgements

This work was a collaboration between researchers at Google and academic partners, including Mike Heddes, Adel Javanmard, MohammadHossein Bateni, and Vahab Mirrokni, whose contributions were critical for the development of this work.

theguardian.com/australia-news/live/2026.headline: Victorian election 2026 live: voters head to the polls as Coalition seeks to topple Labor – latest news

paragraphs.text: What the polls say
The Coalition is poised to win 55 of 88 lower house seats according to a YouGov poll of more than 4300 voters, commissioned by the Herald Sun and News24 and published on election eve.
One Nation would gain 12 seats and the Greens would add five more MPs to their pack of three, according to the analysis conducted between 6 and 23 November.
A Newspoll reported by The Australian late on Thursday had the coalition extending to a 15-point lead over Labor on a two-party preferred basis.
The Coalition’s lead of 57.5% to Labor’s 42.5% compares with the coalition’s 55-45 lead in October before the election campaign began.
If the polls are correct the Victorian Greens will have their most successful campaign on record, gaining between 13% and 17% of primary votes.
Party leader Ellen Sandell received the second highest approval rating among undecided voters during the campaign’s only four-way leaders debate on 17 November.
- Australian Associated Press
Welcome
Good morning, and welcome to the Victorian election live blog.
I’m Josh Taylor and I will be taking you through until later this afternoon.

Going into today, polls suggest the Coalition will comfortably win majority government, while Labor faces an electoral wipeout after 12 years in government, with suggestions the premier, Ben Carroll, could lose his own seat.
More than 2.2 million people had already voted as of Friday, according to the Victorian Electoral Commission, meaning nearly half of those eligible have already cast their vote.
Just as well, too, given the weather in Victoria today. Those democracy sausage sandwiches will be a little wet today with all the rain.

There is a flood warning for parts of west, central and north-east Victoria, with possible minor flooding from Saturday morning for rivers including the Yarra. Rain is likely to continue throughout the day, easing into the evening with up to 30mm of rain expected in Melbourne.
Now let’s get into it.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20q9pw0116o.headline: Eetha, Maharashtra's Vithabhai Narayangaonkar: The 'Tamasha queen' of India whose fans paid for a show that never happened
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj20q9pw0116o.author: Amrita Kadam, Zoya Mateen

paragraphs.text: Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage.
Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child.
In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour.
"She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi.
Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?"
When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children.
"The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled.

Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre.
Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December.
Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life.

Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument.
Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each.
"The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event.
Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds.

How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism.

For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal.

Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them.
It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family.
Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy.

Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin.
Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge.
Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet.
Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra.

During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says.
At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier.

"Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said.

Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says.
There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences.
In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971.

Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters.
When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej."
No one asked for their money back.

But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted.
Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation.
Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours.
Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar.

Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders.
Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported.
Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon.
Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name.
Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy.
Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted.
"It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says.
But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate.
"The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3vg3lkrk03o.headline: Pete Edochie: How Nigeria's Things Fall Apart star became a Nollywood legend
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3vg3lkrk03o.author: Mansur Abubakar, Wycliffe Muia

paragraphs.text: For generations of Nigerians, Pete Edochie was more than a celebrated actor.
He was Okonkwo – the fierce, proud and troubled warrior whose portrayal in Things Fall Apart made him a household name and earned him a place in the hearts of millions.
Even in death, many Nigerians still refer to him by the character's name, a testament to the enduring impact of a role that defined his career.
Edochie died on 25 November, aged 79, in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.

In 1987, Edochie starred in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel. His portrayal of Okonkwo would change his life, establishing him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors and bringing him international recognition.
The series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
Joy Nnamdi, a fan of both the novel and its television adaptation, believes Edochie was the perfect choice for the lead role.
She said nobody else could have brought the character to life as convincingly.
"His character Okonkwo gave a face to the highly celebrated novel," she told the BBC in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos.
The role also cemented his reputation as a hard man, a screen persona he would maintain through much of his career.
"It was very rare to see him laugh in movies. He was the ultimate tough man," Nnamdi added.
With his deep, authoritative voice, imposing presence and effortless command of African proverbs, Edochie had a way of dominating a scene without raising his voice.
Whether playing a village elder, a wealthy businessman or a feared traditional ruler, he became an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.
Edochie went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has grown into one of the world's largest.
From Kenya to South Africa, MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels helped take his films into millions of African homes as Nollywood became a cultural phenomenon across the continent.
Although many of his films were rooted in his Igbo culture, their themes of family loyalty, inheritance disputes, spiritual beliefs and the abuse of power resonated with audiences far beyond Nigeria.
Before becoming a household name in the film industry, however, Edochie had built a successful career in broadcasting.
Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, northern Nigeria, he attended primary and secondary school in Kaduna before studying journalism and television at the School of Journalism and Television in the UK.
He joined the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967, the year Nigeria's civil war broke out.
He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra, and recently described the war years as the greatest personal challenge he ever faced.
"During the war, the experience that we had as Biafrans, you know, survival was difficult. Hunger was driving us into eating all sorts of nonsense," he recalled.

He rose through the ranks to hold senior management positions but then switched to acting. Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals and Billionaire's Club.
His career also bridged the transition from home-video productions to global streaming platforms.
The 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart, which became Netflix's first original Nigerian film, introduced his work to a wider international audience.
He also worked in Ghana, where he starred alongside some of the country's biggest film stars in the 2017 comedy John and John.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, Edochie found an unexpected new audience online.
His distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films became popular social media memes, introducing his work to a younger generation of Africans.
For many who had never watched Things Fall Apart or his early Nollywood films, his stern expressions became a humorous way of conveying disbelief, disapproval or exasperation at everyday situations.
But his reputation as a formidable screen presence was no joke to those who grew up watching him.
Sani Muazu recalls that parents in the northern Nigerian city of Kano would sometimes invoke Edochie's name to keep misbehaving children in check.
"They would tell you: 'Okonkwo will come and visit you if you don't stop' and we would begin acting right," he said.

"To be honest, we grew up scared of him. Even though he was on the screen and not physically present, some of his roles added to our fears because he played some popular occultic roles, and villain roles suited him."
Tributes poured in from fans and fellow actors following news of his death, with many describing him as a giant who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.
Popular actress Genevieve Nnaji paid her tribute in a post on X.

"I will let the assurance of the fact that you are a chosen one; and therefore, have returned to the most high God override my grief and heartbreak. May the heart of a true lion forever rest in peace. We love you," she wrote.
Patience Ozokwor, popularly known as Mama G, who appeared alongside Edochie in several productions, remembered him as a brilliant actor and a source of wisdom.
"He has been a father to stories that are told, like an elder sitting down telling you how things were done in those days," she told BBC News Pidgin.
"I called him any time, any day. He'll tell you what to do and what not to do."
Film director Babangida Bangis told the BBC that Edochie's death was a loss not just for Nigeria or Africa, but for the global film industry.
"Just days ago, during a seminar for filmmakers across the country, his name popped up as an example of brilliance on the screen, longevity and professionalism," he said.
"I think his loss is one for the world, not just Nigeria or Africa. We all grew up watching and loving him."
Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu also mourned the veteran actor, describing his death as a major loss to the country's film industry and cultural heritage.
The president, like many admirers, singled out Edochie's portrayal of Okonkwo, saying the performance and his subsequent roles had established him as one of Nigeria's most accomplished actors.
But beyond the fame and formidable character he portrayed on screen, his family remembers a man whose greatest legacy was the importance he placed on honesty and speaking the truth.
Leo Edochie, his son, told the BBC that his father was a strong-willed man.
"Of all his legacies, I think the whole world would agree that these two were the most important: telling the truth and remaining honest," he said.
He described his father as a man who lived an exemplary life, offering a model that young people could learn from and aspire to follow.
"I don't really have a choice, but the truth is that I have to carry on that legacy for our family," he added.
Edochie's influence also extended to his family, with two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, following him into the Nigerian film industry.
Yet, for an actor so closely associated with stern expressions and intimidating characters, some of his most endearing moments came when he let his guard down.
In 2021, he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for the song Highway, surprising fans with a display of dance moves that showed a lighter, more playful side of the septuagenarian.
It was a refreshing reminder that the man behind the formidable screen persona could also laugh, dance and enjoy himself.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.headline: Angie Martinez hid her explosive Tupac interview for 30 years. Why did she decide to finally press play?
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.author: Nate Jackson

paragraphs.text: There are few voices in New York hip-hop radio more recognizable than Angie Martinez. For over 30 years, the sound of her magnetic Brooklyn swagger and love for hip-hop transmitted through her microphone on Hot 97 FM and Power 105 FM, cementing her title as “The Voice of New York.” But on a recent fall evening in L.A., the hip-hop radio legend is dealing with the pain of losing a part of her that’s much less admired than her radio voice — her appendix.

“I’m really struggling right now, I’m gonna try not to laugh, cry or sneeze,” she tells The Times during an interview with a warm smirk on her face. Her hair is slicked back into a braided ponytail as she slowly sips hot lemon ginger tea and picks at cubes of Monterey Jack cheese and thin marbled slices of prosciutto on a charcuterie board.

Even sitting down in the tranquil, low-lit ambience inside the lobby of the 1 Hotel in West Hollywood, Martinez is trying to avoid agitating the slowly healing stitches on her abdomen underneath her thick gray hoodie. Though having the vestigial organ surgically removed at age 55 isn’t totally unheard of, its timing coincides with her extracting a piece of her history in hip-hop that she’s finally ready to share with the world.

The cassettes of an unreleased two-hour interview she did with Tupac Shakur inside his L.A. apartment in 1996 were recorded three months before he was fatally shot in Las Vegas. But 30 years after the conversation, her decision to co-produce and host “The Tupac Tapes With Angie Martinez,” a four-part video podcast that premiered Friday on Netflix, is her way to honor the West Coast hip-hop legend and examine their eye-opening conversation through a modern lens. It exposes why Martinez, who showed up to the Shakur interview as a bright-eyed, 25-year-old rising personality sporting chunky hooped earrings and a Nautica T-shirt, turned out to be the perfect person for the job. She’s also the person who would keep the recordings hidden for years out of respect for the damage they could’ve done.

“I don’t feel I’m the person to make the Tupac documentary, but I am the person to tell the story of how these tapes came to be, what the climate was for me, especially in New York, how it felt as a young woman going out there to do that,” Martinez said. “That’s my story to tell.”

In the summer of 1996, Martinez sat with Shakur (surrounded by his g-funk proteges, the Outlawz), with just a microphone and a tape recorder. Her intent was to help quash the legendary beef between Shakur and Notorious B.I.G., a.k.a. Biggie Smalls, at the height of the media-fueled East Coast/ West Coast rap war. But when they started talking, Pac’s anger directed at Biggie — his friend-turned-rival — along with now disgraced Bad Boy Records CEO Sean “Diddy” Combs (who is in prison) and acts like Mobb Deep did the exact opposite. Martinez ultimately decided to cut out the bulk of her interview and only broadcast a select 12 minutes on air, leaving the rest to be hidden away until now.

The explosive sit-down didn’t come about in the way most big interviews typically do. Shakur had initially asked Martinez to appear in his music video for “I Ain’t Mad at Cha” — which she politely declined. Not only did she have no desire to be a video girl, but with the East-West rap rivalry inciting violence across the country, an N.Y. radio DJ being involved with Pac’s latest hit would’ve made her a prime target for hometown hate and possibly worse.
“I was just trying to protect myself,” she remembers. “And he understood that, and he was lovely on the phone.”

Shakur had a special level of trust in Martinez as a voice on the radio he deemed credible. During his time in a New York prison serving eight months on a sexual assault conviction, hearing her fair approach to reporting about him on Hot 97 FM enticed him to follow up his music video request with an offer to do an interview with her that she could use for the radio. He said he’d be willing to talk about his feud with Biggie that erupted when Shakur was nearly killed after being ambushed, robbed and shot five times at Quad Recording Studios in Manhattan in 1994. Surprisingly, Shakur said his rage wasn’t meant to be directed at the entire East Coast. Born in East Harlem, he spent his formative years in New York and Baltimore before relocating to Oakland and later L.A., where his rap career took off.

“He was just like, ‘I wouldn’t be mad at the whole coast. That’s f–ing stupid,’” Martinez recalls. “He was laughing, very personable, not this big, bad, scary person. I thought if I could just get everybody to hear what I’m hearing on the phone, everybody could calm down.”

But what transpired over the course of the interview in ‘96 — which Martinez unpacks during four hour-long episodes for Netflix — was nothing close to kumbaya. The tapes capture an unvarnished time capsule of rage and Shakur’s frustrations with the justice system, various rappers and former members of his friend circle, the media and the world. He talked about how street warfare, incarceration and philosophies ingrained in him by the Black Panther movement, of which his mother, Afeni Shakur, was a prominent leader, caused his life to be in danger on a daily basis. Three decades later, Martinez guides several panels of experts on Pac’s life — including Charlamagne Tha God, Joe Budden, Big Boy, Dream Hampton, RZA, Wallo, Matt Barnes, E.D.I. Mean, Lil’ Cease, Ed Lover and others — to break down Shakur’s fiery rhetoric. At times, his answers to Martinez’s questions ranged from poetic and revolutionary to nonsensical and cringe by today’s standards.

From his sexual relationship with Faith Evans, Biggie’s then-wife, to surviving the Quad shooting and retaliating against anyone who he believes crossed him, it’s obvious why broadcasting these tapes on the radio in the ‘90s at the height of the epic rap beef between Tupac and Biggie would’ve been the airwave equivalent to an atomic bomb. On top of that, there are aspects of Shakur’s philosophy on women, homophobia and threats of forced sodomy against the rappers Prodigy and Havoc of Mobb Deep that have definitely aged poorly.

“When you hear this interview, yeah, some of it’s uncomfortable and weird and doesn’t age well,” Martinez said. “We can sit and talk about a recollection of s— that happened, but when you’re listening to an actual audio tape, there’s no prettying it up. It is what it is. He said what he said. I said what I said. Memory is one thing, but actual artifacts don’t lie.”

After listening back to the tapes for the first time in years while putting the Netflix podcast together, Martinez is often critical of herself in hindsight. Would she have challenged Shakur a little more on some of his rhetoric during the interview? Could she have decided on a different 12 minutes of their conversation to air on the radio that might’ve gave us more insight into Tupac the man instead of his myth? The answer to all of that, she says, is undoubtedly yes.

“In that moment, I just was like, ‘Oh man, he’s pissed. I can’t help this situation. It’s so bad.’ But now I’m like, damn, he was hurt, he was angry. But he also had so much going on inside of him,” she says.

Throughout the Shakur interview, a younger version of Martinez struggles to grapple with the rapper’s narrative. While trying to deescalate boiling tensions with reasonable questions, her ability to get the rapper to see where he may be wrong in his perception went beyond her role in hip-hop media. She speaks to him as a friend and a peer trying to stop him from getting in his own way. In the modern era where viral social media clips rule the internet, this kind of unfiltered discussion could probably never have happened.

“Today everything we do is looked at and analyzed, and especially if you do anything high-profile, it’s all out there for the camera even if you’re not a celebrity,” Martinez said. “Everything any of us do in the age that we live in is up for grabs. And I think Pac, yes, he was up for grabs, but I just think he operated like he was not up for grabs. He was just fearless.”

While pursuing the podcast project at Netflix, Martinez reached out to his estate, which was aware of Martinez’s project. However, she says the estate did not participate because of a preoccupation with the long-awaited conclusion of the trial for the rapper’s 1996 murder. That ended in August with Duane “Keffe D” Davis being convicted of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon for orchestrating the fatal shooting in Las Vegas. But it was important that Shakur’s family was represented in the project, so Martinez made sure to include people like Pac’s cousin, entertainment executive Aiyisha T. Obafemi, and Erica Ford, who founded anti-violence group the Code Foundation with Pac and his stepfather, Mutulu Shakur, in 1994.

“It was important to me also that in any panel discussion, that at least one person actually knew Pac,” she said. “I did my best, could there have been other people involved, sure. I could make a list sitting here with you right now of 10 people I would’ve loved to talk to. But with my resources and what we were making, I made what felt right in the moment and I felt really good with how everyone showed up.”

Martinez was adamant she was not trying to do something for the sake of cashing in on Shakur’s legacy, but to add to the wealth of knowledge about his tragically short life 30 years later in the hopes of helping the world better understand him as “a perfect storm of a human being.” At various times she said Shakur’s spirit let her know she was on the right path with the project through a handful of “God winks,” whether it was one of his songs coming on her stereo, or the lights flickering out on the set of the podcast during filming — not once, but twice.

“I don’t claim to be all-knowing. That’s why I didn’t want to make a documentary. I don’t think that’s my place to make a Tupac documentary,” she said. “The story that I’m qualified to tell is these tapes in this very specific moment with this extraordinary person from my very unique seat in the culture. Otherwise what else is there to do? Am I gonna go to the grave with it?”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9d85mlp88o.headline: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash on rescue mission
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9d85mlp88o.author: Jessica Lamb

paragraphs.text: Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq36gk151xkdo.headline: Turkish officials 'destroyed' pro-opposition TV channel, owner tells BBC
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq36gk151xkdo.author: Harry Sekulich

paragraphs.text: Turkish authorities have "destroyed" one of the country's most-watched news channels, its London-based owner has told the BBC.
Speaking to the BBC's Newshour, Cafer Mahiroğlu said that nine people connected to Halk TV were arrested this week on charges including money laundering, bribery and spreading misleading information.

Mahiroğlu said that several of his family members were among those arrested when the pro-opposition channel was taken into government control last month, adding that the allegations against him and Halk TV are "completely wrong".
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor' Office said that two former news anchors of the channel were among the most recent group of people detained.
In a statement, prosecutors accused the anchors of producing "false reports" in exchange for money.
Authorities have also issued an arrest warrant for the channel's news coordinator Kürşad Oğuz who is "abroad", the statement said, without specifying where.
Mahiroğlu told the BBC that he could be sent to prison if he tried to return to Turkey.
"[The government] wants to be in control of the whole media... I'm more worried about my country and my democracy than my channel," he said.

The headquarters of Halk TV was raided by Turkish authorities last month, halting the channel's live broadcasts, the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip Erdoğan and his administration.
The government subsequently appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

Erdoğan's government controls much of the country's media, which ranks among the worst globally for press freedom, external, though the government insists that it does not detain media workers for carrying out journalistic activities.
However, the president has scaled up a crackdown on dissent since his narrow victory in the 2023 presidential election.
Earlier this month, authorities took control of pro-opposition network Sozcu TV.
Erdoğan's main challenger, mayor of Istanbul Ekrem Imamoğlu, has been jailed on corruption charges and for violating election laws, which he and his party have fiercely denied.
Hundreds of Imamoğlu's supporters have faced similar accusations, while the government has also imprisoned other campaigners, lawyers and comedians.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Australia’s east coast deluged by storms as roads flood and damaging winds forecast for NSW and Victoria

paragraphs.text: The final weekend of Australia’s wettest spring on record for an El Niño year is delivering a deluge of storms and heavy rain.
Severe weather and flood watch warnings are in place across the eastern states as a weather band moves from central Queensland through New South Wales to Victoria and Tasmania.
The Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid said El Niño attracted great interest but was only one factor to consider when looking at a season and the continent in its entirety.
“El Niño is part of it, and we have had quite a lot of rainfall in the south-east but that’s … also a balance of what we didn’t have earlier in the winter season,” she said.
Tropical humidity has drifted across the continent and is being swept into the eastern states.
“We are looking at a very active system that’s going to be affecting southern Queensland, inland NSW, Victoria and also into Tasmania,” Reid said.
Damaging winds were forecast for the NSW alpine region and Victoria’s central and eastern districts, which were also expecting heavy rainfall.
The heaviest overnight falls in Victoria were 85.4mm at Amphitheatre Reservoir in the northern Pyrenees region and 72.8mm at Bet Bet Creek in the state’s west.
Victorian State Emergency Service volunteers reported a busy 24 hours, with more than 340 calls for help to 6am on Saturday.
Most calls related to fallen trees (105), building damage (96) and flooding impacts (97).
The state’s north-east and eastern ranges can expect six-hourly rainfall totals from 55mm to 70mm on Saturday morning.

A moderate flood warning is in place for Warrill Creek in Queensland, with initial flood warnings in Tasmania for the Meander and Mersey rivers and flood watches for most of the catchments in western, central and north-east Victoria.
Meanwhile, a heatwave in the Northern Territory is easing but intensifying from severe to extreme in Western Australia’s Kimberley and Pilbara regions.
“It’s only going to be a shortlived heatwave but it is going to be a couple of hot days through there,” Reid said.
“Picking out Kununurra as an example, they’re looking at 42 or 43C for the next few days during the daytime but only dropping down to about 27C overnight.”
An offshore trough off WA’s coast would create a low-intensity heatwave stretching to just north of Perth.
Meanwhile, firefighting crews are facing another difficult day as they continue battling raging bushfires on Tasmania’s remote Flinders Island.
As other parts of Tasmania brace for heavy rains and potential flooding, crews on Flinders Island are battling a blaze that had burned 15,000 hectares by Friday - more than 10 per cent of the island.
Forecast heavy rainfall has yet to reach Flinders Island but Tasmania Fire Service incident controller Steven Richardson said it could create further challenges rather than provide relief.

“At this stage, the weather may actually create further challenges for firefighters on the ground, reducing our ability to strengthen containment lines through backburning and creating wet, slippery conditions,” he said.
“While some warnings have been downgraded, our crews are expecting another long day on the ground focusing on containment and asset protection.”

npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6048749/with-ab.headline: With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas?
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6048749/with-ab.author: Leigh Walden

paragraphs.text: With Abbott out, what does the future look like for data centers in Texas? Texas has been one of the most welcoming states for data centers, but that might change with a new governor coming in.
Politics
Texas has been one of the most welcoming states for data centers, but that might change with a new governor coming in.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Under Republican Governor Greg Abbott, Texas has been one of the country's most welcoming states for new data centers. Times have changed. Abbott lost his bid for reelection, and Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has other ideas about data centers. Leigh Walden of member station KUT in Austin reports.

LEIGH WALDEN, BYLINE: Kate Goodrich is a lobbyist for the tech industry at K&L Gates, a law firm in Austin. And in the days after the election, people in her business were absorbing the change like everyone else.
KATE GOODRICH: The majority of everyone that we're talking to on both sides of the aisle have their mouths somewhere between 1 and 3 inches open still.

WALDEN: Their clients range from individual data center developers to some of the multibillion-dollar companies that operate them, like Microsoft. In November of last year, Texas Governor Greg Abbott declared the state the epicenter of AI development. He has signed laws that made large data centers exempt from sales taxes for the equipment they buy. But then this summer, as he campaigned for a fourth term, he changed his tune and said it was time for Texas to start...
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
GREG ABBOTT: ...Pushing back against these AI data centers that are trying to build in our neighborhoods.

WALDEN: As the public backlash to data centers grew, he also imposed a pause on all new data center projects while the state studied their impact. That pause has already expired. Meanwhile, Democrat Gina Hinojosa said this on CNN right after her surprising victory for governor.
GINA HINOJOSA: Right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.

WALDEN: Now people are watching for what she's going to do as the issue plays out across the country after the midterms. Incoming governors in Kansas and Georgia also promise to pause data centers. But because of the size of its economy, Texas often sets a precedent for how other states do business too. John Hall is the CEO and president of Houston Advanced Research Center, which focuses on environmental policy. He expects Hinojosa to impose a moratorium and then new regulations.
JOHN HALL: Establish it in policy that data centers should have to bring their own water and bring their own power. But in addition to that, offset their emissions.
WALDEN: Austin McCarty, a tech lobbyist at K&L Gates, said some of his clients are okay with more regulation. They think it might build trust and actually improve the industry's reputation.

AUSTIN MCCARTY: It's being dragged down by some folks that are not as prepared as the good actors who have really put in a lot of work to show that they're here to be a part of a really important ecosystem here in Texas.

WALDEN: Some Texans, though skeptical, seem willing to let the industry work on what they see as making amends. Torrie Martin is a horse rancher outside of San Marcos in Central Texas. She's gone to numerous local government meetings to speak against a proposed data center site near her ranch.
TORRIE MARTIN: I am optimistic, but, you know, we have to hold people accountable and pay attention to what is happening.
WALDEN: She thinks it's because of the unpopularity of data centers that laws will be passed and bipartisan agreements reached.

MARTIN: People on either side or all sides are fighting the same fight, which makes me feel more confident in my decision to, you know, stand up so loudly for the ranch lands and agricultural side to Texas.
WALDEN: New state lawmakers will be sworn in January, and then they'll begin a legislative session where data centers will be on the agenda.
From NPR News, I'm Leigh Walden in Austin.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/yuri-f.headline: Yuri and I used to play football together. Then I spotted his name among Russia’s war dead

paragraphs.text: One evening, after weeks spent counting Russia’s war dead, I began looking for names I might recognise.

My colleagues and I had been working our way through more than 11m death certificates leaked from Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, and identifying nearly half a million Russian soldiers who had died in the war in Ukraine.
We had sorted the dead by age, region and cause of death, building the most detailed picture yet of Russia’s losses in nearly five years of war.
Now I typed in the names of the places where I had grown up.

My childhood was spent in Rublevka, a stretch of pine forest west of Moscow that has been home to the Russian elite since Soviet times. With the collapse of communism and Russia’s chaotic embrace of capitalism, the dachas of party officials gave way to the sprawling estates of oligarchs.

Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev established their residences in Rublevka. In more recent years, the area has become a refuge for ousted leaders, among them Ukraine’s Viktor Yanukovych and, as the Guardian previously reported, Syria’s Bashar al-Assad.
I did not expect to find many names there.

Our analysis had shown just how unevenly the burden of the war had fallen across Russian society. In some of the poorest regions, working-age men were up to 32 times more likely to die in the war than men of the same age in Moscow. I knew sons of the Russian elite who had left the country shortly after the invasion, keen to avoid being called up to fight.
My village, Zhukovka, returned no results.
I worked my way along the Rublyovo-Uspenskoye highway, the well-paved road connecting the wealthy settlements west of Moscow. Here and there, a lone death certificate appeared.
Then I typed in Gorki-10, a town a few miles further down the road, named after the famed writer Maxim Gorky, who spent his final years there.
One of the names on my screen was instantly familiar: Yuri Vladimirovich Kyrmyz, aged 31.
Place of death: Makiivka, Svatove district, in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine. Cause of death on 3 February 2025: an explosion during military operations.

Makiivka, a small village on the banks of the Zherebets River, had been the scene of months of bitter fighting as Russian forces sought to retake territory lost during Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive.
Two decades earlier, Yuri and I used to play football together as teenagers.

Though we were never particularly close, he was a reliable presence at our games, a quiet, unassuming defender who rarely had much to say. We had not spoken in years. Until that evening, I had no idea he had gone to fight in Ukraine, let alone that he had died there.
I also do not know what made him join Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Kremlin has worked hard to insulate Moscow and its suburbs from the war. In neighbouring Barvikha, at the Luxury Village shopping complex, visitors can still buy a Ferrari or a Chanel handbag, despite western sanctions. But for all its associations with wealth and power, Rublevka is also home to another Russia.

Parts of Gorki-10 consist of Soviet-era blocks of flats, built for families who serviced the rich or toiled at the local stud farm, which dates back to the 19th century. I remembered that Yuri’s family was not well-off. Before enlisting, Yuri worked as a car dealer.
The signing bonuses and salaries offered by the Russian military, in some cases amounting to several times the average annual wage, would have represented a life-changing sum of money.
He may also have believed in the war.

Yuri was one of millions of Russians of our generation who grew up immersed in the memory of the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany. Victory Day, on 9 May, was one of the biggest occasions of the year, rivalled only by New Year’s Eve. Over the past two decades, Putin has appropriated that collective memory, telling a new generation of Russians that in Ukraine they are fighting the same “Nazi” enemy their grandfathers once faced.

Until I discovered Yuri’s name in the database, the only person I knew to have joined the invasion, other than the soldiers I had interviewed in the course of my reporting, was my former football coach Andrei Solomatin.
In his prime, Solomatin had played for CSKA and Lokomotiv Moscow, won 13 caps for Russia and appeared in all three of the country’s matches at the 2002 World Cup.

But his life unravelled after retirement. There were debts, problems with alcohol and a gradual slide into obscurity. By the time I met him, the former international footballer was eking out a modest living coaching our local Sunday league team.

Our team was an eclectic collection of nationalities, including Dutch (me), British and Nigerian players. I cannot recall Solomatin ever expressing hostility towards Ukraine. Politics, as far as I could tell, did not concern him.
The war changed that.

In autumn 2022, he began delivering aid to Española, a far-right military formation drawn from the ranks of Russian football ultras fighting in occupied Ukraine. By July 2023, he had joined the unit himself.

He was back on television, this time in military fatigues. In interviews, he spoke of his “complete trust” in Putin. The war appears to have given him a sense of public importance he had not enjoyed for years.

Yuri, like hundreds of thousands of other Russian soldiers who have died in Ukraine, left little public trace. Had hackers not obtained the records of Russia’s state statistics agency, I would probably never have learned of his death.
Although in some of the worst-affected parts of Russia nearly everyone knows someone who has died in the war, the full scale of the losses remains hidden from the Russian public.
Asked about the military deaths on Wednesday, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, dismissed the findings, insisting that only official data could be trusted.
Independent Russian journalists were quick to point out the irony, given that the figures came from the Russian state’s own statistics agency.

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/saudi-arabia-vision-.headline: Saudi Arabia shifts Vision 2030 spending amid economic and security pressure
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/saudi-arabia-vision-.author: Jenni Reid

paragraphs.text: Saudi Arabia's economic diversification strategy has moved from "spending and delivery at any cost" to "spending and delivery at the right cost," Economy Minister Faisal Alibrahim told CNBC on Friday.
It comes after the Kingdom scaled back or cut several flagship projects as it endures a sharp economic contraction.

Alibrahim also said Saudi Arabia would "stop at nothing from realizing long-term sustainable stability in the region" amid ongoing Houthi strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure that have killed and injured dozens and repeatedly rocked oil markets.

"The phase we're in today is one where every riyal is deployed with greater precision... it was clear that while we want to diversify or restructure our economy to depend less on government spend, there was a lot of catch-up that needed to be done, and for that, you saw government spend leading the way," Alibrahim told CNBC's Dan Murphy.

"Right now, that is shifting from spending and delivery at any cost to spending and delivering at the right cost. We're moving towards a policy-first approach to many of our policy areas and... objectives. We're also creating a clearer business environment, one that aligns the regulatory environment in the Kingdom with international laws."

That includes the recent announcement of a 15% minimum effective tax rate on multinational profits, which Alibrahim said would "create a clearer environment for the private sector to operate," as the government looks to attract more external investment.
Saudi pulls back non-essential spending

Saudi Arabia has been on a mammoth capital spending spree since it launched its Vision 2030 plan to reduce its dependence on oil revenue in 2016, deploying the resources of its sovereign wealth fund — the Public Investment Fund, or PIF.

But more recently, it has reassessed the cost and commercial prospects of initiatives such as the new economic region NEOM and the futuristic "The Line" city, withdrawn funding from the LIV Golf tournament and halted construction on a planned giant skyscraper in Riyadh. In January, it said it would postpone hosting the 2029 Asian Winter Games, which had been scheduled for Trojena, a planned part of NEOM.

Saudi Arabia is meanwhile grappling with the destabilizing effects of ongoing strikes by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which have hit targets including the PIF tower, Riyadh Airport and the country's largest oil refinery. The danger forced the Kingdom to call off its big international investor conference, dubbed "Davos in the Desert," which was due to be attended by some of the biggest figures in global finance in November.
"The human cost of crisis has been real, and so has been the economic cost," Alibrahim told CNBC.

Alibrahim said infrastructure investments had allowed the Kingdom's energy sector to restore production to near pre-crisis levels. It has meanwhile moved its import and export hub from the east to the west of the country via land-based transport due to the airport strikes, which has restored cargo levels.
He added that the attacks highlight the importance of diversification to the Saudi economy.

Real GDP contracted by 3.8% in the third quarter, according to government figures, with oil activities down 20.4% year-on-year partially offset by a 1.9% rise in non-oil activities. Net foreign direct investment inflows dropped 19.5% year-on-year in the second quarter.
The Saudi Ministry of Finance expects an overall contraction of around 2.1% this year and a rebound of 10.9% next year.

Advisory group Oxford Economics forecasts a more negative outlook. It sees the Saudi economy shrinking 3.4% this year and by 4% in 2027, amid escalating attacks on energy infrastructure even as a new minimum wage and continued Vision 2030 spending are expected to support incomes and domestic demand.
Akanksha Samdani, lead economist at Oxford Economics, said Vision 2030 was entering a new phase focused on returns.

"The government is managing fiscal pressures and shifting budgetary spending towards essential services and strategic priorities, while PIF is becoming more selective in its capital allocation and seeking greater private-sector participation," Samdani said, adding that some giga projects are being scaled back or delayed, while investment continues in sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, tourism, mining and technology.

"Our forecasts already assume that some of the Vision 2030 targets will be achieved later than originally planned. But the overarching goal of economic diversification remains unchanged," Samdani told CNBC by email.

Neil Quilliam, managing director of consultancy Azure Strategy, said investors are assessing whether Houthi attacks demonstrate a persistent vulnerability that could increase the cost and complexity of delivering Vision 2030.

"They have repeatedly demonstrated an ability to target important economic infrastructure and expose weaknesses in Saudi air defences," he told CNBC, with the attacks challenging the "assumption that Saudi Arabia has insulated itself from regional instability."

The economic impact of the strikes will be less about physical damage and more about whether they affect confidence in Saudi Arabia as a destination for tourism, entertainment and sports, a key part of Vision 2030 and a source of foreign capital and expatriate talent, he added.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/mohamm.headline: Palestinian tells of ‘devastating’ struggle after being made redundant by EU in Gaza

paragraphs.text: A Palestinian man who worked for the EU in Gaza has told of a “devastating” struggle to survive after he was made redundant by bosses in Brussels.

He was let go last year after being evacuated to Egypt but his redundancy payment was made to an account to which he has no access. “My family’s situation has become increasingly desperate,” said Mohammad Baraka, a former staffer at the EU border assistance mission (EUBam).
“Both of my daughters have suffered severe psychological distress as a result of the war, displacement and the prolonged uncertainty surrounding our future.”

The 220,000 Israeli shekels (£52,000) payment for almost 20 years’ service was made on 5 August last year to the Bank of Palestine but access to the money has been blocked, a risk he was aware of given the relatively large sum being transferred.

He said he wrote on several occasions to the European Commission, asking it not to make the payment into that bank because of a known risk that a large sum of money could be misconstrued as war funds. “I am now in the devastating position of having money in my name that I cannot access, while my family is experiencing severe financial hardship,” said Baraka.
Instead he had asked for the payment to go to a new account in an Abu Dhabi bank, but that never materialised.

Baraka was evacuated in 2023 after his house in Gaza was bombed and family members killed. The EU tried to relocate him to alternative offices in the West Bank but travel for Palestinians in Gaza was severely restricted. After a hasty three-day concession agreed with the Egyptian government, Baraka was able to leave for Cairo.

As the conflict continued, Baraka was initially able to work remotely from Cairo as an EU employee and had the comfort of a salary, private healthcare and access to schools for his two children. But when Brussels decided to close its EUBam office in Rafah, he was let go, leading to what he says have been traumatic consequences for himself and his wife and two daughters.

He says the evacuation to Egypt with no plan for onward travel to an EU nation or a diplomatically secured place in another country has rendered him stateless, with no residency rights and no right to healthcare or schooling for his seriously ill wife and two daughters, both of whom he says are suffering from the trauma of war.

One of his daughters has an acute mental health condition and Baraka says he cannot pay for her treatment. “I am not asking for charity or special treatment. I am asking for access to my own money, and for accountability over a decision that could have been avoided,” said Baraka.
“I had specifically asked the [EU] mission to transfer my money to my new bank account in Egypt to avoid precisely this situation,” he said.

“If the EU argues that it fulfilled its obligations simply because it transferred the settlement, I believe the legitimate question is whether an employer can consider its responsibility discharged when it knowingly disregards an employee’s repeated warnings about the destination of such a substantial payment.”

Last year he wrote to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, pleading with her to reverse what he called his “unjust dismissal” and asked her to restore his employment, even temporarily, “until a dignified and legal solution is arranged”.

He also wrote to the European ombudsman to ask them to open an investigation but they replied last week to say they had no scope for an inquiry. “We fully appreciate that you and your family are in an immensely difficult position. The hardship you are experiencing as a result of the war and your displacement are clear from your complaint,” wrote Tina Nilsson, the head of inquiries.

“I realise that this conclusion will be disappointing. I nevertheless hope you can understand why, based on the information available, there are insufficient grounds for the ombudsman to intervene further.”
He is now suing the commission for alleged breach of Belgian employment law but the case could take years to be heard.
Without the “laissez-passer” document that allowed him to be evacuated from Gaza, he cannot leave Egypt, he says, putting him in an impossible position.
A spokesperson for the commission said: “Due to the ongoing related court case, we cannot comment on this further.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/dangote-refinery-oil.headline: Africa’s richest man is taking his mega-refinery public in a blockbuster IPO
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/dangote-refinery-oil.author: Sam Meredith

paragraphs.text: One of the world's largest oil refineries is set to become Africa's biggest public firm in a highly anticipated offering that the continent's richest man has marketed as an "IPO for the people."

Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE, founded by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, is expected to begin trading in Lagos on Dec. 1, according to multiple media reports, following regulatory approval. A Dangote Refinery spokesperson did not respond to a CNBC request for comment.

The IPO of a minority stake in the refinery has reportedly been heavily oversubscribed, with investors from 120 countries and all 54 African countries applying to buy shares, Dangote Refinery said. The shares were offered at 525 naira ($0.39).

Reuters' calculations put Dangote Refinery's IPO-implied valuation at about $47 billion, based on the offer price and the company's registered share count. That would make it the biggest stock market listing Africa has ever seen.
