The Lagos-based refinery is regarded as a crown jewel of Nigeria's energy industry given the facility's role in transforming the oil-rich country's fuel market since it started operating in 2024.

"With a minimum subscription of just 10 shares, the offer is designed to give ordinary Nigerians and Africans an opportunity to own a stake in the refinery," Aliko Dangote said at the IPO launch in early September.
"The IPO is positioned not simply as a capital-raising exercise, but as an opportunity for workers, entrepreneurs and everyday Nigerians to participate in the refinery's future growth," he added.
Built for around $20 billion, the Dangote Refinery is now one of the largest in the world, with a crude oil distillation capacity of between 650,000 to 700,000 barrels per day.
It has emerged as a key provider of jet fuel in recent months, with buyers pivoting to West Africa amid Middle Eastern supply disruptions due to the Iran war.
"In theory, it's a win-win situation," Cyril Widdershoven, a maritime, energy and geopolitical analyst at Blue Water Strategy, told CNBC by phone.

Dangote Refinery has bolstered its reputation as a key Atlantic Basin facility amid soaring global demand for refined petroleum products, Widdershoven said, and the company intends to double its refining capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day by 2029, which could further strengthen its competitiveness in global markets.

However, despite the refinery's importance to Nigeria's economy, questions remain over its investment case, Widdershoven said, citing construction costs, commissioning delays, and the possibility that new capacity comes online with weaker margins.
"Right now it's like Anthropic or Nvidia, you are now buying the hype," Widdershoven said.
'An extremely strong year'
The Dangote Refinery has had "an extremely strong year," Mick Strautmann, market analyst at Vortexa, told CNBC by phone.
Between January and October, Vortexa data showed Dangote's seaborne refined product loadings stood at around 400,000 barrels per day, which is roughly 50% more than the same period last year.

More recently, however, the facility has seen refined-product loading jump to a record of 575,000 barrels per day through the first three weeks of November, surpassing an October record of 550,000 barrels per day, Strautmann said.
"It's been able to ramp up quite spectacularly and provide a lot of these products to the market in an extremely high price environment," Strautmann added.

"So, it's been one of the few places that's adding a lot of fuel supply to the Atlantic Basin, and at the same time, you know, to make West Africa less reliant on imports from other regions, particularly Europe for its gasoline supply," he said.

David Omojomolo, an emerging market economist focused on Africa at Capital Economics, said the upcoming Dangote Refinery IPO has captured global attention because the facility is seen as a rare example of an industrial policy success story on the African continent.
"It's been a good news story, and it's been an optimistic one as well," Omojomolo told CNBC.

"I don't want to be a hostage to fortune and say this time is different … but it does feel like a buzz and it's a question as to does it force other, say, billionaire industrialists to put their money where their mouth is in terms of helping the region's industrialisation prospects," he added.

npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6053049/sudans-.headline: Sudan's lost generation: War is stealing the childhood of millions
npr.org/2026/11/27/nx-s1-6053049/sudans-.author: Kate Bartlett

paragraphs.text: Sudan’s lost generation: War is stealing the childhood of millions Three years of war have stolen childhood from millions of children in Sudan, leaving them displaced, hungry and fighting for survival instead of learning in a classroom.
Africa
Three years of war have stolen childhood from millions of children in Sudan, leaving them displaced, hungry and fighting for survival instead of learning in a classroom.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

For millions of children in Sudan, classrooms have been replaced by battlefields. Three years of civil war have left schools destroyed, families displaced and children exposed to drones, famine and forced marriage. Kate Bartlett reports.
(CROSSTALK)
KATE BARTLETT, BYLINE: The happy sounds of children playing belies their circumstances. These children are in a displacement camp in Tawila, in Sudan's North Darfur region.
SAM NUTT: If you ask the children how many of them were displaced by the war, every single hand goes up.

BARTLETT: Dr. Sam Nutt is the head of North American NGO War Child, which supports children in conflict zones with a particular focus on education. She's just returned from a trip to Sudan and described the capital Khartoum as, quote, "post-apocalyptic."

NUTT: If you ask the children one on one how many of them have witnessed someone who has been injured or killed as a result of the conflict, all of them say the same thing. Many of them lost one or both parents.
BARTLETT: Laura Mills from Amnesty International says this is just perpetuating the conflict.

LAURA MILLS: We spoke to many children in particular who told us that, you know, especially because they haven't been able to go to school for years, many of them saw their only option as going back to fight.
(SOUNDBITE OF EXPLOSIONS)

BARTLETT: The U.N. has called Sudan the world's worst humanitarian crisis. The conflict erupted in April 2023 when fighting broke out between Sudanese government troops and a paramilitary group called the Rapid Support Forces or RSF.

BARTLETT: Since then, the war has spread across the country, displacing millions and killing tens of thousands, according to the U.N. Both sides have committed atrocities, with the RSF accused of genocide in the remote western region of Darfur. And with almost 20 million Sudanese already facing acute hunger, U.N. agencies warn the super El Niño could exacerbate food shortages in the coming months. And while it might seem far away, the war in the strategically located mineral-rich country isn't happening in a vacuum, as Dr. Nutt explains.
NUTT: This conflict has significant global tentacles that are of interest to every single American.

BARTLETT: The conflict is not only impacting the surrounding countries, but is funded and supported by others much further away, from Iran and Russia to U.S. ally the United Arab Emirates, accused of backing the RSF, a charge it denies. Amnesty International's Mills again.
MILLS: Eventually, this is just going to lead to a more unstable world where we see the number of wars that are escalating by the day. And it will come back to haunt us.
BARTLETT: As for Sudan's children, there is one story in particular that has stayed with Dr. Nutt.

NUTT: There's one little girl who was 11-years-old in our class who wanted to be a doctor because she wanted to help keep people alive precisely because she had witnessed both of her parents being gunned down in front of her.
BARTLETT: The consequences of this war will also last long after the fighting stops.
Kate Bartlett, NPR News, Johannesburg.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvwy08g70ldko.headline: Bronson Reed: Australian WWE star dies aged 38
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvwy08g70ldko.author: Jessica Lamb

paragraphs.text: Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.
The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.
Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."
They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.
WWE has been contacted for further comment.
Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.
The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.
Owens said Haley loved performing.

"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.
"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."
WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"

WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."
WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.
Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X.
According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November.
He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl.
Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019.
He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.
Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September.
No cause of death was provided at the time.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Victorian election 2026: Coalition projected to win state poll, ending 12 years of Labor government

paragraphs.text: The ABC has projected the Coalition will win the Victorian election, ending Labor’s 12 year run of government in the state.
The national broadcaster’s election and data analyst, Casey Briggs, called the election for the Liberal and National partners at 7.40pm on Saturday evening. .
While it is unclear whether the party will govern in minority or majority, Briggs said there was no pathway for Labor to win a fourth term.

It means the Liberal leader, Jess Wilson, will become premier. At 36, she will be Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Jacinta Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.
The deputy Labor leader, Gabrielle Williams, said she was “deeply saddened” by the result but there was a responsibility for the party to learn from it.
“Clearly we have to be deeply humbled by the results and take the lessons from them,” Williams said.

“We need clearly to take the lessons from the result tonight. But I would go further and say we actually need to go back and have a look at the lessons from 2022 and where those warnings really began to emerge.”
The Labor leader, Ben Carroll, is also facing a swing away from him in seat of Niddrie, in Melbourne’s northwest, which the party has held for its entire 50-year history.
More to come …

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/27/astr.headline: Astronomers ‘disheartened’ by decision allowing SpaceX to deploy satellites for space datacenters

paragraphs.text: Astronomers are pushing back against Elon Musk’s Starmind program to place a huge number of AI computers in space, which was given the green light to proceed by federal communications regulators earlier this week.

The American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the decision by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decision to grant SpaceX a license to deploy as many as 1m satellites in low Earth orbit as a way of moving datacenters into space.

The society said the proposed satellite constellation “would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky”.

The American Astronomical Society has previously raised concerns about the cumulative impact of reflective, bright satellites on astronomy, both optical and infrared, as well as potentially harmful radio frequency interference affecting radio astronomy.

In addition, it said, “atmospheric pollution from the launches and reentries of so many satellites, as well as increased collision risks in orbit, remain significant concerns; both of these factors threaten research astronomy.”
US federal regulators approved a constellation of satellites to process data in space on Wednesday, saying that they would “support America’s booming super intelligence economy”.
The FCC said in a statement that regulators had approved 1m Starmind orbital satellites, or compute modules, built by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
They said that the authorization “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.
“America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence,” said the FCC chair, Brendan Carr.
Proponents of the plan argue that datacenters in space are necessary to offset the electricity and water demands of Earth-based AI computing.

SpaceX argued in its submission to the FCC: “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial datacenters.”

A report published by the government accountability office (GAO) in July said that space-based datacenters “could reduce the land, electricity, and water needed for data centers on Earth” but warned of “engineering and economic barriers to deployment”.

The GAO said datacenters generate excess heat, but space does not cool computing hardware efficiently and “could be a major engineering challenge”. Further, it said, “a significant increase in the number of satellites in orbit could be difficult to manage and cause collisions.”

Under the license approved on Wednesday, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of ⁠the maximum number – or 100,000 – no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said.

Approximately 17,000 satellites currently exist, but there are rising concerns about the amount of space debris in higher orbits. The FCC deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits.
Amazon’s rival satellite unit, Leo, and others have criticized ⁠the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites under the approval.
Opposition to space-based datacenters has also been raised in a report published earlier this month by Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy.

The paper, Space-Based Data Centers Roadmap: The Case for Caution, said that space-based datacenters were likely to become a reality before the risks of large-scale deployment can be fully understood or governed.

“To put even 10% of the artificial intelligence data centers anticipated by 2030 into orbit would require more than 700 launches of large rockets every year, about two per day, in perpetuity,” it said.

In a chapter titled “Night Sky and Astronomy”, the authors warned large satellite constellations “could cause a dramatic transformation of night skies around the world” as well as “large debris fields in low Earth orbit, loss of life and property damage from de-orbiting satellites, depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer and increased global warming”.
It added: “The current governance regimes will not be sufficient to manage these risks, especially as addressing many of the challenges will need to be coordinated on a global scale.”

livescience.com/chemistry/is-it-dangerou.headline: Is it dangerous to mix cleaning products?
livescience.com/chemistry/is-it-dangerou.author: Skyler Ware

paragraphs.text: Household cleaning is often a straightforward, if tedious, task. But some particularly tough spots take more effort. When a stubborn mess needs some extra work, tackling it by combining multiple kinds of cleaning products might seem like a good idea.
But is it dangerous to mix cleaning products? According to one common misconception, doing so could create mustard gas, a toxic synthetic chemical weapon notorious for its use in World War I.
Experts told Live Science that it's not possible to produce mustard gas from these products, but mixing certain chemicals can harm your health.

That's because chemical reactions between some cleaning products can produce gases that irritate parts of the body. For example, mixing bleach with products containing ammonia, such as some glass and stovetop cleaners, produces chloramines. When a person breathes in these compounds, they react with water in the body to form hydrochloric acid. That compound causes burning in the eyes, nose and mucous membranes, said Dr. Mike Chary, an emergency physician at Weill Cornell and co-director of webPoisonControl, a digital platform that guides users faced with poison emergencies.

Ammonia is made up of three hydrogen atoms bound to a central nitrogen atom. When it reacts with bleach, chlorine atoms from bleach can replace one or more of the hydrogen atoms to form chloramines, which are harmful or deadly in high enough concentrations, said Delphine Farmer, an atmospheric chemist at Colorado State University.

"Chloramines are certainly present in a lot of environments," Farmer told Live Science. "We often see them indoors if you just clean with bleach, or you'll get them out of pools. But when you actually mix cleaning products, you can make enough chloramines that they can kill you."
Bleach and ammonia aren't the only compounds that should be kept apart. Mixing bleach with an acid can produce chlorine gas, which irritates the eyes. The gas smells like a swimming pool, Chary said.

But it's not possible to produce mustard gas just by mixing these products. Mustard gas contains sulfur, and although some cleaners have sulfur in them, mustard gas typically doesn’t form at room temperature and pressure, Chary told Live Science.

How dangerous an exposure becomes depends on a few factors, Chary added. The concentration of a hazardous byproduct will be smaller in a larger, well-ventilated room than in a smaller room with no airflow. Existing health conditions, such as asthma or lung disease, could also exacerbate the effects of exposure, Chary said.
Household cleaners also tend to have low concentrations of these chemicals so that any accidental reactions don't produce as much of the byproduct.

"Household bleach is below a certain concentration," Chary told Live Science. "That's primarily designed so that if it gets on you, it isn't going to cause as much damage as industrial-strength bleach. What that also means is that there's less of it per unit to undergo chemical reactions."

If someone mixes any of these chemicals, they typically know right away that there's a problem. Within a few minutes, they might start coughing, their eyes might begin to water, or they might notice a strong odor.
"Most of these things will elicit an aversive response," Chary said. "If you feel something's off, pay attention to that premonition."
Related mysteries

Both Chary and Farmer recommended opening windows and moving outside to fresh air if you accidentally mix cleaning products and notice these effects. Chary noted that if a person requires medical treatment, an exposure to chloramines is usually treated similarly to an asthma attack: Doctors may give medicines such as albuterol to open up the airways, and they’ll monitor patients’ oxygen saturation for signs of lung injuries.

To avoid accidentally mixing chemicals that can create something hazardous, Farmer recommended storing oxidizing cleaners, such as bleach and hydrogen peroxide, separately from other cleaning products. If you must use different kinds of cleaners to tackle a stubborn stain, wait until you can't smell the first one anymore before using the second, she added .

Sometimes, you don't need to use heavy-hitting products at all. "I'm a big fan of reducing exposure to those strong oxidants," Farmer said. "If you can use a simpler compound, that's better. Simple soap and water is amazing."
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/28/col.headline: College football’s latest arms race? A fight for the coolest ‘drone show.’
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/28/col.author: Noah White

paragraphs.text: Drew Martin fashions himself a bit of a thief — at least when it comes to halftime entertainment.

One afternoon a few years back, Martin, deputy athletic director at the University of Texas at Austin, was scrolling from his burnt-orange office chair when a video from an Asian soccer game caught his eye.
Something was happening in the sky.
“If it’s legal,” he recalled thinking, “I want that!”

Martin oversees brand management for one of the country’s largest athletic brands, and community relations in a college town like no other. He had shaped his school into a leader for in-game spectacles. So by that evening, he was talking with a local aerospace company, Verge Aero, that had recently started in the drone business. And not long after that, he was scheming on a whiteboard with UT’s marketing department.

Then, in the fall of 2023, as the Longhorns were walloping Wyoming, the stadium lights went out. Behind Darrell K. Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, the Longhorn logo glowed, lit by what would become college football’s latest craze: a drone show.
“Every game is somebody’s first and somebody’s last,” he said. “So it needs to be special.”

In the big (and sometimes petty) business of college sports, schools have found their latest arms race: a battle for bigger, brighter and pricier drone light shows during night football games. Nearly two dozen Division I schools have put on shows in the past two years, including some of the country’s biggest brands: Texas, Mississippi, Florida, Texas Tech and Ohio State. They typically cost more than $100,000 for four to seven images or movements — a Longhorn at Texas, an oil drill at Texas Tech, a gator chomp at Florida.

“The thought is that you’re bringing in money via attention and fan engagement,” said Scott Linzer, a senior vice president at Skyworx Drone Shows, which has worked with such schools as Florida and Ole Miss. “From our side, it’s hard to know exactly what each school’s thinking. What I can say: It’s never been a better time to be in the drone show business.”

Mississippi’s show during last year’s first round of the College Football Playoff went across ESPN, TNT Sports and the SEC’s social media channels, reaching millions of scrollers. Since then, multiple officials at other Power Four schools said, they have flown staffers to Mississippi night games this year solely to scout its drone shows.

Schools also compete for dates, as only so many U.S. companies put on the shows, which require 300 to 700 drones. Previously, Florida and Auburn were looking at the same date for a show, multiple officials with knowledge of the situation said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. But one of the largest providers, Skyworx, settled with the Gators. Their deal was too good. (The terms were not announced.)

The deals, for the drone companies, can be very good. While collegiate athletic department spending balloons — Division I institutions dropped more than $20.8 billion on athletics in the most recent year of available data — it can’t all go to players, coaches and facilities. Schools are also competing to win the battle of the spectacles.

“You always want to have the most interesting thing,” said Michael Ceilley, Florida’s chief commercial officer. “And when you can cater to the fan while also generating outside interest, that’s good in every way. It’s how you keep people coming.”
And cash, too.

After the covid-19 pandemic, drone shows began popping up at professional sports, including international soccer events. While multiple schools claim to have been the first to bring drones to college football, Texas’s September 2023 show is the earliest found on social media. Mississippi had a show that November and soon gained a reputation for presentations that often featured the “Party in the ‘Sip” message former coach Lane Kiffin championed.

“We watch what other places are doing and then try to see what we can do better,” said Drew Ingraham, a Mississippi senior associate athletic director. “It’s an all-out effort between multiple of our departments, but our goal is to get creative.”
“Ole Miss, by far, is one of the best to work with,” Linzer said. “The willingness to just give anything a shot is off the charts.”

The process is relatively simple. First, you need a night game on the schedule, which is negotiated with your opponent and broadcast partners. Then schools sketch images for their drone show partner, which creates mock-ups of what their art could look like via drones.

The operating company then works with school officials to determine a campus location to lay out hundreds of drones for prep during a packed game day — no small feat in its own right. At showtime, drone pilots code the fleet, preprogramming their coordinated movements, and troubleshoot after the birds leave the ground.

Each school takes a different approach. For established national brands such as Florida and Texas, any addition to game day needs to fit a buttoned-up, specific vibe associated with the school, officials said. Elsewhere, for a fresher college football power player like Texas Tech, things are different.
“We want to stand out,” said Robert Giovannetti, a senior associate athletics director at Tech. “And our brand is recognizable but a bit friskier than everywhere else. So we decided to lean in.”

One of the school’s recent drone shows opened with an image of an oil drill, a nod to the program’s “oil money” donors, the most prominent being Cody Campbell. It had another on Thursday for its Thanksgiving night game against Texas Christian University, which featured a depiction of the state of Texas and a script “Matadors,” one of the school’s nicknames. That one was “unlike any other school’s ever,” Giovannetti contended.

About 375 miles southeast, Martin finished up Thanksgiving dinner and likely kept an eye on the in-state rival. His latest interest is pyrotechnics shot via drones, sparked by watching a stunt during Kendrick Lamar’s Super Bowl 59 halftime show and another late-night Asian sporting event. When “College GameDay” visited for Texas’s game against Ohio State earlier this year, the ESPN show opened with a smoky flash above the set. Since then, more than 10 other schools have incorporated pyrotechnics, and surely none will send credit to Austin.
No shame in the drone show game, though, when chasing the next publicity buzz.
“R and D,” Martin said with a laugh. “Rip off and duplicate.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/us/texas-water-to.headline: How One Woman’s Quest for Clean Water Shook Up Trinidad, Texas

paragraphs.text: It started with a Facebook post in April that showed brown water pooling in a tub. What followed was the unraveling of Trinidad, Texas.

Jennifer Combs, 40, the woman who shared the post, was arrested in May as the city’s police chief claimed she was spreading false information about the water quality in Trinidad, a rural city about 70 miles southeast of Dallas.

After the charges against Ms. Combs were dropped, the police chief of the Trinidad Police Department resigned in June. Two city hall staffers resigned in July, forcing the mayor to hire interim help to run the city.

The turmoil in Trinidad reached a crescendo in September, when the state forced the city’s police department to disband after an investigation, leaving the community of about 800 residents without its own law enforcement.
“The total undoing of our city in the past few weeks since that happened has just been astonishing,” Dennis Haws, the mayor of Trinidad, said, referring to Ms. Combs’ arrest.

Trinidad hasn’t always been this turbulent. The city had long been quiet, anchored by its city hall building on a corner of Park Street by Texas State Highway 31. Down the street from the building, there is a gas station with wide lanes for tractor-trailers and a Dairy Queen, a staple of small towns in Texas.
Mr. Haws, who became mayor last year, moved to Trinidad about five years ago. He said that he has seen little crime since moving to the city.
“It’s just a pretty quiet place to live,” he said, “pretty typical small town Texas kind of feel.”

But there has been one long standing issue in Trinidad: the water. The city has an aging water plant, part of a broader infrastructure problem across Texas that results in billions of gallons of wasted water every year. In Trinidad, Mr. Haws said, the water pipes underground date back to the 1950s or 1960s and hasn’t been properly maintained.

State records dating back to 2003 show dozens of complaints about the water in Trinidad, including five made this year, according to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. Those complaints have increased steadily since 2020.
“It’s just not been very well maintained,” Mr. Haws said about the water system. “It has been an ongoing situation.”
One complaint to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality was filed on April 2, citing concerns from residents about faucets’ spouting brown water.

In early April, Ms. Combs posted an image on Facebook that showed a bathtub filled with brown water. Ms. Combs said a friend who lived in Trinidad shared the picture with her. Ms. Combs does not live in the city but nearby, and reports independently on the area for her website, TruthOutlaw.

“We are receiving reports of possible water quality issues, including concerns about bacteria and unsafe conditions,” the Facebook post said. “We understand not all Trinidad water appears this way. However, if yours does, please let us know. This is about public safety, transparency, and getting answers.”

The Trinidad Police Department pushed back on concerns about the water quality. In a statement shared on Facebook on April 6, the police department said that it was aware of concerns about the water, and that discoloration was possibly the result of rust or sediment that moved through water lines during maintenance. The statement also cautioned that false reports about public services could violate the Texas Penal Code.
About two weeks later, on April 21, the city of Trinidad instructed residents to boil their water for two minutes before drinking it.
Ms. Combs was arrested on May 8 for making a false report or alarm. She spent 23 hours in jail before being bailed out.
“It was very traumatizing,” Ms. Combs said to The New York Times. “I had never even had a speeding ticket before.”
Charles Gregory, the chief of the Trinidad Police Department at the time, addressed concerns about the water and the arrest of Ms. Combs in a Facebook post on May 10.

“It was a very cut-and-dry case,” Mr. Gregory wrote. “Some people believe I should stay quiet, but that’s not who I am. I did not take this position to be a ‘yes man.’ I took an oath to protect this city, to make it better, and that includes standing up for the truth when misinformation is being pushed.”
About two weeks after the arrest, a grand jury in Henderson County declined to indict Ms. Combs, and the case was dismissed.

What followed was a flurry of lawsuits, investigations and resignations. Mr. Gregory resigned from the police department in June without publicly saying why he was stepping down. Then the Texas Rangers, the state’s top investigative agency, started to look into the city's management. Soon after, the Trinidad city administrator and clerk resigned.
Ms. Combs filed a lawsuit in federal court in May against the city of Trinidad, Mr. Gregory and Cameron Beckham, who had also worked for the police department.
“I absolutely knew that I was falsely arrested and should not have been arrested,” Ms. Combs told The Times, adding that she felt that Mr. Gregory was “personally coming after” her.
Lawyers for Mr. Gregory and Mr. Beckham declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing lawsuit.
“Mrs. Combs did not fabricate an emergency,” the lawsuit states. “She did not summon emergency responders. She did not trigger evacuations.”

The lawsuit, which seeks punitive damages, also names Marie Bannister, a Trinidad City Council member, as a defendant. The suit claims that Ms. Bannister was aware of water issues in Trinidad and worked to suppress reports from residents with concerns rather than address them. Ms. Bannister did not respond to a request for comment.

After an investigation into the Trinidad Police Department by the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement in August, the city of Trinidad was told in a letter on Sept. 9 that its police department “failed to meet minimum standards,” thus forcing it to disband its eight-member police force. A state inspection of the Police Department found that the agency could not prove it had at least one bulletproof vest per officer on duty, a proper evidence room and official policies on situations such as use of force and vehicle pursuit.

Mr. Haws has said he was not surprised to learn that the state’s investigation was forcing the city to disband the police department, citing issues in the past. Ms. Combs’s Facebook post about the brown water, Mr. Haws said, was not the only reason the state was investigating the department.
“There’s a 15-year history of an inability to properly maintain a police force,” he said. “But it certainly amplified everything and it put a spotlight on everything.”
At a City Council meeting the next week, Mr. Beckham, who was serving as the interim police chief at the time, said he wanted to keep his department active.
“But if the ship sinks, I’m going down with it. That’s all I have to say,” Mr. Beckham said before leaving the meeting.

Despite the turmoil in Trinidad, Mr. Haws said that some silver linings emerged. The city has contracted with an engineering firm to assess its water infrastructure. Mr. Haws also credited Ms. Combs in part for bringing greater awareness to the water issues in Trinidad, even if it resulted in her arrest.

“That’s the part that has been missed through all of this,” Mr. Haws said. “We’re a small city. We don’t have money laying around to do this with, and her goal was to hopefully put together enough information to go to the state of Texas.”

For now, the Henderson County Sheriff’s Office will help handle policing in Trinidad until the city can reach an agreement with other nearby police agencies. But the water concerns remain an issue. A section of the city was under a boil water notice for two months after Sept. 16. The city temporarily changed the disinfectant in its water system in late October, and residents have been advised that the taste or smell of the water could be different during the switch.
“The citizens, I think, by and large are tired of all of this,” Mr. Haws said. “They just want to live a peaceful life.”

npr.org/2026/11/28/g-s1-155837/democrati.headline: New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
npr.org/2026/11/28/g-s1-155837/democrati.author: Matthew Brown

paragraphs.text: The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.

Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.

The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.

And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.

"Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.
Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.
"There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.

In an interview with NPR, Piper contended that Republican attorneys generals' policies are still broadly supported by voters, but were overshadowed by the unpopularity of the rest of the GOP. He noted that Republican attorneys general candidates ran ahead of GOP candidates for governor and U.S. Senate in some states.

Following the midterm results, Republican attorneys general convened for their fall meeting in Dallas, Texas, where the outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, lost his bid for Senate. He will soon be replaced by a Democrat, Nathan Johnson.

Piper said attendees grimly reflected on their challenges while also strategizing how to position Republican attorneys general to support the GOP as 2028 approaches. He added that the Republican Attorneys General Association are watching for potential "lawfare" by Democrats, including changing the number of Supreme Court justices or welcoming new states into the Union.

"We have to have better quality of candidates at the top of the ticket," Piper said. "We have to have better message discipline, and we need other committees in Washington to focus on what RAGA has done, and that is making sure we're good stewards of resources."

Democratic attorneys general held their own conference in Chicago, which some attendees said was both a celebration of the Democratic victories and an orientation for the incoming Democratic attorneys general.

"While a lot of the focus turns to what's next in Washington, we understand and we're not naive to the fact that we will continue to have a critical role in protecting our republic," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul during a Nov. 19 press briefing with other Democratic attorneys general.

Johnson, the incoming Texas attorney general, said at the same briefing that the wins for Democrats in the state house and governor's mansion could prompt Republicans to cooperate on a "cleansing" anti-corruption agenda. But he also signaled he'd support legislation and legal challenges to President Donald Trump's efforts to build a wall in Big Bend National Park on Texas' border with Mexico.

The Texas attorney general has traditionally brought cases on behalf conservative legal causes that had wide-ranging impacts across the country. The office also served as a training ground for Republican legal talent. U.S. Sen. John Cornyn and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott both served as attorney general before seeking higher office, while Sen. Ted Cruz served as solicitor general in the office before running for Congress. Other staffers have gone on to serve as judges, law clerks and prosecutors.

"Texas was a major intellectual force for the Republican attorneys general, and that's not going to be easily replaced," said James Tierney, a professor at Harvard Law School who has advised more than thirty attorneys general from both parties on staffing and legal philosophy.

"There are a lot of very smart, good lawyers in various AG offices who are very conservative," said Tierney. "But they don't have the heft and the size and the number of attorneys that Texas brings, and so for them, it's a very significant loss."
For Democrats, the recent wins could transform how the states enforce laws, bring legal cases, and support or hinder the Trump administration.

"These new attorneys general are not going to be particularly favorable towards the Trump administration, and will take an oppositional position in a number of different cases," said Anthony Michael Kreis, a constitutional law professor at Georgia State University. That may mean direct lawsuits against the administration in coalition with other attorneys general, Kreis said.

Many incoming Democratic attorneys general campaigned on bringing cases against alleged price gouging and digital surveillance by companies, as well as a tougher approach to antitrust concerns. But they will also face pressure to listen to their local business communities–including major multinational corporations.

"I think it's actually likely to increase bipartisan coalitions, particularly on economic issues," said Swain Wood, a partner at the law firm WilmerHale who now co-chairs the firm's practice advising clients on state attorneys general. Wood, who served as assistant attorney general to North Carolina Democratic Attorney General Josh Stein, cited past landmark settlements against tobacco and opioid distributors as cases where bipartisan groups of attorneys general found common ground.

Attorneys general from both parties have also banded together in recent years on cases about regulating social media platforms. Democrats elected in newly-minted swing states may already face pressure to choose popular or bipartisan legal actions. That's one way to maintain voters' support, as they're likely to face stiff reelection challenges.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y10yydln3o.headline: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y10yydln3o.author: James Chater

paragraphs.text: Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.
The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp80jyz6dl8o.headline: Seven students killed and nearly 100 injured in explosion in Afghanistan, official says
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp80jyz6dl8o.author: Jacob Phillips

paragraphs.text: At least seven students have been killed and 99 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, an official has said.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, a spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.
An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.
