washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/28/a.headline: How one of America’s least-known senators helped pass the permitting bill
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/28/a.author: Theodoric Meyer

paragraphs.text: When Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt (R) appointed Alan Armstrong in March to fill a vacant Senate seat, Stitt sent him to Washington on an unusual mission: Help pass long-stalled legislation to overhaul federal permitting.
Its prospects did not look good.
Senators had spent years discussing a bill to make it easier and quicker to build power plants and transmission lines with the aim of bringing down the cost of power.

The outlines of a compromise were clear: Many Democrats supported the idea because it could help speed the transition to wind and solar power, while Republicans viewed it as a way to cut burdensome regulations. But there was widespread skepticism that Congress could strike a deal in an election year.

“Everybody was like, ‘Oh, good luck,’” Armstrong, a longtime natural gas industry executive, said in an interview. “‘We’re never going to get permitting reform done. You’re crazy if you came here for that.’”
The Senate passed the bill last week less than eight months after Armstrong’s arrival — and right before his time in the Senate is set to end.

Armstrong, a Republican, was appointed to fill the vacancy created when Trump chose Sen. Markwayne Mullin (R) as secretary of homeland security. Armstrong was barred from running for a full Senate term under state law and is set to leave the Senate on Nov. 30.

It’s not uncommon for governors to appoint a caretaker senator who does not run for a full term to fill a vacancy — but it’s rarer for such a senator to throw themselves into passing a single bill. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) described Armstrong on the Senate floor last week as probably the “most effective senator” who had served only 250 days in the chamber.

As the newest senator until the July appointment of Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), Armstrong did not play a leading role in passing the bill. The legislation was hammered out over months by four longtime senators: Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico).
Instead, Armstrong, 64, worked obsessively to build support for passing such a bill among lawmakers and industry leaders.

The legislation is expected to accelerate the construction of a wide variety of infrastructure — including roads, housing and energy projects — if it becomes law. It has the support of fossil fuel and renewable energy interests but has drawn opposition from some Democrats and environmental groups that argue it makes it harder to stop oil and gas projects.

Armstrong estimated he spent more than 90 percent of time in the Senate working on permitting. His fellow Republican senators grew tired of hearing him talk about the bill again and again during their weekly closed-door lunches, he said.

“He was kind of Johnny-one-note,” Capito said. “I mean, that’s all he talked about. And that actually was helpful, because it kept [the spotlight on the issue] while we were negotiating maybe a little more subtly.”

Stitt said he appointed Armstrong after conferring with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) due to Armstrong’s expertise in the permitting process. Armstrong was deeply versed on the issue as a former chief executive of Williams, a natural gas pipeline company — but he knew little about the arcane rules and traditions of the Senate.
Armstrong said he was shocked by the Senate’s “vote-a-rama” tradition, in which senators spend hours voting on amendments late into the night.

“You get all these well-educated, accomplished people to sit around way past their bedtimes until 4 in the morning to really accomplish something that they already knew at 6 o’clock in the evening the night before,” Armstrong said. “And it’s just to grandstand, and it’s just to make a TV recording.”
The permitting bill won the support of almost every Senate Republican but divided Democrats. Some Democrats raised concerns that it would hurt Native American tribes and damage the environment.
The bill has yet to pass the House, and some Democrats have advocated opposing it and writing their own bill once the party regains control of Congress in January.

“We can make it easier to build good things without selling out our friends and neighbors,” Sen. Ed Markey (D-Massachusetts) said in a statement. “Let’s do that in January with a Democratic majority writing the bill, not fossil fuel companies and their lobbyists.”

Others Democrats have warned that waiting would torpedo the bill. Heinrich wrote Monday that “there is no alternative — this year or next — that can become law” because it would need some Republican support in the Senate and Trump’s signature.

One of the 14 Democrats who supported the bill in the Senate was Sen. John Hickenlooper (Colorado), who first met Armstrong when he was an energy executive and Hickenlooper was governor of Colorado. They ran into each other on the Senate floor soon after Armstrong arrived, and Hickenlooper offered to let Armstrong live in the basement apartment of his Capitol Hill rowhouse during his tenure in Washington.
In lieu of rent, Armstrong agreed to supply food and wine for bipartisan dinners that Hickenlooper hosts for senators to discuss tough policy problems — including how to overhaul permitting.
“His value has been to keep pushing,” Hickenlooper said of Armstrong’s role in passing the bill. “He’s got a sense of urgency that’s been unusual for this building.”

Armstrong’s conviction that the United States needed to overhaul its permitting rules was shaped by his years running Williams. In 2016, for instance, New York state blocked construction of the company’s Constitution natural gas pipeline, citing water-quality concerns. The project would’ve moved forward if the permitting bill had been law, Armstrong said.
Still, Armstrong said the bill, if it becomes law, is likely to help Williams in some ways but hurt it in others by making it easier for competitors to build pipelines.

“When you’re the incumbent and nobody else can build anything, your pricing power gets to be pretty outsized,” Armstrong said. “And that’s great for the company in the short term. In the long term, that’s terrible for our country and it’s terrible for our ability to provide low-cost energy, which ultimately is what’s going to keep a company like Williams in business.”

Armstong’s successor, Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), is set to be sworn in next week after winning the race for a full Senate term. Despite his frustrations with aspects of the Senate, Armstrong said he has more hope for the institution now than when he was appointed.

“I arrived in Washington believing that America’s permitting problems could be fixed,” Armstrong said last week in a speech on the Senate floor. “I leave with a much broader conviction: that many of our country’s greatest challenges are within our ability to solve if we are willing to do the very hard work of finding common ground for the benefit of our nation.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/europe/ukra.headline: Ukraine’s Deep Strikes Grow in Scale and Scope Across Russia and Beyond

paragraphs.text: Forty Russian oil and military-industrial sites struck in 50 days, including a fuel terminal on the Arctic White Sea and a missile-propellant plant deep in Siberia. A Russian military cargo ship set ablaze in the Baltic Sea. A warship sunk off the coast of Libya. And, in a flash of fire, a section of roadway on Russia’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea sent crashing into the sea.

Ukraine has been accelerating a deep-strike campaign that now stretches more than 1,500 miles and spans at least five seas, aiming to sever the networks that keep Moscow’s war machine fueled, armed and financed. In doing so, Kyiv is turning Russia’s immense geographic scale and far-flung military and economic assets into a liability.

Russia still holds a clear advantage in long-range strike abilities. Moscow can target any corner of Ukraine with ballistic missiles that Kyiv is largely defenseless against without more U.S.-made interceptors. With its superior troop numbers and weaponry, Russia is calculating that it can outlast Ukraine. Moscow is trying to inflict pain on Ukrainian civilians and push Kyiv closer to surrender by attacking power plants, heating grids and rail infrastructure heading into winter.
But Ukraine has its own cards to play. Ukrainian forces are increasing the tempo of their long-range operations to record levels, firing more than 1,000 drones into Russia on some days.

Kyiv has continued hitting Russian refineries, sending production to a two-decade low, despite President Trump’s demand to stop. Ukraine has conducted audacious long-range attacks even after Elbridge Colby, the U.S. under secretary of defense, scolded Kyiv this month over “the spectacle of deep strikes,” saying they “have not been effective in driving an end to the war.”

Kyrylo Budanov, the head of presidential office in Ukraine, has acknowledged that “long-range strikes alone will not win the war.” But he has argued that every hit “means repairs, lost production, logistics reorganization and additional costs,” making it harder for Russia to sustain the fighting.
The attacks also force Moscow to redeploy air-defense systems away from the front line and move naval assets to protect vessels at sea.
Both sides’ campaigns are spilling well beyond the borders of their enemy.

Moscow is waging a shadow war of arson, sabotage and assassination plots across Europe, alongside incursions in NATO airspace and attacks on ships in the territorial waters of NATO nations. Kyiv, for its part, is hunting far and wide for Russian military assets in an effort to undermine Moscow’s ability to project power.
The breadth of Ukraine’s campaign was driven home this past week when Ukrainian drones struck a Russian military cargo ship, the Sparta II, in the Gulf of Finland in the eastern Baltic Sea.

The next morning, more than 1,000 miles from Ukraine, seven naval drones tore through defensive fire in the Libyan port of Benghazi. The swarm sank the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, along with an onboard combat helicopter, and struck a Russian cargo ship that the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said was hauling weapons.

Officials in the government that controls eastern Libya vowed to retaliate. Mr. Zelensky has defended strikes on Russian targets anywhere in the world as a sovereign right to self-defense, calling them “our long-term security guarantee.”

While Ukraine’s European allies have defended strikes inside Russia, the initial reaction to Ukrainian strikes in the Baltic and Mediterranean Seas has been more cautious, said Aliona Hlivko, the head of St. James’s Foreign Policy Group, a research organization in London.

Some fear that Russia could view such attacks as an escalation, she said, a contention that Mr. Colby, the U.S. defense official, also made. After Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy said that the war “should not and cannot be extended to the Mediterranean,” Mr. Zelensky said he called Ms. Meloni and confirmed that the attack “was conducted without prior coordination with our European partners.”

Others, acknowledging that Europe has “no credible response” to Russia’s shadow war, Ms. Hlivko said, are more supportive of the strikes, as Ukraine offers the only real direct pushback against Moscow. Kyiv, Ukrainian analysts said, is filling a vacuum left by Europe’s fear of direct confrontation with Russia and by the Trump administration’s embrace of Moscow.
“Europe is our rear guard, and we are its army,” Andrii Klymenko, the head of the Black Sea Institute of Strategic Studies, said of Ukraine.
The question of whether Ukraine’s strategy can compel Russia to engage in serious negotiations has highlighted a stark policy rift between the United States and Europe.

After Mr. Colby criticized Ukraine’s long-range campaign during NATO talks in Brussels, European defense chiefs offered retorts. The German defense minister, Boris Pistorius, called Mr. Colby’s remarks “quite a stupid thing.” The British defense secretary, Wes Streeting, said of Ukraine’s campaign, “There’s no doubt in my mind that it is buying time and saving lives.”
Independent analysts have largely aligned with the European perspective.

“Continuing to resource Ukraine’s deep strikes is critical to bringing Russia to negotiations, rather than the Potemkin talks currently being orchestrated by Washington,” Jack Watling, a military expert at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, wrote this past week.

As the Trump administration has tried to jump-start negotiations to end the war by offering incentives to Moscow, Ukraine has unleashed some of its largest assaults of the war. On Nov. 16, the Russian military reported downing 1,336 Ukrainian drones, breaking a record set 18 days before. On Nov. 17, the record fell again, with 1,441 reported interceptions.

Moscow does not say how many Ukrainian drones get through, and it rarely acknowledges damage caused by the attacks. But military analysts using geo-located video footage have verified dozens of significant strikes in recent weeks.

Mr. Putin publicly remarked on Tuesday that Russia’s domestic petroleum market remained difficult and complained that Ukraine had not heeded the Trump administration’s warnings against hitting Russian refineries.

Ukraine is targeting every link in the refinery chain, from upstream pipeline blending and pumping stations to primary refining plants, petrochemical processing facilities and maritime export outlets.

Russian refinery output is roughly 30 percent below the level of a year earlier, according to the International Energy Agency. With gasoline production down 20 percent and diesel down nearly 30 percent, Moscow has restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies.
Ukraine is also targeting the networks that enable Russian missile strikes, including plants critical to weapons production, and the planes and ground launchers used in assaults.

Kyiv’s expanding reach is powered by the rapid growth of its domestic defense industry. Those capabilities have evolved from retrofitting commercial drones to building jet-powered strike systems and heavy cruise missiles capable of carrying a one-ton payload more than 1,800 miles. Ukraine is also racing to produce its own ballistic missiles.

At the same time, Ukrainian engineers are rapidly integrating artificial intelligence across the country’s arsenal. “Hundreds of Ukrainian defense tech companies are already using A.I.,” Mr. Zelensky said on Tuesday.

The increase in domestic output has been paired with joint production agreements with Germany for reconnaissance drones and with Britain to build more than 1,000 long-range strike drones. The push is intended to sustain Ukraine’s deep-strike capacity regardless of political shifts in Washington.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/28/s.headline: She wore yellow to Miley Cyrus’s wedding. I applaud her.
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/28/s.author: Michelle Singletary

paragraphs.text: My shero is the woman in yellow who inadvertently drew attention to a special occasion trend I loathe.
The fashion faux pas police pounced after a guest at Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando’s wedding ceremony in Palm Springs, California, broke the all-black dress code by wearing a mustard-colored outfit.

Miley Cyrus wedding guest is called out for failing to adhere to strict black dress code at her star-studded nuptials as she stands out in bright yellow dress with fans asking 'who is this diva?' https://t.co/Dx5xvjHhq3— Daily Mail (@DailyMail) November 23, 2026

In the comment section of a viral Instagram post, the guest’s sister defended her, insisting it was an honest mistake. Even so, she also offered a mild critique for missing the dress directive, writing that her sibling “should have known better to double check the invite.”
“Where was the wedding planner with the black shawl to give her?” one commenter wrote.
Another wrote: “How embarrassing!”
Really?
I say hallelujah. Heck yes to the yellow dress, even if it wasn’t a deliberate act of defiance against all-too-common bossy dress code edicts.

Whether it’s a milestone birthday, an anniversary dinner or a high-profile wedding, etiquette rules suggest that hosts, as a courtesy, communicate a dress code — formal, semiformal, business — so that people don’t feel over- or underdressed.
Requiring ridiculously specific color palettes — eggshell, not cream; eggplant, not plum; blush, not pink — treats guests like photographic props.
Hosts have every right to plan a celebration that feels meaningful to them, and guests understand there will naturally be some cost and effort in showing up.
Still, genuine hospitality means keeping guests’ financial realities and comfort in mind. Here’s how.
Make it easy for them to show up
There’s a simple equation that applies to important gatherings.
My expression of affection for you is that I’m coming to your event.
Your expression of your caring for me is that you make it as easy as possible for me to attend your special celebration.
This might mean your elderly auntie with chronic back pain may not appreciate having to fly to Fiji for your three-day wedding extravaganza.

I was invited to an all-white party, but it was at the end of the summer season. I wanted to attend because it was part of a financial conference and networking was an important part of the gathering.

Stores stock darker, richer palettes during colder months, making it more difficult to find lighter shades on the rack. So to fit in, I had to shop at several stores to find something suitable for the evening affair. I could have gone rogue, but who wants to subject themselves to the chatter and criticism about not following the rules?
One gentleman at the all-white party arrived wearing the plush white robe provided by the hotel. I admired his ingenuity.
Keep affordability in mind
It’s about balance. If you want a themed event, fine. But plan it so that the cost is minimal.

I get so stressed when I receive invitations with instructions on what I should wear. I have a simple wardrobe, and these themed events often require me to purchase new clothes or accessories I might never wear again.
Many will comply with your demands even when they know it will break their budget.

A 2024 survey by LendingTree found that among the 54 percent of Americans who had attended a wedding in the last five years, 31 percent took on debt to attend. Nearly a quarter amassed $2,500 or more in debt.
Even when people’s better judgment says “RSVP no,” they go anyway. According to the survey, guests who took on the debt felt pressure from the couple, family and friends to attend.

That kind of financial strain shouldn’t be the price of admission. Make coming to your event as inexpensive as possible. You should care enough about your guests to know what they can and can’t afford.
You should not pressure people to spend past their financial comfort zone to prove you are worthy of their presence.
You pay for the extravagance

The definition of hosting has become very warped. People plan big celebrations and then charge guests to attend. And they do so under the guise that if they didn’t pass their costs on to the attendees, they wouldn’t be able to hold their massive party.
There’s nothing wrong with wanting a big, splashy event. But if you’re the host and you’re inviting people to attend, you should pay for the party.
You can have the fanciest engagement, bachelor or bachelorette party you want. But don’t push the financial burden of attending the event on your guests.
Accept a “no” or nonconformity with grace
In the LendingTree survey, 12 percent of folks who declined a wedding invitation said it ruined their relationship with the couple.

Guilt-tripping can be subtle or blunt. But if someone says they can’t afford to attend, including the need to buy a new outfit to match your color aesthetic, and you respond with comments meant to make them feel bad for declining the invitation, you are not a gracious host.
Nor should you criticize a guest who arrives wearing the wrong shade.
Don’t make people’s attendance or color-coded compliance at your affair a test.
Love does not test.

Follow Michelle’s financial advice show, Dollars & Sense with Michelle Singletary, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts. Want Michelle to answer your money question on the show? Email dollarsandsense@washpost.com.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/28/c.headline: Can’t afford a home? Maybe you should buy one with your parents.
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/28/c.author: Maurie Backman

paragraphs.text: During the third quarter of 2026, the median sales price of a new home in the United States was $393,300. Ten years earlier, it was $303,800. Add in the fact that the average 30-year mortgage rate is above 7 percent, and it’s no wonder so many younger buyers are struggling to purchase a home.

If you’re tired of renting but can’t comfortably afford to buy a home on your own, one solution may be to purchase it with your parents and live there together. There are benefits and drawbacks to this type of arrangement, and it’s important to think through them before moving forward.
The pros
When you team up with your parents to purchase a home, you get more buying power, said Daniel Yoon, a real estate agent with eXp Realty in North Chesterfield, Virginia.

“A parent on the loan can help a young buyer qualify for a higher loan amount,” said Yoon. “In a market with few starter homes, the parents’ assistance can be the difference between renting for two more years and getting the keys.”

Daniel Kramp, a real estate broker at Christie’s International Real Estate New York, said that if parents have enough accumulated wealth to purchase the home without financing it, you can avoid borrowing at today’s higher mortgage rates and save money. Your parents’ contribution may also allow you to purchase a nicer, more spacious place than what you can afford on your own.

Even if you end up with a mortgage payment, splitting it with parents could make it easier to manage, said Yoon. And if you’re close to your parents, being under the same roof could benefit everyone. If you have kids, it may allow your parents to help with child care, and it could make it easier for you to become a caregiver for your parents as they age.
The cons
When you buy a home with your parents, you’re not the only one calling the shots.

“If parents are helping with a big down payment and are co-purchasing with you, they also have a say in where they think you should live,” said Kramp. As a result, you may not end up getting the home you want despite having access to more funds.
Things could also get complicated if circumstances change, Yoon said.
“What if one person wants out in three years and the other wants to stay for 15-plus?” he asked.

Your parents might eventually decide to retire to a warmer place, or you might get a job that requires you to relocate. If one owner leaves, the remaining one could get stuck with a more expensive home than they can afford.

Conflict could also arise over things like maintenance, repairs and improvements. You might prefer to outsource snow removal and lawn mowing. Your parents may not want to pay for services you’re all capable of performing yourselves. These could turn into arguments that sour the arrangement.
Approaching a joint purchase

If you like the idea of buying a home with your parents and living there together, first talk everything through. Discuss what that arrangement could look like and acknowledge some of the drawbacks that might arise, like a lack of privacy or disagreements over upkeep and renovations.

“Parent assistance can get a young buyer into a home where rates and prices of today are out of reach individually. It can also tie a family to an agreement that’s hard to undo,” Yoon said. It’s important to be on the same page, he added, because if a major conflict arises it could affect your relationship, not just your finances.

Next, see if there are properties available in your ideal area that can actually accommodate a multigenerational living arrangement. The conversation may be a moot point if you’re unable to find a home that can meet everyone’s needs.

If you decide to move forward, hire an attorney to write a detailed ownership agreement. Make sure it addresses who’s responsible for the down payment and what percentage each person will contribute; how the mortgage is paid; how maintenance and repairs are handled; and what happens when someone wants out.

It should also specify how the title is held so the home transfers smoothly if a parent passes away. A thorough agreement could protect everyone involved in a joint home purchase and help safeguard family relationships as your finances become more closely intertwined.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/mac.headline: The Thanksgiving when actual elephants marched down Broadway
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/mac.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: In 1924, to celebrate the expansion of its Herald Square department store — and to promote the start of the Christmas shopping season — Macy’s invited the public to a Thanksgiving Day parade through Manhattan. Costumed company employees were joined by live Central Park Zoo animals, elephants included, for the 6-mile jaunt down Broadway from Harlem to Herald Square.
Plans included a cage match between grizzly bears. For the finale, Santa Claus climbed atop Macy’s new 34th Street marquee to show off the store’s holiday displays.
The parade would become an annual tradition. Zoo animals would soon be retired, and it would be christened the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1934.
Santa Claus has closed the event nearly every year since, but many traditions now synonymous with it began years or decades after its inception.

It would be a few years before the first giant balloon, the street-smart cartoon character Felix the Cat, made its debut. The event was aired on NBC radio in 1932 and in an experimental shortwave telecast in 1939. CBS broadcast segments from the parade in 1948. NBC, its current home, began broadcasting to a national audience in 1952, according to Macy’s.
The Radio City Rockettes kicked off their first parade performance in 1958. The Tom Turkey float was introduced in 1973. And Broadway performances were added in 1980.
The Thanksgiving Day storm that lashed the East Coast on Thursday led organizers to move this year’s parade to Saturday. It was the first postponement, but not the first time adjustments were needed.
The event was called on account of World War II from 1942 through 1944. A helium shortage in 1958 led organizers to use cranes to hold aloft giant balloons filled with ordinary air.
High winds grounded balloons in 1971. In 1997, a Cat in the Hat balloon hit a lamppost, knocking loose debris that sent a woman into a 24-day coma and injured three other people.
During the coronavirus pandemic, the 2020 production was shrunk to a single block, closed to the public and videotaped over multiple days.
The 100th edition of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade kicks off at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time Saturday.
Photo Almanac is an occasional series from The Washington Post, using photo archives to examine where we’ve been to understand where we are.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/business/ai-offic.headline: A.I. Companies Race for Space in New York, a City That Doesn’t Have Much of It

paragraphs.text: Manhattan is on track to have its strongest year in office leasing since 2000, and artificial intelligence companies are playing a major role in that turnaround.

Their arrival has made New York the A.I. industry’s largest office market outside San Francisco. In the first half of this year, A.I. companies made up more than 8 percent of all new leasing in Manhattan, up from less than 1 percent in 2020, according to a report from Savills, a real estate company, and CompStak, a data provider.

The industry’s expansion in New York to be near companies that buy their products and supply their funding is happening as the office market has grown ever tighter in the city, with many buildings being converted to housing and little new office construction taking place.
The surge has benefited landlords, who can get leases with longer terms and higher rates — and created challenges for A.I. companies seeking more space as they grow.
One such company is Perplexity, the maker of an A.I.-powered search engine that arrived in Manhattan in 2024 and has taken a somewhat unorthodox approach to expanding its footprint in the city.

In 2025, Perplexity signed a lease for an 8,000-square-foot space on the fourth floor of a building in the Union Square neighborhood, then signed a second lease early this year for a 12,000-square-foot space in the building next door, also on the fourth floor. The buildings happen to be owned by the same landlord, the Feil Organization, which proceeded to slice through their exterior walls to unite the floors, creating a sprawling, if quirky, space for the company to spread out.

One side of the office has high ceilings and massive arched windows, while the other has standard ceilings and windows. A ramp in the opening between the buildings was installed to align the floors. ALA Studio, an architecture and design firm, turned the gaping hole into a clean-lined arched passage tiled with penny mosaics — a reference to subway station walls and the lobby floors of historic Manhattan buildings.

Nathan Barksdale, Perplexity’s general counsel and chief operating officer, expressed satisfaction with the design maneuverings on a recent tour of the now 22,000-square-foot space, but he said the company was already searching for more room. (The company lists 92 jobs on its website that could be filled in New York.)
“We’re already looking to expand,” he said.

Perplexity will have to compete with all the other A.I. companies looking for space in New York. The city’s Economic Development Corporation counted more than 2,000 A.I. start-ups in New York last year. Those companies have leased more than six million square feet, said Jonathan Mazur, who leads research at the Newmark Group, a real estate firm.
“The biggest takeaway is the pace of growth,” said Matthew Schreck, a research director at Savills. “A.I., on its own, is already one of the top five industries leasing space in Manhattan.”

Aside from Perplexity, there’s Anthropic, which recently had a record-setting initial public offering and occupies an entire 16-story building in the Hudson Square neighborhood. Harvey AI, which specializes in A.I. tools for legal companies, and Clay, a sales and marketing start-up, have planted flags in Flatiron. OpenAI leased about 90,000 square feet in the Puck Building in SoHo.
(The New York Times is suing OpenAI and Perplexity over alleged copyright violations. The companies deny the claims.)

In Brooklyn, there are companies like Rilla, a homegrown operation that uses A.I. to coach sales teams. The company, which in August moved into 57,000 square feet in Williamsburg, offers an $18,000 stipend annually to employees who rent apartments near the office as an alternative to what its chief executive, Sebastian Jimenez, called an “annoying” commute from Manhattan. Eighty percent of the company’s 130 employees take the stipend, he said.
At Perplexity, Mr. Barksdale is searching for more space in a significantly tighter market than when he began exploring Manhattan real estate.

Both of the company’s buildings, which were 25 percent vacant two years ago, are fully leased today, said Andrew Weiner, head of commercial office leasing for Feil. Mr. Barksdale has toured the top floor of one of the buildings, which will become available in 2028. He has also considered other buildings in Union Square, with the idea of developing what he called a “Perplexity campus” in the neighborhood.

Even as A.I. companies continue to add office space in New York City, there is some concern that the momentum will someday come to a crashing halt as the technology eventually displaces workers, shrinking demand for offices. Some see worrying similarities with the boom-and-bust cycle of the dot-com era.

That kind of outcome is always possible, Mr. Schreck of Savills said, but most A.I. companies are well capitalized, he added, so that even if a business fails, it should be able to fulfill its lease obligations. “I don’t think it would tank the market,” he said, noting that finance and law, in addition to the broader tech sector, are also buttressing the office market today.

livescience.com/animals/birds/it-was-evo.headline: 'It was evolution in a garbage bag': How a box of dead starlings began to unravel the secret to their extraordinary success
livescience.com/animals/birds/it-was-evo.author: Julia M. Zichello

paragraphs.text: In the late 19th century, Eugene Schieffelin, an amateur ornithologist, released around 100 European starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) in New York City's Central Park. He was chairman of the American Acclimatization Society, a group dedicated to introducing the flora and fauna of Europe to North America. The result was a disaster. Within decades, the birds had established themselves in this new habitat and moved across the country, and by 1970 — less than a century after their introduction — there were 200 million of them.

But this rapid expansion revealed something remarkable about one of the world's most invasive bird species: its ability to evolve. In this excerpt from "Bird on the Street: The Unnatural History of Starlings" (Columbia University Press, 2026), author and evolutionary biologist Julia M. Zichello recounts a point in her research when she was starting to figure out these birds' incredible adaptability: when she received a box of dead starlings.

Wildlife control agencies in the United States cull starling populations annually, at airports and on farms, to prevent damage to crops, interference with livestock, and collisions with aircraft. These birds are killed creatively: trapped, gassed, poisoned; their cervical vertebrae dislocated.

Technically, it is not illegal in the United States for someone without a permit to end the life of a starling (as it is for most other birds). In 2014, I sent an email to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal Control Unit requesting starling specimens for my research project.

I remember speaking to a wildlife specialist on the phone who cautiously (but professionally) sounded as though they didn't understand why anyone would want these birds. The starlings were, quite literally, trash. But they graciously sent me the birds anyway (in a box labeled Honey Baked Ham).

Approximately two million starlings are killed every year in the United States by the USDA. And now I had five of them. Intraspecific diversity in anatomy — that is, slight differences between individuals of the same species — can arise from various developmental or evolutionary mechanisms. For example, clear differences emerge throughout development: an old person's anatomy is different from a young person's. There are also anatomical differences between sexes, which are activated by signaling molecules we call hormones.

But other differences between individuals of the same species, controlling for age and sex, can also tell us something important about evolution. In fact, this is where evolution begins. This is microevolution — where variation within a given species is shaped by the constant flux and reciprocal action of mutation, natural selection, the founder effect, migration, and genetic drift.

These evolutionary forces drumbeat through time, with varying speeds, intensities, and moments of confluence and opposition. Determining the strength and contribution of each of these evolutionary forces to the genetic and physical variation we observe within a species is one of the most longstanding and fundamental questions in all of evolutionary biology. Certain evolutionary processes generate differences between individuals, while others homogenize these differences.

For example, mutation is a creative force, which — despite its mostly negative press — can generate new versions of a gene that could turn out to be advantageous in a specific environmental context. Each time a new offspring is born, a few novel mutations arise; these may be advantageous, disadvantageous, or (most often) totally neutral. So mutation creates new variation in a population and makes you a little bit different from each of your parents. Enough reason to celebrate it, really.

The founder effect — a process whereby a new population is established by a small subset of individuals from a larger original population — often reduces genetic variation in the new population. And because genetic diversity is reduced, certain versions of genes (or alleles) can quickly rise in frequency in the new population.

But this is not because the allele is advantageous; it's just because it is the only game in town. This statistical sampling process — called "genetic drift" — is stronger in small populations. The impact that the founder effect has on genetic variation is fairly well understood, but how it shapes physical traits is substantially messier and more mysterious.

This is partly because a single physical (or phenotypic) trait, like wing length, is under the action of many genes at once. Gregor Mendel, the Austrian monk, did some pioneering work in the 1860s with pea plants and discovered how a single gene controlled a single trait, such as flower color or pea texture. But we now know that this elegant one-gene model does not represent how the majority of complex physical traits are genetically programmed.

This non-Mendelian mayhem only added to my interest in how starlings may have changed phenotypically over time due to the founder effect. Patterns of variation — or lack thereof — are evolutionary clues: they can signal that something happened in the past. But figuring out exactly what that something was is part of the inherent challenge of practicing a historical science like evolutionary biology.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro

In starlings, we know from historical records that the U.S. population started out small (around 100 birds) and expanded rapidly to today's population of 93 million. For me, the big question was: do starlings lack genetic and phenotypic diversity because of a dramatic population history forged by human interference?

If you casually look from bird to bird in a starling flock, they look very similar to one another — like glossy little soldiers, sometimes even pecking in the grass and marching forward in unison. But I needed to quantify their differences (or similarities), because there is more to science than just noticing something in the grass.

This approach — looking across a living species as a way of looking backwards in time — is why I was so excited about my five dead starlings. And I could do anything I wanted with them. I could dissect them, take tissue samples for DNA extraction, or turn them into a research specimen for the future. It was evolution in a garbage bag.

Bird on the Street: The Unnatural History of Starlings

Blending natural history with science memoir, Bird on the Street traces how starlings illuminate the mechanisms of evolution and the relationship between humans and wildlife. Following starlings from the streets and skies into museums and laboratories, Julia M. Zichello invites readers into the daily practice of science: the small discoveries and frequent setbacks, moments of doubt as well as wonder. If we set aside our hostility and see starlings for what they are, Zichello argues, we gain new insight into not only evolution and ecology but also ourselves.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/magazine/pedro-pa.headline: Pedro Pascal’s Life Began With a Rupture. He’s Still Coming to Terms With It.

paragraphs.text: There is sometimes a strange alchemy in interviews where you can get to a deeper, more complex place with someone despite your role as a journalist and theirs as a subject. The person being interviewed has to be willing to talk meaningfully about their life, sometimes their past, and reflect on it. Celebrities in particular can be understandably hesitant to do that. There was a personal reason I wanted to try to have that sort of conversation, though, with Pedro Pascal.

Pascal had a dramatic and painful rupture in his childhood in Chile that would shape the rest of his life in ways that he is only just coming to fully understand. His family fled their home country, ended up in exile in Texas and then later moved to Orange County, Calif. While he eventually found home and community in the theater in New York City, his mother never recovered, as he tells me, from the strain of displacement.

Pascal came to fame and professional success late in life, when at 39 he played Oberyn Martell in “Game of Thrones.” That role catapulted him into an A-list career, with roles as an interplanetary bounty hunter in “The Mandalorian” and a fierce father figure in the postapocalyptic saga “The Last of Us,” among others. His latest part is perhaps his most personal. In “Behemoth!” directed by Tony Gilroy and opening Dec. 4, he plays Alex, a nomadic, middle-aged cellist who is trying to come to terms with his life. It’s a role Pascal, now 51, told me he can really identify with.

“Behemoth!” is hard to describe. It’s like being locked in a dream or a memory. But I also think it plays into some of the themes that I want to talk about with you. You play Alex, a celebrated cellist in midlife, and the film unfolds over a series of flashbacks. I’ve seen the film described in a lot of ways, but to me it’s about generational trauma. I agree with you on a deep level. It’s very simple in its characters and in its humanity, but it’s very unusual in its structure. You’re figuring things out as the character is figuring things out. It wasn’t until a particular line in the movie where I realized that this character is, in his way, attempting to end generational trauma. But I didn’t think about that until we were doing it, so I’m very moved that you picked up on that.

Alex says very little in the film. There’s not a lot of dialogue. And there’s been a lot of discussion about how you, as an actor, are able to express things nonverbally in many of your roles. I’ve seen your face described as having incredible emotional depth, and also that you have “sad eyes.” Can you talk me through what is happening in a role like this, where you have to communicate so much but are not talking? There’s something delicious about a character who has a big internal life and is not skilled at expressing themselves externally. To have the entire story inside you and know that you’re only sharing it with the camera. That’s your secret self, almost.

You gave a great Spanish-language interview to your cousin, published in Chile, and you talked about what you give to a role. You said, “I put all my confusion, my joy, my sorrow, my ambivalence, my hostility, my rage, my love, my lust, my greed, my compassion, ignorance and knowledge” into your characters. That is a deep cut.

It is, and I was reading all those words and thinking, God, that must be wrenching. It can be wrenching to experience all of the things in life as we do. This is one of my early interviews, but what I got from that quote was a little bit of earnestness. I’m speaking to one of my older cousins, who was a really big deal to me as a kid. Her father is my godfather. It was always [lowers voice to a pity whisper] “He wants to be an actor.” They would probably all deny it, but I think there was a lot of pity and concern, especially that it was something I was continuing to pursue as a young adult and it wasn’t going my way. So then, for all of them, there was this kind of like: “Holy [expletive]! This son of a bitch got away with it!”

It’s an interesting interview because of her insight into your early life. And I’d like to talk a little about that, because I think that’s where a lot of those emotions come from. My family came from Cuba as political refugees, and there’s something very specific about that experience. Your family had to flee Chile when you were still an infant. Your parents were caught up in what was happening at that moment, a U.S.-backed coup that had thrown out the democratically elected government of leftist Salvador Allende. What was your parents’ involvement? My dad was doing his residency at the hospital of the university in Santiago, and my mother was in college. They were very progressive thinkers and, without too much calculation or preparation, did what they could when they could. Specifically, somebody had been shot in a gunfight and he was brought to my parents’ house knowing that my father was in medicine, and they hid out in our home. I must have been 4 months at the time, which would have made my sister 3 years old. And I remember a story about her being really pissed that there were guns on her bed.

So someone who brought this wounded man to our home was taken into custody, was tortured, and he gave names. And that included the names of both my mother and my father. Like a scene from some kind of political thriller, my father was lucky enough to get word that there was an officer at the hospital asking for him. And then that same officer put his hand on his shoulder and, as my father describes it, says, “Are you Dr. Balmaceda?” God, it’s fascinating to talk about these things because as much as I have tried to get details from my father, it still slips away. I don’t know how much he told me. I don’t know how much I put together myself. I do know that there was a moment of luck when a woman complained that she had been waiting so long in a room and that she was in pain and needed to see a doctor. She was an older woman, and you know in our culture, La mama manda [Mom is in charge].

You have to attend to it immediately. Exactamente. It’s like, “Well, Mom says. …” So I wonder if she knew what she was doing, and I don’t know if my dad knew that she may have known what she was doing to save him. Because he ended up taking her to the room, and he went out the back door, got my mom and then they went into hiding for six months.

They went to the Venezuelan Embassy, and you were taken care of by your cousin’s family because they had to leave without you. Your mother could not leave the embassy grounds, so your aunt would take you to see your parents through a window. Your mother couldn’t touch you, she couldn’t hold you, and you were a baby. Your early life was marked by such separation and fear. How do you think that specific period impacted your whole family? It’s a good question. It’s strange because we found ourselves landed on a different planet altogether — you know what I mean? — in San Antonio, Texas. And I’m none the wiser as a child, going to the movies with my father and being in the public school system in Texas and gradually coming to understand that there’s this entire large family in this world far away. I was sent back to Chile when I was 4 years old, before my parents were allowed back. It sounds like I’m making it up, but I was 4 and my sister was 7 and we flew by ourselves. My parents handed us over to the stewardess, who was just this wonderful-smelling ——

You remember it? I can recall taking a woman’s hand and feeling safe, weirdly. And then being escorted to the family waiting for us in Santiago and spending an entire summer there while it was winter in the States. It’s crazy to think about the things that you didn’t talk about, because obviously my parents needed help. They couldn’t manage things. And so somebody must have come up with the idea of, “Let us take the kids for the summer, sort your [expletive] out.”

My parents fled Cuba. My mother had two children. She was pregnant with a third. She was only 20 years old. And it sent her on this life of constant transition. And in my estimation, it made her a hoarder. She’s got warehouses filled with stuff that just sits there, old VHS machines that she never wants to throw away. And she’s explained that because she lost everything so young and then had this constant movement, things changing all the time, she wants to just hold onto things very tightly. And because I grew up with her, it makes me want to purge and get rid of everything! Did you have something like that? Did that trauma affect them in a particular way and it impacted you? I’m still negotiating with all of that. When we started the interview and we were speaking in Spanish, I was telling you that I feel a little embarrassed by being a first-timer around some of these things at my age. I’ve been having a year where I marvel at how young I feel inside — not in terms of vitality, unfortunately [laughs], but in how young I feel emotionally. How vulnerable I feel. This sounds like this way of tricking you into thinking about “Behemoth!” because the central character is totally evaluating his life and is having all of these memories triggered by music, and we’re part of this life evaluation slash life puzzle that has a big surprise. Well, that’s the [expletive] I’m going through.

You mentioned this very early physical separation as an infant between me and my mother. I’ve been having a lifelong struggle with sleep. I’ve been in therapy for most of my adult life, on and off. You feel like you make a lot of progress, and you slip back a lot, too. All of these things are so nonlinear. I talked to a doctor about this sleep issue over and over again. They start to ask you about your past. And I was like, “Well, it was a pretty tumultuous start.” And they’re like: “Hold on a second. Your mother went into hiding with you?” And I was like: “No, they went into hiding by themselves. My aunts took care of my sister and me.” And they’re like: “So you were physically separated from your mother? For how long?” And I was like, “For six months.” And they’re like, “Everything that was the most familiar to you was suddenly taken away from you.” And I was like: “That’s [expletive] great! What the hell am I supposed to do about that? I don’t have any memory! [Laughs] How am I supposed to fix that?”

I do feel kind of helpless against that sometimes. I also feel very, very grateful. I have such an incredibly rich life. All four of my siblings, we are close, we are thriving. But there’s still perplexity for me over how I navigate the very early conditions that have authored how I live inside my body. Maybe there’s way more therapy than I realize in playing parts. So in a safe environment, you can work out the grief of your own daughter dying in your arms or getting a chance to play a character who is just as nomadic as you are.

What was the catharsis of Alex in “Behemoth!”? He may fail the expectations of relationships that he’s in and is partly a victim to the circumstance of the dysfunctional dance his parents seemed to be trapped in and how they unload that onto him and to his talent. There are so many different reasons he is single and is not setting roots anywhere. And then he begins to make a decision. There comes a point where he is at a stop sign and he has the right blinker on, and then it turns to the left blinker. And that could be one of the first monumental moments in this character’s life, where he is making a decision and stepping toward the truth, because as soon as he makes this decision, it’s green lights toward a revelation. By making the decision to move toward an answer, what do you do with that? [Pascal chokes up] I think it’s an age thing.

Tell me what you’re feeling. I just think it’s moving. It’s moving because you have the opportunity to end a cycle of pain. That’s really beautiful. You talk about how our lives began without our choosing. And that’s what we have, our puzzle pieces. And we can choose to put the puzzle together and look at the picture and understand it, embrace it and understand ourselves as best as we can so that we can give the best of ourselves to the people that we love.

I’m going to bring something up that’s painful, because I think what you’re feeling is part of it. And first I want to say I’m so sorry. Your mother ended up taking her own life when you were in college. And she was your person in the world. I remember looking at that early experience of yours, that rupture, and then wondering how unimaginable it was to lose her that way. How do you understand that now? I want to be very careful how I talk about it because there are people who are still alive, whom I love very much. My mother met my father when she was 15 years old. She was a political refugee in a new country with two kids by the time she was 22 years old, and then in her mid-40s, she was back in Chile, and god knows the kind of complexities within that home that she grew up in, that she fled from as well. Not just the political circumstances but also the psychological circumstances of her own family, and then being returned to all of that. She didn’t make it. I think her heart was broken and she didn’t make it. Some people don’t survive these injuries. There were years leading up to it where she felt in peril to me. And this was my ultimate fear. We were separated by continents and I was desperately trying to get a job. Trying to get a TV series that would mean that I could pay for my mother to come live with me in the States.

You wanted her to come live with you because you saw that she was spiraling? Yeah. And it’s hard because she was not a simple person. She had kids very, very young, but she was a good mom. I think that people want to come up with, in my experience, lazy ways of understanding these kinds of losses, and they want to label it as some sort of diagnosis. I think that the one thing that we’ve never really talked about is that it was heartbreak. I wish I could remember — and I feel so bad because it helped me so much, and I can’t remember who the writer’s name is — but she wrote a book about the end of her marriage. I’m summarizing my memory of it. She was my age and her husband fell in love with someone else. The kids were raised and off to college and the marriage ended. And as a scientist she chose to study heartbreak. I found that to be really, really fascinating. [The book is “Heartbreak,” by Florence Williams.] And she says that you study the body under these circumstances — the death of a loved one, divorce, the death of a child, the death of a parent — and the cortisol levels in your body, actual inflammation of the heart, a lack of sleep, a lack of appetite, extended periods of these things can add up to heart attack, depression, anxiety and the kind of pain that your body is holding that you can no longer withstand. So the idea of choice is one to question, based on each circumstance. Can you imagine the kind of pain that you would be in to have the courage to end your life? [Pascal starts crying] I just have nothing but compassion for that, and I also understand it. I know exactly what it feels like. And what I’ve done is ask for help. I’m so sorry.
I’m so sorry. No, I’m sorry. It’s great to do this on a major public platform. Oh, god.
I’m holding myself a little together. I’m grateful to talk to you about it.

One of the reasons I wanted to talk to you is this inherited trauma of that generation — of all the things that they went through and all the tumult and the secrets that they held to protect us and the hopes that they have for us. I was thinking about that burden for you and how that played out in your career. And why, when people look at you as an actor, they see themselves so deeply reflected. Even with a helmet on.
Maybe not with the helmet on. Even faceless. [Laughs] They literally see themselves because there’s a reflection of their face back at them.

I want to talk about the professional part of this, because what you go into is this interesting period of never quite making it, which you’ve alluded to. You were trying to get pilots. What was going on then? I could come up with a lot of different answers. One boring one, and they talk about this a lot in terms of casting: What age do you come into your own? You look like such a castable 20-year-old, and that look is something that can slip away once you start getting into your 30s. Or it doesn’t develop into something that people consider “castable.” Not handsome enough or, strangely, too Caucasian for the name Pedro.

You changed your name a bunch of times. You started your career with your legal name, Pedro Balmaceda. I didn’t start changing my name until after my mother died because there was such a desperation that I felt. One, I wanted her [last] name, and two, I was in such grief, and getting work would mean that my life would make sense. Especially in New York City, there are crime shows, and I guess they were very limited in terms of casting Latinos, or allowing somebody named Pedro to play somebody named Trevor. I tried to go by Alex, but people calling me Alex felt so weird. I was already in my 20s, and I was like, I can’t do that. For better or worse, my name is Pedro. I’ll keep Pascal. It’s easier to spell, anyone can pronounce it, rather than Balmaceda. And it belongs to my mother. So that was that. There were still years of struggle, but it was a finite decision that was made, and then work started to become more and more consistent. I would get the part of Kevin or the part of Tito. I just started to be very versatile in terms of whatever opportunity presented itself.

You were doing a lot of regional theater at the time: Shakespeare, Ibsen, serious roles. It’s interesting because I didn’t get cast in Ibsen until I changed my name to Alexander. Then I got the part of Oswald in Henrik Ibsen’s “Ghosts.” Those were the types of parts I was desperate to play that I felt were kept from me because I was a white-looking Pedro. But anyway, it’s fair for you to ask about my mom because it identified the journey in a very, very particular way. I was willing to compromise professionally to get a pilot to make money and do the grind out of Los Angeles. Then after she died, I realized that I couldn’t process that grief in that environment. It wasn’t a nurturing enough environment. I had to come back to what felt like home at the time, which was New York, and to my community of friends, and to go after the experience of being in a cast and in a rehearsal process and in the run of a play and within the family of a play.

That makes so much sense. Boy, was it a mistake! It took me off track. I went back to waiting tables and felt like I had taken myself so far away from the goal. I didn’t know what was going to happen. And then finally, my first Off Broadway play, the Cuban playwright Nilo Cruz’s “Beauty of the Father.” He had won the Pulitzer for “Anna in the Tropics,” so it was a big deal. That door opened and I got into the mix and had some consistent Off Broadway work, got my first “Law & Order” and my second “Law & Order,” but I felt a ceiling in New York as far as theater was concerned. It was drying up pretty quick. I wasn’t getting auditions for Broadway, and I was getting into my mid-30s and I’ve got to be able to afford rent.

What did that period teach you? Everything. It made me stronger. It made me develop very, very strong bonds to my theater community. I became a member of the Labyrinth Theater Company. I was around artists. The creative life and being in love with the art of it, being in love with other people’s work, literature, film and creating a moral identity around what it means to be creative.

Correct me if I’m wrong, but what I’m hearing you say is that the work saved you. Without question. It saved me when I was young, too. It saved me as a child. When you say: What are the things that aren’t being spoken about? What are the things that we carry that we don’t realize that we’re carrying? What have our parents not processed and are unconsciously externalizing? Sharing with us in ways that they don’t realize? My father would take us to the movies. I fell in love with movies early, early on. That’s my identity. My truest identity is the person who’s sitting in the theater and who is in school even now.

That’s beautiful. I’m going to do a little bit of a despojo [a spiritual cleansing]. I want to talk about sex onscreen. You were 39 years old when you appeared in your big breakout role in “Game of Thrones.” Your character, Oberyn Martell, was introduced in a brothel as this sexually omnivorous and deadly prince. How do you translate sexual energy onto the screen? [Laughs] I don’t mean to giggle, but it’s a pivot.

It’s a total pivot. I get a little confused when a scene between two people that is physical, sexually, is treated so differently. There are so many different levels of vulnerabilities and forms of expression that can come through language, like we’ve talked about with “Behemoth!” and music, or with physical combat. It’s all language. And so it’s a scene like any other.

In “Behemoth!” you also play this object of desire. What do you think makes someone desirable? Because this is such a thing that people identify you with. It’s not separate. I don’t want to step into any traps, but you know as a Latina that there is culturally an openness and a friendliness and a level of affection that in some cases is deemed as flirtation. Even the idea of flirting has some purity to it. You know what I mean? That you can be a flirt without an end goal, without trying to get something. Maybe that is a piece of myself that I integrate into a character as a way of making them human and relatable. I think that that’s the best way I understand what I think you’re getting at.

As has been much discussed, you have come to epitomize a type of masculinity that is very emotionally available, sensitive, mature. You’re “the internet’s boyfriend.” What do you make of that kind of idealization of you? I think it’s strange. What I think about most is that in this time and the way media exists, so much authors itself without any of your doing. It’s so completely out of your control. It can author itself into the positive. It can author itself into the negative. It has its own life force, and you have no control over it, and that is scary. Also, I’m not young. I’m 51 now. So I’m not going to try to be something. I want you to like my work to a degree. But I guess there’s a conscious decision to just not take it too seriously. And I don’t always protect myself from it, you know? I’m totally human. The algorithm has us completely figured out. I don’t know how to put my phone down better than anybody else, and sometimes things find their way in and it can be really, really painful. And you’re like: Wait a minute, I’m 51 years old. Why do I feel like I’m 14? So it’s something to navigate. What will it be 10 years from now? I’m likely to be free of whatever that is, because at 60 if anyone is thinking about me as an internet boyfriend, we’re writing a whole other story.

persuasion.community/p/teresa-bejan.headline: Teresa Bejan on Why Equality Is More Fragile Than We Think
persuasion.community/p/teresa-bejan.author: Yascha Mounk

paragraphs.text: Teresa M. Bejan is Professor of Political Theory and a Fellow of Oriel College at the University of Oxford. She is the author of Mere Civility: Disagreement and the Limits of Toleration and First Among Equals: Visions of Equality before Egalitarianism.

In this week’s conversation, Yascha Mounk and Teresa Bejan discuss why Oxford’s first-name culture can reinforce hierarchy rather than flatten it, how the Leveller John Lilburn turned an ancient, hierarchical idea of human equality into a radical political demand, and what the forgotten distinction between being equal and being a peer reveals about today’s debates over affirmative action and immigration.
We’re delighted to feature this conversation as part of our series on Liberal Virtues and Values.

This series, made possible with the generous support of the John Templeton Foundation, features content making the case that liberalism has its own distinctive set of virtues and values that are capable not only of responding to the dissatisfaction that drives authoritarianism, but also of restoring faith in liberalism as an ideology worth believing in—and defending—on its own terms.
This transcript has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity.

Yascha Mounk: I always really enjoy talking to you, and I really enjoyed reading your new book. We’ve been talking about it for a long time, and you have a really interesting set of things to talk about and to say about equality, both about the contemporary use of it and the intellectual history of it. I want to start quite concretely. You arrived at Oxford about ten years ago. Oxford has quite an egalitarian norm of calling people by their first names, but you found that in some ways that norm felt less egalitarian than it might appear. Why?

Teresa Bejan: First, it’s probably just worth stopping for a moment, because I think it may come as a surprise to many of your listeners that Oxford is in any way known for egalitarian norms. It’s a very ancient university. My college within the university is celebrating its seven hundredth anniversary this year. What’s important, I think, within Oxford is this sense that every member of the university is an equal member of the university, and therefore we reflect this in the way that we refer to each other by first names. I also think that it’s envisioned as a corrective to the obviously hierarchical and exclusionary nature of the place.

In any event, when I arrived in Oxford over a decade ago, I wasn’t a total outsider. I’d spent a lot of time at Cambridge, I’d spent some time at Oxford before, but I found this norm extremely shocking, because I’d been teaching up to that point in Canada at the University of Toronto, but then also at its branch campus in Mississauga, which has a really healthy majority of first-generation students, immigrant students. It’s very much the satellite campus as an engine of social mobility, but within the university itself, the hierarchical norms were respected. Particularly, you call professors “Professor,” and you don’t presume to use someone’s first name until they tell you otherwise. I’ll confess that when I arrived it was a real, bracing sense of culture shock, because I’d always up to that point been referred to by students with my title.

Mounk: One is the difference of norms, but another point you make about it is that, in some ways, you might think that this flattens social hierarchy, that it means that the just-arrived assistant professor is treated the same way as the already famous professor who’s been there for 50 years. You perceived it differently: the professor who’s famous anyway doesn’t need the title, and for the younger people, actually, the title is what gives them the standing of equals within the academic ranks. To be stripped of it somehow ends up reinforcing hierarchies.

Bejan: Exactly right. Superficially, it seems that the more equal arrangement is to use first names for everyone, but in practice what happens, and what I experienced, was that my senior colleagues, very often male colleagues, would have the privilege of saying, please, please call me John, because students would default to “Professor” in that case. For younger faculty, for female faculty, for ethnic minority faculty, whoever didn’t really look the way that a student might expect an Oxford don to look, it was immediately first names.

The thing that I found particularly shocking was the eagerness of graduate students to police this. In some cases, if I introduced myself by my title, I would be corrected by students. It was just so interesting: it was invariably male students. I remember I gave my very first lecture at Oxford and introduced myself just unthinkingly: I’m Professor Bejan, this is the course, et cetera. I got an email from a student afterward saying that’s not how we do things here.

I was just really interested in conflicting intuitions about what it means to treat people as equals, because certainly, I think, the North American view is that if someone has gone through the process of getting a PhD and achieved this credential and distinguished themselves in this way, you treat them as an equal by giving them their title. I think the other instinct is that, no, no, no, actually titles distract from and introduce noxiously inegalitarian dynamics. My own intuition, not to preempt anything, and I think it’s borne out in experience, is that the problem with defaulting to egalitarian norms, or defaulting to the same for everyone, is that it ends up obfuscating or obscuring the realities of hierarchical power in that situation. I think, in particular, it encourages faculty not to reflect on the duties that they have towards those in their care and under their authority.

Mounk: I’m a little torn about this. I like your instinct to complicate what seems like a simple story, and I have some experiences that resonate with this, but to your comparison between the United States, or North America, and the United Kingdom, I want to add the even less egalitarian example of Germany. Let me say a couple of things.

First, I found it quite interesting when I was an undergrad at Cambridge, which obviously has pretty similar norms to Oxford in a variety of ways. I arrived, and the hierarchy felt like it was incredibly in your face. One example from most colleges in Cambridge and Oxford is that fellows of a college are allowed to walk on the lawn, whereas students and certainly tourists are not allowed to walk on the lawn and will be rudely corrected, or, yes, politely reprimanded, by the porters: “Do not walk on the lawn.” Then I found that it is perhaps in part that hierarchy that allowed a much greater intellectual egalitarianism compared to what I was used to growing up in Germany.

I loved this about my undergraduate experience. In one of my first supervisions, where you write an essay and then you have a one-hour, one-on-one meeting with your supervisor, or your tutor, as it might be called depending on the context, to discuss it, I had been given a bunch of things to read about a topic I knew nothing about. I think it was about whether the height of recruits to the English army had gone up between 1800 and 1830 and what they told us about whether the industrial revolution had increased living standards or not. My supervisor said, “You summarized these readings pretty well, but you don’t really have an argument. What do you think?” I said, “I don’t know what I think. I just read these. You studied this.”

There’s a real assumption, not just that you make an argument, but that you argue with your supervisor, that you defend your corner, and the way you earn respect is to score some points against them, to disagree with them intelligently, and so on. I found, and this is also quite a hierarchical observation, that in a way, I think, it is perhaps the fact that my supervisor could walk across the lawn and I couldn’t, which established a clear social hierarchy between us, that then allowed them, in the intellectual exchange, to treat me as an equal. I share that part of it.
