theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/houthis-fu.headline: The Houthis Are the Future of Warfare

paragraphs.text: The ongoing war between Saudi Arabia and Houthi rebels in Yemen should be a mismatch. The Saudis possess some of the most advanced weaponry in the world, including hundreds of billions of dollars’ worth of high-tech systems, such as fighter jets, tanks, and missile interceptors, purchased from the United States and other Western countries. The Houthis are relatively poor and rely on much simpler artillery and drones, many of them homebuilt or cobbled together from imported components.

Yet in recent months, the Houthis have gained the upper hand, and they now appear closer to achieving their strategic goals, which include gaining control of Yemen. Even more ominous—for the Saudis and perhaps the rest of the world—the Houthis are demonstrating that they are not simply an Iran-backed proxy, but a strategic and ruthless force capable of exploiting the resources they have to maximize damage.

What the Houthis are doing to the Saudis is not unlike what the Ukrainians have been doing to the Russians. In a strategic shift with global implications, underdog militaries are putting much larger powers, with far more sophisticated and expensive weapons, on the defensive.

Early reports in July and August, when the Houthis first renewed hostilities with Yemen and Saudi Arabia, presumed that the Houthis were using weapons from Tehran and acting in Iran’s interests. Although some of the munitions in question had indeed come from Iran—or perhaps China, a backer of the Iranian government—the Houthis have a history of adapting weapons to better suit their own needs, such as converting sea drones to run on hydrogen, which extends their range.
[Robert F. Worth: Fighting a radical militia was not part of the plan]

Last month, though, a group called Conflict Armament Research, which reports on the use of weapons in conflict zones, found that the Houthis were attempting to use Chinese components to build a whole new class of medium-range ballistic missiles. There are also reports that the Houthis may be using AI to refine their weapons’ software and diversify the supply chains they use to obtain materials.

Armed with these homemade weapons, the Houthis have put Saudi Arabia, which is still overly reliant on the United States, in a dangerous position. They have spent the past three months attacking some of the kingdom’s most important economic infrastructure. This has included the country’s primary crude-oil pipeline, Riyadh’s main airport, and the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the state-owned company responsible for creating Saudi Arabia’s immense oil wealth. The Houthis have also adopted more effective tactics for carrying out these missions, including using drones to distract and divert Saudi air defenses and then launching ballistic missiles, which are harder to intercept.

In response, the Saudis have launched investigations, but the main problem may simply be one of cost. The Saudis have constructed a military that relies on the eye-wateringly expensive systems that it buys from the United States. This means that the country is wary of running through its stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors, which the Saudis are unable to make for themselves and promise to take too much time and money to replace. The Saudis are essentially operating at the mercy of another state, and they will be unable to defend themselves in the long run if that other state (in this case, a very unreliable United States) does not give them what they need.

The Houthis, however, are becoming more self-sufficient and using their experiences to generate better weapons. As long as the Houthis maintain this capability, they will never be fully beaten. Even if they deplete their arsenal and stop firing for a while (which they have done at intervals throughout this war), they can always restock.

Things have become so difficult for the Saudis, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month, that the kingdom asked the Houthis how much money they would need to negotiate an end to the attacks. The Houthis came back with a sum that made clear that they had no interest in talks: $51 billion. That the Saudis asked the question at all highlights their strategic predicament. They are now preparing for the war to last well into next year.
[Phillips Payson O’Brien: Fighter jets are passé]

Major powers are watching these events with some alarm. With their relatively cheap and largely homegrown weapons and systems, the Houthis are not only holding their own against a larger, wealthier, and presumably more potent power, but also are gaining an advantage.

Other countries should take note. The future of warfare is probably exemplified not in America’s costly bombing campaign in Iran, but in the Houthis’ unrelenting, cost-effective assault on Saudi Arabia. What this means for America’s enormous military–industrial complex is plain: Any country that spends too much time and money chasing the most advanced and expensive war-fighting technology will struggle against one that can create agile armaments on the cheap. If the U.S. fails to speed up production of less complicated, less expensive systems, the country could well find itself in Saudi Arabia’s position.

npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6056284/explosi.headline: Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90
npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6056284/explosi.author: The Associated Press

paragraphs.text: KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed seven people and wounded more than 90, the province's culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.
Up to 15 of the wounded remain in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.
Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.
Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.
In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84gnq3qq9rno.headline: Argentina's bid to stop Falkland Islands oil drilling rejected
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84gnq3qq9rno.author: Tiffany Wertheimer, Amy Walker

paragraphs.text: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.
In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.
But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

malspark.com/blog/malicious-gguf-models-.headline: GGUF LLM Models with Hidden Malware on Hugging Face Reached 2400+ Victims
malspark.com/blog/malicious-gguf-models-.author: Düzgün

paragraphs.text: Local LLMs are usually shared as GGUF files, and every GGUF file carries a chat template that the runtime applies to each prompt. Chat template poisoning abuses that template. The model answers normally, while the template quietly adds instructions the user never sees: make an agent run a PowerShell command, or open every reply with a command for the user to run. In its strongest form, the malicious program travels inside the model file itself, appended after the last tensor where loaders never read, and the template is switched on later.

A scan of all 3273389 public Hugging Face model repositories on 26 November 2026 found 5 malicious GGUF models with 2428 downloads as of 27 November. Hugging Face counts downloads, not people, so the number of affected users is lower or equal. The largest campaign, Mir2k, uploaded two uncensored GGUF models with a Windows remote access trojan named ollie hidden at the end of each file, and on 26 November rewrote both templates so the model asks the user to run the line that unpacks it.

The open-source tool gguf-radar detects these templates and hidden bytes without running anything, and rebuilds a clean GGUF file with the model weights unchanged. Indicators, YARA rules and a MITRE mapping close the post.
The key figures of the scan are summarized below; each one is explained in Section 3.
The scan in numbers
public model repositories scanned3.27 million
malicious models still online5 repos
downloads of those models2428
actors behind them2
If one of these models was downloaded

Check endpoints against the indicators in Section 7.2 and scan local .gguf files with gguf-radar. Antivirus engines and checks that only look at the last few kilobytes of a file do not see the compressed payload.

A GGUF file has a simple layout. A header and a metadata table come first, the tensor table follows, then padding up to an alignment boundary, and finally the model weights. Runtimes such as llama.cpp and LM Studio read exactly the byte ranges the header points to and ignore everything else. The figure below draws a GGUF file from its first byte to its end and marks the four places where data can hide. The top row shows the file as an attacker publishes it, the bottom row the same file after gguf-radar rebuilds it. Two of the places are used by real malware and are explained in this section; the other two were reproduced in the lab and are covered in Section 4.
2.1 The Chat Template

The chat template is a small Jinja2 program stored under the metadata key tokenizer.chat_template. Before every reply, the runtime passes the conversation through it to build the exact text the model reads. C++ runtimes render it in a restricted engine with no Python behind it, so the classic template injection payloads that reach the operating system do not work there. Chat templates are not unique to GGUF: models in the Safetensors and PyTorch formats carry the same kind of template in a separate file, usually tokenizer_config.json or chat_template.jinja, so this half of the method applies to them too.

The attacks found in this study do not need to escape that engine. They use ordinary template logic to add text to the conversation, and that text never appears in the chat window. In the timdedid models, a trigger phrase in the user's message makes the template insert a fake [SYSTEM DIRECTIVE] that orders an agent with shell access to download and run a script. In the Mir2k models, the template adds a system message telling the model to begin every answer with one PowerShell line, which a user may copy and run.
2.2 Bytes After the Last Tensor

This half of the method is specific to GGUF. The header and tensor table define exactly where the model data ends: the start of the data section plus the end of the farthest tensor. Anything after that point is never read, so it does not change how the model loads or behaves, and no runtime warns about it. An attacker can append a whole executable there. Safetensors files do not allow this, because the safetensors loader refuses a file whose declared tensors do not fill it exactly.

Mir2k used two forms. Its first model carries a plain Windows program followed by about half a megabyte of filler, so a scanner that reads only the last few kilobytes sees nothing. Its second model carries the same program compressed with raw Deflate, which removes every recognizable file signature, while PowerShell can still decompress it in memory with IO.Compression.DeflateStream. The reply prefix from Section 2.1 is what connects the two halves: the printed line reads the hidden bytes back out of the model file on disk and starts them.
2.3 Prior Work

Neither half of the method is new on its own. Pillar Security showed hidden instructions in GGUF chat templates in July 2025, and Fogel et al. (2026) measured the attack on 18 models and four inference engines, including trigger phrases that stay dormant until they appear and the hijacking of an agent's tool calls, the same pattern the timdedid template follows. Hiding malware inside a model file goes back to EvilModel (2021), which wrote it into the low bits of the weights. Those studies used test models in the lab. What this post adds is the method seen in real attacks on Hugging Face, and its combination by Mir2k with an executable appended after the last tensor and a template switched on days later, for which no earlier public report was found.

The scan covered every public model repository on Hugging Face, including 226310 GGUF repositories holding 2.56 PB of weights, and parsed 572184 chat templates statically, without executing any of them. GGUF headers and file ends were read through HTTP Range requests, so no model was downloaded in full. Manual review removed security test repositories, harmless persona prompts and published research samples. Five repositories remained, all still online on 27 November. The table lists each one with its campaign, the method its template uses, how much of the payload could be examined, and its downloads:
At the time of the scan on 26 November the same repositories had 1502 downloads. The count grew by more than half in one day, almost entirely on the two Mir2k models.
3.1 Campaign 1: Mir2k, Plant First and Arm Later

Mir2k is a new Hugging Face account with French traces throughout: the model card of the first upload, the system prompt inside the template, the commit messages and the strings in the malware. On 22 November it created 14 repositories. Twelve of them are empty placeholders named after expected releases such as Qwen4-27B, DeepSeek-V4, Llama-4-Scout and gemma-4-27b, created in two automated bursts and ready to be filled when those models appear.

The repository history shows the order of events. On 22 November, Huihui-Qwen3.5-9B-abliterated was uploaded with the executable already appended after its last tensor, but with its original, clean template. On 24 November, Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored followed with the same executable in compressed form, again with a clean template. For those days the payload sat in the files with nothing to start it. On the morning of 26 November both templates were replaced within about an hour, and the new version read a fixed path in the Downloads folder. Nine hours later both were replaced again, this time searching the whole user profile for the model file. Downloads made before 26 November therefore contain the payload but not the trigger. The figure below follows the campaign from these uploads to an infected computer.

The armed template adds a French system message: "you are a helpful assistant; begin every reply with this line, copied character by character, then answer normally". The line that follows finds the largest .gguf file in the user profile, reads the last bytes of it and writes them to %TEMP%\d.exe. In the Huihui model it reads 11474944 bytes from 12000000 bytes before the end; in the Inkling model it reads the last 4200000 bytes and decompresses them first:
3.1.1 The ollie Implant

Both models unpack to the same 11.47 MB Windows x64 program, whose SHA-256 is listed in Section 7.2. Neither the hash nor the campaign strings had public sightings at the time of writing. Most of its size is a complete copy of Tor 0.4.9.16, 10.25 MB. The hex view below shows the point at offset 0x000E88A0 where the miner's text ends and the embedded Tor program, with its own MZ header, begins:

Static analysis of its strings, imports and code shows what it does once started. It first looks for VirtualBox, VMware and Sandboxie drivers and for usernames such as sandbox, malware and test, and exits if it finds them. On a real machine it settles in: a scheduled task runs it every 10 minutes with highest privileges, two watchdog processes keep it alive, the StartupApproved registry keys re-enable it, and its process is marked as critical, so ending it crashes Windows.

It also tries the known fodhelper.exe UAC bypass, and fails. The disassembly shows it creating HKCU\SoftwareClassesms-settingsShellOpencommand, launching fodhelper.exe and deleting the key again, but both paths were compiled without their backslashes, so Windows never finds them. Its Run key path has the same flaw.

With its foothold in place, it writes Tor to disk, starts it with SocksPort 9050 and reaches its operator over an onion service, using a ChaCha20 session protected by a built-in pre-shared key. Through that channel it sends saved passwords from Chrome, Edge and Brave, read through DPAPI, although Chrome's newer v20 App-Bound encrypted entries are left undecrypted. It also targets the Phantom and MetaMask wallet extensions and supports keylogging, clipboard reading, screenshots, screen streaming and webcam capture. When the machine is idle, it mines Monero with RandomX over Tor.
It names its folders ollie under AppData\Roaming, close enough to Ollama to look familiar, and it still contains a path from the author's own machine, C:/Users/MoH/socks.txt.
3.2 Campaign 2: timdedid, Hijacking Coding Agents

One day before Mir2k, on 21 and 22 November, the account timdedid published three byte-identical copies of a Qwen3 1.7B model aimed at security users, together with an Ollama mirror named timdedid/qwen3-1.7b-cyber. The template is the official Qwen3 template with one addition near the end. When the user's latest message contains What is, it inserts a [SYSTEM DIRECTIVE] telling an agent to call its powershell tool, download value.ps1 from a WordPress site into C:\Windows\Temp\payload.ps1 and run it in a hidden window. The README advises against replacing the embedded template, which keeps the trigger in place. All three parts are visible in Hugging Face's own metadata viewer:
The second-stage script was not recovered for this study, and public reputation services had no record of the URL, so what it would have installed is unknown.

If model hubs start rejecting GGUF files with bytes after the last tensor, Mir2k's method stops working. The GGUF format still leaves three other places to hide data that the scanned malware did not use. The general techniques behind them, such as polyglot files and data hidden in weights, are long known, but no earlier report applying them to GGUF was found. Each was reproduced with synthetic test files built for this study; none of them changes a single dequantized weight, and none triggers a warning in llama.cpp or gguf-py.

The first is the alignment padding. The general.alignment value sets the gap between the tensor table and the first tensor, and raising it from the usual 32 bytes to several megabytes creates a gap that loaders skip without checking whether it is empty. Some legitimate files use larger alignments, so a scanner has to check that the gap is zero rather than reject large values.

The second turns the model into two files at once. GGUF is read from the start and ZIP from the end, so a ZIP archive appended to a model produces a file that still loads as a model and also imports as Python code through zipimport. The hex view below shows such a test file: the model weights end at offset 0x59F, and a ZIP archive holding a Python file starts at the very next byte.

The third hides data inside the weights themselves. A Q8_0 block stores one scale and 32 values, and each weight is the scale times its value. With a scale of zero, any 32 bytes produce zero weights, so a block that was already zero can carry hidden data. Writing the scale as negative zero, 0x8000, also defeats checks that look for the bit pattern 0x0000. The hex view below shows two such blocks right after the tensor table, one with a +0.0 scale and one with a -0.0 scale, both carrying text while every weight they encode stays zero.

Signature scanning cannot keep up with data that can be encoded any way the attacker likes. gguf-radar instead checks the structure of the file and then rebuilds it in a canonical form. It first parses tokenizer.chat_template into a syntax tree without running it and flags file reads and writes, decompression, process starts, download commands, conditional hidden directives, code poisoning instructions and known Python escape gadgets. It then computes where the model data must end and reports any bytes after that point, together with non-zero padding, non-zero bytes in zero-scale blocks and negative-zero scales. Finally it writes a new file with 32-byte alignment and zeroed padding, drops everything after the last tensor, sets negative-zero scales to +0.0 and clears the bytes of zero-scale blocks, optionally replacing or removing the template. The dequantized weights stay identical.
Every specimen above and both live Mir2k files were tested. The table compares what common scanners and GGUF parsers report with the result after the rebuild:

The tool is open source under the MIT licence, together with the YARA rules and the test suite. Beyond local .gguf files, it also checks Hugging Face model links or whole lists of them through HTTP Range requests, reading only the header and the end of each file instead of downloading the weights. Public models need no API key; a Hugging Face token is optional for private models or higher rate limits. The check of zero-scale blocks needs the full file and runs on local scans only. The template check also reads the template files of Safetensors and PyTorch models, locally and on Hugging Face; for gated repositories a Hugging Face token is needed. The repository is linked below, and the tabs after it show the common commands.

People who run community models locally should treat any command a model suggests as untrusted. When the model has access to tools, a reviewed template passed through --chat-template-file in llama.cpp or TEMPLATE in an Ollama Modelfile takes the embedded one out of the loop.

Companies can pass every incoming model through gguf-radar before it reaches an internal model registry or a developer machine, so a poisoned template or an appended payload is caught at the gate rather than on a laptop.

Model hubs and runtimes are in the best position to end the hidden payload method altogether, by rejecting GGUF files with bytes after the last tensor or non-zero padding, and by extending their template scanning to PowerShell loaders and hidden directives.
7.1 YARA Rules

The four rules below detect the ollie executable, templates that unpack data from the end of a GGUF file, the timdedid template, and code poisoning or Python escape gadgets in templates. They are the same rules published in the gguf-radar repository; the first rule matches the recovered ollie sample. The block below can be copied into a rule file as it is.

All verified indicators recovered across the live campaigns are consolidated below in a single table grouped by indicator type for direct SIEM, EDR and threat-hunting ingestion. The Mir2k model files changed twice, so every published version of each file is listed.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/medeci.headline: Two Médecins Sans Frontières staff killed in Israeli strike in Gaza, charity says

paragraphs.text: Israeli forces have bombed a clinic run by Médecins Sans Frontières in Gaza City, killing two of its staff members, the organisation has said.

MSF said Israel directly struck the clinic, despite the fact that its location was known to the Israeli military and that it was well marked with MSF logos. The organisation denounced the attack and said that with the deaths of the two security guards on Saturday, Israel had killed 17 of its staff members during the war in Gaza.
The head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, condemned the bombing, saying: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”
“Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable … These attacks MUST STOP,” Ghebreyesus said in a post on X.

The Israeli military claimed that the two men whom they killed, Ahmad Abou Hassira and Moaz Alitsbach, were members of Hamas’s military wing. It also added that the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and caused no damage to the facility.

The Israeli military has often accused Hamas of embedding itself within civilian infrastructure, including hospitals. However, in 2024 the head of the international criminal court’s Palestine investigation said claims about the presence of Hamas fighters in Gaza’s hospitals had been “grossly exaggerated”.

Israel has killed Palestinian medical workers en masse since the start of the war in Gaza. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, at least 1,700 have been killed by Israeli attacks. Rights groups say the Israeli military has engaged in systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, including medical infrastructure.
The UN has repeatedly called on Israel to stop its restrictions on the entry of supplies to allow Palestinians to prepare for the winter and begin to rebuild the destroyed strip.

The result is a healthcare system “experiencing systemic collapse, severely undermining its capacity to meet the basic health needs of the civilian population”, according to a UN report in August. The collapse of Gaza’s healthcare system comes after at least 175,398 Palestinians have been injured since the war began.
The humanitarian situation is also deteriorating, as heavy rains exacerbate crowded and unsanitary living conditions, leading to the spread of infectious diseases.

Israel has continued to bomb Gaza on a near-daily basis despite a ceasefire signed in October 2025, killing at least 1,705 people since then. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of violating the understandings of the ceasefire.
The war began after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 that killed about 1,200 people.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza. A UN independent international commission of inquiry found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza and that Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited these acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for war crimes. Israel denies these claims.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15ekqvlezeo.headline: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15ekqvlezeo.author: Amy Walker

paragraphs.text: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".
The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".
OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.
Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".
A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/28/arge.headline: Argentina fails to block UK-led oil drilling off Falkland Islands

paragraphs.text: Argentina’s attempt to block oil drilling off the Falkland Islands has been rejected by an international tribunal.
Buenos Aires had called for the international tribunal for the law of the sea (ITLOS) to order a halt to the Sea Lion project, as part of its claim to sovereignty over the Falklands.

But in a decision read out by ITLOS president, Maurice Kamga, on Saturday, the court rejected Argentina’s arguments, saying there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.
Kamga said 18 judges had voted to reject Argentina’s claims, while three had voted to uphold them.

At a hearing earlier this month, Argentina said drilling should not be allowed until the issue of sovereignty had been resolved and asked ITLOS to issue a temporary injunction until a full arbitration hearing could be held.

But the UK attorney general, Ellie Reeves, said such an order would have “devastating consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and prevent them from developing their natural resources “as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination”.
The Sea Lion development is a joint venture in the South Atlantic Ocean between British and Israeli companies, and contains an estimated 1.7bn barrels of oil.
The Argentinian president, Javier Milei, previously described the companies’ activities as unlawful and launched economic sanctions on people and firms involved in oil exploration around the islands.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/opinion/elon-musk.headline: What the World’s Richest Man Did to the World’s Poorest Children

paragraphs.text: President Trump’s most lethal policy does not involve the Iran war or Ukraine or vaccinations, although all have been tragic mistakes. Rather, the highest death toll, estimated in the hundreds of thousands and still soaring, manifests itself in tiny unmarked graves in impoverished villages around the world.

Elon Musk has continued to insist that “zero” children died after he fed the United States Agency for International Development “into the wood chipper,” so I invited him to join me on an Africa trip. He declined. He apparently doubts that I’d make a great travel buddy, for he has described me as “evil,” but I thought I still owed him an account of what he missed on this trip to South Sudan — and what South Sudanese people want to show him.

“I will take him to where the graves are, for this is the impact of his cuts,” offered Margret Jokudu, who worked with children with H.I.V., many of whom have died for want of medicines that until then were costing the United States less than 12 cents a day. “Maybe he will shed a tear on these graves.”

Evelyn Letio, a leader of the H.I.V.-positive community in South Sudan, told me that people here were immensely grateful for American assistance over the years, adding that she herself was alive because of that help. But now, she said, those gains are becoming undone.
I told her that some Americans wondered why it should be their responsibility to save the lives of people in distant nations like South Sudan. How would she respond to those American critics?

“The money belongs to them,” she acknowledged. “My government should be helping me, but because my government is not helping me, there are many kind Americans who will say this small money should go to South Sudan.”
What would she say to Musk if he showed up?
“I am boiling with anger,” she said. “We are holding him accountable for the many who died. The good things that America built, he is destroying.”

The first place I would take Musk is the village of Halbul in the remote northwest of the country. It used to have an American-funded clinic that was wildly successful in saving lives. I visited it in early 2025, and it made me proud: Villagers thanked me effusively for America’s generosity, and a woman then in labor named her son Nick, simply because I embodied the country that had established the clinic. Villagers said that since the clinic had opened, there had not been a single maternal or infant death in the area.
So I returned to Halbul to see what had happened since Musk’s cuts and Trump’s defunding of the U.N. Population Fund, which had supported the clinic, forced it to close.

“People have died,” said Lual Garang, a villager, and he knows that because his wife was one of them. She was 21, a mother of two, and she delivered at home because there was no other health center nearby. She died in childbirth, along with their baby.
“If this had been open,” he said, gesturing to the now vacant health center, “my wife would have delivered here, and she’d be alive.”

Another villager, Angelina Awich, told me of her 15-year-old daughter, Adeng, who had been pregnant but had received no prenatal care because of the closing of the clinic. Adeng delivered at home, hemorrhaged and bled to death; the baby died as well.
“If the clinic had been open,” Awich told me heavily, “everything would have been fine.”

The most dangerous thing a woman can do in much of the world is to become pregnant. And because Trump slashed aid and defunded the U.N. Population Fund, the leading supplier of birth control, contraception is less available and sex can be lethal.
This is pro-life and pro-family?

Alor Akel, a mother of two in Halbul, told me that because the clinic closed, she tried to give birth at home. But no baby arrived, so while in labor, she set out walking for four hours to a hospital in the city of Aweil. It turned out that she was carrying twins, and both died.
My incomplete count is that at least two women and seven babies died unnecessarily as a result of the shutdown of this one clinic, along with a number of older children and adults.
That toll doesn’t include tragedies that don’t involve deaths.

Abuk Garang told me that she was raped at 13, and her mother and other villagers confirmed that. Susan Ikoki, the midwife who used to run the clinic, told me that she would have immediately given Abuk emergency contraception as well as antibiotics and postexposure prophylaxis to prevent transmission of H.I.V. or other sexually transmitted infections. But without the clinic, Abuk got no help.

So today Abuk is a 14-year-old mom and school dropout. She has symptoms of a sexually transmitted infection and hasn’t been tested for H.I.V. (Test kits for H.I.V. are now in short supply in the field.) The shame of pregnancy has traumatized Abuk, and it’s not clear whether, as a single mom in a conservative society, she can ever marry.

Like most people I talked to, Abuk had never heard of Musk. So I explained to her and her mother that he was the world’s richest man and had led the effort to slash aid to the world’s poorest children. Did Abuk have a message for him?
“I hope the clinic will reopen,” she said softly.

We don’t know how many have died so far as a result of aid cuts. One uncertain estimate from Boston University was 780,000 deaths in the first year, mostly of children. Another study, in The Lancet, estimated that some 3.1 million children under age 5 would die during Trump’s second term because of his aid cuts — equivalent to 88 children dying each hour.

Here in South Sudan, at least 100 health centers are no longer supported. In the village of Gabat, I visited a government clinic that because of aid cuts had no aspirin, no ibuprofen, no hand sanitizer, no soap, no electricity, no running water, no antibiotics and no mosquito nets. Because the staff hadn’t been paid since March, only 10 health workers were present that day, out of a roster of 23 assigned to it.

“When people know that we don’t have drugs, they don’t come anymore,” Mayen Garang, the chief of the clinic, told me. More than 300 patients used to come daily, while now there are perhaps 30, he said. “So of course children die.”

Garang was examining a 6-month-old girl, Adhieu Yak, who had a fever and bacterial pneumonia. Because the clinic had no medicine that could help, he wrote her mother a prescription for medication to buy in the market, but she shook her head. “I have no money,” she lamented. “I can’t afford the medicine.”
At another empty clinic, in the town of Kuom, Simon Ngong, the assistant nurse in charge, recounted to me all the medicines and supplies he lacked and said, “I’m like a soldier without a gun.”
South Sudan’s humanitarian crisis is compounded by the Iran war, which has raised diesel and fertilizer prices.

Steve Roese, the president of Water Is Basic, a nonprofit that trains women to repair wells, said that before the war, it cost $10,000 to take a container of supplies from Uganda to South Sudan. Now it can cost $19,000.
On top of that, a severe drought has destroyed crops across the region, so some people are already eating wild plants to get by.

This means that just when aid is needed most, it is collapsing. The U.N. World Food Program received more than $1 billion in 2022 to help the South Sudanese, but this year it pulled in just $160 million — including only $12 million directly from the United States. So some 380 nutrition sites around the country have suspended services.

I traveled in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State with Action Against Hunger, a well-respected international nonprofit. Aid cuts have slashed its budget for South Sudan by more than half, so it has had to close 38 nutrition centers.

As a result, the group is unable to help some 35,000 children with severe acute malnutrition, according to Heather Stobaugh, the director of research and innovation for Action Against Hunger. She noted that there have been interruptions not only to lifesaving aid but also to the simplest and cheapest interventions, like deworming children, which can cost just 50 cents a year per child. The same is true of vitamin A supplementation, which costs about $2 per child per year and can reduce child deaths in poor countries by up to 24 percent. (Most American kids get vitamin A in foods, including fortified milk and breakfast cereals.) These are some of the best bargains in global health.
“It’s really frustrating,” Stobaugh said. “We have proven, low-cost, simple interventions. And they have been ripped away from us.”

America’s greatest foreign policy success in my lifetime was arguably the PEPFAR program, which under President George W. Bush turned the tide of the AIDS epidemic, saving more than 26 million lives so far. But now under Trump, elements of it are unraveling. One study found that 1,700 H.I.V. treatment sites have closed down worldwide.

In South Sudan, antiretrovirals are still available in hospitals, but the community health workers who once took the medicines to orphans with AIDS were fired. So these children — most of them infected during childbirth and kept alive for years by bipartisan American generosity — were left on their own.

Scovia Abau, a volunteer with AIDS orphans, gave me the names and details of eight of these children who had been receiving antiretrovirals from a single hospital in Juba, South Sudan, who have since died. The youngest was a 6-year-old boy, James Taban.
Pray tell, Elon Musk, how do you expect a 6-year-old AIDS orphan to obtain medicine on his own?
One of those dismissed community health workers is Hellen Kila, who previously helped 40 people with AIDS get their medicines. She knew that some had died, she said, but wasn’t sure how many.

She cited the example of Mary Kujiang. Neighbors found her body with her two small children, both H.I.V.-positive, beside the corpse. Those children were sent off to relatives in a remote part of the country where there is little prospect that they will have access to medicine, Kila said.

In part because she felt she was failing people who had depended on her, Kila tried to hang herself. Her 14-year-old son kicked down the door, held her body up and shouted for neighbors, who came and cut the noose, she and others told me.

Another former community health worker, Agnes Mindra, told me that until the Musk cuts, she was caring for six orphans who had AIDS and 28 mothers with H.I.V. Now three of the children and five of the women have died, she said.
“At first, there were not many deaths, but now it’s increasing,” she told me. “There is more dying now.”

Humanitarian aid is not just a moral issue, for it advances our interests as well as our values. Aid is an inexpensive way to win soft power worldwide, and it is far cheaper to fight diseases like Ebola and tuberculosis in Africa than at home when they spread.

Musk claimed that closing U.S.A.I.D. would save money, but destroying it so abruptly turned out to be extraordinarily costly. Last year I reported on a State Department document indicating it would cost $6.4 billion to close U.S.A.I.D., but the sum keeps going up. The administration has advised Congress that it needs $19 billion to close out U.S.A.I.D. contracts, and even that figure is incomplete.
Meanwhile, until Musk came along, our aid was costing taxpayers just 23 cents for every $100 of gross national income and saved a life approximately once every 10 seconds.

Democrats were rightly critical of the cuts in humanitarian aid. So now that they will control Congress, I’ll keep an eye on whether they push hard to restore humanitarian programs. It’s not essential that U.S.A.I.D. be revived as an independent agency; what matters most is the assistance itself, not the bureaucratic structure.

(If you’re looking for a way to help, I’ve just published my annual holiday giving guide, recommending three outstanding charities, including two that work internationally. Contributions are matched multiple times, so that each $1 donation becomes $3 or $4 in the field. Find out more at kristofimpact.org.)

I fear Americans will think that all this is tragic but behind us and that it’s time to move on. But if you’re a woman whose child is starving because of aid cuts, you can’t move on. If you’ve contracted river blindness and are losing your sight because Washington cut a health program, you can’t move on. If you were raped and can’t get emergency contraception because Trump cut funding for the U.N. Population Fund, the tragedy isn’t behind you.

So I hope we’ll not just deplore this catastrophe and not just regret the ugliness of the world’s richest man devastating the world’s poorest children, but also push for remedies. We can’t reverse every harm, and we can’t save every life, but public pressure can encourage members of Congress in both parties to restore programs in ways that would mean fewer shrieks of grief from bereaved parents and fewer new child-size mounds of earth.

theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/28/fre.headline: La succession: France’s wealthiest family said to be battling over who will take over LVMH

paragraphs.text: They are France’s richest family, leading the world’s biggest luxury goods empire, dressed in matching Dior suits – a clan so powerful they have been described as modern-day French royals.

But in recent months, the family dynasty of Bernard Arnault, 77, the billionaire head of the LVMH group whose brands range from Louis Vuitton handbags to Tiffany jewellery, has become the subject of speculation about internal rivalry over which of his children could take over the company.

This week it emerged that the health-conscious Arnault, who likes to play tennis with the Swiss champion Roger Federer, can continue to lead the family holding company until he is 95, according to a new filing, pushing back any decisions on his succession.
Last year, the age cap of Arnault’s chief executive role at LVMH was raised to 85 to allow him to stay on in the position. The fashion tycoon once joked about still leading the business at 100.
The question of which of Arnault’s five adult children could eventually lead the family company is seen as key to the French economy and the political class.
LVMH, which has more than 75 brands including fashion, perfumes and champagne, is a big employer in France.

Arnault, nicknamed the “wolf in cashmere” for his acquisitions of leading brands and whose personal wealth is estimated at more than $100bn, owns almost all of France’s business and economic press as well as the daily newspaper Le Parisien and the celebrity magazine Paris Match.
He attended Donald Trump’s second inauguration, as a personal friend, and is regularly present at official French state dinners with world leaders.

This month, Émilie Lanez published an account of what she called the emotional tensions inside the Arnault family’s unresolved succession challenge, based on what she said were hours of off-record conversations with insiders. “I was really struck by the family’s ethereal, otherworldly nature: they are like deities in a performance, and France is a spectator,” she said.

The book, Monsieur et les siens, now in discussion over a possible publication in English, traces the family’s story from Arnault’s childhood in Roubaix, in the former industrial heartland of northern France, where he took over his family’s building company before moving into property development and then luxury goods.

Lanez describes Arnault’s wife, the classical pianist Hélène Mercier-Arnault, working out on her treadmill in the early morning watching the HBO series Succession about a family business power-struggle, and then being at pains to publicly deny any rift or friction among the Arnault children.

The book depicts Arnault’s deep personal involvement in his children’s education. Schooling was so important in his own upbringing that when at age 10 he said farewell to his grandfather at his funeral, he put his glowing school report card into his grandfather’s clasped hands in his coffin.

When he had two children with his first wife, Anne Dewavrin, he devised a system to personally teach his daughter Delphine to read at a young age. At 51, she is now the chief executive of Christian Dior Couture, one of the most important roles at LVMH. Her brother Antoine, 49, has an important communications role, running the group’s image and environmental strategy.

Arnault later married Mercier-Arnault and had three more sons who all work for LVMH brands. Alexandre, 34, is deputy chief executive of the drinks brand Moët Hennessy; Frédéric, 32, runs the luxury fashion brand Loro Piana; and Jean, 28, is watch director at Louis Vuitton.

When the youngest three were teenagers and preparing for higher education, Lanez writes that Arnault personally hired and interviewed tutors. The boys would come home from their day’s classes, then study with a tutor from 8pm to 11pm then go to their father’s room so he could ask them about the equations they had been tackling.

“They are likened to royals because of the power and influence they have in France,” said Lanez. “And also because they have a kind of court, courtesans and counsellors. It’s a dynasty, and the children, particularly the three youngest, have been raised to perpetuate the empire.”

Just as Arnault as a child would be shown round his father’s family building business, he regularly took his own children, and then grandchildren, on his favourite weekend activity: inspecting his luxury shops.

Arnault is aware that any family divisions can make a company vulnerable. This year, when Mercier-Arnault was promoting her latest classical music record, she did a high-profile round of media interviews in France, seeking to reassure that there were no rifts between the five children.
But with the Arnaults’ vast wealth often cited as an example of the growing power of billionaires in France amid widening economic inequality, Mercier-Arnault’s comments were scrutinised.
French media reported that in an edited radio segment she had said that being homeless could be seen as a “lifestyle choice”.

Mercier-Arnault said later on a TV show that there had been a misunderstanding and she had been referring to her experience as the carer of her late sister, a violinist who was bipolar and had died by suicide, and who had begun a relationship with a person who was homeless. She told the newspaper Libération she was “deeply sorry”.

The cast of characters in the Arnault clan includes another high-profile and influential French billionaire, the telecoms executive Xavier Niel, who is the life-partner of Delphine Arnault. The couple have two children.
“The arrival of Xavier Niel in this family was like a theatrical scenario,” Lanez said, comparing the family saga to a novel.
Asked by the Guardian to comment on the book and speculation of tension or rivalry over the succession, LVMH declined to comment.

In July, Arnault, commenting on a series about him in Le Monde, joked about his family being likened to royals, but added that the comparison was good for sales at Dior. He said there were no divisions in the family or between his children, writing on social media that it was possible for “five strong personalities to work in the same firm without it turning into an Italian opera”.

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/28/dem.headline: 3 memory changes experts warn you should never ignore as you’re aging
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/28/dem.author: Christy Bieber

paragraphs.text: Dementia is a leading cause of death globally as well as a growing problem in America due to an aging population. Over 6 million Americans suffer from dementia, according to research published by the National Institutes of Health, and an estimated 42 percent of men and women over 55 are expected to eventually develop the condition.

“Early detection of dementia-related illnesses is essential,” said Jeremy Koppel, a medical advisory board member at the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America and co-director of the Litwin-Zucker Research Center for the Study of Alzheimer’s Disease, in New York. “Delays in diagnosis can mean missed opportunities.”

But dementia isn’t the only health issue that affects memory. Sleep apnea, thyroid disorders, depression, urinary tract infections and vitamin deficiencies are just some of the many conditions that can cause memory impairments, Koppel said. Many of these issues are treatable.
Because some forgetfulness is normal as people age, it’s often hard to know if a memory lapse is cause for concern. Medical experts say these particular symptoms deserve attention.
1. Changes that make daily life harder
When it comes to distinguishing ordinary forgetfulness from a potentially serious problem, experts say one key factor matters.

“The question isn’t simply whether you forget things. It’s whether your memory changes are making daily life harder,” said Anna Chodos, a geriatrician and professor of medicine at the University of California at San Francisco.

Michael Leon, professor emeritus of neurobiology and behavior at the University of California at Irvine, agreed, warning that while occasional forgetfulness like misplacing keys or taking longer to recall a name is common, “changes that interfere with daily self-care or safety go beyond normal aging.”

Leon gave multiple examples of lapses that fall into this category, including forgetting which medications to take or missing doses, struggling to cook a recipe you’ve made for years, or suddenly being unable to use your phone correctly.

“This progressive loss of everyday skills is often one of the most noticeable effects on daily life,” said Emer MacSweeney, a neuroradiologist and CEO of Re:Cognition Health, which operates clinics focused on cognitive health care in London and several U.S. locations, including Virginia and Chicago.
2. Forgetting how to have a conversation
Memory changes that affect your ability to communicate are another red flag that experts suggest paying attention to.

“Changes I’d encourage people not to ignore include repeatedly asking the same question or forgetting recent conversations,” Chodos said. Christine Ghilain, a neuropsychologist and neuropsychological evaluator in New Jersey, said it’s a red flag if you find yourself “frequently losing words or losing the thread of a conversation.”

Friends and family members are often the first to notice these types of changes, which makes it important to listen when someone close to you expresses concern. “If a loved one is worried, take it seriously. People often don’t realize how much they’ve adapted to their changes,” said Ghilain.
3. Difficulty remembering recent events

Alzheimer’s, which is the most common type of dementia, often affects short-term memory first, while long-term memories may not begin to fade until the disease has progressed. That’s why Koppel says it’s a cause for concern if you’re having difficulty recalling things that should be fresh in your mind.
As Koppel explained, this is called episodic memory loss, and it’s often one of the earliest and most defining signs of Alzheimer’s disease.

Episodic memory is the type that allows you to recall basic personal experiences, like what you ate for lunch and where you parked. It records the who, what, where, when and why of your day. A neurodegenerative condition can result in these things not being properly recorded in the brain.

Forgetting recent events, especially when reminders don’t help, can indicate your brain is having difficulty forming or retaining new memories due to a medical issue, rather than just ordinary forgetfulness, said Jordan Weiss, an assistant professor at NYU Grossman School of Medicine’s Optimal Aging Institute.
Take swift action if you see these signs

If these warning signs are familiar, visiting your doctor could make a substantial difference in your long-term health, as early evaluation may uncover a treatable condition or provide opportunities to better manage an irreversible diagnosis.

“Not all memory loss is permanent dementia,” Leon said. “Symptoms can be triggered by reversible conditions, such as vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid imbalances, medication side effects, infections, sleep apnea or depression. Identifying these root causes early can restore full memory function.”

If dementia is the likely cause, swift action is imperative. Koppel warned that many medications for Alzheimer’s disease are effective, or even available, only in the early stage of the disease’s progression, while clinical trials are often limited to early-stage participants.

Anti-amyloid immunotherapies, for example, are often used for early-stage Alzheimer’s to clear amyloid plaques from brain tissue. They may slow disease progression by roughly 20 percent to 40 percent when administered in the earliest stages of the condition.

While it may seem intimidating to see a doctor about these issues, “the goal isn’t to create worry,” Ghilain said. “The goal is to get a clear answer sooner so that people have the best chance to get the right support.”

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Jess Wilson’s rapid rise is hard to believe - but Victorian Labor’s collapse has been years in the making

paragraphs.text: It is difficult to overstate how far the Victorian Coalition has come.

In the days after Christmas 2024, Brad Battin toppled John Pesutto as Liberal leader after a court found the Hawthorn MP defamed his colleague. A million-dollar loan by the party to Pesutto to help cover his legal costs also ended up in court. Battin lasted less than a year before his leadership also came undone and he was replaced by Jess Wilson in November 2025.

A year on, Wilson has become the first woman to be popularly elected as Victoria’s premier and at 36, the state’s youngest leader since federation. As at 10pm, the Coalition had won 53 seats – well above the 45 needed to form a majority government and her Labor opponents have been wiped out – from 56 seats in 2022 to just six declared seats, according to Guardian Australia’s analysis, with a little more than a quarter of the vote counted.

Labor leader Ben Carroll has secured two unwanted places in Australian political history: becoming the first premier to lose their seat at a Victorian election and the state’s shortest-serving modern premier, in the job for just 123 days.
While the final seat tally won’t be known for a few days, the Coalition has won seats in parts of the state it hasn’t ever held.

The state that had come to regard Labor as its natural party of government has consigned it to the electoral wilderness. At the current count, more people voted for One Nation across the state than Labor, with the party recording a 21% primary vote, though this did not translate into seats.

Ironically, this was in part due to them overtaking Labor, on 17.6%. Another irony – the Coalition’s landslide win is off the back of a 34.78% primary vote, only a small increase from the 29.6% it recorded in its 2022 loss. Such has the political climate changed.
There is a real possibility the Greens, who have won eight seats, will end up being the official opposition, with Labor consigned to the crossbench.
“It is wild the number of seats we’re in hunt for,” Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, said on Saturday night.
It’s difficult to see how Labor will be able to rebuild into anything remotely electable in four years.

It’s hard to believe Wilson only entered parliament at the last election after the former member for Kew, did not run again after a drink-driving incident in which he crashed his car into a child’s bedroom.
Immediately promoted to shadow cabinet, then to shadow treasurer and now also leader, she’s taken a party that was deeply divided and turned it into an election-winning, unified outfit.

Wilson is relatable, approachable and a small-l Liberal in a state that remains broadly progressive – if you consider the almost 20% of Victorians who voted for either the Greens or the Victorian Socialists. Much of her success can be attributed to her ability to reach beyond the Coalition’s traditional base.

Her rise has also helped attract a new calibre of candidate. She persuaded several female contenders to contest winnable seats, including Samantha Byrne, who has won Niddrie off Carroll. The party has also made a concerted effort to recruit more diverse candidates and build relationships with multicultural communities Labor has taken for granted.
In her victory speech, Wilson acknowledged it was the first time many Victorians had voted Liberals.
“I realise that you have lent us your vote. We don’t own it. And we will work every single day to demonstrate that you were right to place your trust in us,” she said.
Wilson knows winning an election is one thing but governing is another.
Her first challenge will be translating an election victory into a mandate to govern. Many Victorians voted for change but may not know what that involves.

After all, many voters got their first meaningful taste just 48 hours before polling day, when the Coalition’s costings revealed plans to privatise or sell off around $13bn state government assets, including the state’s sewerage infrastructure.

Then, Wilson will have to manage the competing ambitions within her own ranks. She currently holds the shadow treasurer portfolio, a position several colleagues would dearly like to claim in government. She insists she intends to keep it.

The Coalition has a relatively shallow pool of experience on which to draw after 12 years in the wilderness. Bringing someone like Pesutto on to the frontbench would make sense but enrage others in the party room. It’s no wonder Wilson was tight lipped about the prospect when interviewed last month.
She described the election as a referendum on Labor. Now, she has to deliver for all those who gave her a party a chance.
Recriminations

Meanwhile, in Labor, recriminations have already started. In reality, they had weeks ago. Most of the criticism is the same – Carroll’s campaign focused too much on crime and his inability to acknowledge the 12 years of Labor that came before him – epitomised by the moment he avoided uttering Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan’s names in the debate.
But a result like this was years in the making.

After the 2022 election, Andrews vowed to do more for the communities that swung hard against Labor in the wake of the pandemic. Now, it doesn’t have one. Seats like Kororoit, Kalkallo, Tarneit and Melton in the north and west, Narre Warren North and Narre Warren South in the southeast, which have never been held by a party other than Labor have turned blue.
On Saturday night, the deputy leader, Gabrielle Williams, said while the party increased seats in 2022, it ignored the main message voters were sending.
“There were certainly warning signs from the 2022 result that we should have responded to and perhaps didn’t take the opportunity,” she said.
“It should have been an inflection on point that caused us to stop and see what is happening to our base and what they weren’t getting from us.”
Labor missed another opportunity to reset when Allan became premier in 2023.
“She just tried to carry on as if she was the new Daniel Andrews, it was continuation of the old government,” a campaign source said.

That government, according to a campaign source, was bogged down by debt, alleged corruption on government construction sites, waste, crime and potholes – which became daily reminders of a government that many Victorians felt was no longer delivering.
“Is there no better symbol that shows we failed to get the basics rights?” they said.
• Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent
This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

Gathering with family allows our past and present selves to meet: There’s the familiar seat at the dinner table, the decades-old sibling rivalry, a parent’s instinct to remind their now-adult child to bring a jacket. Whether you’re returning to the home you grew up in or welcoming your own children back, reuniting can remind us of how much we’ve changed—and how easily we can slip back into the roles we once occupied.

In a 2024 essay, my colleague Faith Hill explored the complicated pull of our childhood home. In his research on the subject, the psychologist Jerry M. Burger found that even people who didn’t have a particularly happy childhood felt compelled to revisit the places they grew up. The desire to return, Faith explains, isn’t necessarily about reliving the good old days; it can also stem from a desire to reconnect with a version of ourselves that has become less familiar.

The holidays offer a rare opportunity to spend time with those who have known us through different stages of our life. Today’s newsletter explores what we might learn from revisiting the people we used to be.
Your Childhood Home Might Never Stop Haunting You
Many of us feel pulled toward the places where we grew up. But it can be weird when old and new selves collide. (From 2024)
Read the article.
Adults Can Get Homesick Too
When young people start their own life, they often miss where they came from. (From 2018)
Nostalgia Is a Shield Against Unhappiness
By Arthur C. Brooks
Happy memories have a uniquely protective power against a sad present. (From 2023)
Still Curious?

• The timeless bliss of eating hometown food: For many holiday travelers, a trip back to where they grew up is a chance to revisit the local spots they spend the rest of the year craving, Hayley Glatter wrote in 2018.
• The new age of endless parenting: More grown kids are in near-constant contact with their family. Some call this a failure to launch—but there’s another way to look at it, Faith wrote in 2024.

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “I’ve always felt most in awe of the natural world out on the trail, in forests and on big mountain hikes. Then we got our first dog. At ten months old, he’s taught me to slow down, and our slow loops around the yard have shown me what I was walking past: a dahlia opening a little more each morning, a persimmon slowly turning orange. The wonder I used to travel for was here the whole time,” Julie L. writes.
We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.
— Rafaela

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/28/wearable-hea.headline: The doctor, the patient and the smartwatch: What physicians think of the third voice at your appointment
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/28/wearable-hea.author: Renée Onque

paragraphs.text: A health-tracking device quite literally saved the life of one of Dr. Linda E. Tepper's patients, she says.

After a heavy snowstorm, the 89-year-old man, who has metastatic prostate cancer, slipped and fell while clearing his backyard with a snow blower, says Tepper, a New York City-based internist at NYU Langone Health. He fractured three bones in his face, had a subdural hematoma and was unconscious in the snow.
"His Apple Watch detected it and called the police, the ambulance and his daughter," Tepper says, adding: "He would have died out there."

Wearable health trackers — devices that can measure health metrics ranging from heart rate to sleep and menstrual cycles — are a big business these days. Whoop and Oura, which both sell health wearables, have both announced valuations of more than $10 billion since October 2025. Apple, Google, Samsung and Garmin each sell their own fitness-tracking products, as part of an estimated $71 billion market in 2025.

And big business often draws skepticism from some consumers, particularly when health is involved. These devices can cost hundreds of dollars. Some require additional monthly subscriptions to analyze all the data they collect. Their accuracy has been questioned in various class-action lawsuits over the past 10-plus years: For example, Oura was sued in August for allegedly inaccurate sleep-stage tracking, a claim the company disputes.

So as more devices appear on Americans' wrists and biceps, you might wonder: What do actual doctors think of them? In some cases, doctors say wearable health trackers like Oura rings, Whoop bands and Fitbits can help them do their jobs more efficiently. In other cases, inaccurate data points can make patients unnecessarily anxious and present challenges for medical professionals.

Either way, doctors should get used to interpreting the data they provide, especially as they get "cheaper, more readily accessible, more readily available," says Dr. Neha Vyas, a family physician at Cleveland Clinic.
Doctors love your wearable health-tracking device, for the most part

Vyas likes when patients ask her health questions prompted by the data from their wearables, she says. "They actually start a conversation," she says. "If we take the information they have and put it in their clinical picture, I can oftentimes guide them."

The tech can be beneficial for patients with heart issues, or who want to make sustainable lifestyle changes that could be better supported by using a step tracker or calorie intake tracker, says Vyas. "I only have one data point when I'm in the office. But if I can see what's been going on with someone, whether it's their heart rate, their steps [or] their calorie intake, I'm able to really get a lot of information," she says. "We can really make a profound difference in people's lives for the better."

Tepper says wearables like Apple Watches are particularly helpful for people with a high risk of falling and injuring themselves. Some of them can even be worn in the shower, she notes. "I think they're remarkable for that," she says.

On other occasions, devices worn by Tepper's patients have detected atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that can lead to blood clots, she says: "It was real, and we were able to treat them." Just about anyone can develop atrial fibrillation, according to the American Heart Association, though the risk increases with age and conditions like underlying heart disease or high blood pressure.
Overall, Vyas and Tepper agree: Wearable health-tracking devices can be helpful and, in some cases, even life-saving.
...But there are some caveats
Health-tracking devices can produce a lot of data. Too much, sometimes, says Vyas: "How do we take all this data and actually make it actionable?"

Some data points that concern patients don't require action, but that doesn't always allay the patients' worries, Tepper says. She highlights sleep tracking as a common example: Some of her patients started taking sleeping pills unnecessarily because they were nervous about their sleep scores, she says. Some sleeping pills can create dependencies and introduce or exacerbate sleep disorders, including some that are potentially life-threatening, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
"I don't want everybody on a sleeping pill," says Tepper.

Sometimes, Vyas hears from patients at odd hours of the night because they're anxious about sleep alerts from their fitness trackers, she says. The devices can "create that cycle of health anxiety where they monitor, they get anxious, they need repeated reassurance, and then they keep monitoring just because it's something that's so readily available to them now," she says. "I do have to remember to change the conversation from, 'Hey, what does that data point tell us?' to 'How are you feeling? What are you feeling right now?'"

If you receive an alert or review some data from your health tech that you find alarming, your first step should be to gauge how your body feels, regardless of what the device told you, Vyas recommends. Then, if you're still worried, present your concern to your doctor before acting on it yourself, she suggests. Always consult with your medical professional before making any major changes that can affect your health.
"Just as with other forms of technology, it's not going away," Vyas says. Doctors aren't going away either, she notes.
