npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6045586/perspec.headline: Perspective: A hero's name lives on
npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6045586/perspec.author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: The ceremonial keel for the aircraft carrier USS Doris Miller will be laid next week.

CNN reported this summer that the Navy was considering naming the ship after President Trump instead. That brief controversy may have distracted from the personal courage of Doris Miller himself. And putting his name on an aircraft carrier is meant to memorialize his heroism.

Doris Miller, known to his shipmates as Dorie, was 22 years old when Japanese forces attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Miller was from a sharecropping family in Waco, Texas, hours away from any coast. But he wanted to see the world and send money to his family, so he enlisted in the Navy.
The U.S. Navy was segregated in those days, like all branches of the armed forces. Black sailors were assigned to custodial roles, in the kitchen and laundry.

Doris Miller became a cook and mess attendant aboard the USS West Virginia, and was in the laundry when bombs began to fall that Sunday morning. He leapt through flames and smoke to move wounded sailors to safer positions, including the ship's badly wounded captain.

Then Doris Miller made his way to a .50-calibre anti-aircraft gun. No Black crew members had been trained for combat duty. But Doris Miller fired that gun at the Japanese planes that were attacking the U.S. fleet, until he ran out of ammunition. And then he pulled men to safety from the oily water, until he was ordered to abandon ship.
More than 2400 Americans died in Pearl Harbor on that date that has lived in infamy. 106 were on the USS West Virginia.

Doris Miller received the Navy Cross for his heroism. It was personally presented by the commander of the US Pacific Fleet, and the citation reads, "for distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage, and disregard for his own personal safety…"
Doris Miller would die in service two years later, in the fiery sinking of the USS Liscome Bay. His body was never recovered.

Seeing Doris Miller's name on an aircraft carrier may remind all of us that courage is not determined by rank or race. Doris Miller served a segregated Navy in a segregated America. He gave his country the highest order of heroism and sacrifice.

theatlantic.com/culture/2026/11/aura-far.headline: Can You Maximize Your Own Coolness?

paragraphs.text: For centuries, aura was understood to be a gift from the gods—an ineffable trait bestowed on special beings. Think of Venus in Botticelli’s 15th-century painting, looking bored yet fabulous as she floats to shore. (As it happens, in that painting, both a god and a nymph named Aura gaze lovingly at Venus.) But now the word is being used more liberally to describe suave celebrities, anime characters, and everyday cool kids alike. It has also gained a new meaning—perhaps most clearly demonstrated by the rise of the phrase aura farming, which evokes hard work rather than divinely granted cool.

Aura farming pulls from gaming-world slang that suggests that people are putting in the effort to level up. (See also: aura level and aura points.) Although aura farming has been around for a bit, its usage was inadvertently boosted last year by Rayyan Arkan Dikha, a young Indonesian boy who went viral for dancing effortlessly on the bow of a fast-moving racing boat, and whose admirers helped popularize the phrase. Soon after, it took off. The concept has since spawned real-life “aura battles,” in which participants invoke jokes, dances, and internet references to prove their greatness. Recently, South Park even released an episode satirizing aura battles; at one point, a character hits his face with a hammer (a clear reference to looksmaxxing) in hopes of chiseling his jawline enough to beat his opponent.

Last year, Oxford University Press shortlisted aura farming for its Word of the Year pick, defining it as “the cultivation of an impressive, attractive, or charismatic persona.” As the publisher jokingly explained in a social-media campaign, an aura farmer might drink matcha, wear wired headphones, and kindly inform you that they went on a date with Luca Guadagnino’s director of photography. In other words, aura farming and its variants reveal a very modern understanding of what it is to be cool: Nowadays, coolness isn’t just God-given—You either got it or you don’t, honey! It’s also seen as something that can, and should, be meticulously optimized.
[Read: Social media broke slang. Now we all speak phone.]

For most of human history, cultures and religions around the world depicted auras via symbols reserved for divine figures, such as deities. Think of the halos used in Buddhist iconography or the billowing garments used in Greco-Roman art. But over time, auras started to be visualized in art more widely. When the first halo appeared in Christian art, in the fourth century C.E., it was reserved for members of the Holy Trinity, Jeremy Stolow, a communications professor at Concordia University, writes in Picturing Aura. But eventually, he notes, halos were used to denote the sanctity of people “across the Christian pantheon,” including saints, popes, prophets, and disciples.

In the late 1800s, scientific breakthroughs shifted how people understood energy and life on Earth, and the concept of auras was further democratized. People began to think “that everybody has an aura, and maybe even not just humans,” Stolow told me—other animals and plants might, too. Discoveries such as the X-ray underscored the notion that invisible things could be made visible, and spiritual groups such as the Theosophists (predecessors of the New Age movement) led a surging interest in energy fields, auras, and clairvoyance. Auras, to some, started to be seen as a legitimate phenomenon for scientific study. Perhaps they were a natural force, like molecules and atoms, that some new gadget would one day lay bare to the naked eye. Throughout the 20th century, Stolow said, use of the word aura skyrocketed as people employed it to describe a kind of subtle emanation.

It’s a nice idea: aura as a secret ingredient of the universe. But these days, the word has evolved into a synonym for swagger. Phoebe Nicholson, an executive editor at Oxford University Press who helped pick the Word of the Year, described how aura’s modern meaning undercuts similar terms, such as X-factor, it girl, and star. Those words arose largely during the golden age of Hollywood in the mid-20th century, when celebrity was typically viewed from a distance, through a lens of “otherworldliness,” she told me, and people were “but peasants looking at it.” Aura farming, though, places coolness within reach: It suggests that although no one is born wearing rhinestones, anyone can put them on and dazzle.
[Read: The new plastic-surgery playbook]

This focus on persona building seems to be a symptom of the broader self-improvement ethos that’s common today. Just as faces and bodies can be tweaked, people’s “subtle emanations” can supposedly be boosted as well. A whole genre of videos has popped up online dispensing advice on how to refine one’s aura. Tips include wearing linen, changing your posture and gait, using a signature scent, and—of course—buying an electrolyte product strategically placed in a video’s corner. Some aura farmers might even shell out $34 a month for an app that promises to help “start upgrading your character” to one with a better mind and soul.

Crucially, this trend of aura enhancement is framed not just in gamified lingo but in economic terms, too. “It’s phrased in this very capitalist language of accumulation,” Stolow said: “I get points; I expend them; I lose them; I invest.” In this way, aura resembles the term identity capital, a concept that sees hobbies, test scores, fashion, and life experiences as wealth-building projects that can be traded in the marketplace of adulthood. Similarly, aura points might be cashed in for attention, renown, a brand deal, a lover.

The catch is that aura levels are subject to the fickle opinions of other people. And delivered in a certain tone, aura farming can be a pejorative—used to cut down those who are trying too hard. One YouTube compilation of “Aura Farming Fails,” for instance, shows a man flexing his muscles in front of a bathroom mirror before accidentally knocking down a soap dispenser.
[Read: Why is everyone talking about getting ‘oneshotted’?]

Here, the bestowers of aura are not gods but social-media commenters: “The role of the spectator is essential,” Stolow noted, “to the whole functioning of this aura economy.” Cultivating aura becomes, for some, a part of online life. But if you botch the attempt or your efforts are too obvious, a jury of your peers can decide that your shine is gone. The fear of losing this quality is, naturally, what drives the demand for all of the products that claim to boost it. “I think we should stop rating looks and coolness,” one character shrewdly concludes near the end of that South Park episode, “so that companies stop preying on people’s insecurities.”

Reading too much into a phrase that’s largely used for fun can, of course, be futile. And people judged others’ attempts at coolness long before the Internet Age. Still, applying video-game language and points systems to real life can cause problems, Adam Aleksic, the author of Algospeak, told me: “We start framing our interactions in these terms.” Put too much stock in your aura level, and you might start seeing your own human value—and that of others—as changeable, rather than inherent. Most of us will never be cool in that effortless Venus way, but mere mortals were never meant to be.

theatlantic.com/science/2026/11/christma.headline: The Forecast for Christmas Is Muddy

paragraphs.text: Snowville, New Hampshire, was named for Joseph Snow, who moved there after fighting in the War of 1812, but the village gets more than its fair share of wintry precipitation. Over the past 10 years, nine of its Christmases have been white.

This year, the chance of a white Christmas—an inch or more of snow on the ground on Christmas morning—is currently about 65 percent in Snowville, according to an online tool from the Weather Company. That’s not too shabby, but it’s also a drop of about 15 percent from normal. The culprit is probably this year’s super El Niño, which is poised to scramble winter weather across the country.

During El Niño, which is part of a climatological cycle that’s been around for at least 250 million years, the winds that normally push west across the Pacific weaken. Warm water starts to pile up around South America. As heat moves from the water into the atmosphere above it, weather patterns change. In the United States, El Niño generally results in a hotter North and a soggier, cooler South.

By itself, El Niño doesn’t warm the planet; it moves existing heat around. But these days, there is more heat than ever to rearrange. “When you throw an El Niño on the shoulders of climate change, we expect that a lot of the country is going to experience above-average temperatures,” Shel Winkley, the chief meteorologist at the nonpartisan science-communication group Climate Central, told me. The odds, he said, lean toward less snow across the U.S., especially in areas where a white Christmas is the norm.

Instead, brace for the possibility of mud. In many places around the country, “brown Christmas is possible,” Shuyi Chen, a meteorology professor at the University of Washington, told me. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s latest Winter Outlook report indicates a roughly 80 percent chance that forceful El Niño conditions will continue through the new year, bringing extra rain to the southern part of the country, especially the Southeast. Florida has already experienced serious flooding in recent weeks; so, too, have California and the Four Corners region.

Brown Christmas is not guaranteed, though. Seven Christmases have coincided with an El Niño since 2003, and snow cover has varied dramatically among them. In 2009, a blizzard blanketed more than half of the mainland United States. In 2023, less than a fifth of the Lower 48 collected snow cover. Plus, this El Niño is coinciding with record-high ocean temperatures and is predicted to be the most powerful since 1950, which means that scientists lack a perfect historical parallel from which to make predictions about this season’s snowfall. Besides, weather is inherently fickle. Forecasters won’t be able to predict how day-to-day fluctuations may interact with the effects of El Niño on Christmas until a week or two in advance.

Perhaps the biggest wild card for the December forecast is the polar vortex, Daniel Cayan, a climate scientist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, told me. This band of strong winds locks in extremely cold air at the top of the globe. The winds arise each fall, when the farthest reaches of the Northern Hemisphere start receiving little sunlight, causing air-temperature differences between the Arctic and the equator to grow. When the sunlight returns in spring, it heats the Arctic stratosphere and causes the vortex to crumble. The dissolving polar vortex can bring about periods of intense cold in the continental U.S. as far south as Florida, and with them, an increased chance of snow.

Usually, the polar vortex deteriorates in March or April; this year, it’s already starting to break down. Researchers aren’t yet sure why, but they have theories. Climate change may play a role. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the rest of the world, and sea ice is growing sparser, which may allow heat to move more easily from the polar ocean to the atmosphere. A warmer Arctic narrows that crucial temperature difference with lower latitudes, weakening the polar vortex and allowing more frigid air to escape to the south.

Whether many Americans will have a muddy Christmas or a white one comes down in large part to a tug-of-war between two age-old phenomena, each of which is behaving abnormally this year. Experts can’t predict exactly how the interaction will play out. Ben Kirtman, an atmospheric-sciences professor at the University of Miami, told me that if sudden warming in the Arctic enables cold air to break out of the polar vortex, it could mean snow.

But without such a well-timed gust, the persistent force of El Niño seems likelier to win out. This year’s super El Niño has already been associated with severe coastal erosion in California, a parade of major hurricanes in the Pacific, and sea turtles showing up far from their normal habitat. A wobbly polar vortex may be no match for it.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/sakana-ais-ceo.headline: Sakana AI’s CEO says its homegrown models are about more than Japan’s national security
techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/sakana-ais-ceo.author: Kate Park

paragraphs.text: Sakana AI, a Japanese AI startup, last month revealed plans to develop its own foundation model. The move has drawn attention for its potential impact on Japan’s defense and cybersecurity sectors as well as concerns about reliance on U.S. and Chinese technologies.

Sakana AI’s co-founder and CEO, David Ha, told TechCrunch that its upcoming foundation model, Sawara, is part of the company’s broader goal of supporting and strengthening Japan’s industrial and manufacturing sectors using AI. In addition, Ha noted rising cybersecurity threats and stressed the need for domestic AI alternatives for sensitive applications, particularly if access to foreign models becomes limited.

“When we started planning for this model, of course, we had physical AI, manufacturing, and industry in mind, and we still do. This is our long-term vision,” Ha said. “But short-term, I think Japan has a real need for security-related capabilities as well.”
Sakana will begin working on Sawara this month, aiming to train and release a smaller-scale model in early 2027, followed by a larger version.

The project comes roughly five months after Sakana launched Fugu, an AI orchestration system that ropes in other large language models, including those developed by U.S. AI labs, to assemble AI agents according to the task at hand. The Tokyo-based startup has also built Namazu, a Japanese-focused language model that fine-tunes existing open-weight models from Meta and DeepSeek to better understand Japanese language, culture, and business needs, including translation, political questions, and AI agent tasks.

“We cannot simply use open-weight models as-is in Japan for enterprises because they’re usually biased towards their creators,” Ha said. “They may refuse to answer questions about Japan or Japanese politics […] they may give Japanese people answers they don’t want to hear.”
However, Ha acknowledged that developing a domestic foundation model alone will not fully eliminate reliance on foreign AI technology.

“The only thing [left] for us to become a full-stack company is the pre-training, Sawara,” Ha continued. “We plan to apply the [Sawara] technology in industry and manufacturing. We’ll train both a small and a large model next year. The small model should be particularly useful for on-premises solutions. Japan needs on-premises deployment capabilities.”

While Fugu incorporates OpenAI’s models, Ha noted that foreign AI models are not enough for certain applications. For example, in cybersecurity, Japan requires that customized models be deployed on-premises.

“Japan will continue to use U.S. systems, but it also wants domestic alternatives,” Ha said. “People often point to Palantir and other systems. I have a great deal of respect for companies such as Snowflake, Palantir, and Datadog. But for national defense, Japan will want its own systems.”

Sakana signed a research contract with Japan’s Ministry of Defense in July to explore how AI could help analyze and integrate information from multiple sources, and it has also worked with the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, on systems for detecting disinformation.

Sakana’s work with Japanese government agencies has shaped its approach to developing Sawara, Ha said. Unlike commercial customers, government agencies often have stricter requirements, including the ability to audit training data, customize AI models and deploy them on-premises.
“Those lessons helped us plan how to develop and deploy Sawara. I think similar requirements exist in many governments,” he said.

While enterprise customers can use a combination of Fugu, Namazu and AI models developed overseas, Sakana’s government-related work currently focuses on two main areas: disinformation detection and analysis, and multimodal systems that integrate data from different government sources.
Going public in Japan
Sakana’s expansion into developing its own foundation models comes amid speculation about a potential IPO following reports by Nikkei and Bloomberg earlier this month.
But Ha said the company doesn’t have any near-term plans to go public.

The reported timing and potential valuation were speculative, Ha said, adding that he did not know when the company might pursue a listing, though he expects his startup to eventually go public in Japan itself.
“We have a gravitational pull to eventually IPO in Japan,” Ha said.

Ha sees Sakana’s future growth tied to the global expansion of Japanese manufacturers. Rather than focusing on selling its models, the company wants to help local companies use AI to become more competitive globally.

“We want to strategically work with the government and Japanese industrial base, make them competitive,” Ha said. “We want to go abroad, go international together with manufacturing and industrial sectors.”

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261128.headline: Scientists may have discovered the hidden root cause of allergies

paragraphs.text: Researchers may have uncovered a previously overlooked biological cause of allergies that challenges decades of medical thinking. Instead of originating in the immune system, allergic diseases may begin with an energy failure inside the cells that form the body's protective barriers, including those lining the skin, gut, nose, lungs, and esophagus.

Professor Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist at Griffith University's School of Medicine and Dentistry, led the research. His team examined what it believes to be the largest collection of multi-omic allergy data assembled to date, encompassing 116 case-control cohorts, 3,776 patients, and 2,164 cohorts. Multi-omic research combines different types of molecular data to provide a more comprehensive picture of the biological processes underlying disease.
The findings point to a potentially fundamental shift in how allergic diseases develop.
Rethinking the Origins of Allergies
"For 60 years, we've taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around," Professor Smith said.
"Allergy diseases, which now affect up to one in three children, may start one step earlier as a power failure in the mitochondria of the epithelial cells which form the body's barrier surfaces.
"The barrier cell can't meet the energy and stress demands of the modern environment, so raises the alarm too easily, and the immune events we recognize as an allergy follow.
"It could help to explain why some children have eczema, food allergies, hay fever, asthma and related conditions."

Mitochondria are tiny structures inside cells that generate most of the energy needed for cellular functions. Epithelial cells depend on this energy to maintain the protective barriers that separate the body from its surroundings, repair damage, and respond to environmental threats. When these energy supplies become compromised, the cells may struggle to perform these essential functions properly.
Evidence of a Hidden Cellular Energy Crisis

The most compelling evidence supporting the hypothesis came from patients with eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic allergic condition that causes inflammation in the esophagus, the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

Across all 13 independent groups of patients with the condition, researchers identified reduced activity in the biological machinery responsible for removing damaged mitochondria. This cellular recycling process is known as mitophagy and is essential for maintaining a healthy population of functioning mitochondria.
The researchers also identified abnormalities in the skin's protective barrier and antioxidant defenses in people with eczema, even in areas of skin showing no signs of inflammation.

However, the same biological pattern did not appear consistently across all allergic diseases. Researchers found no evidence of the signature in established asthma or nasal polyps, while hay fever showed only partial evidence of the proposed mechanism.
Could Modern Life Be Fueling the Allergy Epidemic?

The researchers suggest that many seemingly unrelated risk factors for allergies may converge on a single biological vulnerability: the ability of protective barrier cells to generate enough energy to function properly.
Potential contributors include diets rich in processed foods, air pollution, microplastics, detergents, declining dietary fiber intake, and exposure to antibiotics early in life.

Associate Professor Nic West, a study co-author and molecular immunologist at Griffith University's School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, explained that allergic diseases have long been associated with a wide range of possible causes. However, a single biological explanation capable of accounting for the dramatic increase in allergies within just one generation has remained elusive.
The proposed mechanism may also offer an explanation for why allergic diseases frequently return despite successful treatment.
"The research also explains why allergies can relapse," Associate Professor West said.
"Once inflammation is established, it damages the barrier further.
"Today's drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause."

In other words, if the researchers are correct, allergic inflammation could create a damaging cycle in which weakened barrier cells trigger an immune response, and that response further compromises the protective barrier.
Searching for the Root Cause of Allergies

Professor Smith emphasized that the research presents a hypothesis that requires further testing rather than a definitively established explanation for allergic disease. Nevertheless, it provides researchers with a promising new direction for investigating how allergies first develop.
"We have spent our careers managing the smoke, and for the first time we think we can see the fire, and it is not where everyone was looking," he said.
"This is not a cure but is something we have never had before -- a logical starting point.
"The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops."

Studying infants before they develop allergic conditions could help establish whether mitochondrial dysfunction precedes the onset of allergies or occurs as a consequence of the disease. Making that distinction will be essential to determining whether the proposed mechanism represents a true underlying cause.
The international research team included co-authors from Mount Sinai, Leuven, Cork, Southampton, Zurich, Miami, Singapore, and Aberdeen.
The paper, "The origins of allergy: An outside-in, bioenergetic hypothesis," was published in Allergy.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/wha.headline: What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/wha.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering politics and breaking news

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.
Reporter covering local transportation
Maryland bridge closure alert mistakenly sent callers to sex hotline
People seeking information about a Maryland bridge closure amid Thursday’s storm were in for a surprise: They were mistakenly directed to a sex hotline.
The Maryland Department of Emergency Management sent residents a public safety alert Thursday afternoon warning that the strong Thanksgiving storm had closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
That alert mistakenly directed callers to a sex hotline rather than the Maryland Transportation Authority, or MDTA.

In a statement, Maryland Transportation Authority spokesman Brad Tanner said the authority was “aware of the unfortunate error” included in the emergency alert’s callback number. The agency has corrected the error, Tanner said in the statement.
“We know this was distressing to many Marylanders,” Tanner said. “Emergency alerts are critical, lifesaving tools that require accuracy, and the MDTA takes this error very seriously.”
Thursday’s storm, the worst to hit on Thanksgiving Day in decades, left hundreds of thousands of people without power up and down the East Coast.
The roughly 4.3-mile-long Bay Bridge is notorious for not having shoulders. Some people are so scared of crossing it that they pay other drivers to take them.
This month, the MDTA said plans to replace the bridge are moving forward after securing final federal environmental approval. Construction is expected to begin as soon as 2032, the agency said.
A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”
Virginia sheriff’s office ends agreement with ICE after court ruling

The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia, this week ended its cooperation agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an appeals court upheld a state law limiting local law enforcement cooperation with immigration agents.

Virginia was one of several states this year to place restrictions on participation in ICE’s 287(g) program, which allows state and local officials to be deputized to conduct immigration enforcement. A federal judge temporarily blocked the provision from taking effect in July after the Justice Department sued, but a federal appeals court Monday reversed that decision.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office entered into a 287(g) agreement last year, authorizing its officers to execute ICE administrative warrants, known as detainers, on individuals already in the sheriff’s custody. In an email, sheriff’s office spokesman Tom Julia said the department will abide by the court’s decision. He said the department no longer will keep an individual scheduled for released in custody based on an ICE warrant, but it will continue to honor immigration warrants that are “concurrent” with a person’s release.

So far this year, ICE has issued 673 detainers for noncitizen inmates in the Loudoun County jail, of whom 330 were transferred to ICE custody, according to Julia. The sheriff’s office has not released anyone to ICE since the appeals court ruling, he said.
The agreement had long been a point of contention between Loudoun Sheriff Mike Chapman and the county’s Democratic-controlled board of supervisors.

Loudoun County Board Chair Phyllis J. Randall said in a statement that she was “very pleased” by the sheriff’s decision, adding: “Across our country, poorly trained ICE agents have wreaked havoc, caused death, killed American citizens and terrorized American cities.”
Latin American researcher
Mexico condemns DEA tip line asking people to report corrupt officials in Sinaloa

MEXICO CITY — The Mexican government presented a formal complaint to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico after the Drug Enforcement Administration promoted a tip line for information that would help “expose corruption” and “dismantle narcoterrorist organizations.”

DEA chief Terry Cole, in a post Wednesday on X, shared a dedicated tip line now available in Sinaloa to report alleged members of designated foreign terrorist organizations, corrupt government officials and criminal networks involved in money laundering. Another line will be opened for Jalisco state, he said.

In response, Mexican Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco presented a formal complaint to U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson in an effort to defend Mexico’s sovereignty, President Claudia Sheinbaum said. The DEA did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

“We have made it very clear to the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said during her Friday morning news conference. She described the tip line as a form of U.S. “interference” in Mexico.

While Mexico accepts its responsibility to stop drugs from crossing the border, Sheinbaum said, the U.S. also has a responsibility to reduce drug use among its own population and to detain the cartel members distributing drugs and laundering money within U.S. territory.

The spat comes after the Mexican government, aided by intelligence gleaned by U.S. drones, arrested one of the FBI’s 10 most-wanted fugitives in Sinaloa. Pressured by President Donald Trump’s administration to do more against cartels, Mexico has increased its security operations in Sinaloa, where a violent turf war has taken place after the U.S. arrested drug kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada.

consumerrights.wiki/w/audible_removes_do.author: Consumer Rights Wiki

paragraphs.text: From Consumer Rights Wiki

People who paid for audiobooks with a credit card or with an Audible credit,[1] which the audiobook store Audible says it may issue as "part of a membership plan or a Service promotion", under terms that also say, "We only accept credit cards for payment of your membership fees",[2] can no longer download them directly as computer files from Audible's US website;[3] on the site they can listen with Audible's Cloud Player, which Audible says streams titles "as long as you're connected to the internet".[4] Audible's help says "you can only download titles to your computer using AudibleSync",[1] a Windows 10 and 11 app whose downloads "can only be played by transferring them" to a compatible MP3 player or accessibility device,[5] and it points Mac owners to a separate page to "download audiobooks on a macOS computer".[1] Good e-Reader, an e-reader news site, reported the removal on August 11, 2026 and wrote that the site's web browser interface "now only supports streaming via the online cloud player" or Audible's apps for Android and iOS.[3]
Good e-Reader also wrote that Audible sites in international markets, such as Canada, "still have the download button, for now".[3]
Good e-Reader reported on August 11, 2026 that Audible had removed the "direct option to download audiobooks" on its American site as a computer file from the desktop library website.[3]

Good e-Reader wrote that Amazon had previously retired the legacy Windows app and discontinued Android app support on Windows 11, and that losing the web download button "leaves desktop users with fewer native offline options".[3]

Audible's current US "Download titles" help article says titles can be downloaded with AudibleSync "only if you purchased them with an Audible credit or a credit card".[1] The same article says AudibleSync "does not support bulk downloads".[1]

Audible's help for listening in a browser sends people who want to listen offline to the "Download titles" article.[4] A version of that help article dated July 6, 2026 said people can listen on a laptop or computer with the Cloud Player "since there's no Audible app for PC".[8] The version dated June 8, 2026 did not contain that sentence.[9]
For Mac computers, which run macOS, Apple's desktop operating system, Audible's help describes an "Audible app for macOS" that is installed from the App Store.[10]

Audible's Conditions of Use say Audible may issue credits "redeemable for content" as part of a membership plan or a promotion, and that credits "expire immediately" when a membership is cancelled or terminated unless they are used before then.[2] Audible's homepage tells shoppers that "All titles purchased with a credit are yours to keep forever".[11]

An Audible help page with a 2008 copyright line described settings in Audible Download Manager, Audible's download software, for choosing "where and how you want your downloaded Audible content processed".[12] The news site Windows Central reported on August 4, 2015 that Audiobooks, Audible's app for Windows 10, was available.[13] In an email to users quoted by the news site Softpedia in January 2022, Audible said of its Windows App Store app, "We discontinued this app on January 13, 2022", and said users could continue to listen with it until July 31, 2022.[14] Audible's help center says Microsoft discontinued the Amazon Appstore on Windows 11 and that the Audible Android app "is no longer available or supported on Windows 11".[15]

Audible's Conditions of Use, in the versions dated September 10, 2025 and November 2, 2026, say "When you purchase content from Audible, you are purchasing a license", subject to the rights and restrictions of Audible's License.[16][2] The License, dated February 18, 2025, grants buyers who comply with it and the other Terms, including payment of any applicable fees, a "limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable license" for "personal and non-commercial use of the purchased content".[17] A note in Audible's help on removing titles from the Library says "The titles you purchase with a credit or credit card are yours to keep".[18]

The Conditions of Use dated March 31, 2022 and September 10, 2025 encouraged buyers "to download the content promptly after purchase".[19][16] Both said Audible "may continue" to make purchased content available for re-download but did "not guarantee" it.[19][16] The version dated November 2, 2026 no longer contains those sentences.[2] The 2022, 2025 and 2026 versions all forbid any attempt to "disable, bypass, modify, defeat, or otherwise circumvent" digital rights management (DRM) or any other protection system applied to Audible content.[19][16][2]

Lifehacker writer Emily Long wrote on September 16, 2026 that people who buy titles on Audible would "expect that the files are yours to keep", but that "this isn't a guarantee".[20] Consumer advocate Louis Rossmann said in a March 2024 video that he would no longer pay for audiobooks unless he got a file, such as an Opus or Vorbis file, that he could play on his own device.[21]

The technology news site The Verge reported that, starting February 26, 2025, Amazon was removing a website feature that let buyers download purchased books to a computer and then copy them manually to a Kindle e-reader over USB.[22] A pop-up warning on Amazon's website, reproduced by The Verge, said that from that date "the 'Download & Transfer via USB' option will no longer be available".[22] Amazon spokesperson Jackie Burke said in a statement to The Verge that customers could continue reading books previously downloaded on their Kindle device and access new content through the Kindle app, Kindle for web and Kindle devices with WiFi capability.[22]

The technology site Android Authority reported in December 2025 that, starting January 20, 2026, buyers of a qualifying DRM-free title would be able to download an EPUB (an e-book format that can be used on devices other than a Kindle) or PDF version,[23] while most Kindle books would still not be downloadable.[24]
In a February 2025 video, Rossmann argued that removing the download button helped nobody but maybe rights holders and Amazon, and did not help the end user.[25]
Good e-Reader wrote that for users who want to download their entire library to a PC or Mac "for safe-keeping", the community relies on "dedicated tools that bypass the missing web buttons".[3]
• Libation describes itself as "a free, open-source application for downloading and managing your Audible audiobooks".[26]
• The audible-cli project calls itself "A powerful command-line tool for managing and downloading your Audible audiobooks", a program run through commands such as "audible library list".[27]

• OpenAudible's website says the program connects to an Audible account, downloads the entire library and converts it to MP3 or M4B audio files; it is "Free to try", but "Conversion and splitting require a license", a paid OpenAudible license sold as "one payment, no subscription".[28]

OpenAudible's documentation says that when a user signs in, the program "registers a virtual device with Amazon", and that version 5.0.3 or later "registers new sign-ins as an Android device".[29] Libation's developer wrote on the project's issue tracker in September 2026 that Libation "tries hard to essentially mimic the official app".[30] OpenAudible's documentation says Audible "recently changed which registrations it accepts" and refuses download licenses to "some registrations made by OpenAudible 5.0.2 and earlier".[29] Libation's release notes said that when Audible refuses a license because an account is being throttled, users should "Wait 24 to 48 hours", as it is "Audible rate-limiting, not a Libation bug"; a later release fixed "widespread 'License Denied' / CustomerThrottled failures" caused by Libation registering Android devices with a serial number twice the expected length.[31]
Lifehacker wrote in March 2025 that bypassing DRM "is illegal in the US" under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, "but it may be legal in other regions".[32]

In a September 2025 video, Rossmann said he had used programs that let buyers get audio files of their Audible books, without guilt because he had paid for the books.[33] He said he thought the program was called Open Audible, a Linux program he had downloaded a few years earlier, but that he could be wrong.[33]
