sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261128.headline: Yale scientists may have found a shortcut to the anti-aging benefits of eating less

paragraphs.text: Yale scientists may have uncovered a shortcut to achieving some of the anti-aging benefits of eating less without having to restrict calories. Their discovery centers on an immune system protein that helps protect the body from infections but may also contribute to chronic inflammation as we grow older.

Reducing calorie intake has been shown to extend lifespan in several animal species, including mice, rhesus monkeys, and fruit flies. In some cases, these animals also remain free of disease for longer. However, extreme calorie restriction can come at a significant biological cost. Mice that consume 40% fewer calories, for example, become more vulnerable to infections, experience impaired growth, and are less likely to reproduce.

Researchers have long sought a way to harness the potential longevity benefits of calorie restriction in humans without these harmful consequences. In a new study published in Nature Aging, Yale scientists identified a promising target: an immune system protein known as complement component 3 (C3).

Earlier research from Yale demonstrated that people who reduced their calorie intake by a moderate 14% over two years experienced improvements in immune defense without sacrificing growth or reproductive function.

"This concept demonstrates that aging is actually malleable and a process that can be targeted," says senior author Vishwa Deep Dixit, PhD, Waldemar Von Zedtwitz Professor of Pathology, professor of immunobiology and of comparative medicine, and director of the Yale Center for Research on Aging (Y-Age) at Yale School of Medicine.
Eating Less Reduces a Protein Linked to Aging

For their latest investigation, Dixit and his colleagues at Yale School of Medicine examined blood plasma samples from 42 participants in a two-year clinical trial funded by the National Institutes of Health. The trial, known as CALERIE, stands for Comprehensive Assessment of Long-Term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy.
"It's the only trial of its kind that has been done with such rigor and control and demonstrates relevance to human physiology," Dixit says.
Over the course of the trial, participants successfully lowered their calorie consumption by 11% to 14% without experiencing a sense of deprivation.

By examining blood samples collected over time, the scientists identified more than 7,000 proteins. One particularly intriguing finding was that levels of C3 fell significantly in response to calorie restriction.

C3 is a central component of the complement system, a network of proteins that helps the immune system recognize and eliminate potentially harmful invaders, including bacteria. Although this system is essential for protecting the body, excessive activation may have damaging consequences.

Previous research has linked complement system activity to chronic inflammation, a persistent inflammatory response that can damage healthy tissues over time. Chronic inflammation is considered a major hallmark of biological aging and contributes to the development of numerous age-related diseases.

"But the causal effects of C3 in aging and chronic inflammation have not been identified. So, we were very excited to find that in our study," says Hee-Hoon Kim, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the paper.
A Surprising Discovery Hidden in Body Fat

By comparing protein levels at the beginning and end of the two-year calorie restriction period, the researchers pinpointed white adipose tissue as the primary tissue affected by the dietary intervention. White adipose tissue is the most abundant type of body fat in mammals. Beyond storing energy, it plays important roles in metabolism, hormone production, and immune function.
The researchers then turned to mice to investigate the biological mechanisms behind their findings. Consistent with observations in humans, C3 expression increased as the animals aged.

Further biochemical experiments revealed an unexpected source of this increase: visceral white adipose tissue. Visceral fat accumulates deep within the abdomen, surrounding internal organs, and has been associated with chronic inflammation and metabolic disease.
"We were not expecting that because these proteins are mainly synthesized in the liver," says Manish Mishra, PhD, a postdoctoral associate in the Dixit lab and a co-first author of the study.

Using a technique called single-cell RNA sequencing, which allows scientists to examine gene activity within individual cells, the team traced the production of C3 to specific populations of macrophages associated with aging that reside within fat tissue.
"This whole process was unknown in the beginning," Mishra says. "Just to narrow it down to the subtypes of macrophages responsible for this complement protein production was very challenging."

Macrophages are white blood cells that form part of the body's first line of immune defense. They are best known for surrounding, engulfing, and destroying potentially harmful microorganisms. However, as Dixit explains, they also perform essential functions that help maintain healthy tissues and keep biological processes in balance.
Anti-Aging Benefits May Be Independent of Weight Loss
The discovery raised an important question: Could people benefit from lower C3 activity without having to lose weight?
Initially, the scientists suspected that losing body fat through calorie restriction might reduce the production of C3 and help counter some of the biological processes associated with aging.
There was good reason to suspect a connection. Most participants in the clinical trial lost about 18 pounds during two years of moderate calorie restriction.
However, when the team examined changes in participants' body mass index, they found no correlation between weight loss and reductions in complement protein levels.
"This suggests that calorie restriction has a beneficial effect that is unique to adipose tissues and is likely independent of weight loss," Kim says.

The researchers also tested whether a drug could reproduce this particular benefit of calorie restriction. When they pharmacologically inhibited C3 activation in mice, the animals experienced a reduction in age-related inflammation.

Although the experiments did not establish that blocking C3 extends lifespan or slows aging in humans, they suggest that targeting this protein could reproduce some of the beneficial biological effects of eating less.
When the Immune System Turns Against the Body
According to Dixit, the findings illustrate an important principle in aging research: Biological processes that benefit us when we are young can become harmful later in life.

This idea, known as antagonistic pleiotropy, has its conceptual roots in evolutionary theories of aging developed by biologist Peter Medawar in 1952. The theory of antagonistic pleiotropy was subsequently formalized by evolutionary biologist George C. Williams in 1957.
One example is growth hormone, which is essential for normal growth and development during childhood but may also contribute to the development of cancer later in life.

A similar trade-off may occur with proteins such as C3. Throughout human evolution, these molecules have played a vital role in protecting people from potentially deadly infections. However, as humans increasingly live to advanced ages, excessive activity of these same protective mechanisms may contribute to chronic inflammation and declining health.
Dixit suggests that reducing C3 levels could offer a way to extend health span, the portion of a person's life spent in good health, rather than simply increasing the number of years they live.
Could Existing Drugs Mimic Calorie Restriction?

The Yale team is now investigating whether FDA-approved complement inhibitor drugs could be used to counter the harmful effects of excessive C3 activity and potentially slow aspects of aging in humans.
The challenge will be to reduce damaging inflammation without compromising the immune system's ability to protect the body from infections.
"The idea is not to remove complement systems that are required for us to fight infections," Dixit says. "Instead, the goal is to restore the balance."

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261127.headline: Scientists create stunning, non-fading paint without a single pigment

paragraphs.text: Researchers at Kobe University have developed a coating that produces the rich colors and glossy finish of automotive paint without relying on pigments. The breakthrough overcomes several major limitations of structural color, making it possible to apply colors that resist fading to large, complex surfaces, maintain a consistent hue from different viewing angles, and add protective coatings.

"Color coatings are expected to provide vivid color, brightness, gloss, and long-term durability, yet no existing technology satisfies all of these requirements simultaneously," says Kobe University materials engineer Hiroshi Sugimoto.

Traditional paints typically require relatively thick layers of pigments, which add considerable weight and can fade over time. Structural color, a phenomenon responsible for the brilliant appearance of peacock feathers, offers an alternative that avoids the fading caused by light exposure in organic pigments. However, conventional approaches to structural color require precisely arranged microscopic structures, often produce different colors depending on the viewing angle, and are incompatible with protective coatings.
Unlocking Glossy Color Without Pigments

Sugimoto previously pioneered a new method of producing structural color using tiny silicon spheres that generate consistent colors regardless of viewing angle. His team subsequently adapted the technology for inkjet printing (link). Although the resulting coatings produced color successfully, they scattered reflected light in multiple directions, leaving their surfaces without a glossy finish. The technique that made inkjet printing possible, however, also provided a potential solution to this problem.

Sugimoto explains, "Packing the nanospheres in silica shells not only protects the particles but also controls their spacing and should improve self-assembly into neat arrays." Arranging the particles more uniformly reduces the scattering of reflected light, allowing the coating to develop a glossy appearance.

In a study published in the journal Small Structures, the researchers demonstrated that they could produce and adjust the gloss of structural color coatings on large, three-dimensional surfaces. They also found that applying a protective layer had little effect on the resulting color.

"The most exciting aspect of this work is that it demonstrates glossy, non-iridescent and protection-coated structural color coatings for 3D objects in a single platform, making the technology useful for real-world applications," explains Sugimoto.
Ultra-Lightweight Paint Could Transform Aviation

One of the technology's most remarkable advantages is its extremely low weight. A single layer of silicon nanospheres is sufficient to produce bright colors with high opacity, effectively concealing the underlying surface.

The potential weight savings are particularly striking for aviation. Conventional coatings on wide-body airliners currently add several hundred kilograms to the aircraft's weight. The researchers estimate that a color coating based on their technology could weigh only several hundred grams, less than a carton of milk for an entire airplane.

The materials used to create these coatings also offer environmental advantages. Silicon is nontoxic and can be sourced from the semiconductor industry, while silica is among the most abundant materials in Earth's crust. Combined with their resistance to fading, the minimal material requirements could make future color coatings significantly less resource-intensive.
Taking Structural Color Beyond Paint

Sugimoto is helping establish a company to increase production and bring the technology to industrial markets. The coating process is particularly promising because it can be integrated into several established manufacturing techniques.
"The process is compatible with scalable coating methods such as spray coating, slot-die coating, and roll-to-roll processing."

Beyond commercial paint applications, Sugimoto hopes to use the underlying science to create advanced coatings that perform multiple functions. Future versions could combine vivid structural color with capabilities related to sensing, light-driven chemical reactions, and energy management.

He says: "We want to expand the possibility of applications for the science behind our technology beyond coloration. Looking ahead, we aim to develop multifunctional silicon nanoparticle coatings that combine structural coloration with additional optical functions such as sensing, photocatalysis, and energy management."

This research was funded by the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development (grants JPMJPF2503, JPMJSF2405) and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (grants 24KF0158, 24K01287, 24K22206, 25K01608).

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/science/ai-math-p.headline: A.I. Has Upended Math. Is Physics Next?

paragraphs.text: Janna Levin, a theoretical astrophysicist at Barnard College, is working to explain some of the more baffling aspects of the universe. And she wants to work fast, before artificial intelligence swoops in and beats her to the solution.
“Isn’t that crazy?” Dr. Levin said. “I do feel this urgency. It has to have a time stamp on it, so people will know it was done before A.I. could possibly have done it.”
Dr. Levin was circumspect about giving too many details on the work, lest someone type a few prompts into one of the latest A.I. models and publish the result first.
“It’s just an interesting time that all of us are having to think through,” she said. “What does it mean to create something as a human?”

In the past few months, mathematicians, once optimistic about A.I., have watched with existential alarm as its accelerating smarts seem to be surpassing them. Just over a week ago, a mathematician working at Anthropic announced that he and the company’s Claude A.I. agent had conquered the Riemann hypothesis, arguably the greatest unsolved problem in mathematics.

Some experts worry that soon they will not even be able to understand what the computers prove, much as Isaac Newton, who invented calculus in the 17th century, would struggle if he were suddenly faced with 21st-century math.
Physics is the most mathematical of the sciences. Dr. Levin and others are increasingly worried that the field is about to face its own reckoning with the machines.

But experts have also noted that the discipline is fundamentally different because it seeks to describe how the real universe operates. Rather than making humans obsolete, some argued, A.I. is poised to be a powerful tool in physicists’s quest to reveal new truths about the world we live in.
‘Intellectual Skyscrapers’

The use of computers is nothing new in physics, and physicists have long employed aspects of artificial intelligence such as neural networks, machine learning and data mining to analyze voluminous amounts of data.

But now, the large language models underlying A.I. tools like Claude and ChatGPT from OpenAI incorporate encyclopedic knowledge of nearly everything that every physicist has ever done. This modern iteration of A.I. is accelerating the pace of discovery, offering a high-powered research assistant at all hours that can summarize the state of previous research and serve as a sounding board for debating ideas.

“People draw these parallels to the nuclear era or to the Industrial Revolution,” said Jim Halverson, a theoretical physicist at Northeastern University in Boston who advises an A.I. physics start-up called Physical Superintelligence.
“The industrial era brought us skyscrapers,” Dr. Halverson said, and with A.I., he hopes that physicists can build “intellectual skyscrapers that are a sign of this new era.”

Crucially, unlike in mathematics, neither humans nor the most advanced A.I. models can make significant breakthroughs through “thinking” alone. Theoretical physicists come up with competing, often contradictory ideas that fit with known experimental results. Scientists will still need astronomical observations, collisions in giant particle accelerators and other experimental data to discern which of the proposed theories are accurate descriptions of the physical world and which are simply wrong.

“Nature has to decide, because a theory can be perfectly consistent and still not be the one nature chose,” said Marcela Carena, executive director of the Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics in Canada. An initiative announced by Perimeter in October seeks to both use A.I. to accelerate physics research and use physics to understand how A.I. learns.
While some physicists avoid A.I. entirely, not wishing to inadvertently train the machines with their knowledge and insights, others, especially younger ones entering the field, see A.I. as a boon.

“I haven’t been playing with it so long, but my students are literally 24/7 talking to A.I.,” said Igor Klebanov, a professor of physics at Princeton. “They can’t sleep. They’re so eager, and they say it’s getting dramatically smarter.”
Michael Brenner, a professor of applied mathematics and physics at Harvard University who also leads A.I. scientific research at Google, says now is the greatest time to be a physicist.
“I mean, I wish I were a graduate student now, and I could start from now,” he said.
49 Out of 50
Even in the past few months, A.I. has become much better at physics.

In the spring, Suvrat Raju, a physicist at the International Center for Theoretical Sciences in India, was on sabbatical at the Google DeepMind A.I. research laboratory. He was curious about how well the latest A.I. models would do on problems that experts could solve in about a day — harder than those in a graduate-level physics class but far from groundbreaking research.

He and Praneeth Netrapalli, a colleague at DeepMind, collected from experts 50 unpublished problems in classical physics, quantum field theory, statistical mechanics, cosmology and other fields. Then they prompted A.I. agents from five companies to go solve them.
“When we started the exercise, our idea was that most problems would be too hard for the agents,” Dr. Raju said. “As we went along, the agents started to improve.”
The best-performing agent, the scientists reported, was ChatGPT Astra from OpenAI. Some of Astra’s solutions didn’t match up with what human experts had calculated. But Astra insisted it was correct.
Dr. Raju said they then went back to the experts to check. “In case after case, the experts found some subtle error in their calculations and had to revise their answer,” he said.
In the end, he and Dr. Netrapalli gave Astra a score of 49 out of 50.

On its website, OpenAI this month highlighted Nathaniel Craig, a physicist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who made progress on a question involving the Standard Model, the set of equations encapsulating all the particles and forces of the universe, except for gravity.

In general, theorists want to map the Standard Model onto a four-dimensional grid called a lattice, because that would make it easier to calculate the interactions of particles and look for new, yet-to-be-discovered physical phenomena. But the equations can go haywire when chopped up in that way.

Dr. Craig had the idea of combining two mathematical techniques to map the Standard Model on a lattice in a way that partially solves this problem. The required mathematical bookkeeping was too much for his human brain or traditional computational approaches, he said, but A.I. handled it well.

Astra, the ChatGPT model that Dr. Craig used, even went a step further. When Dr. Craig hit a wall, the A.I. suggested a better technique to avoid equations blowing up to infinity. “It was supercool,” he said.
The Question of Taste
But Dr. Raju said A.I. did not yet match human physicists in perhaps the most important aspect of science: deciding which questions are worth asking.

“So far, I think the models tend to fixate on details and technicalities, and they don’t have the taste that good physicists have,” Dr. Raju said. “If the models were to start formulating interesting problems and pointing out important directions in theoretical physics, I would be persuaded. I haven’t seen that yet.”

He gave the example of Albert Einstein’s paper on special relativity, published in 1905. Much of the groundwork had been performed years earlier, and the notion that the speed of light is constant was already embedded in equations describing electromagnetism.
Einstein’s brilliance was realizing that the constant speed of light was not a quirk of the electromagnetism equations but a fundamental property of the universe.
A.I. has yet to make such a leap of insight. But the first hints of A.I. “taste” may already be showing up.

Christopher Herzog, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London in England, wanted to see what A.I. could do by itself. He did not pose a particular problem. Rather, he told ChatGPT and Claude to go out and find their own topic, collaborate on the research and write a paper that could be published in Physical Review Letters, a top academic journal.

Dr. Herzog constrained the topic to theoretical high-energy physics so that he would have a hope of understanding the results. He had each A.I. agent propose three ideas. Like real physicists, the agents debated and decided which of the six to pursue — without Dr. Herzog offering his opinion, although he said he agreed with their choice.
Then they set off to work. Dr. Herzog’s main role was copying and pasting responses between them, because he had not set up a system for the two agents to talk to each other directly.

Within a couple of hours, the A.I. agents had produced a rough draft, although the prose was not particularly good. “It looks like readable English,” Dr. Herzog said, but it was dense and not well explained.

It took a couple of weeks for Dr. Herzog and his collaborator, Andy Stergiou, to check the work and turn the writing into something that made more sense to a human reader. Then they posted that manuscript online.

“It’s a little bit soul-crushing,” Dr. Herzog said of the effort. “Your only role is to check machines, step by step, and often you think, ‘This looks wrong,’ and then it explains to you what it did, and then it turns out it’s actually right.”
Dr. Herzog said he was not certain what kind of welcome the paper would get from the editors at Physical Review Letters. “There might just be some knee-jerk reaction and send it back,” he said.

Dr. Brenner, of Harvard and Google, was less impressed. If a machine did all of the research, then that might just mean a prestigious journal should raise its bar on what merits publication, requiring results of greater significance.
“What is enough?” Dr. Brenner said. “That’s what we get to find out, and it’s pretty cool.”
‘I’ve Got to Be a Grown-Up’
Dr. Levin and three other theorists in Manhattan — Brian Greene of Columbia, Daniel Kabat of Lehman College and Massimo Porrati of New York University — are still doing physics the old-fashioned way.

They have been working to explain how some mysteries of the universe may arise from the geometry of space-time twisted in higher dimensions. (Basically, if you could travel in a loop around space-time, you would come back mirror-reversed.)

The researchers used this approach in a paper published in March, which showed how twisted space-time could explain why matter and antimatter did not completely annihilate each other in the moment after the Big Bang, leaving nothing to form stars, galaxies and everything else.
They are now racing to apply the idea to another cosmic problem before A.I. figures it out.

Dr. Levin laments that something is lost in the A.I. revolution, because part of the learning and understanding is gained from all the mistakes and dead ends along the way, not just from the correct answers.
“I believe that what the human being is doing is more beautiful, more romantic,” she said. “The pursuit is understanding. It’s not cataloging answers.”
But she also realizes that A.I. is not going away, and she is open to using it in future research.
“I’ve got to be a grown-up about this,” Dr. Levin said. “You can’t be a Luddite, refuse to use phones or not fly in planes. I mean, this is what’s happening. This is the world now.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/27/science/homo-erec.headline: Homo Erectus Lived in Rainforests, Upending Ideas About Their Adaptability

paragraphs.text: Lofty mountaintops. Arid deserts. Frozen tundras.
Modern humans call nearly every environment on Earth home. Turns out our distant ancestors may have, too.

A recent analysis of very old teeth found in southern China suggests that Homo erectus survived in the dense tropical rainforests of the region, adapting to conditions previously thought inhospitable for these hominins.

“This is a new chapter in our understanding of Homo erectus,” said Kira Westaway, an associate professor at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, and an author of the study. “They were more flexible and adaptable than we’ve ever previously thought.”

Homo erectus first appeared in Africa about two million years ago. They are widely believed to be the first hominins to leave that continent, use fire and care for their sick and elderly. After making their way through parts of Europe and Asia, their final days, about 100,000 years ago, seem to have taken place on what is now the Indonesian island of Java. Previous archaeological evidence suggested that the species was best suited to life on open grasslands and savannas, and that it stuck to those environments.
This very rigidity is what some scientists considered the downfall of Homo erectus. Those assumptions, though, now aren’t so clear.

“It seems likely that Homo erectus got outcompeted by us, but that doesn’t mean they couldn’t adapt to that environment,” Susan Antón, an anthropologist at New York University who was not involved in the study, wrote in an email. “It only means that we did it a bit better.”

The new evidence of their dwellings comes from teeth discovered in 2014 and 2024 in two sister caves in the Guangxi province. Dr. Westaway and a team of Australian, Chinese and European researchers examined the stable isotopes present in the teeth, as well as other fossils of plants and animals found in the caves. The scientists also used luminescence dating, a technique that analyzes radiation to reveal when something was last exposed to sunlight.

The tests revealed that the teeth were somewhere between 184,000 and 324,000 years old, that they were from Homo erectus and that those individuals were drinking and eating from the area around them. The results were published in the journal Nature.
At the time, Southern China was covered in tropical rainforests, meaning Homo erectus survived an environment previously thought by experts to be an improbable habitat.
The age of the teeth also represents the most recent evidence of Homo erectus in China to date. Before this discovery, the youngest known remains in China were 400,000 years old.
That timing “helps us understand the ultimate fate of Homo erectus in Asia,” Dr. Westaway said.

Patrick Roberts, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany who was an author on the recent study, has posited that Homo sapiens were “generalist specialists,” suggesting that we outlived our ancestors because of a special ability to adapt to extreme environments and subsist on a wide array of resources.
This recent study, however, “upturns our idea of how unique our species is,” Dr. Roberts said. “Maybe these hominins weren’t as different to us as we first thought.”
Dr. Westaway agreed.
“We like to promote ourselves as this incredible success story,” she said. “But studies like this are starting to redefine what we call ‘successful’ and ‘unsuccessful’ species.”
She hopes to apply these in-depth techniques to other research looking at hominins.
“I think we’ll start to put more flesh on the bones — or in this case, teeth — and start to really tell the story of these people,” she said.

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/oil-price-iran-war-s.headline: The Iran war could shatter rising expectations of surplus oil supply in coming months
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/oil-price-iran-war-s.author: Spencer Kimball

paragraphs.text: Crude oil prices have sold off sharply in November as investors see a recovery in Middle East exports tipping the market into a surplus for the first time since the Iran war began.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, are down about 20% after approaching wartime highs in late October when the contract hit $118 a barrel.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate has also fallen about 21% after topping $104 a barrel in the same period. Brent closed at $95.44 a barrel Friday while WTI settled at $83.08.
U.S. retail gasoline prices have fallen well below $4 a gallon and diesel has eased below $6 a gallon.

In October, investors were pricing in the risk of a major military escalation in the Persian Gulf after the U.S. midterm elections. But President Donald Trump has held back so far from launching renewed military strikes against Iran after the Democrats wiped out Republican congressional majorities.

The selloff this month has likely gone too far, Giovanni Staunovo, a strategist at UBS, wrote in a note clients. The market has become "too comfortable with the supply outlook," Staunovo said. "The rebound in Gulf exports should not be mistaken for a normalization of the oil market," the analyst said.
Fragile surplus

The International Energy Agency has forecast an oil surplus beginning in the fourth quarter. This would represent a major turning point nine months after the Iran war triggered the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market.

Goldman Sachs sees a crude surplus of 2 million barrels per day in 2027 as Gulf producers continue to adapt their supply chains to war in the Middle East. Commodity and ship tracking firm Kpler sees oversupply of 3 million bpd next year.
"If the recovery in the Arabian Gulf region continues, we're going to have oversupply," said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush.
But predictions of a surplus assume a sustained recovery in flows from the Middle East. The IEA also cautioned that downside risks "persist as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security."
"If pigs had wings, they'd fly," said David Goldwyn, who served as the State Department's special envoy for international energy under President Barack Obama, in reference to the surplus forecast.

The more likely scenario is that oil prices trade in a wide range through the end of Trump's term as the security situation in the Gulf remains volatile, McNally at Rapidan said. During periods of relative calm, crude will trade between $70 to $80, he said. Prices could spike well above $100 when the conflict escalates, he said.
"We think there will be more disruptions, more risk and that those surpluses won't materialize next year," McNally said.

Trump recently told Fox News that he might launch renewed strikes on Iran after the new year. A major military escalation in the region would lead to structurally higher prices, said Goldwyn, the Obama administration official. Iran would likely retaliate against U.S. strikes with attacks on ports, refineries or processing facilities, he said.
Market deficit

Crude exports from the Middle East have rebounded since the summer, though they have trended lower in recent weeks and remain well below pre-war levels as tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz are attacked on a near daily basis.
At least 20 attacks on commercial ships have been reported this month, according to maritime security agencies. There were 35 such incidents in October, the highest level since the war began.

Middle east crude exports averaged 12.8 million barrels per day in the week ended Wednesday, about 24% below pre-war levels of 17 million bpd, according to Kpler data. Fuel shipments stood at 3.2 million bpd in the same period, down about 49% from 6.3 million bpd before the war.
Production has also increased in the Americas and demand has pulled back due to seasonal factors associated with the end of the summer driving season and refinery turnarounds, Goldwyn said.

Assuming a persistent surplus, JPMorgan forecasts Brent prices in the high $70s in the first half of 2027 before falling into the $60s in the second half of next year. Goldman Sachs sees Brent trading around $88 a barrel next year and WTI averaging about $78 barrel next year.

But Kpler warned the predicted surplus could easily tip into a deficit again if Iran or its Houthi allies bomb the United Arab Emirates export terminal at Fujairah or key Saudi infrastructure such as the kingdom's facilities at Ras Tanura, Yanbu or its East-West Pipeline.
Low inventories

Any further disruption to Mideast supplies would strike when the world's inventory buffers have already been drawn down to historic lows without time to restock them, Goldwyn said. The CEOs of ExxonMobil and Chevron have warned for months about the depletion of the world's oil stockpiles.

There is room to potentially release another 100 million barrels from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve and for the Europeans to deploy more refined products, Goldwyn said. But neither will be eager to dip into the reserves again, he said.
"If this looks like it's going to be a chronic situation, I think both the U.S and Europeans are going to be reluctant to draw on those reserves just to provide price relief," Goldwyn said.

China is also increasing its crude imports as the situation in the Middle East remains fragile, Staunovo at UBS said. Beijing's decision to dramatically cut its imports earlier this year was one of the major factors keeping prices from shooting even higher during the war.
"Together, these developments are contributing to a decline in oil on water and a tightening physical market," Staunovo said. "This supports our view that oil prices should recover from here."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.headline: How 'beatniks, Communists and nudists' changed the Sunset Strip
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.author: Patt Morrison

paragraphs.text: Oh yeah, the Sunset Strip.
You can say it with a knowing, leering wink, like a burlesque comic.
You can say it with the relish of a real estate agent contemplating a choice listing.
You can say it with the delight of a fan — of comedy, music, hip restaurants, of shopping, chic hotels, of new books and cool old hangouts.
Say it like a local, or like a tourist, but either way, you probably don’t know the half of it.
The Sunset Strip began as a roadway of convenience, a dirt-road link of something under two miles in the 20-plus miles of Sunset Boulevard from downtown to the sea.

“Strip” had nothing to do with casting off clothes. It was called a “strip” because it connected the city limit of Los Angeles (and of the LAPD’s territory) on the east with the tidy and well-policed city of Beverly Hills on the west.

This month marks 60 years since a moment of civic freakout among teenagers and young Angelenos turned the Strip into a testing ground for the 1960s “youthquake,” and for the forces that didn’t want it there.

For some time, kids had been milling in the street and dancing at clubs past the curfew — 10 p.m. — and probably doing some drugs and underage drinking too. But a national moral panic had set in years earlier, with young people at the core of it.
In November 1964, Los Angeles’ TV channel 9’s nighttime announcers were intoning, “Ten o’clock is curfew time in Los Angeles. Do you know where your children are?”
The 1965 Watts uprising had unsettled Americans well beyond the confines of that L.A. neighborhood; just about any disturbance might wind up getting classed as a “riot.”
So what happened on the Sunset Strip over those November and December weeks in 1966?

Kids had been making the Strip a hangout for a while. It was something like L.A.’s version of San Francisco’s counterculture Haight Ashbury district. A favorite spot was Pandora’s Box, an orchid-and-gold-striped, booze-free coffee joint, and in November 1966, its lease was soon to expire (the place would be swiftly closed after the protests, and, the following year, bulldozed).

Until World War II, curfews for most teenagers in L.A. had been 9 p.m. By 1966, the curfew for under-18s in the city and county was 10, an hour when, as kids pointed out, many movies and school dances hadn’t let out yet. Paired up with the curfews were anti-loitering laws against just hanging out; if you weren’t heading to or from someplace after 10, you could be in trouble.

Some merchants and residents along the Strip weren’t pleased with the congregating kids — “beatniks, Communists and nudists” were mentioned — and shared their disaffection with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, which patrolled that segment of Sunset Boulevard.

And then, a dozen days before Thanksgiving, fliers appeared on the Strip announcing a rally protesting the curfew. Word got out via rock and roll radio stations, the kids thronged the street, and deputies dropped the hammer on what became known as “the curfew riots.”

That first weekend, a thousand or so teenagers and 20-somethings showed up. Then, The Times reported, after a carload of off-duty Marines wound up in a fender bender, a brawl began and blew up. A few people threw bottles and broke windows. Law enforcement brought out bullhorns to try to clear the street. Some protesters commandeered a transit bus, shooed out the driver and passengers, broke the windows, dented the roof and deflated the tires. A man who tried to drop burning matches into the bus’ gas tank was arrested.

Over the weeks ahead, several hundred were arrested. For law enforcement, it was a moment to counter the counterculture. Los Angeles County Supervisor Ernest Debs called the protesters “misguided hoodlums,” and the sheriff issued a no-tolerance pledge to prosecute lawbreakers and yank the business licenses of anyone encouraging them. He wanted parents held liable for their “failure” to control their children.

When protesters swarmed across the line into L.A. itself, a L.A. Police Department captain, C.W. Crumley, warned that curfews were necessary lest “juvenile prostitution, venereal disease, narcotics” get out of hand — and that police needed a freer hand to stop them.
Within a few days, it all became a “happening.” Ordinary Angelenos drove to the Strip to gawp at the “teenyboppers,” and the news trucks and radio reporters sometimes outnumbered the “hippies.”

As the days wore on, the young protesters were joined by pastors and sometimes even by parents. Now the kids carried signs: “LAPD is not cool to kids” and “We’re your children! Don’t destroy us.” Some teens wore American Civil Liberties Union armbands. The optics were not working in law enforcement’s favor.

In a letter to a Pasadena newspaper, an Altadena man wrote that he’d visited the Sunset Strip to see for himself, and found “a huge number of normal-looking, short-haired boys and a few beatnik types. I was strongly reminded of a college pep rally,” not a riot.

Actor Peter Fonda was picked up by lawmen, who let him go after he explained that he was researching a film. In December, Sonny and Cher showed up at Pandora’s Box, where they had once performed. Both wore white fur — Sonny in shaggy Mongolian lamb, Cher in mink.

All he did, Sonny said, was remind protesters to be peaceful. But a few days later, the Monterey Park City Council indignantly canceled its invitation to the pop stars to ride on the city’s New Year’s Day 1967 float. It invited country singer Buck Owens instead.

The 1966 “curfew riots” gave us one of the era’s best protest songs, which soon became an antiwar anthem. Musician Stephen Stills witnessed what he called “the absurdity” of November 1966, drove home to Topanga Canyon and, in about 15 minutes, wrote “For What It’s Worth,” soon recorded by his new band, Buffalo Springfield. “For me there was no riot,” he said in The Times. “It was basically a cop dance.”
Given the Strip’s history, there was no small element of hypocrisy to the hand-wringing and policing of late 1966.
Once the area’s early 20th-century poinsettia rows had been plowed under and its avocado groves cut down, the Strip’s geography made it ideal for nightlife, legal or louche.

Gambling, illegal drinking, even fistfights were a constant at nightclubs and cafes that began opening their doors in the 1920s. But because the clientele were in black tie or evening gowns, bore famous names or paid eye-watering tabs and gambling stakes, they often weren’t held to account.

The notorious Clover Club was raided and swiftly reopened so often that in 1936, the management felt constrained to tell The Times, “No payoff of any kind to local or northern politicians was made by the club.”
A sampling of the mayhem:

1928: A fire in the Russian Eagle Café sent patrons on the run, chief among them Charlie Chaplin. The White Russian owner of a next-door shop was convicted of arson for gain. He blamed it on … Commies.

1941: At the chic Mocambo nightclub, Warner Brothers’ star Errol Flynn was stabbed in the cheek with a fork wielded by the wife of a gossip columnist. At the next table, actress Marlene Dietrich, encumbered by a plaster cast on a broken ankle, hustled her legendary gams outta there.
1947: Frank Sinatra slugged a gossip columnist outside Ciro’s nightclub. Days later, he was arrested for battery in a radio studio and ended up paying the columnist $9,000 to settle the case.

1949: Mobster Mickey Cohen was standing outside Sherry’s nightclub, not far from the men’s clothing store he owned, when gangland rivals opened up on him with shotguns. A bodyguard was killed, Cohen got nicked, and newspaper columnist Florabel Muir, who had been inside with Cohen, got peppered in the ass, though the newspapers delicately called it “the thigh area.” Muir seemed to attract mayhem on the Strip.

For years, good-government forces had pleaded to keep mobsters off the Strip. In the 1930s, a huge sign on a vacant lot fronting Sunset read, “Close Clover Gambling Joint — Keep Chicago Out of Hollywood.” An Easter Sunday raid of the Clover and other clubs turned up secret mirrored door panels, thousand-dollar poker chips and dozens of patrons who were all, coincidentally, just leaving.

Time and money exerted their own changes. Las Vegas, with its newer, celebrated strip, began drawing the big gambling money and big-name entertainers. The Sunset Strip’s jazz clubs brought a newer, hipper clientele. The dictatorial movie studios — which paired up their stars, sometimes dressed them from the wardrobe department and sent them off to fetch some flashbulb publicity in the elegant nightclubs on the Sunset Strip — were losing their bossy authority.
Television was entertaining people at home. (One bit in “The Lucy Show” has Lucille Ball picked up for violating the Sunset Strip curfew.)

For six seasons in the ‘50s and ‘60s, the TV show “77 Sunset Strip” tried to capitalize on it all. There was never any such address; it’s always “Sunset Boulevard,” and always, colloquially, with the definite article, “the Sunset Strip.”

The most celebrated place on the Strip, the fabulous Garden of Allah, originally “Alla,” on the south side of Sunset between Crescent Heights and Havenhurst, was a grandly exotic apartment complex and private playland, an outpost for uprooted and celebrated Europeans and New Yorkers. It opened in 1927 and was bulldozed in 1959. What stands there now is yet another shopping plaza.
The nightclub Ciro’s became a rock music venue and eventually the legendary Comedy Store.

And the “hippies” who were ruining the Strip became the reinvention and saving of it, with music clubs whose walls heard the history of modern popular music: folk, rock, pop, glam, heavy metal, punk. David Bowie, John Lennon, Elton John, Joan Baez and Bob Dylan frequented the clubs or went onstage themselves.

In 1939, the mayor of Los Angeles let it be known that L.A. coveted the territory of the Sunset Strip. But it was West Hollywood that in 1984 became a city and claimed the Strip — its rugged roots, its high-priced glamour and its sweet tax revenues — as its own.
Metropolitan Museum Crèche

Among the prized possessions of most churches in Naples are elaborate Baroque Nativity scenes, made of wood, terra-cotta, wax, and delicate fabrics. To this day, there is a whole street devoted to the construction of these detailed set pieces, which, in addition to the Nativity, depict everyday life—fruit sellers, animals, shepherds—in rich detail. The Met owns a large collection, which it displays in a lively tableau at the foot of a giant Christmas tree in the Medieval Sculpture Hall. (Metropolitan Museum of Art; through Jan. 6.)
Radio City “Christmas Spectacular”

Last year, the centenary of the Rockettes was celebrated with a new sound system rather than a new number, but this year that oversight is being corrected. The choreographer Chloé Arnold (“Spirited,” “The Late Late Show with James Corden”) has been hired to sharpen a sometimes neglected aspect of the Rockettes’ tradition: their tap dancing. Her intricate, girl-power routine to a remixed “Carol of the Bells” joins old favorites like “Parade of the Wooden Soldiers,” made in 1933 and built to last. (Radio City Music Hall; through Jan. 4.)
“A Christmas Carol”

Matthew Warchus’s immersive staging of Charles Dickens’s Yuletide classic returns to PAC NYC, albeit with a twist. The crotchety skinflint Ebenezer Scrooge is being played by Andy Karl, cast boldly against type. Karl’s virile charisma energized the lead roles in musicalizations of “Rocky” and “Groundhog Day.” Will a shirtless Scrooge take swings at those pesky charity collectors? Either way, viewers should expect carolling, a complimentary clementine or gingerbread cookie, and, despite Scrooge’s best efforts, Christmas cheer. (PAC NYC; through Jan. 3.)
“A Kidman Carol”

If the thought of another “Christmas Carol” triggers your inner Scrooge, this riff may excite your chilly little heart. Kevin Zak’s unorthodox adaptation camps up the chestnut: on Oscars Eve, Cate Blanchett (Josh Sharp), rich in accolades, is visited by three spirits of Nicole Kidman (Marla Mindelle, fresh off “Titaníque”). They take her on a journey through the Australian outback and a Dickensian Tinsel Town to impart the true meaning of awards season. (New World Stages; through Dec. 30.)

“The Nutcracker” pops up all over town, from Bushwick’s “Nutcracker Rouge” (Théâtre XIV; Dec. 10-13)—a naughty romp that reinvents the Kingdom of the Sweets as a carnal coming-of-age story, replete with trapeze acts and stiletto-heeled burlesque—to Flatbush, where the Kings Theatre brings back “The Hip Hop Nutcracker” (Dec. 23), in which the dances are a reflection of the city’s street life. “The Yorkville Nutcracker,” a cozy production by the late Francis Patrelle, turns thirty this year; the starry guest dancers Miriam Miller and Tyler Angle perform as Sugarplum and her Cavalier. (Kaye Playhouse; Dec. 10-13.) The mother of all “Nutcrackers” is still George Balanchine’s familiar and sumptuous production for New York City Ballet, with its giant tree, heart-in-the-throat snow scene, and windswept Dewdrop solo—a rush of pure movement amid the waltzing flowers. (David H. Koch Theatre; Nov. 27-Jan. 2.)
Yo La Tengo Celebrates Hanukkah

In what has become a cherished annual tradition, the indie-rock band Yo La Tengo returns for a series of Hanukkah shows. Across the holiday’s eight nights, a surprise musician or comedian opens the show, the hosts are joined by guests, and every evening ends with an encore of covers. Past guests have included Lucinda Williams, Fred Armisen, the Sun Ra Arkestra, and Lucy Dacus. As if that wasn’t enough of an enticement, all of the proceeds go to various charities. (Bowery Ballroom; Dec. 4-11.)
“Peter and the Wolf”

Sergei Prokofiev’s “symphonic tale for children” has a dual purpose: to tell an engaging story about a young boy who pulls himself out of a pickle, and to introduce the instruments of the orchestra. Each character—boy, wolf, cat, bird—is associated with a particular instrument. This version, a holiday fixture performed in the little theatre beneath the Guggenheim Museum since 2013, moves the action to Central Park; Isaac Mizrahi narrates with wry humor, the dancers of Dance Heginbotham embody the different characters, and Ensemble Connect plays Prokofiev’s score. (Guggenheim Museum; Dec. 5-13.)

It’s no secret that the city has a special glimmer during the holiday season—it almost feels like angelic voices are serenading you as you walk down the street. In fact, you might not be imagining them. This winter season, there will be festive chanting by the Grace Chorale of Brooklyn (Dec. 19-20), readings and carols by the Dessoff Choirs (Dec. 5), folk songs by the Vienna Boys’ Choir (Dec. 20), candlelight tunes by Voices of Ascension (Dec. 9, 10, 14, and 15), and holiday songs from Cher and Mariah Carey by the New York City Gay Men’s Chorus, in “Yuletide Gay(er)” (Dec. 11-12).
“Messiah”s

Hark, is that the herald angels singing? Oh, wait, no, that’s just every choral group in New York—it’s “Messiah” season! The Oratorio Society will perform it for the hundred-and-fifty-second consecutive time, at Carnegie Hall (Dec. 21), while the New York Classical Players will bring it alive for their first, across the city and in New Jersey (Dec. 4-6). The Brooklyn Chamber Orchestra performs at St. Ann’s Church, featuring the New York Choral Society (Dec. 20)—in Brooklyn, obviously. The New York Philharmonic might take the cake, though—their performance includes one of the most aptly named soloists of the season, the countertenor John Holiday (Dec. 10-13). As Handel said, “Hallelujah!”

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/ai-data-center-const.headline: AI data center boom strains construction labor across the U.S.
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/ai-data-center-const.author: Jonathan Vanian

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump said last week that American companies will face a "tremendous tax" for building data centers outside of the U.S.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything," Trump said at the end of that week's major tech stock selloff.

Amid the nationwide public backlash against data centers and the ongoing market turmoil affecting the artificial intelligence industry itself, there's a more pressing problem with Trump's demand — a worker shortage.

Across the country, tech companies are already competing for a limited pool of electricians, plumbers and other skilled construction workers needed to erect the massive facilities powering the AI boom. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimates the construction industry needs to attract 349,000 net new workers in 2026 just to keep pace with demand.

The pressure is hitting home in Abilene, Texas, where thousands of workers have descended on the region to build massive data center projects. RV parks and temporary housing have expanded to accommodate the influx, while local homebuilders and contractors say they're losing skilled workers to data center jobs offering substantially higher pay.

For Abilene homebuilder Gene Lantrip, the boom has become what he calls "a two-edged sword." Data centers are bringing new business and residents to the city, while making it harder and more expensive to find the workers.

Skilled laborers have been flocking to Texas in droves since 2025 to construct massive data center facilities like the $500 billion Stargate Project for OpenAI, Oracle and Japan's SoftBank. The vast prairie surrounding Abilene is now adorned with mile-wide construction sites and a collection of RV parks and mobile homes to accommodate the region's new blue-collar residents.

Tech giants have pitched these gigantic data center facilities as necessary to train and run powerful foundation models. And because these tech firms want data center campuses to come online quickly, they've been luring construction workers around the U.S. with lavish pay packages to settle down in rural places like Richland Parish, Louisiana, which will be home to Meta's over $50 billion Hyperion data center.

Lantrip said "the economy of Abilene is great because of the data center" and he's busier than ever building houses to accommodate the multitude of new residents. But the overall cost and time to build homes is increasing due in part to having a smaller pool of workers to hire from, he said.

Scotty Wristen, an Abilene master electrician who works with Lantrip, said that some of his electricians decamped to work on AI data centers because of the better pay. Even the local commercial electrical companies in the area have lost workers to the AI data centers, he said.
"I know of one company that lost 42 guys in one day," Wristen said. "If I was young and didn't have a wife and kids, I would probably do it too, because they pay at least triple what I can pay."
Those jobs also include on-the-job training, sponsored by the tech companies.

To boost the supply of construction workers, tech giants like Meta, Google and Amazon are spending millions of dollars on training programs that place aspiring builders at data center sites for hands-on, paid experience. The ABC is currently partnering with Meta on the social media giant's $115 million American Workforce Academy, pitched as "a nationwide, unprecedented fast-track to a long-term career in a skilled trade."

Meta's training program has so far "attracted thousands of folks who want to get into construction and learn a trade and to eventually work in data centers," said Joel Thames, an ABC vice president of health safety, environment and workforce development.It's unclear what happens to towns like Abilene and the throng of data center construction workers once they finish building the facilities. Tech companies will have a tougher time initiating new data center buildouts in the U.S. following the midterm elections in which voters overwhelmingly supported various restrictions on data center related projects.

Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for a statewide data center moratorium until additional rules are in place giving residents more agency to determine whether new facilities should be built. For data center real estate developers like Anita Verma-Lallian, who has projects in Texas and Arizona, any restrictions placed on new initiatives may speed up the completion of the existing buildout.

"What's happened in my view, it's just going to make the demand even higher because the supply is going to be so much more constrained," Verma-Lallian, the CEO of Arizona Land Consulting, said. "We're going to see a rush to get those projects built and online as soon as possible."Verma-Lallian said that there is "going to be some uncertainty" for potential new data center projects in Texas due to any yet-to-be-known restrictions. She views Arizona as being a more favorable environment to data center development and noted that Democratic incumbent Governor Katie Hobbs is "fairly moderate on data centers." If data center construction eventually slows in places like Texas, Verma-Lallian said it's possible that the new labor diaspora "will go to other states or other projects."
WATCH: CNBC traveled to Abilene, Texas to see how the AI data center construction boom is impacting the local economy. CNBC's Jeniece Pettitt and Cameron Costa contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/costa-.headline: Costa Rica bars UN rapporteur on Palestinian territories from entering the country

paragraphs.text: Costa Rica barred entry to the UN special rapporteur on the Israel-occupied Palestinian territories, Francesca Albanese, earning the ire of the UN human rights chief.

Albanese, an Italian national, went to Costa Rica to receive an honorary doctorate from the University of Costa Rica. She was stopped at the airport in San José and not allowed to enter the country, and was transferred to a hotel before she travelled to Mexico on Saturday.

The UN human rights office said that Albanese was stopped from entering the country on “national security grounds”. Costa Rica’s migration office said that its decision was made after she was subject of an “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism.

The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, said that he was “deeply concerned” by the decision to deny Albanese entry. “This is difficult to reconcile with Costa Rica’s longstanding commitment to human rights,” said Türk.

Albanese shared a picture on X of an airport bench and her suitcase, where she was meant to stay the night. “Second night in the airport. Guarded by security at every step. Uncomfortable chairs. Noise. Bright light,” Albanese posted.

Albanese, who acts as an independent expert appointed by the UN human rights council, has been outspoken on Israeli abuses in Gaza and the West Bank. She has drawn ire from Israel and its allies for being one of the first, most prominent officials to accuse Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a claim Israel denies.

The US placed sanctions and revoked the visa of Albanese for her work on Palestine in the summer of 2025, cutting her off from the global financial system. The sanctions make daily life a struggle for Albanese, who has no access to western banks or credit cards.

Albanese called for an investigation into whether her denial of entry into Costa Rica was connected to the US sanctions, in remarks she made remotely at the ceremony for the acceptance of her honorary doctorate.

Costa Rica’s government, headed by the rightwing president, Laura Fernández, is close to the Trump administration and has cooperated with it on security and immigration issues. The government has also intensified its ties with Israel.
Israel’s envoy to the UN, Danny Danon, praised Costa Rica for its decision, accusing Albanese of using her UN position to spread propaganda against Israel.
On Saturday, Albanese was expected leave Costa Rica for Mexico, with the Italian embassy in Mexico working in advance of her visit to ensure there are no obstacles to her entry into the country.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.headline: Inside the L.A. library parking lot that has become a haven for homeless women
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.author: Audrey McGlinchy

paragraphs.text: They filed in when the gates opened at 8:30 p.m. — in a red Honda Fit, a white Dodge and a black van with the middle-row seats wrenched out to make way for a crib mattress and a make-do bed of blankets.
L.A. is a city where the crisis of homelessness is often framed in familiar snapshots: Tents under freeway overpasses and encampments along Skid Row. People sprawled and sun-baked on a sidewalk.

But in a city famous for its car culture, roughly 1 in 4 people experiencing homelessness lives in a vehicle. That amounts to roughly 11,600 people a night sleeping in cars, vans or RVs, according to a Times analysis of homelessness data.

In what has become a common response to vehicular homelessness, especially in California, nonprofits and government agencies have set aside parking lots throughout L.A. as sanctioned places for people to sleep in their cars. Santa Barbara is believed to have opened the first lot of its kind in 2004.
Most of these lots are open to the general population. But the one filling up on this Tuesday night was different. It was for women. Most of them arrived alone — two had children.

The lot is run by Safe Parking LA, a nonprofit that manages six of these spaces throughout the city. It is the largest provider of parking lots authorized for sleeping in L.A., according to one study.

In response to requests from women staying at some of their other lots, Safe Parking LA last year opened a women’s-only lot at a public library. Although women represent about a third of all homeless people in the L.A. area, they make up nearly half of the total count of people living out of cars, vans or RVs, according to a survey published in 2022.

As they rolled through the gate, each woman pulled up a digital permit on her phone, but most didn’t need to. A woman named Jasmin greeted each by name and asked them to sign in. In total, 15 cars would park there this night.
People living in their cars in L.A. report higher rates of employment than the general population experiencing homelessness.
But like much of California, L.A. is expensive — and it doesn’t take a lot for some people to find themselves struggling.
“I see myself outside of it sometimes,” Lisa Sellers said of her current situation. “Like I’m observing it.”

Sellers moved to L.A. eight years ago to pursue acting after working as a celebrity stylist. But since the pandemic, acting and production work has been hard to come by. Especially, she said, since so many auditions have moved to self-tapes and her car makes for a lousy setup.

Nights at this parking lot — The Times is not publishing the exact location because of safety concerns for some of the women — are generally tranquil. In the daytime, the construction site bordering the lot shudders to life.
The excavation seems to be rousting rats, which skitter into the lot at night. When Sellers gets out of her car to use the bathroom, she stomps her feet to make sure no rats get close.
Before Sellers started sleeping in her SUV, she’d rented a one-bedroom apartment in the Baldwin Hills/Crenshaw neighborhood for almost seven years. It had a small patio where she liked to drink tea.

But after suffering years of extreme fatigue, debilitating headaches and skin lesions, she began attributing her health problems to what she said was mold in the walls and gases released from a broken sewer line.

She alerted her landlord and several city departments, but little was fixed, she said, and the health problems persisted. She ended up in the hospital last year and never went back to living in her apartment.
Some of the other women who arrived at the lot this night have pets.

Just before 9 p.m, Old Man escaped from a white Toyota Corolla. The 12-year-old orange cat is one of two that Lynn, a woman in her 50s, lives with in her car. (Because of the stigma associated with homelessness, The Times agreed to withhold the last names of Lynn and another woman interviewed for this article.)

Lynn had been living with her father when, she said, she learned he’d been coaxed into taking out a mortgage after having paid the previous one off. While she tried to find legal help, she was also struggling with medical problems, including nerve damage and fatigue.
When she couldn’t sort out the financial problem with the house, it was foreclosed on. Lynn moved out in 2023. She spent a large chunk of her savings on hotels before moving into her car full time.
Lynn grabbed the cats’ water trough from behind the front seat and used a hand-washing station to refill it. The other side of the back seat floor was taken up by the litter box.
She’s been sleeping at the women’s parking lot most nights since late August.
As a regular, she takes note of who is parked one night and gone the next.
“It does bum me out when I see the cars return night after night,” she said. “[But] when you don’t see a car return, you just hope nothing happened to them.”
Making sure nothing happens to them is part of Alma Falcon‘s job.

Falcon is a caseworker for Safe Parking LA. She arrived at the lot around 8 p.m., as she does every Tuesday, so she can meet with some of the women in person. She brings pamphlets about housing providers or job training programs.
Falcon calls the women who sleep at this lot “the girls.”
She started her career at 19, working in a drug rehab center on the weekends.

She went on to work in an adult rehab center and with survivors of domestic violence. But, she said, some of the first people she ever worked with were girls and maybe, in her mind, they’ve always stayed that way.

By 9 p.m., many of the women were getting ready for bed. One parked next to Lynn flossed her teeth while standing behind the open back door of her SUV. Another changed into leopard-print-and-black pajamas.
For some at this lot, it’s their first time experiencing homelessness. That’s true for many people who end up living in their cars.

Sandy had been homeless once before, she said, for a couple of months in the 1990s. This time, she’s been homeless since the summer, when she had a falling-out with her half sister, whose house she was living in.
Now Sandy lives out of her white sedan with six cats: Midnight, Mino, Marvel, Cupid, Toothless and Sebastian.

Sandy is 64 but looks younger, her voice wistful. A blood disorder keeps her platelet count low and tires her quickly, making it hard to work, she said. She keeps a plastic tray of medications in her glove compartment.

Many shelters or other forms of temporary housing don’t accept people with more than one pet, so Sandy and Lynn have had a harder time finding a way out of their cars. For Sandy, giving up her cats is a nonstarter.

At 10 p.m., she grabbed her toothbrush and a bottle of water and headed to one of the portable toilets. Later, she said, she’ll lie down in the passenger seat of her car and watch YouTube videos on her phone before falling asleep. She’s learning French.
“My heart is to live in France,” she said.

Across the lot, a frangipani bush with its waxy leaves and fragrant flowers sprouted between two rows of parking. One woman walked between the cars, offering up cinnamon muffins she picked up at a discount — $4 for four.
She soon settled into her van on a bed of blankets, floor insulation and a crib mattress. It was close to 11 p.m.
Aside from the light poles, which dim at night, the parking lot at this hour was lighted by the bank next door.
A man rattled the locked gates of the parking lot, yelling about whether the library was open so he could check out a book.
Seated in the driver’s seat of her car, Sellers ticked through photos on her laptop of the apartment she says made her sick. She’s trying to see if there’s a legal case to pursue.
After leaving her apartment, Sellers crashed with friends but eventually moved into her car full time. She’s been using the lot run by Safe Parking LA since June.

She got some relief this past summer when she was invited to teach a course at the Vogue College of Fashion in New York City. Sellers said she was able to stay with extended family and friends and rented a shared apartment for a couple of weeks.
Back in L.A., she’s been working part time at a nonprofit. She picks up small jobs where she can, including a gig moving audience members around at the Grammys earlier this year.
Although Sellers has an income, it’s unstable. She’s not sure she’d qualify for a lease on a new place. Plus she has expenses to consider, such as paying for gas.
“Even living in your car costs money,” she said.
Jennifer Perez was in the first hour of her shift as the security guard for the parking lot, where she’s worked since it opened.

While she watched over the women, Perez’s two daughters were asleep at home. She makes $18 an hour, while her husband — who operates a lift in a Whole Foods warehouse — earns a couple of dollars more.
It’s enough to afford the $2,300-a-month rent on their apartment in Huntington Park, she said, but “I’m still struggling.”
Perez has a front seat at the lot to who stays and who goes. She remembers a mother with her 4-year-old daughter, the same age as Perez’s youngest, who stayed at the lot earlier in the year.
Perez said she heard the woman moved into an apartment in April after several months at the lot. But there’s always a sense of mystery when someone stops showing up.
“I do wonder, like, what happened?” she said around midnight. She wrapped a blanket around herself and settled into the front seat of her car.
Just past 4:30 a.m., Sandy drove toward the gates with her lights off, so as not to wake anyone.

She likes to get up early to avoid traffic. On Tuesdays and Wednesdays, she drives to the technical school where she’s taking classes and sleeps for a couple more hours in the parking lot there before carrying her toothbrush in her bag to the bathroom.
Other mornings she goes to the park.
She knocked on Perez’s window to ask her to open the gate.
Around 5:30 a.m. the sky started to lighten and another car left. Over the next hour and a half, the women woke, used the portable toilets and drove through the lot’s gates.
Just past 7 a.m., Lynn headed to a car wash down the road to vacuum up any spilled cat litter.
The lot closes to the women at 7:30 a.m. Sellers, who likes to sleep as late as she can, was the last to leave.
The lot would open again for the women that night, just like it does every night.

This article is part of The Times’ equity reporting initiative, funded by the James Irvine Foundation, exploring the challenges facing low-income workers and the efforts being made to address California’s economic divide.

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/berkshire-utility-wi.headline: Billions on the line for Berkshire utility as Oregon's high court reviews wildfire claims
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/berkshire-utility-wi.author: Alex Crippen

paragraphs.text: (This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Billions on the line as Oregon's high court reviews wildfire claims

Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp and attorneys for thousands of plaintiffs are welcoming a decision by Oregon's Supreme Court to widen its review of a 2023 lower court trial in which a jury awarded more than one billion in damages over four wildfires in 2020.
The jury found the utility negligently failed to shut down power lines during a powerful windstorm, allowing its equipment to contribute to the fires.

In April, a state appellate court overturned that verdict, ruling the trial judge incorrectly told jurors evidence presented at the trial, which directly involved a small number of claimants, applied to a class of thousands of other plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs appealed that decision to the Oregon Court of Appeals Court where oral arguments focused on the jury instructions.

But now the state's top court will consider all the objections to the original trial that have been raised by both sides, including whether the judge should have allowed it to be a class action suit to begin with.
If the plaintiffs prevail, PacifiCorp could face tens of billions of dollars in damage claims.
If the utility wins, all the litigation could go back to square one.
Either side could potentially try to take the case to the U.S. Supreme Court.
In a news release, a PacifiCorp official says, "We are encouraged by the Court's decision to undertake a complete review of this litigation."
"The Court recognizes the litany of missteps in this case, and we remain confident that sound legal principles and facts will prevail."

Law firms representing the plaintiffs are quoted as saying in a statement, "We are grateful the Supreme Court has accepted the survivors' request for expanded review, and look forward to the Supreme Court's decision."
The court asked for additional written arguments by mid-January and scheduled oral arguments for early April.
Berkshire's Bending Spoon buys were negotiated in five-minute phone calls
Under Warren Buffett as CEO, Berkshire Hathaway would often rapidly close deals, sometimes with just a handshake to start, and no due diligence.
It appears that hasn't changed, at least in the case of the company's now almost $1.4 billion atypical investment in Italy's Bending Spoons.
Barron's is highlighting a post on X with what looks like cell phone video of the company's CEO speaking in Italian to a European audience.

According to the provided translation, Luca Ferrari said both Berkshire's $600 million purchase of shares in the Bending Spoons July IPO, and a subsequent $330 million investment in August, were the result of phone calls lasting no more than five minutes each with Berkshire portfolio manager Ted Weschler.

Ferrari also praised Berkshire for not making any changes to the company's proposed investment contract, saying it was "the only time in my life" a counterparty had not tried to "get something more" after the initial agreement.
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Buffett on what is important and what is knowable (1998)
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger explain why they focus on what certain companies will look like over the long term instead of trying to make predictions about where the economy is headed.
AUDIENCE MEMBER: I have two questions.
Question one: your view on the world financial business environment in the next decade.
Question two — (laughter) — U.S. position for economic competition in the next decade. Thank you.
WARREN BUFFETT: Well, you've asked two big questions, but you're going to get very small answers, I'm afraid. (Laughter)
And that's no disrespect. But we — we just — we don't have that. We don't think about those things very much.
We just are looking for decent businesses. And incidentally, our views in the past wouldn't have been any good on those subjects.
We try to think about two things. We try to think about things that are important and things that are knowable.
Now, there are things that are important that are not knowable. In our view, those two questions that you raised fall in that.
There are things that are knowable but not important. We don't want to clutter our minds up with those.
So we say, "What is important and what is knowable?" And what among the things that fall within those two categories can we translate into some kind of an action that is useful for Berkshire.
And we really — there are all kinds of important subjects that Charlie and I, we don't know anything about, and therefore we don't think about them.
So we have — our view about what the world will look like over the next ten years in business or competitive situations, we're just no good.

We do think we know something about what Coca-Cola's going to look like in ten years, or what Gillette's going to look like in ten years, or what Disney's going to look like in ten years, or what some of our operating subsidiaries are going to look like in ten years.
We care a lot about that. We think a lot about that. We want to be right about that.
If we're right about that, the other things get to be — you know, they're just — they're less important. And if we started focusing on those, we would miss a lot of big things.

I've used this example before, but Coca-Cola went public in, I think, it was 1919. And the first year, one share cost $40. The first year, it went down a little over 50 percent. At the end of the year, it was down to $19. There were some problems with bottler contracts. There's problems with sugar. Various kinds of problems.
If you'd had perfect foresight, you would have seen the world's greatest depression staring you in the face, when the social order even got questioned.
You would have seen World War II. You would have seen atomic bombs and hydrogen bombs. You would have seen all kinds of things.

And you could always find a reason to postpone why you should buy that share of Coca-Cola. But the important thing wasn't to see that. The important thing was to see they were going to be selling a billion eight-ounce servings of beverages a day this year. Or some large number.
And that the person who could make people happy a billion times a day around the globe ought to make a few bucks off doing it.

And so that $40, which went down to $19, I think with dividends reinvested, has to be well over $5 million now. And if you developed a view on these other subjects that in any way forestalled you acting on this more important, specific narrow view about the future of the company, you would have missed a great ride. So that's the kind of thing we focus on.
Charlie?
CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah, we're not predicting the currents that will come, just how some things will swim in the currents, whatever they are.

latimes.com/science/story/2026-11-28/rac.headline: The race for control of NASA's JPL is on
latimes.com/science/story/2026-11-28/rac.author: Noah Haggerty, Corinne Purtill

paragraphs.text: In late October, representatives from more than two dozen companies and universities met with NASA officials on the campus of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in La Cañada Flintridge to discuss the possibility of taking control of the famed space science center — which up until now has been managed solely by the California Institute of Technology.

Alongside Caltech were academic heavy hitters including the University of California, Texas A&M and USC. The group also included companies that run massive labs for the Department of Energy and a cadre of NASA subcontractors deeply familiar with JPL’s inner workings.

The prospect of ending Caltech’s $31-million-per-year management contract follows the termination of a flagship JPL mission to retrieve dust and rock samples from the surface of Mars. Elimination of the program, which was plagued by delays and billions in cost overruns, triggered multiple rounds of grueling layoffs.

Despite this, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman insisted the decision to put control of JPL out to bid was not a direct response to concerns over Caltech’s management. “NASA, since I’ve taken over as administrator, has put several major projects in the hands of the JPL team, which I think speaks to our confidence,” he said. “So, it’s theirs to lose.”

NASA’s hiring of a new manager would topple Caltech’s 90-year reign over the Southern California institution — a period that spans the lab’s founding on Halloween in 1936, the launch of America’s first satellite in 1958, the first successful U.S. spacecraft landings on the moon and Mars in 1966 and 1976 and the first human-made probe to enter interstellar space in 2012.
Beyond Caltech, three of the organizations that attended JPL in late October have publicly expressed interest in submitting a formal bid so far: USC, Texas A&M and Associated Universities Inc.

“We have the greatest respect for Caltech and what they have done over the last number of decades with JPL. They’re a tremendous research university,” USC President Beong-Soo Kim said recently. “This is not something, frankly, that we would have considered had the federal government not indicated that this was something that they were open to.”

Texas A&M, which helps run multiple Department of Energy science and nuclear facilities, is also considering submitting a bid. “NASA’s work at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory is closely aligned with areas where the Texas A&M System has significant strength and growing momentum,” a spokesperson said in a statement to The Times. “We are always interested in opportunities that align with our capabilities and serve the nation.”

AUI, a nonprofit that was established in 1946 by nine Northeastern universities to operate a Department of Energy laboratory in New York, confirmed to The Times it was exploring a bid as well.
