It operates the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, with telescopes across the United States and in Chile, for the National Science Foundation.

The University of California also sent senior leadership members who oversee work with Department of Energy labs, according to public documents, but did not respond to repeated inquiries from The Times.

Battelle Memorial Institute, an Ohio-based nonprofit that serves on the management team for seven Department of Energy labs, sent its vice president for business development and strategic growth to the October meeting, but declined to comment on whether it was considering submitting a bid.

One of the several smaller NASA subcontractors that attended told The Times it had no plans to submit a bid. In bidding competitions for large labs, it’s typical for subcontractors whose work depends on the outcome to provide input during the process.
Caltech does not plan to give up the country’s vanguard of planetary exploration easily.

“The close and enduring partnership among Caltech, JPL and NASA has served America’s preeminence in space exploration remarkably well and continues to do so,” Caltech’s 10th president, Ray Jayawardhana, said as he prepared for his inauguration last month. “I think the value proposition of that partnership is unparalleled and continues to deliver tremendous returns for the nation.”

The competition for control is still in its early stages: NASA has been meeting with interested parties and deciding what exactly it will ask of potential contractors. Bidders, meanwhile, will have to decide whether to enter the race on their own or join forces with other institutions to make a more competitive proposal.

“It’s been under Caltech’s management since essentially inception,“ NASA’s Isaacman said. “From time to time, it’s very helpful to have some amount of competition and see if there’s ways you can improve.”

USC is still weighing whether to submit a solo bid or team up with other interested institutions. AUI, meanwhile, is actively exploring partnerships with other potential bidders. With experience managing large arrays of telescopes, a spokesperson said the nonprofit is particularly interested in bringing its expertise to NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international system of antennas operated by JPL to communicate with space probes — and humans — traveling far from Earth.

NASA plans to officially issue a request for proposals on running JPL in early 2027. Those proposals are expected to be due in late in the year, with NASA selecting a winner in early 2028. Should Caltech lose, the change would occur in October 2028.

While putting the management of a key NASA field center out to competitive bidding is unprecedented, there are examples of it happening at other government labs — most notably at the Department of Energy, where universities and companies have lost long-standing contracts.

Unlike other NASA facilities, JPL was forged by the U.S. War Department in the run-up to World War II. It was part of a larger strategy where the department tapped universities around the country to set up massive research labs for the development of missiles and atomic bombs.
After the war, the department passed many of these university-run labs over to peacetime agencies. JPL went to NASA. The nuclear labs primarily ended up under the Energy Department.
In the decades since, many Department of Energy labs have changed hands through competitions.

For example, the University of California ran Los Alamos National Laboratory in New Mexico for decades. After a series of safety and security incidents — including missing computer disks with classified information and a laser incident that injured an intern — the Department of Energy decided to open the contract for bidding in 2003. The University of California ultimately teamed up with other companies to successfully win control. Today, it is managed by the University of California, Texas A&M and Battelle Memorial Institute.
The government’s competitive procurement process is not a trivial one.

“It’s expensive for the government; it’s expensive for the bidders. It can cost millions of dollars to put together a really good proposal,” said Allison Bawden, managing director of natural resources and environment at the U.S. Government Accountability Office who has studied Department of Energy contract competitions.

Yet, “if you want to see a different type of performance from the contractor or you’re looking for the scope of your work to change,” she said, “just doing a modification of a contract might not get you there.”
Caltech does enjoy a home-field advantage, though, when it comes to managing JPL.

“Caltech, they have the advantage first of all in history, but also of proximity,” said Peter Westwick, a history professor at USC who is not involved in the university’s deliberations on a potential bid. “Anybody who beats them out is going to have to overcome both of those.”

Though USC’s main campus in South Los Angeles is roughly 10 miles farther from JPL than Caltech in Pasadena is, USC boasts closer proximity to the epicenter of Southern California’s aerospace industry in South Bay and Long Beach, including SpaceX in Hawthorne, Kim said.

“If NASA is going to take a different direction, we want to do everything that we can to ensure that Southern California remains central to this new space economy,” he said. “USC is almost ideally situated to help keep that talent in the Southern California region.”
Caltech, however, has managed to stave off existential threats to the lab before.

In the 1980s, the Reagan administration proposed slashing the planetary science missions that had become JPL’s bread and butter. When NASA Administrator James Beggs said such cuts would make JPL “surplus to our needs,” well-connected Caltech leaders convinced Congress and the White House to keep funding Galileo, JPL’s flagship mission at the time to explore Jupiter’s atmosphere.
And even after the loss of the Mars Sample Return mission, JPL managed to restore some faith through the launch of the Roman Space Telescope, which came in ahead of schedule and on budget.

“Caltech is a singular institution that is — across sciences and engineering — preeminent nationally and globally,” Jayawardhana said. “We do very much treasure JPL as a critical element of this ecosystem.”
Times staff writer Jaweed Kaleem contributed to this report.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.headline: Fewer endorsements leave labor in unusual position at start of Becerra era
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.author: Taryn Luna

paragraphs.text: SACRAMENTO — During his election night victory speech in Sacramento, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra held up an orange campaign shirt made by the laborers union.
“LiUNA in the house,” he said to cheers from members of the Laborers’ International Union of North America in California. “I told you they were in the house.”
California’s 41st governor didn’t mention that the laborers were in fact the only union in his house from the start of his campaign.
In a turbulent 2026 gubernatorial race, organized labor had two chances to endorse Becerra when he needed support before the June primary. Most unions blew both opportunities.

Now for the first time in at least a generation, a Democratic governor will take office with significant independence from the most powerful unions — and most other major interest groups — in California.

“He has an opportunity that no other Democratic governor has had in decades,” said Dan Schnur, who teaches political communication at USC and UC Berkeley. “If Becerra wanted to, he would have the freedom to chart a much more independent course than Democratic governors normally have.”
California’s Democratic governors and unions are typically coupled in a powerful political marriage that starts long before election day.

Unions exercise their power by sending legions of workers to knock on doors and canvas for the candidates they endorse and whose values align with their priorities. Endorsements from the biggest unions, such as SEIU California State Council, the California Teachers Assn. and the top unions within the California Federation of Labor, can come with six, or seven-figure political contributions.
Once in office, governors often remember the support and open their doors when union leaders come knocking.

Teachers announced their support for then-candidate Gavin Newsom more than seven months before the 2018 gubernatorial primary. One of his first moves in office was to champion new charter school transparency rules that they had failed to pass for years. Charter school advocates had also spent millions supporting his opponent Antonio Villaraigosa, the former L.A. mayor, which irked Newsom.

For unions, a governor’s help is often critical to push politically thorny policies through the state Legislature and pressure waffling lawmakers to support a bill. For public-sector unions who negotiate union contracts with the governor’s administration, a close relationship can be particularly beneficial to their members.

To the crowded field of Democratic candidates competing in June, public support from powerful unions was seen as a way to lift them out of the pack in the primary and build momentum for their campaigns.

But picking a candidate from among nearly a dozen Democrats with few policy distinctions between them proved unusually challenging for even the most seasoned political operations. The last time there was no clear front-runner in a California gubernatorial primary was in 1998, when former Gov. Gray Davis came from behind in polls.
The California Federation of Labor endorsed four candidates in March. None were Becerra.

After picking Rep. Eric Swalwell before he was accused of sexual assault and dropped out, the California Teachers Assn. settled on billionaire Tom Steyer for its do-over choice because of his promise to raise revenue, including for schools, by increasing taxes on commercial properties, colloquially known as split-roll.

SEIU California backed Swalwell first and then made a safe dual endorsement of Steyer and Becerra. The split support, though it benefited him more than the others, still limited Becerra’s ability to take full advantage of the union’s backing at a time when he was grossly overmatched in fundraising against Steyer, who spent more than $200 million of his own wealth on his campaign.
“Most of labor tried to be for what they thought was going to happen, and they were wrong,” said Rob Stutzman, a Republican political consultant. “None of it panned out.”
The missed opportunity leaves most of labor in an unfamiliar place at the start of the Becerra era: with their hat in hand.
It’s unclear if Becerra will hold a grudge.
Davis still recalls who had his back early and who did not.

“No one is going to fault you for remembering people who helped you in your time of need,” Davis said. “The question is, can you do it in a way that’s fair, that’s transparent, and that doesn’t block more compelling ideas coming from groups that may not have been for you, but came up with a better public policy solution.”
Every gubernatorial transition creates anxiety in Sacramento as interest groups try figure out a new governor, their leadership style and who is in and out of their inner circle.
Stutzman and others doubt that Becerra will turn his back on workers. The incoming governor has a track record of supporting unions and has close relationships with individual local union leaders.

In his election night speech, he described himself as a new sheriff in town with a “law degree and a union card.” He worked as a laborer in college with the same union his father was a member of for 40 years.

That kinship inspired the California State Council of Laborers to endorse Becerra in November 2025 when he was polling in the low single digits. Most other labor organizations jumped on board after he won the primary and he didn’t need their help to trounce his Republican challenger Steve Hilton in the November election

“Xavier was raised on a labor’s pension, a laborer salary,” said Joseph Cruz, the executive director of the laborers. “He understands what our membership’s lives look like every single day. He was family to us, and that was one of the big reasons why we endorsed him. But also because he lived that life, he knew how to connect to my leadership.”
That support proved prescient. When Swalwell dropped out of the race in April, Becerra almost immediately began climbing in public opinion polls.

“I got my guys together and said, “Hey, we’re never going to see this opportunity again in our lifetime where we endorse the candidate at 1 or 2%, who’s a laborer, who now has enough to have a chance,’” Cruz said. “Did he have a clear path to victory? Of course not. But he was in the race at that point.”

The laborers formed an independent expenditure committee in late April with the California Primary Care Assn., another early Becerra backer. The union put in $2 million to start, with another $450,000 before the primary, according to campaign finance filings.

Newsom’s political consultants, Bearstar Strategies, dropped a pro-Swalwell independent expenditure committee and started working with the group supporting Becerra. Several people who worked on Swalwell’s campaign also took jobs with Becerra.

Before the primary, the committee supporting Becerra received big donations from the California Assn. of Realtors, the Pechanga Band of Indians, California Medical Assn., electrical workers, Airbnb and Meta.

California campaign finance law limits the amount of money candidates can directly receive from donors. Supporters can provide unlimited funding to outside independent expenditure committees, also known as political action committees or PACs, that cannot coordinate their spending with the candidates.

Meanwhile, the California Chamber of Commerce, PG&E, Realtors, developers and other business interests continued to funnel a total of $37 million to a never-Steyer committee run by Jim Deboo, a Democratic political consultant and former chief of staff to Newsom. Though the committee was formed to oppose Steyer, hitting his billionaire opponent helped Becerra. In early May, they ran their first ad contrasting the two candidates in support of Becerra.
In comparison, before the primary SEIU-affiliated local unions individually gave Becerra $137,200.

Jennifer Barerra, the chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said her organization opposed Steyer because he campaigned against the business community and made promises that would place more costs and burdens on companies, such as increasing commercial property taxes and enacting single-payer healthcare.

Shortly after the primary, the Chamber made a historic step and endorsed Becerra, the first Democratic governor to win the support of the powerful business group, which often declines to weigh into the race at all.
Becerra expressed a desire to work with the business community, she said, instead of viewing them as an enemy.
“Feeling like a partner and extending a hand versus pointing a finger and blaming them for all the faults of California definitely resonated with the members,” Barerra said.
The incoming governor’s support, and lack thereof, is fueling hope that more advocacy groups will be included at the start of his administration compared with the early days of Newsom’s governorship.

Newsom received strong support from the labor movement and walked into office with a series of progressive policy commitments to make good on that unions helped him push. Over time, Newsom’s positions shifted more moderate and his relationship with the business community improved even as he remained close to labor unions, such as SEIU and CTA.

“It’s very different to start in this place, where I feel like we have a better seat at the table now with Newsom, so to speak, but I think we’re starting in that position with Becerra,” Barerra said.

The unusual dynamics in the race allowed Becerra to cruise to victory in November without making the same kinds of liberal promises to interest groups. But the proposals he has endorsed suggest the governor-elect’s agenda could naturally align with some labor priorities.

In a CNN debate in May, Becerra indicated that he would restore Newsom’s cuts to healthcare coverage for undocumented immigrants, which has included adding premiums for care and freezing enrollment to rein in soaring costs. He has since said he needs to see the state’s balance sheet first.

The Democratic governor-elect also endorsed a concept SEIU has been pushing to penalize large corporations that do not offer affordable healthcare for full-time workers. Though the details of the plan are yet-to-be seen, the idea is to target corporations whose low-income workers continue to receive care through Medi-Cal, forcing taxpayers to pick up the tab.
Becerra also offered what appeared to be an olive branch to the teachers this month.

He named Teri Holloman, the associate executive director of governmental relations for the California Teachers Assn., as his appointments director for his transition into office. The post gives the teachers’ political strategist, a veteran Sacramento operator, an influential role in filling positions on state boards, commissions, departments and agencies in the new governor’s administration.
Christian Grose, a professor of political science and public policy at USC, described Becerra as a leader who will want to work with groups across the political spectrum.
Politicians, he said, also have long memories and there could be some lasting damage for unions that didn’t back him, creating opportunities for others.

“He’s going to also be working with more corporate aligned political advocacy groups, and I actually think some of the more center-left and center-right lobbyists in Sacramento are excited about somebody who wasn’t endorsed extensively by unions,” Grose said.

latimes.com/science/story/2026-11-28/wha.headline: What's next for Southern California's native-born sea turtles?
latimes.com/science/story/2026-11-28/wha.author: Corinne Purtill

paragraphs.text: They scuttled to the water under cover of night, instinctively orienting toward the brightest light on the horizon.

Juiced up on nutrients from their yolk sacs, the tiny olive ridley sea turtles crawled with frantic intensity away from the humans who kept watch over their eggs and down the sandy slopes. Then the first gentle wave washed over them, and whoosh — they were gone.

From the moment a surprise nest of olive ridley sea turtle eggs appeared Sept. 16 on Seal Beach, no one was sure if that clutch of eggs, or a second laid on Huntington Beach three days later, would actually result in turtles.

To the best of anyone’s knowledge, no sea turtle of any species had ever attempted to nest on the U.S. West Coast. No one knew whether the eggs were fertilized, or whether conditions hundreds of miles north of their usual nesting grounds were fit for turtle development.
The answers turned out to be yes.
So far, about 100 hatchlings from 208 eggs laid in Orange County and incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific have been released into the Pacific Ocean.

Now that the first class of native-born California sea turtles has taken to the water, biologists are processing the lessons of this year’s turtle boom and wondering whether this year’s nests are a one-time phenomenon or a sign of things to come.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which has jurisdiction over sea turtles on land, has been clear that the decision to move the Orange County nests to the safety of the Long Beach aquarium won’t necessarily be policy for future nests.
Without intervention, high tides in late September would have destroyed both nests. Given the unprecedented circumstances, federal biologists made a last-minute call to save them.
“That situation was atypical, and the Service will individually assess each instance of turtle nesting in California,” a spokesperson said via email.

The service opted not to move a third olive ridley nest that appeared Nov. 1 on San Buenaventura State Beach in Ventura, after determining that local waters at hatch time would be too cold for baby turtle survival. (Mean December ocean temperatures hover around 58 degrees Fahrenheit in Ventura and 82 degrees in Ostional, Costa Rica, one of the world’s largest olive ridley nesting sites.)

High tides in mid-November swamped the nest and exposed the eggs, which were already incubating in sand significantly colder than the species’ usual nesting grounds and thus unlikely to produce hatchlings. Federal biologists removed and destroyed them.
Both approaches — targeted interventions, and letting nature take its course — are used at sea turtle nesting sites, biologists said.

“Nest relocation, supervised incubation and biologist-assisted hatchling release is common practice around the world on sea turtle nesting beaches and it’s been one of the conservation strategies that has helped sea turtles avoid population crashes in several cases,” said Lindsey Peavey Reeves, a senior scientist with the National Marine Sanctuary Foundation who has studied olive ridleys in the eastern Pacific Ocean for 20 years. “This kind of human intervention is not unusual for sea turtles, just for Southern California.”

Aquarium staff decided to keep interference to a minimum during incubation. The eggs stayed in the same styrofoam coolers they’d been gently packed in on the beach. Apart from swapping the opaque lids for transparent acrylic ones, and installing 24/7 infrared camera systems, the eggs were left largely untouched in their climate-controlled nursery.

“The eggs didn’t give us a lot of feedback on how it was going, so up until when the sand started sinking, we had no idea how well the incubation went,” said Dr. Lance Adams, the aquarium’s director of veterinary services. “I felt like a kid waiting for my birthday to come. It seemed to take forever but then happened fast and was over.”
As of Nov. 23, 107 unhatched eggs remained at the Aquarium of the Pacific. Olive ridleys have a 45- to 60-day incubation period. Nov. 18 marked 60 days since the second of the two nests was laid.
Although additional hatching is still possible, few sea turtle nests have a 100% hatch rate.

Sea turtles produce large clutches of eggs in order to “hedge their bets” that at least some will survive to maturity and produce offspring of their own, Peavey Reeves said. Eggs are often poached by predators in the wild, or destroyed when erosion sweeps away the sand covering them.

“Even with perfect nest environment conditions you can still have sea turtle embryos that begin to develop in the egg and then die prematurely,” said Pamela Plotkin, a retired oceanography professor at Texas A&M University. “You can also have eggs that were not fertilized to begin with and have no embryo development inside.”
Two big questions remain: Will there be more sea turtles on Southern California beaches, and will the first turtles released into these waters return someday to lay eggs of their own?
“I know uncertainty and ‘to be determined’ is not satisfying ... but it’s the reality,” Peavey Reeves said.

The nests appeared amid extraordinary climate conditions. An extreme marine heat wave and a strong El Niño pushed Southern California early autumn water temperatures closer to those of the turtles’ typical nesting grounds.
“If this super El Niño year created once-off conditions for olive ridleys to nest in Southern California, we may not see this behavior again for at least several years,” Peavey Reeves said.
But the extent of the olive ridley’s northward migration may be even larger than previously believed.
Earlier this month, a member of the public discovered the remnants of a turtle nest on a beach in Carpinteria in Santa Barbara County, nearly 100 miles north of the Seal Beach nest.

Analysis at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County determined that the eggs were just days away from hatching when they were destroyed by erosion or some other disturbance, herpetology curator Greg Pauly said, and probably were laid even earlier than those in Orange County.

“What this Carpinteria nest is telling us is that in some situations [in Southern California] we do have conditions that will allow the embryos to fully develop” without human intervention, Pauly said.

It will be 12 to 15 years before any surviving females from the hatchlings released this fall are old enough to reproduce. Female sea turtles of all species typically return to nest on the same beach where they were born. It’s not known for certain how they pull off this navigational feat after thousands of miles of lifetime migration. Evidence suggests that sensory data and cues from the Earth’s magnetic field play a role.

First they must beat formidable odds. Just 1 in 1,000 sea turtle hatchlings survives to adulthood, according to the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Already, some of the Orange County hatchlings almost certainly have fallen prey to fish or seabirds.
But anything can happen out there in the sea. There is always a chance that some will defy the odds, survive into adulthood and make their way back to Orange County to lay eggs of their own.

latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-11-2.headline: Oil-rich Saudi Arabia bets on futuristic luxury cars to build an EV industry
latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-11-2.author: Nabih Bulos

paragraphs.text: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — In the quest to become an EV powerhouse, you’d be hard pressed to find a less likely candidate than Saudi Arabia. After all, the country’s lifeblood is oil and combustion engines’ global thirst for it; going electric seems akin to a candy maker switching to fruits.

Yet on a pleasantly warm October evening in Diriyah, an enclave that qualifies as Beverly Hills to Riyadh’s L.A., a gaggle of curious Saudi men and women paced around and snapped selfies in front of two futuristic-looking cars — the first in the kingdom’s bid to develop its own homegrown electric vehicle industry.

The cars, dubbed Exobot, are the first products of the Saudi automotive startup Ceer, a joint venture launched four years ago between the country’s sovereign Public Investment Fund and Taiwanese electronics manufacturer Foxconn. (BMW is also providing key components.)

Beyond the two fully electric cars on display, a sedan and an SUV, the plan is to eventually offer five more vehicles in Ceer’s portfolio by the end of the decade, and branch out into hybrid and combustion engines.
The expectation is that Ceer will draw $150 million in foreign direct investment, create up to 30,000 direct and indirect jobs, and contribute $8 billion to Saudi Arabia’s GDP by 2034.

That ambition is of a piece with Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s plan to hedge against a post-fossil-fuel future, and transform Saudi Arabia into a commanding presence in the realms of tech, entertainment, tourism and advanced manufacturing.

It’s not the first time Saudi Arabia has forayed into EVs. In 2018, it bought a 5% stake in Tesla before selling it a year later. Also in 2018, the Public Investment Fund plowed money into Lucid Motors, a U.S.-based EV manufacturer, eventually becoming its largest shareholder and opening a factory in the kingdom.
But Ceer goes further than those investments, with the aim of becoming the kingdom’s first original equipment manufacturer. It aims to make almost half of its components locally by 2034.

“Most countries import EV transition, but Saudi Arabia is manufacturing it and building on the strong financial capabilities that they have,” said Joseph Salem, a senior partner specializing in travel, transport and hospitality at the consulting firm Arthur D. Little Middle East.
“The investments today go well beyond selling cars, but also into factories, supplying and charging,” he said.

Walt Madeira, a principal analyst for vehicle forecasting at S&P Global Mobility, compared Ceer to other national automotive manufacturers, such as Turkey’s Togg or Malaysia’s Proton, as opposed to countries like Morocco, which convinced foreign carmakers to manufacture in local factories and export to Europe.
“Saudi Arabia has very ambitious plans. They’re serious in developing the ecosystem,” Madeira said.

The Exobots’ debut arrives at a pivotal moment. Soaring gas prices, spurred by the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran, have energized the global market for EVs and hybrids, with almost a third of cars sold worldwide expected to be electric, according to the International Energy Agency’s Global EV Outlook report this year.

That trend holds for the Middle East, where electric car sales in 2025 reached approximately 75,000 units, a 40% expansion compared with the year before, with the United Arab Emirates representing roughly half of regional demand.

Saudi Arabia remains a relative minnow: EV sales reached 9.2% in the country, according to a November report from Focus2Move, a Rome-based mobility research firm. And though forecasters say the Iran war and the kingdom’s fight with Yemen’s Houthis are hurting demand, the expectation is it will grow quickly.

Though the trends are enticing for any EV aspirant, Ceer enters a market where the bull in the china shop is — ahem — China, with Beijing-backed automakers decimating the bottom lines of storied brands with cheap yet innovative offerings.
And because Chinese automakers are building more cars than China’s market can take, they’ve made strong inroads abroad, including in the Middle East.

The International Energy Agency reported that BYD, China’s largest automaker, accounted for roughly 60% of Middle Eastern EV sales last year; Tesla by contrast got only 15%. Other Chinese makers include Geely, Avatr and Jetour, and together with BYD sell 1 in every 5 cars in the Emirates.

Yet Ceer believes it can compete by emphasizing a theme the crown prince has long focused on throughout his flagship projects: over-the-top luxury, coupled with levels of technology reminiscent of sci-fi movies and games.
That ethos could be seen in the cars displayed in Diriyah, which, according to the enthusiastic salesman on hand and employees, were designed with much input from Bin Salman.

Both models take the notion of a wedge car — a shape famously popularized by iconic vehicles such as the Lamborghini Countach — and dial it up to a cyberpunk-inspired 11. They also feature gull-wing doors and a 94.5-inch windshield that Ceer says is the largest in the world. Inside, the car has a flight yoke rather than a steering wheel.

There are little touches to indicate the cars’ Saudi DNA, from the “Saudi made” badge on the trunk to subtler cues like the shape of the hubcaps, which are supposed to be reminiscent of Saudi architecture; or the 32 LEDs in the car’s front end, a reference to 1932, the year Saudi Arabia was declared a kingdom. Colors, too, are Saudi-inspired, and include options such as “Obaya Black” or “Abha Green.”

Performance figures are supposed to match the cars’ aggressive looks. The models have three electric motors from Rimac, a Croatian manufacturer, and Hyundai; collectively they provide 625 kW, the equivalent of about 850 hp, to propel the sedan from 0 to 60 mph in 2.6 seconds, with a range of over 400 miles.

Both Exobots sell for almost 400,000 riyal (the equivalent of $107,000), planting Ceer in the premium segment against cars from Porsche, Mercedes and Tesla — a different universe from the sub-$15,000 segment dominated by most Chinese carmakers.
“At that price, we’re not looking at the People’s Car,” Madeira said, referencing the Volkswagen Beetle — an example of a car designed to be affordable.

“It’s a strategy where they’re getting higher-income consumers to buy this vehicle, then maybe it trickles down where middle-income consumers can see this higher-priced vehicle and aspire to owning the new model.”
Yet even here Ceer may not be safe from competition. This year, as Chinese makers face a Darwin-esque winnowing at home, they’re branching out into high-end segments.

Geely, for example, has a dedicated premium sub-brand called Zeekr; its newest model, the 9X, comes loaded with gee-whiz tech that only underscores the stodginess of competitors in the U.S. and Europe, including self-parking capabilities and advanced infotainment options.

In the UAE, where the 9X is offered at $100,000, Zeekr’s marketing personnel said they had already received 600 pre-orders for the vehicle by September, with a roughly $3,500 nonrefundable down payment.

In the meantime, like Lucid before it — which the Public Investment Fund has spent billions propping up, despite losing a billion dollars in 2026 alone — Ceer will benefit from Riyadh’s considerable financial muscle and state planning to ensure success.
For example, the government is ramping up investments in charging stations, increasing the few hundred available in the kingdom to 5,000 by 2030 to help encourage EV adoption.

Yet with a projected manufacturing capacity of 240,000 cars per year, Ceer will have to look outward. Madeira said the expectation is that Ceer will be able to sell 50,000 to 70,000 cars regionally for it to be considered a win for Riyadh.

“First they have to be a success within Saudi Arabia before they start going into neighboring countries,” Madeira said, adding that he expected the Exobots’ price would probably hinder sales performance.
“Having said that, I think they’re in it for the long run. They have enough money to sweat it out.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/ini.headline: Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/ini.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.
Reporter covering local transportation
Maryland bridge closure alert mistakenly sent callers to sex hotline
People seeking information about a Maryland bridge closure amid Thursday’s storm were in for a surprise: They were mistakenly directed to a sex hotline.
The Maryland Department of Emergency Management sent residents a public safety alert Thursday afternoon warning that the strong Thanksgiving storm had closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
That alert mistakenly directed callers to a sex hotline rather than the Maryland Transportation Authority, or MDTA.

In a statement, Maryland Transportation Authority spokesman Brad Tanner said the authority was “aware of the unfortunate error” included in the emergency alert’s callback number. The agency has corrected the error, Tanner said in the statement.
“We know this was distressing to many Marylanders,” Tanner said. “Emergency alerts are critical, lifesaving tools that require accuracy, and the MDTA takes this error very seriously.”
Thursday’s storm, the worst to hit on Thanksgiving Day in decades, left hundreds of thousands of people without power up and down the East Coast.
The roughly 4.3-mile-long Bay Bridge is notorious for not having shoulders. Some people are so scared of crossing it that they pay other drivers to take them.
This month, the MDTA said plans to replace the bridge are moving forward after securing final federal environmental approval. Construction is expected to begin as soon as 2032, the agency said.
A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”
Virginia sheriff’s office ends agreement with ICE after court ruling

The sheriff’s office in Loudoun County, Virginia, this week ended its cooperation agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after an appeals court upheld a state law limiting local law enforcement cooperation with immigration agents.

Virginia was one of several states this year to place restrictions on participation in ICE’s 287(g) program, which allows state and local officials to be deputized to conduct immigration enforcement. A federal judge temporarily blocked the provision from taking effect in July after the Justice Department sued, but a federal appeals court Monday reversed that decision.

The Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office entered into a 287(g) agreement last year, authorizing its officers to execute ICE administrative warrants, known as detainers, on individuals already in the sheriff’s custody. In an email, sheriff’s office spokesman Tom Julia said the department will abide by the court’s decision. He said the department no longer will keep an individual scheduled for released in custody based on an ICE warrant, but it will continue to honor immigration warrants that are “concurrent” with a person’s release.

So far this year, ICE has issued 673 detainers for noncitizen inmates in the Loudoun County jail, of whom 330 were transferred to ICE custody, according to Julia. The sheriff’s office has not released anyone to ICE since the appeals court ruling, he said.
The agreement had long been a point of contention between Loudoun Sheriff Mike Chapman and the county’s Democratic-controlled board of supervisors.

Loudoun County Board Chair Phyllis J. Randall said in a statement that she was “very pleased” by the sheriff’s decision, adding: “Across our country, poorly trained ICE agents have wreaked havoc, caused death, killed American citizens and terrorized American cities.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/28/pslf-payment-count-e.headline: He fought the Education Department — and won back his student loan forgiveness credit. What other borrowers can learn
cnbc.com/2026/11/28/pslf-payment-count-e.author: Annie Nova

paragraphs.text: Earlier this year, Nicholas Yund was months away from having his federal student loans forgiven. Then, in early August, the University of Minnesota employee logged into his account and saw his forgiveness date pushed back by nearly two years.
"I could barely breathe," said Yund, 45. "That's when I went online to various Facebook and Reddit groups and saw it was happening to thousands of other people."

Yund's qualifying-payment count fell from 116 to 93, leaving him 27 payments short of the 120 required for Public Service Loan Forgiveness, a federal program created in 2007 that cancels the remaining student loan debt of borrowers working for a government or nonprofit employer.

The reduced payment counts for Yund and other PSLF borrowers result from what the U.S. Department of Education has said is an effort to correct payment-count errors made during the Biden administration.

"These errors resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers," a department spokesperson wrote to CNBC in an email. "The Department remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower's account."
The sudden reductions in payment counts have left borrowers scrambling to determine which months were removed and whether their current timelines are correct.

The American Federation of Teachers recently sued the Trump administration over its management of the PSLF program, claiming that it is unlawfully blocking tens of thousands of borrowers from student loan forgiveness. Filed Oct. 30, the suit is still pending.

For borrowers nearing the finish line, losing qualifying months can mean staying in repayment — and in qualifying public service work — for years longer than expected. It can also delay other financial goals.

Yund said a longer wait for student loan forgiveness would have kept him from putting more money toward retirement savings and enjoying more disposable income. His current student loan balance is around $20,000.
But in the end, he found a way to get his qualifying PSLF payments restored. Here's how.
Yund's fight for student loan forgiveness
When Yund saw his PSLF count drop, he called his loan servicer, Missouri Higher Education Loan Authority, or MOHELA, and asked what had happened. The answer offered little reassurance.

"The agent said they had received lots of calls regarding that issue," Yund said. He said he was told there had been a technical problem but got no explanation of what it meant for his account or when it might be fixed.
A MOHELA spokesperson referred CNBC's questions to the Education Department, which did not respond to questions about Yund's case.
Yund began looking for answers elsewhere.

That month, he opened cases with the Minnesota Attorney General's office and Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar's office. He also had something that could help make his case: a complete record of his payments.
"I kept bank statement records of every payment made as well as downloaded all of my payment history from my student loan servicers," Yund said.

Brian Evans, press secretary at the Minnesota Attorney General's office, said it referred Yund's complaint to the state's Student Loan Advocate, who, he said, "is in a better position to help resolve his complaint."
Klobuchar's office told him it had opened a congressional inquiry with the Education Department on his behalf, according to communications between the senator's staff and Yund reviewed by CNBC.
"Senator Klobuchar's office was very helpful and timely, reaching out to me directly by phone with additional questions and concerns," Yund said.
Those communications show the Education Department responded to the senator's office, saying that its review found that some of Yund's payments did not qualify under standard PSLF.

But the department said that he could receive credit for that period through Temporary Expanded Public Service Loan Forgiveness, or TEPSLF. That program can count payments made under certain repayment plans that are not usually eligible for standard PSLF, provided the borrower meets additional requirements, such as working in a qualifying public service position.
The crispy half chicken
On Sept. 6, Yund logged into his account again. Most of his payments had been restored, but he was still two payments short of his earlier count.
"I was incredibly frustrated with the lack of oversight and errors demonstrated by the Department of Education," Yund said.
But he also saw a reason to keep pushing: "This was an opportunity to advocate for myself and, by extension, draw attention to an important problem we are facing."
His advice to other student loan borrowers? "Be persistent to the point of annoying," he said. "Call your Senators and House Representatives to open cases on your behalf. Do not give up hope."
Be persistent to the point of annoying. Nicholas Yund
Yund is once again nearing debt forgiveness. He had expected it in November; now he anticipates it in January or February.

He already knows how he'll celebrate when he's student loan-free: dinner at Meritage, a popular French brasserie in St. Paul. He knows what he'll order, too. He's had plenty of time to think about it: the crispy half chicken.

washingtonpost.com/national-security/202.headline: The shrinking number of prosecutors bringing DOJ’s high-profile cases
washingtonpost.com/national-security/202.author: Perry Stein

paragraphs.text: Earlier this year, Alessandra Serano, a trusted aide to Attorney General Todd Blanche, flew to South Florida to help prosecutors investigating President Donald Trump’s political foes. Serano, the Justice Department’s first-ever coordinator for child exploitation and human trafficking, zipped back to D.C. last month to ask a judge to sign off on a warrant to search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D).

Stanley Woodward, the third-highest ranking official at the Justice Department, recently put his signature on court filings about Trump’s White House ballroom project, a pre-election lawsuit seeking to potentially block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska and a call for an antitrust investigation into major TV networks that suspended their pooled coverage of the president.
And when the Justice Department charged former FBI director James B. Comey for the third time last month, two close aides to Blanche signed off on the court documents.
As Donald Trump enters his final years in office, the Justice Department is relying on a shrinking number of lawyers to bring the department’s most high-profile and controversial cases.

That marks a sharp change from how the Justice Department operated under previous administrations, during which political appointees rarely waded into courtrooms and instead left the litigating, even in fraught cases, to rank-and-file career prosecutors.

The strategy under Blanche has wound up insulating career staffers from the most controversial cases, enabling them to focus on more traditional Justice Department matters without getting drawn into politically fraught investigations. That also means fewer career prosecutors are at risk of quitting over case assignments they feel could imperil their legal ethics, which was a frequent occurrence during the first year of the Trump administration.

But, according to former Justice Department officials, the reliance on political appointees and what are known as special assistant U.S. attorneys has further eroded trust in the agency and federal law enforcement. Special assistant U.S. attorneys are typically career lawyers already working in the government who are either detailed or appointed to work on a specific case.

This article is based on interviews with current and former Justice Department officials, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to freely discuss their observations of the current administration.

During Trump’s second term, he has repeatedly called for his foes to face investigations and charges, and Justice Department leaders have seemed eager to oblige him. But critics say assigning people viewed as being tied to political appointees to these cases suggests the Trump administration is wielding the law enforcement agency to benefit the president and his allies.

“Cases originate from the ground, not the top,” said Kyle Boynton, a former career civil rights prosecutor who left the department last year. “In this administration, they have been originating from the top. It is such a sharp departure from the expectations that Americans should have of how law enforcement works in this country.”
“That’s why we call it building a case,” he said. “You don’t build a case down from the clouds; you build a foundation first.”

The Justice Department, in a statement, said it was not heavily relying on political appointees to bring these notable cases and that assignments are based on expertise and resources. The agency also said it was taking a “more dynamic approach than previous administrations.”

“To compare Departments across administrations is not an apples-to-apples comparison, as the Biden administration’s approach and priorities created a unique climate coming into 2025,” a spokesperson for the agency said.

The spokesperson said these high-profile matters, including the Florida grand conspiracy investigation and the Omar probe, are not its biggest cases, pointing instead to major fraud and trafficking investigations, which career and political appointees work on together.

Still, Blanche’s approach has coincided with the Justice Department being hollowed out by an exodus of career staffers, most of whom resigned amid upheaval in the agency under Trump or were fired over their reluctance to work on certain cases.

U.S. attorney offices across the country are stretched thin, with some unable to keep up with the mounting workload, which includes an uptick in immigration cases, according to current and former officials.
The Justice Department has defended its staffing decisions, citing declining violent crime rates across the country and saying that it is prosecuting criminals in high numbers.

“The Department is doing more with a leaner workforce because it has stopped funding bloated bureaucracy and activist work outside its core mission,” a department spokesperson said in a statement. “Those who want a Justice Department focused on politics instead of public safety should never again be trusted with the safety of the American people.”

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who later served as Trump’s defense attorney, understands the role of line prosecutors and wants them to keep doing the day-to-day work of investigating and charging strong cases, according to two people familiar with his thinking who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

His decision to assign the department’s most controversial cases to the prosecutors who want to work on them, and who are often political appointees or close to him, has enabled other attorneys to conduct their cases with fewer disturbances, former agency officials said.

But the prosecutors tasked with bringing these fraught cases often have far less experience or skill litigating them than many of the veteran career attorneys who work under them, former Justice Department officials noted.

The former officials said that comparative lack of experience and skill shows, pointing out that the biggest political cases brought by this administration have faltered after they were rejected by grand juries, dismissed by judges or stalled in the investigatory stages. Legal experts said the department’s struggles in court are also a reflection of the sometimes weak cases prosecutors are bringing in these matters.
As Blanche prepares for the second half of Trump’s second term, none of the Justice Department’s defining cases against Trump’s political foes have gone to trial.

Cases against Comey, New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and two former FBI officials who were accused of making false statements about their knowledge of a laptop belonging to Hunter Biden have all been dismissed by judges. The Justice Department is seeking to revive the cases against Comey and James. Another case against Comey could go to trial sometime next year.

Historically, grand juries rarely decline to approve indictments sought by prosecutors. But during Trump’s second term, such panels have rejected indictments in high-profile instances, including attempts to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers, former Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson and people accused of voter fraud.

In Florida, the “grand conspiracy” case — which is examining whether Obama- and Biden-era officials violated Trump’s rights as they investigated him — has yielded no indictments and appears to be faltering.

That investigation is being run out of the U.S. attorney’s office in South Florida, though the Justice Department has kept it separate from the day-to-day operations there, staffing it with political appointees and prosecutors across the country, many of whom volunteered to work on the probe.
The Justice Department in recent weeks dispatched the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles to Florida to work on that investigation.

The prosecutor, Bill Essayli — one of the Justice Department’s most vocal backers of Trump — is a former Republican state politician who has been at the forefront of the administration’s efforts to investigate non citizens accused of voter fraud and prosecute protesters who allegedly impeded immigration officials from doing their jobs.

This new assignment means that Essayli is running one of the biggest U.S. attorney’s office, where he has to oversee hundreds of prosecutors and thousands of cases, while also working as a prosecutor on an investigation on a different coast.
Blanche’s strategy for which officials handle high-profile efforts has also drawn praise.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas, said these cases represent a sliver of the Justice Department’s caseload. Reitz said it makes sense Blanche would want his most trusted allies to handle these sensitive matters while allowing the thousands of career prosecutors to focus on their work.
“Todd is a firm believer that the overwhelming majority of the work that we do is bipartisan, nonpartisan, bread-and-butter law enforcement work,” Reitz said in an interview.

“But like any other administration, there are special projects that arise that involve a special degree of sensitivity that have to be entrusted to certain people,” said Reitz, a conservative prosecutor who has threatened to investigate Democrats over their scrutiny of Trump.

In the first year of the Trump administration, prosecutors and other lawyers have quit the Justice Department after being asked to take actions or work on cases they felt compromised their ethics, The Washington Post has previously reported.

The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section — tasked with investigating and prosecuting public officials — was gutted when many prosecutors refused to sign off on dropping a case against then-New York Mayor Eric Adams (D). Federal prosecutors in New York were also pushed out or quit because of the administration’s desire to drop the case.

In Virginia, at least a half-dozen prosecutors were demoted or pushed out due to fallout from the push to prosecute Comey. In Tennessee, a top prosecutor resigned in protest over the controversial indictment of a Maryland man who had successfully challenged his illegal deportation to El Salvador.

Since the beginning of the administration, more than 7,000 of the agency’s 20,000 or so staffers — a roster that includes lawyers and nonlawyers alike — who work at Justice Department headquarters and U.S. attorney’s offices across the country have left, according to Justice Connection, an advocacy organization founded by former employees. In their place, 3,500 people have been hired, Justice Connection found.
The Justice Department said in response to questions for this article that it has hired more than 1,100 assistant U.S. attorneys, who are the prosecutors who work across the country.

Reitz said when he was installed in July as the U.S. attorney in South Texas, overseeing an office that stretches from Houston to the U.S.-Mexico border, there was a 35 percent vacancy rate in staffing.
The prosecutor said he has chipped away at the vacancy rate, bringing it down to about 25 percent. He achieved that, he said, through $20,000 signing bonuses and relocation stipends.

“We are accomplishing our mission even with a leaner staff, but it is of course true that we can do more with more people,” Reitz said. “I’m not experiencing heartburn yet over declining cases because we don’t have staff.”
Some offices are experiencing that anxiety. People interviewed for this article said departed prosecutors have had to hand off their open cases to remaining staff, leaving whole offices backlogged.
Department leaders are also struggling to address litigation around an unprecedented number of immigration arrests.

Charles Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in the Western District of Washington, wrote in an unusual letter to a federal judge this month that his office did not have staff to defend every “habeas corpus” case mounted by someone challenging their detention.

In these cases, immigrants write petitions to the courts saying that federal officials are unlawfully detaining them. Typically, prosecutors would defend the government, explaining to a judge why the people were rightfully detained.

But Floyd wrote to the judge that such a defense was not possible anymore, saying that “to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which” his office would “no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense.”
Floyd later said his office would again assign staff members to these cases.
Blanche acknowledged in a memo this month that the increase in immigration arrests, and a flood of people challenging their detention, has strained U.S. attorney offices.
The attorney general said he was surging resources in response, requiring attorneys from across the department, including antitrust and civil rights attorneys, to pitch in.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/28/2.headline: Presidential hopefuls focus on cost and corruption this Thanksgiving
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/28/2.author: Alec Dent

paragraphs.text: Holiday weeks tend to be slower for political news, with political arguments moving from the national stage to family dinner tables. But the next presidential campaign cycle still carried on this Thanksgiving, albeit at a bit slower pace.
Here’s what likely 2028 candidates were up to this week between eating turkey and watching football:
Thanksgiving messages focused on rising costs
A number of Democrats considered likely to run for the presidency in 2028 released statements on Thanksgiving emphasizing how expensive life has become for Americans.

As the midterm elections demonstrated, cost of living is top of mind for voters, and an American Farm Bureau Federation survey this month found the average cost of a Thanksgiving meal for 10 people increased by 6 percent from last year.

“It’s Thanksgiving week. The only spending I enjoy is time with family. These high prices for feeding everyone come from the Iran war, the trade war, and the reckless deficit. Needless to say, I am not grateful for those things,” Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) said in a social media post.

“Everything from the turkey to the flight home is more expensive this Thanksgiving under Trump, and families are feeling the squeeze,” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) posted. “Thanksgiving dinner costs rose up to 11% in 2026, with 121,000 fewer Americans expected to travel thanks record fuel costs and soaring airfares.”

“American families are hurting this year. Thanksgiving dinner costs 6% more than last year. Gas is up 17%,” Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) said on X. Khanna called for ending the war with Iran, Medicare-for-all, a $25 minimum wage and making “data centers pay” to address rising costs.
“A turkey costs 10% more than last year. A flight is 22% more. Gas is around $4. Trump keeps lining his pockets while you search yours to make ends meet,” said Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey).
Jensen Huang scandal framed as a corruption issue

Nvidia rehired Jensen Huang as its CEO Monday after President Donald Trump personally intervened on his behalf, prompting criticism from Democrats and Republicans alike about Trump’s unusual role in the decision. Trump has substantial investments in Nvidia and has long been fond of Huang, who was CEO of Nvidia when it made a $25 million pledge to Trump’s ballroom project.
Likely presidential contenders entered the debate about Huang’s return this week and many were focused on potential corruption in the process.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) called Huang’s return “another example of the dangerous combination governing this country: a rigged system that protects those at the very top no matter what, and a corrupt White House that cannot be trusted to put the economic well-being and safety of American families first.”

“You want to know why people are angry? Because they look at this and they say, ‘If you’re rich and powerful and you’re friends with the president, you can get away with everything,’” former New Jersey governor Chris Christie said in an interview with CNBC.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) accused the billionaire class of trying to play by different rules in an interview with the Axios Show.
“The thing that makes people so angry about this is it seems like it’s rules for thee, but not for me,” Moore said. “Frankly, if that was any of us, we would be held to a different type of standard.”
Khanna also called for “fairness,” saying that “Rules should apply to everyone. That’s why I took on the Epstein class.”
“The rich & powerful, like Jensen, do not get to evade export controls or accountability just because it props up the stock price,” Khanna said.

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) told MS NOW that the case was about “billionaires protecting other billionaires” and Trump “protecting his billionaire friend who gave $10 million or more, millions of dollars, to his ballroom project.”
“If something like this would have happened to someone in the Navy or our military, you wouldn’t get a call from the president,” said Kelly, a Naval veteran. “You would get a call from the FBI.”
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) suggested that Trump’s financial stake in Nvidia could have influenced how his administration approached oversight of the company.

“When President Trump came to power, he made the decision, kind of a shocking decision, to allow our most sophisticated AI chips, made by Nvidia, to be sold to the Chinese government, to Chinese companies,” Slotkin said. “Unsurprisingly, we know now, that he has made tremendous money in Nvidia stock because of that decision.”

Focusing on potential corruption in this high-profile incident makes a lot of sense: corruption was one of voters’ top concerns in the midterms and helped propel Democrats to major victories across the country.
The DNC revealed its 2028 debate schedule

The Democratic National Committee said on Monday that it will host a dozen presidential primary debates in the 2028 cycle, with the first scheduled for June 2027. Five debates will take place in 2027, with seven scheduled for 2028.

Also notable: The DNC is requiring debate participants to denounce super PAC spending on their behalf, agree not to participate in unsanctioned debates and skip campaigning in states that disregard the DNC primary calendar. (The latter is significant as the DNC has officially named South Carolina as the first state in its primary calendar, even though New Hampshire state law requires it to hold the nation’s first primary.)
Other 2028 stories from this week

• Vice President JD Vance stopped by Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday with his family to serve lunch to service members ahead of visiting with family in Vance’s home state for Thanksgiving.

• Trump set his sights on California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), a likely 2028 candidate, during a speech at the Justice Department on Monday. Trump criticized Newsom’s effort to commute all death sentences in the California penal system, and accused Newsom of having more sympathy for killers on death row than for victims and their families.

• Pritzker announced that his state will not participate in the new federal school voucher program set to launch in January, saying the program would “siphon money from public schools for private education.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) responded by saying the program will not “‘siphon’ money from public schools; the money is in addition to any state funding.”Former Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin (R) accused Pritzker of siding “with the unions over kids.”
• Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) called for their state to be the home of a Space Force training academy.

• Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky) suggested Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should be removed from office over the Army’s detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives in Iowa. Massie led a failed effort to impeach Hegseth for his role in the Iran war earlier this month.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/28.headline: From frightened fawn in ‘Bambi’ to decorated Marine and Vietnam vet
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/28.author: Amanda Covarrubias

paragraphs.text: Millions of moviegoers knew his voice, if not his name.

Donnie Dunagan gave auditory life to the frightened fawn in Disney’s 1942 animated classic “Bambi,” creating an indelible mark on the minds of moviegoers in the harrowing scene where young Bambi calls for his mother after hunters shoot and kill her.

The movie would be his last. Mr. Dunagan went on to join the Marine Corps at age 18. He served for 25 years and became a decorated veteran, earning three Purple Hearts, among many other medals, and retired as a major.

During most of his time in the Marines, Mr. Dunagan kept his Hollywood past a secret from those who served with him. He didn’t want them confusing their commanding officer with Bambi, and he didn’t want to boast.

“I am a commander in Marine Corps boot camp,” Mr. Dunagan told StoryCorps in 2015. “Hundreds of recruits I’m responsible for. ... I just thought to myself, I don’t think I want all these young Marines to start calling me ‘Major Bambi,’ and I kept my mouth shut.”

He told the Guardian in 2005: “You have to understand what it’s like in the Marine Corps, or in the CIA, or FBI. Those were the best men I ever met in my life, but they would never talk about their past, or boast about their achievements. Because only tacky men did that.”
Mr. Dunagan died Nov. 4 at 92, in San Angelo, Texas, his representatives said. They did not provide a cause of death, but he had suffered from lung cancer.
He came to play the voice of young Bambi in Disney’s 1942 animated classic after being scouted by a talent agent when he was 3 years old.
He appeared in several movies before “Bambi,” including as Peter von Frankenstein, the grandson of the mad scientist, in “Son of Frankenstein” in 1939.
But “Bambi” would turn out to be his last movie role. A decade after it premiered, during the Korean War, he joined the Marines.

He served three tours in Vietnam and trained recruits for combat as the Corps’ youngest drill instructor, according to an Air Force website. He also served as a counterintelligence officer before retiring in 1977.
Donald Roan Dunagan was born Aug. 16, 1934, in San Antonio. During the Depression, his family moved to Memphis, where they lived in a two-room flat.

On a corner down the street, a man would dance “like you would not believe,” he told USA Today. One day his mother took him there, and Donnie started imitating him. They became a duet and soon after performed in a big talent show in Memphis.
“I won the darn thing,” he said. “Someone in the audience got in touch with my parents asking if I could go to Hollywood to audition for a couple roles — they needed a runt kid like me.”
In addition to voicing young Bambi, Mr. Dunagan served as the character’s real-life model for the animators, spending months in front of illustrators, following their commands.

“Look left, look right, look afraid. When Bambi is kissed by a doe, he gives a look of disgust. We spent an hour on that look.” he said. “‘Look like something bad has happened,’ they’d say. But I was having the time of my life. Finally someone said, ‘Pretend like you just had castor oil.’ That did it.”

He called Walt Disney “a wonderful guy” who took him to a meeting in Los Angeles where Disney offered the image of Bambi to the forestry department to use in a campaign to raise awareness about forest fires.
“Look at this face,” Disney said at the meeting, according to Mr. Dunagan. “This is the face of Bambi.”
Mr. Dunagan ended up making seven movies in all, and became his family’s breadwinner. But Hollywood took a toll.

“It turned out that all that money hurt my family,” he told the Guardian. “We’d gone from a one-room tenement to a house in Beverly Hills, and it was too much, too quick. The family just ruptured, and I was then farmed out to a bunch of people.”
After his parents divorced, Dunagan spent time in several boarding homes, played football and boxed in high school, and supported himself before joining the military.

His efforts to hide his “Bambi” past worked until he was near retirement, the same year the animated film was rereleased in theaters. One day his commanding general called him into his office and told him he wanted Mr. Dunagan to audit some auditors on base.

The commanding general pulled down his glasses and patted a red folder on his desk “from an old security clearance I had from years ago,” Mr. Dunagan told USA Today. He began to protest that he was too busy, but the commanding general would have none of it.
“You will audit the auditors,” the commanding general said. “Won’t you … Major Bambi?”
As Mr. Dunagan grew older, he would come to soften his stance toward his most famous Hollywood role. He attended screenings and fan events, while continuing to encourage and support other veterans.
He participated in a DVD release of “Bambi” and spoke at conventions and festivals as an ambassador for the film for many years.
He is survived by his wife of 34 years, Dana Dunagan.
Mr. Dunagan said there were few accomplishments he could have achieved that would have overshadowed his role in “Bambi.”

“I have some holes in my body that God didn’t put there,” Dunagan said in the StoryCorps interview. “I got shot through my left knee. Got an award or two for saving lives over time, but I think I could have been appointed as the aide de camp in the White House. It wouldn’t make any difference.
“It’s Bambi that’s so dear to people, but I love it now when people realize this old jerk is still alive and was Bambi, and I wouldn’t take anything for it, not a darn thing for it.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/arm.headline: Armed man patrolling next to elementary school tests Montana’s gun tolerance
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/arm.author: Annie Gowen

paragraphs.text: The years-long standoff between a gun-wielding man and an elementary school in Billings, Montana, began as a mundane dispute between neighbors — a broken tool, motor oil spilled in the horseradish bed.

It quickly escalated into threats and a restraining order. Eventually one of the neighbors, Gabriel Metcalf, began patrolling his property daily with his gun, directly across the street from Broadwater Elementary School.

He was arrested in 2023 for unlawful possession of a firearm in a school zone. But a federal court overturned his conviction last year, ruling that Montana’s gun laws permitted him to do what he did. He resumed his patrols this September.

Parents and school officials say they are horrified by the sight of Metcalf pacing with a 20-gauge shotgun in front of the home he shares with his mother. They say they are terrified Metcalf could just break down and open fire one day.

To protect students, school administrators have changed the way children walk to school, curtailed recess and hung a huge black tarp over the playground fence. They’re now hoping their legislators can find a solution.

The conflict has tested the limits of Montana’s 2021 law to allow permit-less carry and set off a debate over school safety and fiercely held gun rights in a conservative state where independence and self-reliance are prized.
Tanya Ludwig, a member of the Billings school board who attended the school as a child, wept at a recent meeting.
“This guy could go off and shoot someone,” she said through tears. “I don’t want to have a parent bury a child. It’s not an easy thing to go through. We need to get this addressed.”
Metcalf declined an interview request.

His mother, Vivian Young, says her son is simply trying to keep her safe from a former neighbor who threatened her but has since moved away. She says the family is being victimized by overzealous meddlers, whom she referred to as “Karens.” Her son is just exercising his Second Amendment rights, she said.

“The angry mob is doing everything they can do to harass us,” she said. “All this town needs is a good sale on pitchforks and tiki torches. We would have had them on our lawn. It is so out of control.”
On Nov. 16, the school board voted to allow parents to start fundraising to build a wall around the school to permanently end the view of Metcalf and his patrols. The expected cost is $475,000.
“It’s ridiculous,” Young said. “This is Montana. Everybody’s armed.”

Young, 74, runs a small at-home tailoring business, and Metcalf, 52, lives in a small trailer on the property on Broadwater Avenue. He began patrolling the parcel in 2023 because of the unnerving actions of their neighbor at the time, Young said.

The man began coming over without invitation and doing things like dumping motor oil in her horseradish bed and spraying her bee house with wasp repellent, she said. “He would do these random things — odd, bizarre,” she said.
His behavior soon morphed into violent threats — to kill Young’s pet rabbit and eventually Young herself. She obtained a restraining order against him in 2022.
Metcalf’s near-daily checks on his home’s perimeter raised immediate alarms among parents at the school.
