In August 2023, Metcalf was arrested and charged with unlawful possession of a firearm in a school zone under the federal government’s 1990 Gun-Free School Zones Act, which prohibits unauthorized individuals from possessing a firearm within 1,000 feet of a school. He eventually pleaded guilty and received three years of probation.
But in September 2025, a three-judge panel on the San Francisco-based U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit overturned his conviction by a 2-1 vote.

Metcalf’s lawyers had argued that Montana’s 2021 permit-less carry law — one of 29 across the country — meant Metcalf was legally authorized to possess a firearm as part of the school zone law’s exemptions, which allow “state-licensed individuals” to have firearms near schools. In his opinion, U.S. Circuit Judge Lawrence VanDyke, deemed this argument “plausible.”
VanDyke also wrote that Young’s neighbor had “stalked and threatened Metcalf and his mother” and repeatedly violated the protection order.

“I think this case illustrates the really difficult tension between restrictive federal laws and permissive state laws,” said Joseph Blocher, a law professor at Duke University, who is the director of the school’s Center for Firearms Law. “This is the kind of challenge that arises when states are loosening their gun laws while the federal government is trying to enforce nationwide rules.”
Metcalf resumed his patrols this fall, his mother said, because the family had received death threats over the ongoing drama, as well as an unrelated attempted break-in.

Billings Public Schools Superintendent Erwin Garcia told the board of trustees in September that he drove by the house and saw Metcalf dressed in a face mask and a hoodie toting what he called a “high-caliber weapon.” Young told The Washington Post the weapon was a shotgun.
“It was completely unacceptable,” Garcia said. “This is the time when kids are supposed to be going to school. We’re talking 7:20 or 7:30.”
“But federal judges gave this person his freedom,” the superintendent added. “He’s not doing anything illegal.”
Emergency meetings ensued. The tarp shielding the playground — first added to the fence in 2023 — went back up. Parents began asking to withdraw their kids from the school.
Sgt. Jeff Stovall, spokesman for the Billings Police Department, said the department has increased patrols by school resource officers and others but feels it has few other options to ensure safety.
“We’re at the mercy of the court because precedent has been set,” Stovall said. “Unless there’s an actual crime and probable cause to arrest somebody.”
At the September board meeting, Garcia wondered from the dais if another option might be shutting down the school altogether and somehow finding a place for its 380 students.
“Is this the Montana way?” he asked aloud.

James Reavis, the Democratic state representative who represents the area, said he would propose legislation to address the gun loophole in the next session in January — perhaps by amending the state’s disorderly conduct laws.
“I’m confident we can come up with a bipartisan solution,” he said.
But that feels like an eternity to the parents with children at Broadwater Elementary School.
Katie Brand, a mother of two who lives nearby, told the board in September that she wept with staff when Metcalf reemerged.

“Legislation … feels really impossible at this point and so far down the road,” she said, saying she was concerned about her children’s safety — and her own. “This could be happening to anyone in this city and happen to anyone in this state.”

The parents provided a statement saying that their “priority is ensuring a safe environment for our children to learn and play” and that fundraising efforts are “focused on long-term safety improvements.”
Young said she and her son remain unbowed.
“It has nothing to do with the school,” she said. “People need to resolve to the fact that we have a right to be armed. This is government tyranny.”
Razzan Nakhlawi contributed to this report.

finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/plungi.headline: Plunging Fuel Prices Bring Relief for Drivers and Central Banks
finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/plungi.author: Alex Longley

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- In a few short weeks, global fuel markets have lurched out of crisis, for now at least.
Most Read from Bloomberg

American drivers were spared record gasoline prices when they hit the roads for Thanksgiving, with prices sliding near $3.50 a gallon. The picture is similar elsewhere, with pump costs in Europe down 15% after nine consecutive weekly drops and prices falling from Thailand to Malaysia. Even diesel markets are reversing a near-uninterrupted ascent since the Iran war began.

It's the latest sharp move in oil markets roiled by disruptions to Middle Eastern supplies and Ukrainian attacks on Russian processing plants. Together, the two wars have driven up the cost of living around the world, prompting a wave of interest-rate hikes that has helped derail the bull market in equities.

In recent weeks, though, oil product flows have picked up through the Strait of Hormuz, adding crucial extra barrels to the market. Refineries elsewhere have been running at breakneck speed to fill the supply gap. All the while, demand has cratered, with the International Energy Agency seeing consumption falling almost 3 million barrels a day this year.

Further emergency stockpile releases from IEA member countries are also taking some of the heat out of fuel markets, with European nations set to release at least 15 million barrels of diesel between early November and the end of February, according to the Paris-based watchdog.

Those factors have combined to ease cost pressures that sparked protests in France and Italy and contributed to heavy losses for the Republicans in the US midterm elections. While that's brought some relief to the global economy, the outlook remains uncertain as wartime stress persists.

"The ultimate drivers of these things are events in the world, which are inherently unpredictable," Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey told lawmakers in the UK this week. "If current prices were to stay where they are, the peak of inflation, mechanically, would be lower," he said, referring to both oil and natural gas prices.

Early signs of that relief came on Friday, when inflation in France and Spain slowed much more than anticipated as energy pressures eased. French prices came in about 0.4 percentage points below the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of analysts.

A Bloomberg Economics model shows that a $20 drop in crude oil prices could reduce the US Consumer Price Index by roughly that amount. In recent months, however, central bankers have focused on another gauge of inflationary pressures: crack spreads.

Those gauges, which measure the difference between crude and fuel prices, have been stubbornly wide for much of this year. In the last few weeks, they've reversed, with European gasoline trading at its smallest premium to crude since 2023. Across the US and Asia, equivalent premiums of gasoline and diesel are at multimonth lows.
While prices are cooling into the end of the year, there's still a threat of fresh increases in 2027.

Sky-high crack spreads had incentivized refiners to maximize fuel production, prompting many to defer planned maintenance. Some analysts warn that could lead to larger-than-usual outages, increasing the risk of renewed price spikes during periods of seasonally high demand.

"The next 40 days are going to be deflationary, particularly for gasoline," Tom Kloza, chief energy advisor to Gulf Oil, said in a Bloomberg TV interview. "But watch out in 2027. The seeds for the next rally in gasoline — and perhaps for the next rally in diesel — have been planted here in the last few weeks."

Much will depend on the path ahead in Hormuz, where attacks have grown more intense this month but barrels continue to flow. In the first 15 days of November, about 5.3 million barrels a day of fuel exited the Middle East, both through Hormuz and ports outside of the chokepoint. That's now only about 30% lower than prewar levels, compared with a drop of about half over the summer.

Refiners outside conflict zones have also ramped up production. Last week, US Gulf Coast refiners processed a record 9.8 million barrels of crude a day. Plants across six southern states processed roughly as much oil as the entire Middle East would under normal circumstances.

Uncertainty surrounds demand, which this year has recorded its steepest decline since the pandemic in 2020. With buyers under pressure for much of the year, the recent retreat in prices is showing signs of reviving consumption.

In Europe, German heating oil trading has picked up after consumers held off buying for much of the year because of high prices. As fuel becomes cheaper, a resurgence in buying could help limit further price declines.

"Drivers will be relieved to know that the price of petrol has now fallen," said Simon Williams, head of policy at UK motoring group RAC. He added that the cost of filling up a family car in the country is down by £9 ($11.82) since early October.
Recent oil price declines mean "further reductions are expected at the nation's forecourts," he said.
--With assistance from Prejula Prem, Jack Wittels and Nicholas Lua.

washingtonpost.com/entertainment/tv/2026.headline: Princess Kate’s new film talks about cancer and mortality. Here’s what to know.
washingtonpost.com/entertainment/tv/2026.author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: LONDON — Catherine, Princess of Wales, has released a documentary about her experience with cancer, providing an unusually emotional and intimate account of her journey.

“Heal,” described by Kensington Palace as a “deeply personal” film where Catherine explores “life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort” in the face of serious illness, is a 30-minute film that sees her speaking to other cancer survivors and hiking three of Britain’s highest peaks to raise funds for a cancer charity.

The trailer shows Catherine, 44, describing her inner thoughts and feelings of vulnerability after her cancer diagnosis, in what marks a noticeably different tone from the British royal family’s previous guarded, “never complain, never explain” approach.
Here’s what to know about the film, which will air in Britain on Sunday, and on NBC and Bravo on Monday evening, before streaming on Peacock from Tuesday.
It’s emotionally revealing while staying carefully curated
Return to menu
In a trailer for the documentary, Catherine, who is still popularly known as Kate Middleton, describes how she felt when confronted with cancer and her own mortality.

“Cancer does change you. It changes your body. It changes you physically,” she said. “I think when you’ve had to confront your own vulnerabilities, when you’re faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite.”
“It does open you up; I think it softens your heart. And once you experience something like that, it’s very hard to go back to the person you were before.”

Heal. Premiering this Sunday. Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis. All… pic.twitter.com/jugVnF1qCZ— The Prince and Princess of Wales (@KensingtonRoyal) November 23, 2026

In the film, Catherine describes lying in a hospital room drifting in and out of consciousness and becoming aware someone was holding her hand, the Associated Press reported, after attending a private screening of the film.

“They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there,” she said, without naming the person. “And the presence of someone that stood by me in that time, I’ll forever be grateful for. And it really made me realize the importance of simply being alongside somebody through their darkest times.”

The comments are unusually revealing for Catherine, whose public appearances are typically marked by short interactions at official events. The film is also carefully edited and keeps several personal details private — it does not reveal information about the type of cancer she had, her treatment or future prognosis.
Previous royal generations have been less willing to reveal details about their health or private matters, and King Charles III’s own cancer diagnosis was communicated with a brief written statement.

However, Catherine faced intense speculation about her health in 2024 after she had abdominal surgery and retreated from public view. She later revealed she had been diagnosed with cancer, in a video statement that ended the speculation and offered support to other cancer patients.

The new documentary has been praised by cancer charities that say it will encourage others to talk about their own cancer diagnoses. In Britain, more than 400,000 people are diagnosed with cancer each year, while in the United States more than 1.9 million people were diagnosed in 2023.
Kensington Palace says all funds from the documentary’s distribution have been donated to support “holistic cancer care” at the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity,
It highlights Kate’s deep love of nature
The documentary shows Catherine taking part in the National Three Peaks Challenge this year. This involves climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales, all within 24 hours.
Catherine previously has spoken about the importance of nature to mental health and her recovery, including making a four-part video series over the changing seasons.

In “Heal,” Catherine describes how she missed the outdoors when she was in the hospital. “Even when I physically couldn’t get into nature, I imagined nature from my hospital bed. And now that I’m well enough, I feel a deep longing for all those spaces, for the ocean, for the trees, for the mountains,” she says, according to a Guardian report of the private screening.

The Three Peaks Challenge also is described as an important part of her healing journey, and the trailer shows her striding up rocky peaks in high winds, looking out over the landscape in a baseball cap and grinning while wrapped up against the mist and rain, set to a soaring soundtrack.
Research suggests there are many benefits for mental and physical health from being outdoors, including boosting mood, improving blood pressure and cardiovascular well-being.
It features loving messages from her children
The documentary shows a glimpse into Catherine’s relationship with her three children, who appear in photographs but rarely are heard from in public.
When Catherine reaches the top of England’s Scafell Pike, her brother James Middleton, who has joined her on the climb, plays her voice recordings her children had made to encourage her.
“Remember, I’m always in your heart with you, and I love you very much,” says Prince Louis, 8, the AP reported. “And I’ll be following behind your back with you.”
Prince George, 13, says: “I’m tracking you on Flightradar up the mountains. … You look really, really strong,” adding: “Keep going, and we’re right behind you.”
“Hello, Mummy. I love you so much,” says Princess Charlotte, 11. “We are so proud of you doing your walk and your challenges.”
The documentary emphasizes the importance of family and community support, with Catherine saying at one point, “We’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone.”
It shows her wrapped in a hug with Prince William, cheering on other mountain walkers and walking with James, who previously has highlighted their love of hiking together.

It also shows Catherine and other cancer survivors discussing their experiences, with Catherine saying, “I haven’t really explored this outside my family walls really, so thank you for allowing me the time to do that.”

marketwatch.com/story/we-are-living-in-p.headline: We are living in perilous times if Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dictates your 401(k) balance

paragraphs.text: Why did a futurist with Huang's prescient vision build a company where all roads lead to him?
The turmoil in markets is a cautionary tale of putting so much power in the hands of one man.
Jensen Huang said he'd do better this time. Not everyone is resting easily.

He helped fuel the global AI revolution from the helm of one of the world's most powerful companies. When he became embroiled in a national-security scandal, the fallout led to a couple of trillion dollars in paper losses, give or take a billion. Before his resignation more than two weeks ago, Huang acknowledged that he had an affair with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy; since then, there were reports of two more affairs with female Nvidia employees.

A Moneyist reader asks if any readers are as vulnerable to Nvidia's fortunes as the global economy appears to be. "Did Nvidia's (NVDA) turmoil put your wealth at risk?" the reader asks. "Whose future wealth depends on one man's personal life? I know some people will be deliberately extra when they respond - of course, my whole portfolio didn't tank. Like most people, I'm diversified. But isn't it interesting how our 401(k)s can be affected by one guy in a black leather jacket?"
A 401(k) with 60% to 80% equity exposure lost roughly 5.5% to 7.5% of its on-paper value.

Even before a cloud of uncertainty enveloped Nvidia, the broader AI market and - eventually - the entire stock market, the average retirement balance had fallen in value in the third quarter of the year. The average 401(k) balance in the quarter fell 2% to $152,500, according to an analysis by Fidelity Investments released Monday. IRA balances dropped by 1% to $142,261, while the average 403(b) balance fell by 2% to $142,100.

Based on the S&P 500's SPX 9.3% decline between Nov. 11 and Nov. 20, a typical 401(k) with 60% to 80% equity exposure lost roughly 5.5% to 7.5% of its on-paper value. On an average $152,500 balance, as reported by Fidelity, that translates to $8,500 to $11,350 - or $600 billion to $800 billion across all 401(k) plans. With markets rallying on Monday on the news of Huang's return, 401(k), IRA and 403(b) accounts recovered a portion of those paper losses, though the durability of that rebound is no sure thing.

The turmoil in markets is a cautionary tale of putting so much power in the hands of one man. Huang returned to his role after President Donald Trump implored Nvidia's board of directors to reinstate their former CEO. The board ultimately complied to restore stability to the share price, despite lingering concerns about Huang's governance. Even so, Huang, who presides over a reported 60 direct reports, had not mentored any clear heir apparent.
Related: I hate that Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, but I love what it's done for my 401(k). Am I a hypocrite?
All roads lead to Huang

The stock bounced back, at least when his return was initially announced, in part because Trump believes Nvidia and Huang go together like salt and pepper and are key to the continuing AI boom and the health of the U.S. economy. He has reason to feel this way: The Brookings Institution estimates that investment in data-center buildings, power systems, networking infrastructure, microchips and other equipment will hit $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or roughly 3.63% of gross domestic product per year.

Members of the Moneyist Facebook (META) Group painted a grim picture of this moment. This reader is unsettled by the concentration of market power: "Since the advent of the atom bomb, all futures have been at risk from the whims of one man." And try this on for size: "Anyone who invests in the market is at the whim of the billionaires. Elon Musk tweets and things go berserk." And lastly: "It's always been a risk. Potentially 100 million Americans are invested in Nvidia through mutual funds and retirement accounts."
President Trump believes that Nvidia and Huang go together like salt and pepper.

Huang is instrumental to Nvidia's success and built it into an AI behemoth. In a few short years, he has become a globally recognized tech leader in the iconic style of the late Steve Jobs - even down to the silhouette. Jobs wore his signature black turtleneck and Huang sports a dashing black leather jacket, although he chose a softer, warmer material when he made his triumphant return to Nvidia's HQ in Santa Clara (reportedly a navy cotton Dior shirt).

And yet a futurist with Huang's prescient vision still built a company where all roads lead to him. As tech analyst Daniel Bader noted on CTV News, this is the same man who lied about the affair to his employees, his board of directors, and the general public. "I think that Jensen Huang is the only person who can lead the current version of Nvidia," Bader said, "and I think that coming to terms with that fact was very difficult for both the broader market and internally."

I'm willing to guess that CEOs who neglect to groom successors and perhaps compartmentalize their strategies, supply-chain command and dealmaking do not do so accidentally, but to maintain a tight grip on the corporate helm because their identity is inextricably tied to their role - and the power it brings them. And so here we are. Ultimately, shareholders believed that Nvidia's mission and that of the many tech companies tied to the growth of AI were at risk absent Huang's leadership.
His greatest feat may be making himself irreplaceable - or at least making us all believe that he is.
Related: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

By submitting your story to Dow Jones & Co., the publisher of MarketWatch, you understand and agree that we may use your story, or versions of it, in all media and platforms, including via third parties.

'I've been a stay-at-home mom': I'm 50 and have a chronic illness. My husband lost his job. Should he raid his 401(k)?
I'm terrified of a market crash. Should I put $400,000 of my $1 million retirement savings into an annuity?
