theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/taiwan.headline: ‘Victory for democracy’: Taiwan’s ruling party secures best result in a decade

paragraphs.text: Taiwan’s ruling party secured its best result in a decade in Saturday’s local elections, nearly doubling the number of constituencies it controls, in an outcome expected to anger Beijing.
The Democratic Progressive party (DPP) won at least nine of Taiwan’s 22 mayoral and county magistrate races, up from five in its disastrous showing in the last local elections four years ago.

The DPP is led by Lai Ching-te, Taiwan’s president, who is detested by Beijing. The Chinese Communist party (CCP) regards Lai as a “separatist” who opposes their plans to unify China and Taiwan. China regards Taiwan, a self-governing island, as part of its territory, a stance that the majority of Taiwanese people reject.
Taiwan’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT), won 10 races, down from 14 in the last vote. But it retained control of Taiwan’s capital, Taipei, and the neighbouring New Taipei.

The local elections were fought mainly on bread-and-butter issues such as housing costs and wealth distribution rather than cross-Strait relations. Nevertheless, “China will be breathing a sigh of relief” at the KMT’s success in Taipei and New Taipei, said William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
The KMT promotes closer ties between Taiwan and China and the annual Taipei-Shanghai forum is one of the only major remaining exchanges between China and Taiwan.

The race for Taipei mayor had been a close contest between the KMT’s incumbent, Chiang Wan-an, and Puma Shen, a DPP legislator who has been sanctioned by China. On Saturday afternoon, thousands of supporters gathered outside Shen’s campaign office to watch the results come in.

The mood started out optimistic, with chants of “Puma, keep going!” and “Turn it around!”, but as Chiang extended his lead, a sombre mood descended. Shortly before 8pm, Shen took to the stage to concede defeat, greeted by a prolonged standing ovation.
“The results are in and I’ve lost,” Shen said. Visibly emotional, Shen emphasised that he would continue to work hard.

“Tonight, the people of Taipei made the best decision. As I made clear in previous interviews with foreign media, no matter who wins today, it is a victory for Taipei and a victory for democracy,” he said.
Shen, a criminologist turned politician, is also the co-founder of Kuma Academy, which runs civil defence courses for Taiwanese to prepare for a potential Chinese invasion.

Yan Jing-na, 50, a Shen supporter, cried after he conceded defeat. “I don’t care which party he belongs to. As long as he puts Taiwan’s interests first, I’ll support him,” she said, adding that she thinks it is “cool” that Shen is labelled a “Taiwan independence separatist” by Beijing.
“He has long defended Taiwan’s rights,” she said, “and that’s why I have to support him, because the people of Taiwan have had it tough.”

Yan said Shen had helped raise public awareness of China’s campaign against Taiwan.“So we’re not worried. I think many people are now more aware of China’s influence on Taiwan because of him,” she said.

Taiwanese officials raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference before Saturday’s vote. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

China has also maintained physical pressure around the island. Taiwan’s defence ministry said that 33 Chinese warplanes and eight warships encircled Taiwan on Friday. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office has not yet commented on Saturday’s results.
Lai, Taiwan’s president, said in a Facebook post that he thanked “the people of Taiwan for their support and trust in the DPP’s nominated candidates”. Lai did not mention China in his statement.
Zhan Ying-yi, 51, another Shen supporter, said that he was “disappointed” in the result, “but that’s how democracy works”.

“We can only respect the outcome. After all, we still have the freedom to vote and that is something we should cherish,” he said, adding that the election result had heightened his concerns about the threat posed by China.
“There’s only one thing I fear: that one day we might be ruled by the People’s Republic of China. Then we would lose everything.”

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.headline: Vehicle crashes into gas pump, sparks fire in West Hollywood
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.author: Anthony Solorzano

paragraphs.text: A gas station in West Hollywood was engulfed in flames Friday afternoon after a vehicle crashed into a gas pump, setting off an explosion that charred three vehicles.
The incident took place at WeHo Fuels, located in a strip mall at the intersection of Santa Monica Boulevard and Orlando Avenue, and was reported to authorities at approximately 1:23 p.m.

The fire was ignited after a black SUV crashed into a white sedan and pushed it off the road and into the gas station, according to surveillance footage obtained by ABC 7. The white sedan crashed into a parked grey sedan before crashing into the fuel pump, setting it aflame. A grey pickup truck parked on the other side of the pump quickly caught fire.
“I was pumping gas into my tank when [my truck] caught fire, and I quickly walked away,” César Abarca, the owner of the pickup truck, told Telemundo 52 of the incident.
Abarca’s wife, who was not identified by name by the Spanish news outlet, said she struggled to exit the vehicle after the crash.
“I couldn’t take my seat belt off because of the nerves,” she said. “I was shocked.”

Los Angeles County and Beverly Hills firefighters responded to the call and extinguished the fire. Three ambulances were requested at the scene. The strip mall will remain closed until further notice.
Police officers removed the SUV’s driver from the vehicle after the fire spread. Authorities conducted field sobriety tests on the driver, but he was released. No arrests were made.
One person was taken to the hospital, while the severity of the injuries sustained by those involved was unknown, according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department.
The Sheriff’s Department is continuing to investigate the cause of the crash.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/28/wwe.headline: WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/28/wwe.author: Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering international breaking news
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.
Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.
Reporter covering local transportation
Maryland bridge closure alert mistakenly sent callers to sex hotline
People seeking information about a Maryland bridge closure amid Thursday’s storm were in for a surprise: They were mistakenly directed to a sex hotline.
The Maryland Department of Emergency Management sent residents a public safety alert Thursday afternoon warning that the strong Thanksgiving storm had closed the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
That alert mistakenly directed callers to a sex hotline rather than the Maryland Transportation Authority, or MDTA.

In a statement, Maryland Transportation Authority spokesman Brad Tanner said the authority was “aware of the unfortunate error” included in the emergency alert’s callback number. The agency has corrected the error, Tanner said in the statement.
“We know this was distressing to many Marylanders,” Tanner said. “Emergency alerts are critical, lifesaving tools that require accuracy, and the MDTA takes this error very seriously.”
Thursday’s storm, the worst to hit on Thanksgiving Day in decades, left hundreds of thousands of people without power up and down the East Coast.
The roughly 4.3-mile-long Bay Bridge is notorious for not having shoulders. Some people are so scared of crossing it that they pay other drivers to take them.
This month, the MDTA said plans to replace the bridge are moving forward after securing final federal environmental approval. Construction is expected to begin as soon as 2032, the agency said.
A Denver man is trapping and egging Waymo’s self-driving cars, police say
The Waymo eggings follow a pattern, Denver police say.

First, the middle-aged man parks his silver Toyota Corolla in front of one of the self-driving cars, stopping the vehicle from moving, a police report says. Then, police say, the man takes orange road cones out of his trunk and places them in front of the Waymo so it can’t move.
The man often then pelts the robotic car with eggs and drives away, leaving the Waymo trapped, the police report says.
An investigator working for Waymo told police the company has recorded 30 incidents of a bearded, ponytailed man trapping and egging its vehicles.

Matt Jablow, a spokesperson for the Denver District Attorney’s Office, said in a statement that his office would work with the city attorney’s office “to identify the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”

Since Waymo launched in Denver in September 2025, the vehicles have driven past barricades into a farmers market, come close to driving over a freshly paved road and received a parking ticket, local television station 9News reported.
But Mayor Mike Johnston said this week that Waymo cars are mostly working well in Denver.
“They’re popular, energy-friendly, efficient, and affordable,” he said in a statement. “There have been a few expected hiccups here and there, but overall they’re a good egg.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/guatem.headline: Trump crackdown shatters US hopes for Guatemalans displaced by climate crisis

paragraphs.text: The small plots of farmland in Caparrosa, an Indigenous Maya Ch’orti’ village in eastern Guatemala, are bone dry. It’s mid-June, and the rainy season should have started a month and a half ago, but it’s barely rained at all. The maize is just a few inches tall, and some plots are completely bare.

Lidia Molina is nursing her two-and-a-half-year-old daughter, Karla, sitting on a dusty step next to skinny dogs and chickens. “We haven’t planted our maize yet; it’s too dry,” Molina, 30, said. “We’re hoping it will rain soon, or else we’ll have to make do with whatever my husband sends us.” She is thin and her daughter weighs only 19lb (8.5kg), more typical for a nine-month-old.

The Maya Ch’orti’ have survived centuries of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing by colonial settlers and feudal landowners, maintaining their traditional subsistence way of life despite losing land, water sources, ancestral knowledge and language.

But climate breakdown has pushed them to the brink. Guatemala is one of the top 20 countries most vulnerable to climate change, with two-thirds of the population expected to face water shortages by 2050, according to the United Nations Environmental Program (Unep). Indigenous peoples, who account for nearly half Guatemala’s population of 19 million, are often found in the most remote regions without basic infrastructure such as tap water or irrigation systems. It is these areas that are facing the most severe climate impacts.

In the past 15 years, as erratic rainfall causes subsistence crops to fail, thousands of Guatemalans, many of them Indigenous, are believed to have taken out loans or pawned small plots of ancestral land to fund migration to the United States in hope of finding work to save their families from starvation.

Donald Trump, in his second stint in the White House, has ramped up deportations of migrants, many of whom who had been living and paying taxes in the US for years, severing an economic lifeline for their families back home. Now, as rainfall grows even more unpredictable and dries up regional agricultural labor opportunities, rural communities in Guatemala are running out of options.

Caparrosa, where Molina lives, is located in the ancestral homeland of the Maya Ch’orti’ people, and is one of thousands of tiny rural communities in what is known as the Dry Corridor, a 1,000-mile stretch that covers almost a third of Central America, from southern Mexico to Panama. It’s a spectacular, mountainous and relatively dry area.

For millennia, the dry corridor’s six-month rainy season began in early May, with a relatively dry spell midway through, known as the canicula. Millions of Indigenous and non-Indigenous subsistence farmers timed their plantings – maize, beans and other basic foods – to this seasonal rainfall. Few communities had water capture or irrigation systems.

By the 2000s, the changing climate began to have devastating effects, when heavy rain and flooding caused catastrophic damage in the area. These crisis conditions helped persuade the government to pass its 2013 climate change framework law, making Guatemala the second country in the Americas – after Mexico – to pass explicit climate legislation.
Then came the drought. The rainy season came later and later, and the canicula got longer, hotter and drier.
By 2019, five years of failed harvests had left 1.2 million people in the region needing emergency food aid. Children were dying from malnutrition.

Lidia Molina and her husband, Brian Pérez, are not their real names, which the Guardian is not disclosing, for their security. They were surviving at that time on just a few tortillas each a day, and several of their children showed signs of malnourishment, including distended bellies and hair loss.

The relentless drought triggered the first wave of mass climate displacement from the dry corridor: 188,000 Hondurans and 185,000 Guatemalans traveling in family groups were detained at the US southern border in 2019, an eightfold increase from 2016.
By 2021, the drought had intensified and the situation in Caparrosa was desperate, and so was Pérez.

To escape the worsening drought, Pérez was about to embark on one of the most dangerous migrations in the world with his 10-year-old son Wilson, traveling more than 2,000 miles (3,300km) through Mexico to get to the US border.

To pay his “coyote”, a local guide for informal migration routes, Pérez had handed over the deed to the land where more than a dozen people, the entire extended family, live in a cluster of modest adobe shacks. The land would serve as collateral for a loan to cover the passage, which Pérez hoped to pay off once he found a job in the US.
Fast forward to June 2026. Pérez was not in Caparrosa. Wilson was, and he was 16 by now. The skinny teenager was taller and more solemn and he had a migration nightmare to recount.
The journey across Mexico was really tough, he said, but the US was worse.

Then US president Joe Biden had ostensibly stopped the family separations at the border that surged during Trump’s first term, but that was not the reality Wilson and many others encountered. “They didn’t let us cross, and separated me and my dad,” he told the Guardian.
Biden had also continued enforcing title 42, Trump’s pandemic-era executive order to automatically turn away most asylum seekers without hearing their cases.

Exhausted after a month traveling overland, Pérez and his son Wilson were taken away separately and detained by the US border authorities in a large multi-storey detention center in Texas. Their American dream was over before it had even begun.
“It was really hard [in detention], not much food or water,” Wilson said. “I didn’t see or speak to [my dad] for two months, until they sent us back to Guatemala.”

Since then, his father has been spending long periods away from home, working south of the US border to keep the family from destitution – and to pay back the debt he owes the coyote. He has travelled as far as southern Mexico to work on banana plantations, and sometimes his family don’t know where he is or when he’ll be coming back.

Pérez’s absences mean more responsibility on Wilson to help his grandfather and uncles in the fields when he’s not in school. He held out a large plastic bowl full of maize kernels, saved from last season’s meager crop, ready to plant when it rains again. “It did rain a little a couple of weeks back, but we’d been too busy day laboring for other farmers, so our land wasn’t ready for planting,” said Wilson. “Anyway, we don’t have enough money for fertilizer yet.”

Ironically, synthetic fertilizer is mostly made from the same fossil fuels that, when burned, are the main driver of the greenhouse gas emissions causing global heating – and turbo-charging the drought and erratic rainfall in the Dry Corridor. The cost of synthetic fertilizers has also surged thanks to the illegal wars in Ukraine and Iran.

A week or two later, an update came through from Lidia Molina that Wilson had finally planted the maize after a lightning storm soaked the earth, more than 50 days late. But the rain didn’t last, and not long afterwards they lost the whole crop, Molina said, because the maize was too small and fragile then to endure the canicula.
Yet some communities in the region have found ways to adapt to the changing climate.

In another Ch’orti’ village, Corozal Arriba, just 15 miles north across the mountains from Caparrosa, farming families are producing an abundance of organically farmed fruits and vegetables: tomatoes, eggplant, peppers and potatoes.

Amid the worsening drought, and with no international aid or climate finance or government funding for long-term adaptation measures, the community worked with a grassroots Ch’orti’ organization called Comundich in recent years to build three relatively simple and cheap reservoirs and an irrigation system to pipe in water from a mountain spring. It was a process of trial and error, learning from YouTube videos and local agronomists, but the reservoirs have been a gamechanger: malnutrition and forced migration rates are way down, residents said.
Comundich has helped build almost 20 reservoirs across the territory so far, but there are hundreds of Ch’orti’ villages like Caparrosa where farmers are still 100% dependent on the rain.
Then in late June, just after Wilson planted the maize, which then failed, Pérez got in touch. He was in the United States.

Ten days earlier, he had crossed over the border near the Mexican city of Juárez and its west Texas sister city El Paso, on the other side of the international line that follows the Rio Grande. He had traveled overland for four weeks with 20 or so other Ch’orti’ subsistence farmers, all struggling to support their families. Pérez said that this time he’d used his father’s land as collateral to pay the same coyote, whom he now owes 145,000 quetzales, or almost $20,000.

“I really tried in Guatemala,” Perez said. “And I went to Mexico, working long, hard days in extreme heat in the banana plantations so the coyote wouldn’t take out the house. But you can’t get ahead, and I want more for my family. The weather has changed, it doesn’t rain when it should, and out there it’s just you, the crops and God.”

Droughts, floods, extreme heat, desertification and other climate-related disasters forcibly displaced 250 million people globally over the past decade, the equivalent of 70,000 displacements every day, according to the UN refugee agency. There is no reliable data on how many people from the Dry Corridor have been displaced – internally or across international borders – by climate change. But in the past decade and a half, thousands of poor rural Guatemalans on the frontlines of climate breakdown are believed to have traveled north in hopes of reaching the US.
Under current international law, neither climate change nor famine alone are considered legitimate justifications for claiming asylum.

The US is the biggest historic emitter of the greenhouse gases that cause climate breakdown. It also has a track record of protecting fossil-fuel interests while delaying or blocking action on funding for climate adaptation or reparations being paid by wealthy polluting countries to compensate for climate-driven loss and damage in poor countries like Guatemala.

“Now that I made it to America, little by little I’m going to pay off the debt, and after that the coyote will return the deeds to my mom and dad,” Pérez said. “I’ll only stay until I’ve saved up to make improvements to my house, and then I’ll go back to my family.”

Pérez is aware that the Trump administration is carrying out raids across the US to detain and deport immigrants. He is taking precautions, and rarely goes out except to work as a kitchen hand in a Chinese restaurant, hoping for the best.

Meanwhile, Jorge Cruz, who is from Guayabo, a Ch’orti’ community south-west of Caparrosa, also used his family’s farmland as collateral to head for the US in 2021 and ended up working in construction in Minneapolis. (Cruz is a pseudonym to protect his identity.)
By 2025, he was sending money home to his wife every two weeks and slowly paying off the debt he owed the coyote.

But early one morning last September, he and a colleague were surrounded by ICE trucks after stopping at a gas station to buy coffee and breakfast sandwiches before work. Cruz was arrested, and spent 70 days in an ICE detention center in Wisconsin, before being deported back to Guatemala wearing the same clothes he’d had on that day in September. He lost all his belongings, including the keyboard and guitar he played in the church band, he said.

About a third of Guatemalans put on deportation flights in 2025 had been employed in construction, according to the Guatemalan Institute of Migration, with others working as pilots, accountants, house painters, farmers, mechanics, electricians and waiters, and a whole host of other professions that contributed to the US economy. They were paying US taxes and sending billions of dollars to the Guatemalan economy through remittances.

Trump’s mass deportation campaign shows no sign of abating, despite the drubbing by Democrats in the midterm elections and his anti-immigration tactics being a factor in turning voters against the Republicans.
Still, Pérez, in the United States, is hopeful. In mid-November, he said he had just finished paying off his debts and could now start saving to build a decent house in Caparrosa.
“It’s not easy, but if I keep my head down I think I’ll be fine. It’s a risk, but Wilson is grown now. If something happens to me, he will look after his siblings.”

Cruz, however, speaking to the Guardian in Guatemala City, where he found work in construction after being deported back to Guayabo, said: “I felt like crying when they sent me back with nothing, without having achieved my goal to provide for my children and build a better house.” He added: “But I still have that American dream.”
In the past, deportees would try to reach the US again, but the current immigration crackdown is so cruel that Cruz said, for now, returning feels too risky.

His family home, like most in Guayabo, consists of a couple of simple dusty adobe rooms, with an outdoor toilet, kitchen and sink with tap water a couple of days a week. There are a few bigger, more western-style houses that belong to neighbors with relatives who made it in the US.

For Cruz, like Pérez and most other Guatemalan climate migrants, the expensive and dangerous trek to the US wasn’t a first, second or even third choice. Speaking outside his workplace in Guatemala City, Cruz said he hadn’t finished paying back the loan for his journey, and the coyote still had two land deeds, one for a half-acre plot that Cruz bought after years of working in the sugar plantations. The other is an acre plot owned by his father, Don Clementino, that had once belonged to his grandfather.

“It worries me that the coyote could come here at any time,” Don Clementino said at his home in Guayabo. “That one acre is where I plant corn and beans for the family. The climate isn’t the same any more, so it doesn’t yield much of a harvest, but that’s the only land I have to leave to my children.”

Guayabo is rockier than Caparrosa and particularly arid, with few natural springs and limited access to clean water for drinking, cooking and hygiene. Parasites and other gastrointestinal diseases are common, as are worms and insects that burrow into the skin.

Forced migration is the norm. Historically, a lot of men and boys from Guayabo would spend six months a year working in the sugar cane fields on the Pacific coast. Others have crossed the border to Honduras for the coffee harvest. Both crops involve backbreaking work for low wages, which is relied upon by many Indigenous Guatemalans, who have the highest rates of poverty and child malnutrition in Latin America, according to Unicef.

Mario Ramírez, 58, also of Guayabo, has traveled to Honduras each year to harvest coffee since he was just 11. Back then, the going rate was half a quetzal (50 cents) for every box of coffee beans harvested, a rate that has risen gradually to 20 quetzales ($3).
“The pay is better now, but there’s no coffee to pick because of the weather. The rains have changed,” Ramírez said.

Like subsistence farming, these commodity crops are on the decline due to climate change. And with migration to the United States growing more difficult, the people of Guayabo are left with few options.

Guatemala is suffering far more extreme weather events, drought, floods, and higher temperatures, while the latest El Niño cycle is expected to be punishing. Yet the average rainfall nationally hasn’t really changed over the past few decades. According to Edwin Castellanos, Guatemala’s vice-minister of natural resources and climate change, this presents opportunities.

“The problem is water distribution, and the solution is storage, which isn’t expensive,” Castellanos said. “The ministry of agriculture has programs to promote water storage and irrigation, but the challenge is reaching thousands of farmers. Guatemala is a small country, and we don’t have sufficient resources or personnel.”

Rodimiro Castillo, founder of the grassroots Maya Ch’orti’ group Comundich, believes that the Dry Corridor can be productive and provide a dignified life for the Ch’orti’ people. But only if the approach to adaptation is more radical and begins to address some of the historical injustices dating back to land seizures and ethnic cleansing by colonial settlers and the military dictatorship, which has left large swathes of ancestral Ch’orti’ territory in the hands of private landowners.

“There is water, but it is not in the hands of those who need it, it is in the hands of those who seized it,” said Castillo. “So we are trying to break this narrative that life is not possible in our territory, the Dry Corridor. It is possible.”

The improvised irrigation system in Corozal was proof of concept for Comundich, which is now pitching project ideas to the government and international aid agencies, pushing for more focus on long-term sustainable adaptation measures rather than short-term handouts.

“It changed everything for us,” Elsa Calderón , a subsistence and community organizer in Corozal, said of the reservoir system. “There used to be a lot of malnourished elderly people and children. Some were so terribly thin that they died [but] this hardly happens any more, we grow enough vegetables to eat and sell some at the market.
“We want to build another bigger reservoir,” she told me, “so there’s enough water for our maize and beans, too. That’s our vision.”

Developing countries need an estimated $305bn a year for adaptation projects such as coastal restoration, reforestation, and rainwater capture, storage and irrigation systems for small-scale farmers, according to the latest analysis from Unep. However, there was less than a 10th of this in public finance available from the wealthiest and most-polluting nations for developing countries in 2024.

“People want to remain on their land. They don’t want to be taken to the moon or to Europe, despite the destruction the Global North is causing,” said Adrián Martínez, director of La Ruta del Clima, a climate justice organization based in Costa Rica. “But the scale and timelines for finance are wildly out of step with how urgent the situation is.”

Without a massive injection of international finance now, Castellanos believes that parts of the Dry Corridor will become so arid that adaptation measures will become prohibitively expensive, and farming impossible.

Living off the land is so deep for the Maya Ch’orti’ people, it’s part of who they are, physically and spiritually, and they aren’t willing to accept displacement from their ancestral territory as a fait accompli because of the climate destruction wreaked by others.
Comundich’s Castillo said the communities need the resources and aid agencies to “get out of the way” while they put the resources to best use for future sustainability.

“We want to return to our cosmological vision, to our relationship with nature, to collective strength,” Castillo said. “We have deep roots in the land and in Mother Earth. After all, we are the original people of this place.”

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/middleeast/.headline: Freed From a Notorious Syrian Prison, but Still Trapped by Its Terror

paragraphs.text: Prison is still etched on his body.
A knuckle on his ring finger smashed from a beating.
Above his left eye, a scar.
On the bottom of his feet, more scars.
His broken, rotting teeth.
And his mind.

Months after Ahmed al-Shalh was released from Syria’s most notorious prison, he still sat in the corner of the ramshackle tent his family lived in, knees gripped tight to his chest, the threats of prison guards still echoing in his ears.
When he spoke at all, he spoke in a whisper.
That was more than four years ago — before rebels overthrew the Assad regime, pried open the doors of Syria’s prisons and freed tens of thousands of prisoners like him.

The fanfare over these prisoner releases often gave the impression of a happy end to their suffering. But for many, it was just the beginning of another solitary road, one marked by deep wounds and the struggle to find a place in a broken country trying to rebuild itself.

I began following Mr. al-Shalh only a few months after he got out of prison. Since then, he has reveled in some unexpected wins — he got married and has had two children — while enduring repeated blows. He, his wife and two young children were recently evicted from their apartment because work is scarce, salaries are low and he could not pay the rent. They now live in a small, stuffy modular container — an improvement over the tent his family lived in during the war, but far from the home he envisioned for his young family.
There are few social services to help former prisoners like him. He lives a life of worry, feeling abandoned by the former rebels who run Syria’s government.
The weight of responsibility is so heavy that at times he wishes he never started a family, with three people reliant on him.
“I’m worried about my children’s future,” he said recently. “Sometimes, I wish I never got out of prison.”
Prison

Mr. al-Shalh was 19 when the Assad regime’s security forces stormed into his family’s small house in 2012, dragged him from his bed and threw him into the back of a pickup truck, according to him, his relatives and the Syrian Network for Human Rights, which documented his detention at the time.

It was in the early years of the Syrian uprising that turned into a civil war, and such arrests were common. Mr. al-Shalh was accused of being a rebel fighting against the regime and shooting at government soldiers. He denied it, insisting he had only participated in a few peaceful protests and had never held a gun.
He spent more than 10 years in prison — most of them in the notorious Sednaya prison’s dank, overcrowded cells, with little food or water.

Sometimes, he and other prisoners were made to stand outside for hours, naked under freezing rain, he said. The soles of his feet were beaten with a hose until he could not walk anymore. Interrogations meant beatings with metal rods that left some people dead, he said.
On the morning of May 3, 2022, a prison guard came to Mr. al-Shalh’s cell door and called out his name.
He thought he was about to be executed.
Instead, he was freed.
That day, hundreds of Syrian prisoners were released in surprise amnesties — one of three that year issued by President Bashar al-Assad.
Mr. al-Shalh, 30 by then, said he was given military boots with no laces to wear and a conscription order telling him to report for mandatory military service within 24 hours.
As he left, a prison guard looked at his papers and saw how long Mr. al-Shalh had been imprisoned. He recalled the guard being surprised and saying, “How have we not killed you yet?”
Mr. al-Shalh’s family said they were shocked by his release. They thought he was already dead.

He had lost nearly a third of his body weight in prison. A video captured the moments when Mr. al-Shalh returned to his neighborhood, carried on the shoulders of a cousin — his weak hands held up by two other relatives.
By then, his parents and siblings had fled their home in the coastal city of Latakia because of the war and were living in a camp for displaced people. It was not the homecoming he imagined.
He was no longer sleeping on a cold concrete floor in a crowded cell. Instead, he was in a crowded tent, sleeping on a thin mattress on the cold ground, surrounded by his family.
At times, he said he felt as if he had traded one prison cell for another.
His mother, Muna Ariditi, said she would find him tightly curled up in a fetal position, trying to make himself as small as possible.
“‘Ahmed, you’re not in prison anymore,’” she recalled saying to him, again and again, “I wanted him to forget.”
He could not. He struggled even to leave the tent.
“We lived a lifetime in prison,” he said. “That doesn’t go away overnight.”

At first, he hardly ate, accustomed to the paltry portions in prison. His broken, decayed teeth testify to years of beatings, no dental care and trying to chew olive pits when there was nothing else to eat in prison.
Even the sound of children playing outside put him on edge.

Eventually, his younger brother Mahmoud forced him to go outside. At first, they walked a few feet, around neighboring tents. As Mr. al-Shalh grew stronger — and less frightened — they walked along the windy roads around the camp.
His body ached, and he tired quickly. The only job he said he could get was picking olives during the harvest season for less than $1.50 a day.
“Everyone is asking about the detainees and demanding their release,” he said in his parent’s tent in 2023, before the Assad regime fell. “But when the detainees get out, they won’t hire us.”
“We don’t want your charity,” he said at the time. “Just give us jobs.”
Joining the Rebels
By that time, Mr. al-Shalh’s brother Mahmoud had become a fighter with Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, an Islamist rebel group, one of many factions trying to overthrow the Assad regime.
Soon enough, Mahmoud began taking Mr. al-Shalh to checkpoints and to the front line, to help him venture farther from the tent.
Mahmoud and the other rebels gave Mr. al-Shalh military fatigues to wear. Pretty soon, that was not enough. He wanted to pick up a rifle and fight. He wanted revenge.
He had been imprisoned on accusations of being a rebel.
A decade of imprisonment eventually turned him into one.
“I wanted justice,” he said, “for at least 10 percent of what I suffered in prison.”
The bang of the rifle scared him at first. His body was weak and his eyesight poor. But among the revolutionaries, being a former detainee had cachet.

The civil war had been largely frozen for several years. At the front lines, both sides would fire at each other, with little change on the battlefield. For Mr. al-Shalh, it became the only place he relaxed, shooting toward an unseen enemy and picturing the prison guards at Sednaya.
Then, in November 2024, Mr. al-Shalh and other rebel fighters were told to prepare for a major battle.
By then, though, Mr. al-Shalh had other responsibilities.
A couple of months after he joined the rebels, he and his mother visited a former detainee who had shared a cell with Mr. al-Shalh. During the visit, they met the man’s daughter, Batool al-Asaad.

Having spent his 20s inside a cell, Mr. al-Shalh was eager to catch up on milestones he had missed, marriage chief among them. And unlike many other families, neither Ms. al-Asaad nor her parents had reservations about marriage with a former detainee.

Ms. al-Asaad had already seen how her father, who had been released in 2019, struggled to adjust to life after imprisonment. He, too, could not tolerate any speaking above a whisper for months. It was a challenge, she knew, but one she understood. She and Mr. al-Shalh got married.
When the rebels issued their deployment orders, Ms. al-Asaad begged her husband not to go. By then, they already had a daughter, Muna, named after his mother.
He decided to go anyway. It was his chance to get revenge. Mr. al-Shalh took a final photo of himself with his rifle and dressed in full camouflage, in case he was killed in battle.
After the Dictatorship
Within a few weeks, Syrian rebels toppled the Assad regime, took over the government and established a new military.
Mr. al-Shalh wanted to leave fighting behind, but a lack of any other jobs has kept him in the military ranks.
So one day on the outskirts of Latakia, Mr. al-Shalh sat on guard duty at a military outpost.
His wife called to check when he would be home. Muna, then 1 year old, blabbered over the speakerphone, her voice filling the tiny bunker made of ammunition boxes and a disused refrigerator.
“I’ll see you tomorrow,” Mr. al-Shalh told Muna.

It was her birthday, but there would be no presents or cake. Ms. al-Assad was eight months pregnant at the time with their second child, and even though he did odd jobs to supplement his pay as a soldier, Mr. al-Shalh struggled to buy what they needed for a new baby.
Money Problems
The debts never go away.

A private support group for former detainees helped him buy some jewelry for Ms. al-Asaad when they got married, but she has sold most of it to help pay off their debts. He said he also sold his motorcycle.

This year, their landlord demanded more rent — nothing his $250-a-month military salary could afford — and the family moved into one of the metal prefabricated shelter units erected after the 2023 earthquake. It has no electricity or water. They live in constant fear that thieves will break in and steal what little they have.
The morning after Muna’s birthday, still dressed in fatigues, Mr. al-Shalh arrived at his uncle’s house, where his parents have been living.

I watched as he called out “Mesho,” his nickname for his daughter. She came immediately, crawling excitedly. He smiled widely, scooped her up and planted kiss after kiss on her cheeks and chubby hands.
Sometimes when he is playing with Muna, he laughs in disbelief, having never imagined that he would get out of prison alive, much less build a life.
From his backpack, he takes out two packets of instant coffee for Muna to play with. It is not much, but cradled in her father’s lap, she is happy.
PTSD
When the rebels reached Syria’s capital, Damascus, on Dec. 8, 2024, Mr. al-Shalh was in the coastal city of Latakia, celebrating with his family.

His family watched videos of the rebels storming Sednaya and other prisons, freeing prisoners. It should have been a joyous moment for a former detainee like him, but the sounds and imagery were too much.
“Enough!” he screamed, his family recalled. “Enough!”
Since his release, Mr. al-Shalh has had recurring nightmares, sometimes screaming in his sleep, Ms. al-Asaad said.

In a recurring one, he is back in Sednaya, sitting with prisoners, their backs against the wall as a prison guard approaches, yelling and turning on an electrical prod to beat them. In the nightmare, he presses up against the wall, trying to disappear.
He also emerged from prison with a temper, at times lashing out at his family, then apologizing.
That temper landed him back in prison this year.
In March, a large fight broke out outside his brother’s home. His relatives had accused their neighbors of informing on Mr. al-Shalh back in 2012, leading to his original imprisonment.

Mr. al-Shalh was coming back from his shift, still dressed in military fatigues and carrying his Kalashnikov, as the fight with the neighbors erupted. When he arrived at the scene, he said he tried to remain calm. But then he was hit in the face with a rock, breaking more of his teeth.
“I lost all sense, and I don’t remember what I did,” he said.

He opened fire on the neighbor’s home and two shop fronts, he and relatives said. No one was injured, he said, but he and others on both sides of the melee were arrested. Latakia police did not answer questions about the episode.
Mr. al-Shalh spent a month in a military prison.
“I thought I was back in Sednaya,” he said. He was not mistreated this time, he said, but “I wanted to smash my head against the wall.”
When he was released — after a judge reached a reconciliation agreement between the two families — he said he wanted to go back to Sednaya, as a free man.
Only then, he said, could he put the demons to rest.
Sednaya
Mr. al-Shalh said he wanted to revisit the cells he had been in and find where he had scratched his name on the wall.
For prisoners, scrawling their names on the walls was a way to let people know they had been there, fearing they would be executed and disappear without a trace.

He grows quiet walking the empty halls, using his cellphone’s flashlight to inspect the cell walls. On the home screen of his phone is a picture of Muna smiling on the sand at the beach, her few teeth almost a mirror of her father’s toothy grin.
The young men guarding the prison have given him only an hour. I follow him from cell after cell, where he finds nothing. He is running out of time.
He stops outside the thick metal door of another cell and goes in. Suddenly, he is almost giddy.
He finds his name, scratched in yellow paint. “This is what I’ve been searching for,” he says, beaming.
Leaving the cell, he takes out a cigarette, relaxed.
His name is still here. And so is he.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/us/politics/snap-.headline: Millions of Children Are Losing Food Stamps

paragraphs.text: When Republicans pushed record cuts in food stamps through Congress last year, they insisted that one group of Americans would remain unaffected: children.

But as many as two million children have lost benefits, about one in eight who had them, state data suggests. The drop indicates that the reductions in food stamps, championed by President Trump, have affected a broader and more vulnerable population than predicted.

While it is not wholly clear why families with children have lost aid, the decline has been driven in part by incentives in the law for states to demand more proof of eligibility, which some applicants say makes it hard to get help. Tens of millions of people rely on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamps, making it central to the safety net.

While the cuts were part of a package that included large tax breaks for the wealthy, the overhaul also reflected conservative views that SNAP attracted fraud and discouraged work, hurting people the aid aimed to help. With a decline in SNAP rolls already twice as large as the Congressional Budget Office predicted, the law’s accelerating effects test the idea that a smaller safety net will provide poor people with adequate protection.

The decline in SNAP is especially steep in Louisiana, where enrollment among children has dropped by nearly a quarter since July 2025, when the law passed. With grocery bills at persistent highs, parents losing benefits say that they skip meals to feed children, divert rent money to groceries, serve inexpensive, unhealthy food, and worry to a disturbing degree. Some parents with low wages qualify for SNAP despite working full time.

The strain is evident at the Wilcox Academy of Early Learning, which runs three well-regarded child care centers in New Orleans, a city where Black children are more than 10 times as likely as white children to be poor. Before the cuts, most Wilcox students received SNAP, as did many teachers with children of their own. So many have now lost benefits that parents no longer cater the school festival, and the cook stretches school meals so teachers can take leftovers home.
“They come in asking: Do I have any food for them and their kids?” said the cook, Raymond Brown. “Times are hard if they’re asking me.”

Among those struggling is Ivana Norgah, the gregarious anchor of the toddler room, whose responsibilities include the little people in her lap and a big one at home. At 285 pounds, her son, Kane Mitchell, is a high school lineman with college football hopes.

After losing SNAP in a dispute with the state about whether her fluctuating earnings left her eligible, Ms. Norgah, 43, has become a chronic meal-skipper who pretends she is not hungry when bringing school leftovers to her son. Still, she runs out of staples as basic as peanut butter, and fills him with fast food, at times with loyalty points. “It’s definitely changed the way we eat,” she said.

Mindful of his mother’s feelings, Kane, 16, tries to limit complaints about his grumbling stomach and speaks tactfully of “the red bean situation” — all beans and no meat. “The food — I’m not going to say it’s limited, but it’s, like, limited,” he said.
A Cascade of Consequences

Republicans’ longstanding complaints about SNAP accelerated after the Biden administration unilaterally raised monthly benefits, pushing annual costs above $100 billion. Nearly 42 million Americans received SNAP before the cuts, including 16 million children.

Congress reduced benefits, required more recipients to work, and shifted costs to the states, with new incentives to scrutinize applications. Congressional scorekeepers said the overhaul would cut $187 billion over nine years, or about 20 percent when fully in effect.
In dismissing warnings that children would suffer, Republicans noted that the law’s most prominent feature — the work rules — exempted most families with children.

“If you have young children at home, your benefits are unaffected by this bill,” said Representative Dusty Johnson of South Dakota. Representative Glenn Thompson of Pennsylvania, the chairman of the House Agriculture Committee, said the law would protect “the most vulnerable among us, including children.”

But it ignited large declines among adults and children alike. While only 14 states, including Louisiana, publish children’s caseloads, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning research group, compiled unpublished data from others.

Its sample of 29 states, the most comprehensive count, found that the number of children on SNAP had fallen 14 percent since the law passed. Projecting nationwide, the center estimates that enrollment has dropped by 5.7 million people, and two million are children.
Mr. Johnson and Mr. Thompson, the G.O.P. lawmakers, did not respond to requests for comment.

Enrollment is dropping in part because states demand more proof of eligibility. The law imposes large penalties on states that make excessive errors in awarding benefits. Unless Louisiana reduces errors, it will owe $160 million.

Some parents losing aid are eligible and manage to re-enroll. Others give up. Still others are properly disenrolled, with net incomes above the eligibility line (about $27,000 for a family of three), yet struggle to feed their families.
Camille Conaway, who runs SNAP at Louisiana’s health department, said there was no way to know how many people losing aid remained eligible, but the number could be substantial.

“There are tens of thousands of families that probably still qualify for SNAP — they just didn’t stay on the rolls for whatever reason,” she said. “The goal is always: If you’re eligible, reapply, give us the verification and let’s get you back in.”
Eating Less to Feed the Kids

Steneisha Morehead, a Wilcox teacher with three children, lost SNAP last year amid document requests she found “overwhelming.” She thinks a raise of $1 an hour might have left her ineligible. But she remains unsure. Earning $18 to $20 an hour, Wilcox teachers often hover around the SNAP eligibility line.

Without the monthly benefit of $500, Ms. Morehead, 30, skips meals and has stopped offering her children seconds. She is moving in with her sister, who has SNAP, in hopes of eating more and worrying less. “It’s always on my mind — ‘Am I going to have enough?’” she said.

Another Wilcox teacher, Jennifer James, lost SNAP, got it back and lost it again — a confusing sequence, she said, since her income did not change. Ms. James, 36, said her children had not complained about the switch from produce to processed food. But it has aggravated her lupus disease. Her face burns, her lips swell, and “my chest tightens up like I can’t breathe,” she said.
Chesshiara George, a former Wilcox teacher, lost SNAP for five months. She failed to file proof of her earnings, she said, but the state lost other documents.
Without her $400 monthly benefit, Ms. George, 35, skipped meals, scoured food pantries and sold blood plasma to buy groceries. She calls her guilt and depression about her son’s diet “life altering.”

When the boy, a 5-year-old enthralled with superheroes, noticed her fasting and offered to share, she provided reassurance. Eat up “because you’re a superhero,” she said. “You can save the world for me.”
Bionca Fleury, a Wilcox parent, went nine months without SNAP while trying to confirm eligibility for herself and three daughters. “I was worried every day — ‘What am I going to cook?’” she said.
Her eventual success in reclaiming help, like that of Ms. George, reinforces the idea that eligible families are losing aid.

Her cousin lost SNAP after the state said it was missing wage statements that she insisted she had sent. One argument for safety net programs is that they may protect single mothers from depending on abusive men. A single mother with three children, including a disabled daughter, Ms. Fleury’s cousin began accepting groceries from a man seeking romance. Now, she said, “it’s almost like I’ve got a stalker.”
She regrets his expectations, but not the food.
“I’m a mom. I’m going to do what I have to do,” she said.
Fraud or Red Tape?
Louisiana’s SNAP rolls have lost about 6,000 children a month under the new law.

Ms. Conaway, the state official, noted several potential explanations. Better jobs might have raised parents’ incomes. New work rules (for parents of children 14 or older) might have encouraged employment.

Requests for more proof of eligibility also played a role, she said, with the state demanding written proof of rent and paying a data broker, Equifax, to verify wages. “That’s part of it, yes,” she said. “It’s not aimed at closing anyone’s case — it’s aimed at getting the payment right” and avoiding penalties.

Notably, the state conducts an extra review of working households, because their fluctuating incomes increase the risk of payment errors. Since many working-aged households have children, the review means that the children’s aid that lawmakers vowed to protect tends to face added scrutiny.
Angela Rachidi of the conservative American Enterprise Institute said that much of the decline was likely due to “fewer ineligible households receiving aid,” rather than problems with red tape.

Under previous rules, she said, states had little incentive for strict oversight, since the federal government paid benefits and rarely punished mistakes. Facing the threat of penalties, she said “states were forced to tighten up eligibility.”

While the transition off aid can be difficult, “if you have limits, you have to follow them,” she said. “The solution isn’t to rely on one program to eliminate all hardship. The solution is to create a system of upward mobility.”

Some SNAP critics see falling enrollment as evidence that the program suffered from fraud. Fraud does exist, in a program so large. A friend of Ms. Fleury’s who lost SNAP acknowledged that she was “fabricating” — understating her income to get benefits.

But Ms. Conaway said that most payment errors had come from unintended mistakes, by caseworkers and clients alike, amid complex questions about income and expenses. “In general, payment errors are not fraud,” she said. “The volume is tremendous, and it’s just really hard to get it right.”
‘This too shall pass’

On a recent afternoon, Ms. Norgah, the toddler teacher, arrived at her son’s football practice with precious cargo — chicken and rice from the Wilcox kitchen. “He’s going to love what’s in that pan!” she said.

Like many parents short on food, Ms. Norgah tells herself she can spare her child by eating less. But the reality is more complex. Kane says “I’m hungry” so often that she jokes: “Your name’s not ‘hungry’ — it’s Kane.”

Kane ambled to the car, the hulking star of a contact sport happy to see his mom. Asked to describe their refrigerator, he repeated the word “no” — no juice, no waffles, no neck bones in the beans. Had he gone hungry because they lacked food? He hesitated to upset Ms. Norgah, but said, “Yeah, kind of — I’m not going to lie.”
Then he praised her efforts to keep him fed. “She cares about me eating even more than I care about me eating,” he said.

They both coped by making believe. Ms. Norgah knew she could not fully protect Kane, but told herself she could. Kane knew that his mother skipped meals to feed him, but told himself she did not. “I manipulate my mind to think past it, to pretend she’s full,” he said. “I don’t want to go and be another burden.”
“Never feel like that!” Ms. Norgah said.
“I love my mom,” he said. “I don’t want people to think I come from a bad household.”
Ms. Norgah cried. She allowed herself a boast. When Kane’s teammate texted a picture of his empty refrigerator, Kane found five dollars to send.

The sun had set on an empty field, and the chicken awaited. A gladiator on the gridiron and a man of faith off it, Kane offered a departing thought. “This, too, shall pass,” he said. Then mother and son drove home to eat.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/28/isra.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza kills 2 Doctors Without Borders staff, charity says
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/28/isra.author: Sammy Westfall

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: Is it okay to NOT let guests bring plus-ones to my wedding?
What’s the etiquette for inviting guests to a wedding? Do you automatically include a plus-one for them?

One couple is weighing the rules as the two get ready for their own nuptial celebrations. And in this week’s episode of the “Life Hax” podcast, columnists Shane O’Neill and Carolyn Hax debate the options. (You can find the full episode, which includes more wedding-related dilemmas, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.)

Our letter writer notes that they’ve never needed a date to enjoy a wedding and think it’s “a little silly” to invite plus-ones. They’ve seen different approaches: “We’ve had friends who only invited the partners of guests who were married, engaged, or living together,” they wrote. But “that created way too many weird exclusions.”
So what’s a 30-something to do?
Shane proposes one rubric: “If you know their name and you would be embarrassed to run into them and be like, ‘I didn’t invite you to the wedding,’ invite them to the wedding!”
Carolyn calls that “brilliant.”
The guest list is more about finances than excluding people, Shane adds, because “by the time you’re drunk and doing the Chicken Dance, my worst enemy could be at my wedding.”
Reporter covering breaking news

Humanitarian charity Doctors Without Borders said an Israeli strike killed two of its staff members at a clearly marked Gaza City clinic on Friday — an attack the Israeli military said was targeted at Hamas members “under humanitarian cover.”
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” the group said on X. “This is a direct hit on MSF.”

The Israel Defense Forces said in a statement Saturday that it killed “Hamas terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.” The military said that two men, whom it named, were working as security guards at the clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders “while also serving as terrorists,” without providing evidence. It added that no medical infrastructure in the area was damaged in the strike.
At least 17 members of Doctors Without Borders have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, the charity said.
According to the charity, the premises hit in the attack had been “clearly marked” with its logos and the location had been “communicated to and was known by” the Israeli military.

World Health Organization Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X that attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are “outrageous and unacceptable.” He extended “heartfelt condolences” to Doctors Without Borders colleagues.
Reporter covering international breaking news
WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.
Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.
National correspondent covering Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, with expertise in red states
GOP governors invite Texans to move to their states to flee blue wave
HOUSTON — Republican governors have a message for conservative Texans upset by Democrats sweeping every statewide office: “Texit” and move here!
Sen. Tommy Tuberville, Alabama’s governor-elect, tweeted this week, telling any “red-blooded patriot or business wanting to flee the woke-show that is coming to Texas … Alabama is open for business.”
Not to be outdone, Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry then posted a photo of new billboards he erected in Texas saying: “If you’re from Louisiana, it’s time to come home!”
“Louisiana is leading the nation in economic opportunity,” Landry wrote. “Come home and fill these new job opportunities!”
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt then urged conservative Texans to defect across the northern state line.

“Hey Texans, Oklahoma is open for business, committed to conservative values, and ready to welcome families and entrepreneurs,” Stitt said in a post on X. “Come build your American Dream in Oklahoma!”
Texans — Democrat and Republican alike — had thoughts.
Rep. Joaquin Castro, who as a Texas state lawmaker in 2003 fled to Oklahoma with other Democrats to block Republican congressional redistricting, called Stitt’s invitation “thoughtful” and “kind.”
“I can attest the state was incredibly welcoming,” he said.

Those who rejected the GOP pitch noted that Texas has no state income tax and leads the country in gross domestic product growth and job creation. Others responded with links to Facebook groups offering help to conservative Texans who want to relocate.
“We Texans should all consider Florida or Tennessee now, too,” one retiree in the Houston suburbs posted.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/this-new-sport.headline: This new sports app is designed specifically for women’s sports
techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/this-new-sport.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: A new sports app is looking to change the way fans engage with women’s sports, and it’s doing so without the real-money gambling that has become increasingly common in the sports world.
Called Rival, the app officially launched last weekend on the App Store and Google Play Store, timed to coincide with the National Women’s Soccer League (NWSL) Championship.

With Rival, users can make free-to-play picks, earn points, compete on leaderboards, create and join groups, and connect with other fans. The platform also serves as a hub for discovering women’s sports, bringing together schedules, scores, news, highlights, and information on where to watch.

The app is the brainchild of Kelly DiPaola, whose previous experience includes working for Barbra Streisand and producing unscripted television, including Netflix’s “Selling Sunset.” The idea grew out of her frustration with traditional sports apps, which tend to prioritize scores and statistics over the fan experience. Rather than simply creating another place to check game results, DiPaola envisioned a destination dedicated to women’s sports, where fans could build connections, find community, and feel more invested in the games they follow.

“I’m a passionate sports fan, and my partner, Jodie Taylor, is a former England Lioness and now Technical Director at Arsenal Women,” DiPaola told TechCrunch in an email. “The original spark was my frustration with the disparity in women’s sports coverage on traditional sports betting platforms. I’ve never been particularly good at accepting inequality as the status quo, so I decided to do something about it.”

That vision comes at a time when women’s sports are experiencing record growth in attendance and viewership. Yet greater visibility doesn’t necessarily translate into a better experience for fans, particularly women who participate in mainstream sports communities online.
Platforms such as Reddit, X, and sports-focused forums can expose women — especially women of color and LGBTQ+ athletes — to harassment, abuse, and discriminatory commentary.

The problem is well documented. A 2024 NCAA study found that online abuse targeting student-athletes peaked during March Madness, with women’s basketball players receiving three times as many threats as their male counterparts.

Rival is positioning itself as an alternative to that experience, placing positive social connection and community at the center of its platform. Users can create profiles and statuses, follow other users, and create or join groups around their favorite teams and sports.

“Women’s sports doesn’t just have a visibility problem. It has a participation problem,” DiPaola said. “I wanted to build somewhere that felt like walking into your favorite local bar on a Friday night, where you could turn up on your own and still feel like you belonged, like you were part of something bigger than yourself.”

Although the app is focused on women’s teams and competitions, anyone can join. The platform also includes blocking and reporting tools, private profiles, private groups, in-app support, and moderation features designed to address abusive behavior.

“Our responsibility is to create a safe and welcoming environment for everyone,” DiPaola said. “We have zero tolerance for abuse, harassment, or discrimination, and accounts engaging in such behavior are subject to removal. As our community grows, our moderation capabilities will need to grow with it.”

Another major differentiator is Rival’s decision to avoid real-money sports betting altogether. Instead, the platform centers on what the company describes as “friendly competition,” allowing users to make predictions and compete with friends without putting money on the line.

That distinction is particularly timely as sports betting continues to expand across the U.S., raising concerns about its consequences. According to the American Gaming Association, Americans wagered $166.94 billion on legal sports betting last year. A UCLA study found that, in states allowing online sports gambling, the likelihood of a personal bankruptcy filing increased by around 25%.

At launch, Rival covers 36 leagues and competitions, 1,979 teams, and more than 20,000 athletes internationally. This includes NCAA Women’s Basketball, NCAA Softball, Women’s Professional Football League, EuroLeague, and more.

DiPaola says the company ultimately wants to represent every sport women play, including those that have historically received less coverage. That will mean exploring partnerships to improve data availability for underrepresented sports and leagues.

Looking ahead, Rival also plans to expand its sports coverage, develop its live-picks ecosystem, introduce “richer” social and community features, and bring fan participation closer to live broadcasts.
