bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm752q30q5leo.headline: Myanmar: Dozens killed in military strikes on wedding venue and school
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm752q30q5leo.author: Jack Burgess, BBC Burmese

paragraphs.text: Air strikes by Myanmar's military have killed dozens of people across the South East Asian nation, including at a wedding venue and a school.
Rescuers said at least 21 were confirmed dead, and at least 35 others injured, at the wedding site in Moe Bye village, in the country's southern Shan state, on Saturday afternoon.

On Thursday at least 20 civilians were killed, including students, young monks and teachers, when an air strike hit a school at In Yon village, in central Myanmar's Magway region where resistance forces are active, according to Myanmar's exiled National Unity Government (NUG).
Myanmar's military-led government has not commented on the strikes.
The military also carried out air strikes in Mrauk-U town, in western Myanmar's Rakhine state, on Saturday evening.
At about 20:00 local time (13:30 GMT), a residential area in the town was bombed, reportedly killing more than 10 people and injuring about 20 others.
The area is controlled by the Arakan Army (AA) - one of the strongest ethnic armies fighting the country's military regime.

Military air strikes have been happening almost daily across the country since a coup in 2021 toppled the elected civilian government led by former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, resulting in a lengthy civil war.
Villages have been burned and ground offensives have been carried out by the military on areas it is unable to control, including territories controlled by the NUG and ethnic armed organisations.
The latest strikes come a week after Myanmar was found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
A 2017 military crackdown killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee, but Myanmar denied committing genocide - saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The verdict marked the first time a state had ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/27/belgia.headline: Google told to cease building Belgian datacentre over lack of planning permit

paragraphs.text: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to halt construction work on a large datacentre in the south of the country because the US tech firm’s requests to modify the original terms of the planning permission did not have approval.

“Inspectors visited the site and observed that the building was almost finished, with the structural work completed, even though the permit had been refused,” Raphaël Stokis, a Wallonia regional official, told the public broadcaster RTBF.

Stokis said the 300 workers had been given a verbal order to stop work that had been confirmed in writing to Google. The company said in a statement it was “committed to maintaining an open and collaborative dialogue” with the regional authorities.

Google’s 2025 application to change its plans, notably including a switch from air- to water-cooling, was initially approved by local authorities but later revoked after protests. The company has appealed and a ruling is due early next year.

The vast building, which occupies about 3 hectares (7.4 acres) of a 50-hectare business park on the site of a former coalmine at Aiseau-Presles, about 9 miles west of Charleroi, is one of three originally planned by Google on the site.

Nicolas Yernaux, a regional government spokesperson, told Agence France-Presse on Friday that a report was being submitted to public prosecutors alleging “a major offence: the illegal construction of a building covering 3 hectares”.
The environmental group Greenpeace earlier this week published a report including drone footage that showed Google was carrying on construction work at the site despite lacking the correct permits.

“The tech giant is continuing work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this datacentre was revoked,” Greenpeace said, adding that it had filed an emergency appeal with local planning authorities.
“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region,” the environmental group said. “Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”

Google’s 2024 permit was to construct three smaller air-cooled datacentres, but in 2025 it applied instead to merge two of them into one much larger facility and switch to liquid cooling by drawing 600m3 of water an hour from the nearby Sambre River.

The regional administration initially approved the amendments in April, but residents and protest groups appealed and in August the Wallonia infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, revoked the modified permit over drought concerns.

Google appealed against that decision to Belgium’s council of state and a ruling in the case is expected on 7 January. A company spokesperson said on Friday: “We have halted works consistent with the direction from local authorities and pending additional guidance.

“We have operated in Belgium for over 15 years and remain committed to complying with local laws and an open, collaborative dialogue with government officials and all relevant authorities about our work in Wallonia.”
The legal row is the latest confronting the company in Europe as large tech companies push to build datacentres to support the AI boom.

In October, Finland opened a criminal investigation into possible breaches ⁠of environmental ⁠laws at a planned Google datacentre in the rural north of the country. Work has been halted until environmental impact assessments are completed.

noahpinion.blog/p/its-now-or-never-for-p.headline: It’s now or never for permitting reform in Congress
noahpinion.blog/p/its-now-or-never-for-p.author: IFP

paragraphs.text: This Thanksgiving weekend, I unfortunately suffered a great loss…my sweet rabbit Giggles passed away at the age of 10, due to an ear infection. I’ll write more about him and his life soon. In the meantime, taking a few days off of writing gives me a good opportunity to clear out some of my backlog of guest posts.

This one is especially important. This week the House is set to vote on BAAJA, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This is the most important piece of permitting reform legislation in our lifetimes. For decades, the United States has been building up a regime of anti-development regulations, to the point where it’s basically impossible to build anything of consequence throughout most of the country:

This seemed to work well in the 1990s and the 2000s, when software and finance were America’s biggest engines of growth, and manufacturing was being outsourced to China. But we were simply pushing our physical challenges into the future, and that future can no longer be delayed.

Climate change is much more of an immediate threat today, and yet we can’t build the green energy and the power lines we need in order to bring our emissions down, because the anti-development laws won’t let us. Manufacturing urgently needs to be reshored from China, and yet it’s very hard to build even the most environmentally-friendly factories here, because the anti-development laws won’t let us. Our infrastructure is increasingly unaffordable to maintain, because the anti-development laws make it incredibly hard to get maintenance done. The anti-development laws have our nation by the throat, and they’re throttling the life out of us.

BAAJA is the first serious legislative attempt to dismantle the anti-development regime and replace it with something sane and humane. The Institute For Progress has been at the forefront of promoting and explaining this incredibly important bill. If you want to understand what’s in it, I heavily recommend this explainer by IFP’s Aidan Mackenzie.
So in advance of the big BAAJA vote, I asked Alec Stapp, IFP’s founder, to write a Noahpinion guest post explaining why Congress must vote yes on the bill. Here you go!

We used to be able to build things in this country. But since the 1960s, policymakers have passed a raft of state and federal laws that make it harder to build infrastructure of all kinds, for both good and bad reasons. The substantive protections in laws like the Clean Air Act have delivered enormous benefits relative to their costs. But the procedural rules embedded within some of these laws, especially the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), have created a “litigation doom loop” for projects, while delivering few offsetting benefits.

If an agency fails to document every potentially significant impact, or consider every mitigation measure a plaintiff’s lawyer might dream up, a judge can enjoin the project or vacate its permits and send it back for further review. The uncertainty of these delays raises costs for developers and reduces the scope of projects they consider investing in. It also disproportionately burdens clean energy infrastructure. For example, of the solar projects that required an environmental impact statement between 2010 and 2018, 64% were sued and 32% were ultimately canceled, both higher rates than for fossil fuel projects.

Over the last decade, more and more people have woken up to the costs these procedural roadblocks impose on our everyday lives: higher electricity bills, more expensive fuel, and worse pollution. These are the natural consequences of a permitting system that’s biased toward the status quo by making it difficult to build new infrastructure. In recent years, Congress has made multiple attempts at permitting reform. The two most ambitious efforts — the Building American Energy Security Act of 2022 (BAES) and the Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (EPRA) — ultimately failed. But now new permitting reform champions, including the Senate’s foremost Democratic climate hawks, have pulled together the best bipartisan permitting reform deal yet.

Led by Senators Heinrich, Whitehouse, Capito, and Lee, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would substantially curtail litigation risk for projects while maintaining all of the substantive environmental protections that exist today. And most importantly for clean energy deployment, the bill would give the federal government backstop authority to site and permit the transmission lines needed to connect new clean energy technologies, like solar and geothermal, to the grid and to power electric vehicles and heat pumps. Miraculously, BAAJA is simultaneously good for emissions, affordability, jobs, transit, and housing. And while some environmental groups, such as the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), are opposing the bill, the Democratic stakeholders with the most to gain from a return to building — union workers — have come out strongly in favor of BAAJA.

However, given the midterm results, some Democrats think they should wait until the next Congress to negotiate a new bill that’s more favorable to their priorities. At first blush, pursuing a new bill seems reasonable — after all, Democrats did just win historic margins in each chamber — but on deeper examination, this plan has two major problems:

• Democrats are unlikely to nuke the filibuster next Congress and, even if they did, they would not have veto-proof majorities in either chamber, so any permitting reform deal will still need President Trump’s signature. With the filibuster in place, it will also need at least four Senate Republicans.

• The likely incoming chairmen of two of the most important committees for permitting reform — Rep. Jared Huffman on House Natural Resources and Sen. Jeff Merkley on Senate Environment and Public Works — have opposed every major permitting reform bill of the last five years.

Rep. Huffman and Sen. Merkley are very unlikely to deliver a better deal because they’ve shown, under different balances of power across the last three Congresses, that they oppose all the reforms Republicans care most about — which is a death knell for permitting reform since any deal has to be bipartisan. Rep. Huffman and Sen. Merkley are unusual in this unwillingness to compromise: they opposed every past deal that a majority of their fellow Democrats voted for. This becomes clear when you look at the legislative history for the three main permitting reform deals prior to BAAJA: BAES (2022), the Fiscal Responsibility Act (FRA, 2023), and EPRA (2024).
The Building American Energy Security Act (2022)

In exchange for his vote on the Inflation Reduction Act in August 2022, Sen. Manchin secured a commitment that the Biden Administration and Leader Schumer would work with him on a permitting reform bill. The result was BAES, which would have directed the president to designate 25 priority energy projects for expedited review and expanded federal authority to permit interstate transmission lines. Given that BAES was negotiated under a Democratic trifecta, it did relatively little to advance fossil fuel development. It permitted one pipeline in West Virginia that was important to WV Senators Manchin and Capito. And it set shot clocks and page limits on NEPA environmental reviews, which most Republicans felt was akin to rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic (because the changes didn’t address the underlying litigation risk projects face).

Nevertheless, green groups like the NRDC called the bill “radical” and its Mountain Valley Pipeline provision “draconian.” On December 15, 2022, the Senate voted on adding it to the annual defense bill, the NDAA. The Senate Democratic caucus supported the measure 40-10. But only seven Republicans voted for it, so the final tally of 47-47 fell well short of the 60 votes needed to adopt the amendment. The League of Conservation Voters scored a “no” as the pro-environment vote, which meant it gave positive marks to the Senate Republicans who voted no and negative marks to the Democratic climate hawks who voted yes. Sen. Merkley was one of only 10 members of the Democratic caucus who voted no on this Democratic-led permitting bill. And Rep. Huffman, a lead signer of a 77-member House letter urging leaders to keep the bill out of must-pass legislation, repeatedly called it a “shit sandwich.”
The Fiscal Responsibility Act (2023)

Following the failure of BAES, there was a serious push to add permitting reform to the debt ceiling deal, the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, including transmission reform (the BIG WIRES Act) in exchange for NEPA litigation reforms. But the deal fell apart, and ultimately the only permitting reform in the FRA was the West Virginia pipeline authorization from BAES, some modest NEPA reforms that set deadlines and page limits for environmental reviews but did not limit lawsuits, and a study on the need for transmission reform. The bill passed with overwhelming Democratic support in both the House (165-46) and Senate (46-5). Yet despite the minor nature of these reforms, Rep. Huffman and Sen. Merkley voted no on the whole deal, each citing its permitting provisions among their reasons for opposition.

Prior to his no vote, Rep. Huffman again co-led a sign-on letter from House Democrats to proactively pressure the Biden Administration against any reforms (emphasis added) “gutting or changing” NEPA. In the letter, Rep. Huffman and his colleagues recognized the need for “reforming the transmission planning process and transmission cost allocation process,” but insisted that “these reforms can and must be accomplished without undermining any bedrock environmental laws.” This have-your-cake-and-eat-it-too approach to transmission reform, apart from being substantively wrong (our procedural environmental laws really will require reform if we want a rapid buildout of electrical and clean energy infrastructure), had the foreseeable political effect: Republicans declined the offer.
The Energy Permitting Reform Act (2024)

The most recent permitting reform attempt prior to BAAJA was the Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024. EPRA went much further than BAES or FRA on both clean energy and fossil fuels, giving both Democrats and Republicans more of what they wanted. It had provisions on transmission, judicial review, mining, LNG, geothermal, and leasing. It sailed through the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee with eight of nine Republicans and seven of the 10 senators on the Democratic side voting in favor.

While more ambitious than BAES, EPRA didn’t amend the Clean Water Act, NEPA, or the Endangered Species Act (ESA), changes to which are long-held Republican priorities. House Republicans under Speaker Johnson balked at the bill under pressure from the utilities and President-elect Trump chose not to push for its passage. EPRA was a stark example of how challenging it is to reach a compromise on permitting reform: it didn’t go far enough to win over House Republicans or President-elect Trump, yet Sen. Merkley and Rep. Huffman still publicly opposed it for going too far.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, “BAAJA” (2026)

Now Congress is considering BAAJA. It’s already passed the Senate 62-33. Sen. Merkley and Rep. Huffman have been working hard to tank the deal, with the starkest example being Sen. Merkley’s behavior during the amendment process in the Senate. He put forward, along with fellow Oregonian Sen. Wyden, a partisan amendment that would have been a poison pill for the whole bill.

Sen. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to approve a bipartisan manager’s amendment that included technical fixes to the bill and some modest substantive improvements to address Tribal concerns. Even after the bill had passed, while it could still be amended, Sen. Merkley objected to the manager’s amendment again. By then he could no longer stop the bill. His objection could only make it worse for Democratic priorities (presumably with the goal of making it harder to pass in the House).
The tyranny of the minority

We’re at a crossroads as a country. We should be building all kinds of new infrastructure to support the electrification of the economy — first and foremost, the power lines needed to move electricity from where it’s generated to where it’s needed. But at a time of rising electricity demand, we are actually worse today at getting transmission lines permitted and built than we were 10 years ago:

Sen. Merkley’s brinksmanship is an apt analogy for what’s gone wrong with our permitting system over the last half century. We’ve given a small handful of unrepresentative people a veto over building anything that anyone anywhere doesn’t like, regardless of how many diffuse benefits the project might create. Similarly, Sen. Merkley’s objection to the unanimous consent request, which fellow Democratic Sen. Gallego called a “dirty” move, shows that when one senator holds the other 99 hostage, we get worse outcomes.

Rep. Huffman and Sen. Merkley have now shown four times that they reject the tradeoffs that any bipartisan permitting reform will require; it will be impossible to enact legislation that makes it easier to build transmission or clean energy on their watch next Congress. Rep. Huffman has explicitly said that he won’t countenance the changes to NEPA, NHPA, and ESA that Republicans want. It’s doubtful the two of them can negotiate a deal that even secures the support of every Senate Democrat, let alone four (or more) Senate Republicans and President Trump. The choice for House Democrats isn’t between this deal and a better one next Congress; it’s between this deal and no deal. It’s time to pass the bill in front of them and stop letting a minority deprive the rest of us of a more prosperous and sustainable future.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkgr4g5nrnlo.headline: Two American Airlines planes clip wings before takeoff at Reagan airport
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkgr4g5nrnlo.author: Rebecka Pieder

paragraphs.text: Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday.
One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.
Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.
The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.
"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.

Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.

The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.

A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.
The passenger added that the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and he heard gasps inside the cabin. He described the moment as "tense", but that nobody seemed to be hurt.
As he looked out the window, he saw a piece of the aircraft on the ground. It looked like the "tip of the wing", he said, describing how the other aircraft's wing was overlapping his plane's wing.
The BBC has contacted American Airlines about reports of the broken wingtip.
As they taxied back to the gate, the passenger said he saw a truck pick up the piece that had fallen.
The fact that this isn't the first incident at this airport was "definitely scary", the passenger said.
Last year, there was a deadly mid-air collision between another American Airlines flight and a military helicopter at Reagan National.
The 64 people on the passenger plane and three US Army members on the Black Hawk helicopter all died in the crash.
The aircraft, en route to land at the DC airport after leaving from Wichita, Kansas, was sent careening into the Potomac River upon impact with the military helicopter.
It was later determined that the helicopter was receiving faulty altitude data, causing it to fly higher than intended.
Reagan National Airport is the smaller of the two DC-area airports and caters mostly to domestic flights.
It sits right near the sprawl of the US capital, the White House and the Pentagon.

Earlier this week, the US Army said it planned to resume helicopter test flights near Reagan airport, according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. The flights were paused following last year's incident.
BBC has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/world/middleeast/.headline: Israeli Strike Kills 2 Workers at Gaza Clinic, Doctors Without Borders Says

paragraphs.text: Doctors Without Borders, the aid group, said an Israeli strike on Friday killed two workers at one of its clinics in Gaza, the latest in a series of deadly attacks in the territory in recent days. Israel has said that the attacks targeted Hamas officials.

“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” Doctors Without Borders said in a statement, adding that its facilities were clearly marked as medical buildings. It said the location of the clinic had been shared with the Israeli military and that the deaths brought to 17 the number of Doctors Without Borders workers killed in Gaza.

The Israeli military said in a statement that the men were “Hamas terrorists working under humanitarian cover” as security guards who were preparing attacks against Israeli civilians and troops, without providing any evidence for its claims. The military added that it had taken “precautionary measures” to minimize harm to civilians and that “no damage was caused to medical infrastructure.”
Doctors Without Borders did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Israeli military’s assertions about the workers.

The strike came at the end of a week of intensifying and deadly attacks on Gaza that have killed at least three Hamas officials, according to the Israeli military, despite a nominal U.S.-backed cease-fire that took effect in October 2025. At least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the truce was reached, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

On Thursday, an Israeli strike killed Khaled Abu Nada, a Hamas official and Gaza’s deputy minister of education, along with his wife, according to the authorities in Gaza. Israel accused him of directing funds toward Hamas’s armed forces.

Following the killing of Mr. Abu Nada, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said in a statement that the Israeli military had killed roughly 80 members of Hamas during the past month and vowed to continue pursuing the group’s leaders and operatives.
Hamas said the “assassination” of its leaders violated the cease-fire.

Israel has escalated strikes as Mr. Netanyahu fights for his political life following an inconclusive Israeli election last month. The prime minister is serving as a caretaker leader, with Israeli opposition parties in negotiations to form a new government.

Mr. Netanyahu has been dogged by public anger over the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack in which roughly 1,200 people were killed. The prime minister has regularly raised the specter of further violence targeting Israelis as he bids to remain in power.

In January, Doctors Without Borders said Israel had ordered it to cease operations in Gaza. The Israeli authorities said the aid organization had failed to comply with restrictions that include registering all Gazan employees so that they could be vetted and limiting its criticism of Israel’s conduct of the war. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza in response to the Oct. 7 attack, according to local health officials, and much of the territory has been reduced to rubble.

Doctors Without Borders and other aid groups said the demands contravened international law and violated workers’ privacy rights and European data-protection rules that such groups were legally obligated to follow.

phys.org/news/2026-11-traditional-food-k.headline: How learning on the land is bringing back traditional food knowledge and healing
phys.org/news/2026-11-traditional-food-k.author: Tammara Soma, Morgan Game

paragraphs.text: edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

A viral 2017 poll claimed that 7% of American adults believe chocolate milk comes from brown cows. The results drew a lot of laughs, along with criticism of the poll's accuracy. But nearly a decade later, the results still raise an important question: How much do people really know about where their food comes from and how it's grown?
Grocery prices are skyrocketing in Canada amid a series of crises, from the lingering effects of the COVID-19 pandemic to global conflict, climate change and cyberattacks on grocery chains.

As these events disrupt food supplies, it's time to revisit a skill set humans have valued for millennia—food literacy. Knowing how to grow, harvest, hunt, process and cook our own food can help us become more self-sufficient, and it starts with learning from the land.
Our disconnection from food

The disconnect between the food we eat and the land can be explained by the concept of distancing. It also involves complex power dynamics, financing and entities in the global food system that make our food hard to understand.

Distancing shapes how we value our food, the Earth and the people who work in the food system. Indigenous scholars Linda Clarkson and Vern Morrissette, along with Gabriel Régallet, argue that when we are separated from the source of our sustenance, we lose sight of "our responsibility and our kinship to the Earth." In essence, we collectively forget our responsibilities to the land.

For many Indigenous communities, food can no longer serve as medicine in the way it once did because colonization and the residential school system turned it into a tool of control. These systems forcibly disrupted intergenerational knowledge transfer, removed people from their lands, stigmatized traditional food and knowledge and ruptured relationships that had sustained people for generations.
While many initiatives now offer students and adults opportunities to learn traditional food knowledge, these efforts are not yet mainstream.
Building resilience through land-based learning

One approach to addressing collective forgetting and reclaiming food knowledge is land-based learning, an Indigenous approach to teaching rooted in understanding the land as a teacher. In our ongoing project, "Countering Collective Forgetting: The Role of Land Based Learning," we showcase the important work of those who teach these skills and how they are often undervalued.

Through hands-on teaching, land-based learning encourages adaptive knowledge often gained through the wisdom of Elders. Our research team recently reviewed 137 land-based learning studies. We found that Elder-led mentorship was the most prevalent approach to learning, appearing in 73% of the studies.

To showcase how land-based learning works in practice, we conducted our study on the unceded territories of the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish) and shíshálh (Sechelt) Nations in an area commonly known as the Sunshine Coast of British Columbia. This region is particularly vulnerable to drought, and residents rely on ferry services for 60% of their food, with 40% coming from private barges and transport.

We participated in five land-based learning activities, hosted one learning circle and interviewed eight local land-based learning practitioners. These practitioners included seed savers, farmers, permaculturalists, Indigenous Knowledge Keepers, chefs, schoolteachers and outdoor educators. They comprised a mix of Indigenous and settler residents in their communities.
Our initial findings suggest that food acts as a form of living memory, held and reproduced through stories, relationships and also through engaging with the land.
The land is a teacher, healer

During our learning circle, Alfonso Salinas, a shíshálh educator and cultural ambassador, opened the session with a song and prayer. He described how he was "taken under the wings" of Elders and of shíshálh Nation educator Candace Campo (xets'emits'a), co-founder of Talaysay Tours, a local Indigenous land-based learning and tourism company.

On forest walks, Salinas learned how to use traditional plants and cedar as medicine. He shared his concerns about climate change and how invasive species are increasingly outcompeting native plants such as salmonberries. His message was to never forget to teach the history of the land.
One important piece of history shared by educators from the Sunshine Coast Seed Saving Collective during a seed workshop in September 2025 was that of the Japanese internment camps.
They helped people remember and honor survivors by planting Slocan peas.

Slocan peas are connected to Japanese Canadian families who were interned in the interior of British Columbia during World War II. Slocan peas grew through a period of injustice, carrying a memory of adaptation and resilience. Growing them is a form of healing.

One educator who identified as Red River Métis shared that it's hard to learn from the land when colonial policies continue to create barriers for Indigenous peoples. Zoning rules, the reserve system and resource extraction projects all stand in the way.
Finally, while many of the practitioners volunteered their time out of love, they also recognized this approach isn't sustainable.

Cost was a significant barrier for Robin, a settler who runs farm camps where kids from kindergarten to 12th grade can learn how to grow, process and cook food. She said it was difficult to balance the need to create more affordable land-based learning programs while ensuring that practitioners can continue to teach. "Land-based educators should be paid fair wages," she said.
Supporting traditional food knowledge
Seeds, like knowledge, don't stay viable forever. They have to be planted, harvested, saved and shared for the cycle to continue.

Knowledge from land-based learning carries on the same way, as each generation of learners teaches the next. That cycle can help counter collective forgetting in our food systems, but only if those who dedicate their hearts and time to it have the space, fair wages and support they need.

If we want to close the gap between ourselves and the food we eat, land-based learning offers an important path. To keep traditional food knowledge alive and make our food systems more resilient, we must value the wisdom that allows food to serve as medicine. That work begins by reconnecting with the land and with one another.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/new.headline: New York Mayor Mamdani underwent surgery to repair torn Achilles tendon
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/new.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering politics and breaking news
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) underwent surgery Friday to repair the Achilles tendon he tore during a soccer match last week.

Mamdani’s press secretary, Joe Calvello, said in a statement that the surgery, which lasted just over an hour, “was successful” and that the mayor is expected to make a full recovery. Mamdani was discharged from the hospital the same day as his procedure, Calvello said.
The 35-year-old mayor sustained the injury during a soccer match against local journalists Nov. 19. Mamdani’s team won the game, with the mayor scoring a goal.
At a news conference about closing the Rikers Island jail complex the following day, Mamdani acknowledged that he did not stretch before the game.

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35, and soon after I tore my Achilles, and I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks,” Mamdani told reporters. “And I will play soccer in about nine months.”
Since the incident, Mamdani has continued to make public appearances wearing a medical boot and using crutches.
The mayor’s office did not disclose where the surgery was done but thanked medical staff for the “first-class care” he received.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: Is it okay to NOT let guests bring plus-ones to my wedding?
What’s the etiquette for inviting guests to a wedding? Do you automatically include a plus-one for them?

One couple is weighing the rules as the two get ready for their own nuptial celebrations. And in this week’s episode of the “Life Hax” podcast, columnists Shane O’Neill and Carolyn Hax debate the options. (You can find the full episode, which includes more wedding-related dilemmas, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.)

Our letter writer notes that they’ve never needed a date to enjoy a wedding and think it’s “a little silly” to invite plus-ones. They’ve seen different approaches: “We’ve had friends who only invited the partners of guests who were married, engaged, or living together,” they wrote. But “that created way too many weird exclusions.”
So what’s a 30-something to do?
Shane proposes one rubric: “If you know their name and you would be embarrassed to run into them and be like, ‘I didn’t invite you to the wedding,’ invite them to the wedding!”
Carolyn calls that “brilliant.”
The guest list is more about finances than excluding people, Shane adds, because “by the time you’re drunk and doing the Chicken Dance, my worst enemy could be at my wedding.”
Reporter covering breaking news
Israeli strike on Gaza kills 2 Doctors Without Borders staff, charity says

Humanitarian charity Doctors Without Borders said an Israeli strike killed two of its staff members at a clearly marked Gaza City clinic on Friday — an attack the Israeli military said was targeted at Hamas members “under humanitarian cover.”
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” the group said on X. “This is a direct hit on MSF.”

The Israel Defense Forces said in a statement Saturday that it killed “Hamas terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.” The military said that two men, whom it named, were working as security guards at the clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders “while also serving as terrorists,” without providing evidence. It added that no medical infrastructure in the area was damaged in the strike.
At least 17 members of Doctors Without Borders have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, the charity said.
According to the charity, the premises hit in the attack had been “clearly marked” with its logos and the location had been “communicated to and was known by” the Israeli military.

World Health Organization Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X that attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are “outrageous and unacceptable.” He extended “heartfelt condolences” to Doctors Without Borders colleagues.
Reporter covering international breaking news
WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.
Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.
What it was like to keep a 410-person band in NYC for the rescheduled Macy’s parade

After Macy’s said it would postpone its 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade until Saturday because of inclement weather, performing groups from around the country scrambled to decide whether to extend their stays in New York City or head home without marching down to 34th Street.

For the marching band at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, known as the Marching Illini, the decision to stay “was pretty unanimous,” band director Barry L. Houser said. The logistics of keeping hundreds of band members in Manhattan for two extra days were a challenge, he said, but “everyone’s just been phenomenal.”

First, Houser said, the band had to weigh whether to stay or head back to Illinois to give students time to prepare for their final full week of classes this semester. Then they had to ensure that hotel rooms were available and that they had enough money to extend the trip. The band travels with 436 people, including 410 student performers, Houser said.
Their hotel had room for the whole group to stay, Houser said, but there was a catch: Everyone had to check out and then check back in.
“Adding instruments to that mix in a hotel lobby that is not designed for 436 people — we’ve had to make some accommodations there,” Houser said.
Catering changes and charter bus rescheduling soon fell in line, and the band was able to fundraise more than $175,000 to pay for their extended stay, Houser said.
The Marching Illini’s parade set is poised to include a custom arrangement of “Chicago” by Sufjan Stevens. Video from the band’s rehearsal of the piece went viral this week.
On Sunday, the band will board buses for the long drive back to Champaign, just in time for their last full week of classes.
The trip to Manhattan from Illinois, Houser said, was about 19 hours long.
Data reporter focusing on climate and the environment
Where high tides set records on both coasts this week
Oceans raged along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts of the U.S. this week as a combination of king tides, strong swells and a winter storm sent water levels into record territory.

Along the Mid-Atlantic coast, a winter storm that brought 60 mph to 70 mph winds and waves up to 20 feet coincided with some of the highest tides of the year to send ocean waters rushing into communities along the coast.
“Everything was in the right place for a worst-case scenario,” said Larry Brown, a meteorologist in the National Weather Service’s Wakefield, Virginia, office.

Waters surged 1.5 feet beyond the prior record at the tide station at Wachapreague, Virginia, according to preliminary data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The previous record was set during Tropical Storm Ernesto in 2006, and the station dates back to 1978.

Along the California coast, a record El Niño has caused warmer-than-usual waters to accumulate, raising sea levels by more than a foot in some areas. When king tides arrived earlier this week they were accompanied by a strong ocean swell that generated 20-foot to 30-foot waves. The combination sent waves over roads and into homes and businesses, and caused part of a pier to collapse.
Tides set records at stations from San Diego to Monterey, and more intense king tides are expected in December and January.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/openais-new-co.headline: OpenAI’s new countersuit accuses Apple of ‘unlawfully pressuring vendors’
techcrunch.com/2026/11/28/openais-new-co.author: Anthony Ha

paragraphs.text: After Apple sued OpenAI this summer over allegations that the AI company had stolen trade secrets, OpenAI has fired back with a countersuit of its own.

According to Bloomberg, the new suit claims that as OpenAI prepared to enter the hardware market, Apple responded by “by unlawfully pressuring vendors not to work with OpenAI and using expansive employment restraints to limit OpenAI’s access to talented engineers.”
The suit also accuses Apple of stealing OpenAI’s trade secrets.

Apple told the Financial Times that the countersuit is “a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit, in which OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using Apple’s confidential information.”

Apple previously alleged that OpenAI leaders, including Chief Hardware Officer Tang Tan, asked candidates to bring Apple hardware components to their job interviews and coached them on how to evade security procedures. OpenAI responded that it has “no interest in other companies’ trade secrets.”
The dueling lawsuits mark a dramatic souring of the relationship between two companies that in 2024 partnered to integrate OpenAI’s ChatGPT with Apple’s Siri.

npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6056359/epa-res.headline: EPA says initial tests show no toxic lead contamination in Iowa following detonation
npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6056359/epa-res.author: Kat Lonsdorf

paragraphs.text: Initial lab results from the controlled detonation of roughly five tons of unstable lead azide at a U.S. Army ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa showed no elevation of lead in water sources in the surrounding environment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday.

"We will continue to provide updates in the coming days as new lab results for over 3,200 air, soil, dust and water samples (collected pre and post detonation) rapidly return and get validated," the agency wrote in a post on X.
The EPA says a team of 300 personnel and contractors spent the days immediately following Wednesday's blast collecting samples, in addition to monitoring for airborne lead for 30 consecutive hours.
Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade or break down over time. It's especially dangerous to children and pregnant people, and experts say there is no safe level of exposure.

Military explosives experts detonated 68 drums of aging lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown after it was found to be at risk of spontaneous explosion. Residents within five miles of the plant were ordered to evacuate, and many others told to stay inside, amid fears of a toxic plume of the chemicals.

In the hours immediately after the explosion, U.S. Army officials called the detonation a success, saying that the mitigation measures put in place – including layers of contaminant and downward-facing explosives meant to drive the blast into the ground – had "exceeded expectations."

Still, many residents and some elected officials have criticized the military for a lack of transparency in the operation, including Iowa Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who has called for an investigation into why the lead azide was allowed to get to this precarious point.
"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," he said after the detonation. "Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared."
Sue Dyer, a corn and bean farmer about 18 miles southwest of the blast site, agreed that the biggest problem was communication, calling it "horrible."
"We didn't know anything about this until last week," she told NPR's Scott Simon in an interview on Saturday morning.
Dyer said that people in the community are all across the spectrum in terms of how worried they are after the detonation, even with reassurances from the federal government.

"Some people are sure that we're absolutely fine, and some people think we're absolutely dead. So put me somewhere in the middle until I have the data to make an opinion," she said, noting she is waiting for independent sampling results as well as those from the EPA.
Dyer says she had samples taken from her farmland before the blast and plans on taking her own samples again in the coming days, in hopes to get her farm verified lead-free.
"But what do you do if there's lead there?" Dyer asked. "I'm very hopeful that everything's fine, but I'm also a realist."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-28/.headline: A magnitude 5 earthquake rattles Southern California

paragraphs.text: A magnitude 5.0 earthquake rattled Southern California on Saturday morning.

The temblor, centered about three miles west of the Hermosa Beach Pier, was felt over a wide swath of the region, though there were no immediate reports of major damage. A plume of smoke was seen rising from the Chevron refinery in El Segundo.

“It is one of the larger ones we’ve had in the Los Angeles area in quite a while,” seismologist Lucy Jones, a Caltech research associate, said. The last magnitude 5-or-greater quake in the L.A. County-Orange County metropolitan area was the magnitude 5.1 quake in Brea in 2014. A bit farther out, a magnitude 5.1 quake southeast of Ojai hit in 2023.

It’s highly improbable that there was major damage from the earthquake, Jones said. The intensity of shaking closest to the epicenter “is the level that scares people a lot,” but wasn’t high enough to cause major damage, Jones said.
Saturday’s earthquake hit at 9:30 a.m. and was followed by smaller aftershocks.
“Moderate” shaking was felt closest to the epicenter, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. In El Segundo, pictures fell off a bookcase, include a ceramic cup and a photo frame.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.headline: L.A. acting class teaches lawyers to influence jurors, banter in court
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-27/.author: Sonja Sharp

paragraphs.text: High on adrenaline and king-sized bars of Payday and 100 Grand, a punchline’s worth of plaintiff’s lawyers clowned around a Mid-Wilshire office tower one recent afternoon, learning how to talk nonsense and influence jurors.
“Who hasn’t been made uncomfortable yet?” asked actor and attorney Brian Breiter, who leads this popular workshop for litigators.
Eugenia Bagdassarian, a personal injury lawyer with towering curls, tentatively raised her hand.
By this point, she and her classmates had already crawled around on all fours, held a cocktail party in gibberish and exchanged invisible gifts, among other ego-piercing exercises.

Such games are stock-in-trade for beginner improv classes, dozens of which can be found in Los Angeles on any given day. Once the sole province of aspiring actors and up-and-coming comics, improv has long since spread to corporate team-building, pediatric play therapy and even dating.
Still, Improv for Trial stands apart. In this elite workshop, buttoned-up attorneys learn how to let go and “just do” in service of winning civil cases and the occasional criminal conviction.

(Though he has taught thousands of law students, prosecutors, public defenders and plaintiff’s attorneys, Breiter generally bars civil defense lawyers from his improv courtroom, in part because he considers most too risk averse, and in part to disadvantage the competition.)

To nonlawyers who deal daily with the vagaries of our judicial system, the utility of such a course is obvious: a trial requires sustained close attention from jurors who don’t want to be there, something even a law professor may struggle to command.
“This is my favorite thing to do,” said Joseph Limbaugh, Breiter’s longtime acting partner and co-teacher. “Some of this stuff I’ve never tried with lawyers before.”

After each game, Breiter would debrief. Imaginary gifts became an object lesson for voir dire, the nonsense-party, nonverbal communication. Talking around the letter “r” or “s” or “t” was meant to help navigate motions about what evidence can be presented at a trial.

“The most important thing is hyper-listening, being super observant and understanding how you are perceived,” Breiter explained. “I would do a trial 10 different ways depending on the audience I have.”

For most of the last 15 years, Breiter and Limbaugh have taught this class in a purpose-built theater, complete with plush velvet curtains, a movable witness stand, and half a dozen Muppet-style hand-and-rod puppets slumped on a hat rack in the corner.
“Puppets allow you to say and do things that you as a human can’t,” Breiter said.
“I feel like puppets and masks are the only magic left in the world,” Limbaugh agreed.
Around the room hung framed posters of Hollywood court movies, including “A Few Good Men,” “My Cousin Vinny” and “Legally Blonde.”

Breiter’s most infamous wins are nearly as dramatic: closing arguments performed as a game show, Oscar the Grouch interrupting to ventriloquize arguments for the defense, a baking competition enacted through mime.

To those outside the law, all this might appear like a Tinseltown affectation. In a city where accident attorneys are their own brand of roadside celebrity, even lawyers struggle to grasp the utility at first.
“I have no idea what to expect, except the email said ‘wear comfortable clothes,’” said Jacob Seropian, a last-minute addition to the class.
To understand why this class is so popular, it helps to understand just how different courtroom dramas are from courts in real life.
There’s a reason Hollywood can’t quit the legal procedural.
The American judicial system is “adversarial,” meaning tension is built into the process. So too are stakes. Trials are a war of narrative. Lives hang in the balance.

This is true not only in criminal court, where liberty and justice spar out of necessity (see: “To Kill a Mockingbird”), but increasingly in the civil division (See: “Philadelphia”), where everything from domestic military deployments to the limits of social media have been fought — often, though not always — before juries.
Yet many of this country’s busiest halls of justice are not ready for prime time.
In courtrooms smelling of burnt dust and WPA-era plumbing, most of what happens is stultifying.

Journalists distill hours of crushing boredom into a highlight reel with context and observation that sets the most significant moments apart from the tedious accretion of detail necessary to fit a messy set of facts inside a tidy set of laws.

But jurors don’t have that luxury. They must sit attentively through days, weeks and sometimes months of testimony without the benefit of snappy experts, clever editors or a union paycheck to guide them.
“When you watch these TV lawyers, they’re actors so they know how to perform their role,” Breiter said. “Most lawyers don’t know how to tell a story. They don’t even know what a story is.”

There are several good reasons for this. First, even in Los Angeles, most lawyers are not actors. Second, the law is bound by a library’s worth of complex rules. Third, attorneys are trained to be ruthlessly analytical.
Breiter’s goal is to loosen those binds so that lawyers can connect with lay people, and move them.
“The audience can’t walk out. You have them captive there,” he said of the jury. “You have to be appreciative of their time and make it enjoyable when it can be.”
To that end, he frequently casts his student-audience as jurors — a role lawyers adopt almost unconsciously, and with total fluency.
“Who here speaks another language?” Breiter asked while debriefing the gibberish exercise.

Constantinos “Dean” Pavlakos raised his hand, showing off a muscled arm inked with Greek iconography. At Breiter’s instruction, he answered questions in fractured English for a mock voir dire, reacting gamely as the teacher recruited other attorney-jurors to his cause in a pedagogical version of crowd work.
These exercises build toward the marquee concept in Breiter and Limbaugh’s workshops: Status.

Black’s Law Dictionary defines status as “a person’s legal condition” including their rights, duties and liabilities. In Limbaugh and Breiter’s stage court, it’s a term of art invented by the late acting teacher Keith Johnstone, of whom the pair are disciples.
Johnstone’s school of theater is less “yes, and” and more relationship building.
For Breiter and Limbaugh, status is a framework for radical empathy — that is, inhabiting another person’s perspective in the pursuit of justice — albeit justice in the form of money damages.

In the lesson’s status exercises, students practiced observing and projecting power dynamics. Participants loomed and shied, minced and strutted, advanced and retreated, first in opposition, then in concert, until at last each was charged with addressing their peer-jury with an improvised speech about an unfamiliar topic while attempting to maintain eye contact with everyone simultaneously.
It was torture that induced rib-aching laughter.
Attorneys have a common, cringey habit of reminding jurors just how essential they are to the legal system.
Improv for Trial puts that platitude into practice.

In reality, justice requires millions of ordinary people to open that letter no one wants and show up to that leaky, roach-infested courthouse where no one wants to be, on the off chance they might be selected to decide the fate of a stranger.
When court is a bore, justice suffers along with the jury.
“Jurors dread going to court,” Breiter said. “If they’re going to take 8 to 25 days out of their life and sit there, you better make it entertaining.”
For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed.
Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them!
This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully.
That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero.
Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others.
The Temporary New Policy
Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved.
Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted.

I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible.
Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding.

nytimes.com/2026/11/27/business/media/ol.headline: It’s Boom Times for Old TV Shows. New TV, Not So Much.

paragraphs.text: TJ Helmstetter used to watch lots of new TV shows.

These days, though, his streaming habits are stretching into other decades. Mr. Helmstetter, a 42-year-old political consultant who lives in Washington, just streamed for the first time all 275 episodes of “Cheers,” the hit NBC comedy in the 1980s and ’90s. He and his husband also recently watched crime dramas from the 2010s like “Broadchurch” and “Major Crimes.”

Some new shows made the cut, like “Furious,” a police thriller on Hulu. But between professional obligations and being “decision fatigued” amid a sea of streaming options, the bar is getting much higher to start an original series, Mr. Helmstetter said.
“My brain can’t handle something new and I have been in that mode for like the last year or so,” he added.

He is not alone. Viewership for older television series and movies on streaming services has been on a rapid rise in recent years, according to a pair of research firms. Viewership for newer series, not so much.
There are plenty of reasons people are turning to older fare like “Girls,” “Mad Men,” “Glee” and “The West Wing.”

The industry is making significantly fewer scripted and reality series compared with just four years ago, leaving viewers hunting for other content in a post-Peak TV era. Some streamers have been struggling to get audiences to show up for new shows, and an even harder time keeping them there for subsequent seasons.

Netflix, the biggest subscription streamer of them all, recently ousted its top programming leader as it struggles to find new giant hits. And viewers said it is comforting to revisit old classics or finally check them off their watch list.

Back libraries, of course, have long been the backbone of cable television and streaming. Plenty of people have discovered older series in the streaming era, like “Suits,” on Netflix. But now they’re finding them on other apps, like HBO Max, too: “The Big Bang Theory” became the most-watched show in America over the summer, according to Nielsen, even though it has been off the air for seven years.
As viewership for older series rises, it underscores the challenges all studios and entertainment executives are confronting in trying to get new TV shows in front of audiences.

As recently as 2023, original programming accounted for 17 percent of streaming usage, according to Nielsen. For much of the last year, that figure has fallen to 13 percent or lower, despite an overall spike in streaming viewership.

Data from Luminate, another research firm, is even starker: Viewing of library content jumped more than 40 percent among major subscription streaming services in the third quarter this year, compared with the same period of time last year. Viewership for new TV series and movies during the same time period declined modestly.

There are also fewer sustainable new hits this year. According to Nielsen’s weekly streaming ratings charts, an original series drew a total of at least two billion minutes of viewing time in any given week 21 times last year. (That’s the company’s benchmark for a very big hit; “Stranger Things,” “Bridgerton” and “The Lincoln Lawyer” were among the shows that cleared that number.) This year, that figure has dropped to nine.
Other popular distractions, including sporting events, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and video games like Grand Theft Auto VI, could also be playing a role.

Robert Greenblatt, a former top executive at NBC and WarnerMedia and an executive producer of “The Gilded Age,” said that it’s much easier to be a producer for a popular recurring series right now than it is to bring “a whole new show to the marketplace.”

“We’re still being pummeled by new shows on every streaming service and rather than try to figure out what’s worth committing to, it’s easier to just escape into ‘Seinfeld’ or ‘Downton Abbey’ because you know exactly what you’re getting,” he said.
Some viewers have complained it is harder than ever to even discover that a new show exists, something executives describe as a “discoverability” problem.

Emily Bianchi, a 37-year-old who lives outside Detroit, said that despite paying for subscriptions for at least seven streaming services, she has found herself spending most of her viewing time recently with older shows like “Mad Men,” which premiered in 2007 on AMC, and “Dexter,” which debuted in 2006 on Showtime.

“It’s hard to know where to find shows,” she said. “The only social media I’m on is Instagram and Threads and if it’s not popping up on my feed then I really just have no idea. You’re kind of on your own to find that stuff.”

Lisa Baar, a 66-year-old retiree who lives in Virginia Beach, said she and her husband were taken with Damien Lewis’s performance during a recent rewatch of “Band of Brothers,” the 2001 HBO mini-series. That inspired them to watch for the first time another show of his, “Homeland,” which ran on Showtime between 2011 and 2020. They devoured it, and she thought it was better than any new show that she has seen recently.
“We’ll start watching a new show and it never sticks,” she said.

The majority of older TV shows also have far more episodes than newer shows, which gives them a big leg up in viewing time tallies. HBO’s “Succession,” a three-time best drama winner in the 2020s at the Emmy Awards, had all of 39 episodes; “The West Wing,” a four-time winner from the 2000s, had 156. Twenty years ago, “Grey’s Anatomy” used to have 25 episodes a season — this season the episode count is whittled down to 13.

Executives are aware of that imbalance. Casey Bloys, the chief content officer at Skydance’s streaming division and the longtime programming head at HBO, has said that he programmed “The Pitt,” which runs at 15 episodes every season, because of the importance of making shows that future generations can spend dozens of hours with.

“Those libraries are incredibly important and have fueled streaming,” he said in an interview with The New York Times last year. “One of the thoughts we had was, well, if we don’t make new ones, you’re not going to have another library in the future like that.”

John Landgraf, the longtime head of FX, underscored a similar point this year. In July, Mr. Landgraf undertook an unusual experiment and greenlit a new premiere episode to get audiences to give his comedy “Adults” another chance. The show’s viewership figures were low, but he had a feeling it has the potential to be a “Friends” for a future generation.

“Why, as an industry, are we not making more deep library?” he told The Times over the summer. “That seems crazy to me when I can see what our viewers are doing. They’re consuming our deep library. It’s one of our most valuable assets.”

Mr. Helmstetter, and his husband, Mike Naple, said they are not afraid of watching a new show. But they are more deliberate than they used to be. They will often go through a checklist: Who’s starring? Has it been nominated for an Emmy? Which night can they focus and watch, and not have another device out?

“Often times, I’ll be like, ‘All right, we’ve got these new shows that are coming up, I think these are going to be good,’” Mr. Naple said. “And then it’s, like, ‘Well, no, I don’t want to do something new.’ Then we’re watching Season 5 of ‘Project Runway.’”

phys.org/news/2026-11-symmetry-shortcut-.headline: Symmetry shortcut narrows the search for hidden magnetic patterns
phys.org/news/2026-11-symmetry-shortcut-.author: Sam Jarman

paragraphs.text: November 28, 2026 report
by Sam Jarman, Phys.org
edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

In some magnetic materials, the spins of individual atoms line up in highly ordered patterns but point in directions that almost completely cancel out, leaving the material unmagnetized. The exact arrangement of these spins can strongly affect how electrons move through a material, shaping both its electrical and magnetic properties. But because a single crystal can support such a huge number of plausible spin patterns, it would be impossible to test them one at a time.

Two independent research teams have now revealed how this search could be dramatically narrowed down. One team was led by Qihang Liu at the Southern University of Science and Technology in China, and the other by Takuya Nomoto at Tokyo Metropolitan University in Japan. Using differing methods, both teams have reproduced the known spin patterns of real magnets with strikingly different crystal structures.
Both studies have been published in Physical Review X.
Impossible search

While the arrangement of atoms in a crystal can be easily worked out, its magnetic structure is far harder to pin down and usually requires specialized measurements such as neutron diffraction. Researchers usually interpret these measurements using standard symmetry methods, which work out which spin patterns fit the shape of the crystal.

However, these methods often leave key details unresolved, such as the angles between neighboring spins or whether equivalent atoms carry spins of equal strength. In recent years, physicists have shown that treating rotations of the spins separately from the symmetry of the crystal itself can reveal patterns that would be missed by conventional methods.

Building on this idea, Liu's and Nomoto's teams each questioned whether crystal symmetry could narrow the search even further. To do this, the two groups first generated manageable lists of candidate patterns, then ranked them with computer simulations in two stages. First, they compared how the spins lined up relative to each other. Then they brought in spin–orbit coupling to work out how the favored patterns were oriented within the crystal.
Two different approaches

From here, the two teams diverged in their approaches. In their study, Liu's team searched for patterns repeating over regions up to four times the size of the crystal's basic building block, without having to specify the repeat length in advance. They then reproduced the known spin patterns in three very different magnets: a straight-line arrangement in MnTe, a triangular pattern in Mn₃Sn and a fully 3D arrangement in CoNb₃S₆. In a broader test, they recovered the reported magnetic structures for 73% of 1,178 materials screened.

In their own study, Nomoto's team sped up the second stage by reusing the arrangement of electrons calculated in the first round. They found that the observed pattern came out lowest in energy in 83% of 271 cases where the repeat length was already known.

Looking ahead, the two teams now hope to run stronger tests, making predictions from crystal structures measured before magnetic order sets in—before comparing them with later diffraction measurements. If successful, their approach could ultimately open up new routes to finding materials for spin-based memory and electronics.

marketwatch.com/story/my-husband-spent-8.headline: My husband spent $80,000 on a boat, yet says my plans for a $100,000 pottery studio are irresponsible. Who's right?

paragraphs.text: 'We have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.'
"My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from." (Photo subject is a model.)

My husband and I have been married for 31 years. He's 65 and I'm 62. I work part-time in a dental office and we have a house that's fully paid off. It's worth about $900,000. Best of all, we have $2.9 million in retirement accounts. That includes some money that we inherited about 10 years ago.

For the last 15 years, I have dreamed of opening my own pottery studio. I've taken lessons at our Saturday market for several years, and I find it extremely meditative and also a wonderful pastime. There's a space near an old rail depot, about 900 square feet, which would be perfect for a pottery studio, where I could teach others. By my estimations, insurance, equipment and rent would require about $100,000.

My husband, however, is skeptical. He says that's a lot of money to spend on something that I'm trying to profit from. My sister says it's bad timing given that we're both heading into retirement. Three years ago, he purchased a boat for $80,000 and spent $12,000 on a new motor and fishfinder. He barely used it, and finally sold it at a loss.

I'm not claiming my pottery studio will make us rich, but I'm perfectly willing to come up with a business plan and set a budget, with a red line on the amount of money I would be prepared to lose. I'd actually also start a lot smaller and build up if the price is right. We could have 30 years ahead of us in retirement, and I want to spend it doing something that brings me a lot of joy.
Am I being unrealistic?
A 62-Year-Old Wife
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
Related: 'I like the idea of a big return': My financial adviser wants me to invest $350,000 in a UAE data center. Is this risky?
Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started.
From your letter, it doesn't sound like pottery is just a business for you.

For you, pottery is a passion, and it's important to have something you like doing in retirement. If you are going to choose to open a business, it should be something you will love because it won't always be easy, and you may need to rely on that bedrock of belief when the going gets tough. That's in addition to financial projections, advice from an accountant, knowing where you draw a hard line on the budget if sales dry up, and even a Plan B for the space.

I'm not going to tell you to open a business and spend $100,000, which could be a little on the high side, although you will know more when you compare this plan to similar-sized businesses and complete your due diligence. More important, I'm not going to tell you not to do it, and I don't think anyone else should, either, at least not without hearing you out, visiting the proposed site and, crucially, seeing your business plan. What stands out from your letter is your husband's immediate, possibly knee-jerk, opposition.

However, pointing out that he bought an $80,000 motorboat and ended up throwing good money after bad and selling it at a loss may be fair, but it doesn't help your cause. Yes, he decided to pursue something that he eventually tired of or decided wasn't worth all the hassle and expense. He's the one who apparently lost interest in a project after spending nearly six figures, not you. But it won't help to trade successes and failures in a tit-for-tat argument.
If a pottery studio is a vocation, you have earned the right to at least look into it.

It may be that you don't have to lease this building, as romantic as it sounds. You could rent a space at a retirement center or local school, at least initially, invest in the equipment to host pottery classes, build up word of mouth or an online presence and see how much demand is out there. That way, you won't be locked into a lease if the demand is not there. It will also help you envision what success means to you. Is it teaching a twice-weekly class? Or running a full-time studio?

You raise a great point when you say your retirement is not about doing nothing, or spending all of your time on the golf course or tennis court, or sitting in your garden reading - rather, it's about pursuing work that fulfills you. If pottery is a vocation for you, you have earned the right to at least look into it, given that you have worked for probably 40-plus years in jobs that helped you and your husband build a $2.9 million nest egg, even if those jobs were not your first choice.

For what it's worth, your business plan should include projected costs, including the lease, insurance, equipment, advertising, branding and marketing; projected revenue; the target market (there may be schools or senior centers nearby that would jump at the opportunity for their community to learn pottery); and, of course, the competition (find out if there are similar businesses in your area and, if so, how close they are and what they charge for classes).
Related: 'I don't want to die on the sales floor': I'm 67 and earn $19.50 an hour at a big-box store. When can I finally retire?
Running the numbers

You won't win this argument on statements that your husband is the proverbial pot calling the kettle black, and you may not "win" the argument at all. But you will lend more credence to your pottery studio idea through data. You have $2.9 million for retirement, a mortgage-free house worth $900,000, hardly any debt, a husband who has already retired, Social Security coming down the pike, and you continue to work part-time, although that may have to end if you set up this studio.

To put your small business in context: Startup costs of $100,000 represent 3.45% of your retirement account balance. That's not nothing, but neither is it an outrageous, extravagant risk, particularly given that this is an investment to further a pastime that brings you joy and, hopefully, makes money. What is your annual income now? What will it be in five years? What are your annual expenses? How much of your retirement is in traditional accounts versus Roth?

Another missing piece of this puzzle: Do you have a "fun money" account, an emergency fund or CDs or bonds to draw from? Otherwise, you would have to take this money from your investments. That would mean you need to take more than $100,000, because you would have to pay tax on the money you withdraw from a traditional IRA or 401(k). You would lose future investment returns (which you would ideally recoup, even if only in part, from your studio).
A $100,000 startup cost represents 3.45% of your retirement-account balance.

Tell your husband that you're not giving up before you've even started, just as you would not expect him to give up on a passion project without at least stress-testing the finances. The unspoken part of this conversation, particularly after his motorboat project, is hanging over you. It does not sound like you are asking him for permission, per se - rather, you are requesting his support, and I assume you have both contributed to your retirement fund, either as a corporate worker or a homemaker.

Agree on a maximum amount you can afford to lose on a studio. You will need working capital, particularly in the early stages, when you are building your reputation. This is an opportunity to step back and ask what you want from retirement. How do you want to spend your savings? What kind of issues require unanimous agreement? (Did you agree to the motorboat purchase, for instance?) How will you navigate such issues while respecting each other's space?

A woman named Kyla Glendenning opened up a pottery studio in Fort Lauderdale and said she had revenue of $71,000 in the first six months, but spent nearly $20,000 on Facebook advertisements. That tells me, in addition to the costs of setting up a studio, signing a lease and buying equipment, that your biggest challenges will be getting the word out that you exist. Her online tutorials and videos on social media - where I found her - also require both time and money.
Don't let anyone crack your bowls before they've even hit the kiln.
Related: My wife says we can't afford to retire. I vetoed her $8,000 trip to Italy. We're in our 60s and have $4 million. Do I keep working?
