marketwatch.com/story/a-66-year-old-nurs.headline: A 66-year-old nurse is facing down retirement with just $500 saved. Who's to blame?

paragraphs.text: 'Retirement is a financial status, not an age'
"When you spend every dollar on lifestyle habits and car loans for decades instead of saving, you don't get to act surprised when the math doesn't work." (Photo subject is a model.)

Regarding the 66-year-old nurse (I'm 66, rely on Social Security and have just $500 in savings. What hope do I have?) having less than $500 to her name after a career in nursing isn't bad luck - it's the result of lifelong financial choices. Even putting aside $1,000-a-year over a few decades would have left her in a completely different position.

It's her fault. Retiring with zero savings isn't a viable plan, and there's no point in worrying about Social Security earnings limits when you don't have enough to live on. She didn't have a low-wage job; she had a solid career as a nurse, which makes the lack of a basic budget or safety net all the more frustrating.

When you spend every dollar on lifestyle habits and car loans for decades instead of saving, you don't get to act surprised when the math doesn't work. Retirement is a financial status, not an age - and without savings, she simply can't afford to stop working until 70. This is the problem with America. No one wants to be held accountable, even to themselves.
How many Starbucks did she have a week?
You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.
Don't miss: 'I experienced many years of poverty': I worked until 70. Why do wealthy retirees look down on those with less savings?
She could have been living paycheck-to-paycheck like millions of Americans or she could have, as you say in your letter, lost sight of the bigger picture.
Asking "why?" is often a fruitful question, if we keep an open mind.

We don't know how much that nurse was paid, and we don't know whether she was divorced or had difficulty paying rent. She could have lived paycheck-to-paycheck on stagnant wages and lost sight of the challenges that lie ahead. Most nurses work grueling 12-hour shifts. They don't retire out of entitlement; they retire because their knees and backs have given out.

Kindness is free, and it's often key to understanding what went right and wrong in people's lives, including our own. The average annual salary for nurses rose over the past 30 years from roughly $40,000 in the 2000s to $97,500 today, but those salaries depend on the medical facility, city/town and specialty. That income falls to $42,000 a year for nursing assistants and $64,400 for licensed vocational nurses.

I don't wish to change your view of her circumstances or why she is in the position she is in. Your views are your own. Yes, we all must take responsibility for our situation in life. We agree on that. But I prefer to frame her story as one of roads not taken and financial literacy, or lack thereof. She may also have had a catastrophic life event: divorce, a medical crisis or caring for an elderly relative.
Kindness is free and it's often key to understanding what went wrong.

This woman, for better or for worse, felt left out of the political discourse and conversations centering members of the middle class as a person who is living close to the poverty line. She collects $2,000 in Social Security, and also suggested that she is scared about what will happen when she is no longer able to work. She lives in a two-bedroom apartment with a roommate who is receiving disability benefits.

She may not be aware: When she reaches her full retirement age - 66 and 10 months or 67 years of age - there is no limit on how much she can earn without reducing how much she receives in Social Security benefits. Best of all, if any benefits were withheld earlier, the Social Security Administration will recalculate and increase her monthly check once she hits her FRA.

The nurse whose situation frustrates you is not unique. Multiple studies contend that just under half of retirees have less than $100,000 saved for retirement and, according to a 2025 report from the Transamerica Institute, 12% of retirees have no savings, and more than half (53%) rely on Social Security as their primary source of income throughout their retirement.
Don't miss: Spooked by Nvidia's turmoil? Play Grand Theft Auto VI instead of peeking at your 401(k).
Financial fragility

"Retirees face financial fragility, especially being vulnerable to economic uncertainty, inflation, rising healthcare costs, and financial market volatility - all factors that can easily erode their buying power on limited income," the report said. "Many are concerned about their health in older age and their ability to afford long-term care, yet many also have not solidified plans."

Achieving a secure retirement is, for some people, easier on paper. Lower-income workers who come up short in retirement often did not have a 401(k) at work, for instance, and research suggests that they tend to be women, who still experience a gender pay gap in part due to the kinds of jobs they have traditionally inhabited, as well as single adults and racial minorities.

Financial literacy has improved in recent decades. One study by researchers from Texas Tech University and the University of Michigan found that financial literacy declines steadily in older age, even though confidence in money-related decisions remains high. Average financial literacy scores increase up to 50 years of age and then begin to fall with age, they concluded.
Not everyone has the same start in life and chooses well-paid careers.

Access to education plays a role. Some 81% of college graduates versus 39% of adults with no college education have savings, and 68% of non-Hispanic white adults have a retirement savings plan versus 42% of people of color, Gallup found. Men (61%) are also more likely than women (57%) to have a retirement plan. (Women are more likely to be caretakers and homemakers.)

There's a lot, in fairness, that goes into making up the puzzle of any person's life story. Did I have an inheritance? What career did I choose? Was there a 401(k)? Did I suffer from an unexpected job loss, or a downturn in the market just as I was entering retirement? If we are honest, our journeys are a combination of upbringing, hard work, planning and dumb luck.

The 66-year-old's Social Security suggests she probably worked as hard as you or me. You learned either from your peers, parents or reading the financial press and, regardless of your profession, did not live above your means because you knew you had to put money aside for retirement and because you had the ability to do so. That's smart and savvy. But not everyone has the same start in life or chooses a well-paid career.
Some people have a margin of error to learn from their mistakes; others, alas, don't.
Related: Are you middle class? No, you're not. Here's why.

fortune.com/2026/11/28/cyberattacks-air-.headline: After the ‘Black October’ hacking spree, another wave of cyberattacks tests the West’s digital foundations as military and spy agencies are targeted
fortune.com/2026/11/28/cyberattacks-air-.author: Jason Ma

paragraphs.text: Hackers haven’t eased off this month after waging a massive crime spree in October, and are now targeting foundational institutions of Western power, including top national security agencies.

Last month, cyberattacks hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. Targets included the Federal Election Commission, Sony, John Deere, Oracle Health, Burger King Japan, and the State Bank of India. Cyberattacks even reached freezers across Europe and at U.S. military bases, with temperatures hiked high enough to spoil frozen food. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.”

Cybersecurity experts also rushed to fix vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language that’s used in nearly 70% of all websites. Black October reached a crescendo with the largest crypto heist in history: North Korean hackers swiped $6.3 billion from Binance.

But November has seen a new string of cyber incidents. Sources told Reuters on Friday that hackers broke into Cloud One, the U.S. Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform. The breach was discovered in the past month during upgrades to the system. It was unclear who was behind it, how far the intruders got, or whether any data was taken, the report said.

The attackers used a software vulnerability to reach the platform’s control plane, which is comparable to a universal remote, according to Reuters. In theory, access at that level could let intruders check the operational status of military aircraft or track the movement of spare parts.
“A breach here is a big deal,” a source told Reuters.

Cloud One was designed as a single home for the Air Force’s IT needs, running scores of applications — including a system that consolidates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America as well as a system that tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force locations worldwide.

Since the breach was discovered, efforts to move back-office applications onto Cloud One have been paused, while updates to applications already on the platform have been blocked, sources told Reuters.

Meanwhile, sources told the New York Times on Tuesday that the Central Intelligence Agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency recently discovered a cybersecurity breach that exposed some of their unclassified information.
It affected an open-source intelligence analysis system and a computer network that looks for intelligence insights in public, the report added.

Earlier this month, CNN reported that hackers penetrated the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, marking the second such incident in recent months. A possible cyberattack also forced the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network to take some services offline.

Meanwhile, the Pentagon has been dealing with the fallout from a breach last year that exposed Social Security numbers, dates of birth and other military personnel information. Similarly, a leak dubbed “Icepick” exposed personnel records for Department of Homeland Security employees and contractors last month.

In Europe, FIFA said Thursday that hackers stole personal and business information from FIFA the global governing body for soccer. And the UK’s Department for Work and Pensions, which administers Britain’s welfare system, took many of its services offline on Friday as officials declined to rule out a cyberattack.
Companies weren’t spared wither. Travel-booking platform Expedia confirmed Thursday to Skift that hackers breached its systems via a third-party data provider.
Researchers say there is little evidence that ordinary hackers are using AI to exploit complex vulnerabilities. Instead, the technology is mostly being used to scale up phishing campaigns.
At the same time, AI models can find vulnerabilities far faster than humans, setting off a race in where defenders try to find and fix flaws before attackers exploit them.

In fact, the string of cyberattacks followed a series of network outages caused by companies rushing out security patches. On Nov. 12, Microsoft’s suite of software tools went offline, shutting down email and calendars as well as collaboration and AI functions.

Days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. And the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network also went down.
The Trump administration has insisted that the surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.
Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.
One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.
“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”

cbsnews.com/news/cyberattack-hits-uk-wor.headline: Cyberattack hits U.K. work and pensions department, some systems still offline

paragraphs.text: November 28, 2026 / 1:40 PM EST / CBS/AP
Britain's department that handles benefit payments to millions of people confirmed Saturday it was hit by a cyberattack that prompted it to take its systems offline over the past couple of days.
The Department for Work and Pensions, the biggest-spending government department, said in a statement it had experienced "an attempt to gain unauthorized access to our systems."
It did not disclose any other information about the source of the attack.
"Our team and specialist cyber experts continue to investigate a cyberattack on DWP's systems," the department said.
It said that it's continuing to work with the National Cyber Security Centre and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre to understand what occurred.
The incident, which was first detected on Thursday night, saw a range of services taken offline as a precautionary measure, several of which remained offline on Saturday.
The department's statement did not say how much longer the systems would be offline.
The department has said there was no evidence of any personal details being compromised, and pensions and benefit payments continued to be made as normal.
On Friday, the prime minister's office said there was no evidence a "malicious actor" had targeted other government departments.

Mike Bracken, who once led the U.K. Government Digital Service, told CBS News partner BBC News that the cyberattack should be a "wake-up call" for governments to "think about their approach to technology" and its resilience.

"The renewal of systems without a more thoughtful approach to technology, and technology's role in our public policy, is a fundamental problem," he said, adding, "It's about designing an infrastructure that is secure and resilient that we want to have work for us for decades to come."

The cyberattack is the latest in a series of cybersecurity incidents to hit the United Kingdom. Most notably, a number of U.K. meat suppliers said in early November their fridges heated up overnight as they were affected by hacks targeting software used by supermarkets across Europe.

Earlier this month, the country's cyberchief said the U.K. will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia, increasingly use AI in their cyber activity.

Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Center, said that could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks, as the technology will allow "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long" to be discovered and exploited "at a scale that was once unimaginable."
Supermarkets, water control systems, more hacked around U.S., world

latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-27/s.headline: An expert's guide to low-stress holiday gift-giving
latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-27/s.author: Anh Do

paragraphs.text: As she browsed the twinkling collectibles at Downtown Disney District, the glitzy, character-driven shopping destination in Anaheim, Maria Howard picked plenty of goodies to fill a gift basket for a grandchild on the way. At her side, Michelle Lopez pointed to a row of shimmering Mickeys and Minnies, looking for just the right mouse pair to anchor the hamper.

On this Friday, the mother-daughter duo devoted an afternoon to what they called “fun and fantasy.” Howard, a retired restaurant server, was expecting her first granddaughter a few weeks before Thanksgiving. She doesn’t have time “to buy for anyone else,” she says. “I can’t even predict Christmas. In December, I’ll definitely need help checking off my list. I’ll be running around until the last minute.”

It’s the same for Lopez, a medical clerk from South Los Angeles. She already felt tense getting ready to be a new parent. She had hopes of stockpiling presents and crossing off some holiday obligations, yet was resigned to “sending a mall gift card to all my friends and relatives,” she said. “What else can we do?”
My answer: A lot is under your control. Think creatively. Act thoroughly.
I met the pair while filling a bin of baubles — to tick off my own gift list. Season to season, my goal is to stress less, buy early.

This happens to be the time of year when I start wrapping presents. Yes, November. That’s because I started holiday shopping in August. Yes, August. Since Christmas 2001, I’ve experimented with ways to ease into the holly-laden winter minus the mess and achieve more breathing room.
To start with and to simplify, here are my top tips:

• Choose three stores. The first should be an all-consuming stop or a department store that sells most everything. The second should be an online shop, so the vendor can handle your big lift — by this, I mean shipping. If possible, order enough to reach the threshold of free shipping — conveniently handled by the seller. None of us needs to spend time standing in endless lines at the post office. Third, go local and support a neighborhood business, charity shop or crafts fair. (Check out The Times’ list of 125 local gift shops as part of the annual Gift Guide.) This trio should cover the majority of your gifting needs so you’re not driving around to a dozen places for, say, 20 gifts, especially in a year when gas prices (gasp!) cause a case of the shudders. (If you like specifics, this year I’ve chosen the Lego Store, Tiny and Snail and Fugetsu-Do).

• Create an inventory of gift supplies. Gently hoard assorted rolls of wrapping paper, decorative bags, ribbons, bows, invisible tape, colored twine, gift tags, holiday cards, gift card holders, burlap wine pouches, vessels, vellum paper, cellophane, cookie tins ... You get the idea. I have a closet in my home devoted to this. I keep it well-stocked, matched to holidays or celebrations like a baby shower or a graduation, and popping with patterns so there’s an abundant and colorful supply.

• Leverage the deals — like those on Black Friday, Small Business Saturday, Museum Store Sunday, Cyber Monday and Giving Tuesday — to push you near the finish line. And in the case of the latter, yes, for the friend who “has it all,” wait for that Tuesday and make a donation in their honor.

• On the first weekend of December, start purchasing the perishables. That means blooms, pastries, potted plants or seasonal gourmet temptations. You also can fill a gold or silver bin with tropical fruits from the Asian supermarket — think cherimoya, rambutan or starfruit — and make sure your gift is delivered fresh to your recipients. (Again, for specifics, I’ve chosen Farmgirl Flowers, Socola Chocolatier and Trader Joe’s).That allows the people you care for to enjoy them in the countdown to jam-packed holiday gatherings (and the little indulgence doesn’t get lost in the bustle of preparations). It’s a small lift in hectic times.
Now, don’t fret. Here’s how to expand and execute the above steps.

• Look at the ages of your recipients and group them for streamlined shopping. For example, I choose the same or similar items according to sets I’ve designated. This can range from the elementary school set and the teenage set to the retiree set and the office co-workers set.

• Next, look at the shops or vendors that you’ve selected from the tips above and see what set fits where — then buy accordingly. To follow this, I’ve been combing through the aisles and getting gifts like lunch boxes for my friends’ 12-and-under kids at the Lego Store. Think beyond bricks and pieces. They carry fun merchandise.
• Keep in mind that a set can refer to a family. If you usually give to your best friend, their partner and children, narrow your selections to one store or one website to save energy and hours.

• If the set method isn’t ideal, try themes. One fall, I pre-shopped based on a coffee theme and bought different flavors coupled with a home-state mug for the whole roster of my favorite board of directors. That same month, I used a “Discover SoCal” theme to order a series of museum tickets for my neighbors. Or buy ethical or fair trade.

• Speaking of tickets, don’t forget that members of your inner circle might relish seeing what’s in their own backyard. As giver, I’d get passes to a home and garden tour organized in the same county as the receiver, or to a food festival. With all these categories, set a budget and stick to it. Know that the gift you share can be an activity for the near future. Not everything has to be experienced in the moment when, perhaps, your gift recipients are completely inundated with festivities. (As part of the Gift Guide, the Times has a list of 19 experiences to give.)

Then there are special requests. A colleague asked me what she should give her cousin marrying in December and honeymooning in France for Christmas. It’s not mandatory to be bound to a wedding registry. I found a vintage travel trunk, and we filled it with guidebooks, a Julia Child cookbook, a basic phrase book, bookmarks, a journal, a Parisian memoir and the pièce de résistance, a portable electronic translator.

Examine the nature of the event. What are the elements tailored to the bride and groom — or to anyone at the center of a celebration? Take your cues and choose to honor the sense of place, the poetry, the colors or the backstory of the person in the spotlight and gift from there.

Another colleague told me his parents prefer “gifts of a practical nature. No fancy labels. Just something they can use right away.” We settled on separate meat and poultry boxes packaged with dry ice.

I have some aunties who are particular about the scented products they use. At one Christmas Eve gathering, I created a display of Acure, Aveeno and Crabtree & Evelyn lotions, hand washes, ointments and perfumes. I provided a stash of poinsettia- and pine tree-themed bags, and they could stroll around the room, taking their pick. (No gift receipt required for exchange, thank heavens).

Still, like Howard and Lopez, we all face a time crunch. When playing benefactor — but at your wit’s end — go for the presents I consider perennials: luggage tags, hand creams, grocery store gift cards, ginger tea and personalized note cards. Really, everyone uses them. And they’re thoughtful stocking stuffers, a saving grace when my personal list totals as many as 76 people this year. (The Times also has a new list of 28 stocking stuffers.)
Let us remember: Every day is a gift. May we happily unwrap it with others.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/us-civil-r.headline: US civil rights group challenges ICE subpoenas as attack on speech
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/us-civil-r.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: The Trump administration is abusing the grand jury process in an effort to unmask social media users anonymously criticising its immigration enforcement tactics, civil rights lawyers have claimed.

A federal class action filed on Friday, backed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), seeks a court order enjoining the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security from conducting a “bad-faith investigation” that violates the anonymous individuals’ First Amendment free speech rights.
Recommended Stories

The scope of the investigation remains a mystery, but the ACLU says government lawyers have issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas seeking to identify critics and provide their personal information to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) investigators.

ACLU lawyers sued on behalf of four unnamed social media users, asking the district court in Washington to block subpoenas seeking account information for users of social media companies, including Meta, Bluesky and X, formerly known as Twitter. Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the ACLU case’s unsealing on Wednesday.

Boasberg scheduled a January 6 hearing for arguments on the ACLU’s request for a preliminary injunction against the government. The administration has until December 14 to respond in writing to the ACLU’s allegations.

Spokespeople for DHS and US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office in Washington did not immediately respond to The Associated Press’s requests for comment. Pirro, Attorney General Todd Blanche and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin are named as defendants in the ACLU’s lawsuit.
ACLU lawyers say Pirro’s office has used the term “Investigation 18” to describe efforts to identify and obtain the personal information.
“The investigation,” the ACLU says, “is a bad-faith fishing expedition initiated to gather intrusive intelligence and facilitate retaliation against dissenters.”

The ACLU says its lawsuit in Washington is the “first systemic civil challenge, and the first case that will be litigated in public view, to the Trump administration’s abuse of grand jury unmasking subpoenas.”

“The government is weaponizing the grand jury process to retaliate against people for expressing their political views online,” Laura Moraff, staff lawyer with the ACLU, said in a statement. “The First Amendment guarantees our right to criticize the government, including anonymously, and no one should fear being investigated for disagreeing with the president. This crackdown on dissent is antithetical to our nation’s core values.”

The ACLU argues that the subpoenas to social media platforms are part of a broader pattern of intimidation. DHS has sent hundreds of administrative subpoenas to tech companies in the past year to seek information about online ICE critics, the ACLU says.

The civil rights organisation says the Trump administration has shifted to using grand jury subpoenas — a more secretive process — after encountering pushback to the administrative subpoenas from users and tech companies.

The ACLU lawsuit’s plaintiffs include a Bluesky user who wrote about an ICE-related shooting in New York by posting: “Burn ICE to the ground. Burn DHS to the ground. Salt the earth.” Another plaintiff is a college student whose posts on X included an expletive directed at DHS, ICE and Trump.

“Defendants’ rampant use of subpoenas to unmask critics of the federal government is occurring against the backdrop of repeated suggestions that Defendants are building a database of dissenters,” ACLU lawyers wrote.
Laura Follansbee, staff lawyer with the ACLU of DC, claimed the use of grand jury subpoenas was “an alarming abuse of power”.
“The use of subpoenas to punish social media users for their speech is chilling not only for our clients but for others who fear being targeted because of their political beliefs,” Follansbee said.

fortune.com/2026/11/28/steelers-aaron-ro.headline: The Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers. They still owe him about $8.56 million
fortune.com/2026/11/28/steelers-aaron-ro.author: Ashley Lutz

paragraphs.text: Aaron Rodgers no longer has a team. He still has a paycheck.

The Pittsburgh Steelers released the 42-year-old quarterback on Wednesday, hours after he accused head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep in team meetings during an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show. Under his contract, the team remains on the hook for roughly $8.56 million of his salary.

That figure comes from the structure of the one-year deal Rodgers signed in May. According to an ESPN breakdown, the contract totaled $22,502,750: a $500,000 roster bonus and a $2,750 workout bonus, both already paid, plus a fully guaranteed $22 million base salary. Rodgers had collected about $13.44 million of that salary through the first 11 weeks of the 18-week regular season.

Because no team claimed him off waivers on Thursday, Pittsburgh is obligated for the rest of that guarantee. A team that claimed him would have assumed the contract. None did, and NFL insiders Tom Pelissero and Dianna Russini both reported no immediate interest from other teams.
What Rodgers will be paid in 2026
If the guarantee holds, Rodgers will finish 2026 with about $22.5 million from Pittsburgh, up from the $13.65 million base value of his first Steelers contract a year earlier.

The deal could have reached $25 million. Insider Jordan Schultz reported $2.5 million in incentives that paid $625,000 for each Steelers playoff win, provided Rodgers played 75% of regular-season snaps. Those bonuses were tied to Pittsburgh’s postseason, which he is no longer part of.

He can still add to the total. If he signs elsewhere, it would likely be at the veteran minimum of about $75,000 a week, and the Steelers would remain responsible for the rest of his salary, sports litigator Jay Reisinger told Pittsburgh’s WTAE.
Can Pittsburgh get the money back?

Possibly, but not easily. The NFL’s collective bargaining agreement lets a club deny termination pay to a player released for conduct detrimental to the team, a call that ultimately goes to an arbitrator. ESPN reported that if the Steelers filed and won such a grievance, they would get the remaining $8.56 million back as a salary-cap credit after the season. Until then, his $22.5 million cap charge for 2026 is unaffected.

There is no indication yet that the team plans to try, Front Office Sports reported Friday, and the NFL Players Association would be expected to fight any attempt. Reisinger told WTAE the likelier outcome is a settlement “somewhere south of $7 million.”

Rodgers has offered his own account of the split. In a message read by Al Michaels during Amazon Prime Video’s Black Friday broadcast, he said the team went public first and added: “They also barred me from the facility. That’s why I went to McAfee.” Steelers owner Art Rooney II has said he has “100% confidence in Mike McCarthy.”
The fallout has reached the box office, too. Steelers ticket prices on the secondary market fell 36% in three days after the release, Front Office Sports reported.
A fortune built mostly on salary

Rodgers’ net worth has never been publicly disclosed. His documented pay is about $417 million in career NFL earnings including this season, according to Spotrac. That is nearly $400 million more than Mason Rudolph, the backup who replaced him and led Pittsburgh to a 27-5 win over Denver on Friday.

Endorsements add to his assets. Rodgers left Nike for a multiyear deal with Adidas in 2015, as Fortune reported at the time, and Forbes estimated his 2022 earnings at $68 million, including $11 million off the field.

Rodgers turns 43 on Dec. 2. In May, he said 2026 would be his final NFL season. If no team calls, his last check from the league will come from a franchise that no longer wants him around, and may yet try not to send it.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/former-min.headline: Former minister arrested in Paraguay’s latest Ueno Bank failure fallout
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/former-min.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Paraguay’s former economy minister Carlos Fernandez Valdovinos has turned himself in to police.
On Friday, he became the latest former official placed under arrest following the collapse of one of the country’s largest banks.
Recommended Stories

The Ueno Bank crisis, which saw millions locked out of their life savings earlier this month, has already prompted the impeachment of President Santiago Pena, who has been arrested along with several other former top officials.

An arrest warrant for Valdovinos, seen by the AFP news agency, accused the 61-year-old of “alleged criminal acts of administration for personal gain, aggravated passive bribery, criminal association and money laundering”.
The public prosecutor’s office alleged that while he was minister in July last year, he approved the transfer of tens of millions of dollars in pension fund money to Ueno Bank.
He left office in August, after which he signed a multi-million-dollar consulting contract with the business group that controlled Ueno Bank.
Prosecutors believe the lucrative contract may have been linked to the pension fund transaction.
The Ueno Bank crisis
The crisis erupted on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.

In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million customers. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions. It left people struggling to access their savings, wages and pension payments, and raised questions about the government’s handling of public money.

The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.
His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings. He was removed from office on November 6.
The bank had grown quickly under Pena’s presidency from a financial technology company into a large firm handling state pensions and the accounts of several government entities.

Pena is accused of using his position to direct millions in government funds to Ueno and concealing or downplaying its financial troubles, despite warnings of risky lending practices, while having financial ties to the bank. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares last year.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/hun.headline: Hundreds died in the Cocoanut Grove fire. What doctors learned saved many more.
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/hun.author: Matthew Hay Brown

paragraphs.text: If you had been fortunate enough to have been pulled from the Cocoanut Grove after its papery tropical decor caught flame 84 years ago Saturday, your chances of surviving what’s still the nation’s deadliest nightclub fire would have depended in large part on the hospital to which you were sent.

At Boston City Hospital, burn victims received the then-standard treatment for burn wounds — and suffered the standard mortality rate. But at Massachusetts General Hospital, Oliver Cope, the acting chief of surgery, tried something different.

An estimated 1,000 people, more than double the Boston venue’s legal capacity, had packed the building on the evening of Nov. 28, 1942, when the fire broke out. (The crowd would have been larger, and the disaster likely still greater, had Boston College won its football game that day. We’ll get back to that.)

The flames spread quickly from the basement Melody Lounge to the main level of the building, the size of a city block. Panicked patrons jammed the front entrance revolving door. Six of the nine other exit doors were locked, apparently to prevent guests from skipping out on their tabs. Some doors were behind curtains, or opened inward, useless before a stampeding crowd. To get to the victims, firefighters had to break through walls.
A call for ambulances drew responses from not only the city but also suburbs and military installations. City officials warned the hospitals of mass casualties.

They were ready. Since the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor the previous December drew the United States into World War II, both Boston City and Mass General prepared emergency plans for more attacks, according to Mass General. Each received grant money to study burn injuries, and laid in supplies. The city of Boston had rehearsed a disaster response only the weekend before.
Of the Cocoanut Grove victims taken to Boston City that Saturday night, 114 were alive Sunday morning.
First, they were administered morphine, a powerful opiate that was hardly sufficient for the excruciating, sometimes lethal standard treatment.
Multiple people were required to hold each writhing patient still enough for the doctors to proceed. They cut and scraped away burn blisters and dead tissue. Then they applied tannic acid.

The goal was to turn the surviving skin into an infection-resistant leather. Even when successful, recovery took months. The disfiguring scars were permanent. A third of the Cocoanut Grove victims so treated still died.

Of the victims taken to Mass General, 39 survived the first night. Cope, a professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, saw an opportunity. He’d been thinking about burn wounds since Pearl Harbor, and had hypothesized a treatment that would likely be less traumatic than tanning — and possibly more effective.

Under his direction, patients were given penicillin, an early use of the antibiotic, to protect against bacterial infection. Then their wounds were wrapped in petroleum jelly-infused gauze, not scraped or tanned, and left to heal.
It worked: All 39 patients survived to discharge, and the so-called soft treatment became the new standard. It was used for Allied soldiers during the war and further refined in the ensuing decades.

“The 171 victims who made it alive to Boston City and Mass General hospitals became subjects in the most comprehensive clinical trial in the annals of burn treatment,” author Barbara Ravage wrote in Burn Unit: Saving Lives After the Flames. “New ideas were tried, old methods discarded, and the agenda for burn research was set for the next quarter century.”
Even with the treatment breakthrough, 492 people, more than the Cocoanut Grove’s legal capacity of 460, died as a result of the fire.

It could have been worse. The B.C. Eagles, 8-0 and ranked first in the nation entering the day, had planned to celebrate an undefeated season at the venue that night. But they were stunned that afternoon by archrival Holy Cross in one of college football’s greatest upsets, a 55-12 rout at Fenway Park that dashed their national championship hopes. They canceled the party.

Barnet “Barney” Welansky, the Cocoanut Grove’s owner, was convicted in 1943 of 19 counts of involuntary manslaughter. The case established that a business owner could be held accountable for failing to meet an appropriate duty of care to his customers. He was sentenced to 12 to 15 years in prison but released after four with cancer and died a short tine later.
The fire and its aftermath led also to reforms in fire codes and enforcement, and advances in the understanding of grief and post-traumatic stress disorder.

While it was “catastrophic,” physicians Jeffrey C. Schneider and Coleen M. Ryan wrote for Harvard Medical School in 2013, it “nonetheless served as an engine for research and innovation that has since saved many more lives than were lost — a fitting memorial” to those who died or whose lives were forever changed.
Photo Almanac is an occasional series from The Washington Post, using photo archives to understand where we are today by examining where we’ve been.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/israels-ei.headline: Netanyahu offers to rotate Israeli premiership with Gadi Eisenkot
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/28/israels-ei.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Prime Ministerial hopeful Eisenkot offers immediate talks with Netanyahu to test whether Likud is ‘ready for genuine unity’.

Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has proposed a rotating premiership with his main rival Gadi Eisenkot, who responded by offering immediate talks to see if the Likud leader is serious about a proposal for the country’s future government.

“If Likud is ready for genuine unity, I am prepared to see how serious it is over the next 24 hours,” Eisenkot said in a statement on Saturday. “I invite Netanyahu and his team to join me tonight … to conduct genuine and accelerated negotiations,” he added, naming a hotel near Tel Aviv as the location for talks.
Recommended Stories
Eisenkot is the leader of the centrist Yashar party and was tapped by Israel’s president to form a new government.
Earlier on Saturday, Netanyahu said on X that he was willing to let Eisenkot serve first as prime minister in a rotating premiership agreement as part of a unity government.
He said that with Likud being the largest in the country, he should “naturally” lead the unity government, but he would be willing to abandon that principle this time.

“Given the gravity of the existential danger and the possibility that a government will be formed that lacks the ability to confront it, my responsibility as a leader requires me to set everything aside, including the principle of the largest party, and agree that Gadi Eisenkot will serve first as prime minister, while I will serve as alternate prime minister at the beginning of the term,” Netanyahu said.

Eisenkot had pledged on Friday to announce the formation of Israel’s next government by the official deadline of December 6, without using the option of a 14-day extension. He also accused Netanyahu of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections. The prime ministerial hopeful has so far struggled to put together a ruling coalition.

“I expect that, in light of this agreement on my part, we will immediately begin genuine, sincere and accelerated negotiations in which the other side will also be willing to make similar compromises and concessions, to establish a national unity government that will repel these dangers and ensure Israel’s security and future,” Netanyahu said.
‘Deceitful tactics’

Israel’s public broadcaster Kan earlier reported that the offer had already been proposed unofficially, so Likud could assume “plausible deniability” as the party remains conflicted on the terms of the proposal.
The October 27 elections failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.
Netanyahu and his traditional alliance of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties won 53 seats, short of a majority in the 120-seat parliament, while Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats.
Netanyahu’s announcement underscores the pressure he also faces as Eisenkot wins support from potential partners that could hand him a governing majority or allow him to form a coalition government.
After his proposal, the leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, who has also publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu in the past, rejected the latest offer.
“Enough tricks and deceitful tactics, Netanyahu has lost and our duty is to respect the will of the voter and form a government of change and rescue,” he posted on X.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, which is an alliance of Arab-led parties, also said that Netanyahu was attempting to thwart a change of government.

“The democratic majority has decided: this blood-stained, neglectful government must go,” he wrote on X. “It is time to fulfil the shared will of the entire public, Jews and Arabs alike, and remove Netanyahu this very week.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/28/benjam.headline: Netanyahu offers to rotate Israeli premiership with main rival Eisenkot

paragraphs.text: Israel’s caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday proposed a rotating premiership with his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, who would go first, with the latter expected to announce the formation of a new government within days.

Proposing a unity government in a social media post, Netanyahu said “my responsibility as a leader requires me to set everything aside ... and agree that Gadi Eisenkot will serve first as prime minister, while I will serve as alternate prime minister at the beginning of the term”.
The offer came one day after Eisenkot vowed to announce the formation of Israel’s next government by the official deadline of 6 December, without using the option of a 14-day extension.
He is expected to form a coalition with anti-Netanyahu parties, but his centrist Yashar party has also been conducting negotiations with Netanyahu’s rightwing Likud.
On Friday, however, Eisenkot accused Likud of stalling coalition talks in an effort to bring about new elections.
“Likud ... has been unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table,” Eisenkot said in a statement.
His wide-ranging camp has faced divisions over whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, the Arab-majority lists, or form a unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu opponents scoffed at his offer of a rotating premiership.

Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Arab-majority Joint List, which is expected to support an Eisenkot-led government without joining it, wrote: “The democratic majority has decided: this bloodstained, neglectful government must go. It is time to fulfill the shared will of the entire public, Jews and Arabs alike, and remove Netanyahu this (upcoming) week.”

Former premier Yair Lapid, who co-chairs the centrist Beyachad (Together) party, wrote: “Netanyahu’s proposal is yet another transparent con by a serial fraudster who has deceived every partner and violated every agreement.”
Eisenkot’s Yashar party has so far agreed coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Together, they have a combined total of 36 lawmakers – far short of the 61 needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.

Israeli media reported that Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Arab-Israeli party Ra’am, is expected on Saturday to recognise Hamas as a “terror group” – a move that could pave the way for his party to join a possible Eisenkot-led coalition.
But some of Eisenkot’s allies have voiced opposition to relying on the support of the Arab-majority lists, which made unprecedented gains in the election.
Meanwhile, Britain, France and six other countries on Saturday issued a joint statement calling for postponed Palestinian legislative elections to take place in the first three months of 2027.

The vote was “essential” for a “democratic renewal” in the Palestinian territories and “is inseparable from the preservation of the two-state solution, which we remain steadfastly committed to”, they said.
The other countries behind the joint statement were Canada, Australia, Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway and Poland.
Last month, the Palestinian president, Mahmoud Abbas, postponed legislative elections to September next year.
The first legislative elections since 2006, which the international community has strongly advocated for, had been scheduled for 28 November, with a presidential election expected in early 2027.
“Twenty years after the last national election in Palestine”, Palestinians were still being denied “the right to express themselves democratically through the ballot box”, the eight countries said.
“The holding of free and transparent elections is essential to preserve the democratic principles that must remain at the heart of Palestinian institutions.”
The ministers also warned that their continued support for the Palestinian Authority went hand in hand with commitments on reform and democratic renewal.
Abbas’s office in October blamed the delay on “obstacles imposed by Israeli measures ... as well as the need to create appropriate political, security and on-the-ground conditions”.
Israel, which held its own elections late last month, rejected any responsibility for the delay.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/col.headline: College Board says it is investigating possible AI hack
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/28/col.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering politics and breaking news

College Board, the nonprofit organization that administers standardized tests and hosts an online application used to award financial aid, said that it suspects artificial intelligence tools were recently used to gain unauthorized access to students’ and professionals’ account information.
The organization disclosed the breach in a statement Friday, saying it “took immediate action” to protect its users and systems.

“Our preliminary assessment is that this activity involved sophisticated AI tools that have recently been leveraged to gain access to the systems of other major institutions worldwide,” College Board said in the statement. “While our investigation is ongoing, we have determined that the activity involved access to the systems students and professionals use to create new College Board accounts and to submit CSS Profile applications for financial aid.”

The organization did not disclose the scale of the breach or details on what data was accessed, but said it “allowed the actors to access basic account information for a subset of users and to initiate password resets in some cases.”

As of Saturday afternoon, College Board’s CSS Profile applications remained temporarily disabled in response to the suspicious activity. The organization said there is no evidence to suggest that its repository of test scores and content was improperly accessed.
Groupthink can be a good thing in browser tabs

The tab groups feature in a browser can bring order to the chaos of having dozens of pages opened in a browser window by letting you file pages about shared subjects (say, recipes or travel) in distinct collections. Every major browser supports them, with the option to open a link in a current or new tab group usually behind a contextual menu you bring up with a right-click or a long press of the screen.

Browsers differ, however, in how they synchronize tab groups between your computers. Apple’s Safari does this best, automatically syncing all of your tab groups between Mac, iPhone and iPad copies of that browser and making them accessible via a prominent toolbar icon. It’s at the top right corner in the macOS and iPadOS versions of Safari, at the bottom of the screen in iOS.

Google’s Chrome implements its tab group sync somewhat less elegantly, hiding access to your groups behind an item halfway down the catchall menu list you open via a vertical-ellipsis icon at the top right. Microsoft’s Edge, based on Chrome’s underlying code, works in much the same way except its menu icon is a horizontal ellipsis at the top right in its Mac and Windows apps and at the bottom right of its iOS and Android releases. Mozilla Firefox, however, doesn’t support tab-group sync, leaving it in last place in this feature ranking.
New York Mayor Mamdani underwent surgery to repair torn Achilles tendon
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) underwent surgery Friday to repair the Achilles tendon he tore during a soccer match last week.

Mamdani’s press secretary, Joe Calvello, said in a statement that the surgery, which lasted just over an hour, “was successful” and that the mayor is expected to make a full recovery. Mamdani was discharged from the hospital the same day as his procedure, Calvello said.
The 35-year-old mayor sustained the injury during a soccer match against local journalists Nov. 19. Mamdani’s team won the game, with the mayor scoring a goal.
At a news conference about closing the Rikers Island jail complex the following day, Mamdani acknowledged that he did not stretch before the game.

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35, and soon after I tore my Achilles, and I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks,” Mamdani told reporters. “And I will play soccer in about nine months.”
Since the incident, Mamdani has continued to make public appearances wearing a medical boot and using crutches.
The mayor’s office did not disclose where the surgery was done but thanked medical staff for the “first-class care” he received.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: Is it okay to NOT let guests bring plus-ones to my wedding?
What’s the etiquette for inviting guests to a wedding? Do you automatically include a plus-one for them?

One couple is weighing the rules as the two get ready for their own nuptial celebrations. And in this week’s episode of the “Life Hax” podcast, columnists Shane O’Neill and Carolyn Hax debate the options. (You can find the full episode, which includes more wedding-related dilemmas, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.)

Our letter writer notes that they’ve never needed a date to enjoy a wedding and think it’s “a little silly” to invite plus-ones. They’ve seen different approaches: “We’ve had friends who only invited the partners of guests who were married, engaged, or living together,” they wrote. But “that created way too many weird exclusions.”
So what’s a 30-something to do?
Shane proposes one rubric: “If you know their name and you would be embarrassed to run into them and be like, ‘I didn’t invite you to the wedding,’ invite them to the wedding!”
Carolyn calls that “brilliant.”
The guest list is more about finances than excluding people, Shane adds, because “by the time you’re drunk and doing the Chicken Dance, my worst enemy could be at my wedding.”
Reporter covering breaking news
Israeli strike on Gaza kills 2 Doctors Without Borders staff, charity says

Humanitarian charity Doctors Without Borders said an Israeli strike killed two of its staff members at a clearly marked Gaza City clinic on Friday — an attack the Israeli military said was targeted at Hamas members “under humanitarian cover.”
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” the group said on X. “This is a direct hit on MSF.”

The Israel Defense Forces said in a statement Saturday that it killed “Hamas terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.” The military said that two men, whom it named, were working as security guards at the clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders “while also serving as terrorists,” without providing evidence. It added that no medical infrastructure in the area was damaged in the strike.
At least 17 members of Doctors Without Borders have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, the charity said.
According to the charity, the premises hit in the attack had been “clearly marked” with its logos and the location had been “communicated to and was known by” the Israeli military.

World Health Organization Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X that attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are “outrageous and unacceptable.” He extended “heartfelt condolences” to Doctors Without Borders colleagues.
Reporter covering international breaking news
WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.
Initial tests show no lead in drinking water near Iowa detonation site, EPA says

The Environmental Protection Agency says preliminary tests indicate the controlled detonation that took place in Middleton, Iowa, on Wednesday did not lead to an increase in lead levels in sources of drinking water in the surrounding area.

The Army detonated nearly 10,000 pounds of degrading lead explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant, saying this was necessary because the stockpile of lead azide had become so unstable it feared it would spontaneously explode.
The operation was postponed several times amid a legal challenge and outcry from residents and local officials who feared the blast would create a plume of toxic lead dust.

The EPA said Saturday it “found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake.”
It added that it had also monitored air quality for 30 consecutive hours after the detonation and detected no airborne lead.
The agency is still processing tap water, soil, dust and air samples, and says results will be posted online.
Activists in Iowa have said public pushback to the Army’s original proposal had made the explosion safer and more transparent, The Post reported.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/us/dead-fish-myst.headline: This Seattle Engineering Marvel Hid a Mystery: Pyramids of Dead Fish

paragraphs.text: Travis Eiler explores sunken planes, shipwrecks and forgotten bridges in the murky waters of the Pacific Northwest, yet the recreational diver still wasn’t prepared for his unsettling discovery last fall in Seattle’s Lake Washington: fish, arrayed in neat pyramids, seemingly unharmed, except they were dead.
“It was like some kind of bizarre science experiment,” Mr. Eiler said.

The finding — and the mystery that ensued — threatened to waylay a $765 million engineering marvel overhead, the world’s first floating rail bridge that stretches the region’s light rail system across the 1.5-mile-wide lake.

Since the 1960s, Puget Sound leaders had dreamed of a transit bridge connecting Seattle’s urban core with communities on the east side of the lake, but Seattle-area voters repeatedly rejected rapid transit measures. In 1989, engineers incorporated space for future transit into the Interstate 90 floating bridge over Lake Washington, part of a highway that stretches from Seattle to Boston. But legal battles still kept the trains at bay.

Voters finally approved a sales tax dedicated for transit in 2008, but an engineering challenge remained. More than 200 feet deep in spots, Lake Washington has a soft, muddy bottom that makes support piers impossible, but a floating rail bridge seemed far-fetched. Pontoons pitch and roll with the waves, while light rail requires high-voltage power lines that must stay steadily aligned. And the electrical current used to power light rail can corrode the steel inside concrete pontoons.
Brad Owen, an engineer and executive with the Seattle-area transit authority Sound Transit, said the hardest part of a floating bridge wasn’t keeping it afloat; “it’s the motion that stops you.”

So crews insulated the tracks, invented articulated steel joiners that flex with the water’s motion and dangled dozens of electrical cables — known as anode strings — into the lake to draw stray current safely away from the pontoons.

Some 252,000 people rode the bridge on opening day, waiting an hour or more for the smooth, fast ride and sweeping views of Mount Rainier. Ridership on the line that rolls over Lake Washington has roughly quadrupled, and Seattle residents are so enthusiastic about transit these days that they voted this month to double the city’s transit sales tax, a small portion of which will help Sound Transit’s continued expansion.
“Everybody wants it, they want it to their neighborhood, and they wanted it yesterday,” said Dow Constantine, Sound Transit’s chief executive.
Deep below water, however, lay a problem.

Unlike other recreational divers who head for the brighter, marine-rich waters of Puget Sound, Mr. Eiler prefers to explore the lake’s darkness and its sunken World War II-era airplanes and “modern ruins,” such as collapsed bridges.

He and his diving partner, Shahein Moussavi, were hunting for concrete bridge remnants last fall when they found a stack of dead fish, so neatly placed that “it almost looked like a net had been dropped down and opened,” Mr. Eiler said.

Subsequent dives revealed more than a dozen other mounds of dead perch, carp and chinook salmon — a big problem in a region where salmon are protected by federal tribal treaties. Scavengers like crayfish and sculpin hadn’t touched the carcasses, suggesting whatever killed them was either poisoning the water or generating an electrical field that kept bottom-dwellers away.

Last November, the divers emailed photos of the dead fish to a Washington Department of Transportation worker. When no one responded, Mr. Eiler and Mr. Moussavi in July alerted conservationists and tribal leaders, who pressed state officials to act. This time, the culprit was revealed: The dead fish were all beneath those anode strings dangling from the bridge to help prevent corrosion.
Were the deaths caused by electrical current coming off the bridge’s cables, engineers wondered, or by a chemical reaction between that current and lake-bed sediments?

Anti-corrosion systems are common on floating bridges for cars and trucks, and engineers and planners assumed the low-voltage current generated by the light-rail bridge wouldn’t cause a problem. They also initially didn’t include plans for routine underwater inspections because the anti-corrosion cables could be pulled out for safety checks.
Nothing in the planning “indicated that this system should not work,” Mr. Constantine said.

This fall, state and tribal biologists and engineers tested both the fish and the water and determined that resting the anodes on the lake’s bottom silt had created concentrated, localized electrical fields strong enough to stun or kill fish. That explained both the lack of visible injuries on the carcasses and scavengers’ reluctance to eat them. Sound Transit lowered the voltage coming off the cables, lifted lines that had been resting on the lake bed and began installing protective cages around the anodes, adding several million dollars to the cost of the bridge.
In all, Sound Transit says around 2,000 fish died, mostly invasive species rather than salmon.
When Mr. Eiler and Mr. Moussavi dived under Lake Washington again a few weeks ago, they found what they had hoped for. No stacks of dead fish and plenty to explore.

nytimes.com/2026/11/28/nyregion/small-bo.headline: A Big Bookstore Arrives Near a Shop on the Corner. This Isn’t a Movie.

paragraphs.text: Walking between the new mother-daughter-owned bookstore, the Rabbit Books and Bar, at East 11th Street and Avenue A and the new, big Barnes & Noble catty-corner, Julia DeMarco observed life imitating art.

“It reminds me of a movie,” said Ms. DeMarco, 29, who lives in the East Village. “Meg Ryan runs an independent bookstore, and Tom Hanks opens this big conglomerate nearby and puts her out of business.”

With apologies for that spoiler, the movie Ms. DeMarco referred to is the 1998 romantic comedy “You’ve Got Mail,” directed by Nora Ephron. On Monday night inside the Rabbit, its co-owner Marianna Vaidman Stone squeezed her eyes shut and pressed her hands into a tabletop at the utterance of its name.

“Of course I saw the movie,” she said. And she estimated that “You’ve Got Mail” was now mentioned more in online comments about her store than, for example, its poetry gatherings, wine list or comfortable reading nooks.
“I intend,” Ms. Vaidman Stone added, “for my ending to be different.”
The Rabbit opened on Aug. 11. The Barnes & Noble followed on Nov. 18. Some bibliophiles cheered.
“They’re both a welcome addition for their own unique reasons,” said Karen Martinez, an East Village resident for 20 years.

Coming on the heels of an article in The Atlantic that declared “The End of Reading Is Here,” bookstore openings come across as New York City’s vigorous rebuttal. Businesses and events that sell and glorify books are surging. Recently in these pages, readers (yes, readers) have learned about a 66-hour live recitation of Robert Caro’s “The Power Broker,” a new “Moby Dick”-themed bar and neighborhood book crawls.
Now the staredown between the Rabbit and the Barnes & Noble — which is the city’s biggest new bookstore in a decade — has some pondering how sustainable in-person book buying is.
“Is there a market for this many bookstores?” Chris Brown, a 28-year-old Stuyvesant Town resident, asked as he exited the Rabbit. “I wonder who will survive the longest.”
In response to emailed questions, a Barnes & Noble spokesperson said that the stores would complement more than they would compete, and that their proximity was a boon for both.
“Bookstores attract book buyers,” the spokesperson wrote.

Blaming Barnes & Noble for burying independent bookstores may actually seem quaint now, with the explosion of Amazon and online book sales. In 2018, the New York Times columnist David Leonhardt was moved to write, “It’s plausible that Barnes & Noble will not survive.” Once ubiquitous around New York City, by 2023 Barnes & Noble had only three stores left in Manhattan and one in Brooklyn.

After Amazon recast Barnes & Noble as David instead of Goliath, book lovers began cheering the chain as proof that physical bookstores would not vanish. A 2022 Times headline noted that Barnes & Noble had gone “from villain to hero.” Nationwide, the chain has expanded from fewer than 600 stores in 2023 to more than 740 today, per a news release from a Barnes & Noble media contact, Debb Hanks (no relation to Tom).

Its resurgence, though, is not universally welcomed. On Avenue A, people could be heard shouting at the gleaming displays in the windows, “Shop local!” John Dorney, 28, said the new store felt “predatory.”

Still, other neighbors who pride themselves on supporting independent businesses conceded that if a chain store had to move into that long-vacant 11,000-square-foot space, this was far from the worst.
“If we’re going to have a new, big shop, I’m glad it’s a bookstore,” said Anna Levak, 56, after she strolled through the new Barnes & Noble with her 14-year-old daughter, Lila.

Amenities that used to give Barnes & Noble an advantage over smaller competitors are inverted on Avenue A. It is the Rabbit that has the cozy bar, plush sofas, and tables for cappuccinos, cabernets, snacks and book-themed board games. While the Barnes & Noble does have colorful, cushioned sitting cubes in its large children’s section, the store otherwise has only a few hardwood chairs — and no food, drink or restrooms.
“They’re going to put the Barnes & Noble out of business,” Amar Jivraj, 28, gloated upon leaving the Rabbit.

Ms. Vaidman Stone, 55, said she hoped the stores could serve as “the gateway to the literary playground of the East Village.” Born in Moscow, Ms. Vaidman Stone fled antisemitism in the Soviet Union to emigrate to the United States with her family in 1979. Her grandfather and father later opened an American gas station and incorporated it under the letters “KROL” — the root of the word “krolik,” which in Russian means “rabbit.” The small, clever animal became a family totem.

When Ms. Vaidman Stone decided to switch careers from public policy work to creating “a book-centered place of human connection,” she named it to honor her family. The name is also a homage to the world’s diverse array of literature, so much of which features rabbit characters — from ancient folklore to “Alice in Wonderland” and “Watership Down.”

In January, she signed her 10-year lease for an ample corner space, previously filled by a 7-Eleven, across Avenue A from a vibrant new country music bar, Lucinda’s. When she learned that Barnes & Noble would open catty-corner, she called it “a blow.”
Her daughter and co-owner, Emily Stone, looked on the bright side.
“I’m happy to have more bookish people in the area,” said Ms. Stone, 25, as she poured a customer a glass of rosé.

nytimes.com/2026/11/27/world/europe/fran.headline: France’s Bookstores, Beloved Curators of Literature, Are in a Deep Crisis

paragraphs.text: When old friends and loyal customers gathered for a book club in Strasbourg, France, last month, the only thing missing was the books. The group met in an empty room that had housed one of the city’s most beloved bookstores, Dinali, before it closed its doors this summer after 54 years.

“It’ll take some time before I can fully come to terms with it,” said Jennifer Goepp, who had owned the store with her husband, Thierry, and was welcoming the book club members to what was left of it.

The Goepps are not alone. Last year, 85 bookstores went out of business in France. It was the first year in recent history that the country had seen more bookstores close than open. Earlier this year, Gibert Joseph, France’s largest independent bookstore chain, founded in 1888, filed for bankruptcy protection.

“We’re drowning right now,” said Alexandra Charroin Spangenberg, the head of the national booksellers’ union. “If we lose the network of independent bookstores,” she said, “we lose part of France’s cultural identity.”

With more than 3,200 shops, France has one of the most deeply rooted bookstore cultures in the world, surviving a broader shift to online book-buying better than many places. The United States, with nearly five times the population, has only about 500 more bookshops. Bookstores help give French literature its idiosyncratic character by giving shelf space to aspiring writers whose work might be overlooked in mass-market online book selling.

Being an independent bookseller — a “libraire,” as the French call it — is not like any other retail job. People can study the trade at universities and earn a widely respected diploma. “I think of it as a calling rather than a job,” said Ms. Charroin Spangenberg, who owns a bookstore in St.-Étienne, a town in central France.

Yet France leaves its libraires little room to absorb rising costs. They run an average profit margin of 1 percent, making them among the country’s least profitable retailers, according to the booksellers’ union.
“A baker, when the price of butter and flour goes up, simply raises the price of his baguette,” Mr. Goepp said. “We can’t.”

That’s because, under a 1981 law named after Jack Lang, the culture minister at the time, publishers fix book prices nationwide. The main purpose is to protect small bookshops from predatory discounting by large retail chains. But the law leaves booksellers with little flexibility to set their own prices. By September, retail prices overall were up more than 3 percent from a year earlier, but book prices rose only about 1 percent.

Shops like Dinali must also compete with the likes of Amazon. Over the years, the Lang law was amended to limit the sway of online sellers — fixing e-book prices and restricting deals on delivery fees — but their selection and fast delivery still give them an edge over bricks-and-mortar stores.

“I buy online when I can’t find what I need in a bookstore,” said Hugo Muré, 22, a law student who shopped at Dinali. Mr. Muré said he often needed titles that arrived much faster online, adding: “I can’t afford to wait.”
The post-pandemic boom, when shoppers rallied to support independent businesses, has long faded. Shops like Dinali have recorded a near 14 percent drop in sales since 2021, according to the union.

These pressures eroded Dinali’s profit margins until there was no choice but to shut down. After running a deficit for three years, Mr. Goepp said he and his wife made the decision to close all three Dinali stores in Strasbourg in late 2025.
“We realized that the next step would mean cutting staff positions,” said Ms. Goepp, who added that would have hurt their ability to curate their shelves thoughtfully.

Sophie Noël, a sociologist at Panthéon-Assas University in Paris, said, “These bookstores really give a voice to, and provide opportunities for, books that would never be able to gain traction through other channels.”
“Take Samuel Beckett,” she said.

The Nobel-winning Beckett was born in Dublin but lived most of his life in France, frequently writing in French. Still, he initially had little commercial success there. Between the spring of 1947 and the summer of 1948, he sold exactly four copies of his novel “Murphy.” The risk taken by small bookstores to keep stocking him allowed him to slowly build a readership in a way that helped sustain his career, particularly until his play “Waiting for Godot” brought him global acclaim.

Customers said they were drawn to Dinali by its distinctive selection, and mourned the loss like a death in the Strasbourg community. For Françoise Houari, 58, a longtime customer, the book club helped cushion the blow.

At last month’s meeting, about a dozen members perched on plastic chairs, amid ripped-out floorboards, presenting the books they had chosen. Ms. Houari brought a “mendiant,” a traditional Alsatian cake made from stale brioche, alongside her choice of book, Douce Dibondo’s “Le Mouvement.” Mr. Goepp chose a pastry recipe book, a nod to the new career he is starting at 63.

The Goepps have turned the store’s old main space, on a cobblestone street with half-timbered houses in Strasbourg’s old town, into a chocolate store and cafe. It has an upstairs reading space, where they display the old Dinali sign on a shelf, flanked by books.
Ms. Charroin Spangenberg, the union head, is less hopeful about the future. “We’re going to have to get through this crisis,” she said, “and our concern is how many of us will survive.”

cbsnews.com/news/israel-gaza-msf-doctors.headline: Israeli strike kills 2 Doctors Without Borders guards whom Israel claims were Hamas fighters
cbsnews.com/news/israel-gaza-msf-doctors.author: Duarte Dias

paragraphs.text: Doctors Without Borders, also known by their French acronym MSF, said Friday night two of its staff who worked as guards were killed in an Israeli strike on a clinic in Gaza. The Israeli military accused the men of being Hamas fighters.
"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen," the humanitarian organization said in a post on X. "This is a direct hit on MSF," it added.
In the statement, MSF also said its premises are marked with logos and its locations are communicated to the Israeli military.
"We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability," the statement said.
In response, the Israeli Defense Forces named the two men killed as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, and claimed they were terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.

"While also serving as terrorists, the two worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF). This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the IDF said in a statement released on Friday.

The Israeli military also disputed the claim that MSF facilities were targeted in the attack, claiming that no damage was caused to medical infrastructure. It added that it had used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to minimize "the expected harm to civilians."
MSF say the deaths bring the total number of their workers killed in Gaza to 17.
Mourners gathered Saturday for the two men's funeral prayers. Ahmad Abu Haseira, a relative of one of the killed men, said they were unarmed and wore MSF uniforms at the time of the attack.
A local MSF employee, Ahmad Shehada, said the two were making their rounds to check the clinic's facilities when a missile struck.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

phys.org/news/2026-11-lab-electrons-gain.headline: Lab experiment shows how electrons gain energy during magnetic reconnection
phys.org/news/2026-11-lab-electrons-gain.author: Sam Jarman

paragraphs.text: November 28, 2026 report
by Sam Jarman, Phys.org
edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

Within a plasma, magnetic field lines can break apart and join up again in a new arrangement, releasing huge amounts of stored magnetic energy in the process. Named magnetic reconnection, this phenomenon is known to power dramatic solar flares and has also been recreated in lab experiments on Earth.
So far, however, some key details about the process remain poorly understood. In particular, physicists have yet to explain how energy is transferred to a plasma's electrons during reconnection.

Through new research published in Physical Review Letters, a team led by Sonu Yadav at West Virginia University has found direct evidence that this handover is carried out by "lower-hybrid drift waves": ripples that form at the sharp boundaries created by reconnection.
Elusive energy boost

To date, physicists have proposed several ways that electrons could be indirectly energized by reconnection. Previous theories have suggested that while some electrons may be sped up directly by the electric fields the process creates, others gain energy by bouncing off shrinking loops of magnetic field.

A combination of simulations, lab experiments and spacecraft observations has now all pointed to lower-hybrid drift waves as another possibility: these waves form where the plasma's density drops steeply over a short distance, which is exactly what happens at the edges of reconnection regions. Until now, however, researchers had yet to observe how electrons respond to these waves.
Merging plasma

To address the challenge, Yadav's team used the PHASMA facility at West Virginia University: a vacuum chamber almost 5 meters (16 feet) long. Inside, they created two twisted columns of magnetized helium plasma and pushed them together to trigger reconnection.

Because each merger played out in almost exactly the same way, the researchers could run the experiment many times. In some runs, they measured the waves with electrical probes—while in others, they recorded the electrons' speeds by measuring their scattering of laser light. They then compared their observations with theoretical predictions for lower-hybrid drift waves.
Electron energy transfer

As the waves grew, extra clusters of electrons appeared at speeds matching how fast the waves moved along the magnetic field. Over around two microseconds, these peaks spread out into flat regions in the electrons' range of speeds, closely matching the team's theoretical predictions.

The same electron signatures also appeared at two different points along the reconnection boundary, showing that the effect wasn't limited to a single spot. Together, the results suggest that the waves act as go-betweens, passing magnetic energy to the electrons.

Yadav's team now hopes their result could help to solve a key mystery of magnetic reconnection by giving theories of wave-driven electron heating a benchmark to test against. It could also help researchers to improve their models of energy flow within plasma, and perhaps even make better sense of spacecraft measurements close to sites where magnetic reconnection occurs.
