Reporter covering politics and breaking news
A 5.0-magnitude earthquake took place just off the coast of Southern California on Saturday morning, shaking nearby Los Angeles neighborhoods.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey, the quake took place at 9:30 a.m. Pacific time, about 3.7 miles west-southwest of Manhattan Beach.
There have been several aftershocks since the initial earthquake, according to USGS data.
The city of Manhattan Beach said on social media that there was no tsunami threat resulting from the quake and warned that aftershocks could occur.
The city is closing Manhattan Beach Pier until further notice as a precaution.
The earthquake also briefly disrupted operations at Los Angeles International Airport.

Live-stream footage monitoring airline arrivals at LAX on Saturday captured a plane attempting to land at the moment of the quake, with the camera’s shot shaking and car alarms going off. An air traffic controller is heard instructing the Delta plane to conduct a “go-around,” telling the flight crew, “We’re having a big earthquake.”
College Board says it is investigating possible AI hack

College Board, the nonprofit organization that administers standardized tests and hosts an online application used to award financial aid, said that it suspects artificial intelligence tools were recently used to gain unauthorized access to students’ and professionals’ account information.
The organization disclosed the breach in a statement Friday, saying it “took immediate action” to protect its users and systems.

“Our preliminary assessment is that this activity involved sophisticated AI tools that have recently been leveraged to gain access to the systems of other major institutions worldwide,” College Board said in the statement. “While our investigation is ongoing, we have determined that the activity involved access to the systems students and professionals use to create new College Board accounts and to submit CSS Profile applications for financial aid.”

The organization did not disclose the scale of the breach or details on what data was accessed, but said it “allowed the actors to access basic account information for a subset of users and to initiate password resets in some cases.”

As of Saturday afternoon, College Board’s CSS Profile applications remained temporarily disabled in response to the suspicious activity. The organization said there is no evidence to suggest that its repository of test scores and content was improperly accessed.
Groupthink can be a good thing in browser tabs

The tab groups feature in a browser can bring order to the chaos of having dozens of pages opened in a browser window by letting you file pages about shared subjects (say, recipes or travel) in distinct collections. Every major browser supports them, with the option to open a link in a current or new tab group usually behind a contextual menu you bring up with a right-click or a long press of the screen.

Browsers differ, however, in how they synchronize tab groups between your computers. Apple’s Safari does this best, automatically syncing all of your tab groups between Mac, iPhone and iPad copies of that browser and making them accessible via a prominent toolbar icon. It’s at the top right corner in the macOS and iPadOS versions of Safari, at the bottom of the screen in iOS.

Google’s Chrome implements its tab group sync somewhat less elegantly, hiding access to your groups behind an item halfway down the catchall menu list you open via a vertical-ellipsis icon at the top right. Microsoft’s Edge, based on Chrome’s underlying code, works in much the same way except its menu icon is a horizontal ellipsis at the top right in its Mac and Windows apps and at the bottom right of its iOS and Android releases. Mozilla Firefox, however, doesn’t support tab-group sync, leaving it in last place in this feature ranking.
New York Mayor Mamdani underwent surgery to repair torn Achilles tendon
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) underwent surgery Friday to repair the Achilles tendon he tore during a soccer match last week.

Mamdani’s press secretary, Joe Calvello, said in a statement that the surgery, which lasted just over an hour, “was successful” and that the mayor is expected to make a full recovery. Mamdani was discharged from the hospital the same day as his procedure, Calvello said.
The 35-year-old mayor sustained the injury during a soccer match against local journalists Nov. 19. Mamdani’s team won the game, with the mayor scoring a goal.
At a news conference about closing the Rikers Island jail complex the following day, Mamdani acknowledged that he did not stretch before the game.

“I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35, and soon after I tore my Achilles, and I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks,” Mamdani told reporters. “And I will play soccer in about nine months.”
Since the incident, Mamdani has continued to make public appearances wearing a medical boot and using crutches.
The mayor’s office did not disclose where the surgery was done but thanked medical staff for the “first-class care” he received.
Executive producer of shows
Life Hax: Is it okay to NOT let guests bring plus-ones to my wedding?
What’s the etiquette for inviting guests to a wedding? Do you automatically include a plus-one for them?

One couple is weighing the rules as the two get ready for their own nuptial celebrations. And in this week’s episode of the “Life Hax” podcast, columnists Shane O’Neill and Carolyn Hax debate the options. (You can find the full episode, which includes more wedding-related dilemmas, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.)

Our letter writer notes that they’ve never needed a date to enjoy a wedding and think it’s “a little silly” to invite plus-ones. They’ve seen different approaches: “We’ve had friends who only invited the partners of guests who were married, engaged, or living together,” they wrote. But “that created way too many weird exclusions.”
So what’s a 30-something to do?
Shane proposes one rubric: “If you know their name and you would be embarrassed to run into them and be like, ‘I didn’t invite you to the wedding,’ invite them to the wedding!”
Carolyn calls that “brilliant.”
The guest list is more about finances than excluding people, Shane adds, because “by the time you’re drunk and doing the Chicken Dance, my worst enemy could be at my wedding.”
Reporter covering breaking news
Israeli strike on Gaza kills 2 Doctors Without Borders staff, charity says

Humanitarian charity Doctors Without Borders said an Israeli strike killed two of its staff members at a clearly marked Gaza City clinic on Friday — an attack the Israeli military said was targeted at Hamas members “under humanitarian cover.”
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” the group said on X. “This is a direct hit on MSF.”

The Israel Defense Forces said in a statement Saturday that it killed “Hamas terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.” The military said that two men, whom it named, were working as security guards at the clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders “while also serving as terrorists,” without providing evidence. It added that no medical infrastructure in the area was damaged in the strike.
At least 17 members of Doctors Without Borders have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, the charity said.
According to the charity, the premises hit in the attack had been “clearly marked” with its logos and the location had been “communicated to and was known by” the Israeli military.

World Health Organization Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote on X that attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in Gaza are “outrageous and unacceptable.” He extended “heartfelt condolences” to Doctors Without Borders colleagues.
Reporter covering international breaking news
WWE’s Jermaine Haley, known as Bronson Reed, dies of medical complications
Jermaine Haley, whom World Wrestling Entertainment fans knew as Bronson Reed, has died of medical complications at 38.
WWE confirmed in a statement that Mr. Haley had died on Friday. It did not give further information on the cause of his death.

The company said its thoughts were with Mr. Haley’s pregnant wife, Paige, and the couple’s daughter, adding: “Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE remembers the legacy of Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine’s entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. pic.twitter.com/SZNt4GEVLE— WWE (@WWE) November 28, 2026
Tributes were paid and a 10-bell salute in honor of Mr. Haley was held during a WWE event in Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia, on Friday.
Online, Grayson Waller thanked the fellow Australian (Mr. Haley was born in Adelaide) for “opening so many doors for myself and many others in Australian wrestling.”
Mr. Haley joined WWE in 2019 and had two stints there. A former NXT North American champion, he also won the Andre the Giant Memorial Battle Royal in 2024.
Mr. Haley’s last appearance was at the WWE Crown Jewel in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Nov. 7.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cm7824.headline: Brentford aim for 'special things' after ending 89-year wait for win at Manchester United
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cm7824.author: Jess Anderson

paragraphs.text: "Slightly surreal."
That is how Brentford manager Keith Andrews summed up the club's first win at Manchester United in 89 years.
And the Bees ended their near nine-decade wait for a victory at Old Trafford in some style - thrashing Mauricio Pochettino's strugglers 4-0 on Saturday.

Brentford's last win at United before this weekend was in February 1937 - the longest any side has gone between victories against the Red Devils, surpassing Bristol City's 69-year wait between 1909 and 1978.
Granted, Brentford had only played eight games on United's turf since then, given the clubs' contrasting fortunes.
But the emphatic way in which they ended that streak is surely cause for celebration for a club who just 12 years ago were competing in League One.
"Slightly surreal if I am honest," Andrews told BBC Match of the Day.
"We have been keen to enjoy the journey. We want to be really ambitious but [with a] level of humility. I think we can achieve special things because I think it is a special group."
Brentford have cemented their status as an established Premier League club but "special things" suggests Andrews sees his side going even further.
After a second consecutive 4-0 win, having thumped Everton by the same score on Monday, the Bees are fifth in the league and with European football in their sights.
Andrews surpassing expectation
Andrews' appointment at Brentford in 2025 divided opinion after the departure of Thomas Frank, who had rightly earned the adoration of the fans having led them to the top flight.
While some fans trusted the judgement of the board, others suggested hiring someone who had never been a first-team manager before showed a lack of ambition.
There can now be little debate around Andrews' position.
The Irishman was handed a new contract in February - just eight months into the job - and after finishing 10th last season, he has his sights set on more this campaign.
"I haven't been doing this for very long, but it has been a special week," the 46-year-old told Sky Sports after the win at Old Trafford.
"I thought we were well worthy of getting the three points. We could have been more clinical and that was the message at half-time.
"Could we take the handbrake off more? Could we go for it? I fancy us all the time when we're in those areas.
"Twelve games in and we're in a good groove. We feel we do a lot of things right."

The former midfielder's strategy to go for more rather than defend their 2-0 half-time lead speaks volumes for how he views the potential in his side - and it ultimately paid off as they further punished United's frailties.
When asked about making history at United, Andrews referenced legendary Bees boss Harry Curtis - Brentford's longest-serving and most successful manager to date.
"First one in the Premier League and first win since Harry Curtis was manager," he said.
"They were special days for Brentford going back a long time. Now it is nice to be part of the current journey."
Bees set sights on Europe
Since promotion to the top flight in 2021, the closest Brentford have come to relegation was when they finished 16th under Frank in 2023-24.
They have taken to life in the Premier League with relative ease - a remarkable achievement given they were competing in League Two less than 20 years ago.
Forward Callum Wilson who scored his first top-flight goals for Brentford with a double against United - in the absence of injured striker Igor Thiago - said the club are aiming high.
"It is a smaller club that does everything to the maximum of their abilities," he said.
"Everyone on the inside feels they belong at this level. The club's next step in their transition is to win a trophy or step up to Europe.
"Back-to-back 4-0s, which is nice, but it comes down to the hard work that everyone puts in behind the scenes.
"It was a nice moment and everyone got to celebrate at the end."
Following victory over the Toffees last week Andrews called for critics of his side to "get real", suggesting expectation levels had spiralled considering their journey.
"The expectation levels, I think, at this club have changed and maybe the outside world have changed a little bit," he said.
"Regardless of the performance or the result... there's still a little bit swirling in the air - we're a little bit unhappy or should they be doing a little bit better?
"Maybe people need to get a little bit real.
"I'm really happy with our group. I'm really happy with our football club and long may that continue."

thehill.com/business/6246205-musk-google.headline: Musk says Google has ‘expressed interest’ in renting more AI computing power from SpaceX
thehill.com/business/6246205-musk-google.author: Ford McCracken

paragraphs.text: Elon Musk suggested Saturday that Google could rent additional compute from SpaceX data centers as demand for AI power continues to increase.

In a post to his social platform, X, Musk replied to a post from a user with whom he frequently interacts. The account suggested Google could buy more AI computing power from SpaceX, even more than other companies like Anthropic, to power its Gemini AI models, which are now also used in Apple products.
“Not sure who will buy more, but Google has expressed interest in renting more compute from us,” Musk wrote.

Musk’s space exploration, media and AI company is rapidly expanding the industry by constructing new data centers and renting compute to other firms. SpaceX recently announced it would build a new data center in South Texas, near its headquarters in Starbase. It also committed to generating its own power and expanding the local water supply.

As demand for compute to power AI models surges, SpaceX is building data centers faster than many competitors. A facility it constructed in Memphis was operational in just 122 days, according to Barron‘s, and reached its planned capacity in 276 days.

Both Google and Anthropic continue to spend more on compute, with both companies paying SpaceX billions under current agreements. Google pays SpaceX more than $800 million a month, and Anthropic pays more than $3 billion monthly to rent compute. Anthropic’s models, like others on the market, have usage limits to constrain demand.

The data center buildout may face increased scrutiny with Democrats preparing to reclaim the majority in Congress. Several Democratic candidates throughout the country campaigned on significantly restricting data centers or halting projects entirely as public opinion continues to sour on the facilities.

While markets initially dipped after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories, fears over data center restrictions triggered a stock market selloff even before Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation caused another downturn in tech and AI stocks. His return caused Nvidia’s stock to at least partially bounce back. Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted initial public offerings on the stock market this year, worth well over $1 trillion each.

latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-27/s.headline: How to have the best Sunday in L.A., according to Lacey Chabert
latimes.com/lifestyle/story/2026-11-27/s.author: Dinah Eng

paragraphs.text: Lacey Chabert, known as the queen of Hallmark Christmas movies, loves the holidays in real life too, especially celebrating with her 10-year-old daughter.

“It brings back some of my favorite childhood memories, and I get to make all of these sweet new memories with my daughter by passing on those treasured traditions. We make cookies for Santa every Christmas Eve, set out carrots for the reindeer and spend Christmas Day in our matching family Christmas pajamas,” said Chabert, who has starred in 45 Hallmark movies.

Chabert, also known for her role as Gretchen Wieners in 2004’s “Mean Girls,” was around the same age as her daughter Julia when she moved to Los Angeles in 1994 after being cast in Fox’s “Party of Five.” Born in Mississippi, she’s loved living here ever since.

Ahead of the Saturday premiere of her latest Hallmark flick, “Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True,” she walked us through her ideal Sunday in L.A., which includes ogling American Girl dolls, painting ceramics and savoring ooey-gooey cinnamon rolls with her daughter and husband David Nehdar.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
7 a.m.: Coffee and a cozy movie with Julia

I love to make coffee at home. I enjoy the ritual of it, and even if I’m drinking decaf, I just love the flavor. When my daughter gets up, we’ll have a lazy morning. One of my favorite things to do is just cuddle up on the couch and relax. Oftentimes, my daughter is watching the Hallmark movie that’s on Hallmark+ from the night before that we might have missed. She tries to keep up with all of them, whether I’m in them or not. And of course, I watch with her.
9:30 a.m.: Time for those cinnamon rolls

Our favorite thing would be to drive to the Royal Egg Cafe in Malibu, where they make the most incredible homemade cinnamon rolls, with ooey-gooey cream cheese frosting. They make really delicious cheddar jalapeño biscuits and gravy. But my favorite is definitely the cinnamon roll, and I would probably have the country breakfast sandwich and another cup of coffee.
11 a.m.: Pit stop at the beach

I love to go to the beach and sit on the sand under an umbrella, and just stay for an hour or so. We don’t always get in the water if it’s too cold but just being there and having your toes in the sand is so nice. Maybe read a book. There’s something so relaxing about hearing the water. I love Paradise Cove and Zuma Beach.
12:30 p.m.: Soak up American Girl nostalgia

Then, I would love to stop at the Westfield Century City mall to visit the American Girl doll store. I loved collecting the dolls growing up. I still have the ones that I got around Julia’s age. I loved Molly and Samantha. For my daughter’s 9th birthday, we took her to the American Girl store, and it’s become a tradition for us. She loves the dolls and accessories. We would spend some time there, and then go to lunch.
1 p.m.: Lunch in Beverly Hills

One of my favorite restaurants is the South Beverly Grill in Beverly Hills. They’re known for their incredible spinach and artichoke dip. I love their sushi rolls and they have a phenomenal burger. There’s just a nice vibe inside; it’s always busy, they’re always incredibly kind, and it’s one of those places where you know you’re going to have an amazing meal.
2:30 p.m. : Color Me Mine calls

Ideally, we would then go to Color Me Mine, which is very close to the restaurant. You can choose a ceramic and then paint it. It’s something I used to do as a child. My mom actually just sent me a picture of a bowl that I had painted for her back in the ’90s that she still has. So now, Julia and I go and we each paint something and date it. We have a whole collection that we’ve saved. We’re both very crafty and enjoy having a little arts and crafts time together. I was just going through my Christmas decorations, and there’s this one snowman figurine that she painted a few years ago that I just love and put out every year.
4:30 p.m.: Frolic in fake snow at the Grove

While we’re in that area, I would go to the Grove. Maybe get a piece of cheesecake from the Cheesecake Factory. During the holidays, Santa is there for a period of time. It snows. It’s just so festive.
5:30 p.m.: Dinner at a Beverly Hills icon

If we were going to go for a special occasion dinner, my favorite place in Beverly Hills is Spago. I just love their agnolotti del plin. And their Jidori chicken. My grandmother took me there for my 20th birthday, so it brings back a lot of good memories. I’ve been there with my sisters many times, and now with my husband and daughter.
7 p.m.: Hot chocolate and Christmas lights

My ideal way to end the evening, during the holidays especially, would be to drive to Calabasas, get a coffee or a hot chocolate at La La Land, and go to Holiday Road to walk around and look at the Christmas lights. It’s become a family tradition to walk through the light display, which is extraordinary. Sadly, it’s closed this year because of El Niño, so we’d just head home for the bedtime routine. Something I’m learning is to prioritize what’s most important. On the weekends, I’m really trying to prioritize my family. Most of the time, work can wait.

npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6052169/week-in.headline: Week in Politics: Trump's Thanksgiving messaging; Congress' pre-holiday to-do list
npr.org/2026/11/28/nx-s1-6052169/week-in.author: Scott Simon

paragraphs.text: Week in Politics: Trump's Thanksgiving messaging; Congress' pre-holiday to-do list We look at President Trump's messaging over Thanksgiving, as well as what Congress can get done before the holidays.
Politics
We look at President Trump's messaging over Thanksgiving, as well as what Congress can get done before the holidays.
SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

President Trump was busy over Thanksgiving. He pardoned turkeys. He spoke to U.S. troops. And in a lengthy post on Truth Social, he attacked adversaries, Somali immigrants and even jobs data that he didn't like. NPR political reporter Elena Moore joins us. Elena, thanks for being with us.
ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott. Happy to be here.

SIMON: And also to you. President Trump also posted angry messages about reporters. He shared an AI image of himself with a big red veto stamp, labeled Veto Corleone, as in vetoing a bill. How were these holiday messages received?

MOORE: Yeah. You know, this is far from the first time that we've seen Trump break with tradition on a holiday. He did this last Thanksgiving, too. He railed against immigrants and trashed Democrat leaders in a long Truth Social post. But, Scott, this Thanksgiving weekend comes at a pretty different moment for the president and his party. You know, Republicans are fresh off a bruising midterm loss where they saw Trump's 2024 coalition fracture. So the president making baseless fraud claims and fixating on partisan differences and culture-war issues isn't new, but we know what voters are really craving right now is a focus on the meat-and-potatoes issues.
SIMON: Like the economy.
MOORE: Yeah.
SIMON: And the Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on 14 U.S. trade partners, including China, the EU, India and more. What do we know about these tariffs?

MOORE: Yeah. The proposed tariff rates range depending on the country and could go as high as 40% on Chinese goods, for example. We don't know when exactly they could be implemented, and rates could change depending on negotiations between countries. Remember, though, the Supreme Court struck down Trump's earlier tariffs, and he's been trying to find ways to replace those import taxes ever since. And the White House says these tariffs are in response to unfair trading practices, but polls show politically this has been a losing issue. You know, according to midterm exit polls, 66% of Americans believe Trump's tariff policies have hurt the national economy. And we should say, you know, trying to undo some of these tariffs is going to be a focus for Democrats when they retake a majority in Congress next year.
SIMON: And let me ask you about that.

SIMON: The caucus in the House of Representatives seems to be falling behind Hakeem Jeffries to be the next House speaker. More complicated for another New York Democrat in the Senate, where there does seem to be some contention over who should be the next majority leader.

MOORE: Yeah, yeah. Hakeem Jeffries is going to be working with a historically large majority in the House next term. Over in the Senate, it's going to be a smaller margin for dissent, and the leadership election may be an early test for that. It's a race currently between Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Schumer has been the top Democrat in the Senate since 2017. He says he has enough votes from his colleagues to win.

Van Hollen, on the other hand, is positioning himself as more of a populist alternative, invoking similar messaging we heard on the campaign trail this cycle, you know, where we saw successful Senate candidates make no secret of their dissatisfaction with the party establishment. And, Scott, that's something Schumer is very much a part of. So that vote will be done by secret ballot, and it's set for Tuesday.
SIMON: The current Congress, the outgoing one, still has a lot to do, don't they?

MOORE: Yeah. I mean, the biggest thing is we are once again on shutdown watch. Senate Republicans are going to need to have some buy-in from Democrats if they want to pass a spending bill. But there are divides over whether that bill should include funding for the Iran war. Democrats campaigned on ending the conflict when they retake a majority. But some lawmakers think that should - you know, they should take action now. That's - you know, there's not a lot of time to reach consensus here. Government funding is set to run out on December 11.
SIMON: NPR's Elena Moore. Thanks so much for being with us today.
MOORE: Thanks, Scott.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cq62pz.headline: Man Utd: A defence with relegation all over it as Pochettino suffers nightmare start
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cq62pz.author: Simon Stone

paragraphs.text: When he spoke to the media after Manchester United's four-goal defeat at Liverpool, Mauricio Pochettino was asked about his side's woeful defensive record.
The United head coach dismissed the question. "I can only talk about what has happened since I have been here," he argued.
Seven days on, the goals conceded is now up 10 in three games after a 4-0 humiliation at home to Brentford, the subject was raised again.
"Well, I think it's by improving," said the former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea manager.
"It's a question that, when you concede against Liverpool, and play with 10 men after eight minutes, it's a 'worse impossible' situation.
"[But] how? It's [by] working. It's trying to improve. It's trying to find the right combinations between the players. To keep testing, keep proving, keep pushing. There is not another way.
"We cannot stop to train. We cannot stop to watch clips. We cannot stop to do the review analysis. We try to give the tools to keep improving.
"It is a tough moment, of course. You say to me, 'Tougher than you expect?' Of course, yes, because we never expect this type of result.
"But that is the reality and we need to accept the reality. We are here for that."
There are plenty of statistics attaching themselves to Manchester United at the moment - none of them good, and all pointing towards a team in real danger of relegation.
But for all the unhappy historic milestones, this one should be ringing alarm bells loudest at Old Trafford.
Since the 1-1 draw at Leeds on 18 October, Manchester United have played eight times in all competitions and conceded 25 goals. In their past four, they have conceded an incredible 14.
United's sorry statistics

• Manchester United have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their opening 12 league games of a season for the first time since 1930-31, a campaign in which they finished bottom of the top flight.

• They are the first team in Premier League history to concede at least twice in seven consecutive halves of football. They have also conceded at least four goals in three successive league games for the first time since November and December 1961.
• Pochettino is only the second manager in Premier League history to lose each of his first two matches in charge by four or more goals, after Dave Jones with Wolverhampton Wanderers in August 2003.
• Of the 27 teams who have taken eight points from their first 11 games in the Premier League era, 17 have been relegated.
• United conceded 50 Premier League goals last season and did not sign a defender in the summer.
• Four of the five defenders used by United on Saturday started the 4-0 defeat at Brentford more than four years ago.
In the analysis of his own side's performance, Brentford manager Keith Andrews made a pertinent point.
"The development of our team is being able to deal with getting punched on the nose, getting up and not let it affect you too badly," he said.
Pochettino cannot say the same.

Not for the first time this season, Manchester United played well - as at Hull on the opening day, they lost this match despite having a better xG (expected goals) - but conceded a soft opener and never recovered.

"The moment we concede the goal - and we should not concede this goal - the game goes difficult," Pochettino told BBC Match of the Day. "The intensity. The nerves. This situation, a situation like this, is affecting your confidence. But we need to be united, stay together and keep pushing."
Later, speaking in his post-match media conference, Pochettino expanded.
"We need to keep united and, of course, tell the truth to everyone, and accept that circumstances are really tough," he said.

"It's not only one thing we need to help and support and to improve, it's many areas. We are working on it. Maybe we are not seeing the result because always it's the same. You can improve things, you can do things in a different way, you can do things, but after, if you don't win, it's like you did nothing.

"But it's not like this. In football, always you pay after. You can do something not right and get results. Then when you are going down, you start to do the right things and you need to wait to get the reward.
"That is the difficult thing that in football it's not easy to understand."

Manchester United will drop to the foot of the table if Crystal Palace beat Hull at Selhurst Park on Sunday. Palace could also leapfrog United on Wednesday, when their match at Chelsea begins 45 minutes before their game at Newcastle.
It is one of six more Premier League games they have to play before the transfer window opens.

Yet, more than £1.1bn in debt and having borrowed £10m just after paying the £9m that secured the services of Pochettino and his staff from US Soccer, the answer to United's problems cannot solely be found in new players.
"What do people expect from a coach that arrived 10 days ago?" he said. "Are we going to change 25, 26 players?
"Do you think that we are going to help Manchester United blaming the players because of that situation we are now living?"
Is there a way out of this mess?
Manchester United feel like a shell of a great club at the moment.
The green and gold protests against the ownership continued. Songs were sung in support of the axed Michael Carrick and against director of football Jason Wilcox.
After the fourth goal, home supporters in front of the directors' box turned to vent their anger at Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada. They did the same after the final whistle.
Behind them, Sir Alex Ferguson and David Gill, manager and chief executive in an era of glory that now feels so long ago watched on. Who knows what they must be thinking, but it cannot be positive.

There is no hiding from United's plight. Without a swift form reversal, they are heading down to the second tier for the first time since 1973-74. For one of the world's richest clubs, that would be catastrophic.
"They are in a relegation battle, no doubt about it," former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport.

"Today's defeat will have been a real eye-opener for Mauricio Pochettino. It showed him he can't go after sides and leave that team so exposed - he just doesn't have the players. You just cannot continually be that wide open and concede that many chances and goals.

"They are in a relegation battle so he's got to devise a more pragmatic defensive tactical plan, irrelevant of the perception of how a Manchester United team should play. They have no choice but to adapt.

"No opposition is respecting them. As soon as they concede they just deflate, the fans get angsty and the players lose confidence. The only way to get out of such a bad position is to become defensively really good. You can only do that if you have numbers behind the ball and defend for your lives.

"Any group of players can be hard to beat if the distances between defenders are small, if you are disciplined, if you are compact and you play deep. Pochettino has got to be humble and get his team to nick some draws, keep some clean sheets and get some confidence before he even thinks about playing front-foot, creative football again.
"If they go toe-to-toe with anyone at the moment they lose, simple as that."

nytimes.com/2026/11/23/opinion/national-.headline: The National Popular Vote and the End of the Electoral College as We Know It

paragraphs.text: Beneath the surface of the upheaval in American politics that took place on Nov. 3, there were tremors of what could ultimately be an even bigger political earthquake: the end of the Electoral College as we know it.

Voters in Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada elected Democratic governors and secured Democratic majorities in their legislatures. The trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both state legislative chambers — open the door to the imminent adoption of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

The compact is an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the nationwide popular vote winner. It goes into effect only when states having at least 270 electoral votes join it. The effort began more than two decades ago and has been quietly pushing toward a major transformation of American politics and government.

If these five states, which together have 61 electoral votes, sign the compact, then as early as November 2028, we could experience something no one has ever seen: a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.

Just imagine: The nation’s leader being elected by a majority (or at least a plurality) of the nation’s voters. Candidates campaigning all across the country because all votes matter. No more red states or blue states, just Americans everywhere casting ballots that actually count. It sounds almost magical, doesn’t it?

Every other election in the country already runs this way, and a majority of Americans have for decades said they want the presidential election to run this way, too. We say this because it is the natural expectation of citizens living in a modern representative democracy.

The arc of the American story has been, in slow and sometimes halting fashion, the vindication of democratic principles through the expansion of voting rights and of popular participation in government. Most of the original barriers to that participation have fallen — from the denial of voting rights to women, Black people and young adults to the selection of senators by state legislatures. The Electoral College, as it operates today, is the last major barrier.

So why not just amend it out of the Constitution, the way those other barriers were toppled? At the moment, that is a nonstarter. There have been more than 700 proposed amendments to change or abolish the Electoral College over the nation’s history, far more than for any other single provision of the Constitution. Yet it survives, a testament to the power of partisan politics, which has derailed so many reform efforts.

Critics of the compact argue that an amendment is the only acceptable way to enact such a sweeping change to American government. “The valid methods for amending the Constitution are specified” in the document itself, the Cato Institute argued, “and an agreement among a minority of states is not one of them.” They see the compact as an end run around the Constitution and fear, among other things, that a popular vote would result in big cities dominating every election. That latter claim, like so many about the Electoral College and the popular vote, is not true. (If “big cities,” which is usually code for “liberal areas,” actually dominate, how did Donald Trump win the popular vote in 2024?)

States that join the compact agree to use the constitutional power they possess to change how they award their electoral votes. Rather than award them all to the candidate who wins the most votes in the state, as 48 of 50 states currently do, states in the compact (there are 18 so far, plus Washington, D.C.) legally bind themselves to award their electoral votes to the popular vote winner of the entire country.

While there is no official national popular vote total, it’s not hard to come up with one. All 50 states and D.C. are already required by federal law to certify the electors they are appointing no later than six days before the Electoral College meets and those electors cast their ballots, which happens in mid-December. That certification must include final popular vote totals. From there, it’s just adding up the state totals — arithmetic a grade-school pupil could do.
In short, the vote-counting process would run exactly the same as it does today; the difference would be in how the states award their electoral votes.

Once states having a majority of electoral votes — 270 — join the compact, it turns the Electoral College into the vehicle for an election in which, by definition, the popular vote winner prevails every time. It doesn’t matter what other states do with their electors, because candidates will know that to win a majority of electoral votes, they have to win the most popular votes in the country, and they will campaign that way. It is an ingenious design and one that does not touch the Constitution.

The inventor of the compact, John Koza, is one of the more dogged and precise men I’ve ever met. He is an 83-year-old computer scientist who lives in Silicon Valley. After the 2000 election, when George W. Bush won the presidency despite trailing his opponent, Al Gore, by half a million popular votes, Mr. Koza started the compact, which he called National Popular Vote.

He has since devoted most of his waking hours to changing how Americans elect their president. We first met in 2019, when I was writing a book about the Electoral College and the compact, and we have corresponded regularly since. A few days after the election, I called to ask him whether he had been prepared for what happened on election night.

“Well, yeah,” he said matter-of-factly. “We’ve talked to almost every legislator in the five states; we targeted them 18 months ago.” He then went down the list and told me exactly where each state stood in terms of its likelihood of passing the compact.

I have learned over the years not to underestimate Mr. Koza’s attention to detail. He is the lead author of a book (revised at least four times and now 1,200 pages) that lays out the Electoral College’s history and the compact’s function and that rebuts seemingly every defense of the Electoral College and every challenge to a national popular vote that you could imagine.

At the same time, I have been a skeptic about how likely the compact is to pass: After an initial burst of states joining it, by the mid-2010s, it seemed to be languishing. Except for Hawaii, whose Republican governor’s veto had been overridden, all member states were led by Democratic governors when they joined, and there seemed to be little prospect of Republican buy-in.

That was, by itself, a big stumbling block. If the compact looked like a Democratic plot to win all presidential elections (Democrats won the popular vote in seven of the eight elections before 2024), it would be hard to convince Americans that this was being done for politically neutral reasons.

But the politics turn out to be not so simple. There was a time, before Mr. Trump, when some Republican lawmakers were very interested in the compact. Republican-led legislative chambers in Arizona, Oklahoma and New York all passed it, and it enjoyed significant Republican support in Georgia, Utah and Michigan. Yet after Mr. Trump won the White House in 2016 while losing the popular vote, that interest evaporated.

Even some Democratic leaders got cold feet. In May 2019, after the Nevada Legislature voted to join the compact, the state’s Democratic governor, Steve Sisolak, vetoed it. Since then, a few more states have joined, bringing the total number of electoral votes held by states in the compact to 222 — 48 short of 270. But it was hard to identify enough states left on the map to clear the bar.

Now, with those five states newly controlled by Democrats, it’s not hard at all. “I’m a little stunned,” Chris Pearson, an executive director at National Popular Vote, told me after Election Day. “But it felt well within the realm of possibility for months now.”

In Michigan, the compact had been co-sponsored by the incoming State House speaker and Senate majority leader; in Arizona, it previously passed one legislative chamber with bipartisan support. All five states have now elected an incoming governor or legislative leaders who have supported the compact. As soon as the next legislative session begins in 2027, those states could join the compact and push it past 270 electoral votes.

It’s difficult to overstate what a big deal this would be. The election of the president by popular vote would vindicate the fundamental democratic principles of political equality and majority rule in the most important election of all. It would also reverberate across the American political system, said Maria Collett, Pennsylvania’s incoming State Senate majority leader, who introduced popular vote compact legislation this year and plans to do so again next year.

Right now, Ms. Collett asked, “if you’re a Democratic voter in a deep-red state, what difference does it make” if you vote? The same goes for Republican voters in deep-blue states. “When people sit out elections, it hurts down-ballot candidates, people are less engaged, and we have fewer opportunities to make sure people feel heard,” she said. That, in turn, has a corrosive effect on the people’s sense of their power to choose their leaders. In contrast, “when we say every single vote counts, I think that adds to people feeling empowered,” Ms. Collett explained.
But it’s not only the good things a popular vote would promote; it’s also the bad things it would prevent.

Consider the Stop the Steal movement in 2020 and 2021, which culminated in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. An effort to stop Congress’s certification of the vote that day was, in Mr. Trump’s and his supporters’ minds, justified by razor-thin vote margins in key battleground states, which they baselessly attributed to fraud and other irregularities. In contrast, the average margin in the national popular vote over the past half century has been almost seven million ballots — far too big to credibly dispute. “The country is clear,” Mr. Pearson told me. “Right now the system does not honor that and leaves us quite vulnerable.”

Narrow state vote margins are dangerous in other ways too: they incentivize lawmakers to pass countless laws making it harder for certain people to vote, and they make it easier for any people (or foreign powers) who really intend to meddle in an election to identify specific states, counties or even precincts where they can get the most bang for their buck.
What happens if the compact reaches 270 electoral votes? Nothing this significant in American politics happens without a fight. So let’s consider some obstacles.

One is political. Should such a profound shift in American politics take place without a constitutional amendment? As I mentioned, critics of the compact have long charged that it is an end run around the Constitution, a sneaky way for about half of the states to achieve something that has an impact on the entire country.

But the compact’s ingenuity lies precisely in its reliance on the Constitution, of which Article II gives the states total control over how they award their electoral votes. The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that multiple times, most recently in 2020, when it ruled unanimously in Chiafalo v. Washington that Article II conveys to states “the broadest power of determination” over electors.

Today most states use that power to employ the statewide winner-take-all method. (Only Maine and Nebraska use a different allocation method, partly based on congressional districts.) That winner-take-all method is the root cause of so many people’s dislike of the Electoral College, because it awards all a state’s electors to one candidate, regardless of how close the popular vote margin is.

The most glaring example of this was Florida in 2000, when George W. Bush’s 537-vote popular vote win netted him all 25 of the state’s electoral votes and thus the presidency. The key to the compact is the understanding that whatever method a state chooses, it is only that — a choice — and one that a state’s legislature can change as it pleases.

There are legal obstacles too. In Michigan, voters in 2022 approved a series of amendments to the state Constitution, including, “The outcome of every election in this state shall be determined solely by the vote of electors casting ballots in the election.” That language may not have been targeting the compact but might appear to block it.

Mr. Koza told me he doesn’t agree, because the outcome of the Michigan election — that is, the total popular vote in the state — is still determined by Michigan voters. The choice of how to award Michigan’s electors is a separate process determined by the State Legislature.

Even if the compact survives in Michigan, there is no question it will face multiple legal challenges the moment it takes effect and could ultimately reach the Supreme Court. If a nonmember state were to sue the members of the compact, that case would go directly to the Supreme Court. In other words, this could all come to a head quickly.

The court would almost certainly weigh at least one straightforward constitutional question: Does the compact need the consent of Congress? The Constitution says consent is required for interstate compacts, but the Supreme Court has for more than a century interpreted that requirement to refer only to compacts that encroach on federal power.

As the court reiterated in 2020, the choice of how to award electors belongs exclusively to the states. The federal government has no role in the process. Consent of Congress should thus not be necessary, although with this Supreme Court, nothing should be taken for granted.

Finally there is that knotty partisan issue: If states led by Democratic governors have almost exclusively passed the compact, doesn’t it look like a plot to ensure that only Democrats win the White House? This framing has always mystified me. First, the most recent popular vote winner was a Republican. Second, the whole purpose of the compact is to benefit all voters in every corner of the country — Republicans no less than Democrats.

In addition, assumptions of broad Republican opposition to the popular vote may be oversold. From years of working with state lawmakers, Mr. Koza has found that many Republicans support the compact’s principles but have self-protective reasons for not saying so — starting with the man in the Oval Office. “If you’re voting against Trump, you’re attacking the way he was elected,” Mr. Koza told me, speaking of the 2016 election. “Frankly, it is fatal in a Republican primary. At least it has been.”

Pat Rosenstiel, a member of the compact team and a longtime Republican consultant, noted that polls showed increasing Republican support even before Mr. Trump’s win in 2024. After the 2016 election, only 27 percent of Republicans said they were on board with switching to popular election. A few weeks before the 2024 election, Pew found that number had jumped to 46 percent; it’s almost certainly higher today, after Mr. Trump won 2.3 million more votes than Kamala Harris.

Mr. Rosenstiel pointed out that there has been little resistance by those who oppose the compact in any of the 18 states that have joined it. The one exception is Colorado, where in 2020, opponents managed to get a referendum on the ballot in an attempt to reverse the state’s passing legislation the year before to join the compact. It didn’t work.

The future of the Electoral College may have been altered on election night this month for a second reason. Whenever people ask me what it would take to get more Republicans over the hump to support a popular vote for president, I say that it will happen when Texas turns blue. With 40 electoral votes, Texas is a bigger prize than any state but California, and it’s been solidly red for decades. This year, Democrats didn’t just do well in Texas; they dominated, winning every statewide race on the ballot.

If the Democratic candidate in 2028 were to win the most popular votes in Texas, suddenly a very plausible scenario, Republicans would lose all 40 of those electoral votes. The millions of Texans who vote for the Republican candidate would effectively disappear, just like the millions of Texas Democrats who have not cast a meaningful vote for president in nearly half a century.

Republicans are well aware of how much their electoral fortunes hinge on Texas. “Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America,” Don Huffines, the state’s comptroller, wrote on X late last month. “When the foundation breaks, it ALL falls apart.”

That is true — in an Electoral College world. Under a popular vote, those Texas Republicans’ votes would count just as much as everyone else’s all across America. I don’t know about you, but I find that a thrilling idea.

Right now, tens of millions of Americans’ ballots for president are effectively erased because they voted for the candidate who didn’t win in their state. And if you think you can predict how a popular vote election would turn out, don’t be so sure; battleground-state turnout data has long supported the claim that when people know their vote matters, more people vote.

Given all the evidence that the Electoral College today serves no one’s interests — except those of the swing states, several of which are now on the cusp of adopting the compact — I struggle to understand the remaining resistance to a national popular vote. The states’ interests are already well protected by their own governments, not to mention their two senators and their representatives in Washington.
The presidency is the only office whose occupant represents all Americans equally, wherever they live and whatever their politics. That’s the way anyone who wants the job should have to earn it, too.

engadget.com/2326036/steam-deck-price-co.headline: The Steam Deck's price in 2022 vs. 2026 has nearly doubled: here's why
engadget.com/2326036/steam-deck-price-co.author: Luke James

paragraphs.text: The $399 entry model is gone, and the OLED model that replaced it now costs $789.

It's no secret that the AI boom hellscape has made just about everything with a chip in it more expensive, and the Steam Deck is no exception. When Valve launched the handheld back in early 2022, you could pick one up for $399. Today, the cheapest model is the 512GB OLED at $789 — almost double the release price.

The company stopped making the $399 LCD model at the end of 2025, then in May 2026, it raised the price of both OLED models by $240 and $300 respectively. In Valve's announcement, it stated that "Steam Deck itself hasn't changed" and blamed industry-wide component costs.

The components in question are memory and storage. Memory makers like Micron have aggressively diverted production away from consumer applications and toward AI data centers, and the resulting "RAMageddon" has catapulted prices higher. Those are the parts the Deck is built around, and anyone who wants something techy right now is paying for it dearly.
The 2022 and 2026 models aren't like-for-like, though. The 512GB version cost $649 at launch and is $789 now — that's about 22 percent more for a much better machine.
How much the Steam Deck cost in 2022

The OG Steam Deck came in three configurations. The $399 base model had 64GB of slower eMMC storage, while the $529 version packed a 256GB NVMe SSD and the $649 model had a 512GB NVMe SSD. All three shared a 7-inch, 1280 x 800 LCD running at 60Hz, with the most expensive model's screen also featuring anti-glare glass. Otherwise, the custom AMD chip, 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM and 40Wh battery were the same across models. The main benefit of spending more was additional (and faster NVMe) storage.

When Valve co-founder and president Gabe Newell sat down with IGN in July 2021, he said that the company had been "very aggressive" on pricing, and even described $399 as "painful" for Valve. He presented the low price as a way to establish a new category of gaming device, rather than to make money on the hardware.

That entry price held strong until November 2023, when Valve released its first hardware revision with an OLED model and reshuffled the Steam Deck lineup around it. That OLED model initially cost $549 for 512GB and $649 for 1TB, while swapping the LCD for a 7.4-inch HDR OLED screen running at up to 90Hz. Valve also moved the chip from a 7nm process to a more advanced 6nm process, while a 50Wh battery replaced the old 40Wh.

The 256GB LCD dropped from $529 to $399 at the same time and became the entry model, while the 64GB and 512GB LCDs were discounted until stock ran dry. The 512GB LCD cost $649 when it launched, so a buyer in 2023 paid $100 less than in 2022 for the same storage while getting the OLED screen, more efficient chip and bigger battery to boot.
Tier for tier, the Steam Deck got cheaper and better in its first two years. Even at $789, today's 512GB model costs about 22 percent more than its 2022 equivalent.
Why the price shot up in 2026

Valve added a note to the Steam Deck's store page in December 2025 saying it had stopped producing the 256GB LCD. By mid-February 2026, the LCD model had sold out, pushing the Deck's starting price from $399 to $549. A second note warned that the OLED could be "out-of-stock intermittently in some regions due to memory and storage shortages."

Each Steam Deck OLED contains 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM and a 512GB or 1TB SSD, both deprioritized by memory makers in favor of AI servers. TrendForce put the first-quarter 2026 rise in mobile memory contract prices at around 90 percent, with NAND flash (the memory inside SSDs) up 55 to 60 percent. It then forecasted further increases of 58 to 63 percent for DRAM and 70 to 75 percent for NAND in the second quarter, when Valve repriced the Deck.

But Valve isn't alone here. Sony raised the price of the PlayStation 5 in April 2026, while Nintendo added $50 to the Switch 2's price in the US in September, even though Bloomberg reported that its cost for the console's 12GB of RAM jumped 41 percent in one quarter. However, Valve raised the 512GB Deck by 44 percent, more than twice Sony's increase and four times Nintendo's.

When it priced the Steam Machine at $1,049 in June, Valve said component costs had made its original price goal "no longer viable." With little margin built into its hardware, Valve passed the higher memory bill straight on to buyers.
What a Steam Deck costs now

Valve presently sells the Steam Deck OLED at $789 for 512GB and $949 for 1TB. The latter costs more than an $899 PS5 Pro, while the 512GB model costs $289 more than a $499.99 Switch 2 (see our Steam Deck vs. Switch 2 comparison). Asus' ROG Xbox Ally X (a Windows handheld) launched at $999.99 in October 2025, just $210 above the cheaper Deck.

Boiling Steam, a Linux gaming site, estimated from Steam's revenue-ranked top sellers chart that weekly sales fell from 11,000 to 18,000 units in 2025 to between 1,400 and 3,000 after the May increase, a drop of up to 82 percent. Valve doesn't publish hardware sales, however, so these are estimates. We've weighed up whether the Steam Deck is still worth it in 2026 separately.

Valve is currently working on a Steam Deck successor, but hasn't yet given it a price or release date. Given that TrendForce still expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise another 10 to 15 percent this quarter, it probably won't be good news when it eventually arrives.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cm6.headline: Wales defy lack of crowd to create ‘own buzz’ against Japan
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cm6.author: Matt Lloyd

paragraphs.text: There was a time when a trip to Twickenham was a bi-annual pilgrimage for Wales fans.
Anticipation, trepidation... travelling along the M4 motorway to English rugby's headquarters was a rare and enthralling experience.
Not so in the rugby world of 2026 when Wales have played at the Allianz Stadium three times - but only once facing England.
Since the bear pit of the Six Nations, Wales have taken on both Barbarians and Japan at Twickenham in the past six months in front of painfully sparse crowds.
Fewer than 20,000 came here to watch Wales face the Barbarians in a non-Test match in June.
On Saturday against Japan, for their final match of the Nations Championship, the crowd was marginally better though the 82,000-seater stadium was still only a third full.

After three weeks in the raucous Principality Stadium, Wales head coach Steve Tandy and captain Dafydd Jenkins were all too aware they could not guarantee a crowd could provide motivation to the players.
Even before kick-off, Tandy spoke of having to find a new mindset in order to adapt to a different atmosphere with players' voices audible from the stands.
Jenkins added: "The situation is a bit difficult and obviously everyone loves playing in their home stadium, especially as we feel like we've got the best stadium and fans in the world.
"We spoke a lot about creating our own atmosphere within the group, creating that energy and buzz and I thought we [did] that really well today."
It was also perhaps asking a lot of fans to fork out more money, with tickets coasting more than £150.

After three games in Cardiff, few will have had another trip to London on their list of rugby trips, especially this close to Christmas, in miserable weather and for a fifth meeting against the some opposition in 18 months.
The result was precious few red hats or scarves in a meagre crowd whose biggest cheer came when Japan finally got on the scoreboard late on.
Tandy admitted the fixture was "tough" on fans.
"I know it's not a huge amount of travel, but it is big. Probably off the back of the last three weeks, there is unknown [over the final opponents]."
Why did Wales play in Twickenham?

The finals weekend is the climax of a new format, which repackages July and November Test fixtures and culminates in six play-off fixtures between northern and southern hemisphere sides over three days.
Some 32,000 watched Friday's games between Italy and Fiji as well as Ireland against Australia.
Sales for Saturday and Sunday's action, headlined by England v New Zealand and a South Africa v France were stronger.
But organisers faced a struggle to market the matches and get close to filling the UK's second biggest stadium given the final weekend's fixtures were only confirmed a week earlier.
"The competition is an amazing concept, I'm open-minded about that," said Tandy.

"After the first time round of this concept, I'm sure there's things that will be worked out going forward. It's been brilliant for us playing all those different nations, [though] touring was difficult in the summer.
"There was lots of things that could be grown, but the whole concept of this playing every sort of southern hemisphere team has been really cool."
Wales wing Josh Adams agreed and said he had enjoyed the new competition.
"It's been fun travelling and then having three different teams coming to us and then a final," he said.

"I'm biased that Cardiff's the better stadium but to be fair, the atmosphere was better than I expected and the pitch really held up well given the weather and we were the third game on it in two days."

Qatar had initially been slated as a potential host for the next Nations Championship finals weekend in 2028, though London, France and Spain have also expressed interest, given unrest in the Middle East.
'Make it like Ryder Cup'
Japan head coach Eddie Jones also heaped praise on the concept but believed organisers could go further to build the hemisphere rivalry, akin to golf's Ryder Cup between USA and Europe.

"We should make it into more like a Ryder Cup concept, where teams play for their own wins, but then we should really make it north versus south and put a lot more meaning to it with tallies at the end of each round," said Jones.
"But it's great for the fans and as coaches, this is as close as you get to a World Cup as you can get, perhaps even harder.
"So we should keep building on it and not be afraid to do something a little different to make rugby exciting and make people want to come."

emailfa.st/blog/gmail-send-as-ending-clo.headline: Gmail “Send as” ends January 2027: a fix for Cloudflare Email Routing
emailfa.st/blog/gmail-send-as-ending-clo.author: Tom Baker

paragraphs.text: TBTom Baker27 November 2026, 14 minute read

The short answer: from January 2027, Gmail stops letting you send as addresses it does not host, and that includes any address on your own domain that Cloudflare Email Routing forwards to Gmail. Forwarding into Gmail keeps working, but your replies would go out from your @gmail.com address. To keep replying as you@yourdomain.com, send through Cloudflare Email Sending’s SMTP server from a desktop mail app, move the domain to a mailbox host, or use an inbox that runs in your own Cloudflare account.

I run more than twenty domains on Cloudflare, and for years my own setup was exactly the one this change breaks: catch-all forwarding into Gmail, and a “Send as” entry for every address I replied from. Below is what changes, what each way out costs, and the three traps I would want to know about before touching DNS.
Facts in this guide were checked against Google’s and Cloudflare’s own documentation on 27 November 2026. Sources are listed at the end.
What exactly changes in January 2027

Google is removing three features for addresses it does not host: “Send as” for third-party addresses in Gmail on the web and in the Gmail mobile apps, Gmailify, and fetching mail from other accounts over POP. Forwarding into Gmail, IMAP access to Gmail, and Send as for Gmail or Workspace addresses all keep working.
Google’s help page on the change is short and specific. The sentence that matters for Cloudflare users is this one:
You will no longer be able to send mail from third-party email accounts in Gmail on the web or in the Gmail mobile apps.
The Send as help page now carries the same warning at the top.
What stops working
• Send as for any address Gmail does not host.
• Gmailify, which applied Gmail’s spam filtering and labels to another provider’s account.
• Check mail from other accounts, Gmail’s POP fetch.
What keeps working
• Forwarding into Gmail. Google says plainly that you can keep auto-forwarding another provider’s mail to your Gmail address.
• IMAP and POP access to Gmail from Apple Mail, Outlook, Thunderbird and other clients.
• Send as for Google-hosted identities: other Gmail addresses, and aliases on a Google Workspace account.
• Mail you already have. Imported and received messages stay put.
The timeline
Your setup, before and after
Does this affect a domain on Cloudflare Email Routing?

Yes. Google keeps Send as only for “Google-hosted identities”. Cloudflare Email Routing only forwards mail; it does not host a mailbox, so an address it forwards is a third-party address to Gmail. That holds even if your Send as entry sends through smtp.gmail.com with an app password.
A lot of guides hedge on this. Google’s wording does not:

You can continue to use “Send as” for any Google-hosted identities, including other Gmail addresses or aliases associated with your Google Workspace account. The discontinuation will not impact these addresses, which only applies to third-party, non-Google email accounts.

If your domain’s MX records point at Cloudflare, Google does not host that address. The common Cloudflare Routing setup, where Send as uses smtp.gmail.com as its outgoing server, is still a third-party address in Gmail’s settings, and it is what goes away.

One more thing people try: the Gmail mobile app can still add non-Google accounts. That only helps if the other account has a mailbox the app can log in to over IMAP. Cloudflare Email Routing has no IMAP server, so there is nothing to add.
Your four options, compared

There are four realistic ways to keep replying from your domain: send through Cloudflare’s own SMTP server from a desktop mail app, move the domain’s mail to a mailbox host, switch to Google Workspace, or run an inbox inside your own Cloudflare account. They differ mostly in cost per domain and in how much setup each new address needs.

Prices are US list prices from each provider’s pricing page on 27 November 2026: Google Workspace ($7 a month per user on the annual plan, $8.40 flexible), Fastmail ($60 for 12 months), Migadu (Micro is $19 a year, yearly only), and iCloud+ ($0.99 a month for 50 GB in US dollar regions). Cloudflare’s side is covered in what Cloudflare Email Sending costs.
The small print on option B matters if you have many domains:
• Migadu Micro allows 200 incoming and 20 outgoing messages a day across the account, and its domain limit is “almost unlimited”.
• iCloud+ Custom Email Domain allows up to five domains with up to 10 addresses each, and needs an Apple Account with two-factor authentication.
• A domain’s MX records can only point one way. Moving to any host means Cloudflare Email Routing stops receiving for that domain.
Which one should you pick?
• One domain, you like Gmail, and you are happy to reply from a desktop app: option A. It is the smallest change.
• A few domains, and you want a phone app and IMAP: option B. Migadu Micro is the cheapest; Fastmail is the most polished.
• A team that already lives in Google Docs and Calendar: option C. It is the only option that keeps Send as inside Gmail itself.

• Many domains, catch-all on all of them, and a Mac: option D. Adding a domain costs nothing extra, and every address on it can reply as itself. I compare every app that does this in every inbox for Cloudflare Email Routing, compared.
Option A step by step: Apple Mail and Cloudflare’s SMTP server

Cloudflare Email Sending has an SMTP endpoint at smtp.mx.cloudflare.net, port 465, implicit TLS only. Onboard your domain for Email Sending, create an API token with the Email Sending: Edit permission, then add the server to your mail app with the username api_token and the token as the password.
Cloudflare added authenticated SMTP submission on 8 June 2026, as a beta, alongside the Workers binding and the REST API. It is the piece that makes option A possible without writing any code.
1. Onboard the domain for Email Sending
In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to Compute > Email Service > Email Sending, select Onboard Domain and pick the domain. Cloudflare adds these records:

MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route1.mx.cloudflare.net MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route2.mx.cloudflare.net MX cf-bounce.yourdomain.com route3.mx.cloudflare.net TXT cf-bounce.yourdomain.com "v=spf1 include:_spf.mx.cloudflare.net ~all" TXT cf-bounce._domainkey.yourdomain.com (DKIM public key) TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com (only if you have no DMARC record yet)
These live on the cf-bounce subdomain and sit alongside your Email Routing records on the root domain, so receiving is not affected. Read the DMARC trap below before you press Done.
2. Create the API token
Create a Cloudflare API token with the Email Sending: Edit permission. Cloudflare accepts account-owned tokens, which it recommends, and user-owned ones.

Treat it like a password. Cloudflare’s SMTP reference is explicit: anyone with the token can send email from any onboarded domain on the account. If you onboard twenty domains, one leaked token can send as all twenty.
3. Test it before you touch your mail app
This is the test from Cloudflare’s docs. Swap in your token and two addresses:

cat > mail.txt <<'MAIL' From: you@yourdomain.com To: you@gmail.com Subject: Cloudflare SMTP test Sent through smtp.mx.cloudflare.net. MAIL curl --ssl-reqd \ --url "smtps://smtp.mx.cloudflare.net:465" \ --user "api_token:<API_TOKEN>" \ --mail-from "you@yourdomain.com" \ --mail-rcpt "you@gmail.com" \ --upload-file mail.txt
On the Workers Free plan this only works if the recipient is a verified destination address in your account. Anything else is refused at RCPT TO with 550 5.7.1. Sending to anyone needs Workers Paid.
4. Apple Mail settings

In Mail, open Settings > Accounts, choose the account you read your forwarded mail in, open Server Settings, and choose Edit SMTP Server List from the Outgoing Mail Account menu. Add a server and turn off Automatically manage connection settings.

Then add your domain addresses to the account. In Account Information, open the Email Address menu and choose Edit Email Addresses to list every address you want in the From menu. Check the From address before you send a reply.
Cloudflare does not offer port 587 with STARTTLS, or port 25, for sending. If Mail says the server is unavailable, the TLS setting is the first thing to check.
5. The Apple Mail catch

Apple Mail sends everything from an account through that account’s one outgoing server. If the account is your Gmail account and you point it at Cloudflare, mail from your @gmail.com address goes to Cloudflare too, and Cloudflare refuses it with 550 5.7.1 Sender denied, because gmail.com is not a domain you onboarded.
Two ways round it:
• Send only domain mail from that account, and send personal Gmail from the Gmail website or app.
• Use Thunderbird, which lets each identity have its own outgoing server.
Thunderbird, and catch-all addresses

Thunderbird handles this better. Add the Cloudflare server under Outgoing Server (SMTP) with the same values: port 465, connection security SSL/TLS, authentication Normal password, username api_token. Then create an identity for your domain and give it that server.

If you use catch-all, open the identity’s settings and set Reply from this identity when delivery headers match to *@yourdomain.com. A reply to mail sent to an address you never created will then go out from that address, not your default one. Apple Mail has no equivalent; you can only reply from addresses you have listed.
Three traps nobody mentions

Onboarding Email Sending adds a DMARC record with a p=reject policy if your domain has none, which can make your existing Gmail Send as replies bounce. Cloudflare’s Email preview stores the content of what you send for about seven days, on by default. And Email Sending is a beta product that Cloudflare describes as transactional only.
1. The DMARC record Cloudflare adds

When you onboard a domain for Email Sending, Cloudflare adds a DMARC record on _dmarc.yourdomain.com only if the domain has none, and its default policy is p=reject. Cloudflare’s own advice is to keep p=reject only if Email Service is the only thing sending for the domain, and to use p=none while other services still send.

Gmail Send as is one of those other services. A reply sent through smtp.gmail.com as you@yourdomain.com is signed by Gmail, not by your domain, so it does not pass DMARC for your domain. With p=reject in place, receivers are told to refuse it.
So during the switch:
• Check whether you already have a record: dig +short TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com
• If Cloudflare adds one, change it to p=none in DNS > Records while Gmail Send as still sends anything. Cloudflare does not lock it or overwrite your edit.
• Move to p=quarantine, then p=reject, once Gmail is no longer sending as the domain.
2. Email preview keeps a copy of what you send

Email Sending has an Email preview setting that stores sent messages so you can read them in the Activity log. Previews are kept for about seven days, and new sending domains have it turned on automatically.

For an app sending password resets, that is a handy debugging tool. For personal replies to customers, lawyers or your accountant, it means the full text of what you sent can be read in your Cloudflare dashboard by anyone with access to it for a week. To turn it off, go to Email Sending, select the domain, open Settings and switch off Enable email preview.
3. It is a beta, and Cloudflare calls it transactional

Cloudflare’s docs label Email Sending Beta, and its FAQ says Email Service “supports transactional email only”, in answer to a question about marketing mail. One person replying to the people who wrote to them is not marketing. But it is a different use from the order confirmations Cloudflare’s examples are built around, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.

The practical limits are covered in the routing and sending limits: 50 recipients per message, 25 MiB per message, and a daily quota that Cloudflare does not publish and that starts conservative on new accounts.
What it costs to reply through Cloudflare

Replying through Cloudflare Email Sending needs the Workers Paid plan: $5 a month for the whole Cloudflare account, with 3,000 outbound emails a month included and $0.35 per 1,000 after that. A person replying from any number of domains will almost always pay just the $5, or $60 a year.

The 3,000 is per account, not per domain, and it resets with your billing cycle. Receiving through Email Routing stays free and unlimited on every plan, according to Cloudflare’s pricing page. If your account already pays for Workers Paid for something else, replying costs nothing extra until you pass 3,000 a month.
For the full table of what each option costs over three years, including Workspace and Fastmail, see the cheapest way to get email on multiple domains.
Migration checklist before January
• List every Send as address in Gmail under Settings > Accounts and Import. Note which domain each belongs to.
• List your Cloudflare routing rules, including any catch-all. Addresses you reply from under a catch-all will not appear in Gmail’s list, so check your Sent folder too.
• Pick a path from the four options above, per domain if you need to.
• Set up sending authentication for the new path: onboard the domain for Email Sending, or add the new host’s SPF and DKIM records.
• Check DMARC before and after onboarding, and set p=none while Gmail still sends as the domain.
• Send test replies to a Gmail, an Outlook.com and an iCloud address. Open the original message in each and check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass for your domain.
• Remove the old Send as entries once replies go out the new way, then tighten DMARC and update your signatures.
Where EmailFast fits

I make EmailFast, which is option D. It is a Mac app that receives every address on every domain through Cloudflare Email Routing with catch-all, keeps the mail in a small mailbox in your own Cloudflare account, and replies from whichever address each message was sent to through Cloudflare Email Sending. There is no Gmail in the loop, so the January change does not touch it.

It sets up the records, routing and sending for each domain you tick, and incoming mail is sealed on arrival with a key only your Macs hold. You can see exactly what it creates in your account and how the sealing works. It is $129 once, plus Cloudflare’s Workers Paid plan if your account does not have it. It is in beta at the moment.
If you are happy in Gmail with one domain, option A is enough. If you have twenty domains and a catch-all on each, that is the problem I built it for.
Sources, read 27 November 2026
• Cloudflare: SMTP reference
• Cloudflare: Email Service FAQ
Questions

Yes. Google keeps “Send as” only for Google-hosted identities, such as other Gmail addresses and Google Workspace aliases. An address that Cloudflare Email Routing forwards is not hosted by Google, even if you set it up to send through smtp.gmail.com.

Possibly not. Google's timeline says Gmail may restrict new configurations during the Q3 to Q4 2026 transition period, before full removal in January 2027. Do not plan a migration around adding new addresses now.

Workers Paid is $5 a month for the whole Cloudflare account and includes 3,000 outbound emails a month, then $0.35 per 1,000. A person replying from a few domains will almost always pay the $5 minimum, which is $60 a year.
